Jun Lu

Preface

This book aims to provide an introduction to linear models and the theoretical foundations that underpin them. Our goal is to offer a rigorous treatment of the subject for readers who already have some familiarity with ordinary least squares (OLS) regression.

In machine learning, where outputs often involve nonlinear functions, and deep learning seeks to capture complex nonlinear relationships through multiple computational layers, the underlying principles still rest on simple linear models. This highlights the importance of understanding the theory and application of linear models as a basis for more advanced techniques.
The book then covers various aspects of linear models, with a particular emphasis on the method of least squares as the primary tool for solving regression problems. Least squares minimizes the sum of squared errors to estimate the regression function that yields the smallest expected squared error.

Primarily serving as a concise yet comprehensive overview, this book emphasizes the significance of key theoretical concepts behind linear models, including distribution theory, minimum variance estimation, and analysis of variance.
We begin with the ordinary least squares framework and explore it from multiple perspectives. We then introduce random disturbances modeled as Gaussian noise. This leads naturally to the concept of likelihood, enabling us to define the maximum likelihood estimator and develop corresponding distributional theories.
The distribution theory of least squares allows us to address a variety of statistical questions and introduces several practical applications. We also prove that the least squares estimator is the best unbiased linear estimator in terms of mean squared error—moreover, it approaches the theoretical performance limit.
Finally, we extend our discussion to include Bayesian approaches to linear models and touch upon related advanced topics.

The mathematical prerequisites for this book are modest: a first course in linear algebra and basic statistics. Beyond this, the development is self-contained, with detailed and rigorous proofs provided throughout.

The main objective of this book is to offer a self-contained introduction to the core concepts, mathematical tools, and rigorous analysis behind linear models, enabling a smooth transition to the discussion of their methods and applications in subsequent sections.
However, we acknowledge the limitations of this work—we cannot cover all useful or interesting results related to linear models. Due to space constraints, we do not include separate treatments of certain topics such as LASSO and ridge regression. For a more in-depth exploration of these subjects, we refer readers to specialized literature on linear models and regularization techniques.

Keywords

Fundamental theory of linear algebra, Orthogonal projection matrix, Out-of-sample error, Gauss-Markov, Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB), Minimum variance unbiased estimator, Distribution theory of linear models, Asymptotic theory, Connection between Bayesian approach and Gaussian process, Variable selection, Large-scale optimization, Generalized linear models.

Chapter 1
Introduction

1.1
Introduction and Background

T
This book is meant to provide an introduction to linear models and their underlying theories. Our goal is to give a rigorous introduction to the readers with prior exposure to ordinary least squares.
While machine learning often deals with nonlinear relationships, including those explored in deep learning with intricate layers demanding substantial computation, many algorithms are rooted in simple linear models.

The exposition approaches linear models from various perspectives, elucidating their properties and associated theories.
In regression problems, the primary tool is the least squares approximation, minimizing the sum of squared errors.
This is a natural choice when we’re interested in finding the regression function, which minimizes the corresponding expected squared error.

This book is primarily a summary of purpose, emphasizing the significance of important theories behind linear models, e.g., distribution theory, minimum variance estimator.
We begin by presenting ordinary least squares from various distinct points of view, upon which we disturb the model with random noise and Gaussian noise.
The introduction of Gaussian noise establishes a likelihood, leading to the derivation of a maximum likelihood estimator and the development of distribution theories related to this Gaussian disturbance, which will help us answer various questions and introduce related applications.
The subsequent proof establishes that least squares is the best unbiased linear model in terms of mean squared error, and notably, it approaches the theoretical limit.
The exploration extends to linear models within a Bayesian framework and a generalized linear model framework.
The mathematical prerequisites are a first course in linear algebra and statistics. Beyond these basic requirements, the content is self-contained, featuring rigorous proofs throughout.

Linear models play a central role in machine learning, particularly as the concatenation of simple linear models has led to the development of intricate nonlinear models like neural networks.
The sole aim of this book is to give a self-contained introduction to concepts and mathematical tools in theory behind linear models and rigorous analysis in order to seamlessly introduce linear model methods and their applications in subsequent sections.
It is acknowledged, however, that the book cannot comprehensively cover all valuable and interesting results related to linear models. Due to constraints, topics like the separate analysis of LASSO and ridge regression are not exhaustively discussed here.
Interested readers are directed to relevant literature in the field of linear models for more in-depth exploration.
Some excellent examples include
Strang 2009
;
Panaretos 2016
;
Hoff 2009
;
Strang 2021
;
Beck 2014
;
Jackson 2024
.

In the remainder of this chapter, we briefly introduce and review some basic notation and concepts from mathematics. Additional definitions will be introduced as needed throughout the text for clarity.

1.2
Linear Algebra

In all cases, scalars will be denoted in a non-bold font possibly with subscripts (e.g.,
a
,
\alpha
,
\alpha_{i}
). We will use
boldface
lowercase letters possibly with subscripts to denote vectors (e.g.,
\boldsymbol{\mu}
,
\bm{x}
,
\bm{x}_{n}
,
\bm{z}
) and

boldface
uppercase letters possibly with subscripts to denote matrices (e.g.,
\bm{X}
,
\bm{L}_{j}
). The
i
-th element of a vector
\bm{z}
will be denoted by
z_{i}
in non-bold font.
In the meantime, the
normal fonts
of scalars denote
random variables
(e.g.,
a
and
\textnormal{b}_{1}
are random variables, while italics
a
and
b_{1}
are scalars);
the normal fonts of
boldface
lowercase letters, possibly with subscripts, denote
random vectors
(e.g.,
{\mathbf{a}}
and
{\mathbf{b}}_{1}
are random vectors, while italics
\bm{a}
and
\bm{b}_{1}
are vectors);
and the normal fonts of
boldface
uppercase letters, possibly with subscripts, denote
random matrices
(e.g.,
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}_{1}
are random matrices, while italics
\bm{A}
and
\bm{B}_{1}
are matrices).

Subarrays are formed by fixing a subset of indices of a matrix.
The element located in the
i
-th row and
j
-th column of a matrix
\bm{X}
(i.e., the
(i,j)
entry) is denoted by
x_{ij}
; in this case,
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
can be denoted as
\bm{X}=\{x_{ij}\}_{i,j=1}^{n,p}=[x_{ij}]
.
Furthermore, it will be helpful to utilize the
Matlab-style notation
, the
i
-th row to the
j
-th row and the
k
-th column to the
m
-th column submatrix of the matrix
\bm{X}
will be denoted by
\bm{X}_{i:j,k:m}\equiv\bm{X}[i:j,k:m]
. A colon is used to indicate all elements of a dimension, e.g.,
\bm{X}_{:,k:m}\equiv\bm{X}[:,k:m]
denotes the
k
-th column to the
m
-th column of the matrix
\bm{X}
, and
\bm{X}_{:,k}\equiv\bm{X}[:,k]
denotes the
k
-th column of
\bm{X}
.
Alternatively, the
k
-th column of
\bm{X}
may be denoted more compactly by
\bm{x}_{k}
; and the
k
-th row of
\bm{X}
can be denoted as
\bm{x}^{(k)}
.

When the index is not continuous, given ordered subindex sets
{\mathbb{I}}
and
{\mathbb{J}}
,
\bm{X}[{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}]
denotes the submatrix of
\bm{X}
obtained by extracting the rows and columns of
\bm{X}
indexed by
{\mathbb{I}}
and
{\mathbb{J}}
, respectively; and
\bm{X}[:,{\mathbb{J}}]
denotes the submatrix of
\bm{X}
obtained by extracting the columns of
\bm{X}
indexed by
{\mathbb{J}}
, where again the colon operator implies all indices.

Definition 1
(Matlab notation).

Suppose
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and
{\mathbb{I}}=\{i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{k}\}
and
{\mathbb{J}}=\{j_{1},j_{2},\ldots,j_{l}\}
are two index vectors.
Then
\bm{X}[{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}]
denotes the
k\times l
submatrix

\bm{X}[{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}]=\begin{bmatrix}x_{i_{1},j_{1}}&x_{i_{1},j_{2}}&\ldots&x_{i_{1},j_{l}}\\
x_{i_{2},j_{1}}&x_{i_{2},j_{2}}&\ldots&x_{i_{2},j_{l}}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
x_{i_{k},j_{1}}&x_{i_{k},j_{2}}&\ldots&x_{i_{k},j_{l}}\\
\end{bmatrix}.

Whilst,
\bm{X}[{\mathbb{I}},:]
denotes the
k\times p
submatrix, and
\bm{X}[:,{\mathbb{J}}]
denotes the
n\times l
submatrix analogously.
We should also notice that the range of the index satisfies:

\left\{\begin{aligned} 0&\leq\min({\mathbb{I}})\leq\max({\mathbb{I}})\leq n;\\
0&\leq\min({\mathbb{J}})\leq\max({\mathbb{J}})\leq p.\end{aligned}\right.

And in all cases, vectors are formulated in a column rather than in a row. A row vector will be denoted by a transpose of a column vector, such as
\bm{x}^{\top}
. A specific column vector with values is separated by the semicolons
``;"
, e.g.,

\bm{x}=[1;2;3]\qquad\text{(column vector)}

is a column vector in
3
. Similarly, a specific row vector with values is separated by the comma
``,"
, e.g.,

\bm{y}=[1,2,3]\qquad\text{(row vector)}

is a row vector with 3 values.
Alternatively, a column vector can also be written as the transpose of a row vector. For instance,
\bm{y}=[1,2,3]^{\top}
is a column vector.

The transpose of a matrix
\bm{X}
will be denoted by
\bm{X}^{\top}
,
and its inverse will be denoted by
\bm{X}^{-1}
. We will denote the
p\times p
identity matrix by
\bm{I}_{p}
. A vector or matrix of all zeros will be denoted by a
boldface
zero
\boldsymbol{0}
, whose size should be clear from context; or we denote
\boldsymbol{0}_{p}
to be the vector of all zeros with
p
entries.
Similarly, a vector or matrix of all ones will be denoted by a
boldface
one
\bm{1}
, whose size is clear from context; or we denote
\bm{1}_{p}
to be the vector of all ones with
p
entries.
Subscripts are often omitted when the dimensions are evident from the context.

Definition 2
(Eigenvalue, Eigenvector).

Given any vector space
{\mathbb{F}}
and any linear map
\bm{X}:{\mathbb{F}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{F}}
(or simply a real matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
), a scalar
\lambda\in{\mathbb{K}}
is called a (right) eigenvalue, or proper value, or characteristic value of
\bm{X}
, if there exists a nonzero vector
\bm{u}\in{\mathbb{F}}
such that

\bm{X}\bm{u}=\lambda\bm{u}.

And
\bm{u}
is called a (right) eigenvector of
\bm{X}
associated with
\lambda
.

On the other hand,
\kappa
is referred to as a left eigenvalue if there exists a nonzero vector
\bm{v}\in{\mathbb{F}}
such that

\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{X}=\kappa\bm{v}^{\top}.

And
\bm{v}
is called a left eigenvector of
\bm{X}
associated with
\kappa
.

When it is clear from the context, we will simply use the term “eigenvalue/eigenvector” instead of “right eigenvalue/eigenvector.”

For simplicity, we focus only on real-valued matrices unless otherwise specified. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, all eigenvalues discussed are assumed to be real as well.

In simple terms, an eigenvector
\bm{u}
of a matrix
\bm{X}
represents a direction that remains unchanged when transformed into the coordinate system defined by the columns of
\bm{X}
.
In fact, real-valued matrices can have complex eigenvalues. However, all eigenvalues of symmetric matrices are guaranteed to be real (see Theorem
).

Definition 3
(Spectrum and Spectral Radius).

The set of all eigenvalues of a matrix
\bm{X}
is called the spectrum of
\bm{X}
, and is denoted by
\Lambda(\bm{X})
.
The largest magnitude among the eigenvalues is known as the spectral radius of
\bm{X}
, denoted by
\rho(\bm{X})
:

\rho(\bm{X})=\mathop{\max}_{\lambda\in\Lambda(\bm{X})}\left\lvert\lambda\right\rvert.

Moreover, the tuple
(\lambda,\bm{u})
is referred to as an
eigenpair
. Intuitively, the above definitions mean that multiplying matrix
\bm{X}
by the vector
\bm{u}
results in a new vector that is in the same direction as
\bm{u}
, but only scaled by a factor
\lambda
. For any eigenvector
\bm{u}
, we can scale it by a scalar
s
such that
s\bm{u}
is still an eigenvector of
\bm{X}
. That’s why we say that the eigenvector is an eigenvector of
\bm{X}
associated with the eigenvalue
\lambda
. To avoid ambiguity, we usually assume that the eigenvector is normalized to have length one and the first entry is positive (or negative) since both
\bm{u}
and
-\bm{u}
are eigenvectors.

In linear algebra, every vector space has a basis, and every vector in that space can be expressed as a linear combination of the basis vectors. Based on this idea, we define the span and dimension of a subspace using the concept of a basis.

Definition 4
(Subspace).

A nonempty subset
\mathcal{V}
of
n
is called a subspace if
x\bm{a}+y\bm{a}\in\mathcal{V}
for every
\bm{a},\bm{b}\in\mathcal{V}
and every
x,y\in\real
.

Definition 5
(Span).

If every vector
\bm{v}
in a subspace
\mathcal{V}
can be expressed as a linear combination of
\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,

\bm{x}_{n}\}
, then we say that these vectors span the subspace
\mathcal{V}
.

The concept of linear independence of a set of vectors is central to linear algebra. Two equivalent definitions are given below.

Definition 6
(Linearly independent).

A set of vectors
\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
is said to be linearly independent if there is no combination can get
a_{1}\bm{x}_{1}+a_{2}\bm{x}_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}\bm{x}_{n}=0
except all
a_{i}
’s are zero. An equivalent definition is that
\bm{x}_{1}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
, and for every
k>1
, the vector
\bm{x}_{k}
does not belong to the span of
\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{k-1}\}
.

Definition 7
(Basis and dimension).

A set of vectors
\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
is called a basis of a subspace
\mathcal{V}
if they are linearly independent, and they span
\mathcal{V}
. Every basis of a given subspace contains the same number of vectors, and the number of vectors in any basis is called the dimension of the subspace
\mathcal{V}
. By convention, the trivial subspace
\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
is said to have dimension zero.
Furthermore, every subspace with a nonzero dimension has an orthogonal basis; in other words, the basis of a subspace can be chosen orthogonal (Definition
).

Definition 8
(Column space (range)).

Let
\bm{X}
be an
n\times p
real matrix. The column space (or range) of
\bm{X}
is defined as the set of all vectors that can be expressed as a linear combination of its columns:

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})=\{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\exists\bm{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{p},\,\bm{v}=\bm{X}\bm{u}\}.

Similarly, the row space of
\bm{X}
is the set of all vectors spanned by its rows. Equivalently, it is the column space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
:

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})=\{\bm{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\exists\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\,\bm{u}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{v}\}.

Definition 9
(Null space (nullspace, kernel)).

Let
\bm{X}
be an
n\times p
real matrix. The null space (or kernel, or nullspace) of
\bm{X}
is defined as the set:

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})=\{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\,\bm{X}\bm{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\}.

In some cases, the null space of
\bm{X}
is also referred to as the right null space of
\bm{X}
.
And the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
is defined as

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})=\{\bm{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\,\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{u}=\boldsymbol{0}\}.

Similarly, the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
is also referred to as the left null space of
\bm{X}
.

Both the column space of
\bm{X}
and the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
are subspaces of
n
. In fact, every vector in
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
is orthogonal to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
and vice versa. Similarly, every vector in
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
is also orthogonal to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
and vice versa.

Definition 10
(Rank).

The
rank
of a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is defined as the dimension of its column space. That is, the rank of
\bm{X}
is equal to the maximum number of linearly independent columns of
\bm{X}
, and is also the maximum number of linearly independent rows of
\bm{X}
. The matrix
\bm{X}
and its transpose
\bm{X}^{\top}
have the same rank. We say that
\bm{X}
has full rank if its rank is equal to
\min\{n,p\}
. Specifically, given a vector
\bm{u}\in\real^{n}
and a vector
\bm{v}\in\real^{p}
, then the
n\times p
matrix
\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top}
obtained by the outer product of vectors is of rank 1. In short, the rank of a matrix is equal to:

the number of linearly independent columns;

the number of linearly independent rows;

and remarkably, these are always the same (see Lemma
).

Definition 11
(Orthogonal complement in general).

The orthogonal complement
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}\subseteq\real^{n}
of a subspace
\mathcal{V}\subseteq\real^{n}
consists of all vectors that are perpendicular to every vector in
\mathcal{V}
. That is,

\mathcal{V}^{\perp}=\{\bm{v}\in\real^{n}:\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{u}=0,\ \forall\,\bm{u}\in\mathcal{V}\}.

These two subspaces are disjoint and together span the entire space
n
.
The dimensions of
\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
add up to the dimension of the entire space:
\dim(\mathcal{V})+\dim(\mathcal{V}^{\perp})=n
. Furthermore,
(\mathcal{V}^{\perp})^{\perp}=\mathcal{V}
.

Definition 12
(Orthogonal complement of column space).

Let
\bm{X}
be an
n\times p
real matrix. The orthogonal complement of the column space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, denoted by
\mathcal{C}^{\bot}(\bm{X})
, is the subspace defined as:

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\bot}(\bm{X})

\displaystyle=\{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\,\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{u}=\boldsymbol{0},\,\forall\,\bm{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\}

\displaystyle=\{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\,\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{w}=\boldsymbol{0},\,\forall\,\bm{w}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\}.

Then we have the
four fundamental spaces
for any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with rank
r
:

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
: Column space of
\bm{X}
, i.e., linear combinations of columns with dimension
r
.

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
: (Right) null space of
\bm{X}
, i.e., all
\bm{u}
satisfying
\bm{X}\bm{u}=\boldsymbol{0}
with dimension
p-r
.

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
: Row space of
\bm{X}
, i.e., linear combinations of rows with dimension
r
.

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
: Left null space of
\bm{X}
, i.e., all
\bm{v}
satisfying
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{v}=\boldsymbol{0}
with dimension
n-r
.

Furthermore,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
is the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
is the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
. The proof is further discussed in Theorem
.

We establish the equivalence stated in Definition
.

Lemma 13
(Dimension of column space and row space).

The dimension of the column space of a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is equal to the dimension of its
row space, i.e., the row rank and the column rank of a matrix
\bm{X}
are equal.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We first notice that the null space of
\bm{X}
is orthogonal complementary to the row space of
\bm{X}
:
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\bot\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
(where the row space of
\bm{X}
is equivalent to the column space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
).
That is, vectors in the null space of
\bm{X}
are orthogonal to vectors in the row space of
\bm{X}
. To see this, suppose
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1}^{\top};\bm{x}_{2}^{\top};\ldots;\bm{x}_{n}^{\top}]
is the row partition of
\bm{X}
. For any vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
, we have
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
, that is,
[\bm{x}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta};\bm{x}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta};\ldots;\bm{x}_{n}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}]=\boldsymbol{0}
.
And since the row space of
\bm{X}
is spanned by
\{\bm{x}_{1}^{\top},\bm{x}_{2}^{\top},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}^{\top}\}
, thus,
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is perpendicular to any vectors from
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
. This indicates
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\bot\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
.

Now, assuming the dimension of the row space of
\bm{X}
is
r
,
let
\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{r}
be a set of vectors in
p
and form a basis for the row space
.
Consequently, the
r
vectors
\bm{X}\bm{r}_{1},\bm{X}\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{X}\bm{r}_{r}
are in the column space of
\bm{X}
; furthermore, they are linearly independent. To see this, suppose we have a linear combination of the
r
vectors:
\beta_{1}\bm{X}\bm{r}_{1}+\beta_{2}\bm{X}\bm{r}_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{r}\bm{X}\bm{r}_{r}=0
, that is,
\bm{X}(\beta_{1}\bm{r}_{1}+\beta_{2}\bm{r}_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{r}\bm{r}_{r})=0
, and the vector
\bm{v}=\beta_{1}\bm{r}_{1}+\beta_{2}\bm{r}_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{r}\bm{r}_{r}
is in null space of
\bm{X}
. But since
\{\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{r}\}
is a basis for the row space of
\bm{X}
,
\bm{v}
is thus also in the row space of
\bm{X}
. We have shown that vectors from null space of
\bm{X}
is perpendicular to vectors from row space of
\bm{X}
, thus
\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{v}=0
and
\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\ldots=\beta_{r}=0
. Then,
\bm{X}\bm{r}_{1},\bm{X}\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{X}\bm{r}_{r}
are in the column space of
\bm{X}
and they are independent
. This means that the dimension of the column space of
\bm{X}
is larger than
r
. This result shows that
row rank of
\bm{X}\leq
column rank of
\bm{X}
.

If we apply this process again to
\bm{X}^{\top}
, we will have
column rank of
\bm{X}\leq
row rank of
\bm{X}
. This completes the proof.

From the previous proof, we can also conclude that if
\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{r}
is a set of vectors in
p
that forms a basis for the row space of
\bm{X}
, then
\bm{X}\bm{r}_{1},\bm{X}\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{X}\bm{r}_{r}
forms a basis for the column space of
\bm{X}
.
We formalize this result in the following lemma.

Lemma 14
(Column basis from row basis).

For any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, let
\{\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{r}\}
be a set of vectors in
p
, which forms a basis for the row space of
\bm{X}
. Then, the set
\{\bm{X}\bm{r}_{1},\bm{X}\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{X}\bm{r}_{r}\}
is a basis for the column space of
\bm{X}
.

Definition 15
(Orthogonal matrix, semi-orthogonal matrix).

A real square matrix
\bm{Q}\in\real^{n\times n}
is an orthogonal matrix if the inverse of
\bm{Q}
equals its transpose, that is
\bm{Q}^{-1}=\bm{Q}^{\top}
and
\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{Q}=\bm{I}
. In other words, suppose
\bm{Q}=[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}]
, where
\bm{q}_{i}\in\real^{n}
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, then
\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{q}_{j}=\delta(i,j)
with
\delta(i,j)
being the Kronecker delta function.
For any vector
\bm{x}
, the orthogonal matrix will preserve the length:
\left\lVert\bm{Q}\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}
, where
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}
denotes the
\ell_{2}
norm (Definition
).
Note that, since the orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}
contains unit-length columns, the columns are mutually orthogonormal. However, the terminology of orthogonormal matrix is
not
used due to historical convention; instead, the term orthogonal matrix is standard even though it implies orthonormal columns.

On the other hand, if
\bm{Q}
contains only
\gamma<n
of these columns, then
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{Q}=\bm{I}_{\gamma}
stills holds, where
\bm{I}_{\gamma}
is the
\gamma\times\gamma
identity matrix. But
\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{I}
will not be true.
In this case,
\bm{Q}
referred to as a semi-orthogonal matrix.

The vectors
\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{\gamma}\in\real^{n}
are
mutually orthogonal
when their dot products
\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{q}_{j}
are zero whenever
i\neq j
. When each vector is divided by its length, the vectors become orthogonal unit vectors. Then the vectors
\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{\gamma}
are called
mutually orthonormal
. We usually put the orthonormal vectors into a matrix
\bm{Q}
.

When
n\neq\gamma
: the matrix
\bm{Q}
is easy to work with because
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{Q}=\bm{I}\in\real^{\gamma\times\gamma}
.

When
n=\gamma
: the matrix
\bm{Q}
is square,
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{Q}=\bm{I}
means that
\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}^{-1}
, i.e., the transpose of
\bm{Q}
is the inverse of
\bm{Q}
. Then we also have
\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{I}
, i.e.,
\bm{Q}^{\top}
is the two-sided inverse of
\bm{Q}
. We call this
\bm{Q}
an
orthogonal matrix
.

Definition 16
(Idempotent Matrix).

A matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
is called idempotent if
\bm{X}^{2}=\bm{X}
.

Definition 17
(Permutation matrix).

A permutation matrix
\bm{P}\in\real^{n\times n}
is a square binary matrix that has exactly one entry of 1 in each row and each column, and 0’s elsewhere.

Row point.

That is, the permutation matrix
\bm{P}
has the rows of the identity
\bm{I}
in any order, and the order decides the sequence of the row permutation. If we want to permute the rows of a matrix
\bm{X}
, we multiply on the left
\bm{P}\bm{X}
.

Column point.

Or, equivalently, the permutation matrix
\bm{P}
has the columns of the identity
\bm{I}
in any order, and the order decides the sequence of the column permutation. To apply a column permutation to
\bm{X}
, we multiply on the right
\bm{X}\bm{P}
.

The permutation matrix
\bm{P}
can be more efficiently represented via a set
{\mathbb{J}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{n}
of indices such that
\bm{P}=\bm{I}[:,{\mathbb{J}}]
, where
\bm{I}
is the
n\times n
identity matrix. And notably, the elements in vector
{\mathbb{J}}
sum to
1+2+\ldots+n=\frac{n^{2}+n}{2}
.

Example 18
(Permutation).

Suppose

\bm{X}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\
4&5&6\\
7&8&9\end{bmatrix}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{P}=\begin{bmatrix}&1&\\
&&1\\
1&&\end{bmatrix}.

The row and column permutations are given by

\bm{P}\bm{X}=\begin{bmatrix}4&5&6\\
7&8&9\\
1&2&3\\
\end{bmatrix}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{X}\bm{P}=\begin{bmatrix}3&1&2\\
6&4&5\\
9&7&8\end{bmatrix},

respectively,
where the order of the rows of
\bm{X}
appearing in
\bm{P}\bm{X}
matches the order of the rows of
\bm{I}
in
\bm{P}
,
and the order of the columns of
\bm{X}
appearing in
\bm{X}\bm{P}
matches the order of the columns of
\bm{I}
in
\bm{P}
.

Definition 19
(Determinant: Laplace Expansion by Minors).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
be any square matrix, and let
\bm{X}_{ij}\in\real^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}
denote the submatrix of
\bm{X}
obtained by deleting the
i
-th row and
j
-th column.
The determinant of
\bm{X}
can be computed recursively using the following equations:

\det(\bm{X})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{i+k}a_{ik}\det(\bm{X}_{ik})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k+j}a_{kj}\det(\bm{X}_{kj}),

(1.1)

where the first equation is the Laplace expansion by minors along row
i
, and the second equation is the Laplace expansion by minors along column
j
.
Equivalently, given a cardinality
r
, and consider an index set
{\mathbb{J}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
with cardinality
r
(
\left\lvert{\mathbb{J}}\right\rvert=r
) and its complementary set
{\mathbb{J}}^{c}=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\backslash{\mathbb{J}}
, we have:

\displaystyle\det(\bm{X})=\sum_{{\mathbb{I}}}(-1)^{\gamma}\det(\bm{X}[{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}])\det(\bm{X}[{\mathbb{I}}^{c},{\mathbb{J}}^{c}])=\sum_{{\mathbb{I}}}(-1)^{\gamma}\det(\bm{X}[{\mathbb{J}},{\mathbb{I}}])\det(\bm{X}[{\mathbb{J}}^{c},{\mathbb{I}}^{c}]),

where
\gamma=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}i+\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{J}}}j
, and the sum is taken over all the index sets
{\mathbb{I}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
with cardinality
r
.
When
r=1
, this reduces to (
).

The determinant of a square matrix maps the matrix into a scalar value.
In the case of a
2\times 2
matrix, the determinant represents the area of the parallelogram spanned by the column vectors of the matrix. It is positive if the orientation is counterclockwise and negative if clockwise.
For a
3\times 3
matrix, the determinant corresponds to the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three column vectors of the matrix. Again, the sign indicates whether the orientation is preserved or reversed.
For a matrix representing a linear transformation in
n
-dimensional space, the absolute value of the determinant gives the factor by which the volume changes under this transformation. If the determinant is positive, the orientation (or handedness) of the basis is preserved; if negative, it is reversed.
A matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero. This means that the transformation does not collapse the space into a lower dimension or a single point, which would happen if the determinant were zero.
The determinant of a matrix is equal to the product of its eigenvalues. This means that the determinant reflects the combined effect of all the stretching factors applied by the matrix to the eigenvectors.
We provide a few properties of the determinant.

Lemma 20
(Properties of determinant).

We have the following properties for determinant of matrices:

The determinant of the product of two matrices is
\det(\bm{X}\bm{Y})=\det(\bm{X})\det(\bm{Y})
;

The determinant of the transpose is
\det(\bm{X}^{\top})=\det(\bm{X})
;

Suppose matrix
\bm{X}
has an eigenvalue
\lambda
, then
\det(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})=0
;

Determinant of any identity matrix is
1
;

Determinant of an orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}
:

\det(\bm{Q})=\det(\bm{Q}^{\top})=\pm 1,\qquad\text{since }\det(\bm{Q}^{\top})\det(\bm{Q})=\det(\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{Q})=\det(\bm{I})=1;

Given any square matrix
\bm{X}
and orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}
, we have

\det(\bm{X})=\det(\bm{Q}^{\top})\det(\bm{X})\det(\bm{Q})=\det(\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Q});

Suppose
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
, then
\det(-\bm{X})=(-1)^{n}\det(\bm{X})
.

Positive definiteness or positive semidefiniteness is one of the highest accolades to which a matrix can aspire.
In Section
, we will introduce the Cholesky decomposition, which applies specifically to positive definite matrices. We begin with the following definition.

Definition 21
(Positive definite and positive semidefinite).

A matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
is said to be positive definite (PD) if
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}>0
for all nonzero
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{n}
, denoted by
\bm{X}\succ\boldsymbol{0}
.
And a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
is called positive semidefinite (PSD) if
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\geq 0
for all
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{n}
, denoted by
\bm{X}\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
.

We can show that a matrix
\bm{X}
is positive definite if and only if all of its eigenvalues are strictly positive. Similarly,
\bm{X}
is positive semidefinite if and only if all of its eigenvalues are nonnegative.

This result leads to the following theorem:

{theoremHigh}
[Eigenvalue characterization theorem]
A matrix
\bm{A}
is positive definite if and only if it contains only
positive eigenvalues
. Similarly, a matrix
\bm{A}
is positive semidefinite if and only if it contains only
nonnegative eigenvalues
.
Moreover, we have the following implications:

\bm{A}-\gamma\bm{I}\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
if and only if
\lambda_{\min}(\bm{A})\geq\gamma
;

\bm{A}-\gamma\bm{I}\succ\boldsymbol{0}
if and only if
\lambda_{\min}(\bm{A})>\gamma
;

\bm{A}-\gamma\bm{I}\preceq\boldsymbol{0}
if and only if
\lambda_{\max}(\bm{A})\leq\gamma
;

\bm{A}-\gamma\bm{I}\prec\boldsymbol{0}
if and only if
\lambda_{\max}(\bm{A})<\gamma
;

\lambda_{\min}(\bm{A})\bm{I}\preceq\bm{A}\preceq\lambda_{\max}(\bm{A})\bm{I}
,

where
\lambda_{\min}(\bm{A})
and
\lambda_{\max}(\bm{A})
represent the minimum and maximum eigenvalues of
\bm{A}
, respectively, and
\bm{B}\prec\bm{C}
means
\bm{C}-\bm{B}
is PSD.

Given the eigenpair
(\lambda,\bm{x})
of
\bm{A}
, the forward implication can be shown that
\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{x}=\lambda\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}>0
such that
\lambda=(\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{x})/(\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x})>0
(resp.
\geq 0
) if
\bm{A}
is PD (resp. PSD).
The full proof of this equivalence can be proved using the spectral theorem (Theorem
).
This theorem provides an alternative definition of positive definiteness and positive semidefiniteness in terms of the eigenvalues of the matrix, which is a fundamental property for the Cholesky decomposition.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Power of PSD)

Let
\bm{A}
be PSD. Show that
\bm{A}^{k}
is also PSD for
k=1,2,\ldots
.

From an introductory course on linear algebra, we have the following remark on the equivalent claims of nonsingular matrices.

Remark 22
(List of equivalence of nonsingularity for a matrix).

Given a square matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
, the following claims are equivalent:

\bm{X}
is nonsingular;

\bm{X}
is invertible, i.e.,
\bm{X}^{-1}
exists;

\bm{X}\bm{u}=\bm{y}
has a unique solution
\bm{u}=\bm{X}^{-1}\bm{y}
;

\bm{X}\bm{u}=\boldsymbol{0}
has a unique, trivial solution:
\bm{u}=\boldsymbol{0}
;

Columns of
\bm{X}
are linearly independent;

Rows of
\bm{X}
are linearly independent;

\det(\bm{X})\neq 0
;

\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}))=0
;

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, i.e., the null space is trivial;

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})=\real^{n}
, i.e., the column space or row space span the entire
n
;

\bm{X}
has full rank
r=n
;

The reduced row echelon form is
\bm{R}=\bm{I}
;

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is symmetric positive definite (PD);

\bm{X}
has
n
nonzero (positive) singular values;

All eigenvalues are nonzero.

It is important to keep the above equivalence in mind. Additionally, the following remark presents equivalent statements that apply to singular matrices as well.

Remark 23
(List of equivalence of singularity for a matrix).

For a square matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
with an eigenpair
(\lambda,\bm{u})
, the following claims are equivalent:

(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
is singular;

(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
is not invertible;

(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})\bm{v}=\boldsymbol{0}
has nonzero
\bm{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
solutions, and
\bm{v}=\bm{u}
is one of such solutions;

(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
has linearly dependent columns;

\det(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})=0
;

\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I}))>0
;

Null space of
(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
is nontrivial;

Columns of
(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
are linearly dependent;

Rows of
(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
are linearly dependent;

(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
has rank
r<n
;

Dimension of column space = dimension of row space =
r<n
;

(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})^{\top}(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
is symmetric semidefinite;

(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
has
r<n
nonzero (positive) singular values;

Zero is an eigenvalue of
(\bm{X}-\lambda\bm{I})
.

Given a vector or a matrix, its norm should satisfy the following three criteria.

Definition 24
(Vector norm and matrix nrom).

Given a norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
defined on either vectors or matrices, for any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and any vector
\bm{x}\in\real^{n}
, the following three properties must be satisfied:

Nonnegativity.
\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert\geq 0
or
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert\geq 0
, and the equality is obtained if and only if
\bm{X}=\boldsymbol{0}
or
\bm{x}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

Positive homogeneity.
\left\lVert\lambda\bm{X}\right\rVert=\left\lvert\lambda\right\rvert\cdot\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert
or
\left\lVert\lambda\bm{x}\right\rVert=\left\lvert\lambda\right\rvert\cdot\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert
for any
\lambda\in\real
.

Triangle inequality.
\left\lVert\bm{X}+\bm{Y}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert+\left\lVert\bm{Y}\right\rVert
, or
\left\lVert\bm{x}+\bm{y}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert+\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert
for any matrices
\bm{X},\bm{Y}\in\real^{n\times p}
or vectors
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.

Based on this definition of norms, we can now define specific types of vector norms, namely the
\ell_{1}
,
\ell_{2}
, and
\ell_{\infty}
norms for a vector.

Definition 25
(Vector
\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ell_{\infty}
,
\ell_{p}
norms).

For a vector
\bm{x}\in\real^{n}
, the
\ell_{2}
vector norm is defined as
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}=\sqrt{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\ldots+x_{n}^{2}}
.
Similarly, the
\ell_{1}
norm can be obtained by

\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_{i}|.

And the
\ell_{\infty}
norm can be obtained by

\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\mathop{\max}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}|x_{i}|.

More generally, the
\ell_{p}
norm is defined as
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{p}=\sqrt[p]{\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_{i}|^{p}}
for
p\geq 1
.

\paragrapharrow

Dual norm.
Consider the
\ell_{p}
vector norm. From
Hölder’s inequality
, we have

\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{y}\leq\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{p}\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{q},

where
p,q>1
satisfy
\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1
, and
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
. Equality holds if the two sequences
\{\left\lvert x_{i}\right\rvert^{p}\}
and
\{\left\lvert y_{i}\right\rvert^{q}\}
are linearly dependent. This implies

\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{q}=1}\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{y}=\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{p}.

(1.2)

For this reason,
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{q}
is called the
dual norm
of
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{p}
.
On the other hand, for each
\bm{x}\in\real^{n}
with
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{p}=1
, there exists a vector
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
such that
\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{q}=1
and
\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{y}=1
.
Notably, the
\ell_{2}
norm is self-dual, while the
\ell_{1}
and
\ell_{\infty}
norms are dual to each other.

Definition 26
(Set of primal counterparts).

Let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
be any norm on
n
. Then the set of primal counterparts of
\bm{a}
is defined as

\Lambda_{\bm{a}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{\bm{u}\in\real^{n}}\left\{\left\langle\bm{a},\bm{u}\right\rangle\mid\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert\leq 1\right\}.

(1.3)

That is,
\left\langle\bm{a},\bm{a}^{\dagger}\right\rangle=\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{*}
for any
\bm{a}^{\dagger}\in\Lambda_{\bm{a}}
, where
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{*}
denotes the dual norm.
It follows that

1.

If
\bm{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
, then
\left\lVert\bm{a}^{\dagger}\right\rVert=1
for any
\bm{a}^{\dagger}\in\Lambda_{\bm{a}}
.

2.

If
\bm{a}=\boldsymbol{0}
, then
\Lambda_{\bm{a}}=\{\bm{x}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert\leq 1\}
.

Example 27
(Set of Primal Counterparts).

A few examples for the sets of primal counterparts are shown below:

If the norm is the
\ell_{2}
norm, then for any
\bm{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
,

\Lambda_{\bm{a}}=\left\{{\bm{a}}/{\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}}\right\}.

If the norm is the
\ell_{1}
norm, then for any
\bm{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
,

\Lambda_{\bm{a}}=\left\{\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}(\bm{a})}\lambda_{i}\sign(a_{i})\bm{e}_{i}\mid\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}(\bm{a})}\lambda_{i}=1,\lambda_{j}\geq 0,j\in{\mathbb{I}}(\bm{a})\right\},

where
{\mathbb{I}}(\bm{a})\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}|a_{i}|
.

If the norm is the
\ell_{\infty}
norm, then for any
\bm{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
,

\Lambda_{\bm{a}}=\left\{\bm{x}\in\real^{n}\mid x_{i}=\sign(a_{i}),i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{\neq}(\bm{a}),|x_{j}|\leq 1,j\in{\mathbb{I}}_{0}(\bm{a})\right\},

where

{\mathbb{I}}_{\neq}(\bm{a})\triangleq\left\{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\mid a_{i}\neq 0\right\}
and
{\mathbb{I}}_{0}(\bm{a})\triangleq\left\{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\mid a_{i}=0\right\}.

These examples play a crucial role in the development of non-Euclidean gradient descent methods, which will be discussed in Sections
.

Given a specific norm definition, we introduce the concepts of an open ball and a closed ball as follows:

Definition 28
(Open ball, closed ball).

Let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{p}:\real^{n}\rightarrow\real_{+}
be the
\ell_{p}
norm function. The open ball centered at
\bm{c}\in\real^{n}
with radius
r
is defined as

{\mathbb{B}}_{p}(\bm{c},r)\triangleq\{\bm{x}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{c}\right\rVert_{p}<r\}.

Similarly, the closed ball centered at
\bm{c}\in\real^{n}
with radius
r
is defined as

{\mathbb{B}}_{p}[\bm{c},r]\triangleq\{\bm{x}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{c}\right\rVert_{p}\leq r\}.

For example,
{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[\boldsymbol{0},1]
represents the unit closed ball w.r.t. to the
\ell_{2}
norm.
To simplify notation, we omit the subscript 2 for
\ell_{2}
norms and
\boldsymbol{0}
for balls centered at zero, e.g.,
{\mathbb{B}}[1]\triangleq{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[\boldsymbol{0},1]
.
As a special case, the notation
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\triangleq{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[\boldsymbol{0},k]
denotes the set of
k
-sparse vectors, i.e., containing vectors that have only
k
(or less) nonzero elements.
More generally, let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
be any norm, the induced open and closed balls are denoted as

{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}(\bm{c},r)\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}[\bm{c},r].

For a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, we define the (matrix) Frobenius norm as follows.

Definition 29
(Matrix Frobenius norm).

The Frobenius norm of a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is defined as

\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1,j=1}^{n,p}(a_{ij})^{2}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})}=\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})}=\sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\sigma_{r}^{2}},

where
\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{r}
are nonzero singular values of
\bm{X}
, and
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
denotes the trace of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
, i.e., sum of diagonal elements of the matrix.

The spectral norm is defined as follows.

Definition 30
(Matrix spectral norm).

The spectral norm of a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is defined as

\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}=\mathop{\max}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq\boldsymbol{0}}\frac{\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}}=\mathop{\max}_{\bm{u}\in\real^{p}:\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{u}\right\rVert_{2},

which is also the maximum singular value of
\bm{X}
, i.e.,
\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}=\sigma_{\max}(\bm{X})
.

We note that the Frobenius norm serves as the matrix counterpart of the6 vector
\ell_{2}
norm.
For simplicity, we do not give the full subscript of the norm for the vector
\ell_{2}
norm or Frobenius norm when it is clear from the context which one we are referring to:
\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}
and
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}
.
However, for the spectral norm, the subscript
\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}
should
not
be omitted.

The vector space
n
, together with a given norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
, is called a
normed vector space
.
On the other hand, one way to define norms for matrices is by viewing a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
as a vector in
np
, e.g., using the vectorization of the matrix.
What distinguishes a matrix norm is a property called
submultiplicativity
:
\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{Y}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{Y}\right\rVert
if
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
is a submultiplicative matrix norm (see discussions below).

In some texts, a matrix norm that is not
submultiplicative
is termed as a
vector norm on matrices
or a
generalized matrix norm
.
The submultiplicativity of a matrix norm is important for the analysis of square matrices, although the definition of a matrix norm applies to both square and rectangular matrices.
For a submultiplicative matrix norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
that satisfies
\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{Y}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{Y}\right\rVert
, considering
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
, it follows that

\left\lVert\bm{X}^{2}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert^{2}\quad\implies\quad\left\lVert\bm{X}^{k}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert^{k},\ \forall\,k\in\{1,2,\ldots,\}.

(1.4)

Therefore, if the matrix is idempotent, i.e.,
\bm{X}^{2}=\bm{X}
, we have
\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert\geq 1
, which also indicates

\left\lVert\bm{I}\right\rVert\geq 1,\quad\text{if}\quad\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert\text{ is submultiplicative}.

(1.5)

On the other hand, if
\bm{X}
is nonsingular, we have the inequality for submultiplicative norms:

1\leq\left\lVert\bm{I}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-1}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert\left\lVert\bm{X}^{-1}\right\rVert.

That is, a submultiplicative norm has
\left\lVert\bm{I}\right\rVert\geq 1
and is
normalized
if and only if
\left\lVert\bm{I}\right\rVert=1
.

Proposition 31
(Submultiplicativity and orthogonally invariance of Frobenius/spectral).

The Frobnenius and spectral norms are submultiplicative. That is,

\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}\left\lVert\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{2}.

The two norms are also and orthogonally invariant. That is, let
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times p}
be orthogonal matrices, and let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
. Then,

\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}=\left\lVert\bm{U}\bm{X}\bm{V}\right\rVert_{F}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{U}\bm{X}\bm{V}\right\rVert_{2}.

1.3
Famous Inequalities

In this section, we introduce some famous inequalities that will be often used.
When considering random matrices, the
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
is considered one of the most important and widely used inequalities in mathematics.

Lemma 32
(Cauchy-Schwarz inequality).

For any random
n\times p
matrices
{\mathbf{X}}
and
{\mathbf{Y}}
(see Section
for more details), we have

\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}{\mathbf{Y}}\right\rVert\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}\right\rVert^{2}\right]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{Y}}\right\rVert^{2}\right]^{1/2},

where the inner product is defined as
\langle{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{Y}}\rangle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}{\mathbf{Y}}\right\rVert\right]
.

The result can be applied to non-random matrices and vectors.

Lemma 33
(Cauchy-Schwarz matrix (vector) inequality).

For any
n\times p
matrices
\bm{X}
and
\bm{Y}
, we have

\left\lVert\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{Y}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert\cdot\left\lVert\bm{Y}\right\rVert.

This is a special form of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, where the inner product is defined as
\langle\bm{X},\bm{Y}\rangle=\left\lVert\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{Y}\right\rVert
.

Similarly, for any vectors
\bm{u},\bm{v}
, we have

\left\lvert\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{v}\right\rvert\leq\|\bm{u}\|\cdot\|\bm{v}\|.

(1.6)

In the two-dimensional case, it becomes

(ac+bd)^{2}\leq(a^{2}+b^{2})(c^{2}+d^{2}).

The vector form of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality plays a crucial role in various branches of modern mathematics, including Hilbert space theory and numerical analysis
(
Wu and Wu 2009
)
.
Here, we present the proof for the vector form of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for simplicity. To see this, given two vectors
\bm{u},\bm{v}\in\real^{n}
, we have

\displaystyle 0\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(u_{i}v_{j}-u_{j}v_{i})^{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{i}^{2}v_{j}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{i}^{2}u_{j}^{2}-2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{i}u_{j}v_{i}v_{j}

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}^{2}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}^{2}\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}^{2}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{j}^{2}\right)-2\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}v_{i}\right)^{2}

\displaystyle=2\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert^{2}\cdot\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2}-2\left\lVert\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2},

from which the result follows.
The equality holds if and only if
\bm{u}=k\bm{v}
for some constant
k\in\real
, i.e.,
\bm{u}
and
\bm{v}
are linearly dependent.

Lemma 34
(Markov’s inequality).

Let
x
be a nonnegative random variable. Then, given any
\epsilon>0
, we have

\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\geq\epsilon]\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]}{\epsilon}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We notice the trick that
0\leq\epsilon\mathds{1}\{{\textnormal{x}}\geq\epsilon\}\leq{\textnormal{x}}
since
x
is nonnegative. This implies
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mathds{1}\{{\textnormal{x}}\geq\epsilon\}]\leq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]
. We also have

\mathbb{E}\left[\epsilon\mathds{1}\{{\textnormal{x}}\geq\epsilon\}\right]=\epsilon\mathbb{E}\left[\mathds{1}\{{\textnormal{x}}\geq\epsilon\}\right]=\epsilon\left(1\cdot\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\geq\epsilon]+0\cdot\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}<\epsilon]\right)=\epsilon\cdot\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\geq\epsilon]\leq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}].

This completes the proof.

Lemma 35
(Chebyshev’s inequality).

Let
x
be a random variable with finite mean
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]<\infty
. Then, given any
\epsilon>0
, we have

\Pr[|{\textnormal{x}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]|\geq\epsilon]\leq\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]}{\epsilon^{2}}.

Chebyshev’s inequality can be easily verified by defining
{\textnormal{y}}=({\textnormal{x}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}])^{2}
(which is nonnegative) and applying Markov’s inequality to
y
.

1.4
Differentiability and Differential Calculus

Differentiability and differential calculus form the backbone of mathematical analysis, particularly in the study of functions defined over multidimensional spaces. This section delves into the fundamental concepts that enable us to understand how functions change with respect to their variables, providing a rigorous technique for analyzing and optimizing complex systems.

At the heart of this discussion is the concept of the directional derivative, which measures the rate of change of a function
f
at a point
\bm{x}
in the direction of a vector
\bm{d}
.

Definition 36
(Directional derivative, partial derivative).

Given a function
f
defined over a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
and a nonzero vector
\bm{d}\in\real^{n}
. Then the directional derivative of
f
at
\bm{x}
w.r.t. the direction
\bm{d}
is given by, if the limit exists,

\mathop{\lim}_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{f(\bm{x}+t\bm{d})-f(\bm{x})}{t}.

And it is denoted by
f^{\prime}(\bm{x};\bm{d})
or
D_{\bm{d}}f(\bm{x})
.
The directional derivative is sometimes called the Gâteaux derivative.

For any
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, the directional derivative at
\bm{x}
w.r.t. the direction of the
i
-th standard basis
\bm{e}_{i}
is called the
i
-th partial derivative and is denoted by
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}(\bm{x})
,
D_{\bm{e}_{i}}f(\bm{x})
, or
\partial_{i}f(\bm{x})
.

If all the partial derivatives of a function
f
exist at a point
\bm{x}\in\real^{n}
, then the
gradient
of
f
at
\bm{x}
is defined as the column vector containing all the partial derivatives:

\nabla f(\bm{x})\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}(\bm{x})\\
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{2}}(\bm{x})\\
\vdots\\
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}(\bm{x})\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\in\real^{n}.

A function
f
defined over an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
is called
continuously differentiable
over
{\mathbb{S}}
if all the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on
{\mathbb{S}}
.
In the setting of continuously differentiability, the directional derivative and gradient have the following relationship:

f^{\prime}(\bm{x};\bm{d})=\nabla f(\bm{x})^{\top}\bm{d},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{for all }\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{S}}\text{ and }\bm{d}\in\real^{n}.

(1.7)

And in the setting of continuously differentiability, we also have

\mathop{\lim}_{\bm{d}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}}\frac{f(\bm{x}+\bm{d})-f(\bm{x})-\nabla f(\bm{x})^{\top}\bm{d}}{\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert}=0\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{for all }\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{S}},

(1.8)

or

f(\bm{y})=f(\bm{x})+\nabla f(\bm{x})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})+o(\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{x}\right\rVert),

(1.9)

where the
small-oh
function
o(\cdot):\real_{+}\rightarrow\real
is a one-dimensional function satisfying
\frac{o(t)}{t}\rightarrow 0
as
t\rightarrow 0^{+}
.

The partial derivative
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}(\bm{x})
is also a real-valued function of
\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{S}}
that can be partially differentiated. The
j
-th partial derivative of
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}(\bm{x})
is defined as

\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{j}\partial x_{i}}(\bm{x})=\frac{\partial\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}(\bm{x})\right)}{\partial x_{j}}(\bm{x}).

This is called the (
j,i
)-th
second-order partial derivative
of function
f
.
A function
f
defined over an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq
is called
twice continuously differentiable
over
{\mathbb{S}}
if all the second-order partial derivatives exist and are continuous over
{\mathbb{S}}
. In the setting of twice continuously differentiability, the second-order partial derivative are symmetric:

\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{j}\partial x_{i}}(\bm{x})=\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}}(\bm{x}).

The
Hessian
of the function
f
at a point
\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{S}}
is defined as the symmetric
n\times n
matrix

\nabla^{2}f(\bm{x})\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{1}^{2}}(\bm{x})&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{1}\partial x_{2}}(\bm{x})&\ldots&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{1}\partial x_{n}}(\bm{x})\\
\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{2}\partial x_{1}}(\bm{x})&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{2}\partial x_{2}}(\bm{x})&\ldots&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{2}\partial x_{n}}(\bm{x})\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{n}\partial x_{1}}(\bm{x})&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{n}\partial x_{2}}(\bm{x})&\ldots&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{n}^{2}}(\bm{x})\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

We then provide a simple proof of Taylor’s expansion for one-dimensional functions.

{theoremHigh}
[Taylor’s expansion with Lagrange remainder]
Let
f(x):\real\rightarrow\real
be
k
-times continuously differentiable on the closed interval
{\mathbb{I}}
with endpoints
x
and
y
, for some
k\geq 0
. If
f^{(k+1)}
exists on the interval
{\mathbb{I}}
, then there exists a
\xi\in(x,y)
such that

\displaystyle f(x)

\displaystyle=f(y)+f^{\prime}(y)(x-y)+\ldots+\frac{f^{(k)}(y)}{k!}(x-y)^{k}+\frac{f^{(k+1)}(\xi)}{(k+1)!}(x-y)^{k+1}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\frac{f^{(i)}(y)}{i!}(x-y)^{i}+\frac{f^{(k+1)}(\xi)}{(k+1)!}(x-y)^{k+1}.

Taylor’s expansion can be extended to a function of vector
f(\bm{x}):\real^{n}\rightarrow\real
or a function of matrix
f(\bm{X}):\real^{m\times n}\rightarrow\real
.

Taylor’s expansion, or also known as
Taylor’s series
, approximates the function
f(x)
around a value
y
using a polynomial in a single variable
x
. To understand the origin of this series, we recall from the elementary calculus course that the approximated function of
\cos(\theta)
around
\theta=0
is given by

\cos(\theta)\approx 1-\frac{\theta^{2}}{2}.

This means that
\cos(\theta)
can be approximated by a second-degree polynomial.
If we want to approximate
\cos(\theta)
more generally with a second-degree polynomial
f(\theta)=c_{1}+c_{2}\theta+c_{3}\theta^{2}
, an intuitive approach is to match the function and its derivatives at
\theta=0
. That is,

\left\{\begin{aligned} \cos(0)&=f(0);\\
\cos^{\prime}(0)&=f^{\prime}(0);\\
\cos^{\prime\prime}(0)&=f^{\prime\prime}(0);\\
\end{aligned}\right.\quad\implies\quad\left\{\begin{aligned} 1&=c_{1};\\
-\sin(0)&=0=c_{2};\\
-\cos(0)&=-1=2c_{3}.\\
\end{aligned}\right.

Solving these equations yields
f(\theta)=c_{1}+c_{2}\theta+c_{3}\theta^{2}=1-\frac{\theta^{2}}{2}
, which matches our initial approximation
\cos(\theta)\approx 1-\frac{\theta^{2}}{2}
around
\theta=0
.

For high-dimensional functions, we have the following approximation results.

{theoremHigh}
[Mean value theorem]
Let
f(\bm{x}):{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a continuously differentiable function over an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
, and given two points
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Then, there exists a point
\boldsymbol{\xi}\in[\bm{x},\bm{y}]
such that

f(\bm{y})=f(\bm{x})+\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\xi})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{x}).

{theoremHigh}

[Linear approximation theorem]
Let
f(\bm{x}):{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a twice continuously differentiable function over an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
, and let
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Then, there exists a point
\boldsymbol{\xi}\in[\bm{x},\bm{y}]
such that

f(\bm{y})=f(\bm{x})+\nabla f(\bm{x})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f(\boldsymbol{\xi})(\bm{y}-\bm{x}),

or

f(\bm{y})=f(\bm{x})+\nabla f(\bm{x})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})+o(\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}),

or

f(\bm{y})=f(\bm{x})+\nabla f(\bm{x})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})+\mathcal{O}(\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}).

This theorem suggests that the error in the linear approximation is of the order of the square of the distance between
\bm{x}
and
\bm{y}
.

{theoremHigh}
[Quadratic approximation theorem]
Let
f(\bm{x}):{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a twice continuously differentiable function over an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
, and let
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Then it follows that

f(\bm{y})=f(\bm{x})+\nabla f(\bm{x})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f(\bm{x})(\bm{y}-\bm{x})+o(\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}),

or

f(\bm{y})=f(\bm{x})+\nabla f(\bm{x})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{x})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f(\bm{x})(\bm{y}-\bm{x})+\mathcal{O}(\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{3}).

This theorem indicates that the error in the quadratic approximation is of the order of the cube of the distance between
\bm{x}
and
\bm{y}
, making it a more accurate approximation when
\bm{y}
is close to
\bm{x}
.

1.5
Statistics and Common Probability Distributions

A random variable is a variable that assumes different values randomly that models uncertain outcomes or events. We denote the random variable itself with a lowercase letter in
normal fonts
, and its possible values with lowercase letters in
italic fonts
.
For instance,
y_{1}
and
y_{2}
are possible values of the random variable
y
.
In the case of vector-valued variables, we represent the random variable as
{\mathbf{y}}
and one of its realizations as
\bm{y}
.
Similarly, we denote the random variable as
{\mathbf{Y}}
and one of its values as
\bm{Y}
when we are working with matrix-valued variables.
However, a random variable merely describes possible states and needs to be accompanied by a probability distribution specifying the likelihood of each state.

\paragrapharrow

Probability and statistics.
In a general sense, one can describe statistics as the mathematical discipline whose purpose is to use empirical data generated by a random phenomenon, in order to make inferences about certain deterministic characteristics of the phenomenon, while simultaneously quantifying the uncertainty inherent in these inferences.

Let’s take a step back and examine the key components of this definition. What exactly is a
random phenomenon
?
A random phenomenon can be thought of as a system or process whose outcome, denoted
x
, is uncertain.
This means that even if we have complete knowledge of all aspects of the system, we still cannot predict its outcome with certainty.
In mathematical terms, such phenomena are modeled using probability theory: the outcome
x
is represented as a random variable, and the model describing the phenomenon is its
probability distribution function
, also known as the
cumulative distribution function (CDF)
, defined as:

F(x)\equiv\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x].

Now, suppose there is a characteristic
\boldsymbol{\theta}
of the phenomenon that affects the probabilities associated with the outcomes of
x
. Such a characteristic is referred to as a
parameter
. Since the probability of the event
\{{\textnormal{x}}\leq x\}
depends on
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, the function
F(x)
must also depend on
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. Therefore, we write it as:

F(x;\boldsymbol{\theta})={\Pr}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x].

In probability theory, if we know both the functional form of
F(x;\boldsymbol{\theta})
and the true value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, we can then calculate the probability
\Pr_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x]=F(x;\boldsymbol{\theta})
for any possible outcome
x
.
However, in statistics, we deal with the inverse problem: suppose that we know the precise functional form of
F(x;\boldsymbol{\theta})
, but do not know which is the true
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. If we have an outcome
x
(a realization of
x
), the central question becomes: is it possible to say something useful about
\boldsymbol{\theta}
? It seems that we should be able to do so. Since
\boldsymbol{\theta}
influences what outcomes are most probable, then knowing an outcome should give us information on which
\boldsymbol{\theta}
are plausible. The topic of statistics will be how exactly to make this connection rigorous and show how to exploit it in order to (a) make the best possible use of our data
x
to better inform ourselves about
\boldsymbol{\theta}
and (b) understand how certain we can be about our inferences on
\boldsymbol{\theta}
for the given data
x
. In summary, the discussion of statistics includes:

1.

There is a distribution
F(x;\boldsymbol{\theta})
depending on an unknown
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{p}
.

2.

We observe the realization of
n
independent identically distributed random variables
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
that follow this distribution.

3.

We wish to use our
n
observations (the realizations of
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
) in order to make statements about the true value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
and to quantify the uncertainty associated with those statements.

\paragrapharrow

Discrete random variables.
Random variables can be either discrete or continuous. A discrete random variable has a finite or countably infinite number of states. These states need not be integers; they can also be named states without numerical values. Conversely, a continuous random variable is associated with real values.

A probability distribution describes the likelihood of a random variable or set of random variables.
The characterization of probability distributions varies depending on whether the variables are discrete or continuous.

For discrete variables, we employ a
probability mass function (p.m.f., PMF)
. Probability mass functions are denoted with a capital
\Pr
.
The probability mass function maps a state of a random variable to
the probability of that random variable taking on that state. The notation
\Pr({\textnormal{y}}=y)
(or
f_{{\textnormal{y}}}(y)
,
\Pr_{{\textnormal{y}}}(y)
) represents the probability that
y
equals
y
, with a probability of 1 indicating certainty and a probability of 0 indicating impossibility.
Alternatively, we define a variable first and use the
\sim
notation to specify its distribution later:
{\textnormal{y}}\sim\Pr({\textnormal{y}})
.

Probability mass functions can operate on multiple variables simultaneously, constituting a
joint probability mass distribution functions
or
joint frequency functions
.
For example,
\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x,{\textnormal{y}}=y)
denotes the probability of
x=x
and
y=y
simultaneously, and we may also use the shorthand
\Pr(x,y)
or
\Pr_{{\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}}}(x,y)
. Moreover, if the PMF depends on some known parameters
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, then it can be denoted by
\Pr(x,y\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
(or
\Pr_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(x,y)
,
f(x,y;\boldsymbol{\theta})
) for brevity.

In many cases, our focus lies in determining the probability of an event, given the occurrence of another event. This is referred to as a
conditional probability
.
The conditional probability that
{\textnormal{x}}=x
given
{\textnormal{y}}=y
is denoted by
\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x\mid{\textnormal{y}}=y)
.
This can be calculated using the formula

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x\mid{\textnormal{y}}=y)=\frac{\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x,{\textnormal{y}}=y)}{\Pr({\textnormal{y}}=y)}.

This formula serves as the cornerstone in
Bayes’ theorem
(see Theorem
).

On the contrary, there are instances when the probability distribution across a set of variables is known, and the interest lies in determining the probability distribution over a specific subset of them.
The probability distribution over the subset is referred to as the
marginal probability mass distribution
.
For example, suppose we have discrete random variables
x
and
y
, and we know
\Pr({\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}})
. We can find
\Pr({\textnormal{x}})
using summation:

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x)=\sum_{y}\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x,{\textnormal{y}}=y).

\paragrapharrow

Continuous random variables.
When dealing with continuous random variables, we represent probability distributions using a
probability density function (p.d.f., PDF)
instead of a probability mass function. For a function
p
to qualify as a probability density function, it must adhere to the following properties:

The domain of
p
must be the set of all possible states of
y
;

We do not require
p(y)\leq 1
as that in the PMF. However, it must satisfies that
\forall\,y\in{\textnormal{y}},p(y)\geq 0
.

Integrates to 1:
\int p(y)dy=1
.

A probability density function
p(y)
(or denoted as
f_{{\textnormal{y}}}(y)
,
p_{{\textnormal{y}}}(y)
) does not provide the probability of a specific state directly.
Instead, the probability of falling within an infinitesimal region with volume
\delta y
is given by
p(y)\delta y
.
Moreover, if the probability density function depends on some known parameters
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, it can be denoted by
p(x\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
,
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(x;\boldsymbol{\theta})
or
f(x;\boldsymbol{\theta})
for brevity.

\paragrapharrow

Distribution function.
On the other hand, a probability distribution can be characterized by the cumulative distribution function (c.d.f., CDF).
Let
x
be a random variable with the distribution function
F(x)=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x]
, where
F(x)
is nondecreasing and right continuous and satisfies

0\leq F(x)\leq 1,\qquad F(-\infty)=0,\qquad F(\infty)=1.

The expected value
\mu
and variance
\omega^{2}
of
x
in the continuous case are defined as

\mu=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}xdF(x),\qquad\omega^{2}=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{x}}-\mu)^{2}]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(x-\mu)^{2}dF(x).

Similarly, in the discrete case, they are defined as

\mu=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\sum_{x}x\Pr(x),\qquad\omega^{2}=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{x}}-\mu)^{2}]=\sum_{x}(x-\mu)^{2}\Pr(x).

It is easy to see that

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}])^{2}.

(1.10)

Exercise
\thetheo
(Uniform distribution)

Let
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\text{Uniform}(x\mid a,b)
be a uniform distributed variable such that
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(x)=\frac{1}{b-a}
if
a\leq x\leq b
and
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(x)=0
otherwise. Show that

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{a+b}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{(b-a)^{2}}{12}.

Let
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]^{\top}
be a vector of random variables. The
joint probability distribution function
(or simply probability distribution function) of the random vector—denoted as
F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(\bm{x})
,
F(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})
, or
F(\bm{x})
—is defined as

F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\leq x_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\leq x_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x_{n}].

It holds that

When all the variables are discrete, as discussed above, the joint probability mass function or the joint frequency function can be characterized as

f_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}=x_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}=x_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}=x_{n}].

On the contrary, if the variables are continuous, the
joint probability density function
is a function
f_{{\mathbf{x}}}:\real^{n}\rightarrow[0,\infty)
(or simply
f(\bm{x})
,
p_{{\mathbf{x}}}(\bm{x})
,
p(\bm{x})
) such that

F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=\int_{-\infty}^{x_{1}}\ldots\int_{-\infty}^{x_{n}}f_{{\mathbf{x}}}(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n})dy_{1}\ldots dy_{n}.

In this case, when
f_{{\mathbf{x}}}
is continuous at
\bm{x}=[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}]^{\top}
, we have

f_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial x_{1}\partial x_{2}\ldots\partial x_{n}}F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}).

The variables are independent if and only if

\displaystyle F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})

\displaystyle=F_{{\textnormal{x}}_{1}}(x_{1})\cdot F_{{\textnormal{x}}_{2}}(x_{2})\cdot\ldots\cdot F_{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}}(x_{n});

\displaystyle\text{or}\quad f_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})

\displaystyle=f_{{\textnormal{x}}_{1}}(x_{1})\cdot f_{{\textnormal{x}}_{2}}(x_{2})\cdot\ldots\cdot f_{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}}(x_{n}).

The
conditional or marginal probability density functions
for the continuous cases are similar to the discrete cases, except that integration is employed instead of summation. For example,
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(x)=\int f_{{\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}}}(x,y)dy
.

Specifically, the joint distribution of
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
and
{\textnormal{x}}_{j}
is
F(x_{i},x_{j})\equiv\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\leq x_{i},{\textnormal{x}}_{j}\leq x_{j}]
. Then the covariance
\omega_{ij}
between
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
and
{\textnormal{x}}_{j}
is defined by

\omega_{ij}\triangleq\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i},{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]\triangleq\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\mu_{i})({\textnormal{x}}_{j}-\mu_{j})]=\int_{x_{i},x_{j}=-\infty}^{\infty}(x_{i}-\mu_{i})(x_{j}-\mu_{j})dF(x_{i},x_{j}).

Then
\omega_{ij}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]-\mu_{i}\mu_{j}
, where
\mu_{i}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]
. The covariance matrix
\boldsymbol{\Omega}\in\real^{n\times n}
of the random vector
{\mathbf{x}}
is defined by

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}({\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top})-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top},

(1.11)

where
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}]=[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\ldots,\mu_{n}]^{\top}
. A few useful properties are provided below.

The variance of two random variables expresses the degree of linear dependency between the two. Moreover, the correlation between the two is defined as

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{orr}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]\triangleq\frac{\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]}{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]}}.

(1.12)

The variance and correlation of two random variable convey the equivalent dependence information.
However, the correlation is invariant to changes of scale, and the range of the correlation is
[-1,1]
.
It also holds that

\left\lvert\mathbb{C}\mathrm{orr}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]\right\rvert\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]}.

(1.13)

Lemma 37
(Linear transformation).

Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}
, where
\bm{A}\in\real^{m\times n}
is a given matrix, and let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
be a random vector with the mean vector
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}
and covariance matrix
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
. Then

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{y}}]=\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}]=\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{A}^{\top}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
The first property follows directly from the definition of expected value. The second is proved as

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{A}^{\top}]=\bm{A}\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}]\bm{A}^{\top}=\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{A}^{\top}.

This completes the proof.

In the special case when
\bm{A}=\bm{a}^{\top}
is a row vector,
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{a}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}
is a linear functional of
{\mathbf{x}}
. Then, if
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}
,
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{a}
.

Lemma 38
(Quadratic transformation).

Let
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
be a symmetric matrix, and let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
be a random vector with expected value
\boldsymbol{\mu}=[\mu_{i}]
and covariance matrix
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=[\omega_{ij}]
. Then,

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}),

where
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega})
denotes the trace of
\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}
, i.e., sum of diagonal elements of the matrix.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}
,
it follows that
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]
.
Substitute the expectations
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]=\mu_{i}\mu_{j}+\omega_{ij}
:

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}]=\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\mu_{i}\mu_{j}}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}}+\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\omega_{ij}}_{\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega})}.

Thus, the lemma is proven.

Alternatively, for
{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}
, we have

\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}

\displaystyle=(\boldsymbol{\mu}+{\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{A}(\boldsymbol{\mu}+{\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})+({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}).

Thus, it follows that

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})+({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})]=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{tr}[({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})]\right]

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{tr}[\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}]\right]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{=}}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathrm{tr}\left[\mathbb{E}[\bm{A}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}]\right]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathrm{tr}\left[\bm{A}\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}]\right]=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathrm{tr}\left[\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\right],

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the trace trick, and the equality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from the linear property of traces.
For any matrix
\bm{A},\bm{B},\bm{C}
, the trace trick is

\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\bm{B}\bm{C})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{B}\bm{C}\bm{A})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{C}\bm{A}\bm{B}),

if all
\bm{A}\bm{B}\bm{C}
,
\bm{B}\bm{C}\bm{A}
, and
\bm{C}\bm{A}\bm{B}
exist.
This completes the proof.

We will often engineer this
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\boldsymbol{0}
so that the key thing we care about is just
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega})
.
If we assume that
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\boldsymbol{0}
and the variance is
\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
, then
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}]=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
.
Note that
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is a known value. Then, we search the universe to find an
\bm{A}
such that
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=1
, which would give us an unbiased estimate of
\sigma^{2}
; see Definition
for a reference.

1.5.1
Common Univariate Probability Distributions

In the rest of this section, we provide rigorous definitions for common probability distributions.

Definition 39
(Gaussian or normal distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the Gaussian distribution (a.k.a., the normal distribution) with mean and variance parameters
\mu
and
\sigma^{2}>0
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
, if

f(x;\mu,\sigma^{2})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(x-\mu)^{2}\right\}=\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{2\pi}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\tau}{2}(x-\mu)^{2}\right\}.

The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mu,\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\sigma^{2}=\tau^{-1},

where
\tau
is also known as the precision of the Gaussian distribution.
The cumulative distribution function (c.d.f., CDF) of Gaussian is

F(x;\mu,\sigma^{2})=\Pr({\textnormal{x}}<x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\int_{-\infty}^{x}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(z-\mu)^{2}\right\}dz.

Specifically, we denote
\Phi(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{y}\mathcal{N}(u\mid 0,1)du=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{y}\exp(-\frac{u^{2}}{2})du
as the cumulative distribution function of
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
, the standard normal distribution.
Figure
illustrates the impact of different parameters
\mu,\sigma^{2}
for the Gaussian distribution.

Suppose
\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{N}\}
are drawn independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) from a Gaussian distribution of
\mathcal{N}(x\mid\mu,\sigma^{2})
.
For analytical simplicity, we may rewrite the Gaussian probability density function as follows:

\displaystyle p(\mathcal{X}\mid\mu,\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=\prod^{N}_{i=1}\mathcal{N}(x_{i}\mid\mu,\sigma^{2})

(1.14)

\displaystyle=(2\pi)^{-N/2}(\sigma^{2})^{-N/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\left[N(\overline{x}-\mu)^{2}+N\sum_{n=1}^{N}(x_{n}-\overline{x})^{2}\right]\right\}

\displaystyle=(2\pi)^{-N/2}(\sigma^{2})^{-N/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\left[N(\overline{x}-\mu)^{2}+NS_{\overline{x}}\right]\right\},

where
S_{\overline{x}}\triangleq\sum_{n=1}^{N}(x_{n}-\overline{x})^{2}
and
\overline{x}\triangleq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}
.

Figure 1.1:
Gaussian probability density functions for different values of the mean and variance parameters
\mu
and
\sigma^{2}
.

While the product of two Gaussian variables remains an open problem, the sum of Gaussian variables can be characterized by a new Gaussian distribution.

Remark 40
(Sum of Gaussians).

Let
x
and
y
be two Gaussian distributed variables with means
\mu_{x},\mu_{y}
and variance
\sigma_{x}^{2},\sigma_{y}^{2}
, respectively.

When there is no correlation between the two variables, then it follows that

{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{x}+\mu_{y},\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{y}^{2}).

When there exists a correlation of
\rho
between the two variables, then it follows that

{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{x}+\mu_{y},\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{y}^{2}+2\rho\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y}).

Gaussian distributions have strong concentration properties. The following tail bound on a Gaussian random variable is an important result.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Chernoff bound for centered Gaussian)

For
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
, show that

p(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq t)\leq 2e^{-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}.

Hint: Use Chernoff bound.

The
Laplace
