distribution, also known as the
double exponential
distribution, is named after
Pierre-Simon Laplace
(1749–1827), who obtained the distribution in 1774
(
Kotz et al. 2001
;
Härdle and Simar 2007
)
.
This distribution finds applications in modeling heavy-tailed data due to its tails being heavier than those of the normal distribution, and it is used extensively in sparse-favoring models since it expresses a high peak with heavy tails (same as the
\ell_{1}
regularization term in non-probabilistic or non-Bayesian optimization methods).
In Bayesian modeling, when there is a prior belief that the parameter of interest is likely to be close to the mean with the potential for large deviations, the Laplace distribution serves as a suitable prior distribution for such scenarios.

Definition 41
(Laplace distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the Laplace distribution with location and scale parameters
\mu
and
b>0
, respectively, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{L}(\mu,b)
, if

f(x;\mu,b)=\frac{1}{2b}\exp\left(-\frac{\left\lvert x-\mu\right\rvert}{b}\right).

The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{L}(\mu,b)
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mu,\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=2b^{2}.

Figure
compares different parameters
\mu
and
b
for the Laplace distribution.

Figure 1.2:
Laplace probability density functions for different values of the parameters.

More often than not, we repeat an experiment multiple times independently with two alternative outcomes, say “success” and “failure”, and we want to model the overall number of successes.
We are inevitably taken to the binomial distribution if each experiment is modeled as a Bernoulli distribution.
This simulates the overall proportion of heads in a run of
n
separate coin flips.

Definition 42
(Binomial distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the binomial distribution with parameter
p\in(0,1)
and
n\in\mathbb{N}
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathrm{Binom}(n,p)
, if

f(x;n,p)=\binom{n}{x}p^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},

where
\binom{n}{x}
is known as the binomial coefficient.
The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathrm{Binom}(a,b)
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=np,\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=np(1-p).

Figure
compares different parameters of
p
with
n=10
for the binomial distribution.

A distribution that is closely related to the Binomial distribution is called the Bernoulli distribution.
A random variable is said to follow the
Bernoulli
distribution with parameter
p\in(0,1)
, denoted as
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(p)
, if

f(x;p)=p\mathds{1}\{x=1\}+(1-p)\mathds{1}\{x=0\},

(1.15)

with mean
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=p
and variance
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=p(1-p)
, respectively.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Bernoulli and binomial)

Show that if
{\textnormal{x}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\textnormal{y}}_{i}
with
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bern}(p)
, then we have
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathrm{Binom}(N,p)
.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Scaled binomial)

When considering proportions instead of counts, we scale the binomial variable
x
by dividing it by the number of trials
n
. Define
y
as the random variable representing the proportion of successes:

{\textnormal{y}}=\frac{{\textnormal{x}}}{n}

Then,
y
can be seen as having a “scaled” or “rescaled” binomial distribution, with the PMF adjusted accordingly:

\Pr({\textnormal{y}}=y)=\binom{n}{ny}p^{ny}(1-p)^{n(1-y)}

for values of
y
that are multiples of
1/n
, i.e.,
z=0,\frac{1}{n},\frac{2}{n},\dots,1
.
Show that

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}]=p\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.

The scaled binomial distribution is particularly useful when modeling data that represent proportions or rates, such as the proportion of individuals responding to a treatment in clinical trials or the success rate of an event over multiple attempts.
In statistical modeling, especially within the framework of generalized linear models (GLMs), using the scaled binomial allows for direct modeling of probabilities or proportions while accounting for the number of trials. This approach simplifies the interpretation of model coefficients and predictions, focusing on the expected proportion of successes rather than the raw count; see Example
.

Figure 1.3:
Binomial distribution probability mass
functions for different values of the parameters
p
with
n=10
.

The
exponential
distribution is a probability distribution commonly used in modeling events occurring randomly over time, such as the time elapsed until the occurrence of a certain event, or the time between two consecutive events.
It is a special Gamma distribution (see definition below) with support on nonnegative real values.

Definition 43
(Exponential distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the exponential distribution with rate parameter
\lambda>0
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{E}(\lambda)
, if

f(x;\lambda)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\lambda\exp(-\lambda x),&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x\geq 0;\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x<0.\end{aligned}\right.

We will see this is equivalent to
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}(1,\lambda)
, a Gamma distribution.
The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{E}(\lambda)
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\lambda^{-1},\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\lambda^{-2}.

The support of an exponential distribution is on
(0,\infty)
.
Figure
compares different parameters
\lambda
for the exponential distribution.

Note that the average
\lambda^{-1}
is the average time until the occurrence of the event of interest, interpreting
\lambda
as a rate parameter.
An important property of the exponential distribution is that it is “memoryless,” meaning that the probability of waiting for an additional amount of time
x
depends only on
x
, not on the past waiting time.

Remark 44
(Property of exponential distribution).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{E}(\lambda)
. Then we have
\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq x+s\mid{\textnormal{x}}\geq s)=\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq x)
.

Figure 1.4:
Exponential probability density functions for different values of the rate parameter
\lambda
.

Definition 45
(Gamma distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the Gamma distribution with shape parameter
r>0
and rate parameter
\lambda>0
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}(r,\lambda)
, if

f(x;r,\lambda)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\lambda^{r}}{\Gamma(r)}x^{r-1}\exp(-\lambda x),&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x\geq 0.\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x<0,\end{aligned}\right.

where
\Gamma(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{x-1}\exp(-t)dt
is the Gamma function, and we can just take it as a function to normalize the distribution into sum to 1. In special cases when
y
is a positive integer,
\Gamma(y)=(y-1)!
.
We will delay the introduction of Chi-squared distribution in Definition
.
The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}(r,\lambda)
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{r}{\lambda},\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{r}{\lambda^{2}}.

Figure
compares different parameters for the Gamma distribution.

It is important to note that the definition of the Gamma distribution does not constrain
r
to be a natural number; instead, it allows
r
to take any positive value.
However, when
r
is a positive integer, the Gamma distribution can be interpreted as a sum of
r
exponentials of rate
\lambda
(see Definition
).
The summation property holds true more generally for Gamma variables with the same rate parameter. If
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}
and
{\textnormal{x}}_{2}
are random variables drawn from
\mathcal{G}(r_{1},\lambda)
and
\mathcal{G}(r_{2},\lambda)
, respectively, then their sum
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}+{\textnormal{x}}_{2}
is a Gamma random variable from
\mathcal{G}(r_{1}+r_{2},\lambda)
.

In the Gamma distribution definition, we observe that the Gamma function can be defined as follows:

\Gamma(y)=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{y-1}e^{-x}dx,\qquad y\geq 0.

Utilizing integration by parts
\int_{a}^{b}u(x)v^{\prime}(x)dx=u(x)v(x)|_{a}^{b}-\int_{a}^{b}u^{\prime}(x)v(x)dx
, where
u(x)=x^{y-1}
and
v(x)=-e^{-x}
, we derive

\displaystyle\Gamma(y)

\displaystyle=-x^{y-1}e^{-x}|_{0}^{\infty}-\int_{0}^{\infty}(y-1)x^{y-2}(-e^{-x})dx

\displaystyle=0+(y-1)\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{y-2}e^{-x}dx=(y-1)\Gamma(y-1).

This demonstrates that when
y
is a positive integer, the relationship
\Gamma(y)=(y-1)!
holds true.

(a)

Gamma probability density
functions for different values of the parameters
r
and
\lambda
.

(b)

Chi-squared probability density
functions for different values of the parameter
p
.

Figure 1.5:
Comparison between the Gamma distribution and the Chi-squared distribution.

Though the Chi-squared distribution is a special case of the Gamma distribution, it holds particular significance in statistical theory.

Definition 46
(Chi-squared distribution,
\chi^{2}
-Distribution).

Let
{\textnormal{a}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
(equivalently,
{\mathbf{a}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{I}_{p})
; see Definition
).
Then,
{\textnormal{x}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}{\textnormal{a}}_{i}^{2}
follows the Chi-squared distribution (or Chi-square distribution,
\chi^{2}
-distribution) with
p
degrees of freedom.
We write
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\chi_{(p)}^{2}
, and it is equivalent to
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}(p/2,1/2)
in Definition
. The probability density function is given by

f(x;p)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{2^{p/2}\Gamma(\frac{p}{2})}x^{\frac{p}{2}-1}\exp(-\frac{x}{2}),&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x\geq 0;\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x<0.\end{aligned}\right.

The mean, variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\chi_{(p)}^{2}
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=p,\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=2p.

Figure
compares different parameters
p
for the Chi-squared distribution.

The definition shows that if
{\mathbf{a}}=[{\textnormal{a}}_{1},{\textnormal{a}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{a}}_{p}]^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{I}_{p})
(the multivariate Gaussian distribution; as a hindsight, see Definition
), then
{\textnormal{x}}={\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{a}}\sim\chi_{(p)}^{2}
.
Given an orthogonal projection matrix
\bm{H}
of rank
r<p
(as a hindsight, see Definition
), then it follows that

{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}\bm{H}{\mathbf{a}}\sim\chi_{(r)}^{2},\text{ with orthogonal projector $\mathrm{rank}(\bm{H})=r<p$}.

(1.16)

Suppose that
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
where
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\real^{p}
and
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}
is nonsingular. Then,

({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\sim\chi^{2}_{(p)}.

(1.17)

To see this, we note that
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is symmetric and positive definite. Then, we can write that
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}
, where
\bm{Q}
is an
p\times p
orthogonal matrix and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{p})
with
\lambda_{j}>0
(as a hindsight, see Theorem
).
Then, define
{\mathbf{y}}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\bm{Q}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})
, which is a standardized version of
{\mathbf{x}}
. Vector
{\mathbf{y}}
then is normally distributed by Lemma
:

{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{I}_{p}).

It follows that the elements of
{\mathbf{y}}
are independent and that
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
. So,

({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})={\mathbf{y}}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}\sim\chi^{2}_{(p)}
.

Definition 47
(Inverse-Gamma distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the inverse-Gamma distribution with shape parameter
r>0
and scale parameter
\lambda>0
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}^{-1}(r,\lambda)
, if

f(x;r,\lambda)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\lambda^{r}}{\Gamma(r)}x^{-r-1}\exp(-\frac{\lambda}{x}),&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x>0;\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x\leq 0.\end{aligned}\right.

The mean and variance of inverse-Gamma distribution are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\lambda}{r-1},\,&\mathrm{if\,}r\geq 1;\\
&\infty,\,&\mathrm{if\,}0<r<1.\end{aligned}\right.\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\lambda^{2}}{(r-1)^{2}(r-2)},\,&\mathrm{if\,}r>2;\\
&\infty,\,&\mathrm{if\,}0<r\leq 2.\end{aligned}\right.

Figure
illustrates the impact of different parameters
r
and
\lambda
for the inverse-Gamma distribution.

If
x
is Gamma distributed, then
{\textnormal{y}}=1/{\textnormal{x}}
is inverse-Gamma distributed.
Note that the inverse-Gamma density is not simply the Gamma density with

x
replaced by
\frac{1}{y}
. There is an additional factor of
y^{-2}
. The inverse-Gamma distribution is useful as a prior for positive parameters. It imparts a quite heavy tail and keeps probability further from zero than the Gamma distribution (see examples in Figure
).

functions for different values of the parameters
r
and
\lambda
.

Inverse-Chi-squared probability density
functions for different values of the parameters
v
and
s^{2}
.

Comparison between the inverse-Gamma distribution and inverse-Chi-squared distribution for different values of the parameters.

Definition 48
(Inverse-Chi-squared distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the inverse-Chi-squared distribution with parameter
\nu>0
and
s^{2}>0
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}^{-1}(\frac{\nu}{2},\frac{\nu s^{2}}{2})
, if

f(x;\nu,s^{2})=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{{(\frac{\nu s^{2}}{2})}^{\frac{\nu}{2}}}{\Gamma(\frac{\nu}{2})}x^{-\frac{\nu}{2}-1}\exp(-\frac{\nu s^{2}}{2x}),&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x>0;\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x\leq 0.\end{aligned}\right.

And it is also compactly denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathrm{\chi^{-2}}(\nu,s^{2})
. The parameter
\nu>0
is called the degrees of freedom, and
s^{2}>0
is the scale parameter. And it is also known as the scaled inverse-Chi-squared distribution.
The mean and variance of the inverse-Chi-squared distribution are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\nu s^{2}}{\nu-2},\,&\mathrm{if\,\,}\nu\geq 2;\\
&\infty,\,&\mathrm{if\,\,}0<\nu<2.\end{aligned}\right.\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{2\nu^{2}s^{4}}{(\nu-2)^{2}(\nu-4)},\,&\mathrm{if\,\,}\nu\geq 4;\\
&\infty,\,&\mathrm{if\,\,}0<\nu<4.\end{aligned}\right.

To establish a connection with the inverse-Gamma distribution, we can set
S=\nu s^{2}
. Then the inverse-Chi-squared distribution can also be denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}^{-1}(\frac{\nu}{2},\frac{S}{2})
if
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathrm{\chi^{-2}}(\nu,s^{2})
, the form of which conforms to the univariate case of the inverse-Wishart distribution (see
Lu 2023b
).
Figure
illustrates the impact of different parameters
\nu
and
s^{2}
for the inverse-Chi-squared distribution.

Definition 49
(Beta distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the Beta distribution with parameter
a>0
and
b>0
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)
, if

f(x;a,b)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{B(a,b)}x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1},&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}0\leq x\leq 1.\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,otherwise\,\,},\end{aligned}\right.

where
B(a,b)
denotes Euler’s Beta function and it can be seen as a normalization term. Equivalently,
B(a,b)
can be obtained by

B(a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)},

where
\Gamma(\cdot)
is the Gamma function.
The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{a}{a+b},\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{ab}{(a+b+1)(a+b)^{2}}.

Figure
compares different parameters of
a
and
b
for the Beta distribution. When
a=b=1
, the Beta distribution reduces to a uniform distribution in the range of 0 and 1; see Exercise
.

Figure 1.7:
Beta distribution probability density
functions for different values of the parameters
a
and
b
. When
a=b=1
, the Beta distribution reduces to a uniform distribution in the range of 0 and 1.

The
Poisson
distribution is a discrete probability distribution that characterizes the number of events in a fixed interval of time or space, given the average number of events in that interval.
The Poisson distribution is frequently employed for modeling count data, such as the number of calls received by a call center in an hour or the number of emails received in a day provided that the probability of a “success” for any given instance is “very small.”
To name more examples where the Poisson distribution can be applied, e.g., the number of stars in a random area of the space; the distribution of bacteria on a surface; the number of typographical errors on a typed page; the number of wrong connections to a phone number.

Definition 50
(Poisson Distribution).

A random variable
{\textnormal{x}}\in\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}
is said to follow the Poisson distribution with rate parameter
\lambda>0
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{P}(\lambda)
, if

f(x;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^{x}}{x!}\exp(-\lambda).

The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{P}(\lambda)
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\lambda,\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\lambda.

The support of an exponential distribution is on
\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}=\{0\}\cup\mathbb{N}
.
Figure
compares probability mass functions of different parameter values
\lambda
for the Poisson distribution.

The mean and variance of the Poisson distribution are equal.
Roughly speaking, a Poisson distribution is the limit of a binomial distribution when
n\rightarrow\infty
and
\pi=\lambda/n
, i.e., the number of trials diverges to infinity but the probability of success decreases to zero linearly with respect to the number of trials. This is also known as the
law of rare events
.
Therefore, the Poisson distribution is often employed to model rare events like radioactive decays.

Figure 1.8:
Poisson probability mass functions for different values of the parameter
\lambda
.

The sum of independently identical Poisson distributed random variables again follows a Poisson distribution.

{theoremHigh}
[Sum of Independently Distributed Poisson]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{P}(\lambda_{i})
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
. Then
{\textnormal{y}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{P}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i})
.

For simplicity, we consider two independent Poisson random variables
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{P}(\lambda_{1})
and
{\textnormal{y}}\sim\mathcal{P}(\lambda_{2})
.
Define
\lambda\triangleq\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}
and
{\textnormal{z}}\triangleq{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}
. Then
z
is a Poisson random variable with parameter
\lambda
. To see this, we have

\displaystyle p(z)

\displaystyle=P({\textnormal{z}}=z)=\sum_{k=1}^{z}P({\textnormal{x}}=k)\cdot P({\textnormal{y}}=z-k)=\sum_{k=1}^{z}\frac{\lambda_{1}^{k}}{k!}\exp(-\lambda_{1})\cdot\frac{\lambda_{2}^{z-k}}{(z-k)!}\exp(-\lambda_{2})

\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(-\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2})}{z!}\sum_{k=1}^{z}{z\choose k}\lambda_{1}^{k}\lambda_{2}^{z-k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\frac{\exp(-\lambda)}{z!}(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2})^{z}=\frac{\lambda^{z}}{z!}\exp(-\lambda),

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the
binomial theorem
.
Working for general, once we know the sum of two Poisson random variables, we can keep adding more and more of them to obtain another Poisson variable.

{theoremHigh}

[Poisson and Multinomial]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{P}(\lambda_{i})
be independent for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,K\}
. Then the conditional distribution of
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{k}]^{\top}
given
\sum_{i=1}^{K}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}=N
is
\mathrm{Multi}_{K}(N,\{p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{K}\})
with

p_{i}=\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\ldots+\lambda_{K}},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{for all }i\in\{1,2,\ldots,K\}.

1.5.2
Common Multivariate Probability Distributions

In this section, we further provide common multivariate probability distributions.

Multivariate Gaussian Distribution

A
multivariate Gaussian distribution
(also referred to as a
multivariate normal distribution
or simply Gaussian distribution) is a continuous probability distribution characterized by a jointly normal distribution across multiple variables.
It is fully described by its mean vector (of size equal to the number of variables) and covariance matrix (a square matrix of size equal to the number of variables).
The covariance matrix encodes the pairwise relationships between variables in terms of the covariance between them.
Widely applied in diverse domains like machine learning, statistics, and signal processing, the multivariate Gaussian proves (or simply called Gaussian when it’s clear from the context) instrumental in modeling complex data distributions.
We first present the rigorous definition of the multivariate Gaussian distribution as follows.

Definition 51
(Multivariate Gaussian distribution).

A random vector
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{D}
is said to follow the multivariate Gaussian distribution (multivariate normal, MVN) with parameters
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\real^{D}
and
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{D\times D}
, denoted by
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
, if

\displaystyle f(\bm{x};\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})

\displaystyle=(2\pi)^{-D/2}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{-1/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right\},\penalty\

where
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\real^{D}
is called the mean vector, and
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{D\times D}
is positive definite and is called the covariance matrix.
\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert=\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
is the determinant of the matrix
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
.
The mean, mode, and covariance of the multivariate Gaussian distribution are given by

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\mu},\qquad\mathrm{Mode}[{\mathbf{x}}]=\boldsymbol{\mu},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}.

The covariance matrix can be obtained by

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}]-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}.

Figure
compares Gaussian density plots for different kinds of covariance matrices.
The multivariate Gaussian variable can be drawn from a univariate Gaussian density; see Problem
.

(a)

Gaussian,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}.

(b)

Gaussian,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&3\end{bmatrix}.

(c)

Gaussian,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&\textendash 0.5\\
\textendash 0.5&1.5\end{bmatrix}.

(d)

Gaussian,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\
0&2\end{bmatrix}.

(e)

Gaussian,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}.

(f)

Gaussian,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}3&\textendash 0.5\\
\textendash 0.5&1.5\end{bmatrix}.

Figure 1.9:
Density and contour plots (
blue
=low,
yellow
=high) for the multivariate Gaussian distribution over the
\mathbb{R}^{2}
space for various values of the covariance/scale matrix with a zero-mean vector. Fig
and
: A spherical covariance matrix has a circular shape;
Fig
and
: A diagonal covariance matrix is an
axis aligned
ellipse;
Fig
and
: A full covariance matrix has an elliptical shape.

Similar to the likelihood under univariate Gaussian distribution (Equation (
)), especially in deriving the conjugate Bayesian result,
the likelihood of
N
random observations
\mathcal{X}=\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{N}\}
generated by a multivariate Gaussian with mean vector
\boldsymbol{\mu}
and covariance matrix
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is given by

\displaystyle p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\prod^{N}_{n=1}\mathcal{N}(\bm{x}_{n}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})

(1.18)

\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=}(2\pi)^{-ND/2}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{-N/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\sum^{N}_{n=1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right\}

\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{=}(2\pi)^{-ND/2}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{-N/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{S}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\right\}

\displaystyle\overset{(c)}{=}(2\pi)^{-ND/2}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{-N/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{N}{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\overline{\bm{x}})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\overline{\bm{x}})\right\}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{S}_{\overline{x}})\right\},

where

\bm{S}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\triangleq\sum^{N}_{n=1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\bm{x}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top},\quad\bm{S}_{\overline{x}}\triangleq\sum^{N}_{n=1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\overline{\bm{x}})(\bm{x}_{n}-\overline{\bm{x}})^{\top},\quad\overline{\bm{x}}\triangleq\frac{1}{N}\sum^{N}_{n=1}\bm{x}_{n}.

(1.19)

The matrix
\bm{S}_{\overline{x}}
is the
matrix of sum of squares
and is also known as the
scatter matrix
.
The equivalence between equation (a) and equation (c) follows from the following identity (similar reasoning applies to the equivalence between equation (a) and equation (b)):

\displaystyle\sum^{N}_{n=1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})=\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{S}_{\overline{x}})+N\cdot(\overline{\bm{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\overline{\bm{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}),

(1.20)

where the trace of a square matrix
\bm{A}
is defined to be the sum of the diagonal elements
a_{ii}
of
\bm{A}
:
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A})=\sum_{i}a_{ii}
.

Proof
[Proof of Identity
1.20
]
There is a “trick” involving the trace that makes such calculations easy (see also Chapter 3 of
Gentle 2007
):

\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{x}=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{x})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{x}\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{A})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\bm{x}\bm{x}^{\top}),

(1.21)

where the first equality follows from the fact that
\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{x}
is a scalar and the trace of a product is invariant under cyclical permutations of the factors.

We can then rewrite
\sum^{N}_{n=1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})
as

\displaystyle\sum^{N}_{n=1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\overline{\bm{x}})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\bm{x}_{n}-\overline{\bm{x}})+\sum^{N}_{n=1}(\overline{\bm{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\overline{\bm{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})

(1.22)

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{S}_{\overline{x}})+N\cdot(\overline{\bm{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\overline{\bm{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}).

This concludes the proof.

Given fixed mean
\boldsymbol{\mu}
and covariance
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
parameters, we have

\displaystyle p(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})

\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\propto\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\bm{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{x}+\bm{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}\right\}.

(1.23)

Properties of Multivariate Gaussian Distribution

The entropy of Gaussians (measured in natural units) is discussed in Problem
.
The affine transformation, rotation, independence of linear combinations of multivariate Gaussian distribution also follows the multivariate Gaussian distribution.

Lemma 52
(Affine transformation of multivariate Gaussian distribution).

Given fixed matrices and vector,
\bm{A},\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times d}
and
\bm{c}\in\real^{p}
,
let
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x})
and
{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{y})
be independent variables (of length
d
).
Then,

{\mathbf{z}}=\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}+\bm{B}{\mathbf{y}}+\bm{c}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}+\bm{B}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}+\bm{c},\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x}\bm{A}^{\top}+\bm{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{y}\bm{B}^{\top}).

Given further
\bm{d}\in\real^{d}
, then
\bm{d}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}
follows from a univariate Gaussian:

\bm{d}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x},\bm{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x}\bm{d}).

The result can be proved using the moment generating function of multivariate Gaussian distributions.
The result also relies on the
sum of independent Gaussians
:

\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}\big(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i},\sum_{i=1}^{n}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}\big)\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{if }{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}),\ \forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.

Moreover, let
\bm{A}=\bm{e}_{i}^{\top}
be a unit basis vector, then
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}=\bm{e}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{x,i},\sigma_{x,ii}^{2})
, where
\mu_{x,i}
represents the
i
-th component of
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}
and
\sigma_{x,ii}^{2}
denotes the
i
-th diagonal of
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x}
.

Lemma 53
(Rotations on multivariate Gaussian distribution).

Rotations on the Gaussian distribution do not affect the distribution.
That is, for any orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}
with
\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{Q}=\bm{I}
, if
{\mathbf{v}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
, then
\bm{Q}{\mathbf{v}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
.

Lemma 54
(Independence of linear combinations in Gaussian Distributions).

Suppose
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\in\real^{p}
, and let
\bm{A}\in\real^{m\times p}
,
\bm{B}\in\real^{d\times p}
be real matrices. Then,

\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}

is independent of

\bm{B}{\mathbf{x}}

\quad\iff\quad

\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{B}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

(1.24)

The proof again relies on the moment generating function of Gaussian distributions and we shall not provide the details.

\paragrapharrow

“Standardization and decorrelation.”
The distribution
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{I})
is called the
standard multivariate Gaussian distribution
.
Given
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
, then the
decorrelation
of
{\mathbf{x}}
follows that

{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\quad\implies\quad{\mathbf{z}}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{I}).

(1.25)

This also shows that if
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
, then

{\mathbf{x}}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{where }\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{I}).

(1.26)

Suppose
\{\bm{x}_{i},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
are
n
random samples of
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
and let
\overline{\bm{x}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}
. Then, it follows that

\sqrt{n}(\overline{\bm{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}).

(1.27)

\paragrapharrow

Partition of Gaussian.
Let
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
where
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\real^{p}
. Consider the partition of
{\mathbf{x}}

\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\\
{\mathbf{x}}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}&\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\right).

Then
{\mathbf{x}}_{1}
and
{\mathbf{x}}_{2}
are independent if and only if
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Furthermore, Let
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{p}]^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
. Then,

the
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
’s are mutually independent if and only if
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is diagonal.

(1.28)

Rigorously, this can be proved as follows:

Proof
[of Equation (
)]
Suppose that the
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
’s are independent. The property below Lemma
yields
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2})
for some
\sigma_{i}>0
. Thus the density of
{\mathbf{x}}
is

\displaystyle p_{{\mathbf{x}}}(\bm{x})\

\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}p_{{\textnormal{x}}_{i}}(x_{i})=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x_{i}-\mu_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right\}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}\left\lvert\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2})\right\rvert^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{-2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{-2})(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right\}.

Hence
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2}))
, i.e., the covariance
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is diagonal.

Conversely, assume
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is diagonal, say
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2})
. Then we can reverse the steps of the first part to see that the joint density
p_{{\mathbf{x}}}(\bm{x})
can be written as a product of the marginal densities
p_{{\textnormal{x}}_{i}}(x_{i})
, thus proving independence.

It also follows that functions of independent vectors should also be independent. That is, it should be that
g_{1}({\mathbf{x}}_{1})
and
g_{2}({\mathbf{x}}_{2})
are independent for all
g_{1},g_{2}
.
Suppose that
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
is i.i.d.
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
. Then, we can define a vector populated by
\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}
and
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}
:

\begin{bmatrix}\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\\
\vdots\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{p}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{p}&\frac{1}{p}&\ldots&\frac{1}{p}\\
&\bm{I}_{p}-\frac{1}{p}\bm{J}_{p}&\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\\
\vdots\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{p}\end{bmatrix}\qquad\text{where}\qquad\bm{J}_{p}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&\cdots&1\\
1&\ddots&&1\\
1&&\ddots&\vdots\\
1&1&\cdots&1\end{bmatrix}\in\real^{p\times p}.

It then follows that

\begin{bmatrix}\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\\
\vdots\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{p}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}\mu\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0\end{bmatrix},\sigma^{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{p}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{I}_{p}-\frac{1}{p}\bm{J}_{p}\end{bmatrix}\right).

Therefore, we find that
\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}
is independent of
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{p}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}
.
In many applications, we may construct a random variable:

t\triangleq\sqrt{p}\frac{(\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}-\mu)/\sigma}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{p-1}\sum(y_{i}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}})^{2}/\sigma^{2}}},

in which case, the numerator and the denominator are independent variables.

\paragrapharrow

Quadratic of Gaussian.
The definition of the Chi-squared distribution (Definition
) shows

\sum_{i=1}^{p}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}\sim\chi^{2}(p),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{if }{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

Therefore, we also have

{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\implies{\mathbf{z}}=({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\sim\chi^{2}(p),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{where }{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{p}.

(1.29)

We may also be interested in the quadratic form of
{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}
where
\bm{A}
is symmetric. We provide some important results below.

{theoremHigh}
[Quadratic of Gaussians]
We have the following results with quadratic forms of Gaussians:

Given
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\lambda\bm{I})
(of length
p
) and symmetric matrix
\bm{A}\in\real^{p\times p}
. Then, it follows that

\frac{{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}}{\lambda}\sim\chi^{2}_{(n)},

if and only if
\bm{A}
(
\bm{A}^{2}=\bm{A}
) is idempotent with rank
n<p
.

Given
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
(of length
p
) and symmetric matrix
\bm{A}\in\real^{p\times p}
. Then, it follows that

{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}\sim\chi^{2}_{(n)},

if and only if
\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is idempotent with rank
n<p
.

\paragrapharrow

Marginal and conditional distributions.
Let
{\mathbf{x}}
and
{\mathbf{y}}
be jointly Gaussian random vectors with

{\mathbf{z}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{x}}\\
{\mathbf{y}}\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}\\
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\bm{A}&\bm{C}\\
\bm{C}^{\top}&\bm{B}\end{bmatrix}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}\\
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\bm{A}}&\widetilde{\bm{C}}\\
\widetilde{\bm{C}}^{\top}&\widetilde{\bm{B}}\end{bmatrix}^{-1}\right).\penalty\

where
{\mathbf{x}}
and
{\mathbf{y}}
are
independent
if and only if
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}}]=\bm{C}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Then every marginal distribution of a multivariate Gaussian distribution is itself a multivariate Gaussian distribution, and the conditional distribution
{\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{y}}
also follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution:

\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x},\bm{A}),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{y}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}+\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}),\bm{A}-\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top})

(1.31)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}-\widetilde{\bm{A}}^{-1}\widetilde{\bm{C}}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}),\widetilde{\bm{A}}^{-1});

\displaystyle{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y},\bm{B}),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{\mathbf{y}}\mid{\mathbf{x}}=\bm{x}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}+\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}),\bm{B}-\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{C})

\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}-\widetilde{\bm{B}}^{-1}\widetilde{\bm{C}}^{\top}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}),\widetilde{\bm{B}}^{-1}).

Proof
[Short proof]
Suppose
{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}={\mathbf{x}}-\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}
. Then

{\mathbf{z}}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}\\
{\mathbf{y}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}&-\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{I}\end{bmatrix}{\mathbf{z}}.

Using Lemma
, we can show that
{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}
and
{\mathbf{y}}
are independent.
Then, the conditional distribution of
{\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{y}}
can be obtained by
{\mathbf{x}}={\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}+\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}{\mathbf{y}}
and following the distribution law.
The second part can be proved similarly.

This relationship is useful for finding Gaussian-related distributions. See the exercise below.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Affine dependence of Gaussian variables)

Suppose random vectors
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
and
{\mathbf{y}}\mid{\mathbf{x}}=\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{A}\bm{x}+\bm{b},\bm{M})
.
Note
{\mathbf{y}}
is not simply the affine transformation
\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}+\bm{b}
, but it follows that
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{A}\bm{x}+\bm{b}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{M})
.
Show that

{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\bm{b},\bm{M}+\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{A}^{\top}),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}\big(\bm{L}\big\{\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{M}^{-1}({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{b})+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}\big\},\bm{L}\big),

where
\bm{L}=(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}+\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{M}^{-1}\bm{A})^{-1}
.

Hint: compute the cross-covariance of
{\mathbf{x}}
and
{\mathbf{y}}
by
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}}]=\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x})({\mathbf{y}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y})^{\top}]=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{A}^{\top}
where
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}=\boldsymbol{\mu}
and
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{y}}]=\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\bm{b}
, and use Woodbury matrix identity:
(\bm{A}+\bm{B}\bm{D}\bm{C})^{-1}=\bm{A}^{-1}-\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{B}(\bm{D}^{-1}+\bm{C}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{B})^{-1}\bm{C}\bm{A}^{-1}
for appropriate matrices
\bm{A},\bm{B},\bm{C}
, and
\bm{D}
; see, for example,
Lu 2021b
.

\paragrapharrow

Product of Gaussians.
The product of two Gaussians also follows a Gaussian distribution (although no longer normalized)
(
Ahrendt 2005
)
.
Given two Gaussians
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{a})
and
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{b})
(both of length
p
), it follows that

\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{a})\cdot\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{b})\propto z_{c}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}),

(1.32)

where

\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}=(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{a}^{-1}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{b}^{-1})^{-1},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{and}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{a}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{b}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b}).

That is, the resulting precision matrix is the sum of precision matrices of the two components.
And
z_{c}
is a normalization constant

\displaystyle z_{c}=\left\lvert 2\pi\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{a}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{b}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}^{-1}\right\rvert^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{a}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{b}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{b})\right\}.

Multivariate Student’s
t
Distribution

The multivariate Student’s
t
-distribution is a continuous probability distribution over multiple variables that generalizes the Gaussian distribution to allow for heavier tails,
i.e., the probability of extreme values is higher than that in a Gaussian distribution.
The multivariate Student’s
t
distribution (simply called Student’s
t
distribution when it’s clear from the context) will be often used in the posterior predictive distribution of multivariate Gaussian parameters. We rigorously define the distribution as follows.

Definition 55
(Multivariate Student’s
t
distribution).

A random vector
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{D}
is said to follow the multivariate Student’s
t
distribution with parameters
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\real^{D}
,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{D\times D}
, and
\nu
, denoted by
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\nu)
, if

\displaystyle f(\bm{x};\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\nu)

\displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(\nu/2+D/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)}\frac{\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{-1/2}}{\nu^{D/2}\pi^{D/2}}\times\left[1+\frac{1}{\nu}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right]^{-(\frac{\nu+D}{2})}

\displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(\nu/2+D/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)}|\pi\bm{V}|^{-1/2}\times\left[1+\frac{1}{\nu}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\bm{V}^{-1}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right]^{-(\frac{\nu+D}{2})},

where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is called the scale matrix and
\bm{V}=\nu\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
, and
\nu
is the degree of freedom. This distribution has fatter tails than a Gaussian one. The smaller the
\nu
is, the fatter the tails. As
\nu\rightarrow\infty
, the distribution converges towards a multivariate Gaussian.
The mean, mode, and covariance of the multivariate Student’s
t
distribution are given by

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\bm{x}]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\mu},\qquad\mathrm{Mode}[\bm{x}]=\boldsymbol{\mu},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\bm{x}]=\frac{\nu}{\nu-2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}.

Note that the
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is called the scale matrix since it is not exactly the covariance matrix as that in a multivariate Gaussian distribution.

Specifically, When
D=1
, it follows that

\displaystyle\tau(x\mid\mu,\sigma^{2},\nu)

\displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(\frac{\nu+1}{2})}{\Gamma(\frac{\nu}{2})}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{\nu\pi}}\times\left[1+\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{\nu\sigma^{2}}\right]^{-(\frac{\nu+1}{2})}.

(1.33)

When
D=1,\boldsymbol{\mu}=0,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=1
, then the p.d.f. defines the univariate
t
distribution.

\displaystyle\tau(x\mid\nu)

\displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(\frac{\nu+1}{2})}{\Gamma(\frac{\nu}{2})}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu\pi}}\times\left[1+\frac{x^{2}}{\nu}\right]^{-(\frac{\nu+1}{2})}.

Figure
compares the Gaussian and the Student’s
t
distribution for various values such that when
\nu\rightarrow\infty
, the difference between the densities is approaching zero. Given the same parameters in the densities, the Student’s
t
in general has longer “tails” than a Gaussian, which can be seen from the comparison between Figure
and Figure
.
This provides the Student’s
t
distribution an important property known as
robustness
, which means that it is much less sensitive than the Gaussian in the presence of outliers
(
Bishop 2006
;
Murphy 2012
)
.

\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\

(b)

Gaussian,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\

(c)

Gaussian,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&\textendash 0.5\\
\textendash 0.5&1.5\end{bmatrix}.

(d)

Student
t
,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\

t
,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&1\end{bmatrix},\nu=3.

Stu
t
,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\

Density and contour plots (
blue
=low,
yellow
=high) for the multivariate Gaussian distribution and multivariate Student’s
t
distribution over the
\mathbb{R}^{2}
space for various values of the covariance/scale matrix with zero-mean vector.

\nu
such that the difference between (a) and (f) in Fig

A Student’s
t
distribution can be written as a
Gaussian scale mixture

\tau(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\nu)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathcal{N}(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/z)\cdot\mathcal{G}\big(z\mid\frac{\nu}{2},\frac{\nu}{2}\big)dz.

(1.34)

This can be thought of as an “infinite” mixture of Gaussians, each with a slightly different covariance matrix. In other words, a Student’s
t
distribution is obtained by adding up an
infinite number of Gaussian distributions having the same mean vector but different covariance matrices.
From this Gaussian scale mixture view, when
\nu\rightarrow\infty
, the Gamma distribution becomes a degenerate random variable with all the nonzero mass at the point unity such that the multivariate Student’s
t
distribution converges to a multivariate Gaussian distribution.

\paragrapharrow

Affine transformations of Student’s
t
.
Similar to the multivariate Gaussian distribution, the affine transformation of a Student’s
t
also follows another Student’s
t
.
Suppose
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\nu)
(of length
D
) and given a fixed matrix
\bm{A}\in\real^{P\times D}
and a fixed vector
\bm{b}\in\real^{P}
. Then it follows that

\bm{A}{\mathbf{x}}\sim\tau(\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\bm{b},\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{A}^{\top},\nu).

(1.35)

Therefore, we can sample
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\nu)
by sampling
{\mathbf{y}}\sim\tau(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{I},\nu)
and letting
{\mathbf{x}}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\bm{L}{\mathbf{y}}
, where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}
is the Cholesky decomposition of
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
(Theorem
).

\paragrapharrow

Marginal and conditional distributions of Student’s
t
.
Similar to the multivariate Gaussian distribution, let
{\mathbf{x}}
and
{\mathbf{y}}
be jointly Student’s
t
random vectors with

{\mathbf{z}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{x}}\\
{\mathbf{y}}\end{bmatrix}\sim\tau\left(\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}\\
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\bm{A}&\bm{C}\\
\bm{C}^{\top}&\bm{B}\end{bmatrix},\nu\right)=\tau\left(\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}\\
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\bm{A}}&\widetilde{\bm{C}}\\
\widetilde{\bm{C}}^{\top}&\widetilde{\bm{B}}\end{bmatrix}^{-1},\nu\right),

where
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{d_{x}}
and
{\mathbf{y}}\in\real^{d_{y}}
.
Then every marginal distribution of a Student’s
t
distribution is itself a Student’s
t
distribution, and the conditional distribution
{\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{y}}
also follows a Student’s
t
distribution:

\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}\sim\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x},\bm{A},\nu),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{y}

\displaystyle\sim\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}+\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}),m_{x}(\bm{A}-\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}),\nu+d_{x})

(1.36)

\displaystyle=\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}-\widetilde{\bm{A}}^{-1}\widetilde{\bm{C}}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}),m_{x}\widetilde{\bm{A}}^{-1},\nu+d_{x});

\displaystyle{\mathbf{y}}\sim\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y},\bm{B},\nu),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{\mathbf{y}}\mid{\mathbf{x}}=\bm{x}

\displaystyle\sim\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}+\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}),m_{y}(\bm{B}-\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{C}),\nu+d_{y})

\displaystyle=\tau(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}-\widetilde{\bm{B}}^{-1}\widetilde{\bm{C}}^{\top}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x}),m_{y}\widetilde{\bm{B}}^{-1},\nu+d_{y}),

where

\displaystyle m_{x}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\nu+d_{y}}\left[\nu+(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y})^{\top}\bm{B}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y})\right];

\displaystyle m_{y}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\nu+d_{x}}\left[\nu+(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x})^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}(\bm{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x})\right].

Wishart Distribution and Variants

A generalization to the inverse-Gamma distribution (Definition
) is the
inverse-Wishart
distribution, serving as a conjugate prior for the full covariance matrix of a multivariate Gaussian distribution.
That is, the inverse-Wishart distribution is a probability distribution of random positive definite matrices that can be used to model random covariance matrices.

Before delving into the topic of the inverse-Wishart distribution, it’s important to note that it originates from the Wishart distribution, a multidimensional generalization of the Gamma distribution. As stated by
Anderson 2003
in 1962, “
The Wishart distribution ranks next to the (multivariate) normal distribution in order of importance and usefulness in multivariate statistics.
”

Definition 56
(Wishart distribution).

A random symmetric positive definite matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\real^{D\times D}
is said to follow the Wishart distribution with parameter
\bm{M}\in\real^{D\times D}
and
\nu
, denoted by
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu)
, if

\displaystyle f(\boldsymbol{\Lambda};{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{M}},\nu)

\displaystyle=\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\right\rvert^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\frac{\nu-D-1}{2}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{M}^{-1}})\right\}\left[2^{\frac{\nu D}{2}}\pi^{D(D-1)/4}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}|\bm{M}|^{\nu/2}}\prod_{d=1}^{D}\Gamma\big(\frac{\nu+1-d}{2}\big)\right]^{-1},

where
\nu\geq D
and
\bm{M}
is a
D\times D
symmetric positive definite matrix, and
\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\right\rvert=\det(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})
is the determinant of matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
.
The parameter
\nu
is called the number of degrees of freedom, and
\bm{M}
is called the scale matrix.
The mean and variance of the Wishart distribution are given by

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\Lambda}]

\displaystyle=\nu\bm{M}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\lambda_{ij}]=\nu(m_{ij}^{2}+m_{ii}m_{jj}),

where
m_{ij}
is the (
i,j
)-th element of
\bm{M}
.
It can be shown that when
\nu\rightarrow\infty
, then
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}/\nu
converges in probability to
\bm{M}
(using law of large numbers and the Cramér-Wold device).

When
D=1
and
\bm{M}=1
, the Wishart distribution reduces to the Chi-squared distribution (Definition
) such that:

\mathrm{Wi}(x\mid 1,\nu)=\chi^{2}(x\mid\nu).

An interpretation of the Wishart distribution is as follows. Suppose we independently sample vectors
\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{z}_{\nu}\in\real^{D}
from
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{M})
. The sum of squares matrix of the collection of multivariate vectors is given by

\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\bm{z}_{i}\bm{z}_{i}^{\top}=\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z},

where
\bm{Z}
is the
\nu\times D
matrix with
i
-th row being
\bm{z}_{i}
. It is evident that
\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z}
is positive semidefinite (PSD) and symmetric. If
\nu>D
and the
\bm{z}_{i}
’s are linearly independent, then
\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z}
will be positive definite (PD) and symmetric.
In other words,
\bm{Z}\bm{x}=\boldsymbol{0}
only happens when
\bm{x}=\boldsymbol{0}
. We can repeat over and over again, generating matrices
\bm{Z}_{1}^{\top}\bm{Z}_{1},\bm{Z}_{2}^{\top}\bm{Z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{Z}_{l}^{\top}\bm{Z}_{l}
. The population distribution of these matrices follows a Wishart distribution with parameters
(\bm{M},\nu)
. By definition,

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Lambda}

\displaystyle=\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z}=\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\bm{z}_{i}\bm{z}_{i}^{\top}\qquad\implies\qquad\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\Lambda}]=\mathbb{E}[\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z}]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\bm{z}_{i}\bm{z}_{i}^{\top}\right]=\nu\mathbb{E}[\bm{z}_{i}\bm{z}_{i}^{\top}]=\nu\bm{M}.

When
D=1
, this reduces to the case that if
z
is drawn from a zero-mean univariate normal random variable, then
z^{2}
is drawn from a Gamma random variable. To be specific,

\mathrm{suppose}\qquad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,a),\qquad\mathrm{then}\qquad z^{2}\sim\mathcal{G}(a/2,1/2).

Remark 57
(Properties of Wishart distribution).

We present several properties of the Wishart distribution without providing their proofs:

“Decorrelation.” Suppose
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu)
with
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\real^{D\times D}
.
Then, it follows that
\bm{M}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{M}^{-1/2}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\nu,\bm{I}_{D})
.

Quadratic transformation. Suppose
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu)
with
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\real^{D\times D}
and
\bm{A}\in\real^{P\times D}
.
Then, it follows that
\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{A}^{\top}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{A}\bm{M}\bm{A}^{\top},\nu)
.

Suppose
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu)
with
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\real^{D\times D}
,
\bm{a}\in\real^{D}
, and
\nu>D-1
.
Then, it follows that
\frac{\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{M}^{-1}\bm{a}}{\bm{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\bm{a}}\sim\chi^{2}_{(\nu-D-1)}
.

Suppose
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu)
with
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\real^{D\times D}
and
\bm{a}\in\real^{D}
.
Then, it follows that
\frac{\bm{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{a}}{\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{M}\bm{a}}\sim\chi^{2}_{(\nu)}
.

Sum of independent Wisharts
. Given independent random matrices
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{i}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu_{i})
with
\nu=\sum_{i}\nu_{i}
.
Then, it follows that
\sum_{i}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{i}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu)
.

Sum of independent Wisharts
. Similarly, given independent random matrices
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu)
and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{1}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu_{1})
.
Then, it follows that
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{2}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{1}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu-\nu_{1})
.

“Standardization”. Suppose
\{\bm{x}_{i},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
are random samples of
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
, let
\overline{\bm{x}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}
and
\bm{S}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\bm{x}_{i}-\overline{\bm{x}})(\bm{x}_{i}-\overline{\bm{x}})^{\top}
.
Then, it follows that
(n-1)\bm{S}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma},n-1)
. And it can be shown that
\overline{\bm{x}}
and
\bm{S}
are independent (the distribution of
\overline{\bm{x}}
is shown in (
)).

Just like the relationship between the inverse-Gamma distribution and the Gamma distribution that if
x\sim\mathcal{G}(r,\lambda)
, then
y=\frac{1}{x}\sim\mathcal{G}^{-1}(r,\lambda)
. There is a similar connection between the inverse-Wishart distribution and the Wishart distribution.

Since we often use the inverse-Wishart (IW) distribution as a prior distribution for a covariance matrix, it is often useful to replace
\bm{M}
in the Wishart distribution with
\bm{S}=\bm{M}^{-1}
. This results in that
a random
D\times D
symmetric positive definite matrix
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
follows an inverse-Wishart
\mathrm{IW}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mid\bm{S},\nu)
distribution if
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
follows a Wishart
\mathrm{Wi}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mid\bm{M},\nu)
distribution.

Definition 58
(Inverse-Wishart distribution).

A random symmetric positive definite matrix
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{D\times D}
is said to follow the inverse-Wishart distribution with parameters
\bm{S}\in\real^{D\times D}
and
\nu
, denoted by
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\sim\mathrm{IW}(\bm{S},\nu)
, if

\displaystyle f(\boldsymbol{\Sigma};{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}\bm{S}},\nu)=\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}-\frac{\nu+D+1}{2}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}({\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}\bm{S}})\right\}\times\left[2^{\frac{\nu D}{2}}\pi^{D(D-1)/4}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}|\bm{S}|^{-\nu/2}}\prod_{d=1}^{D}\Gamma\big(\frac{\nu+1-d}{2}\big)\right]^{-1},

where
\nu\geq D
,
\bm{S}
is a
D\times D
symmetric positive definite matrix, and
\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert=\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
.
The parameter
\nu
is called the number of degrees of freedom, and
\bm{S}
is called the scale matrix.
The mean and mode of the inverse-Wishart distribution are given by

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}]

\displaystyle=\nu\bm{S}^{-1}=\nu\bm{M},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}]=\frac{1}{\nu-D-1}\bm{S},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathrm{Mode}[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}]=\frac{1}{\nu+D+1}\bm{S}.

Note that, sometimes, we replace
\bm{S}
by
\bm{M}=\bm{S}^{-1}
such that
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}]=\nu\bm{M}
, which does not involve the inverse of the matrix.

When
D=1
, the inverse-Wishart distribution reduces to the inverse-Gamma such that
\frac{\nu}{2}=r
and
\frac{S}{2}=\lambda
(see Definition
):

\mathrm{IW}(y\mid S,\nu)=\mathcal{G}^{-1}(y\mid r,\lambda).

Note that the Wishart density is not simply the inverse-Wishart density with

\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
replaced by
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}
. There is an additional factor of
\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{-(D+1)}
. See Theorem 7.7.1 in
Anderson 2003
that the Jacobian of the transformation
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}
is
\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{-(D+1)}
. Substitution of
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}
in the definition of the Wishart distribution and multiplying by
\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right\rvert^{-(D+1)}
can yield the inverse-Wishart distribution.

Example 59
(Wishart and inverse-Wishart).

Consider a random matrix
{\mathbf{G}}\in\real^{\nu\times m}
, each row of which is drawn independently from the distribution
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{M})
, where
\bm{M}\in\real^{m\times m}
is symmetric positive definite.
Then, as mentioned above, the probability distribution of the
m\times m
random matrix
{\mathbf{G}}^{\top}{\mathbf{G}}
is called the Wishart distribution with
\nu
degrees of freedom, denoted as
\mathrm{Wi}(\bm{M},\nu)
. Moreover, the distribution of the matrix
({\mathbf{G}}^{\top}{\mathbf{G}})^{-1}
is called the inverse Wishart distribution and is denoted by
\mathrm{IW}(\bm{M}^{-1},\nu)
.

Now suppose that
{\mathbf{G}}\in\real^{\nu\times m}
, each entry
{\textnormal{g}}_{ij}
of which is drawn independently from
\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{m})
. Then, the matrix
{\mathbf{G}}^{\top}{\mathbf{G}}
follows the Wishart distribution
\mathrm{Wi}(\frac{1}{m}\bm{I}_{m},\nu)
that satisfies:

\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{tr}({\mathbf{G}}^{\top}{\mathbf{G}})^{-1}\right]=\frac{m^{2}}{\nu-m-1},

(1.37)

since
({\mathbf{G}}^{\top}{\mathbf{G}})^{-1}\sim\mathrm{IW}(m\bm{I}_{m},\nu)
.

1.6
Matrix Decomposition

This section introduces several matrix decomposition methods, which can be instrumental in proving theories related to linear models or least squares models.

1.6.1
Cholesky Decomposition

Positive definiteness or positive semidefiniteness (Definition
) is one of the most desirable properties a matrix can have. In this section, we introduce decomposition techniques for positive definite matrices, with a focus on the well-known
Cholesky decomposition
.
The Cholesky decomposition is named after a French military officer and mathematician, André-Louis Cholesky (1875–1918), who developed this method in his surveying work. It is primarily used to solve linear systems involving positive definite matrices.

To establish the existence of the Cholesky decomposition, we rely on the well-known Sylvester’s criterion.

{theoremHigh}
[Sylvester’s criterion]
Let
\bm{A}_{k}=\bm{A}[1:k,1:k]\in\real^{k\times k}
,
k=1,2,\ldots,n
, be the leading principal submatrices of the symmetric matrix
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
. Then
\bm{A}
is positive definite if and only if
\det(\bm{A}_{k})>0
,
k=1,2,\ldots,n
.

The proof can be found, for example, in
Lu 2021b
.

Here, we establish the existence of the Cholesky decomposition using an inductive approach. Alternative proofs also exist, such as those derived from the LU decomposition
(
Lu 2022c
)
.

{theoremHigh}

[Cholesky decomposition]
Every positive definite (PD) matrix
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
can be factored as

\bm{A}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R},

where
\bm{R}\in\real^{n\times n}
is an upper triangular matrix
with positive diagonal elements
. This decomposition is called the
Cholesky decomposition
of
\bm{A}
, and
\bm{R}
is known as the
Cholesky factor
or
Cholesky triangle
of
\bm{A}
.
Specifically, the Cholesky decomposition is unique (Corollary
).

Alternatively,
\bm{A}
can be factored as
\bm{A}=\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}
, where
\bm{L}=\bm{R}^{\top}
is a lower triangular matrix
with positive diagonals
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We will prove by induction that every
n\times n
positive definite matrix
\bm{A}
has a decomposition
\bm{A}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
. The
1\times 1
case is trivial by setting
R\triangleq\sqrt{A}
, so that
A=R^{2}
.

Suppose any
k\times k
PD matrix
\bm{A}_{k}
has a Cholesky decomposition. We must show that any
(k+1)\times(k+1)
PD matrix
\bm{A}_{k+1}
can also be factored as this Cholesky decomposition, then we complete the proof.

For any
(k+1)\times(k+1)
PD matrix
\bm{A}_{k+1}
, write
\bm{A}_{k+1}
as

\bm{A}_{k+1}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{A}_{k}&\bm{b}\\
\bm{b}^{\top}&d\end{bmatrix}.

Since
\bm{A}_{k}
is PD, by the inductive hypothesis, it admits a Cholesky decomposition
\bm{A}_{k}=\bm{R}_{k}^{\top}\bm{R}_{k}
. Define the upper triangular matrix

\bm{R}_{k+1}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{k}&\bm{r}\\
0&s\end{bmatrix}.

Then,

\bm{R}_{k+1}^{\top}\bm{R}_{k+1}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{k}^{\top}\bm{R}_{k}&\bm{R}_{k}^{\top}\bm{r}\\
\bm{r}^{\top}\bm{R}_{k}&\bm{r}^{\top}\bm{r}+s^{2}\end{bmatrix}.

Therefore, if we can prove
\bm{R}_{k+1}^{\top}\bm{R}_{k+1}=\bm{A}_{k+1}
is the Cholesky decomposition of
\bm{A}_{k+1}
(which requires the value
s
to be positive), then we complete the proof. That is, we need to prove

\displaystyle\bm{b}

\displaystyle=\bm{R}_{k}^{\top}\bm{r}\qquad\text{and}\qquad d=\bm{r}^{\top}\bm{r}+s^{2}.

Since
\bm{R}_{k}
is nonsingular, we can solve uniquely for
\bm{r}
and
s
:

\displaystyle\bm{r}

\displaystyle=\bm{R}_{k}^{-\top}\bm{b}\qquad\text{and}\qquad s=\sqrt{d-\bm{r}^{\top}\bm{r}}=\sqrt{d-\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{A}_{k}^{-1}\bm{b}},

where we assume
s
is nonnegative. However, we need to further prove that
s
is not only nonnegative, but also positive. Since
\bm{A}_{k}
is PD, from Sylvester’s criterion (Theorem
), and the fact that if matrix
\bm{M}
has a block formulation:
\bm{M}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{A}&\bm{B}\\
\bm{C}&\bm{D}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
, then
\det(\bm{M})=\det(\bm{A})\det(\bm{D}-\bm{C}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{B})
, we have

\det(\bm{A}_{k+1})=\det(\bm{A}_{k})\det(d-\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{A}_{k}^{-1}\bm{b})=\det(\bm{A}_{k})(d-\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{A}_{k}^{-1}\bm{b})>0.

Because
\det(\bm{A}_{k})>0
, we then obtain that
(d-\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{A}_{k}^{-1}\bm{b})>0
, and this implies
s>0
.
This completes the proof.

Corollary 60
(Uniqueness of Cholesky decomposition).

The Cholesky decomposition
\bm{A}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
for any positive definite matrix
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
is unique.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
Suppose the Cholesky decomposition is not unique. Then, there exist two distinct decompositions such that
\bm{A}=\bm{R}_{1}^{\top}\bm{R}_{1}=\bm{R}_{2}^{\top}\bm{R}_{2}
. Rearranging, we obtain

\bm{R}_{1}\bm{R}_{2}^{-1}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}\bm{R}_{2}^{\top}.

Since the inverse of an upper triangular matrix is also upper triangular, and the product of two upper triangular matrices is upper triangular, we conclude that the left-hand side of the above equation is an upper triangular matrix, while the right-hand side is a lower triangular matrix. Consequently,
\bm{R}_{1}\bm{R}_{2}^{-1}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}\bm{R}_{2}^{\top}
must be a diagonal matrix, and
\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}\bm{R}_{2}^{\top}=(\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}\bm{R}_{2}^{\top})^{\top}=\bm{R}_{2}\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}
.
Let
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\triangleq\bm{R}_{1}\bm{R}_{2}^{-1}=\bm{R}_{2}\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}
be the diagonal matrix. We notice that the diagonal value of
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
is the product of the corresponding diagonal values of
\bm{R}_{1}
and
\bm{R}_{2}^{-1}
(or
\bm{R}_{2}
and
\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}
). Explicitly, writing the matrices as

\bm{R}_{1}=\small\begin{bmatrix}r_{11}&r_{12}&\ldots&r_{1n}\\
0&r_{22}&\ldots&r_{2n}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\ldots&r_{nn}\end{bmatrix},\hskip 18.49988pt\normalsize\bm{R}_{2}=\small\begin{bmatrix}s_{11}&s_{12}&\ldots&s_{1n}\\
0&s_{22}&\ldots&s_{2n}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\ldots&s_{nn}\end{bmatrix},

we find that

\displaystyle\bm{R}_{1}\bm{R}_{2}^{-1}=\small\begin{bmatrix}\frac{r_{11}}{s_{11}}&0&\ldots&0\\
0&\frac{r_{22}}{s_{22}}&\ldots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\ldots&\frac{r_{nn}}{s_{nn}}\end{bmatrix}=\small\begin{bmatrix}\frac{s_{11}}{r_{11}}&0&\ldots&0\\
0&\frac{s_{22}}{r_{22}}&\ldots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\ldots&\frac{s_{nn}}{r_{nn}}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize=\bm{R}_{2}\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}.

Since both
\bm{R}_{1}
and
\bm{R}_{2}
have positive diagonals, this implies
r_{11}=s_{11},r_{22}=s_{22},\ldots,r_{nn}=s_{nn}
.
Thus, we conclude that
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\bm{R}_{1}\bm{R}_{2}^{-1}=\bm{R}_{2}\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}=\bm{I}
, which implies
\bm{R}_{1}=\bm{R}_{2}
, contradicting our initial assumption that the decomposition is not unique. Therefore, the Cholesky decomposition is unique.

We now state some useful properties of positive definite matrices. From the Cholesky decomposition follows a well-known characterization.

{theoremHigh}

Let
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
be symmetric, and let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
have full column rank. Then
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{X}
is positive definite. In particular, any principal
p\times p
submatrix

\begin{bmatrix}a_{i_{1}i_{1}}&\ldots&a_{i_{1}i_{p}}\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
a_{i_{p}i_{1}}&\ldots&a_{i_{p}i_{p}}\end{bmatrix}\in\real^{p\times p},\quad 1\leq p<n,

is positive definite. From
p=1
it follows that all diagonal elements in
\bm{A}
are real positive.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Suppose
\bm{A}
is positive definite,
\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq 0
, and
\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
. Then since
\bm{X}
has full column rank, it follows that
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
and

\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\alpha}>0.

The result now follows because any principal submatrix of
\bm{A}
can be written as
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{X}
, where the columns of
\bm{X}
are taken to be the columns
k=i_{j}
,
j=1,2,\ldots,p
, of the identity matrix.

Corollary 61
.

The element of maximum magnitude of a real symmetric positive definite matrix
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
lies on the diagonal.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
From Theorem
and Sylvester’s criterion it follows that

\det\left(\begin{bmatrix}a_{ii}&a_{ij}\\
a_{ij}&a_{jj}\end{bmatrix}\right)=a_{ii}a_{jj}-{a_{ij}}^{2}>0,\quad 1\leq i,j\leq n.

(1.38)

Hence
{a_{ij}}^{2}<a_{ii}a_{jj}\leq\max_{1\leq i\leq n}a_{ii}^{2}
.

1.6.2
CR and Rank Decomposition

The CR decomposition, as introduced in
Strang 2021
;
Strang and Moler 2022
, is presented as follows without a proof; see
Strang and Moler 2022
for more details.

{theoremHigh}
[CR decomposition]
Any rank-
r
matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
admits the following decomposition:

\underset{n\times p}{\bm{X}}=\underset{n\times r}{\bm{C}}\,\,\,\underset{r\times p}{\bm{R}}

where
\bm{C}
contains the first
r
linearly independent columns of
\bm{X}
, and
\bm{R}
is an
r\times p
matrix used to reconstruct the columns of
\bm{X}
from the columns of
\bm{C}
. In particular,
\bm{R}
is the reduced row echelon form (RREF) of
\bm{X}
without the zero rows.

This decomposition leads to a potential reduction or increase in storage requirements, transitioning from
np
floating-point numbers to
r(n+p)
floating-point numbers.

The CR decomposition represents a particular instance of rank decomposition. To provide a rigorous demonstration of the existence of rank decomposition, we present the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[Rank decomposition]
Any rank-
r
matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
admits the following decomposition:

\underset{n\times p}{\bm{X}}=\underset{n\times r}{\bm{D}}\,\,\,\underset{r\times p}{\bm{F}},

where
\bm{D}\in\real^{n\times r}
has rank
r
, and
\bm{F}\in\real^{r\times p}
also has rank
r
, i.e.,
\bm{D}
and
\bm{F}
have full rank
r
.

The storage for the decomposition is then reduced or potentially increased from
np
floating-point numbers to
r(n+p)
floating-point numbers.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By ULV decomposition in Theorem
, we can decompose
\bm{X}
by

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{L}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{V}.

Let
\bm{U}_{0}=\bm{U}_{:,1:r}
and
\bm{V}_{0}=\bm{V}_{1:r,:}
, i.e.,
\bm{U}_{0}
contains only the first
r
columns of
\bm{U}
, and
\bm{V}_{0}
contains only the first
r
rows of
\bm{V}
. Then, we still have
\bm{X}=\bm{U}_{0}\bm{L}\bm{V}_{0}
, where
\bm{U}_{0}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
\bm{V}_{0}\in\real^{r\times p}
. This is also known as the reduced ULV decomposition. Let {
\bm{D}=\bm{U}_{0}\bm{L}
and
\bm{F}=\bm{V}_{0}
}, or {
\bm{D}=\bm{U}_{0}
and
\bm{F}=\bm{L}\bm{V}_{0}
}, we find such rank decompositions.

The rank decomposition is not unique. Even by elementary transformations, we have

\bm{X}=\bm{E}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Z}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{E}_{2},

where
\bm{E}_{1}\in\real^{n\times n},\bm{E}_{2}\in\real^{p\times p}
represent elementary row and column operations, and
\bm{Z}\in\real^{r\times r}
. The transformation is rather general, and there are dozens of these
\bm{E}_{1}
,
\bm{E}_{2}
, and
\bm{Z}
. By similar construction on this decomposition as shown in the proof above, we can recover another rank decomposition.

Similarly, one can obtain matrices
\bm{D}
and
\bm{F}
through methods such as SVD, URV, CR, CUR, and various other decomposition algorithms.
However, we may connect different rank decompositions by the following lemma.

Lemma 62
(Connection between rank decompositions).

For any two rank decompositions of
\bm{X}=\bm{D}_{1}\bm{F}_{1}=\bm{D}_{2}\bm{F}_{2}
, there exists a nonsingular matrix
\bm{P}
such that

\bm{D}_{1}=\bm{D}_{2}\bm{P}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{F}_{1}=\bm{P}^{-1}\bm{F}_{2}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
\bm{D}_{1}\bm{F}_{1}=\bm{D}_{2}\bm{F}_{2}
, we have
\bm{D}_{1}\bm{F}_{1}\bm{F}_{1}^{\top}=\bm{D}_{2}\bm{F}_{2}\bm{F}_{1}^{\top}
. It is evident that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{F}_{1}\bm{F}_{1}^{\top})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{F}_{1})=r
such that
\bm{F}_{1}\bm{F}_{1}^{\top}
is a square matrix with full rank and thus is nonsingular. This implies
\bm{D}_{1}=\bm{D}_{2}\bm{F}_{2}\bm{F}_{1}^{\top}(\bm{F}_{1}\bm{F}_{1}^{\top})^{-1}
. Let
\bm{P}=\bm{F}_{2}\bm{F}_{1}^{\top}(\bm{F}_{1}\bm{F}_{1}^{\top})^{-1}
, we have
\bm{D}_{1}=\bm{D}_{2}\bm{P}
and
\bm{F}_{1}=\bm{P}^{-1}\bm{F}_{2}
.

1.6.3
QR Decomposition

In many applications, we are interested in the column space of a matrix
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]\in\real^{n\times p}
. The successive spaces spanned by the columns
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots
of
\bm{X}
are

\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\bm{x}_{3}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\ldots,

where
\mathcal{C}([\ldots])
is the subspace spanned by the vectors included in the brackets.
Moreover, the notion of orthogonal or orthonormal bases within the column space plays a crucial role in various algorithms, allowing for efficient computations and interpretations.
The idea of QR decomposition involves the construction of a sequence of orthonormal vectors
\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots
that span the same successive subspaces. That is,

\mathcal{C}([\bm{q}_{1}])=\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1}]),\qquad\mathcal{C}([\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}])=\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2}]),\qquad\mathcal{C}([\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\bm{q}_{3}])=\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\bm{x}_{3}]),\ldots.

We illustrate the result of QR decomposition in the following theorem, the proof of which will be discussed in the sequel.

{theoremHigh}
[QR decomposition]
Every
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]
(whether independent or dependent columns) with
n\geq p
admits the following decomposition:

\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R},

where

1.

Reduced
:
\bm{Q}
is
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}n\times p}
with orthonormal columns, and
\bm{R}
is an
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p\times p}
upper triangular matrix, known as the
reduced QR decomposition
;

2.

Full
:
\bm{Q}
is
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}n\times n}
with orthonormal columns, and
\bm{R}
is an
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}n\times p}
upper triangular matrix, known as the
full QR decomposition
.
If we further restrict the upper triangular matrix to be a square matrix, the full QR decomposition can be denoted by

\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},

where
\bm{R}_{0}
is an
p\times p
upper triangular matrix.

Specifically, when
\bm{X}
has full rank, i.e.,
\bm{X}
has linearly independent columns,
\bm{R}
also exhibits linearly independent columns, and
\bm{R}
is nonsingular in the
reduced
case.
This implies that the diagonals of
\bm{R}
are nonzero. Under this condition, when we further restrict that elements on the diagonal of
\bm{R}
to be positive, the
reduced
QR decomposition is
unique
. The
full
QR decomposition is normally not unique since the right-most
(n-p)
columns in
\bm{Q}
can be arranged in any order.

(a)

Reduced QR decomposition.

(b)

Full QR decomposition.

Figure 1.11:
Comparison between the reduced and full QR decompositions. White entries are zero, and
blue
entries are not necessarily zero.
Gray
columns denote silent columns.

If we obtain the reduced QR decomposition, a full QR decomposition of an
n\times p
matrix with linearly independent columns goes further by appending additional
n-p
orthonormal columns to
\bm{Q}
, transforming it into an
n\times n
orthogonal matrix. Simultaneously,
\bm{R}
is augmented with rows of zeros to attain an
n\times p
upper triangular matrix.
We refer to the additional columns in
\bm{Q}
as
silent columns
and the additional rows in
\bm{R}
as
silent rows
.
The difference between the reduced and the full QR decomposition is shown in Figure
, where silent columns in
\bm{Q}
are denoted in gray, blank entries indicate zero elements, and blue entries are elements that are not necessarily zero.

Project a Vector Onto Another Vector

To achieve the QR decomposition, we first discuss how to project a vector onto another vector, based on which the Gram-Schmidt process is employed iteratively.

Projecting a vector
\bm{a}
onto another vector
\bm{b}
involves determining the vector on the line of
\bm{b}
that is closest to
\bm{a}
.
The resulting projection vector, denoted as
\widehat{\bm{a}}
, is a scalar multiple of
\bm{b}
.
Let
\widehat{\bm{a}}=\widehat{x}\bm{b}
, then
\bm{a}-\widehat{\bm{a}}
is perpendicular to
\bm{b}
, as shown in Figure
.
This leads to the following outcome about projecting vector
\bm{a}
onto vector
\bm{b}
:

\bm{a}-\widehat{\bm{a}}
is perpendicular to
\bm{b}
, so
(\bm{a}-\widehat{x}\bm{b})^{\top}\bm{b}=0
:
\widehat{x}
=
\frac{\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{b}}{\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{b}}
and
\widehat{\bm{a}}=\frac{\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{b}}{\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{b}}\bm{b}=\frac{\bm{b}\bm{b}^{\top}}{\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{b}}\bm{a}
.

(a)

Project onto a line.

(b)

Project onto a space.

Figure 1.12:
Project a vector onto a line and onto a space.

Project a Vector Onto a Plane

Projecting a vector
\bm{a}
onto a space spanned by
\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}
involves determining the vector closest to
\bm{a}
within the column space of
[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}]
.
The resulting projection vector, denoted as
\widehat{\bm{a}}
, is expressed as a linear combination of
\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}
:
\widehat{\bm{a}}=\widehat{x}_{1}\bm{b}_{1}+\widehat{x}_{2}\bm{b}_{2}+\ldots+\widehat{x}_{p}\bm{b}_{p}
.
This scenario can be formulated as a least squares problem, wherein the normal equation
\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{B}\widehat{\bm{x}}=\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{a}
is solved, where
\bm{B}=[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}]
and
\widehat{\bm{x}}=[\widehat{x}_{1},\widehat{x}_{2},\ldots,\widehat{x}_{p}]
.
For each vector
\bm{b}_{i}
, the projection of
\bm{a}
in the direction of
\bm{b}_{i}
can be similarly obtained by

\widehat{\bm{a}}_{i}=\frac{\bm{b}_{i}\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}}{\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\bm{b}_{i}}\bm{a},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}.

Let
\widehat{\bm{a}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{\bm{a}}_{i}
, this results in

\bm{a}^{\perp}=(\bm{a}-\widehat{\bm{a}})\perp\mathcal{C}(\bm{B}),

i.e.,
(\bm{a}-\widehat{\bm{a}})
is perpendicular to the column space of
\bm{B}=[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}]
, as shown in Figure
.
See Section
for more details about projection matrices.

Existence of the QR Decomposition via the Gram-Schmidt Process

We proceed by establishing the Gram-Schmidt process through vector projection.
Given three independent vectors
\bm{a}_{1},\bm{a}_{2},\bm{a}_{3}
and the space spanned by the three vectors, denoted as
\mathcal{C}{([\bm{a}_{1},\bm{a}_{2},\bm{a}_{3}])}
, i.e., the column space of matrix
[\bm{a}_{1},\bm{a}_{2},\bm{a}_{3}]
. We intend to construct three orthogonal vectors
\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\bm{b}_{3}
such that
\mathcal{C}{([\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\bm{b}_{3}])}
=
\mathcal{C}{([\bm{a}_{1},\bm{a}_{2},\bm{a}_{3}])}
.
We then normalize these orthogonal vectors by dividing each by its length, resulting in three orthonormal vectors:
\bm{q}_{1}=\frac{\bm{b}_{1}}{\left\lVert\bm{b}_{1}\right\rVert}
,
\bm{q}_{2}=\frac{\bm{b}_{2}}{\left\lVert\bm{b}_{2}\right\rVert}
, and
\bm{q}_{2}=\frac{\bm{b}_{2}}{\left\lVert\bm{b}_{2}\right\rVert}
.

For the first vector, we directly set
\bm{b}_{1}=\bm{a}_{1}
. The second vector,
\bm{b}_{2}
, must be perpendicular to the first.
This is achieved by considering the vector
\bm{a}_{2}
and subtracting its projection along
\bm{b}_{1}
:

\displaystyle\bm{b}_{2}

\displaystyle=\bm{a}_{2}-\frac{\bm{b}_{1}\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}}{\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\bm{b}_{1}}\bm{a}_{2}=(\bm{I}-\frac{\bm{b}_{1}\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}}{\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\bm{b}_{1}})\bm{a}_{2}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{Projection view})

\displaystyle=\bm{a}_{2}-\underbrace{\frac{\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\bm{a}_{2}}{\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\bm{b}_{1}}\bm{b}_{1}}_{\widehat{\bm{a}}_{2}},\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{Combination view})

where the first equation shows that
\bm{b}_{2}
is a multiplication of a matrix and
\bm{a}_{2}
, i.e., project
