\bm{a}_{2}
onto the orthogonal complement space of
\mathcal{C}{([\bm{b}_{1}])}
. The second equation shows that
\bm{a}_{2}
is a linear combination of
\bm{b}_{1}
and
\bm{b}_{2}
.
Clearly, the space spanned by
\bm{b}_{1}
and
\bm{b}_{2}
is the same space spanned by
\bm{a}_{1}
and
\bm{a}_{2}
. The situation is shown in Figure
, in which we choose
the direction of
\bm{b}_{1}
as the
x
-axis in the Cartesian coordinate system
.
\widehat{\bm{a}}_{2}
is the projection of
\bm{a}_{2}
onto the line
\bm{b}_{1}
. It can be clearly shown that the part of
\bm{a}_{2}
perpendicular to
\bm{b}_{1}
is
\bm{b}_{2}=\bm{a}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{a}}_{2}
from the figure.

For the third vector
\bm{b}_{3}
, it must be perpendicular to both the
\bm{b}_{1}
and
\bm{b}_{2}
, which is actually the vector
\bm{a}_{3}
subtracting its projection along the plane spanned by
\bm{b}_{1}
and
\bm{b}_{2}
:

\displaystyle\bm{b}_{3}

\displaystyle=\bm{a}_{3}-\frac{\bm{b}_{1}\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}}{\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\bm{b}_{1}}\bm{a}_{3}-\frac{\bm{b}_{2}\bm{b}_{2}^{\top}}{\bm{b}_{2}^{\top}\bm{b}_{2}}\bm{a}_{3}=(\bm{I}-\frac{\bm{b}_{1}\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}}{\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\bm{b}_{1}}-\frac{\bm{b}_{2}\bm{b}_{2}^{\top}}{\bm{b}_{2}^{\top}\bm{b}_{2}})\bm{a}_{3}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{Projection view})

(1.39)

\displaystyle=\bm{a}_{3}-\underbrace{\frac{\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\bm{a}_{3}}{\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\bm{b}_{1}}\bm{b}_{1}}_{\widehat{\bm{a}}_{3}}-\underbrace{\frac{\bm{b}_{2}^{\top}\bm{a}_{3}}{\bm{b}_{2}^{\top}\bm{b}_{2}}\bm{b}_{2}}_{\bar{\bm{a}}_{3}},\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{Combination view})

where the first equation shows that
\bm{b}_{3}
is a multiplication of a matrix and
\bm{a}_{3}
, i.e., project
\bm{a}_{3}
onto the orthogonal complement space of
\mathcal{C}{([\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2}])}
. The second equation shows that
\bm{a}_{3}
is a linear combination of
\bm{b}_{1}
,
\bm{b}_{2}
, and
\bm{b}_{3}
.
Again, it can be shown that the space spanned by
\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\bm{b}_{3}
is the same space spanned by
\bm{a}_{1},\bm{a}_{2},\bm{a}_{3}
. The situation is shown in Figure
, in which we choose
the direction of
\bm{b}_{2}
as the
y
-axis of the Cartesian coordinate system
.
\widehat{\bm{a}}_{3}
is the projection of
\bm{a}_{3}
onto the line
\bm{b}_{1}
, and
\bar{\bm{a}}_{3}
is the projection of
\bm{a}_{3}
onto the line
\bm{b}_{2}
. It can be shown that the part of
\bm{a}_{3}
perpendicular to both
\bm{b}_{1}
and
\bm{b}_{2}
is
\bm{b}_{3}=\bm{a}_{3}-\widehat{\bm{a}}_{3}-\bar{\bm{a}}_{3}
from the figure.

Finally, we normalize each vector by dividing its length, resulting in three orthonormal vectors:
\bm{q}_{1}=\frac{\bm{b}_{1}}{\left\lVert\bm{b}_{1}\right\rVert}
,
\bm{q}_{2}=\frac{\bm{b}_{2}}{\left\lVert\bm{b}_{2}\right\rVert}
, and
\bm{q}_{2}=\frac{\bm{b}_{2}}{\left\lVert\bm{b}_{2}\right\rVert}
.

(a)

Project
\bm{a}_{2}
onto the space perpendicular to
\bm{b}_{1}
.

(b)

Project
\bm{a}_{3}
onto the space perpendicular to
\bm{b}_{1}
and
\bm{b}_{2}
.

Figure 1.13:
Gram-Schmidt process.

This idea can be extended to a set of vectors rather than only three. And we refer to this process as the
Gram-Schmidt process
. After this process, the matrix
\bm{X}
will be triangularized. The method is named after Jørgen Pedersen Gram and Erhard Schmidt, but it appeared earlier in the work of Pierre-Simon Laplace in the theory of Lie group decomposition.

The Gram–Schmidt process is not the sole algorithm for obtaining the QR decomposition.
There are several other QR decomposition algorithms available, such as
Householder reflections
and
Givens rotations
, which exhibit greater robustness in the presence of round-off errors; see Section
.
These QR decomposition methods may also alter the order in which the columns of
\bm{X}
are processed.

Properties of the QR Decomposition

\paragrapharrow

Orthonormal basis.
For any matrix
\bm{X}
, we have the property:
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
is the orthogonal complement of the column space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
in
n
:
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}))=n
;
This relationship is known as the rank-nullity theorem, and its proof can be found in Theorem
.
Specifically, QR decomposition yields a basis for this subspace.
In singular value decomposition, we will also find the basis for
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
.

{theoremHigh}

[Orthonormal basis in
n
]
Given the full QR decomposition of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full rank
p
, we have the following property:

\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\ldots,\bm{q}_{p}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
;

\{\bm{q}_{p+1},\bm{q}_{p+2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Following from the Gram-Schmidt process, it is trivial that
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{k}\}
is equal to
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k}\}
for all
k\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
. Thus,
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}\}=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{p}\}
, and
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{p}\}
is an orthonormal basis for the column space of
\bm{X}
.
Additionally, we have
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})\bot\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, and
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}))=n-\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}))=n-p
.
Since the space spanned by
\{\bm{q}_{p+1},\bm{q}_{p+2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}\}
is also perpendicular to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
with dimension
n-p
, thus,
\{\bm{q}_{p+1},\bm{q}_{p+2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}\}
is an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
.

\paragrapharrow

Uniqueness of the QR decomposition.The QR decomposition is generally not unique.

Example 63
(Non-uniqueness of the QR decomposition).

Suppose the matrix
\bm{X}
is given by

\bm{X}=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\
3&2\end{bmatrix}.

The QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
can be obtained by

\displaystyle\bm{X}

\displaystyle=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.6\\
0.6&-0.8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5&2\\
0&-1\end{bmatrix}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{R}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&-0.6\\
0.6&0.8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5&2\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}

\displaystyle=\bm{Q}_{3}\bm{R}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.8&-0.6\\
-0.6&0.8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-5&-2\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bm{Q}_{4}\bm{R}_{4}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.8&0.6\\
-0.6&-0.8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-5&-2\\
0&-1\end{bmatrix}.

Thus, the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
is not unique.

However, the uniqueness of the
reduced
QR decomposition for a full column rank matrix
\bm{X}
is guaranteed when
\bm{R}
has positive diagonals.

{theoremHigh}
[Uniqueness of the reduced QR decomposition]
Suppose matrix
\bm{X}
is an
n\times p
matrix with full column rank
p
and
n\geq p
. Then, the
reduced
QR decomposition is unique if the main diagonal values of
\bm{R}
are positive.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Suppose the
reduced
QR decomposition is not unique, we can complete it into a
full
QR decomposition, then we can find two such full decompositions satisfying
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}_{1}=\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{R}_{2}
.
This implies
\bm{R}_{1}=\bm{Q}_{1}^{-1}\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{R}_{2}\triangleq\bm{V}\bm{R}_{2}
, where
\bm{V}\triangleq\bm{Q}_{1}^{-1}\bm{Q}_{2}
is an orthogonal matrix. Write out the equation, we have

\displaystyle\bm{R}_{1}

\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}r_{11}&r_{12}&\dots&r_{1p}\\
&r_{22}&\dots&r_{2p}\\
&&\ddots&\vdots\\
\lx@intercol\hfil\raisebox{5.59721pt}[0.0pt]{\Huge 0}\hfil\lx@intercol&&r_{pp}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\ldots&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}v_{11}&v_{12}&\ldots&v_{1n}\\
v_{21}&v_{22}&\ldots&v_{2n}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
v_{n1}&v_{n2}&\ldots&v_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}nn}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}s_{11}&s_{12}&\dots&s_{1p}\\
&s_{22}&\dots&s_{2p}\\
&&\ddots&\vdots\\
\lx@intercol\hfil\raisebox{5.59721pt}[0.0pt]{\Huge 0}\hfil\lx@intercol&&s_{pp}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\ldots&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{V}\bm{R}_{2},

This implies

r_{11}=v_{11}s_{11},\qquad v_{21}=v_{31}=v_{41}=\ldots=v_{n1}=0.

Since
\bm{V}
contains mutually orthonormal columns, and the first column of
\bm{V}
is of norm 1. Thus,
v_{11}=\pm 1
.
We notice that
r_{ii}>0
and
s_{ii}>0
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
by assumption such that
r_{11}>0
and
s_{11}>0
, implying that
v_{11}
can only be positive 1. Since
\bm{V}
is an orthogonal matrix, we also have

v_{12}=v_{13}=v_{14}=\ldots=v_{1n}=0.

Applying this process to the submatrices of
\bm{R}_{1}
,
\bm{V}
, and
\bm{R}_{2}
, we will find the upper-left submatrix of
\bm{V}
is the identity matrix:
\bm{V}[1:p,1:p]=\bm{I}_{p}
such that
\bm{R}_{1}=\bm{R}_{2}
. This implies
\bm{Q}_{1}[:,1:p]=\bm{Q}_{2}[:,1:p]
and leads to a contradiction. And thus the reduced QR decomposition is unique.
We complete the proof.

LQ Decomposition

We have proved the existence of the QR decomposition via the Gram-Schmidt process, in which case we are interested in the column space of a matrix
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]\in\real^{n\times p}
. The successive spaces spanned by the columns
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots
of
\bm{X}
are

\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\bm{x}_{3}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\ldots,

The concept behind QR decomposition involves generating a sequence of orthonormal vectors
\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots
, spanning the same successive subspaces:

\left\{\mathcal{C}([\bm{q}_{1}])=\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1}])\right\}\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\{\mathcal{C}([\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}])=\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2}])\}\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\ldots,

However, in many applications (see
Schilders 2009
), interest extends to the row space of a matrix
\bm{Y}=[\bm{y}_{1}^{\top};\bm{y}_{2}^{\top};\ldots;\bm{y}_{n}^{\top}]\in\real^{n\times p}
, where, abusing the notation,
\bm{y}_{i}
denotes the
i
-th row of
\bm{Y}
. The successive spaces spanned by the rows
\bm{y}_{1},\bm{y}_{2},\ldots
of
\bm{Y}
are

\mathcal{C}([\bm{y}_{1}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\mathcal{C}([\bm{y}_{1},\bm{y}_{2}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\mathcal{C}([\bm{y}_{1},\bm{y}_{2},\bm{y}_{3}])\,\,\,\,\subseteq\,\,\,\,\ldots.

The QR decomposition thus has a counterpart that identifies the orthogonal row space.
By applying QR decomposition on
\bm{Y}^{\top}=\bm{Q}_{0}\bm{R}
, we recover the LQ decomposition of the matrix
\bm{Y}=\bm{L}\bm{Q}
, where
\bm{Q}=\bm{Q}_{0}^{\top}
and
\bm{L}=\bm{R}^{\top}
. The LQ decomposition is helpful in demonstrating the existence of the UTV decomposition in Section
.

{theoremHigh}

[LQ decomposition]
Every
n\times p
matrix
\bm{Y}
(whether linearly independent or dependent rows) with
p\geq n
admits the following decomposition:

\bm{Y}=\bm{L}\bm{Q},

where

1.

Reduced
:
\bm{L}
is an
n\times n
lower triangular matrix and
\bm{Q}
is
n\times p
with orthonormal rows. This is known as the
reduced LQ decomposition
;

2.

Full
:
\bm{L}
is an
n\times p
lower triangular matrix and
\bm{Q}
is
p\times p
with orthonormal rows. This is known as the
full LQ decomposition
. If we further restrict the lower triangular matrix to be a square matrix, the full LQ decomposition can be denoted as

\bm{Y}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{L}_{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{Q},

where
\bm{L}_{0}
is an
n\times n
square lower triangular matrix.

Similarly, a comparison between the reduced and full LQ decomposition is shown in Figure
.

(a)

Reduced LQ decomposition.

(b)

Full LQ decomposition.

Figure 1.14:
Comparison between the reduced and full LQ decomposition. White entries are zero, and blue entries are not necessarily zero. Gray columns denote silent rows.

1.6.4
Schur and Spectral Decomposition

{theoremHigh}

[Schur decomposition]
Any real square matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
with real eigenvalues admits the following decomposition:

\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{U}\bm{Q}^{\top},

where
\bm{Q}
is an orthogonal matrix, and
\bm{U}
is an upper triangular matrix. That is, any square matrix
\bm{X}
with real eigenvalues can be triangularized.

When dealing with a symmetric matrix
\bm{X}=\bm{X}^{\top}
, we find that
\bm{Q}\bm{U}\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{Q}^{\top}
.
Consequently,
\bm{U}
is a diagonal matrix. And this diagonal matrix actually contains the eigenvalues of
\bm{X}
. All the columns of
\bm{Q}
are eigenvectors of
\bm{X}
.
This leads us to the conclusion that symmetric matrices are inherently diagonalizable, even in the presence of repeated eigenvalues.

Moreover, the matrix
\bm{X}
and
\bm{U}
are in the notion of similar matrices.

Definition 64
(Similar matrices).

For any nonsingular matrix
\bm{P}
, the matrices
\bm{X}
and
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}
are called similar matrices.

Lemma 65
(Eigenvalue, trace and rank of similar matrices).

Given a nonsingular matrix
\bm{P}
,
any eigenvalue of
\bm{X}
is also an eigenvalue of
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}
.
The converse is also true that any eigenvalue of
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}
is likewise an eigenvalue of
\bm{X}
.
In other words,
\Lambda(\bm{X})=\Lambda(\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1})
, where
\Lambda(\bm{Z})
represents the spectrum of matrix
\bm{Z}
(Definition
).

Furthermore, the trace and rank of
\bm{X}
are equal to those of matrix
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}
for any nonsingular matrix
\bm{P}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For any eigenpair
(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta})
of
\bm{X}
, we have
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}
. Consequently,
\lambda\bm{P}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}\bm{P}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, demonstrating that
\bm{P}\boldsymbol{\beta}
is an eigenvector of
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}
associated with
\lambda
.

Similarly, for any eigenpair
(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta})
of
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}
, we have
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}
. Then,
\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\bm{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, indicating that
\bm{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}
is an eigenvector of
\bm{X}
corresponding to
\lambda
.

Regarding the the trace of
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}
, we can establish that
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}\bm{P})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X})
, where the first equality comes from the fact that the
trace of a product is invariant under cyclical permutations of the factors:

\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\bm{B}\bm{C})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{B}\bm{C}\bm{A})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{C}\bm{A}\bm{B}),

if all
\bm{A}\bm{B}\bm{C}
,
\bm{B}\bm{C}\bm{A}
, and
\bm{C}\bm{A}\bm{B}
exist.

Regarding the rank of
\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1}
, we separate it into two claims as follows.

Rank claim 1:
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Z}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
if
\bm{Z}
is nonsingular.

We will begin by demonstrating that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Z}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
if
\bm{Z}
is nonsingular.
Consider any vector
\bm{n}
in the null space of
\bm{X}
, that is,
\bm{X}\bm{n}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Consequently,
\bm{Z}\bm{X}\bm{n}=\boldsymbol{0}
, that is,
\bm{n}
also resides in the null space of
\bm{Z}\bm{X}
.
This, in turn, implies
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\bm{Z}\bm{X})
.

Conversely, for any vector
\bm{m}
in the null space of
\bm{Z}\bm{X}
, i.e.,
\bm{Z}\bm{X}\bm{m}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we can deduce that
\bm{X}\bm{m}=\bm{Z}^{-1}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{0}
. That is,
\bm{m}
also lies in the null space of
\bm{X}
. And this indicates
\mathcal{N}(\bm{Z}\bm{X})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.

Combining the two arguments presented above leads to the following conclusion:

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{Z}\bm{X})\quad\longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Z}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}).

Rank claim 2:
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{Z})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
if
\bm{Z}
is nonsingular.

We observe that the row rank of a matrix is equivalent to its column rank (Lemma
).
Therefore,
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{Z})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})
. Since
\bm{Z}^{\top}
is nonsingular, as per claim 1, we can conclude that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{\top})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, where the last equality follows again from the fact that the row rank is equal to the column rank for any matrix. This establishes that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{Z})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, as claimed.

Since
\bm{P}
and
\bm{P}^{-1}
are nonsingular, we can conclude that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{P}\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{P}^{-1})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, where the first equality follows from claim 1, and the second equality follows from claim 2. We complete the proof.

Existence of the Schur Decomposition

To prove Theorem
, we need to use the following lemma.

Lemma 66
(Submatrix with same eigenvalue).

Suppose the square matrix
\bm{X}_{k+1}\in\real^{(k+1)\times(k+1)}
has real eigenvalues
\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k+1}
. Then, we can construct a
k\times k
matrix
\bm{X}_{k}
with eigenvalues
\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},\ldots,\lambda_{k+1}
by

\bm{X}_{k}=\begin{bmatrix}-\bm{p}_{2}^{\top}-\\
-\bm{p}_{3}^{\top}-\\
\vdots\\
-\bm{p}_{k+1}^{\top}-\end{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{p}_{2}&\bm{p}_{3}&\ldots&\bm{p}_{k+1}\end{bmatrix},

where
\bm{p}_{1}
is an eigenvector of
\bm{X}_{k+1}
with norm 1 corresponding to the eigenvalue
\lambda_{1}
, and
\bm{p}_{2},\bm{p}_{3},\ldots,\bm{p}_{k+1}
are any mutually orthonormal vectors that are orthogonal to
\bm{p}_{1}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\bm{P}_{k+1}=[\bm{p}_{1},\bm{p}_{2},\ldots,\bm{p}_{k+1}]
. We have
\bm{P}_{k+1}^{\top}\bm{P}_{k+1}=\bm{I}
and

\bm{P}_{k+1}^{\top}\bm{X}_{k+1}\bm{P}_{k+1}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{X}_{k}\end{bmatrix}.

For any eigenvalue
\lambda=\{\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},\ldots,\lambda_{k+1}\}
, by Lemma
, we have

\displaystyle\det(\bm{X}_{k+1}-\lambda\bm{I})

\displaystyle=\det(\bm{P}_{k+1}^{\top}(\bm{X}_{k+1}-\lambda\bm{I})\bm{P}_{k+1})=\det(\bm{P}_{k+1}^{\top}\bm{X}_{k+1}\bm{P}_{k+1}-\lambda\bm{P}_{k+1}^{\top}\bm{P}_{k+1})

\displaystyle=\det\left(\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}-\lambda&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{X}_{k}-\lambda\bm{I}\end{bmatrix}\right)=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda)\det(\bm{X}_{k}-\lambda\bm{I}),

where the last equality follows from the fact that if matrix
\bm{M}
has a block formulation:

\bm{M}=\footnotesize\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{E}&\bm{F}\\
\bm{G}&\bm{H}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
, then
\det(\bm{M})=\det(\bm{E})\det(\bm{H}-\bm{G}\bm{E}^{-1}\bm{F})
.
Since
\lambda
is an eigenvalue of
\bm{X}
and
\lambda\neq\lambda_{1}
, then
\det(\bm{X}_{k+1}-\lambda\bm{I})=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda)\det(\bm{X}_{k}-\lambda\bm{I})=0
means that
\lambda
is also an eigenvalue of
\bm{X}_{k}
.

We then prove the existence of the Schur decomposition by induction.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We note that the theorem is trivial when
n=1
by setting
Q=1
and
U=A
. Suppose the theorem is true when
n=k
for some
k\geq 1
. If we prove the theorem is also true when
n=k+1
, then we complete the proof.

Suppose for
n=k
, the theorem is true for
\bm{X}_{k}=\bm{Q}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}\bm{Q}_{k}^{\top}
.

Suppose further
\bm{P}_{k+1}
contains orthogonal vectors
\bm{P}_{k+1}=[\bm{p}_{1},\bm{p}_{2},\ldots,\bm{p}_{k+1}]
as constructed in Lemma
, where
\bm{p}_{1}
is an eigenvector of
\bm{X}_{k+1}
corresponding to the eigenvalue
\lambda_{1}
, and its norm is 1; and
\bm{p}_{2},\ldots,\bm{p}_{k+1}
are orthonormal to
\bm{p}_{1}
. Let the other
k
eigenvalues of
\bm{X}_{k+1}
be
\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},\ldots,\lambda_{k+1}
. Since we assume the theorem is true for
n=k
, we can find a matrix
\bm{X}_{k}
with eigenvalues
\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},\ldots,\lambda_{k+1}
. So we have the following property by Lemma
:

\bm{P}_{k+1}^{\top}\bm{X}_{k+1}\bm{P}_{k+1}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{X}_{k}\end{bmatrix}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{X}_{k+1}\bm{P}_{k+1}=\bm{P}_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{X}_{k}\end{bmatrix}.

Let

\bm{Q}_{k+1}\triangleq\bm{P}_{k+1}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{k}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

Then, it follows that

\displaystyle\bm{X}_{k+1}\bm{Q}_{k+1}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}_{k+1}\bm{P}_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{k}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{P}_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{X}_{k}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{k}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{P}_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{X}_{k}\bm{Q}_{k}\end{bmatrix}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\bm{P}_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{P}_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{k}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{U}_{k}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{Q}_{k+1}\bm{U}_{k+1},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the the assumption for
n=k
, and the last equality follows from the fact that
\bm{U}_{k+1}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{U}_{k}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
.
We then have
\bm{X}_{k+1}=\bm{Q}_{k+1}\bm{U}_{k+1}\bm{Q}_{k+1}^{\top}
, where
\bm{U}_{k+1}
is an upper triangular matrix, and
\bm{Q}_{k+1}
is an orthogonal matrix since
\bm{P}_{k+1}
and

\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{k}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
are both orthogonal matrices.
This completes the proof.

Other Forms of the Schur Decomposition

From the proof of the Schur decomposition, we obtain the upper triangular matrix
\bm{U}_{k+1}
by appending the eigenvalue
\lambda_{1}
to
\bm{U}_{k}
. From this process, the values on the diagonal are always eigenvalues. Therefore, we can decompose the upper triangular into two parts.

Corollary 67
(Form 2 of Schur decomposition).

Any square matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
with real eigenvalues admits the following decomposition:

\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Q}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}+\bm{T}\qquad\textbf{or}\qquad\bm{X}=\bm{Q}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}+\bm{T})\bm{Q}^{\top},

where
\bm{Q}
is an orthogonal matrix,
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n})
is a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of
\bm{X}
, and
\bm{T}
is a strictly upper triangular matrix (with zeros on the diagonal).

A strictly upper triangular matrix is an upper triangular matrix having 0’s along the diagonal as well as the lower portion. Another proof for this decomposition is that
\bm{X}
and
\bm{U}
(where
\bm{U}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Q}
) are similar matrices so that they have the same eigenvalues (Lemma
). And the eigenvalues of any upper triangular matrices are on the diagonal.
To see this, for any upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}\in\real^{n\times n}
, where the diagonal values are
r_{ii}
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, we have

\bm{R}\bm{e}_{i}=r_{ii}\bm{e}_{i},

where
\bm{e}_{i}
is the
i
-th basis vector in
n
.
So we can decompose
\bm{U}
into
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
and
\bm{T}
.

Spectral Decomposition

{theoremHigh}

[Spectral decomposition]
A real matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times n}
is symmetric if and only if there exists an orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}
and a diagonal matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
such that

\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top},

where the columns of
\bm{Q}=[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}]
are eigenvectors of
\bm{X}
and are mutually orthonormal, and the entries of
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n})
are the corresponding eigenvalues of
\bm{X}
, which are real. Specifically, we have the following properties:

1.

A symmetric matrix has only
real eigenvalues
.

2.

The eigenvectors can be chosen
orthonormal
.

3.

The rank of
\bm{X}
is the number of nonzero eigenvalues.

4.

If the eigenvalues are distinct, the eigenvectors are linearly independent.

To prove the existence of the spectral decomposition, we need the following lemmas.

Lemma 68
(Symmetric matrix property 1 of 4: real eigenvalues).

The eigenvalues of any symmetric matrix are all real.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose eigenvalue
\lambda
is a complex number
\lambda=a+ib
, where
a
and
b
are real. Its complex conjugate is
\bar{\lambda}=a-ib
. Similarly, we have the complex eigenvector
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{c}+i\bm{d}
and its complex conjugate
\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{c}-i\bm{d}
, where
\bm{c}
and
\bm{d}
are real vectors. We then have the following property:

\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}\qquad\underrightarrow{\text{ leads to }}\qquad\bm{X}\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bar{\lambda}\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\qquad\underrightarrow{\text{ transpose to }}\qquad\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bar{\lambda}\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}.

We take the dot product of the first equation with
\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and the last equation with
\boldsymbol{\beta}
:

\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\qquad\text{and }\qquad\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bar{\lambda}\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}.

Then we have the equality
\lambda\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bar{\lambda}\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
. Since
\bar{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\bm{c}-i\bm{d})^{\top}(\bm{c}+i\bm{d})=\bm{c}^{\top}\bm{c}+\bm{d}^{\top}\bm{d}
is a real number, the imaginary part of
\lambda
is zero and
\lambda
is real.

Lemma 69
(Symmetric matrix property 2 of 4: orthogonal eigenvectors).

The eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues of any symmetric matrix are orthogonal so that we can normalize eigenvectors to make them orthonormal since
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}\underrightarrow{\text{ leads to }}\bm{X}\frac{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}}=\lambda\frac{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}}
which corresponds to the same eigenvalue.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose eigenvalues
\lambda_{1}
and
\lambda_{2}
correspond to eigenvectors
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
, respectively, such that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}
and
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}=\lambda_{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
. We have the following equality:

\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}=\lambda_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}\qquad\implies\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}=\lambda_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}^{\top}\qquad\implies\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}=\lambda_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2},

and

\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}=\lambda_{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}\qquad\implies\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}=\lambda_{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2},

which implies
\lambda_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}=\lambda_{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
. Since the eigenvalues
\lambda_{1}\neq\lambda_{2}
, the eigenvectors are orthogonal.

For any matrix multiplication, the rank of the multiplication result is does not exceed the rank of the inputs. However, the symmetric matrix
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is rather special in that the rank of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is equal to that of
\bm{X}
which will be used in the proof of the singular value decomposition in the sequel.

Lemma 70
(Rank of
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{Y}\in\real^{p\times k}
. Then the matrix multiplication
\bm{X}\bm{Y}\in\real^{n\times k}
has
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
)
\leq
min(
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}
),
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{Y}
)).

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For matrix multiplication
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
, we have

All rows of
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
are combination of the rows of
\bm{Y}
, the row space of
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
is a subset of the row space of
\bm{Y}
. Thus
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
)
\leq
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{Y}
).

All columns of
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
are combination of columns of
\bm{X}
, the column space of
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
is a subset of the column space of
\bm{X}
. Thus
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
)
\leq
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}
).

Therefore we have,
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
)
\leq
min(
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}
),
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{Y}
)).

For the third property of symmetric matrix, we need the definition of similar matrices and the property about eigenvalues of similar matrices (see Lemma
).

Lemma 71
(Symmetric matrix property 3 of 4: orthonormal eigenvectors for duplicate eigenvalue).

If
\bm{X}
has a duplicate eigenvalue
\lambda_{i}
with multiplicity
k\geq 2
, then there exist
k
orthonormal eigenvectors corresponding to
\lambda_{i}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We note that there is at least one eigenvector
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
corresponding to
\lambda_{i}
. And for such an eigenvector
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
, we can always find additional
n-1
orthonormal vectors
\bm{y}_{2},\bm{y}_{3},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}
so that
\{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1},\bm{y}_{2},\bm{y}_{3},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}\}
forms an orthonormal basis in
n
. Put the
\bm{y}_{2},\bm{y}_{3},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}
into matrix
\bm{Y}_{1}
and
\{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1},\bm{y}_{2},\bm{y}_{3},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}\}
into matrix
\bm{P}_{1}
:

\bm{Y}_{1}=[\bm{y}_{2},\bm{y}_{3},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}]\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{P}_{1}=[\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1},\bm{Y}_{1}].

We then have

\bm{P}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Y}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}\end{bmatrix}.\qquad(\text{Let $\bm{B}=\bm{Y}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}$})

As a result,
\bm{X}
and
\bm{P}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1}
are similar matrices such that they have the same eigenvalues since
\bm{P}_{1}
is nonsingular (even orthogonal here, see Lemma
). We obtain

\det(\bm{P}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1}-\lambda\bm{I}_{n})=\penalty\ \penalty\ (\lambda_{i}-\lambda)\det(\bm{Y}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}-\lambda\bm{I}_{n-1}).

If
\lambda_{i}
has a multiplicity
k\geq 2
, then the term
(\lambda_{i}-\lambda)
occurs
k
times in the polynomial from the determinant
\det(\bm{P}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1}-\lambda\bm{I}_{n})
, i.e., the term occurs
k-1
times in the polynomial from
\det(\bm{Y}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}-\lambda\bm{I}_{n-1})
. In other words,
\det(\bm{Y}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n-1})=0
and
\lambda_{i}
is an eigenvalue of
\bm{Y}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}
.

Let
\bm{B}=\bm{Y}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}
. Since
\det(\bm{B}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n-1})=0
, the null space of
\bm{B}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n-1}
is not none. Suppose
(\bm{B}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n-1})\bm{n}=\boldsymbol{0}
, i.e.,
\bm{B}\bm{n}=\lambda_{i}\bm{n}
and
\bm{n}
is an eigenvector of
\bm{B}
.

From
\bm{P}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}\end{bmatrix},

we have
\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}z\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize=\bm{P}_{1}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}z\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}
, where
z
is any scalar. From the left side of this equation, we have

\displaystyle\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}z\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}

\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1},\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}z\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}=\lambda_{i}z\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}+\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{n}.

(1.40)

And from the right side of the equation, we have

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}z\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}

\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}&\bm{Y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}z\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}&\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{B}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}z\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}

(1.41)

\displaystyle=\lambda_{i}z\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}+\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{B}\bm{n}=\lambda_{i}z\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}+\lambda_{i}\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{n},

where the last equality follows from the fact that
\bm{B}\bm{n}=\lambda_{i}\bm{n}
.
Combining Equation (
) and Equation (
), we obtain

\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{n}=\lambda_{i}\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{n},

which means that
\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{n}
is an eigenvector of
\bm{X}
corresponding to the eigenvalue
\lambda_{i}
(the same eigenvalue corresponding to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
). Since
\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{n}
is a combination of
\bm{y}_{2},\bm{y}_{3},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}
, which are orthonormal to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
, the vector
\bm{Y}_{1}\bm{n}
can be chosen to be orthonormal to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
.

To conclude, if we have one eigenvector
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
corresponding to
\lambda_{i}
whose multiplicity is
k\geq 2
, we could construct the second eigenvector by choosing one vector from the null space of
(\bm{B}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n-1})
constructed above. Suppose now, we have constructed the second eigenvector
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i2}
, which is orthonormal to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
.
For such eigenvectors
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i2}
, we can always find additional
n-2
orthonormal vectors
\bm{y}_{3},\bm{y}_{4},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}
so that
\{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1},\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i2},\bm{y}_{3},\bm{y}_{4},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}\}
forms an orthonormal basis in
n
. Put the vectors
\bm{y}_{3},\bm{y}_{4},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}
into matrix
\bm{Y}_{2}
and
\{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1},\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i2},\bm{y}_{3},\bm{y}_{4},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}\}
into matrix
\bm{P}_{2}
:

\bm{Y}_{2}=[\bm{y}_{3},\bm{y}_{4},\ldots,\bm{y}_{n}]\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{P}_{2}=[\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1},\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i2},\bm{Y}_{1}].

We then have

\bm{P}_{2}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Y}_{2}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{C}\end{bmatrix},

where
\bm{C}=\bm{Y}_{2}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{2}
such that
\det(\bm{P}_{2}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}_{2}-\lambda\bm{I}_{n})=(\lambda_{i}-\lambda)^{2}\det(\bm{C}-\lambda\bm{I}_{n-2})
. If the multiplicity of
\lambda_{i}
is
k\geq 3
,
\det(\bm{C}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n-2})=0
and the null space of
\bm{C}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n-2}
is not none so that we can still find a vector from the null space of
\bm{C}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n-2}
and
\bm{C}\bm{n}=\lambda_{i}\bm{n}
. Now we can construct a vector
\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}\\
z_{2}\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}\in\real^{n}
, where
z_{1}
and
z_{2}
are any scalar values, such that

\bm{X}\bm{P}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}\\
z_{2}\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{P}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&\lambda_{i}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{C}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}\\
z_{2}\\
\bm{n}\end{bmatrix}.

Similarly, from the left side of the above equation we will get
\lambda_{i}z_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}+\lambda_{i}z_{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i2}+\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{2}\bm{n}
. From the right side of the above equation we will get
\lambda_{i}z_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}+\lambda_{i}z_{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i2}+\lambda_{i}\bm{Y}_{2}\bm{n}
. As a result,

\bm{X}\bm{Y}_{2}\bm{n}=\lambda_{i}\bm{Y}_{2}\bm{n},

where
\bm{Y}_{2}\bm{n}
is an eigenvector of
\bm{X}
and is orthogonal to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i1}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i2}
. And it is easy to construct the eigenvector to be orthonormal to the first two.

The process can go on, and finally, we will find
k
orthonormal eigenvectors corresponding to
\lambda_{i}
.

Actually, the dimension of the null space of
\bm{P}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1}-\lambda_{i}\bm{I}_{n}
is equal to the multiplicity
k
. It also follows that if the multiplicity of
\lambda_{i}
is
k
, there cannot be more than
k
orthogonal eigenvectors corresponding to
\lambda_{i}
. Otherwise, it will lead to the contradiction that we could find more than
n
orthogonal eigenvectors.

The proof of the Spectral Theorem
is evident from the lemmas above. Also, we can use Schur decomposition to prove the existence of spectral decomposition (see Theorem
).

Lemma 72
(Symmetric matrix property 4 of 4: rank of symmetric matrix).

If
\bm{X}
is an
n\times n
real symmetric matrix, then rank(
\bm{X}
) =
the total number of nonzero eigenvalues of
\bm{X}
.
In particular,
\bm{X}
has full rank if and only if
\bm{X}
is nonsingular. Furthermore,
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
is the linear space spanned by the eigenvectors of
\bm{X}
that correspond to nonzero eigenvalues.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For any symmetric matrix
\bm{X}
, we have
\bm{X}
, in spectral form, as
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
and also
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Q}
. Since we have shown in Lemma
that the rank of the matrix multiplication
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
)
\leq
min(
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}
),
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{Y}
)). Therefore, we have

From
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
, we have
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})
;

From
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Q}
, we have
\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
,

The inequalities above give us a contradiction. And thus
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})
, which is the total number of nonzero eigenvalues.

Since
\bm{X}
is nonsingular if and only if all of its eigenvalues are nonzero,
\bm{X}
has full rank if and only if
\bm{X}
is nonsingular.

{theoremHigh}

[Unique power decomposition of PD/PSD matrices]
Any
n\times n
PSD (resp. PD) matrix
\bm{A}
can be
uniquely
factored as a power of another PSD (resp. PD) matrix
\bm{B}
such that
\bm{A}=\bm{B}^{k}
with
k=\{1,2,\ldots\}
, where
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{B})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{A})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We first show the existence of such a positive semidefinite matrix
\bm{B}
that satisfies
\bm{A}=\bm{B}^{k}
.

Existence.

Since
\bm{A}
is symmetric and positive semidefinite, its spectral decomposition is given by
\bm{A}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
, where
\bm{Q}
is orthogonal and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
is diagonal containing the eigenvalues of
\bm{A}
. Since eigenvalues of PSD matrices are nonnegative (Theorem
), the
k
-th square root of
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
exists. We can define
\bm{B}\triangleq\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/k}\bm{Q}^{\top}
such that
\bm{A}=\bm{B}^{k}
, where
\bm{B}
is apparently PSD.

Uniqueness.

Suppose the factorization is not unique. Then, there exist two positive definite matrices
\bm{B}_{1}
and
\bm{B}_{2}
such that

\bm{A}=\bm{B}_{1}^{k}=\bm{B}_{2}^{k}.

Their spectral decompositions are given by

\bm{B}_{1}=\bm{Q}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{B}_{2}=\bm{Q}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{2}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}.

We notice that
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{1}^{k}
and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{2}^{k}
contain the eigenvalues of
\bm{A}
, and both eigenvalues of
\bm{B}_{1}
and
\bm{B}_{2}
contained in
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{1}
and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{2}
are nonnegative (since both
\bm{B}_{1}
and
\bm{B}_{2}
are PSD). Without loss of generality, we suppose
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{1}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{2}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/k}
, and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n})
such that
\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\lambda_{n}
. Utilizing the equation
\bm{B}_{1}^{k}=\bm{B}_{2}^{k}
, we have

\bm{Q}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}=\bm{Q}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\quad\implies\quad\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}.

Let
\bm{Z}\triangleq\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}
(which is orthogonal), this implies that
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
and
\bm{Z}
commute, and
\bm{Z}
must be a block-diagonal matrix whose partitioning conforms to the block structure of
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
. This results in
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/k}=\bm{Z}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/k}\bm{Z}^{\top}
and

\bm{B}_{2}=\bm{Q}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/k}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}=\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/k}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}=\bm{B}_{1}.

Thus, the decomposition is unique. In a similar manner, we can establish the unique decomposition of a PD matrix
\bm{A}=\bm{B}^{k}
, where
\bm{B}
is also PD.
For a more detailed discussion, see
Koeber and Schäfer 2006
;
Horn and Johnson 2012
, which provides an alternative proof using polynomials.

1.6.5
Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

Employing QR decomposition, we factor the matrix into an orthogonal matrix.
Unlike the factorization into a single orthogonal matrix, singular value decomposition (SVD) yields two orthogonal matrices. We illustrate the result of SVD in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[Reduced SVD for rectangular matrices]
Any real
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
with rank
r
admits the following decomposition:

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top},

where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{r\times r}
is a diagonal matrix
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\ldots,\sigma_{r})
with
\sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\sigma_{r}
, and:

The elements
\sigma_{i}
’s are the nonzero
singular values
of
\bm{X}
, in the meantime, they are the (positive) square roots of the nonzero
eigenvalues
of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
.

Columns of
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times r}
contain the
r
eigenvectors of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
corresponding to the
r
nonzero eigenvalues of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
.

Columns of
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times r}
contain the
r
eigenvectors of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
corresponding to the
r
nonzero eigenvalues of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
.

Moreover, the columns of
\bm{U}
and
\bm{V}
are called the
left and right singular vectors
of
\bm{X}
, respectively.

Furthermore, the columns of
\bm{U}
and
\bm{V}
are orthonormal (by Spectral Theorem
).

In particular, we can write out the matrix decomposition
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}
, which is a sum of
r
rank-one matrices.

If we append additional
n-r
silent columns that are orthonormal to the
r
eigenvectors of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
, just like the silent columns in QR decomposition, we will have an orthogonal matrix
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
. A similar procedure applies to the columns of
\bm{V}
.
The comparison between the reduced and full SVD is shown in Figure
, where white entries are zero, and blue entries are not necessarily zero.

(a)

Reduced SVD decomposition.

(b)

Full SVD decomposition.

Figure 1.15:
Comparison between the reduced and full SVD. White entries are zero, and blue entries are not necessarily zero

Existence of the SVD

To prove the existence of the SVD, we need to use the following lemmas. We may notice that the singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
. While, negative values do not have square roots such that its eigenvalues must be nonnegative.

Lemma 73
(Nonnegative eigenvalues of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
).

For any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
has nonnegative eigenvalues.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Given an eigenvalue and its corresponding eigenvector
\lambda
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}
of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
, we have

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}\qquad\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}.

Since
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 0
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\geq 0
. It then follows that
\lambda\geq 0
.

Since
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
has nonnegative eigenvalues, we then can define the singular value
\sigma\geq 0
of
\bm{X}
such that
\sigma^{2}
is the eigenvalue of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
, i.e.,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{v}=\sigma^{2}\bm{v}
. This is essential for establishing the existence of SVD.

We have shown in Lemma
that
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
)
\leq
min(
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{X}
),
\mathrm{rank}
(
\bm{Y}
)).
However, the symmetric matrix
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is rather special in that the rank of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is equal to
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
. And the proof is provided in the following lemma.

Lemma 74
(Rank of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
).

For any matrix
\bm{X}
,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}
have same rank.
Similarly,
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
and
\bm{X}
have same rank:

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}).

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
, that is, a vector in the null space of
\bm{X}
such that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Then,

\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\eta}=\boldsymbol{0}\qquad\implies\qquad\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\eta}=\boldsymbol{0},

which means
\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\implies\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
. Therefore,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
.

Conversely, suppose
\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
, we have

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\eta}=\boldsymbol{0}\implies\boldsymbol{\eta}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\eta}=0\implies\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\eta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=0\implies\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\eta}=\boldsymbol{0}.

This shows that
\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})\implies\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
. Therefore,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
. Combining both inclusions, we conclude:
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
and
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}))=\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}))
. Applying the fundamental theorem of linear algebra in Theorem
, we conclude that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}
have the same rank.

By applying the same reasoning to
\bm{X}^{\top}
, we can also show that
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
and
\bm{X}
share the same rank.
The ordinary least squares estimate is a result of this conclusion.

In the form of SVD, we claimed the matrix
\bm{X}
is a sum of
r
rank-one matrices, where
r
is the number of nonzero singular values. And the number of nonzero singular values is actually equal to the rank of the matrix.

Lemma 75
.

The number of nonzero singular values of a matrix
\bm{X}
equals the rank of
\bm{X}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
The rank of any symmetric matrix (here
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
) equals the number of nonzero eigenvalues (with repetitions) by Lemma
. So the number of nonzero singular values equals the rank of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
. By Lemma
,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}
have the same rank, so the number of nonzero singular values equals the rank of
\bm{X}
.

We are now ready to prove the existence of SVD.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is a symmetric matrix, by Spectral Theorem
and Lemma
, there exists an orthogonal matrix
\bm{V}
such that

{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2}\bm{V}^{\top}},

where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
is a diagonal matrix containing the singular values of
\bm{X}
, i.e.,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2}
contains the eigenvalues of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
.
Specifically,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\ldots,\sigma_{r})
and
\{\sigma_{1}^{2},\sigma_{2}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{r}^{2}\}
are the nonzero eigenvalues of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
with
r
being the rank of
\bm{X}
. I.e.,
\{\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r}\}
are the singular values of
\bm{X}
. In this case,
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times r}
.
Start from
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\bm{v}_{i}
,
\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,r\}
, i.e., the eigenvector
\bm{v}_{i}
of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
corresponding to
\sigma_{i}^{2}
:

1. Multiply both sides by
\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}
:

\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{v}_{i}\qquad\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\qquad\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}\right\rVert=\sigma_{i}.

2. Multiply both sides by
\bm{X}
:

\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}\,\,\,\,\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\,\,\,\,\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}\frac{\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\frac{\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}}\,\,\,\,\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\,\,\,\,\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{u}_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\bm{u}_{i},

where we notice this form can find the eigenvector of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
corresponding to
\sigma_{i}^{2}
, and the eigenvector is
\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}
. Since the length of
\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}
is
\sigma_{i}
, we then define
\bm{u}_{i}\triangleq\frac{\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}}
with norm 1.
These
\bm{u}_{i}
’s are orthogonal because
(\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i})^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{v}_{j})=\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{v}_{j}=\sigma_{j}^{2}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\bm{v}_{j}=0
. That is,

{\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2}\bm{U}^{\top}}.

Since
\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}=\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}
, we have

[\bm{X}\bm{v}_{1},\bm{X}\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{X}\bm{v}_{r}]=[\sigma_{1}\bm{u}_{1},\sigma_{2}\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{r}\bm{u}_{r}]\qquad\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\bm{X}\bm{V}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma},

Since
\bm{V}\bm{V}^{\top}\neq\bm{I}
, we cannot obtain the reduced SVD directly.
Suppose we append the semi-orthogonal matrix
\bm{V}
into an orthogonal matrix
\widetilde{\bm{V}}=[\bm{V},\bm{V}_{2}]
, and append the semi-orthogonal matrix
\bm{U}
into an orthogonal matrix
\widetilde{\bm{U}}=[\bm{U},\bm{U}_{2}]
. We then obtain

\bm{A}\widetilde{\bm{V}}=\widetilde{\bm{U}}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{where}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\quad\implies\quad\bm{A}=\widetilde{\bm{U}}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\widetilde{\bm{V}}^{\top},

i.e., the full SVD (since
\widetilde{\bm{V}}\widetilde{\bm{V}}^{\top}=\bm{I}
).
Simplifying the product, we get:

\bm{A}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}+\bm{U}_{2}\cdot\boldsymbol{0}\cdot\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top},

i.e., the reduced SVD,
which completes the proof.

Eckart-Young-Mirsky Theorem

Suppose we want to approximate the rank-
r
matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
by a rank-
k
matrix
\bm{Y}
(
k<r
). The approximation is measured using the Frobenius norm (Definition
):

\bm{Y}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{Y}}\,\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}.

Then we can recover the optimal rank-
k
approximation using the following theorem
(
Stewart 1993
)
.

{theoremHigh}

[Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem w.r.t. Frobenius norm]
Given a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
1\leq k\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r
, and let
\bm{X}_{k}
be the
truncated SVD
(TSVD) of
\bm{X}
with the largest
k
terms, i.e.,
\bm{X}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}
from the SVD of
\bm{X}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}
by zeroing out the
r-k
trailing singular values of
\bm{X}
. Then
\bm{X}_{k}
is the optimal rank-
k
approximation to
\bm{X}
in terms of the Frobenius norm, satisfying
\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{X}_{k}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i\geq k+1}\sigma_{i}^{2}
.

Four Orthonormal Bases in SVD

For any matrix, we have the following property:

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
is the orthogonal complement of the row space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
in
p
:
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}))=p
;

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
is the orthogonal complement of the column space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
in
n
:
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}))=n
;

This is called the fundamental theorem of linear algebra and is also known as the rank-nullity theorem (Theorem
).
In specific, the construction of SVD yields a set of orthonormal bases for the four subspaces in the fundamental theorem of linear algebra.
To show this, we require the following fact.

Lemma 76
(Subspace of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be given. Then,

The column space of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is identical to the column space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
(i.e., row space of
\bm{X}
):
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
; this also shows
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
by fundamental theorem of linear algebra in Theorem
.

The column space of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
is identical to the column space of
\bm{X}
:
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
; again, this also shows

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
, we have

\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}\implies\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0},

i.e.,
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\implies\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
. Therefore,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
.
Furthermore, let
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
, we have

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}\implies\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=0\implies\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=0\implies\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0},

i.e.,
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})\implies\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
. Therefore,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.
As a result, by “sandwiching,” it follows that

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}).

According to the fundamental theorem of linear algebra in Theorem
, we have

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}).

Applying the same process to
\bm{X}^{\top}
leads to the second part of the lemma.

{theoremHigh}

[Four orthonormal bases in SVD]
Given the full SVD of matrix
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
, where
\bm{U}=[\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{n}]
and
\bm{V}=[\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{p}]
are the column partitions of
\bm{U}
and
\bm{V}
, respectively. Then, we have the following property:

\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of the row space,
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
;

\{\bm{v}_{r+1},\bm{v}_{r+2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{p}\}
is an orthonormal basis of the null space,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
;

\{\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of the column space,
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
;

\{\bm{u}_{r+1},\bm{u}_{r+2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{n}\}
is an orthonormal basis of the left null space,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
From Lemma
, for symmetric matrix
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
, its column space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
is spanned by the eigenvectors.
Therefore, the set
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2}\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
forms an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
.
Thus,
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
also serves as an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
by Lemma
.

Furthermore, the space spanned by
\{\bm{v}_{r+1},\bm{v}_{r+2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{n}\}
is an orthogonal complement to the space spanned by
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
. Hence,
\{\bm{v}_{r+1},\bm{v}_{r+2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{n}\}
constitutes an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.

Applying this process to
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
proves the remaining claims in the lemma.
Alternatively, we can see that
\{\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{r}\}
forms a basis for the column space of
\bm{X}
by Lemma
, since
\bm{u}_{i}=\frac{\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}},\,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,r\}
.

The relationship among the four subspaces is demonstrated in Figure
, where
\bm{X}
maps each row basis vector
\bm{v}_{i}
into the column basis vector
\bm{u}_{i}
by
\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}=\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,r\}
.

Figure 1.16:
Orthonormal bases that diagonalize
\bm{X}
from SVD.
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, and
\{\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
. Connection between the row space basis and column space basis:
\bm{X}
transfers the row basis
\bm{v}_{i}
into the column basis
\bm{u}_{i}
by
\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}=\bm{X}\bm{v}_{i}
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,r\}
.

1.7
Pseudo-Inverse

If the matrix
\bm{X}
is nonsingular, the solution to the linear system
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
can be directly obtained by taking the inverse of
\bm{X}
, yielding
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{-1}\bm{y}
.
However, when
\bm{X}
is not square or is singular, the inverse does not exist. In such cases, we can still define a generalized inverse known as the
pseudo-inverse
, represented as a
p\times n
matrix denoted by
\bm{X}^{+}
.

Before discussing the pseudo-inverse in detail, we will briefly introduce related concepts such as one-sided inverses, generalized inverses, and reflexive generalized inverses.
That said, readers who are already familiar with these ideas may choose to skip ahead without losing the overall understanding of the pseudo-inverse.

1.7.1
One-Sided Inverse

We begin by providing a formal definition of the one-sided inverse:

Definition 77
(One-sided inverse).

For any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, a matrix
\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}
is called a left inverse of
\bm{X}
if it satisfies the condition:

\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{X}=\bm{I}_{p}.

In such cases, the matrix
\bm{X}
is said to be left-invertible.
Similarly, a matrix
\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}
is referred to as a right inverse of
\bm{X}
if the following holds:

\bm{X}\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}=\bm{I}_{n}.\penalty\

Here,
\bm{X}
is said to be right-invertible.

Lemma 78
(One-sided invertible).

For any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, the following hold:

\bm{X}
is left-invertible if and only if
\bm{X}
has full column rank (which implies
n\geq p
);

\bm{X}
is right-invertible if and only if
\bm{X}
has full row rank (which implies
n\leq p
).

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose
\bm{X}
has full column rank. Then the matrix
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\in\real^{p\times p}
attains full rank (by Lemma
). Therefore,
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})=\bm{I}_{p}
. This implies that
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
acts as a left inverse of
\bm{X}
.

Conversely, suppose
\bm{X}
is left-invertible with
\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{X}=\bm{I}_{p}
. Since all rows of
\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{X}
are combinations of the rows of
\bm{X}
, meaning the row space of
\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{X}
is a subset of the row space of
\bm{X}
. We then have
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})\geq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{I}_{p})=p
, indicating
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, and
\bm{X}
has full column rank.

Similarly, we can show that
\bm{X}
is right-invertible if and only if
\bm{X}
has full row rank, and
\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}
serves as a right inverse of
\bm{X}
.

From the proof above, we see that
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
is a specific left inverse of
\bm{X}
when it has full column rank.
Similarly,
\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}
acts as a specific right inverse of
\bm{X}
when it has full row rank.
However, obtaining the inverse of a nonsingular
p\times p
matrix involves a complex process, requiring
2p^{3}
floating-point operations (flops)
(
Lu 2021b
)
.
In our case, finding the inverses of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
would require
2p^{3}
and
2n^{3}
flops, respectively.
A more straightforward approach to acquire a one-sided inverse involves using elementary operations.

Assume that
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full column rank.
We can apply
row elementary operations
, represented by a matrix
\bm{E}\in\real^{n\times n}
, to the augmented matrix
[\bm{X},\bm{I}_{n}]
, resulting in

\bm{E}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}&\bm{I}_{n}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{p}&\bm{G}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Z}\end{bmatrix},

(1.42)

where
\bm{G}\in\real^{p\times n}
,
\bm{I}_{n}
is an
n\times n
identity matrix,
\bm{I}_{p}
is a
p\times p
identity matrix, and
\bm{Z}
is an
(n-p)\times n
matrix.
Then, it can be easily verified that
\bm{G}\bm{X}=\bm{I}_{p}
, establishing
\bm{G}
as a left inverse of
\bm{X}
.

Similarly, consider
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full row rank. By applying
column elementary operations
, denoted by
\bm{E}\in\real^{p\times p}
, to the matrix
[\bm{X}^{\top},\bm{I}_{p}]^{\top}
, we obtain

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}\\
\bm{I}_{p}\end{bmatrix}\bm{E}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{n}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{G}&\bm{Z}\end{bmatrix},

(1.43)

where
\bm{Z}
is a
p\times(p-n)
matrix.
Then,
\bm{G}\in\real^{p\times n}
is a right inverse of
\bm{X}
.

More generally, the following two propositions provide the methods for discovering more left inverses or right inverses of a matrix.

Proposition 79
(Finding left inverse).

Suppose
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is left-invertible (
n\geq p
). Then,

\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}=[(\bm{X}_{1}^{-1}-\bm{Y}\bm{X}_{2}\bm{X}_{1}^{-1}),\bm{Y}]\bm{E},

is a left inverse of
\bm{X}
, where
\bm{Y}\in\real^{p\times(n-p)}
can be any matrix, and
\bm{E}\bm{X}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
is the row elementary transformation of
\bm{X}
such that
\bm{X}_{1}\in\real^{p\times p}
is invertible (since
\bm{X}
has full column rank
p
) and
\bm{E}\in\real^{n\times n}
.

We can verify that
\bm{G}
in Equation (
) is a specific left inverse of
\bm{X}
by setting
\bm{Y}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Since
\bm{E}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{G}\\
*\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
,
\bm{X}_{1}=\bm{I}_{p}
, and
\bm{X}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we have

\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}=[(\bm{X}_{1}^{-1}-\bm{Y}\bm{X}_{2}\bm{X}_{1}^{-1}),\bm{Y}]\bm{E}=\bm{G}+\bm{Y}\bm{Z}=\bm{G},

where the last equality follows from the assumption that
\bm{Y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

Proposition 80
(Finding right inverse).

Suppose
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is right-invertible (
n\leq p
). Then,

\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}=\bm{E}\begin{bmatrix}(\bm{X}_{1}^{-1}-\bm{X}_{1}^{-1}\bm{X}_{2}\bm{Y})\\
\bm{Y}\end{bmatrix},

is a right inverse of
\bm{X}
, where
\bm{Y}\in\real^{(p-n)\times n}
can be any matrix, and
\bm{X}\bm{E}=[\bm{X}_{1},\bm{X}_{2}]
is the column elementary transformation of
\bm{X}
such that
\bm{X}_{1}\in\real^{n\times n}
is invertible (since
\bm{X}
has full row rank
n
) and
\bm{E}\in\real^{p\times p}
.

Similarly, we can verify that
\bm{G}
in Equation (
) is a specific right inverse of
\bm{X}
by setting
\bm{Y}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Since
\bm{E}=[\bm{G},\bm{Z}]
,
\bm{X}_{1}=\bm{I}_{n}
, and
\bm{X}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we have

\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}=\bm{E}\begin{bmatrix}(\bm{X}_{1}^{-1}-\bm{X}_{1}^{-1}\bm{X}_{2}\bm{Y})\\
\bm{Y}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{G}+\bm{Z}\bm{Y}=\bm{G},

where again the last equality holds because
\bm{Y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

1.7.2
Generalized Inverse (g-inverse)

We mentioned previously that if the matrix
\bm{X}
is nonsingular, the linear system
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
can be easily solved using the inverse of
\bm{X}
, resulting in
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{-1}\bm{y}
. However, for an
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
, the inverse does not exist if
\bm{X}
is neither square nor nonsingular.

Nevertheless, when
\bm{y}
lies in the column space of
\bm{X}
, we can still determine the solution to the linear system. The association between the solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and the target vector
\bm{y}
is expressed by the
generalized inverse
(or
inner inverse or
\{1\}
-inverse
) of
\bm{X}
:
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}

(
Nashed 1973
)
.

Definition 81
(Generalized inverse).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix of rank
r
, where
r\leq p\leq n
.
Then, a generalized inverse (g-inverse)
\bm{X}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
of
\bm{X}
is a matrix that satisfies

(C1)\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X},

or equivalently,

(C1.1)\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}=\bm{y}

for any vector
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

To demonstrate the equivalence between
(C1)
and
(C1.1)
, that is, we want to show
\bm{X}
satisfies
(C1)
if and only if it satisfies
(C1.1)
. For any
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, a
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}
exists such that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
. If
\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}^{-}
satisfy
(C1)
, then

\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\qquad\implies\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}=\bm{y},

indicating that
\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}^{-}
also satisfy
(C1.1)
. Conversely, if
\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}^{-}
satisfy
(C1.1)
, then:

\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}=\bm{y}\qquad\implies\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},

which implies
\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}^{-}
also satisfy
(C1)
.

Multiply on the left of
(C1)
by
\bm{X}^{-}
and utilize the definition of the projection matrix in Definition
(i.e., an idempotent matrix), we obtain
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
such that
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
is idempotent, which implies
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
is a projection matrix (not necessarily an orthogonal projection, i.e., a symmetric and idempotent matrix).

Lemma 82
(Projection matrix from generalized inverse).

For any matrix
\bm{X}
and any of its generalized inverse
\bm{X}^{-}
,
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
is a projection matrix but not necessarily an orthogonal projection matrix. Same claim can be applied to
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
as well.

Lemma 83
(Rank of generalized inverse).

For any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and any of its generalized inverse
\bm{X}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
, the following inequality holds:

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-})\geq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}).

Specifically, we also have
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
From condition
(C1)
, we know that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})
. Moreover,

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}),

where the first inequality follows because the columns of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
are linear combinations of the columns of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
, and the second inequality follows because the rows of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
are linear combinations of the rows of
\bm{X}^{-}
.

For the second part, we have

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})\geq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})\geq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}),

where the first inequality follows because the columns of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
are linear combinations of the columns of
\bm{X}
, and the second inequality follows because the columns of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
are linear combinations of the columns of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
.
From
(C1)
again,
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})
, which implies by “sandwiching” that

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}).

Similarly, we also have

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})\geq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})\geq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}),

where the first inequality follows because the rows of
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
are linear combinations of the rows of
\bm{X}
, and the second inequality follows because the rows of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
are linear combinations of the rows of
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
. By “sandwiching” again, we have

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}),

which completes the proof.

In Lemma
, we demonstrated that a left inverse exists if and only if
\bm{X}
has full column rank, and a right inverse exists if and only if
\bm{X}
has full row rank.
However, these full-rank conditions are not required for the existence of a generalized inverse. When such full-rank conditions are satisfied, the following property holds:

Lemma 84
(Full-rank generalized inverse).

Given any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and its generalized inverse
\bm{X}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
, the following statements hold:

1.

\bm{X}
has full column rank if and only if
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{I}_{p}
;

2.

\bm{X}
has full row rank if and only if
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}=\bm{I}_{n}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For (i), suppose
\bm{X}
has full column rank, and we have shown in Lemma
that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})
. Thus,
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, and
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\in\real^{p\times p}
is nonsingular. We have

\bm{I}_{p}=(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})^{-1}=\bm{X}^{-}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})^{-1}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}.

Conversely, suppose
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{I}_{p}
, which implies
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=p
. From
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, we have
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
such that
\bm{X}
has full column rank.

Similarly, we can show
\bm{X}
has full row rank if and only if
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}=\bm{I}_{n}
.

Lemma 85
(Constructing generalized inverse).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be any matrix with a generalized inverse
\bm{X}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
.
Then there exists a
p\times n
matrix
\bm{A}
such that the matrix

\overline{\bm{X}}=\bm{X}^{-}+\bm{A}-\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}

(1.44)

is also a generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
.
Moreover, for any generalized inverse
\overline{\bm{X}}
of
\bm{X}
, there exists some matrix
\bm{A}
so that Equation (
) is satisfied.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Write out the equation

\displaystyle\bm{X}\overline{\bm{X}}\bm{X}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{-}+\bm{A}-\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})\bm{X}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}+\bm{X}\bm{A}\bm{X}-(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})\bm{A}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})

\displaystyle=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}+\bm{X}\bm{A}\bm{X}-\bm{X}\bm{A}\bm{X}=\bm{X}.

Therefore,
\overline{\bm{X}}
satisfies condition
(C1)
and is indeed a generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
.

Now suppose that
\bm{B}
is any generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
, and define
\bm{A}\triangleq\bm{B}-\bm{X}^{-}
. Recall that
\bm{X}\bm{B}\bm{X}=\bm{X}
, we have

\displaystyle\bm{X}^{-}+\bm{A}-\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{-}+(\bm{B}-\bm{X}^{-})-\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}(\bm{B}-\bm{X}^{-})\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}

\displaystyle=\bm{B}-\bm{X}^{-}(\bm{X}\bm{B}\bm{X})\bm{X}^{-}+\bm{X}^{-}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})\bm{X}^{-}

\displaystyle=\bm{B}-\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}+\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}=\bm{B},

which implies that the matrix
\bm{A}
can be constructed for any generalized inverse
\bm{B}
of
\bm{X}
.

We end up this section by providing more properties of the generalized inverse.

Lemma 86
(Generalized inverse properties).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be any matrix and let
\bm{X}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
be a generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
.
Then the following properties hold:

1.

(\bm{X}^{\top})^{-}=(\bm{X}^{-})^{\top}
, i.e.,
(\bm{X}^{-})^{\top}
is a generalized inverse of
\bm{X}^{\top}
;

2.

For any scalar
a\neq 0
,
\frac{1}{a}\bm{X}^{-}
is a generalized inverse of
a\bm{X}
;

3.

If
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times p}
are both nonsingular, then
\bm{B}^{-1}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{A}^{-1}
is a generalized inverse of
\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{B}
;

4.

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]

(i).
From condition
(C1)
,
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}
, we have
\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{-})^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}
such that
(\bm{X}^{-})^{\top}
is a generalized inverse of
\bm{X}^{\top}
.

(ii).

It can be easily verified that
(a\bm{X})(\frac{1}{a}\bm{X}^{-})(a\bm{X})=(a\bm{X})
such that
\frac{1}{a}\bm{X}^{-}
is a generalized inverse of
a\bm{X}
for any
a\neq 0
.

(iii).

We realize that
(\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{B})(\bm{B}^{-1}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{A}^{-1})(\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{B})=\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{B}=\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{B}
, which implies
\bm{B}^{-1}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{A}^{-1}
is a generalized inverse of
\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{B}
.

(iv).

Note that the columns of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
are linear combinations of the columns of
\bm{X}
, so:
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
. From Lemma
, we know
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})
, then
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
. Similarly, we could prove
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.
This completes the proof.

1.7.3
Reflexive Generalized Inverse (rg-inverse)

Figure 1.17:
Relationship of different inverses: inverse, one-sided inverse, reflexive generalized inverse, and generalized inverse.

Definition 87
(Reflexive Generalized Inverse).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix of rank
r
, where
r\leq\min\{p,n\}
. Then, a reflexive generalized inverse (rg-inverse)
\bm{X}_{r}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
of
\bm{X}
is a matrix that satisfies the conditions:

(C1)\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}_{r}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X},\qquad\text{$\bm{X}_{r}^{-}$ is an inner inverse}

and

(C2)\qquad\bm{X}_{r}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}_{r}^{-}=\bm{X}_{r}^{-}.\qquad\text{$\bm{X}_{r}^{-}$ is an outer inverse}

In other words,
\bm{X}_{r}^{-}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}
, and at the same time,
\bm{X}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}_{r}^{-}
.

Note that
(C1)
shows that
\bm{X}_{r}^{-}
is a
generalized inverse
(or
inner inverse
,
\{1\}
-inverse
) or
\bm{X}
; while
(C2)
shows that
\bm{X}
is a generalized inverse of
\bm{X}_{r}^{-}
.
Equivalently, we say that
\bm{X}_{r}^{-}
is an
outer inverse
or a
\{2\}
-inverse
of
\bm{X}
by
(C2)

(
Nashed 1973
;
Björck 2024
)
.

Suppose the matrix
\bm{X}
is of rank
r
. Then, it can be factored as
\bm{X}=\bm{E}_{1}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{r}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\bm{E}_{2}
, where
\bm{E}_{1}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{E}_{2}\in\real^{p\times p}
are elementary transformations on
\bm{X}
. Then, we can construct such a reflexive generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
as

\bm{X}_{r}^{-}=\bm{E}_{2}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{r}&\bm{A}\\
\bm{B}&\bm{B}\bm{A}\end{bmatrix}\bm{E}_{1}^{-1},

(1.45)

where
\bm{A}\in\real^{r\times(n-r)}
,
\bm{B}\in\real^{(p-r)\times r}
can be any arbitrary matrices.
This shows that the reflexive generalized inverse is generally
not unique
.
This construction of the reflexive generalized inverse also shows that a reflexive generalized inverse exists for any matrix
\bm{X}
.
Therefore, compared to one-sided inverses—which only exist under strict full-rank conditions—the reflexive generalized inverse is a more general concept.

Lemma 88
(Reflexive generalized inverse from g-inverse).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be any matrix, and suppose
\bm{A}
and
\bm{B}
are both generalized inverses of
\bm{X}
.
Define the matrix:

\bm{Z}\triangleq\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{B}.

Then,
\bm{Z}
is a reflexive generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
.

It can be easily verified that
\bm{X}\bm{Z}\bm{X}=\bm{X}
and
\bm{Z}\bm{X}\bm{Z}=\bm{Z}
for the lemma above.

Lemma 89
(Reflexive generalized inverse from g-inverse).

For any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, the following two matrices
\bm{A}
and
\bm{B}
are two reflexive generalized inverses of
\bm{X}
:

\displaystyle\bm{A}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-}\bm{X}^{\top},

\displaystyle\bm{B}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-},

where
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-}
is a g-inverse of
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
, and
(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-}
is a g-inverse of
(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By Lemma
, we have
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.
Then there exists a set of vectors
\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{z}_{n}\in\real^{p}
such that the
i
-th column of
\bm{X}^{\top}
can be expressed as
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{z}_{i}
.
Let
\bm{Z}\triangleq[\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{z}_{n}]
, so we have:

\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Z}.

Using this identity and the condition
(C1)
of g-inverse, compute:

\displaystyle\bm{X}\bm{A}\bm{X}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{Z})^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}

(1.46)

\displaystyle=\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{X}.

Now, let’s examine
\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{A}
:

\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{A}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-}\bm{X}^{\top}.

The same argument applies to
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}
. Thus,

\bm{A}\bm{X}\bm{A}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{A}.

(1.47)

Combining Equation (
) and Equation (
), we conclude that
\bm{A}
is a reflexive generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
. Similarly, we can show
\bm{B}
is a reflexive generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
as well.

From the definition, it is clear that a reflexive generalized inverse is a special type of generalized inverse. However, under certain conditions, these two types of inverses are equivalent.

Lemma 90
(Reflexive generalized inverse in g-inverse).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be any matrix, and let
\bm{X}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
be a generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
.
Then,
\bm{X}^{-}
is a reflexive generalized inverse of
\bm{X}
if and only if
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose
\bm{X}^{-}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}
, , so by definition:
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}
. Suppose further,
\bm{X}^{-}
is also a rg-inverse, then
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}=\bm{X}^{-}
. We have

\displaystyle\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})

where the two inequalities follows from Lemma
. This implies
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-})
.

Conversely, suppose
\bm{X}^{-}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}
, then
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}
. And suppose further that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-})
, we have

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}),

where the first inequality follows because the rows of
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
are combinations of the rows of
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
, and the second inequality follows because the columns of
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
are combinations of the columns of
\bm{X}^{-}
.
This implies
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{-})
and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{-})
. Then, there exists a set of vectors
\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1},\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{2},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}\in\real^{p}
such that the column-
i
of
\bm{X}^{-}
can be expressed as
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}
. That is, for
\bm{A}=[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1},\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{2},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}]
, we have

\bm{X}^{-}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{A}.

We realize again that
\bm{X}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
, then

\bm{X}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{A})\bm{X}=\bm{X}\bm{A}\bm{X},

where the last equality follows form condition
(C1.1)
; and thus,
\bm{A}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}
. From Lemma
,
\bm{X}^{-}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{A}
is a rg-inverse of
\bm{X}
, which completes the proof.

To summarize this section, we now provide insight into the rank relationships in reflexive generalized inverses.

Proposition 91
(Rank of reflexive generalized inverse).

Consider a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and its generalized inverse
\bm{X}_{r}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
.
Utilizing the result in Lemma
and the result from the rank of g-inverses in Lemma
, we have

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}_{r}^{-})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{r}^{-})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}_{r}^{-}\bm{X}).

Lemma 92
(Reflexive generalized inverse properties).

Given a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and its reflexive generalized inverse
\bm{X}_{r}^{-}\in\real^{p\times n}
, the following properties hold:

1.

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{r}^{-})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}_{r}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.

2.

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}_{r}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}_{r}^{-})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{r}^{-})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}_{r}^{-})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose
\bm{X}^{-}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}
,
we show in Lemma
that
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
. Since
\bm{X}^{-}_{r}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}
, and
\bm{X}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}^{-}_{r}
, we complete the proof.

1.7.4
