Pseudo-Inverse

As previously mentioned, for a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, we can find its pseudo-inverse, a
p\times n
matrix denoted by
\bm{X}^{+}
.
In simple terms, when
\bm{X}
multiplies a vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
that lies in its row space, this produces
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
in the column space (see Figure
).
Both of these spaces have the same dimension
r
, i.e., the rank of
\bm{X}
.
When restricted to these subspaces,
\bm{X}
behaves like an invertible matrix, and
\bm{X}^{+}
acts as its inverse. Specifically:

If
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is in the row space of
\bm{X}
, then
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}
.

If
\bm{y}
is in the column space of
\bm{X}
, then
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{y}
(see Figure
).

The null space of
\bm{X}^{+}
coincides with the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
. It contains the vectors
\bm{y}
in
n
with
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Those vectors
\bm{y}
are orthogonal to every vector
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
in the column space of
\bm{X}
. We delay the proof of this property in Theorem
.

More formally, the
pseudo-inverse
, also known as the
Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse
,
\bm{X}^{+}
, is defined by the unique
p\times n
matrix satisfying the following four conditions, often referred to as the
Penrose conditions

(
Penrose 1955
)
:

\boxed{\begin{aligned} &(C1)\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}&=&\bm{X}\qquad&(\bm{X}^{+}\text{ is a g-inverse of }\bm{X})\\
&(C2)\qquad\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}&=&\bm{X}^{+}\qquad&(\bm{X}\text{ is a g-inverse of }\bm{X}^{+})\\
&(C3)\qquad(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{\top}&=&\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\qquad&(\text{$\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}$ is symmetric})\\
&(C4)\qquad(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}&=&\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}\qquad&(\text{$\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}$ is symmetric})\\
\end{aligned}}

(1.48)

Although we mostly work with real matrices, when
\bm{X}\in{\mathbb{F}}^{n\times p}
(where
{\mathbb{F}}
denotes either for real or
\mathbb{C}
for complex numbers), the pseudo-inverse satisfies similar conditions using the conjugate transpose:

\boxed{\begin{aligned} &(C1)\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}&=&\bm{X}\qquad&(\bm{X}^{+}\text{ is a g-inverse of }\bm{X})\\
&(C2)\qquad\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}&=&\bm{X}^{+}\qquad&(\bm{X}\text{ is a g-inverse of }\bm{X}^{+})\\
&(C3)\qquad(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{*}&=&\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\qquad&(\text{$\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}$ is Hermitian})\\
&(C4)\qquad(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})^{*}&=&\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}\qquad&(\text{$\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}$ is Hermitian})\end{aligned}}

(1.49)

In Lemma
, we claimed that
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}
and
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}
are idempotent if
\bm{X}^{+}
is a g-inverse of
\bm{X}
, and thus they are both projection matrices (Definition
, i.e., an idempotent matrix). Since
\bm{X}^{+}
is the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
, by conditions
(C3)
and
(C4)
, these projections are symmetric such that they not just general projections, but orthogonal projections (Lemma
, symmetric idempotent matrices are called orthogonal projectors).

The existence of the pseudo-inverse for any matrix is supported by the CR or rank decomposition of the matrix.

Lemma 93
(Existence of pseudo-inverse).

Every matrix
\bm{X}
has a pseudo-inverse.

Proof
[of Lemma
] Given the CR decomposition (Theorem
) or the rank decomposition (Theorem
) of
\bm{X}=\bm{C}\bm{R}\in\real^{n\times p}
, let

\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{R}^{+}\bm{C}^{+}=\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top},

where
\bm{R}^{+}=\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}
and
\bm{C}^{+}=(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}
. Notably,
\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top}
and
\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C}
are invertible since
\bm{C}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
\bm{R}\in\real^{r\times p}
have full rank
r
due to the properties of the CR decomposition.

Now, we verify the Penrose conditions:

\displaystyle(C1)\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bm{C}\bm{R}\left(\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}\right)\bm{C}\bm{R}=\bm{C}\bm{R}=\bm{X},

\displaystyle(C2)\qquad\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}\right)\bm{C}\bm{R}\left(\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{+},

\displaystyle(C3)\qquad(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{\top}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bm{C}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{C}^{\top}=\bm{C}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bm{C}\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+},

\displaystyle(C4)\qquad(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{R}=\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{R}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bm{R}^{\top}(\bm{R}\bm{R}^{\top})^{-1}(\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C})^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C}\bm{R}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}.

Since all four Penrose conditions are satisfied,
\bm{X}^{+}
is indeed the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
, proving that the pseudo-inverse exists for any
\bm{X}
.

Lemma 94
(Uniqueness of pseudo-inverse).

Every matrix
\bm{X}
has a unique pseudo-inverse.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose
\bm{X}_{1}^{+}
and
\bm{X}_{2}^{+}
are two pseudo-inverses of
\bm{X}
. Then

\displaystyle\bm{X}_{1}^{+}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X}\bm{X}_{1}^{+}=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\bm{X})\bm{X}_{1}^{+}=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{2}^{+})(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{1}^{+})\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C2),(C1)$})

\displaystyle=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{2}^{+})^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{1}^{+})^{\top}=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X}_{2}^{+\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}_{1}^{+\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C3)$})

\displaystyle=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X}_{2}^{+\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X}_{2}^{+\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C1)$})

\displaystyle=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{2}^{+})^{\top}=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X}\bm{X}_{2}^{+}=\bm{X}_{1}^{+}(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\bm{X})\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C3),(C1)$})

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X})(\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\bm{X})\bm{X}_{2}^{+}=(\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}(\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C4)$})

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{1}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}\bm{X}_{2}^{+\top}\bm{X}_{2}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}_{2}^{+\top}\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C1)$})

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}\bm{X}_{2}^{+}=\bm{X}_{2}^{+}\bm{X}\bm{X}_{2}^{+}=\bm{X}_{2}^{+}.\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C4),(C2)$})

This shows that any two pseudo-inverses of
\bm{X}
must be equal. Therefore, the pseudo-inverse is unique.

Lemma 95
(Property of pseudo-inverse).

For any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, it follows that

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
From the first Penrose condition of the pseudo-inverse (see (
)), we know:

\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}=\bm{X}.

Take the transpose of both sides:

(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}\qquad\implies\qquad\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}.

From the third Penrose condition of the pseudo-inverse,
(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{\top}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}
. Substituting this into the equation above, we get

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}.

This completes the proof.

This equality reflects the fact that
\bm{X}^{+}
“projects” vectors in the row space of
\bm{X}
back onto the column space of
\bm{X}
(see below for more details). Specifically:

\bm{X}^{+}
maps any vector
\bm{y}
to the least squares solution of the system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
(we will explore this further in the book).

When
\bm{X}^{+}
is applied to
\bm{X}
, it effectively reconstructs
\bm{X}
in a way that respects its column space and null space.

The equality
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}
encodes the idea that applying
\bm{X}^{+}
to
\bm{X}
does not distort the action of
\bm{X}^{\top}
on vectors.

We are now ready to present the four fundamental subspaces associated with the pseudo-inverse.

{theoremHigh}
[Four subspaces in pseudo-inverse]
Given the pseudo-inverse
\bm{X}^{+}
of
\bm{X}
, the following properties hold:

The column space of
\bm{X}^{+}
is the same as the row space of
\bm{X}
;

The row space of
\bm{X}^{+}
is the same as the column space of
\bm{X}
;

The null space of
\bm{X}^{+}
is the same as the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
;

The null space of
\bm{X}^{+\top}
is the same as the null space of
\bm{X}
.

The relationships among these four subspaces are illustrated in Figure
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
\bm{X}^{+}
is a special rg-inverse, by Lemma
, we have

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})

\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})

\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{+}).

Additionally, from conditions
(C3)
and
(C4)
in the definition of pseudo-inverses, we know that:

(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{\top}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}.

Using the fundamental theorem of linear algebra (Theorem
), we realize that
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})
is the orthogonal complement to
\mathcal{N}((\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{\top})
, and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})
is the orthogonal complement to
\mathcal{N}((\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top})
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})\perp\mathcal{N}((\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{\top})

\displaystyle\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\perp\mathcal{N}((\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})^{\top})

\displaystyle\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}).

This implies

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{+})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+})\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}).

That is,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{+})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
.
By the fundamental theorem of linear algebra, this also implies:
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+\top})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{+\top})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.

Figure 1.18:
Column space and row space of the pseudo-inverse
\bm{X}^{+}
.
\bm{X}
transfers from the row space to the column space.

maps from the column space to the row space. The decomposition of

into

and the transformation to
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}
are discussed in Section

\paragrapharrow

Pseudo-inverse in different cases.
We conclude this section by presenting the pseudo-inverse for various types of matrices. Specifically, we define it in the following cases:

Case
n>p=r
.

That is, the matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full column rank. In this case,

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is a
p\times p
invertible matrix. And we define the left-pseudo-inverse:

{\text{left-pseudo-inverse}=\bm{X}^{+}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}},

which satisfies

\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{I}_{p}.

But

\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\neq\bm{I}.

We can also show that
(\bm{X}^{+})^{+}=\bm{X}
. If
n>p=r
, we have

\displaystyle(\bm{X}^{+})^{+}

\displaystyle=[(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}]^{+}=\bm{X}^{+\top}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top})^{-1}

\displaystyle=\left[(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\right]^{\top}\left\{\left[(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\right]\left[(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\right]^{\top}\right\}^{-1}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\left\{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\right\}^{-1}=\bm{X}.

Case
p>n=r
.

That is, the matrix
\bm{X}
has full row rank.
In this case,

\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
is an
n\times n
invertible matrix. And we define the right-pseudo-inverse:

{\text{right-pseudo-inverse}=\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}},

which satisfies

\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}=\bm{I}_{n}.

But

\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{X}\neq\bm{I}.

(1.50)

Similarly, we can show
(\bm{X}^{+})^{+}=\bm{X}
if
p>n=r
.

Case rank-deficient.

We delay the pseudo-inverse for rank-deficient matrices in the next section via the SVD.

Case
n=p
with full rank.

\bm{X}
is a square invertible matrix, then both the left and right pseudo-inverses reduce to the standard inverse of
\bm{X}
:

\displaystyle\text{left-pseudo-inverse}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{+}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{-1}\bm{X}^{-\top}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{-1};

\displaystyle\text{right-pseudo-inverse}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}^{-\top}\bm{X}^{-1}=\bm{X}^{-1}.

1.7.5
Pseudo-Inverse in SVD

Given the SVD of a matrix
\bm{X}
, we provide further discussion on the pseudo-inverse in different cases.
For the full SVD of matrix
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
, we consider the following cases:

Case
n>p=r
.

Since the matrix
\bm{X}
has independent columns, the left-pseudo-inverse can be obtained by

\displaystyle\text{left-pseudo-inverse}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{+}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}=(\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\bm{U}^{\top}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}\bm{V}^{\top}\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\bm{U}^{\top}=\bm{V}[(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}]\bm{U}^{\top}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top},

where the last equality follows because
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}=(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}
.

Case
p>n=r
.

Since the matrix
\bm{X}
has independent rows, the right-pseudo-inverse can be obtained by

\displaystyle\text{right-pseudo-inverse}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}=(\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top})^{\top}[(\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top})(\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top})^{\top}]^{-1}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\bm{U}^{\top}(\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\bm{U}^{\top})^{-1}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{U}^{-\top}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{U}^{-1}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{U}^{-1}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top},

where the last equality follows because
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top})^{-1}
.

Case rank-deficient.

\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}
,
where the upper-left side of
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\in\real^{p\times n}
is a diagonal matrix
\mathrm{diag}(\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}},\frac{1}{\sigma_{2}},\ldots,\frac{1}{\sigma_{r}})
. It can be easily verified that this definition of the pseudo-inverse satisfies the four conditions in Equation (
).

In all cases, we have
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}
as the pseudo-inverse of
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
with
1/\sigma_{1},1/\sigma_{2},\ldots,1/\sigma_{r}
on its diagonal. We thus conclude the pseudo-inverse from SVD:

\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{V}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{U}^{\top},\quad\text{with }\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\text{ and }\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\in\real^{r\times r}.

(1.51)

See also Table
.

Table 1.2:
Pseudo-inverse in SVD.

If
\bm{X}
is nonsingular, then
\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{-1}
, so (
) is a generalization of the usual inverse.
The pseudo-inverse of a scalar is

\sigma^{+}=\begin{cases}1/\sigma,&\text{if }\sigma\neq 0;\\
0,&\text{if }\sigma=0.\end{cases}

This shows the important fact that the pseudo-inverse
\bm{X}^{+}
is not a continuous function of
\bm{X}
, unless we allow only perturbations that do not change the rank of
\bm{X}
. The pseudo-inverse has the property

\bm{X}^{+}=\lim_{\delta\to 0}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\delta\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}.

Using the SVD representation of pseudo-inverses in (
), we can derive additional properties of the pseudo-inverse of a matrix
\bm{X}
.

Lemma 96
(Properties of pseudo-inverse using SVD).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
. The following properties of the pseudo-inverse follow from (
).

1.

\bm{X}^{+}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{+}
.

2.

When
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, this becomes
\bm{X}^{+}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top},\ (\bm{X}^{\top})^{+}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
.

3.

(\bm{X}^{+})^{+}=\bm{X}
.

4.

(\alpha\bm{X})^{+}=\alpha^{+}\bm{X}^{+}
.

5.

(\bm{X}^{+})^{\top}=(\bm{X}^{\top})^{+}
.

6.

(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{+}=\bm{X}^{+}(\bm{X}^{\top})^{+}
.

7.

\bm{X}
,
\bm{X}^{\top}
,
\bm{X}^{+}
, and
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}
all have rank equal to
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})
.

8.

If
\bm{U}
and
\bm{V}
are orthogonal,
(\bm{U}\bm{X}\bm{V}^{\top})^{+}=\bm{V}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}
.

9.

If
\bm{X}=\sum_{i}\bm{X}_{i}
, where
\bm{X}_{i}\bm{X}_{j}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0}
,
\bm{X}_{i}^{\top}\bm{X}_{j}=\boldsymbol{0}
,
i\neq j
, then
\bm{X}^{+}=\sum_{i}\bm{X}_{i}^{+}
.

10.

If
\bm{X}
is normal (
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
), then
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}
and
(\bm{X}^{n})^{+}=(\bm{X}^{+})^{n}
.

For the pseudo-inverse, the relations
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}
and
(\bm{X}\bm{Y})^{+}=\bm{Y}^{+}\bm{X}^{+}
are not in general true. For example, let
\bm{X}=\footnotesize[1,0]
and
\bm{Y}=[1,1]^{\top}
. Then
\bm{X}\bm{Y}=1
, but

\bm{Y}^{+}\bm{X}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}[1,1]\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix}\normalsize=\frac{1}{2}.

Necessary and sufficient conditions for the identity
(\bm{X}\bm{Y})^{+}=\bm{Y}^{+}\bm{X}^{+}
to hold were established by
Greville 1966
. The following theorem provides an important sufficient condition under which this equality holds.

{theoremHigh}

[Sufficient Condition for
(\bm{X}\bm{Y})^{+}=\bm{Y}^{+}\bm{X}^{+}
]
If
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
\bm{Y}\in\real^{p\times m}
, and
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Y})=p
,
then

(\bm{X}\bm{Y})^{+}=\bm{Y}^{+}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{Y}^{\top}(\bm{Y}\bm{Y}^{\top})^{-1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The last equality follows from Lemma
.
. The first equality follows from the proof of Lemma
and is verified by showing that the four Penrose conditions are satisfied.

\paragrapharrow

Another way to see the subspaces in pseudo-inverse via SVD.
Using SVD, we provide an alternative perspective on demonstrating the four fundamental subspaces associated with the pseudo-inverse introduced in Theorem
and Figure
.
From Lemma
, consider the symmetric matrix
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top}
and its spectral decomposition:
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top}=\bm{V}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}\bm{V}^{\top}
.
The column space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top})
is spanned by the eigenvectors of this decomposition.
Therefore, the set
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2}\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
forms an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top})
.

We now establish the following results:

1.

Since
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top}
is symmetric, its row space coincides with its column space.

2.

Every column of
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top}
is a linear combination of the columns of
\bm{X}^{+}
. Therefore, the column space of
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top}

\subseteq
the column space of
\bm{X}^{+}
, i.e.,
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top})\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+})
.

3.

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{+})
by Lemma
.

Consequently, the row space of
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top}
= the column space of
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top}
= the column space of
\bm{X}^{+}
, i.e.,
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}^{+\top})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+})
.
Consequently,
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
constitutes an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+})
. We also proved in Theorem
that
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of the row space of
\bm{X}
(i.e., basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
). Thus,
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, as shown in Figure
.

Similarly, if we apply this process to
\bm{X}^{+\top}\bm{X}^{+}
, we can show that the row space of
\bm{X}^{+}
is equal to the column space of
\bm{X}
, and the null space of
\bm{X}^{+}
is equal to the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
.

Now, consider a vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}
in the row space of
\bm{X}
.
Since
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
forms an orthonormal basis for the row space of
\bm{X}
, we can express
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}
as
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}x_{i}\bm{v}_{i}
(see Theorem
). For a vector
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}
in the column space of
\bm{X}
, we have
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}
and

\bm{X}^{+}\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\bm{v}_{i}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}x_{i}\bm{v}_{i}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}x_{i}\bm{v}_{i}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}.

For any vector
\bm{e}
in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
, we have
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{e}=\boldsymbol{0}
, since
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{+})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
. Any vector
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
can be decomposed into
\bm{y}=\widehat{\bm{y}}+\bm{e}
, where
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is a vector in the column space of
\bm{X}
, and
\bm{e}
is a vector in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
. That is,

\bm{X}^{+}\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+},

where
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}
lies in the row space of
\bm{X}
.

In conclusion, for any vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}
in row space of
\bm{X}
, we have

\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+}\quad\implies\quad\bm{X}^{+}\widehat{\bm{y}}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{+},

and the relationship is illustrated in Figure
.

KL of Gaussians.
Given two probability distribution function

and

, we denote the

between

and

D_{\mathrm{KL}}[P\parallel Q]=\int P(\bm{x})\ln\left(\frac{P(\bm{x})}{Q(\bm{x})}\right)d\bm{x}\geq 0
, where the equality is obtained only when
P=Q
.
Given

. This expression is commonly used as the KL loss in fitting variational autoencoders
(
Lu 2021a
)
.

KL of Gaussians.

12.

Properties of expectation of conditionals.

Let
x
and
y
be two random variables, and let
h
be a function.
Show that

(a).

Note that
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]
is a function of
y
. However, if
x
is independent of
y
, then
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]={\textnormal{x}}
.

(b).

\mathbb{E}[c\mid{\textnormal{x}}]={\textnormal{x}}
, where
c
is a constant.

(c).

Linearity:
\mathbb{E}[a{\textnormal{x}}_{1}+b{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]=a\cdot\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]+b\cdot\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]
.

(d).

Conditional constant:
\mathbb{E}[h({\textnormal{y}}){\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]=h({\textnormal{y}})\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]
, where
h({\textnormal{y}})
is called a
conditional constant
w.r.t.
y
.

(e).

Monotonicity: if
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\leq{\textnormal{x}}_{2}
, then
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\leq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]
.

(f).

Tower property:
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\mid h({\textnormal{y}})\right]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid h({\textnormal{y}})]
; that is,
h({\textnormal{y}})
conveys information at most as
y
.

(g).

Unbiasedness:
\mathbb{E}\big\{\mathbb{E}[h({\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}})\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\big\}=\mathbb{E}[h({\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}})]
; specially,
\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\big]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]
.

(h).

Least squares:
\mathbb{E}\big[\big({\textnormal{y}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid{\textnormal{x}}]\big)^{2}\big]\leq\mathbb{E}\big[\big({\textnormal{y}}-h({\textnormal{x}})\big)^{2}\big]
for any function
h
. This also means
g({\textnormal{x}})\triangleq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid{\textnormal{x}}]
is the best estimate in the least squares sense.

13.

Sum of random variables by convolution.

Let
x
and
y
be continuous random variables with probability density functions
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}
and
f_{{\textnormal{y}}}
. Show that the density function of
{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}
is the convolution of
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}
with
f_{{\textnormal{y}}}
:

f_{{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}}(u)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(u-v)f_{\textnormal{y}}(v)\,dv.

14.

Properties of variance and correlation.

Let
{\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},{\textnormal{y}},{\mathbf{x}}
be random variables or vectors, and let
a,b
be constants.
Show that

Let
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
be a real symmetric matrix. Then
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is positive semidefinite (Definition
) if and only if
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is the covariance matrix of some random vector
{\mathbf{x}}
.

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}])^{2}=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{x}}]
.

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[a{\textnormal{x}}+b]=a^{2}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]
.

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}\big[\sum_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\big]=\sum_{i}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]+\sum_{i\neq j}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i},{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]
.

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]
.

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[a{\textnormal{x}}_{1}+b{\textnormal{x}}_{2},{\textnormal{y}}]=a\cdot\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{y}}]+b\cdot\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2},{\textnormal{y}}]
; that is, covariance is linear in one variable.

If
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}^{2}]<\infty
, then the following are equivalent:

(i)

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]
;

(ii)

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]=0
;

(iii)

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\pm{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]+\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]
.

Note that independence will imply these three last properties, but none of these properties imply independence.

Let
h
be a nondecreasing function such that
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]<\infty
and
\mathbb{E}[h({\textnormal{x}})^{2}]<\infty
. Then
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}},h({\textnormal{x}})]>0
.

Let

and

be two random variables. The

of

given

is defined as

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\triangleq\mathbb{E}\big[\big({\textnormal{x}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\big)^{2}\mid{\textnormal{y}}\big]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]-(\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}])^{2}.

(1.52)

The conditional variance tells us how much variance is left if we use

Chapter 2
Least Squares Approximations

2.1
Least Squares Approximations

L
Linear models is a fundamental technique in solving regression problems, and its core method is the least squares approximation, which aims to minimize the sum of squared errors between predicted and observed values.
This approach is particularly appropriate when the goal is to estimate the regression function that minimizes the expected squared error loss.
linear models have found wide application across various domains. Examples include decision making
(
Dawes and Corrigan 1974
)
, time series analysis
(
Christensen 1991
;
Lu 2017
;
Lu and Yi 2022
)
, and fields such as production science, social science, and soil science
(
Fox 1997
;
Lane 2002
;
Schaeffer 2004
;
Mrode 2014
)
.

We consider the system

\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},

(2.1)

where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
represents the input data matrix (or
predictors
,
predictor variables
,
covariates
,
features
).
These predictors may be numerical by nature, or derived from categorical variables through encoding.
In general, each column will be a function of the actual covariates
\bm{z}_{i}
; for example
\bm{x}_{i}=\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\bm{z}_{i}),i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
.
And
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
is the observation vector (or
target, response, output variables, outcomes
),
n
represents the number of observations (sample size), and
p
denotes the number of features (dimension value).
The vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
constitutes a vector of weights of the linear model, which is called the
coefficient vector
or
weight vector
.
In practice, a
bias term
(also called the
intercept
) is often included by adding a column of ones as the first column of
\bm{X}
. This allows the least squares method to solve:

\widetilde{\bm{X}}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[\bm{1},\bm{X}]\begin{bmatrix}\beta_{0}\\
\boldsymbol{\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{y}.

(2.2)

Equivalently, for each data point
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, we have

y_{i}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x_{i1}+\beta_{2}x_{i2}+\ldots+\beta_{p-1}x_{i,p-1}.

For simplicity, we will denote
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
and
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
simply as
\bm{X}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, respectively, in all subsequent discussions unless otherwise specified.

\paragrapharrow

General thoughts.
In many practical applications, we want to find an approximate solution to a problem or set of equations that, for noise reasons or whatever other reasons, does not have a solution, or not unrelatedly does not have a unique solution. A canonical example of this is given by the very
overdetermined
(i.e., overconstrained)
least squares (LS, or ordinary least squares, OLS)
problem or called the
large sample problem
(
n\gg p
in (
)), and this will be our focus for the next several sections.

The least squares method originated from the need to reduce the impact of measurement errors when fitting a mathematical model to observed data. One way to achieve this is by using more measurements (
n
) than unknown parameters (
p
) in the model.

While some (but not all) of the concepts we discuss can also apply to
underdetermined
(i.e.,
underconstrained
) LS problems (see Section
), we will primarily focus on the simpler and more commonly used case of overdetermined LS problems.

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
be given. If
n\gg p
, in which case there are significantly more rows/constraints than columns/variables, then in general, there does not exist a vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
such that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
.
Define the column space of
\bm{X}
, denoted
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, as
\{\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\mid\forall\,\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in\real^{p}\}
.
Thus, the meaning of
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
has no solution is that
\bm{y}
has a part that sits outside the column space of
\bm{X}
.
That is,
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, but
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
is a
p
-dimensional subspace of
n
, and so with even a little noise, numerical instability, etc., there will be a part of
\bm{y}
that is not captured as a linear combination of the columns of
\bm{X}
.
In other words, the error
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
cannot be reduced to zero.

In this case, a popular way to find the “best” vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
such that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\approx\bm{y}
is to minimize the norm of the residuals, i.e., to solve
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert
, where
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
is some norm. The most popular choice is the Euclidean or
\ell_{2}
norm (Definition
).
In this case, the LS problem is to minimize the sum of squares of the residual, i.e., to solve

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}.

(2.3)

If we let
\bm{X}^{+}
denote the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
(Section
), then the solution to this minimization problem is:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}.

(2.4)

The vector
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is called a least squares solution, i.e.,
\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
is minimized.

Actually, we should note that
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}+\boldsymbol{\xi}
, where
\boldsymbol{\xi}\perp\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, i.e., where
\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\real^{n}
is any vector orthogonal to the row span of
\bm{X}
(
\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
), solves the LS problem given in (
).
Among all such solutions, the one given by
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
is the minimal (
\ell_{2}
) norm solution to the LS problem.
We will be interested in working with this shortest or minimum-norm solution (Theorems
and
).

In most practical settings, the matrix
\bm{X}
will have full column rank, especially when working with real-world data, which often naturally avoids collinearity, or after preprocessing steps that ensure linear independence among the columns. In this case, the least squares solution simplifies to:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}\equiv(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}.

(2.5)

\paragrapharrow

Numerical methods and loss functions.
In (
), we show that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
minimizes the residual norm:
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}
.
However, the term
least squares
comes from the fact that what we are actually minimizing is the square of this norm:
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
, i.e., the least sum of squared errors.
This is equivalent to minimizing the norm itself because the square function is monotonically increasing for nonnegative values. That is:

\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}\equiv\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}.

In many computer programs using numerical methods, e.g.,
gradient descent and conjugate descent methods
,
f_{1}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
is defined as the
loss function
(or called
objective function
,
cost function
) rather than
\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}
since the gradient of the former one can be derived easily:

\nabla f_{1}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=2(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}).

Due to the factor of 2 in the gradient, it is often more convenient to define the loss function as:

f_{2}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2},

which simplifies expressions during optimization.
Another common variation is to normalize the loss by the number of samples
n
, resulting in:

f_{3}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\qquad\text{or}\qquad f_{4}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where
n
is the sample size.
There are several reasons why normalization by
n
is beneficial:

Mathematical convenience.
The term
\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
represents the squared error summed over all
n
samples. Without dividing by
n
, the loss value grows proportionally with the number of samples. This makes it harder to interpret or compare across datasets of different sizes.

Dividing by
n
normalizes the loss to represent the
average squared error per sample
, which is independent of the dataset size. This allows for more meaningful comparisons between models trained on datasets of varying sizes.

Numerical stability.
For large datasets, the unnormalized loss
\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
can become very large, leading to potential numerical instability during optimization. Dividing by
n
keeps the loss values in a reasonable range, improving numerical stability.

Using the normalized form often makes gradient-based optimization methods (e.g., stochastic gradient descent) more stable because the gradients are scaled appropriately.

Statistical estimation.
In statistics, the least squares problem can be viewed as maximizing the likelihood under the assumption that the errors are normally distributed. The normalized loss
\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
corresponds to the
mean squared error (MSE)
, which is a commonly used metric in statistical modeling.

Consistency.
Many other loss functions in machine learning (e.g., cross-entropy loss, hinge loss) are expressed as averages over the samples. Dividing by
n
ensures consistency with these conventions, making it easier to switch between different loss functions or combine them in composite objectives.

In other words, dividing the least squares loss by
n
serves to normalize the loss, making it interpretable, mathematically convenient, statistically meaningful, consistent with other loss functions, and numerically stable. While it does not affect the solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
itself, it improves the overall process of optimization and interpretation.
In this book, we will use these forms interchangeably depending on context and convenience.

\paragrapharrow

Matrix LS problems.
In many scenarios, we may also consider the
matrix least squares
(a.k.a.,
multiple-response least squares
) problem, which is formulated as:

\bm{B}^{*}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times q}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{B}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times q}}\sum_{i=1}^{q}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i}-\bm{y}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(2.6)

where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
\bm{B}=[\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1},\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\beta}_{q}]\in\real^{p\times q}
, and
\bm{Y}=[\bm{y}_{1},\bm{y}_{2},\ldots,\bm{y}_{q}]\in\real^{n\times q}
.
This, apparently, can be solved using
q
least squares problems (
).
In other words, the problem is
column-wise decomposable
.
However, when the number of responses
q
is much larger than both the number of samples
n
and the number of features
p
(i.e.,
q\gg\max\{n,p\}
), it becomes impractical to transmit or store the full response matrix
\bm{Y}
, especially in communication-constrained environments.
To address this issue, we introduce
sketched least squares with quantized response
, which reduces the amount of data that needs to be communicated while still allowing for accurate estimation. This approach will be discussed in detail in Section
.

\paragrapharrow

General insights.
This LS problem is ubiquitous and has many well-known interpretations.
From a statistical perspective, it provides the
best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE)
under certain assumptions about the data-generating process; see Section
.
From a geometric perspective, the solution corresponds to the orthogonal projection of the response vector
\bm{y}
onto the column space of the design matrix
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
; see Section
.
Note that the latter interpretation is basically a statement about the data at hand, while the former interpretation is basically a statement about models and unseen data. This parallels the algorithmic-statistical approaches:

Algorithmic perspective
(see Chapter
). From an algorithmic perspective, the relevant question is: How long does it take to compute the least squares solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
? The answer to this question is that it takes
\mathcal{O}(np^{2})
time. This can be accomplished using one of several numerical algorithms—with the Cholesky decomposition (which is good if
\bm{X}
has full column rank and is very well-conditioned); or with a variant of the QR decomposition (which is somewhat slower, but more numerically stable); or by computing the full SVD
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
(which is often, but certainly not always, overkill, but which can be easier to explain), and letting
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}
.
Although these methods differ significantly in terms of implementation and numerical behavior, asymptotically they all require roughly the same amount of time—on the order of a constant multiple of
np^{2}
.

Statistical perspective
(see Chapters
and
). From a statistical perspective, the relevant question is: Under what conditions is computing
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
the appropriate choice?
The answer to this question is that this LS optimization is the right problem to solve when the relationship between the responses and predictors is roughly linear, when there are no small number of components that are particularly important or influential (called leverage points), and when the error processes generating the data are “nice” (in the sense that the errors have mean zero, constant variance, are uncorrelated, and are normally distributed; or when we have adequate sample size to rely on large sample theory).
When these assumptions hold, the LS estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
has strong theoretical guarantees. However, if the assumptions are violated—even slightly—the performance of LS can degrade significantly.
Thus, from a statistical perspective, a natural next question to ask is: What should one do when the assumptions underlying the use of LS methods are not satisfied or are only imperfectly satisfied?

In the remaining sections of this chapter, we will explore least squares solutions from several complementary perspectives: calculus, convex optimization, linear algebra, and geometry.
That is, to obtain and to interpret the least squares solutions from each of these viewpoints.

2.2
Least Squares in the Big Picture

We return to the basic problem
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, which
is at the core of our discussion. For the least squares problem, we consider the following questions:

Q1: What is the least squares solution?

Q2: When can uniqueness of the least squares solution be claimed?

Q3: When can uniqueness of the least squares solution with minimum-norm be claimed?

To address these questions, we require the following lemma regarding the optimality condition for the least squares problem.

Lemma 97
(Optimality condition of LS).

Given
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, let

{\mathbb{B}}\triangleq\{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\min\}

denote the set of all least squares solutions. Then,
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in{\mathbb{B}}
if and only if the following orthogonality condition holds:

\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})=\boldsymbol{0}.\penalty\

(2.7)

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Assume that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfies
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{e}=\boldsymbol{0}
, where
\bm{e}\triangleq\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Then for any
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}
, we have

\widetilde{\bm{e}}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{e}+\bm{X}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq\bm{e}+\bm{X}\bm{d}.

From this we obtain

\widetilde{\bm{e}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{e}}=(\bm{e}+\bm{X}\bm{d})^{\top}(\bm{e}+\bm{X}\bm{d})=\bm{e}^{\top}\bm{e}+\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{d}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
,
which is minimized when
\bm{d}=\boldsymbol{0}
; that is,
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Conversely, suppose
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{e}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\alpha}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
. If
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\gamma\boldsymbol{\alpha}
, then

\widetilde{\bm{e}}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{e}-\gamma\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\alpha}

and

\widetilde{\bm{e}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{e}}=\bm{e}^{\top}\bm{e}-2\gamma\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\gamma^{2}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\alpha})^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\alpha}<\bm{e}^{\top}\bm{e}

for sufficiently small
\gamma>0
. Hence
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is not a least squares solution, which leads to a contradiction. Hence,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{e}
must be zero.

We now present a unified view of the least squares problem in the following theorem. The underlying ideas will become clearer as we proceed. This theorem answers the question Q1 introduced at the beginning of this section.

{theoremHigh}
[A unified view of least squares problems]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.
Then the least squares problem
f(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
has a minimizer
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{n}
if and only if there exists a vector
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\real^{p}
such that

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha},

(2.8)

where
\bm{X}^{+}
denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
(Section
):

This shows that the least squares has a
unique
minimizer of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
only when
\bm{X}^{+}
is a left inverse of
\bm{X}
(Definition
, and
\bm{X}
is left-invertible only when
\bm{X}
has full column rank by Lemma
). The solution in (
) is a special case of this result.

The optimal value is
f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})\bm{y}
.

If
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
:
\left\lVert\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}
.

This means that any vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
that minimizes
f(\boldsymbol{\beta})
must be in this form, where:

\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
(by Theorem
) is the particular solution (the minimum-norm solution).

(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
(by Theorem
) is the homogeneous solution that accounts for the freedom in
\boldsymbol{\beta}
coming from the null space of
\bm{X}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By Lemma
, the solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
must satisfy
\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})=\boldsymbol{0}
.
This equation means that the vector
\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
is orthogonal to the column space of
\bm{X}
, i.e., the error
\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
lies in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
:

\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\perp\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}).

(2.9)

To solve for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, we recognize that the equation
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
may not always have an exact solution (i.e., when
\bm{y}\notin\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
). Instead, we seek the minimum-norm solution that minimizes
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}
.
The pseudo-inverse
\bm{X}^{+}
provides the best possible solution by giving the unique minimum-norm least squares solution (see the argument in the sequel):

\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{particular}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}.

(2.10)

To see
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{particular}}
satisfies (
), we have

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{particular}}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
, where we used the fact that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}
(Lemma
).

However, this is just one possible solution.
To see the full solution set, we consider two cases.

Case 1:
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

For this case, the solution in (
) is obvious by the properties (
\bm{X}(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\boldsymbol{0}
) and uniqueness of the pseudo-inverse of a matrix (Lemma
).

Case 2:
\bm{y}\notin\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

Let
\bm{e}\triangleq\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{particular}}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
. Since we can looking for solutions
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
that satisfy
\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. Two possible scenarios are:

\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{y}=\bm{e}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{e}.

The former scenario implies that
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{particular}}=\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{y}
, which leads to
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\frac{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{particular}}}{2}
, i.e.,
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, matching Case 1.
Therefore, only the second scenario applies.
Since
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is in
p
, the full space of solutions consists of the particular solution
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{particular}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
plus any vector in the null space of
\bm{X}
(i.e., any
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{null}}
that satisfies
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{null}}=\boldsymbol{0}
,
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{null}}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\triangleq\{\bm{z}\mid\bm{X}\bm{z}=\boldsymbol{0}\}
).
Thus, the general solution for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
must then take the form:

\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{null}},\qquad\text{with}\quad\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{null}}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}).

(2.11)

Since
\bm{X}-\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}=\boldsymbol{0}
by (
), the projection onto the null space of
\bm{X}
is given by:

\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{null}}=(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha},\quad\text{for some }\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\real^{p}.

(2.12)

This follows because
(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})
is a projection matrix onto
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
(see Theorem
and Section
for more details).

On the other hand, since
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\text{null}}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{+})\equiv\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
(see Theorem
, Theorem
), it follows that

\left\lVert\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This shows that
\left\lVert\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}
if
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
and completes the proof.

Definition 98
(Normal equation).

We can express the zero gradient of
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
w.r.t.
\boldsymbol{\beta}
as
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
. The equation is also known as the normal equation.
Gauss developed an elimination method for solving the normal equation that uses pivots chosen from the diagonal
(
Stewart 1995
)
. Then all
reduced matrices are symmetric, and the storage and number of needed operations are reduced
by half. Later, the preferred way to implement this elimination process became the Cholesky decomposition.

The above analysis shows that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is a least squares solution if and only if the residual
\bm{e}\triangleq\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is perpendicular to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
from the normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{e}=\boldsymbol{0}
:

\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\perp\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}).

(2.13)

For this reason, the residual
\bm{e}
is sometimes denoted as
\bm{y}^{\perp}\triangleq\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Based on this, we can now state the following equivalent characterizations of a least squares solution.

Corollary 99
(Least squares solution).

The following statements are equivalent:

1.

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
solves the least squares problem
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}
.

2.

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfies the normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
.

3.

The residual
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is orthogonal to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

Since the least squares estimate is widely used in regression problems, it is important to understand how it generates predictions. After obtaining the least squares estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
from the data matrix
\bm{X}
and the response vector
\bm{y}
, the predicted value of
\bm{y}
is given by

\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

For a new input vector
\bm{x}_{\text{new}}
, the corresponding
prediction
(also referred to as the “
curve-fit
”) is simply computed as

\widehat{y}_{\text{new}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}.

Theorem
shows that
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
is a minimum-norm solution for the least squares problem in general.
Based on the properties of the pseudo-inverse, we can distinguish several important cases:

Large-sample least squares problem.
If
n>p=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, then the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
is given by
\bm{X}^{+}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
. This shows

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}.

That is, the least squares solution is
unique
and answers the question Q2 introduced at the beginning of this section.
This scenario—where there are more observations than predictors—is often referred to as the
large-sample LS problem
. It will be discussed further in
Sections
,
,
,
,
, and Chapter
.

Rank-deficient least squares problem.
If
n>p>\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, then the matrix
\bm{X}
does not have full rank and
\bm{X}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}
is a minimizer, where
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}
denotes the SVD of
\bm{X}
. This rank-deficient LS problem will be further discussed in Theorem
, and Sections
and
.

High-dimensional least squares problem.
If
p\geq n=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, then the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
is given by
\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}
.
In this case, the general least squares solution becomes

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha}.

Here, the minimum-norm solution is
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\triangleq\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}
.
This high-dimensional LS problem will be further discussed in Section
.

\paragrapharrow

Matrix least squares problems.
When the response variable
\bm{y}
is extended from a vector to a matrix
\bm{Y}
, the problem becomes what is known as a
matrix least squares problem
.
A direct consequence of Theorem
is the following result for such problems.

Corollary 100
(Matrix least squares).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
.

Given further
\bm{Y}\in\real^{p\times q}
, then the least squares problem
f_{1}(\bm{B})=\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{B}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
has a minimizer
\widehat{\bm{B}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{Y}\in\real^{p\times q}
.

Given further
\bm{Y}\in\real^{q\times p}
, then the least squares problem
f_{2}(\bm{B})=\left\lVert\bm{B}\bm{X}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
has a minimizer
\widehat{\bm{B}}=\bm{Y}\bm{X}^{+}\in\real^{q\times n}
.

Rank-Deficient Least Squares Problems

If
r=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})<p
, then
\bm{X}
has a null space of dimension
p-r>0
. Then the problem
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}
is
rank-deficient
, and its solution is not unique. If
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is a particular least squares solution, then the set of all least squares solutions is
{\mathbb{B}}=\{\boldsymbol{\beta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\boldsymbol{\alpha}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\}
. In this case we can seek the least squares solution of minimum-norm
\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}
, i.e., solve

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in{\mathbb{B}}}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2},\qquad{\mathbb{B}}=\{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}=\min\}.

(2.14)

This solution is always unique (question Q3 introduced at the beginning of this section); see Theorem
.
For the least squares problem, the set of all minimizers
{\mathbb{B}}
is convex.
To see this, let
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1},\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}\in{\mathbb{B}}
and
\lambda\in[0,1]
. Then we have:

\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}(\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\lambda\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}+(1-\lambda)\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}\right\rVert_{2}=\mathop{\min}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}.

Therefore, the convex combination
\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
also belongs to
{\mathbb{B}}
, which confirms that
{\mathbb{B}}
is a convex set.

Consistent System

Consider the linear system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
, where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
If there is at least one solution to this system, it is called
consistent
; otherwise, it is called
inconsistent
. It can be shown that the system is consistent if and only if
\mathrm{rank}([\bm{X},\bm{y}])=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, i.e., the
augmented matrix

[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
has the same rank as the observed coefficient matrix
\bm{X}
.
This condition also implies that
\bm{y}
lies in the column space of
\bm{X}
.
For consistent systems, we can distinguish the following two cases:

When
\bm{X}
has full column rank
p
, the linear system has a
unique
solution:
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
. Refer to its description in the left inverse (Theorem
).

When
\bm{X}
has full row rank
n
, the linear system has at least one solution:
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}\bm{y}
, where
\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}
is a right inverse of
\bm{X}
. Refer to its description in the right inverse (Theorem
).

If the system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
is consistent, then the minimum-norm solution satisfies the normal equation of second kind; see Theorem
below for more details:

\text{(NE2)}:\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\quad\implies\quad\quad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{y}.

(2.15)

If
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=n
, then
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
is nonsingular, and the solution to (
) (i.e., the minimum-norm solution) is
unique
:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}\equiv\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}.

(2.16)

Uniqueness of LS Problems

From the result in (
) and Corollary
, we obtain the following characterization of a solution to the least squares problem (
). It includes both the over- and underdetermined cases.

{theoremHigh}

[Minimum-norm solution]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.
And let
\boldsymbol{\beta}
be a solution of the problem
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}
. Then
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is a
unique
least squares solution of minimum-norm if and only if
\boldsymbol{\beta}\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
or, equivalently,
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}
,
\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in\real^{n}
.
That is, for
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
of any dimension and rank, the least squares solution of minimum norm
\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}
is
unique
and characterized by the conditions

\bm{e}\triangleq\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\perp\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}).

(2.17)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Assume
\boldsymbol{\beta}\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.
Let
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
be any least squares solution, and set
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\alpha}
, where
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
. Then
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\boldsymbol{0}
, so
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is also a least squares solution. Since
\boldsymbol{\beta}\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
and
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
, by the Pythagorean theorem,
\big\lVert\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, which is minimized when
\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
The reverse claim follows from the normal equation.

Augmented LS Problem

From the normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
, we show that the error component
\bm{e}\triangleq\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
satisfies the orthogonality condition
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{e}=\boldsymbol{0}
. These forms a symmetric augmented system of
n+p
equations:

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}&\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{e}\\
\boldsymbol{\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{y}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},\quad\bm{y}\in\real^{n}.

(2.18)

Apparently, this augmented system is a special case of the following augmented system, which we call the
augmented LS (AuLS) problem
:

(\text{AuLS}):\qquad\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}&\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\\
\boldsymbol{\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{y}\\
\bm{z}\end{bmatrix},\quad\bm{y}\in\real^{n},\quad\bm{z}\in\real^{p},

(2.19)

On the other hand, we also consider the high-dimensional problem (consistent underdetermined linear system), of which the minimum-norm solution is

(\text{MN}):\quad\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\ \text{s.t.}\ \bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{z}\quad\implies\quad\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\quad\implies\quad\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{z},

where
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{z}
is called the normal equation of the second kind; see (
).
Therefore, the minimum-norm solution is also a special case of the AuLS system by setting
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}
.

Therefore, both the standard least squares and minimum-norm problems are special cases of the augmented LS problem.
Such AuLS systems represent the equilibrium of a physical system and occur in many applications; see
Strang 1988
;
Björck 2024
for more details.
The system is nonsingular if and and only if
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, and its inverse is

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}&\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}-\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}&\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\\
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}&-(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\end{bmatrix},\quad\text{when }\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p.

(2.20)

Note that
\bm{H}\triangleq\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
is the orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
; see Section
.

{theoremHigh}

If
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, then the augmented system (
) has a unique solution that solves the primal and dual least squares problems,

\displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\bm{z}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta},

(2.21)

\displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\real^{n}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{z}.

(2.22)

Proof

Differentiating (
2.21
) gives
\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})=\bm{z}
, which with
\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
is the augmented system (
). This system is also obtained by differentiating the Lagrangian

L(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\bm{y})^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\bm{y})+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\bm{z})

for (
2.22
) and equating to zero, where
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is the vector of Lagrange multipliers.

Special Least Squares Systems

If the columns
\bm{X}[:,j]
of
\bm{X}
are mutually orthogonal, then least squares problems simplify considerably. The reason is that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is diagonal and then so is
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
in the full rank case. The result is that

\widehat{\beta}_{j}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ij}y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ij}^{2}}=\frac{\bm{X}[:,j]^{\top}\bm{y}}{\left\lVert\bm{X}[:,j]\right\rVert_{2}^{2}},\qquad\forall\,j\in\{1,2\ldots,p\}.

This means the coefficients can be computed independently, one at a time, without needing to solve a system of equations.
In the even more special case that each of
\bm{X}[:,j]
is a unit vector (or the columns
\bm{X}
are mutually orthogonormal), then
\widehat{\beta}_{j}=\bm{X}[:,j]^{\top}\bm{y}
.

Orthogonal predictors bring great simplification. The cost of computation is only
O(np)
. The variance of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is
\sigma^{2}\mathrm{diag}(1/\left\lVert\bm{X}[:,j]\right\rVert_{2}^{2})
(see Chapter
for more details) so the components of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
are uncorrelated. In the Gaussian case, the
\widehat{\beta}_{j}
are statistically independent in addition to the computational independence noted above.

Leave One Out Formula

In this subsection we explore what happens to a (full-rank) least squares model when one data point (a row in
\bm{X}
) is added or removed. We begin with the
Sherman-Morrison formula
. Suppose that
\bm{A}
is an invertible
n\times n
matrix, and let
\bm{u}
and
\bm{v}
be
n
-dimensional vectors such that
1+\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{u}\neq 0
. Then

(\bm{A}+\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top})^{-1}=\bm{A}^{-1}-\frac{\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}}{1+\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{u}}.

(2.23)

This can be proved by multiplying the right-hand side of the equation by
\bm{A}+\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top}
and checking that the product equals the identity matrix. The condition
1+\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{u}\neq 0
ensures that the updated matrix
\bm{A}+\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top}
remains invertible if
\bm{A}
is nonsingular.

Now suppose we delete the
i
-th observation from the data
\bm{X}
.
Then
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}
is replaced by
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})_{(-i)}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}
, where
\bm{x}_{i}\in\real^{p}
is a column vector representing the
i
-th row of
\bm{X}
, using a subscript of
(-i)
to denote the removal of the
i
-th observation. We can fit this into (
) by taking
\bm{u}=\bm{x}_{i}
and
\bm{v}=-\bm{x}_{i}
. Then,

\displaystyle(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}_{(-i)}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}+\frac{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}}{1-\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}}

\displaystyle\triangleq(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}+\frac{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}}{1-h_{ii}},

where we let
\bm{H}\triangleq\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
, and
h_{ii}\triangleq\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}
.
We also find that
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y})_{(-i)}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{x}_{i}y_{i}
.
Therefore, the leave-one-out update for the least squares solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
becomes

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{(-i)}

\displaystyle=\Big((\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}+\frac{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}}{1-h_{ii}}\Big)\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{x}_{i}y_{i}\right)

\displaystyle=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}y_{i}+\frac{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}{1-h_{ii}}-\frac{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}h_{ii}y_{i}}{1-h_{ii}}

\displaystyle=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\frac{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}{1-h_{ii}}-\frac{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}y_{i}}{1-h_{ii}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{i}(y_{i}-\widehat{y}_{i})}{1-h_{ii}},

where
\widehat{y}_{i}\triangleq\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Thus, the prediction for
y_{i}
when
(\bm{x}_{i},y_{i})
is removed from the least squares fit is

\widehat{y}_{i,(-i)}\triangleq\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{(-i)}=\widehat{y}_{i}-\frac{h_{ii}(y_{i}-\widehat{y}_{i})}{1-h_{ii}}.

Multiplying both sides by
1-h_{ii}
and rearranging gives:

\widehat{y}_{i}=h_{ii}y_{i}+(1-h_{ii})\widehat{y}_{i,(-i)}.

(2.24)

Equation (
) has an important interpretation. The least squares fit
\widehat{y}_{i}
is a weighted combination of
y_{i}
itself and the least squares prediction we would have made for it, had it been left out of the fitting. The larger
h_{ii}
is, the more that
\widehat{y}_{i}
depends on
y_{i}
. It also means that if we want to compute a “leave one out” residual
y_{i}-\widehat{y}_{i,(-i)}
, we don’t have to actually take
(\bm{x}_{i},y_{i})
out of the data and rerun the estimate. We can instead use

y_{i}-\widehat{y}_{i,(-i)}=\frac{y_{i}-\widehat{y}_{i}}{1-h_{ii}}.

(2.25)

This analysis will be important for the diagnostics for linear models; see Section
.

2.3
OLS in Calculus

Fermat’s theorem
, also known as
Fermat’s theorem on stationary points
, is a fundamental result in calculus and mathematical optimization. It provides a necessary condition for a function to have a local optimum (either a local maximum or a local minimum) at a point inside the domain of the function.
For a univariate function, Fermat’s theorem states the optimality condition for a optimal point that lies in the interior of a set, i.e., a one-dimensional constrained optimization problem.

Proposition 101
(Fermat’s theorem: necessary condition for univariate functions).

Let
f:(a,b)\rightarrow\real
be a univariate differentiable function defined over an interval (
a,b
).
If a point
\widehat{\theta}\in(a,b)
(i.e.,
\widehat{\theta}\in\text{int}([a,b])
) is a local maximum or minimum, then
f^{\prime}(\widehat{\theta})=0
.

In other words, if a function
f
has a local maximum or minimum at a point
\widehat{\theta}
, and
f
is differentiable at that point, then the slope of the tangent line at
\widehat{\theta}
must be zero; that is, the derivative of
\widehat{\theta}
is zero.

It is important to note that this condition is necessary but
not
sufficient for
\widehat{\theta}
to be a local extremum. There are cases where the derivative is zero, but the point is neither a maximum nor a minimum—for example, at an inflection point.

Additionally, Fermat’s theorem does
not
apply to boundary points of the domain of
f
, or to points where
f
is not differentiable.

Most objective functions, especially those with multiple local minima, also contain local maxima and other critical points that satisfy the necessary condition given by Fermat’s theorem. To distinguish true local minima from these irrelevant or non-optimal critical points, we rely on additional theorems and conditions, which help us better characterize and classify such points.

We now state the first-order necessary condition for a local minimum point in multivariate optimization.

Proposition 102
(First-order necessary condition for a minimum point).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a differentiable function. If
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is a (local) minimizer for
f
, then

\nabla f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\boldsymbol{0}.

This is known as a stationary point of
f
.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Let
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, and define the one-dimensional function
g(\mu)=f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\mu\bm{e}_{i})
. Note that
g
is differentiable at
\mu=0
and that
g^{\prime}(0)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
. Since
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is a local minimum point of
f
, it follows that
\mu=0
is a local minimum point of
g
, which immediately implies that
g^{\prime}(0)=0
by Proposition
. This equality is exactly the same as
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=0
. Since this holds for any
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, we obtain
\nabla f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\boldsymbol{0}
.

When objective
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is differentiable, and the parameter space of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
includes the entire space
p
(so that the minimum occurs in the interior of the domain), the least squares estimate must occur at a point where the gradient of the function is zero. We thus come into the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[Least squares by calculus]
Assume the observed data matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full rank (i.e., the columns of
\bm{X}
are linearly independent) with
n\geq p
. Consider the overdetermined system
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, the least squares solution by calculus via setting the derivative in every direction of
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
to be zero is
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
.
The value
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}\equiv\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
is known as the
ordinary least squares (OLS)
estimate or simply least squares (LS) estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
From Proposition
, a function
f(\boldsymbol{\beta})
attains a minimum at a point
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
if its gradient
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\boldsymbol{0}
.
In our case, the objective function is
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, whose gradient is
2\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-2\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
.
The condition
2\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-2\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
thus aligns with the normal equation (Definition
).
The matrix
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is invertible since we assume
\bm{X}
is fixed and has full rank (Lemma
). So the OLS solution of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
, from which the result follows.

(a)

A convex function.

(b)

A concave function.

(c)

A random function.

Figure 2.1:
Three functions.

However, we cannot be certain whether the least squares estimate obtained in Theorem
corresponds to a minimum, maximum, or neither. An illustrative example is shown in Figure
.
Our current understanding only confirms that the function
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
has a single critical point (a root of its gradient), which is a
necessary
condition for a minimum—but not necessarily a
sufficient
one.
Further clarification on this issue is provided in the following remark. Alternatively, a more general explanation can be given using convex analysis (see Section
).

Remark 103
(Verification of least squares solution).

Why does a zero gradient imply the least mean squared error?
We avoid discussing convexity (as we will shortly see) in detail here in order to keep things simple. However, we directly verify that the OLS solution indeed minimizes the sum of squared errors.
For any
\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, consider the following expansion:

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\bm{X}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert\bm{X}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\big(\bm{X}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\big)^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert\bm{X}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+2(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

where the third term is zero due to the normal equation, and it also follows that
\big\lVert\bm{X}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 0
. Therefore,

\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This shows that the OLS estimate corresponds to a minimum, rather than a maximum or saddle point, using a calculus-based argument.
In fact, the condition arising from the least squares estimate is also referred to as the sufficiency of stationarity under convexity. When
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is defined across the entire space
p
, this condition is alternatively recognized as the necessity and sufficiency of stationarity under convexity.

A natural question arises: Why does the normal equation magically produce a solution for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
?
A simple example will help clarify this idea. The equation
x^{2}=-1
has no real solution. But
x\cdot x^{2}=x\cdot(-1)
has a real solution
\widehat{x}=0
, in which case
\widehat{x}
makes
x^{2}
and
-1
as close as possible.

Example 104
(Multiplying from left can change the solution set).

Consider the matrix

\bm{X}=\left[\begin{matrix}-3&-4\\
4&6\\
1&1\end{matrix}\right]\mathrm{\,\,\,and\,\,\,}\bm{y}=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\
-1\\
0\end{matrix}\right].

It can be easily verified that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
has no solution for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
(an inconsistent system). However, if we multiply from left by

\bm{Z}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&6\\
0&1&-4\end{bmatrix}.

Then the new system
\bm{Z}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{Z}\bm{y}
has a solution:
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[1/2,-1/2]^{\top}
.
This specific example shows why the normal equation can give rise to the least squares solution. Multiplying from the left of a linear system will change the solution set. The normal equation, especially, results in the least squares solution.

2.4
OLS in Convex Optimization

Mathematical Tools

We briefly introduce the concept of convex optimization.

Definition 105
(Convex set).

A set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
is called convex if, for any
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
\lambda\in[0,1]
, the point
\lambda\bm{x}+(1-\lambda)\bm{y}
also belongs to
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Geometrically, convex sets contain all line segments
that join two points within the set (Figure
). Consequently, these sets do not feature any concave indentations.

Figure 2.2:
A set is considered convex if it includes all convex combinations of its points. If there exists even one convex combination that lies outside the set, then by definition, the set is not convex. Therefore, a convex set must have a shape without any inward “dents” or “bulges”. It’s worth noting that the collection of sparse vectors does not satisfy this criterion and thus forms a non-convex set.

A related concept is that of convex functions, which exhibit specific behavior under convex combinations. We now recall the definition:

Definition 106
(Convex functions).

A function
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
defined over a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
is called convex if

f(\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{\gamma})\leq\lambda f(\boldsymbol{\theta})+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}),\text{ for any }\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in{\mathbb{S}},\lambda\in[0,1].

Moreover,
f
is called strictly convex if
