f(\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{\gamma})<\lambda f(\boldsymbol{\theta})+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}),\text{ for any }\boldsymbol{\theta}\neq\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in{\mathbb{S}},\lambda\in(0,1).

A well-known inequality derived from the concept of convex functions is provided below without a proof.

{theoremHigh}
[Jensen’s inequality]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a convex function defined on a convex subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
. For any finite sequence of points
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{m}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and any sequence of nonnegative weights
\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{m}
such that
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}=1
, Jensen’s inequality states:

f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}).

If
f
is concave, the inequality is reversed.
In the context of probability theory, if
{\mathbf{x}}
is a random vector with values in
{\mathbb{S}}
and
f
is a convex function, Jensen’s inequality can be stated as follows:

f(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}])\leq\mathbb{E}[f({\mathbf{x}})],

where
\mathbb{E}[\cdot]
denotes the expectation operator over the random vector
{\mathbf{x}}
. For a concave function, the inequality is again reversed.

Convex functions do not necessarily have to be differentiable. However, when they are differentiable, such functions can be characterized by the gradient inequality.

{theoremHigh}
[Gradient Inequality]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a continuously differentiable function defined on a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
. Then,
f
is convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

f(\boldsymbol{\theta})+\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}-\boldsymbol{\theta})\leq f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}),\text{ for any $\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in{\mathbb{S}}$}.

(2.26)

Similarly, the function is strictly convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

f(\boldsymbol{\theta})+\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}-\boldsymbol{\theta})<f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}),\text{ for any $\boldsymbol{\theta}\neq\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in{\mathbb{S}}$}.

(2.27)

This indicates that the graph of a convex function lies above its tangent plane at any point. For concave or strictly concave functions, the inequality signs are reversed.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Convexity of quadratic functions)

Let
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\bm{A}\boldsymbol{\theta}+\bm{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}+c
, where
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
is symmetric,
\bm{b}\in\real^{n}
, and
c\in\real
. Show that
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
is convex (resp. strict convex) if and only if
\bm{A}\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
(resp.
\bm{A}\succ\boldsymbol{0}
).

A
convex optimization problem
(or simply a convex problem) involves minimizing a convex function over a convex set:

\textbf{(Convex Optimization)}:\qquad\begin{aligned} &\min\quad f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\quad&&\text{(convex function)}\\
&\text{s.t.}\quad\boldsymbol{\theta}\in{\mathbb{S}}\quad&&\text{(convex set)}.\end{aligned}

(2.28)

{theoremHigh}

[Local is global in convex optimization]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a convex function (resp. strictly convex function) defined over the convex set
{\mathbb{S}}
.
If
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
is a local minimum of
f
over
{\mathbb{S}}
, then
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is the global minimum (resp. strict global minimum, i.e., the only global minimum point) of
f
over
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is a local minimum of
f
over
{\mathbb{S}}
, there exists a scalar
\tau>0
such that
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\geq f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
for any
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in{\mathbb{S}}
satisfying
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in{\mathbb{B}}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\tau]
. Now let
\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in{\mathbb{S}}
satisfy
\boldsymbol{\gamma}\neq\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
. It suffices to show that
f(\boldsymbol{\gamma})\geq f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
. Let
\lambda\in(0,1]
be such that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\lambda(\boldsymbol{\gamma}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\in{\mathbb{B}}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\tau]
. An example of such
\lambda
is
\lambda=\frac{\tau}{\left\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\gamma}\right\rVert_{2}}
. Since
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\lambda(\boldsymbol{\gamma}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\in{\mathbb{B}}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\tau]\cap{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\leq f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\lambda(\boldsymbol{\gamma}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})),

and hence by Jensen’s inequality (Theorem
)

f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\leq f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\lambda(\boldsymbol{\gamma}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}))\leq(1-\lambda)f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\lambda f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}).

Therefore, we obtain
f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\leq f(\boldsymbol{\gamma})
.

A slight modification of the above argument shows that any local minimum of a strictly convex function over a convex set is indeed a strict global minimum of the function over the set.

The optimal set of the convex problem (
) is the set of all minimizers, that is,
\Theta=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}\{f(\boldsymbol{\theta}):\boldsymbol{\theta}\in{\mathbb{S}}\}
. This definition of an optimal set is also valid for general problems.
A notable property of convex problems is that their optimal sets are also convex.

{theoremHigh}

[Convexity of the optimal set in convex optimization]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a convex function defined over the convex set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}
. Then the set of optimal solutions of the problem,

\Theta=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}\{f(\boldsymbol{\theta}):\boldsymbol{\theta}\in{\mathbb{S}}\},

is convex. If, in addition,
f
is strictly convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
, then there exists
at most one
optimal solution.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
If
\Theta=\varnothing
, the result follows trivially.
We then assume that
\Theta\neq\varnothing
and denote the optimal value by
f^{*}
. Let
\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in\Theta
and
\lambda\in[0,1]
. Then, by Jensen’s inequality
f(\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{\gamma})\leq\lambda f^{*}+(1-\lambda)f^{*}=f^{*}
, and hence
\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{\gamma}
is also optimal, i.e., belongs to
\Theta
, establishing the convexity of
\Theta
. Suppose now that
f
is strictly convex and
\Theta
is nonempty; to show that
\Theta
is a singleton, suppose in contradiction that there exist
\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in\Theta
such that
\boldsymbol{\theta}\neq\boldsymbol{\gamma}
. Then
\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and by the strict convexity of
f
we have

f\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\right)<\frac{1}{2}f(\boldsymbol{\theta})+\frac{1}{2}f(\boldsymbol{\gamma})=\frac{1}{2}f^{*}+\frac{1}{2}f^{*}=f^{*},

which leads to a contradiction to the fact that
f^{*}
is the optimal value.

Stationarity is a
necessary optimality condition
for local optimality (Proposition
). However, when the objective function is additionally assumed to be convex, stationarity is a
necessary and sufficient condition
for optimality.

{theoremHigh}

[Necessity/sufficiency of constrained convex]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{n}\rightarrow\real
be a continuously differentiable convex function over a closed and convex set
{\mathbb{S}}
. Then
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is a stationary point of

\text{(P)}\qquad\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\in{\mathbb{S}}}f(\boldsymbol{\theta})

if and only if
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is an optimal solution of (P).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
If
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is an optimal solution of (P), then by Proposition
, it follows that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is a stationary point of (P). To prove the sufficiency of the stationarity condition, assume that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is a stationary point of (P). For any
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, we have:

f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\geq f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\nabla f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\geq f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}),

where the first inequality follows from the gradient inequality for convex functions (Theorem
), and the second inequality follows from the definition of a stationary point. This shows that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is indeed the global minimum point of (P), completing the proof.

LS in Convex Optimization

The theorems on convex functions help answer Questions Q2 and Q3 posed at the beginning of Section
rigorously.
We previously briefly answer the question Q2, the uniqueness of the least squares solution, in the large-sample least squares problem. If
n>p=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
, the least squares solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
is unique.
In fact, this is the
only
case in which the least squares solution is guaranteed to be unique.

Note that both Q2 and Q3 can be formulated as convex optimization problems:

\displaystyle\text{(P2)}:

\displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}f(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-2\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y};

(2.29)

\displaystyle\text{(P3)}:

\displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in{\mathbb{B}}}g(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad{\mathbb{B}}\triangleq\{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\min\}.

Here, both
f(\boldsymbol{\beta})
and
g(\boldsymbol{\beta})
are convex functions (Exercise
), and the set
{\mathbb{B}}
is convex (see Theorem
).
Therefore, both (P2) and (P3) are convex optimization problems.
Theorem
proves that if the function is strictly convex, then the solution is unique.
Apparently,
g(\boldsymbol{\beta})
is strictly convex (this again confirms Theorem
and Q3).
And
f(\boldsymbol{\beta})
is strictly convex only when
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is positive definite, which is the case only when
\bm{X}
has full column rank (i.e.,
n>p=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
).
This answers the question Q2 rigorously.

2.5
OLS in Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra

Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra

For any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, it can be easily verified that any vector in the row space of
\bm{X}
is perpendicular to any vector in the null space of
\bm{X}
. Suppose
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{n}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
, then
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{n}=\boldsymbol{0}
such that
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{n}
is perpendicular to every row of
\bm{X}
, supporting our claim. This implies the row space of
\bm{X}
is the orthogonal complement to the null space of
\bm{X}
.

Similarly, we can also show that any vector in the column space of
\bm{X}
is perpendicular to any vector in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
. Furthermore, the column space of
\bm{X}
together with the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
span the entire space of
n
which is known as the fundamental theorem of linear algebra.

{theoremHigh}
[Fundamental theorem of linear algebra]
Orthogonal Complement and Rank-Nullity Theorem: for any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, we have

The null space
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
is the orthogonal complement to the row space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
in
p
:
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}))=p
;

The null space
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
is the orthogonal complement to the column space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
in
n
:
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}))=n
;

For rank-
r
matrix
\bm{X}
,
\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}))=\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}))=r
, that is,
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}))=p-r
and
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}))=n-r
.

Figure 2.3:
Two pairs of orthogonal subspaces in
p
and
n
.
\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}))+\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}))=p
and
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}))=n
. The null space component goes to zero as
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}\in\real^{n}
.
Simultaneously, the row space component transforms into the column space by
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\bm{r}}=\bm{X}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\bm{r}}+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\bm{n}})=\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

The fundamental theorem contains two parts, the dimension of the subspaces and the orthogonality of the subspaces. The orthogonality can be readily verified as we have shown at the beginning of this section. When the row space has dimension
r
, the null space has dimension
p-r
. This cannot be easily stated, and we prove it as follows.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Following the proof of Lemma
, let
\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{r}
be a set of vectors in
p
that form a basis for the row space.
Then,
\bm{X}\bm{r}_{1},\bm{X}\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{X}\bm{r}_{r}
is a basis for the column space of
\bm{X}
. Let
\bm{n}_{1},\bm{n}_{2},\ldots,\bm{n}_{k}\in\real^{p}
form a basis for the null space of
\bm{X}
. Following again the proof of Lemma
,
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})\bot\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, thus,
\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{r}
are perpendicular to
\bm{n}_{1},\bm{n}_{2},\ldots,\bm{n}_{k}
. Then,
\{\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{r},\bm{n}_{1},\bm{n}_{2},\ldots,\bm{n}_{k}\}
is linearly independent in
p
.

For any vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}
,
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
is in the column space of
\bm{X}
. Thus, it can be expressed as a linear combination of
\bm{X}\bm{r}_{1},\bm{X}\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{X}\bm{r}_{r}
:
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_{i}\bm{X}\bm{r}_{i}
, which states that
\bm{X}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_{i}\bm{r}_{i})=\boldsymbol{0}
, and
\boldsymbol{\beta}-\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_{i}\bm{r}_{i}
is thus in
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
. Since
\{\bm{n}_{1},\bm{n}_{2},\ldots,\bm{n}_{k}\}
is a basis for the null space of
\bm{X}
,
\boldsymbol{\beta}-\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_{i}\bm{r}_{i}
can be expressed by a combination of
\bm{n}_{1},\bm{n}_{2},\ldots,\bm{n}_{k}
:
\boldsymbol{\beta}-\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_{i}\bm{r}_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}b_{j}\bm{n}_{j}
, i.e.,
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_{i}\bm{r}_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}b_{j}\bm{n}_{j}
. That is, any vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}
can be expressed by
\{\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{r},\bm{n}_{1},\bm{n}_{2},\ldots,\bm{n}_{k}\}
and the set forms a basis for
p
. Thus the dimension add up to
p
:
r+k=p
, i.e.,
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}))=p
. Similarly, we can prove
\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}))=n
.

Figure
demonstrates two pairs of such orthogonal subspaces and shows how
\bm{X}
takes
\boldsymbol{\beta}
into the column space. The dimensions of the row space of
\bm{X}
and the null space of
\bm{X}
add up to
p
. And the dimensions of the column space of
\bm{X}
and the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
add up to
n
. The null space component goes to zero as
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}\in\real^{n}
, which is the intersection of the column space of
\bm{X}
and the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
. The row space component transforms into the column space as
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\bm{r}}=\bm{X}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\bm{r}}+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\bm{n}})=\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

LS in Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra

Figure 2.4:
Least squares:
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
minimizes
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is in the row space of
\bm{X}
.
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
.

The solution to the least squares problem aims to minimize the error
\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
in terms of mean squared error.
Since
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
is a combination of the columns of
\bm{X}
, it remains within the column space of
\bm{X}
.
Therefore, the optimal choice is to select the nearest point to
\bm{y}
within the column space
(
Strang 1993
;
Lu 2021c
)
. This point is the projection
\widehat{\bm{y}}
of
\bm{y}
onto the column space of
\bm{X}
. Then the error vector
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
has the minimum length. In other words, the best combination
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is the projection of
\bm{y}
onto the column space. The error
\bm{e}
is perpendicular to the column space. Therefore,
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
(from the fundamental theorem of linear algebra):

\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},

which agrees with the normal equation as we have defined in Section
.
The relationship between
\bm{e}
and
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is shown in Figure
, where
\bm{y}
is decomposed into
\widehat{\bm{y}}+\bm{e}
.
We can always find this decomposition since the column space of
\bm{X}
and the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
are orthogonal complement to each other, and they collectively span the entire space of
n
.
Moreover, it can be demonstrated that the OLS estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
resides in the row space of
\bm{X}
, i.e., it cannot be decomposed into a combination of two components—one in the row space of
\bm{X}
and the other in the null space of
\bm{X}
(refer to the expression for
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
via the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
in Section
, where
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is presented as a linear combination of the orthonormal basis of the row space; or refer to Theorem
).

To conclude, we avoid solving the equation
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
by removing
\bm{e}
from
\bm{y}
and addressing
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
instead, i.e.,

\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}=\widehat{\bm{y}}+\bm{e}\,\,\mathrm{is\,impossible;}\qquad\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\widehat{\bm{y}}\,\,\mathrm{is\,possible.}

2.6
OLS in SVD for General Matrices

Prior to delving into the geometric aspects of least squares, we will first elucidate least squares through singular value decomposition (SVD), as they constitute fundamental components for the subsequent discussions.

2.6.1
Least Squares via SVD for General Matrices

Returning to the least squares problem, our prior assumption was that
\bm{X}
has full rank.
However, if
\bm{X}
does not have full column rank,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
becomes non-invertible. In such cases, we can employ the SVD decomposition of
\bm{X}
to address the least squares problem with a rank-deficient
\bm{X}
.
The methodology for solving the rank-deficient least squares problem is illustrated in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[LS via SVD for general matrices]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and let
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
be its full SVD decomposition with
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times p}
being orthogonal matrices, and
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r\leq\min\{n,p\}
. Suppose
\bm{U}=[\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{n}]
and
\bm{V}=[\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{p}]
are the column partitions of
\bm{U}
and
\bm{V}
, respectively, and the observed output vector is
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.
Then the ordinary least squares solution with the minimal
\ell_{2}
norm to the linear system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
is given by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{\bm{u}_{i}^{\top}\bm{y}}{\sigma_{i}}\bm{v}_{i}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}\equiv\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y},

(2.30)

where the upper-left side of
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\in\real^{p\times n}
is a diagonal matrix
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}^{+}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}
with
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}^{+}=\mathrm{diag}(\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}},\frac{1}{\sigma_{2}},\ldots,\frac{1}{\sigma_{r}})
, and
\bm{X}^{+}
denotes the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
(Section
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Expressing the loss to be minimized:

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}\bm{U}\bm{U}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{=}}\left\lVert\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{V}\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle*}}{{=}}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\sigma_{i}\alpha_{i}-\bm{u}_{i}^{\top}\bm{y})^{2}+\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}(\bm{u}_{i}^{\top}\bm{y})^{2},

where the equality
({\dagger})
follows since
\bm{U}
is an orthogonal matrix, and the equality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from the invariance under orthogonal transformations, the equality (
*
) follows by letting
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\triangleq\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and the last equality follows since
\sigma_{r+1}=\sigma_{r+2}=\ldots=\sigma_{n}=0
.

Since
\boldsymbol{\beta}
only appears in
\boldsymbol{\alpha}
, setting
\alpha_{i}=\frac{\bm{u}_{i}^{\top}\bm{y}}{\sigma_{i}}
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,r\}
minimizes the loss above.
The result remains the same for any values of
\alpha_{r+1},\alpha_{r+2},\ldots,\alpha_{p}
.
From a regularization point of view, we can set them to be 0 (the same as searching for minimum norm of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
).
This yields the SVD-based OLS solution:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{\bm{u}_{i}^{\top}\bm{y}}{\sigma_{i}}\bm{v}_{i}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y},

where
\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}\in\real^{p\times n}
is known as the
pseudo-inverse
of
\bm{X}
. Refer to Section
for a detailed discussion about the pseudo-inverse, where we also prove that
the column space of
\bm{X}^{+}
is equal to the row space of
\bm{X}
, and the row space of
\bm{X}^{+}
is equal to the column space of
\bm{X}
.

Figure 2.5:
\bm{X}^{+}
: Pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
. A more detailed discussion of the four subspaces in pseudo-inverse is discussed in Section
(see Figure
).

Proposition 107
(LS in the Four Subspaces of Linear Algebra via SVD).

Assume
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and does
not
necessarily has full rank with
n\geq p
. Consider the overdetermined system
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
Then, we can factor
\bm{y}
into
\widehat{\bm{y}}+\bm{e}
, where
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is in the column space of
\bm{X}
(in
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
), and
\bm{e}
is in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
(in
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
). We can always find this decomposition since the column space of
\bm{X}
and the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
span the entire space
n
. The relationship between vectors
\bm{e}
and
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is shown in Figure
. Let
\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}
be the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
. The pseudo-inverse
\bm{X}^{+}
agrees with
\bm{X}^{-1}
when
\bm{X}
is invertible. Then, we have the following properties (also shown in Figure
):

For
\bm{e}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, it follows that
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{e}=\boldsymbol{0}\in\real^{p}
.

Given the OLS solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
via SVD, it follows that
\bm{X}^{+}\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

OLS solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is in the row space of
\bm{X}
, i.e., it cannot be decomposed into a combination of two components that are in the row space of
\bm{X}
and the null space of
\bm{X}
, respectively. This is the reason why
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, as shown in Figure
, is in the row space of
\bm{X}
rather than in
p
in general.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Since
\bm{e}
is in
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
and it is perpendicular to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, and we have shown in Theorem
that
\{\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, then the first
r
components of
\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{e}
are all zeros. Therefore,
\bm{X}^{+}\bm{e}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{+}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{e}=\boldsymbol{0}
(see also Figure
where we transfer
\bm{e}
from
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
into the zero vector
\boldsymbol{0}\in\real^{p}
by
\bm{X}^{+}
). Therefore, it follows that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{+}(\widehat{\bm{y}}+\bm{e})=\bm{X}^{+}\widehat{\bm{y}}
.

Furthermore, we have also shown in Theorem
that
\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
. Thus,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{\bm{u}_{i}^{\top}\bm{y}}{\sigma_{i}}\bm{v}_{i}
is in the row space of
\bm{X}
.

In the following sections, we will also demonstrate that the vector
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is the closest point to
\bm{y}
within the column space of
\bm{X}
. This point is the (orthogonal) projection
\widehat{\bm{y}}
of
\bm{y}
onto the column space of
\bm{X}
.
Then the error vector
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
has the minimum length (norm).

Besides the OLS solution derived from SVD, practical implementations of solutions through normal equation may encounter numerical challenges when
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is close to singular. In particular, when two or more columns in
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
are nearly co-linear,
the resulting parameter values can become excessively large.
Such near degeneracies will not be uncommon when dealing with real-world data sets.
Addressing these numerical challenges can be effectively achieved through the application of SVD as well
(
Bishop 2006
)
.

2.6.2
Least Squares with Norm Ratio Method

Continuing from the previous section, let
\bm{X}_{k}\in\real^{n\times p}
be the optimal rank-
k
approximation to the original
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
(Theorem
). Define the
Frobenius norm ratio

(
Zhang 2017
)
as

\nu(k)\triangleq\frac{\left\lVert\bm{X}_{k}\right\rVert_{F}}{\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}}=\frac{\sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\sigma_{k}^{2}}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\sigma_{h}^{2}}},\quad h=\min\{n,p\},

where

\bm{X}_{k}
is the truncated SVD of
\bm{X}
with the largest
k
terms, i.e.,
\bm{X}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}
from the SVD of
\bm{X}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}
. And
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{F}
is the matrix Frobenius norm (Definition
).
We determine the minimum integer
k
satisfying

\nu(k)\geq\alpha

as the
effective rank estimate

\widehat{r}
, where
\alpha
is the threshold capped at a maximum value of 1, and it is usually set to
\alpha=0.997
.
Once we have determined the effective rank
\widehat{r}
, we substitute it into Equation (
), yielding:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i=1}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\widehat{r}}}\frac{\bm{u}_{i}^{\top}\bm{b}}{\sigma_{i}}\bm{v}_{i},

which can be regarded as an approximation to the OLS solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
And this solution corresponds to the OLS solution of the linear equation
\bm{X}_{\widehat{r}}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{b}
, where

\bm{X}_{\widehat{r}}=\sum_{i=1}^{\widehat{r}}\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}.

The introduced filtering method is particularly valuable when dealing with a noisy matrix
\bm{X}

(
Zhang 2017
)
.

2.6.3
High-Dimensional Least Squares Problems

Although Theorem
applies to general types of matrices
\bm{X}
,regardless of whether they have a large sample size or are rank-deficient,
we now focus on the problem of finding a solution to the linear system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}

where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full row rank and
p>n
, i.e., the
high-dimensional least squares problem
. Although there is no unique solution in general, the minimum (
\ell_{2}
) norm solution is unique.
The minimum-norm solution is defined as follows:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t. }\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}.

The solution to the minimum-norm problem is

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}

The above matrix
\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}
exists as long as
\bm{X}
has full row rank. To show that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
is a valid solution, we can substitute
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
into the constraint equation:

\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}=\bm{y}.

To prove that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
has the smallest (
\ell_{2}
) norm among all solutions of
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
, we first show that the difference vector
(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}})
is orthogonal to
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
. For any
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}\in\real^{p}
such that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}=\bm{y}
, it follows that

\displaystyle(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime})^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}

\displaystyle=(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime})^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}))^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=(\bm{y}-\bm{y})^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0},

whence we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\big\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}+\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\big\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This proves that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}
is a solution to the minimum-norm problem.
Recall that any matrix
\bm{X}
can be written as the full SVD:

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top},

where
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times p}
.
Since
\bm{X}
has full row rank. Substituting the SVD into the expression for
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
, we obtain:

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{U}^{\top}(\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{U}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{U}^{\top}(\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2}\bm{U}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2})^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y},

which again agrees with Theorem
.

2.7
OLS in Geometry and Orthogonal Projection

As discussed earlier, the OLS estimate involves minimizing
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, which searches for an estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
such that
\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is in
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
so as to minimize the distance between
\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
\bm{y}
. The nearest point is the
projection

\widehat{\bm{y}}
. The predicted value
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is the projection of
\bm{y}
onto the column space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
by a
projection matrix

{\bm{H}\triangleq\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}}
when
\bm{X}
has full column rank with
n\geq p
:

\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{H}\bm{y},

where the matrix
\bm{H}
is also known as the
hat matrix
, since it “put a hat” on
\bm{y}
to produce
\widehat{\bm{y}}
.

This shows
h_{ij}
, the entry
(i,j)
of
\bm{H}
measures the influence or statistical leverage exerted on the prediction
\widehat{y}_{i}
by the observation
y_{j}
.
Relatedly, if the
i
-th diagonal element of
\bm{H}
is particularly large, then the
i
-th data point (
i
-th row of
\bm{X}
) is particularly sensitive or influential in determining the best LS fit, thus justifying the interpretation of the elements
h_{ii}
as
statistical leverage scores

(
Mahoney et al. 2011
)
.
These leverage scores have been used extensively in classical regression diagnostics to identify potential outliers by, e.g., flagging data points with leverage score greater than 2 or 3 times the average value in order to be investigated as errors or potential outliers
(
Chatterjee and Hadi 1988
)
.

But what is a projection matrix? Merely stating that
\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
is a projection requires elucidation.
Before the discussion on the projection matrix, we first provide some basic properties about symmetric and idempotent matrices, which will find extensive application in subsequent sections.

2.7.1
Properties of Symmetric and Idempotent Matrices

Symmetric idempotent matrices exhibit specific eigenvalues, a crucial aspect for the subsequent sections on the distribution theory of least squares.

Lemma 108
(Eigenvalue of symmetric idempotent matrices).

The only possible eigenvalues of any symmetric idempotent matrix are 0 and 1.

In Lemma
, we will show that the eigenvalues of idempotent matrices (not necessarily symmetric) are 1 and 0 as well, which relaxes the conditions required here (both idempotent and symmetric). However, the method used in the proof is quite useful so we keep both of the claims.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\bm{X}
be a symmetric idempotent matrix. By spectral theorem (Theorem
), we can decompose
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
, where
\bm{Q}
is an orthogonal matrix, and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
is a diagonal matrix. Therefore, it follows that

\displaystyle(\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top})^{2}

\displaystyle=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}\qquad\implies\qquad\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}

(2.31)

\displaystyle\qquad\implies\qquad\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{2}\bm{Q}^{\top}

\displaystyle=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}\qquad\implies\qquad\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{2}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\qquad\implies\qquad\lambda_{i}^{2}=\lambda_{i},

where the first equality follows since
\bm{X}
is symmetric and idempotent.
Thus, the eigenvalues of
\bm{X}
satisfy that
\lambda_{i}\in\{0,1\},\ \forall\,i
. This completes the proof.

In the previous lemma, we used the spectral theorem to show that the eigenvalues of any symmetric idempotent matrix are 0 or 1. This approach is common in linear algebra and appears frequently in statistical theory (see later sections on distribution theory; Chapter
). With a slight modification, we can remove the symmetry condition entirely and extend the result to general idempotent matrices.

Lemma 109
(Eigenvalue of idempotent matrices).

The only possible eigenvalues of any idempotent matrix are 0 and 1.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\boldsymbol{\beta}
denote an eigenvector of the idempotent matrix
\bm{X}
corresponding to the eigenvalue
\lambda
. That is,

\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
Also, we have

\displaystyle\bm{X}^{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{2})\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})=\bm{X}(\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta})=\lambda\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\lambda^{2}\boldsymbol{\beta},

which implies
\lambda^{2}=\lambda
, and
\lambda
is either 0 or 1. This completes the proof.

We also demonstrate that the rank of a symmetric idempotent matrix is equal to its trace, a result that will be highly beneficial in the subsequent sections.

Lemma 110
(Rank and trace of symmetric idempotent matrices).

For any
n\times n
symmetric idempotent matrix
\bm{X}
, the rank of
\bm{X}
equals its trace.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
From Spectral Theorem
, the matrix
\bm{X}
admits the spectral decomposition
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
.
Since
\bm{X}
and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
are similar matrices, their rank and trace are the same (see Lemma
). That is,

\displaystyle\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{rank}(\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n}));

\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n})),

By Lemma
, the only eigenvalues of
\bm{X}
are 0 and 1. Then, it follows that

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X})
.

In the previous lemma, we prove the rank and trace of any symmetric idempotent matrix are the same.
However, this result also holds under a weaker condition—namely, just idempotency. We now present a more general version of the lemma. Although the second proof applies to a broader class of matrices, we again include both versions because the techniques used in each are valuable and commonly applied in linear algebra.

Lemma 111
(Rank and trace of an idempotent matrix).

For any
n\times n
idempotent matrix
\bm{X}
, the rank of
\bm{X}
equals its trace.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Any
n\times n
rank-
r
matrix
\bm{X}
admits CR decomposition
\bm{X}=\bm{C}\bm{R}
, where
\bm{C}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
\bm{R}\in\real^{r\times n}
have full rank
r

(see Section
).
Then, it follows that

\displaystyle\bm{X}^{2}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}\quad\implies\quad\bm{C}\bm{R}\bm{C}\bm{R}=\bm{C}\bm{R}\quad\implies\quad\bm{R}\bm{C}\bm{R}=\bm{R}\quad\implies\quad\bm{R}\bm{C}=\bm{I}_{r},

where
\bm{I}_{r}
is the
r\times r
identity matrix. Thus, the trace is

\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{C}\bm{R})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{R}\bm{C})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{I}_{r})=r,

where the second equality uses the cyclic property of the trace, which completes the proof.

2.7.2
By Geometry and Orthogonal Projection

Formally, we define the projection matrix as follows:

Definition 112
(Projection matrix).

A matrix
\bm{H}\in\real^{n\times n}
is called a projection matrix or projector onto a subspace
\mathcal{V}\in\real^{n}
if and only if
\bm{H}
satisfies the following properties:

(P1).
\bm{H}\bm{y}\in\mathcal{V}
for all
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
: Any vector can be projected onto the subspace
\mathcal{V}
.

(P2).
\bm{H}\bm{y}=\bm{y}
for all
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{V}
: Projecting a vector that is already in that subspace has no further effect.

(P3).
\bm{H}^{2}=\bm{H}
, i.e., applying the projection twice is the same as applying it once, because the vector is already in the subspace. This property is known as idempotence.

Since we project a vector in
n
onto a subspace of
n
, any projection matrix must be square.
Otherwise, we will project onto the subspace of
m
rather than
n
.
We realize that
\bm{H}\bm{y}
is always in the column space of
\bm{H}
.
One might then ask: what is the relationship between the subspace
\mathcal{V}
and the column space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})
.
In fact, the column space of
\bm{H}
is equal to the subspace
\mathcal{V}
onto which we are projecting.

Suppose
\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})
, and suppose further that
\bm{y}
is already in the subspace
\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})
, i.e., there is a vector
\boldsymbol{\alpha}
such that
\bm{y}=\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\alpha}
. Given only the condition (P3) above, we have,

\bm{H}\bm{y}=\bm{H}\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{y}.

That is, condition (P3) implies conditions (P1) and (P2).
Therefore, the definition of a projection matrix can be simplified to require only that
\bm{H}
is idempotent.

Intuitively, we also want the projection
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{H}\bm{y}
of any vector
\bm{y}
to be perpendicular to the residual vector
\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
such that the distance between
\widehat{\bm{y}}
and
\bm{y}
is minimized, which aligns with the principle of least squares error minimization. Such a projection is called an
orthogonal projection
.

Definition 113
(Orthogonal and oblique projection matrix).

A matrix
\bm{H}
is called an orthogonal projection matrix or an orthogonal projector onto a subspace
\mathcal{V}\in\real^{n}
if and only if
\bm{H}
is a projection matrix, and the projection
\widehat{\bm{y}}
of any vector
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
is orthogonal to
\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
, i.e.,
\bm{H}
projects onto
\mathcal{V}
and along
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
, the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{V}
.

Otherwise, if
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is not orthogonal to
\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
, then the projection matrix is called an oblique projection matrix or an oblique projector. A comparison between orthogonal and oblique projections is shown in Figure
.

(a)

Orthogonal projection: project
\bm{y}
to
\widehat{\bm{y}}
.

(b)

Oblique projection: project
\bm{y}
to
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}
or
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}
.

Figure 2.6:
Projection onto the hyperplane of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, i.e., the column space of
\bm{X}
.

Note that in the context of orthogonal projection, the term does not imply that the projection matrix itself is orthogonal (Definition
).
Instead, it means that the projected vector
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is perpendicular to the residual vector
\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
. This specialized orthogonal projection matrix will be implicitly assumed as such in the subsequent discussion unless explicitly clarified.

An
elementary projector
is a projector exactly one of whose eigenvalues is 0.
Then we have the following result:

Exercise
\thetheo
(Elementary projection matrix)

Let
\bm{x}\in\real^{n}
be nonzero. Show that
\bm{H}\triangleq\bm{I}-\frac{1}{\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}}\bm{x}\bm{x}^{\top}
is an elementary projection matrix satisfying (a).
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{H})=n-1
; (b).
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{x}\}^{\perp}
; (c).
\mathcal{N}(\bm{H})=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{x}\}
.
For the other way around, if
\bm{H}\in\real^{n\times n}
is a projector with
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{H})=n-1
, show that there is a nonzero vector
\bm{x}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{H})
such that
\bm{H}=\bm{I}-\frac{1}{\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}}\bm{x}\bm{x}^{\top}
.

Lemma 114
(Symmetric orthogonal projection matrix).

A projection matrix
\bm{H}
is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if
\bm{H}
is symmetric.
That is:

If
\bm{H}^{2}=\bm{H}
and
\bm{H}^{\top}=\bm{H}
, then
\bm{H}
is an orthogonal projector.

If
\bm{H}^{2}=\bm{H}
and
\bm{H}^{\top}\neq\bm{H}
, then
\bm{H}
is an oblique projector.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose
\bm{H}
is an orthogonal projection matrix, which projects vectors onto a subspace
\mathcal{V}
. Then any vectors
\bm{v}
and
\bm{w}
can be decomposed into a vector lies in
\mathcal{V}
(
\bm{v}_{p}
and
\bm{w}_{p}
) and a vector lies in
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
(
\bm{v}_{n}
and
\bm{w}_{n}
), so that

\displaystyle\bm{v}

\displaystyle=\bm{v}_{p}+\bm{v}_{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{w}=\bm{w}_{p}+\bm{w}_{n}.

Since the projection matrix
\bm{H}
projects vectors onto
\mathcal{V}
, it follows that
\bm{H}\bm{v}=\bm{v}_{p}
and
\bm{H}\bm{w}=\bm{w}_{p}
, whence we have

\displaystyle(\bm{H}\bm{v})^{\top}\bm{w}

\displaystyle=\bm{v}_{p}^{\top}\bm{w}=\bm{v}_{p}^{\top}(\bm{w}_{p}+\bm{w}_{n})

\displaystyle\qquad\bm{v}^{\top}(\bm{H}\bm{w})

\displaystyle=\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{w}_{p}=(\bm{v}_{p}+\bm{v}_{n})^{\top}\bm{w}_{p}

\displaystyle=\bm{v}_{p}^{\top}\bm{w}_{p}+\bm{v}_{p}^{\top}\bm{w}_{n}=\bm{v}_{p}^{\top}\bm{w}_{p};

\displaystyle=\bm{v}_{p}^{\top}\bm{w}_{p}+\bm{v}_{n}^{\top}\bm{w}_{p}=\bm{v}_{p}^{\top}\bm{w}_{p},

where the last equations follow from the fact that
\bm{v}_{p}
is perpendicular to
\bm{w}_{n}
, and
\bm{v}_{n}
is perpendicular to
\bm{w}_{p}
.
Therefore, we conclude that

\displaystyle(\bm{H}\bm{v})^{\top}\bm{w}=\bm{v}^{\top}(\bm{H}\bm{w})\quad\implies\quad\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{H}^{\top}\bm{w}=\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{H}\bm{w},

which implies
\bm{H}^{\top}=\bm{H}
.

Conversely, if a projection matrix
\bm{H}
(not necessarily an orthogonal projection) is symmetric, then any vector
\bm{v}
can be decomposed into
\bm{v}=\bm{H}\bm{v}+(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{v}
. If we can prove
\bm{H}\bm{v}
is perpendicular to
(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{v}
, then we complete the proof. To see this, we have

\displaystyle(\bm{H}\bm{v})^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{v}

\displaystyle=\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{H}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{v}=\bm{v}^{\top}(\bm{H}^{\top}-\bm{H}^{\top}\bm{H})\bm{v}

\displaystyle=\bm{v}^{\top}(\bm{H}-\bm{H}\bm{H})\bm{v}=\bm{v}^{\top}(\bm{H}-\bm{H})\bm{v}=\boldsymbol{0},

which completes the proof.

We claimed earlier that orthogonal projection minimizes the distance between a vector
\bm{y}
and its projection
\widehat{\bm{y}}
.
We now rigorously prove this important property.

{theoremHigh}
[Minimum distance in orthogonal projection]
Let
\mathcal{V}
be a subspace of
n
and
\bm{H}\in\real^{n\times n}
be an orthogonal projection matrix onto
\mathcal{V}
. Then, given any vector
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, it follows that

\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad\forall\,\bm{v}\in\mathcal{V}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
\bm{H}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}\in\real^{n\times n}
be the spectral decomposition of the orthogonal projection matrix
\bm{H}
,
where
\bm{Q}=[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}]
is the column partition of
\bm{Q}
, and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n})
. Let
\dim(\mathcal{V})=r
. Then, from Lemma
, the only possible eigenvalues of the orthogonal projection matrix are 1 and 0. Without loss of generality, let
\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\ldots=\lambda_{r}=1
and
\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_{r+2}=\ldots=\lambda_{n}=0
. Then, it follows that

\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
n
.

\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{V}
. So for any vector
\bm{v}\in\mathcal{V}
, we have
\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}=0
for
i\in\{r+1,r+2,\ldots,n\}
.

Then we have,

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}-(\bm{H}\bm{y})^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{=}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}-\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{H}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle*}}{{=}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}-\lambda_{i}\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle+}}{{=}}0+\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}-\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}+\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bot}}{{=}}\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the invariance under orthogonal transformation, the equality (
{\ddagger}
) follows since
\bm{H}
is symmetric,
the equality (
*
) follows from
\bm{H}\bm{Q}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
, the equality (
+
) follows since the eigenvalues are 1 or 0, and the equality (
\bot
) follows since
\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}=0
for
i>r
.
This completes the proof.

Next, we examine the geometric relationship between a vector
\bm{y}
and its orthogonal projection
\bm{H}\bm{y}
.

Lemma 115
(Angle between the original and projected vectors).

Let
\bm{H}
be an orthogonal projection onto
\mathcal{V}
. Then,

1.

\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{H}\bm{y})\geq 0
, meaning the angle between
\bm{y}
and
\bm{H}\bm{y}
is less than or equal to
90^{\circ}
;

2.

\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, meaning the length of the projected vector is no greater than the original vector.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
According to the definition of the orthogonal projection, we have
\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{H}\bm{y})=\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{H}(\bm{H}\bm{y})=\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{H}^{\top}(\bm{H}\bm{y})=\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 0
.
And we could decompose
\bm{y}
by

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{H}+\bm{H})\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}\bm{H}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This completes the proof.

In conclusion, to determine the OLS solution, we define the
projection matrix
as an idempotent matrix.
For it to represent an orthogonal projection, we add the condition that the matrix must also be symmetric. Through this orthogonal projection, we illustrate that the distance between the original vector and its projection is minimized.

We now further explore the relationship between the OLS solution and orthogonal projection.

Proposition 116
(Projection matrix from a set of vectors).

Let
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}\in\real^{n}
be linearly independent vectors such that
\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}])=\mathcal{V}
, and assume
n\geq p
.
Then, the orthogonal projection onto the subspace
\mathcal{V}
can be expressed as:

\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top},

where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is the matrix whose columns are
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}
.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
It can be easily verified that
\bm{H}
is symmetric and idempotent. By SVD of
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
, we have
\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\bm{U}^{\top}
. Let
\bm{U}=[\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{n}]
be the column partition of
\bm{U}
. From Theorem
,
\{\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{p}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
. And
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}
in
\bm{H}
is an
n\times n
matrix, where the upper-left part is a
p\times p
identity matrix and the other parts are zero. Apply this observation of
\bm{H}
into spectral theorem,
\{\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{p}\}
is also an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})
.
Thus, it follows that
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, and the orthogonal projection
\bm{H}
is projecting onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, from which the result follows.

The proposition above brings us back to the result we have shown at the beginning of this section.
For the OLS estimate to minimize
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, which searches for an estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
so that
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is in
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, minimizing the distance between
\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
\bm{y}
. An orthogonal projection matrix
\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
can project
\bm{y}
onto the column space of
\bm{X}
, and the projected vector is
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{H}\bm{y}
.
By Theorem
, this projection ensures the squared distance between
\widehat{\bm{y}}
and
\bm{y}
is minimized.

To repeat, the hat matrix
\bm{H}
has a clear geometric interpretation: it drops a perpendicular to the hyperplane. Here,
\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
drops
\bm{y}
onto the column space of
\bm{X}
:
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{H}\bm{y}
.
Idempotency also has a geometric interpretation. Additional
\bm{H}
’s also drop a perpendicular to the hyperplane. But it has no additional effect because we are already on that hyperplane. Therefore,
\bm{H}^{2}\bm{y}=\bm{H}\bm{y}
. This scenario is shown in Figure
. The sum of squared error is then equal to the squared Euclidean distance between
\bm{y}
and
\widehat{\bm{y}}
. Thus, the least squares solution for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
corresponds to the orthogonal projection of
\bm{y}
onto the column space of
\bm{X}
.

Lemma 117
(Column space of projection matrices).

We notice that the hat matrix
\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
is used to project any vector in
n
onto the column space of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
. In other words,
\bm{H}\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
. Notice again that
\bm{H}\bm{y}
is nothing but a combination of the columns of
\bm{H}
, thus
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

More generally, for any projection matrix
\bm{H}
that projects a vector onto a subspace
\mathcal{V}
, then
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})=\mathcal{V}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}\bm{C}
(let
\bm{C}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
), the columns of
\bm{H}
are combinations of columns of
\bm{X}
. Thus,
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
. By Lemma
, we have

\displaystyle\mathrm{rank}(\bm{H})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{H})=\mathrm{tr}\big(\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\big)

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}\big((\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\big)=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{I}_{p})=p.

where the third equality follows from the fact that the trace of a product is invariant under cyclical permutations of the factors:
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\bm{B}\bm{C})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{B}\bm{C}\bm{A})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{C}\bm{A}\bm{B})
.
Thus, the rank of
\bm{H}
equals the rank of
\bm{X}
such that
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

2.7.3
Properties of Orthogonal Projection Matrices

Proposition
shows that
\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
is the orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
if
\bm{X}
has full column rank, which is the hat matrix we used in the least squares solution.
More generally, we have the following result.

{theoremHigh}
[Orthogonal projector onto general subspaces]
Let
\mathcal{V}
be a subspace in
n
with dimension
r
. Let
\bm{Q}_{1}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
\bm{Q}_{2}\in\real^{n\times(n-r)}
be semi-orthogonal matrices (i.e., their columns are mutually orthonormal; Definition
) such that
\mathcal{C}(\bm{Q}_{1})=\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{Q}_{2})=\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
, where
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
denotes the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{V}
. Then the orthogonal projectors onto
\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
are given by

\bm{H}_{1}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{H}_{2}=\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top},

(2.32)

respectively.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We have
\bm{H}_{1}^{2}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}=\bm{H}_{1}
since
\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}=\bm{I}_{r}
. This shows that
\bm{H}_{1}
is a projector onto
\mathcal{V}
.
Since
\bm{H}_{1}
is symmetric, this completes the proof for the first part.
The second part follows from a similar argument.

As a direct consequence of the above analysis, Theorem
shows four orthogonal projectors in the context of SVD of a matrix.

{theoremHigh}
[SVD-related orthogonal projections]
Let
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
be the full SVD of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with rank
r
. Suppose we have the following column partitions

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\bm{U}=&\bm{U}_{1}&\bm{U}_{2}\\
&n\times r&n\times(n-r)\\
\end{array},\qquad\begin{array}[]{ccc}\bm{V}=&\bm{V}_{1}&\bm{V}_{2}\\
&p\times r&p\times(p-r)\\
\end{array},

where
\bm{U}_{1}
and
\bm{V}_{1}
consist of the first
r
columns of
\bm{U}
and
\bm{V}
, respectively.
Then the four orthogonal projections can be obtained by

\displaystyle\bm{V}_{1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}

\displaystyle=\text{projection onto $\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})$},\quad

\displaystyle\bm{V}_{2}\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}

\displaystyle=\text{projection onto $\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})$},

\displaystyle\bm{U}_{1}\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}

\displaystyle=\text{projection onto $\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})$},\quad

\displaystyle\bm{U}_{2}\bm{U}_{2}^{\top}

\displaystyle=\text{projection onto $\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})$}.

Furthermore, there are also four orthogonal projectors associated with the pseudo-inverse of a matrix.

{theoremHigh}
[Pseudo-inverse-related orthogonal projections]
Given any matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and its pseudo-inverse
\bm{X}^{+}\in\real^{p\times n}
, the following hold:

\bm{H}\triangleq\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}
is the orthogonal projector onto the column space of
\bm{X}
.

\bm{I}-\bm{H}
is the orthogonal projector onto the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
.

\bm{P}\triangleq\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}
is the orthogonal projector onto the row space of
\bm{X}
.

\bm{I}-\bm{P}
is the orthogonal projector onto the null space of
\bm{X}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
\bm{H}^{\top}=(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})^{\top}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{H}
from the definition of the pseudo-inverse, we see that
\bm{H}
is symmetric. Moreover,
\bm{H}
is idempotent, which confirms that
\bm{H}
is an orthogonal projector.
From Table
, we conclude that
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
. This implies that
\bm{H}
is the orthogonal projector onto the column space of
\bm{X}
. Similarly, we can prove
\bm{P}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}
is the orthogonal projector onto the row space of
\bm{X}
.

In fact,
(\bm{I}-\bm{H})
is also symmetric idempotent if
\bm{H}
is symmetric idempotent.
In general, when
\bm{H}
projects onto a subspace
\mathcal{V}
, the matrix
\bm{I}-\bm{H}
projects onto the orthogonal complement
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
. Using the notation from Theorem
, it follows that
\bm{H}_{2}\equiv\bm{I}-\bm{H}_{1}
since
\bm{Q}\triangleq[\bm{Q}_{1},\bm{Q}_{2}]
is orthogonal such that
\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}+\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}=\bm{I}
.
Alternatively, we have the following result.

Proposition 118
(Project onto
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
).

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a subspace, and let
\bm{H}
be an orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{V}
. Then,
\bm{I}-\bm{H}
is the orthogonal projection matrix onto
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
.

The claim can be extended further that suppose
\mathcal{V}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{V}_{2}\subseteq\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
. Then,
\bm{H}_{1}
is the orthogonal projector that projects onto
\mathcal{V}_{1}
and
\bm{H}_{2}
is the orthogonal projector that projects onto
\mathcal{V}_{2}
if and only if
\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
First,
(\bm{I}-\bm{H})
is symmetric,
(\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}=\bm{I}-\bm{H}^{\top}=\bm{I}-\bm{H}
since
\bm{H}
is symmetric. And

(\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{2}=\bm{I}^{2}-\bm{I}\bm{H}-\bm{H}\bm{I}+\bm{H}^{2}=\bm{I}-\bm{H}.

Thus,
\bm{I}-\bm{H}
is an orthogonal projection matrix. By spectral theorem again, let
\bm{H}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
. Then,
\bm{I}-\bm{H}=\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}-\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}(\bm{I}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\bm{Q}^{\top}
. Hence the column space of
\bm{I}-\bm{H}
is spanned by the eigenvectors of
\bm{H}
corresponding to the zero eigenvalues of
\bm{H}
(by Proposition
), which coincides with
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
.

For the second part, since
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H}_{1})=\mathcal{V}_{1}
and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H}_{2})=\mathcal{V}_{2}
, every column of
\bm{H}_{1}
is perpendicular to each column of
\bm{H}_{2}
. Thus,
\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Conversely, suppose
\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
, then
\bm{H}_{1}(\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y})=\boldsymbol{0}
for all
\bm{y}
. Thus
\mathcal{V}_{1}\perp\mathcal{V}_{2}
.

In particular, from the above result, it can be easily verified when
\mathcal{V}_{1}=\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{V}_{2}=\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
, we have
\bm{H}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})=\boldsymbol{0}
.

A projection matrix that projects any vector onto a subspace is not unique in general. However, when we restrict to orthogonal projections, the corresponding projection matrix becomes unique.

Proposition 119
(Uniqueness of orthogonal projection).

If
\bm{P}
and
\bm{H}
are orthogonal projection matrices onto the same subspace
\mathcal{V}
, then
\bm{P}=\bm{H}
.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
For any vector
\bm{v}
in
n
, it can be factored into a vector
\bm{v}_{p}
in
\mathcal{V}
and a vector
\bm{v}_{n}
in
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
such that
\bm{v}=\bm{v}_{p}+\bm{v}_{n}
and
\bm{v}_{p}^{\top}\bm{v}_{n}=0
. Then, we have

\bm{P}\bm{v}=\bm{v}_{p}=\bm{H}\bm{v},

such that
(\bm{P}-\bm{H})\bm{v}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Since any vector
\bm{v}\in\real^{n}
is in the null space of
\bm{P}-\bm{H}
, it follows that
\bm{P}-\bm{H}
is of rank 0, and
\bm{P}=\bm{H}
.

A direct consequence of Proposition
and Theorem
is the following result on the uniqueness of orthogonal projectors constructed from different sets of orthonormal bases.

Corollary 120
(Uniqueness of orthogonal projection).

Let
\bm{U},\bm{Q}\in\real^{n\times r}
be semi-orthogonal matrices such that
\bm{U}\neq\bm{Q}
and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{U})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{Q})
. Then the orthogonal projectors
\bm{H}_{1}\triangleq\bm{U}\bm{U}^{\top}
and
\bm{H}_{2}\triangleq\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}
are the same.

The proof is straightforward from Proposition
and Theorem
. Alternatively, we provide a self-contained proof below.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
Given that the column spaces of
\bm{U}
and
\bm{Q}
are the same, there exists an orthogonal matrix
\bm{Z}\in\real^{r\times r}
such that
\bm{U}=\bm{Q}\bm{Z}
.
The existence of such a matrix
\bm{Z}
is trivial since
\mathcal{C}(\bm{U})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{Q})
. To see that
\bm{Z}
is orthogonal, we have
\bm{I}_{r}=\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{U}=\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{Q}\bm{Z}=\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z}
. Therefore,
\bm{Z}
is orthogonal.

Now, let’s calculate
\bm{U}\bm{U}^{\top}
:

\bm{U}\bm{U}^{\top}=(\bm{Q}\bm{Z})(\bm{Q}\bm{Z})^{\top}=\bm{Q}\bm{Z}(\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Q}^{\top})=\bm{Q}(\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top})\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}.

This completes the proof.

Remark 121
(Equivalence between SVD and QR projections).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
have full column rank.
Suppose
[\bm{U}_{1},\bm{U}_{2}]\boldsymbol{\Sigma}[\bm{V}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}]^{\top}
and
[\bm{Q}_{1},\bm{Q}_{2}]\bm{R}
(with
\bm{U}_{1},\bm{Q}_{1}\in\real^{n\times p}
) are the full SVD and QR decompositions of
\bm{X}
, respectively.
Then,
\bm{U}_{1}\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}
and
\bm{U}_{2}\bm{U}_{2}^{\top}=\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}
are two set of orthogonal projectors onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, respectively.

Proposition 122
(Nested projection).

Let
\mathcal{V}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{2}\subseteq\real^{n}
be two nested linear subspaces.
Suppose
\bm{H}_{1}
is the orthogonal projection onto
\mathcal{V}_{1}
, and
\bm{H}_{2}
is the orthogonal projection onto
\mathcal{V}_{2}
.
Then the following properties hold:

1.

\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}=\bm{H}_{1}=\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}
;

2.

\bm{H}_{2}-\bm{H}_{1}
is also an orthogonal projection.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
For all
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, we have
\bm{H}_{1}\bm{y}\in\mathcal{V}_{1}
. This implies
\bm{H}_{1}\bm{y}\in\mathcal{V}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{2}
. Thus,

\bm{H}_{2}(\bm{H}_{1}\bm{y})=\bm{H}_{1}\bm{y}.\qquad(\text{from Definition\penalty\ \ref{definition:projection-matrix}})

Then
(\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}-\bm{H}_{1})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
for all
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
. That is, the dimension of the null space
\mathcal{N}(\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}-\bm{H}_{1})=n
and the rank of
\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}-\bm{H}_{1}
is 0, which results in
\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}=\bm{H}_{1}
.

For
\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}
, both
\bm{H}_{1}
and
\bm{H}_{2}
are symmetric such that
\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}=\bm{H}_{1}^{\top}\bm{H}_{2}^{\top}=(\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1})^{\top}=\bm{H}_{1}^{\top}=\bm{H}_{1}
, which completes the proof of part (i).

To see the second part, we notice that
(\bm{H}_{2}-\bm{H}_{1})^{\top}=\bm{H}_{2}-\bm{H}_{1}
and

\displaystyle(\bm{H}_{2}-\bm{H}_{1})^{2}

\displaystyle=\bm{H}_{2}^{2}-\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}-\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}+\bm{H}_{1}^{2}=\bm{H}_{2}-\bm{H}_{1}-\bm{H}_{1}+\bm{H}_{1}=\bm{H}_{2}-\bm{H}_{1},

which states that
\bm{H}_{2}-\bm{H}_{1}
is both symmetric and idempotent. This completes the proof.

To conclude, we claim that orthogonal projection matrices are positive semidefinite (PSD).

Proposition 123
(Symmetric projection).

Any orthogonal projection matrix
\bm{H}
is positive semidefinite.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Since
\bm{H}
is symmetric and idempotent. For any vector
\bm{x}
, we have

\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{H}\bm{x}=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{H}\bm{H}\bm{x}=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{H}^{\top}\bm{H}\bm{x}=\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}\geq 0.

Thus,
\bm{H}
is PSD.

2.7.4
Properties of Oblique Projection Matrices

Proposition
highlights the role of orthogonal projection in the standard least squares problem. This projection plays a central role in estimating the best fit solution by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. However, in more general settings where the errors are not assumed to be isotropic or homoskedastic, such as in the
generalized least squares (GLS)
framework, the notion of projection becomes more nuanced. In these cases, we encounter an oblique projection, which allows for projections along directions that are not necessarily orthogonal with respect to the standard Euclidean inner product. We will explore this concept in detail in Section
, where we discuss how GLS accounts for correlations and heteroskedasticity in the error terms through the use of a weighting matrix.

As mentioned previously, a matrix
\bm{P}\in\real^{n\times n}
that satisfies
\bm{P}^{2}=\bm{P}
and
\bm{P}^{\top}\neq\bm{P}
is an
oblique projector
(Lemma
). It splits any vector
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
into a sum
\bm{y}=\bm{P}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{y}
:

\bm{P}\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{P})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{P}\bm{y}\not\perp(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{y}.

Consider first the two-dimensional case. Let
\bm{u}
and
\bm{v}
be unit vectors in
2
such that
\cos(\theta)=\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{v}>0
.
If
\bm{u}\neq\bm{v}
, then

\bm{P}\triangleq\bm{u}(\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{u})^{-1}\bm{v}^{\top}=\frac{1}{\cos(\theta)}\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top}
is the oblique projector onto
\bm{u}
along the orthogonal complement of
\bm{v}
. That is,
\bm{P}\bm{y}
is a scalar multiple of
\bm{u}
and
\bm{v}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
for any
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.

\bm{P}^{\top}=\bm{v}(\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{v})^{-1}\bm{u}^{\top}=\frac{1}{\cos(\theta)}\bm{v}\bm{u}^{\top}
is the oblique projector onto
\bm{v}
along the orthogonal complement of
\bm{u}
. That is,
\bm{P}\bm{y}
is a scalar multiple of
\bm{v}
and
\bm{u}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
for any
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.

If
\bm{u}=\bm{v}
, then
\bm{P}
is an orthogonal projector and
\cos(\theta)=1
(see the subsection below Theorem
, the projections used in the QR decomposition). When
\bm{v}
is almost orthogonal to
\bm{u}
, then
\left\lVert\bm{P}\right\rVert_{2}=1/\cos(\theta)
becomes large.

We showed in Proposition
that
\bm{H}\triangleq\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
is an orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
if
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full column rank.
Using the matrix
\bm{X}
, we can also find an oblique projector by introducing a positive definite matrix.

Proposition 124
(Oblique projector onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
have full column rank
p
(
p\leq n
), and let
\boldsymbol{\Omega}\neq\bm{I}\in\real^{n\times n}
be positive definite. Then,

\bm{P}\triangleq\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1},

(2.33)

is an oblique projector
onto

\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})

along
the space
\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})^{\perp}
:

\bm{P}\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\qquad\text{and}\qquad(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{y}\in\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})^{\perp}\equiv\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}).

(2.34)

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Let
\mathcal{C}\triangleq\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, and let
\mathcal{C}^{\perp}
be the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{C}
.
Since
\bm{P}^{2}=\bm{P}
,
\bm{P}
is a projector.
For any
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
,
\bm{P}\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.
On the other hand, if
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, say
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, then:

\bm{P}\bm{y}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}.

So
\bm{P}
is a projector onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

Let
\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{\bm{u}\in\real^{n}\mid\bm{P}\bm{u}=\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
We want to prove
\mathcal{S}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathcal{C}^{\perp}
.
To see this, we first suppose
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{S}
, i.e.,
\bm{P}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Since
\bm{X}
has full column rank, then

(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{\top}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}\qquad\implies\qquad(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{\top}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}\iff\bm{X}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y})=\boldsymbol{0}.

Therefore,
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}^{\perp}\implies\bm{y}\in\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathcal{C}^{\perp}\implies\mathcal{S}\subseteq\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathcal{C}^{\perp}
.

Conversely, suppose
\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{z}
with
\bm{z}\in\mathcal{C}^{\perp}
.
Then,

\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{z}=\boldsymbol{0}.

Therefore,
\bm{P}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
This concludes that
\bm{P}
is an oblique projection onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, along
\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})^{\perp}
.

More generally, we have the following result.

{theoremHigh}
[Oblique projector onto general subspaces]
Let
\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{W}
be two complementary subspaces in
n
:

\mathcal{V}\cap\mathcal{W}=\boldsymbol{0}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{V}\cup\mathcal{W}=\real^{n}.

Let
\bm{U}_{1}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
\bm{V}_{1}\in\real^{n\times(n-r)}
be semi-orthogonal matrices (i.e., their columns are mutually orthonormal; Definition
) such that
\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{1})=\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{C}(\bm{V}_{1})=\mathcal{W}^{\perp}
, where
\mathcal{W}^{\perp}
is the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{W}
. Then the oblique projector
onto

\mathcal{V}

along

\mathcal{W}
is

\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}=\bm{U}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}.

(2.35)

Similarly, let
\bm{U}_{2}\in\real^{n\times(n-r)}
and
\bm{V}_{2}\in\real^{n\times r}
be semi-orthogonal matrices such that
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}=\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{2})
and
\mathcal{W}=\mathcal{C}(\bm{V}_{2})
. Then,

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{\mathcal{W},\mathcal{V}}=\bm{V}_{2}(\bm{U}_{2}^{\top}\bm{V}_{2})^{-1}\bm{U}_{2}^{\top};

(2.36)

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}+\bm{P}_{\mathcal{W},\mathcal{V}}=\bm{I};

(2.37)

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}^{\top}=\bm{P}_{\mathcal{W}^{\perp},\mathcal{V}^{\perp}}.

(2.38)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We have
\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}^{2}=\bm{U}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}=\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}
. This shows that
\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}
is a projector onto
\mathcal{V}
.

Forward implication.

Let
\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{\bm{u}\in\real^{n}\mid\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}\bm{u}=\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
We want to prove
\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{W}\equiv\mathcal{C}(\bm{V}_{2})\equiv\mathcal{C}(\bm{V}_{1})^{\perp}\equiv\mathcal{N}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top})
.
To see this, we first suppose
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{S}
, i.e.,
\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Since
\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1}=\bm{I}_{r}
, we have

\bm{U}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}\qquad\implies\qquad\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}.

Therefore,
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top})\implies\bm{y}\in\mathcal{W}\implies\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{W}
.

Backward implication.

Conversely, suppose
\bm{y}\in\mathcal{W}
such that
\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Then,
\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
This concludes that
\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}
is an oblique projection onto
\mathcal{V}
, along
\mathcal{W}
.

Similarly,
\bm{P}_{\mathcal{W},\mathcal{V}}=\bm{V}_{2}(\bm{U}_{2}^{\top}\bm{V}_{2})^{-1}\bm{U}_{2}^{\top}
is the projector onto
\mathcal{W}
along
\mathcal{V}
.
To prove (
2.37
), we first note that the assumption implies
\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{V}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\bm{U}_{2}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Then,

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}+\bm{P}_{\mathcal{W},\mathcal{V}}

\displaystyle=\bm{U}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}+\bm{V}_{2}(\bm{U}_{2}^{\top}\bm{V}_{2})^{-1}\bm{U}_{2}^{\top}

\displaystyle=[\bm{U}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}]\left([\bm{V}_{1},\bm{U}_{2}]^{\top}[\bm{U}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}]\right)^{-1}[\bm{V}_{1},\bm{U}_{2}]^{\top}

\displaystyle=[\bm{U}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}][\bm{U}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}]^{-1}[\bm{V}_{1},\bm{U}_{2}]^{-\top}[\bm{V}_{1},\bm{U}_{2}]^{\top}=\bm{I}.

The equality (
2.38
) follows from the expression
\bm{P}_{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W}}^{\top}=\bm{V}_{1}(\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}
.
This completes the proof.

Suppose
\bm{H}\in\real^{n\times n}
is an orthogonal projector onto a subspace
\mathcal{V}
where
\dim(\mathcal{V})=r
. And let
\bm{U}_{1}\in\real^{n\times r}
be a semi-orthogonal matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis for the subspace
\mathcal{V}
.
Then we have
\bm{H}\equiv\bm{U}_{1}\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}
(Theorem
and Corollary
).
Since
\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1}=\bm{I}_{r}
, it holds that

\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\big\lVert\bm{U}_{1}\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}\bm{v}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1}\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}\bm{U}_{1}\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}\bm{v}=\big\lVert\bm{U}_{1}^{\top}\bm{v}\big\rVert_{2}^{2},\;\forall\;\bm{v}\in\real^{n},

(2.39)

where the first inequality follows by Lemma
.

Exercise
\thetheo

Show that the converse of the above result is also true: a projector
\bm{H}
is an orthogonal projector only if (
) holds for all
\bm{v}\in\real^{n}
.

Hint: See the comparison between orthogonal and oblique projections, as shown in Figure
.

2.8
OLS in Geometry with Noise Disturbance

We revisit the concept of the orthogonal projection matrix in the context of the least squares problem.

Remark 125
(Important facts about hat matrix (part 1)).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p0}
.

1. As we assume
\bm{X}
is fixed and has full rank with
n\geq p
. It is known that the rank of
\bm{X}
is equal to the rank of its Gram matrix, defined as
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
, such that

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}).

2. The rank of an orthogonal projection matrix is the dimension of the subspace onto which it projects. Hence, the rank of
\bm{H}
is
p
when
\bm{X}
has full rank and
n\geq p
:

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{H})=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top})=p.

3. The column space of
\bm{H}
is identical to the column space of
\bm{X}
.

Now suppose the ideal output
\bm{y}
comes from some true function
g(\bm{X})\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
such that the observed output
{\mathbf{y}}
is modeled as

{\mathbf{y}}=g(\bm{X})+\boldsymbol{\epsilon},

(2.40)

where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
represents additive noise, making
{\mathbf{y}}
a random variable.
That is, the real observation
{\mathbf{y}}
is disturbed by some noise random variable.
In this case, we assume that the observed values
\bm{y}
differ from the true function
g(\bm{X})=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
by additive noise.
This situation is illustrated in Figure
, which provides a geometric interpretation of the least squares problem and serves as a foundation for further developments in this book.
The main components of the model are:

Vector of outputs (responses):
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
is an
n\times 1
vector of observations of the output variable, and
n
is the sample size.

Design matrix:
\bm{X}
is an
n\times p
matrix of inputs, and
p
is the dimension of the inputs for each observation.

Vector of parameters:
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}
is a
p\times 1
vector of regression coefficients.

Vector of noises:
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\real^{n}
is an
n\times 1
vector of noises.

Vector of errors (residuals):
\bm{e}\in\real^{n}
is an
n\times 1
vector of errors. For predicted outputs
\widehat{\bm{y}}
,
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
.
Note that
\bm{e}
is different from
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
: the former results from our linear model fit, while the latter is unobservable. In some literature,
\bm{e}
is denoted as
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
to emphasize its relationship with
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
.

Figure 2.7:
Projection onto the hyperplane of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, with the output disturbed by noise
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
.

By introducing the noise vector, we can derive additional important properties of the hat matrix:

Remark 126
(Important facts about hat matrix (part 2)).

In light of Remark
, we have

4. Error vector
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}=\underline{(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{y}}=(\bm{I}-\bm{H})(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=\underline{(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
: projecting
\bm{y}
onto the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
is equivalent to projecting
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
onto the same space.
This result follows naturally from the geometric interpretation shown in Figure
.

5. The predicted output
\widehat{\bm{y}}
and the residual vector
\bm{e}
are orthogonal. Additionally,
\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
and
\bm{e}
are also orthogonal.

6. By the Pythagorean theorem applied to projections:
\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
and
\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.

7. Pythagoras in general: for any orthogonal projection matrix
\bm{P}
, we have
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{P}\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.

This general form of the Pythagorean identity can be verified as follows:

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{P}\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{P}^{\top}\bm{P}\bm{x}+\bm{x}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{P})^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{x}

\displaystyle=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{P}\bm{x}+\bm{x}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{x}=\bm{x}^{\top}\big[\bm{P}\bm{x}+(\bm{I}-\bm{P})\bm{x}\big]=\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

2.9
OLS in Pseudo-Inverse

By Theorem
, when
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
does not necessarily have full rank, the unique least squares solution of minimum norm is characterized by

\bm{e}\triangleq\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\perp\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}\perp\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}).

(2.41)

The full SVD
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}

provides orthogonal bases for these two subspaces (Theorem
), making the SVD an ideal tool for solving least squares problems.
Consider the minimum-norm least squares problem:

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in{\mathbb{B}}}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2},\quad{\mathbb{B}}\triangleq\{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}=\min\}.

The problem has a unique solution that can be written as
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
(Theorem
),
where the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}
is:

\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{V}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{U}^{\top},\quad\text{with }\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\text{ and }\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\in\real^{r\times r}.

By the uniqueness of
\bm{X}^{+}
(Lemma
), this does not depend on the particular choice of
\bm{U}
and
\bm{V}
in the SVD.

The pseudo-inverse and the singular vectors of
\bm{X}
also provide simple expressions for orthogonal projections onto the four fundamental subspaces of
\bm{X}
.
These expressions can be verified using the Penrose conditions (see (
), Theorems
and
) and the SVD:

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})}
