\displaystyle=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{U}_{1}\bm{U}_{1}^{\top},\qquad

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}=\bm{V}_{1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top},

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})}

\displaystyle=\bm{I}-\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{U}_{2}\bm{U}_{2}^{\top},\qquad

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})}

\displaystyle=\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{+}\bm{X}=\bm{V}_{2}\bm{V}_{2}^{\top},

where
\bm{U}_{1}=[\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{r}]
,
\bm{V}_{1}=[\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}]
, and
r=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
.

If only some of the four Penrose conditions hold, the corresponding matrix is referred to as a generalized inverse.
Any matrix
\bm{X}^{-}
satisfying the first Penrose condition
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}
is called an
inner inverse or
\{1\}
-inverse
. If it satisfies the second condition
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}=\bm{X}^{-}
, it is called an
outer inverse or a
\{2\}
-inverse
.

Let
\bm{X}^{-}
be an inner-inverse of
\bm{X}
. Then for all
\bm{y}
such that the system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
is consistent,
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}
is a solution. The general solution can be written

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}+(\bm{I}-\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\alpha},\qquad\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\real^{p}.

(2.42)

This form is similar to the one using the pseudo-inverse given in (
). However,
\bm{X}^{-}
is in general not unique, and
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}
may not yield a minimum-norm solution of the least squares problem; see below.

\paragrapharrow

Penrose (
C1
)+(
C3
), and least squares inverse.
For any inner-inverse of
\bm{X}
, it holds that

(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})^{2}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-},\qquad(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})^{2}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}.

This shows that both
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
and
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
are idempotent matrices, and hence (in general, oblique) projectors; see Section
.
The residual norm
\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}
is minimized when
\boldsymbol{\beta}
satisfies the normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
. Suppose that an inner-inverse
\bm{X}^{-}
also satisfies the third Penrose condition:

(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})^{\top}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}.

Then
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
becomes the orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, and in this case,
\bm{X}^{-}
is called a
least squares inverse
.
From the two conditions
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}
and
(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-})^{\top}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}
, we obtain:

\bm{X}^{\top}=(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}.

Therefore,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
,
which shows that
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}
satisfies the normal equation and therefore is a least squares solution.

\paragrapharrow

Penrose (
C1
)+(
C4
).
A dual result also holds.
If
\bm{X}^{-}
is an inner inverse and
(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})^{\top}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
, then
\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
is the orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, and
\bm{X}^{-}
is called a minimum-norm inverse. If
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
is consistent, the unique solution for which
\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}
is smallest satisfies the normal equation of the second kind; see (
):

\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{y}.

For a minimum-norm inverse
\bm{X}^{-}
, we again use the identity
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}=\bm{X}
and
(\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})^{\top}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}
to derive:

\bm{X}^{\top}=(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X})^{\top}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}.

Hence,
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{X}^{-}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma})=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}
, which shows that
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{-}\bm{y}
is the solution of minimum norm.

\paragrapharrow

Consistency guarantee.
In the above paragraph, we assumed that the linear system is consistent.
Consistency can be guaranteed under certain conditions using the concept of left and right inverses (Definition
).
We now show that the linear system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
has a unique solution under specific conditions.

{theoremHigh}
[Unique linear system solution]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be left-invertible (
n\geq p
), and let
\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\in\real^{p\times n}
denote a left inverse of
\bm{X}
. Then, the linear system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
has a
unique
solution if and only if

(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}.

In this case, the unique solution is given by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Suppose
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
is the solution of
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
, then

\displaystyle\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})

\displaystyle=\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{y};

\displaystyle\bm{X}(\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\bm{y}.

That implies
\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{y}=\bm{y}
and
(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

Conversely, suppose
(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
, and let
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{y}
. Substituting
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{y}
into
(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we have

\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\bm{y},

which implies
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\bm{X}_{L}^{-1}\bm{y}
is a solution of
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
whenever
(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

To prove the uniqueness, suppose
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}
are two solutions of
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
. We have
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}=\bm{y}
, hence
\bm{X}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1})=\boldsymbol{0}
. Since
\bm{X}
is left-invertible, so that
\bm{X}
has full column rank
p
.
The dimension of the row space of
\bm{X}
is
p
as well such that the null space of
\bm{X}
is of dimension 0 (i.e.,
\dim(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top}))+\dim(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}))=p
by the fundamental theorem of linear algebra, see Theorem
). Therefore,
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}
, which completes the proof.

According to the fundamental theorem of linear algebra (Figure
),
if
\bm{X}
is left-invertible, its row space spans the entire
p
(indicating
\bm{X}
has full column rank
p
). The condition
(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{X}\bm{X}_{L}^{-1})\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
implies that
\bm{y}
is in the column space of
\bm{X}
such that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
has at least one solution, and the above proposition shows that this solution is unique.

{theoremHigh}

[Always have solution]
Suppose
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is right-invertible (which implies
n\leq p
), and let
\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}
be a right inverse of
\bm{X}
.
Then, for any
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, the linear system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
has at least one solution, and one such solution is given by:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}\bm{y},

where
\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}
is a right inverse of
\bm{X}
and the right inverse is not necessarily unique.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
It is straightforward to verify that

(\bm{X}\bm{X}_{R}^{-1})\bm{y}=\bm{I}_{n}\bm{y}=\bm{y},

which shows that
\bm{X}_{R}^{-1}\bm{y}
is a solution of
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
.

We observe that if
\bm{X}
is right-invertible, then it has full row rank
n
. According to the fundamental theorem of linear algebra (Figure
),
the column space of
\bm{X}
spans the entire space of
n
if
\bm{X}
is right-invertible
. Hence, any vector
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
lies in the column space of
\bm{X}
, and the system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
always has at least one solution.

2.10
Generalized Least Squares (GLS)

We will briefly introduce the
generalized least squares (GLS)
problem in this section.
In Section
, we will discuss the Bayesian approach to linear models or generalized linear models.
The Gauss-Markov extension to the GLS problem is discussed in Theorem
.

\paragrapharrow

Generalized least squares problem.
We consider the following
generalized least squares (GLS)
problem

\displaystyle(\textbf{LS}):\qquad

\displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})

(2.43)

\displaystyle\implies(\textbf{GLS}):\qquad

\displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}),

(2.44)

where
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is positive definite. Since
\boldsymbol{\Phi}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}
is also positive definite, one may wonder why we use
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}
instead of
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
.
The reason is that
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
has a covariance interpretation within the Gauss-Markov model; see Theorem
.
However, when developing numerical methods for solving the GLS problem, the notion
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
is frequently used; see Section
.

Several perspectives can be taken on the GLS solution or prediction:

1.

The least squares solution of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is the value
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
that satisfies the
generalized normal equation

(\textbf{GNE}):\qquad\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}.

(2.45)

This can be obtained, for example, using the first-order optimality condition (Proposition
).

2.

Equivalently, the solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfies the
orthogonality condition

\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{e}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(2.46)

3.

The predicted vector for
\bm{y}
(when
\bm{X}
has full column rank and
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is PD) is given by

\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}.

(2.47)

This represents the oblique projection of
\bm{y}
using the oblique projector onto
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
along the space
\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})^{\perp}
(Proposition
).

The GLS problem can be solved or interpreted through basic LS solutions in three ways:

Let
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
be the spectral decomposition of
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
. Since
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is positive definite, then by Theorem
the square root of
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
exists such that
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\bm{Q}^{\top}\triangleq\bm{G}\bm{G}^{\top}
.
Therefore,
(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})=\left\lVert\bm{G}^{-1}\bm{y}-\bm{G}^{-1}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
such that the GLS problem of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is equivalent to the basic LS problem of

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\lVert\widetilde{\bm{y}}-\widetilde{\bm{X}}\boldsymbol{\beta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\text{where }\widetilde{\bm{y}}\triangleq\bm{G}^{-1}\bm{y},\ \widetilde{\bm{X}}\triangleq\bm{G}^{-1}\bm{X}.

(2.48)

\boldsymbol{\Omega}
can also be uniquely denoted as
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\bm{M}^{2}\triangleq(\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\bm{Q}^{\top})(\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\bm{Q}^{\top})
, where
\bm{M}
is also positive definite (Theorem
). Thus, the GLS problem can be written as another LS problem of the form (
), where
\widetilde{\bm{y}}\triangleq\bm{M}^{-1}\bm{y}
and
\widetilde{\bm{X}}\triangleq\bm{M}^{-1}\bm{X}
.

\boldsymbol{\Omega}
admits the Cholesky decomposition
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}
.
Thus, the GLS problem can be written as another LS problem of the same form (
), where
\widetilde{\bm{y}}\triangleq\bm{L}^{-1}\bm{y}
and
\widetilde{\bm{X}}\triangleq\bm{L}^{-1}\bm{X}
.

Among these three approaches, the third one—based on the Cholesky decomposition—is generally the most straightforward.
The GLS problem can be solved by first computing
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}
and then solving the transformed systems
\bm{L}\widetilde{\bm{X}}=\bm{X}
and
\bm{L}\widetilde{\bm{y}}=\bm{y}
. The normal equation
\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{y}}
are formed and solved by Cholesky factorization; see Section
. Alternatively, one may apply QR factorization to the transformed design matrix:

\bm{L}^{-1}\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},\quad\bm{Q}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Q}_{1}&\bm{Q}_{2}\end{bmatrix},

(2.49)

which leads to the solution:
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{L}^{-1}\bm{y}
; see Section
.

Computing the Cholesky factorization
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}
requires approximately
\sim n^{3}/3
floating-point operations (flops) for a dense matrix
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
.
Forming the transformed matrices
\widetilde{\bm{X}}=\bm{L}^{-1}\bm{X}
and
\widetilde{\bm{y}}=\bm{L}^{-1}\bm{y}
requires a further
\sim n^{2}p
flops. This may be prohibitive unless
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
has a favorable structure. When
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is a banded matrix with small bandwidth
w
, the cost of the Cholesky factorization reduces to roughly
\sim nw(w+3)
flops.

\paragrapharrow

Weighted least squares (WLS). The
weighted least squares
problem is a special GLS problem in which
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is chosen to be a diagonal matrix. When the diagonal matrix is the identity matrix, WLS reduces to the ordinary least squares problem. See also Problem
.

\paragrapharrow

Generalized minimum-norm problem.
Consider a consistent linear system
\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{z}
of full row rank, the
generalized minimum-norm (GMN) problem
is

(\textbf{GMN}):\qquad\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{z}.

(2.50)

The corresponding
generalized normal equation
of the second kind is

(\textbf{GNE2}):\qquad\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{z},\qquad\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\gamma}.

(2.51)

If
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}
is the Cholesky factorization, then
\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\left\lVert\bm{L}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. Hence problem (
) is equivalent to seeking the minimum-norm solution of the system

\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\bm{z}\quad\text{with}\quad\widetilde{\bm{X}}\triangleq\bm{L}^{-1}\bm{X},\ \widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq\bm{L}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}.

Alternatively, using the QR factorization gives
\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{L}^{-\top}\bm{Q}_{1}(\bm{R}^{-\top}\bm{z})
; see Section
.

Similar to the augmented LS problem (
),
Problems GLS and GMN are special cases of the generalized augmented LS problem:

\text{(GAuLS)}:\qquad\bm{F}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\\
\boldsymbol{\beta}\end{bmatrix}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Omega}&\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\\
\boldsymbol{\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{y}\\
\bm{z}\end{bmatrix}\quad\bm{y}\in\real^{n},\quad\bm{z}\in\real^{p}.

(2.52)

This system matrix
\bm{F}
is nonsingular if and only if
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
and

\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})\cap\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}.

In fact, if
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is positive definite, then it follows that the matrix
\bm{F}\in\real^{(n+p)\times(n+p)}
of system (
) has
n
positive and
p
negative eigenvalues
(
Björck 2024
)
. For this reason, (
) is called a saddle point system. Eliminating
\boldsymbol{\alpha}
in (
) gives the generalized normal equation for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
,

\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}-\bm{z}.

(2.53)

An explicit expression for the inverse of augmented matrix
\bm{F}
is obtained from the Schur complement of
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
in
\bm{F}
; see, for example,
Lu 2021b
:

\bm{F}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Omega}&\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}(\bm{I}-\bm{T})&\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}\bm{S}^{-1}\\
\bm{S}^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}&-\bm{S}^{-1}\end{bmatrix},

(2.54)

where

\bm{S}\triangleq\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X},\qquad\bm{T}\triangleq\bm{X}\bm{S}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{\top}.

In terms of the QR factorization (
), the inverse is

\bm{F}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{L}^{-\top}\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{L}^{-1}&\bm{L}^{-\top}\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}^{-\top}\\
\bm{R}^{-1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{L}^{-1}&-\bm{R}^{-1}\bm{R}^{-\top}\end{bmatrix}.

(2.55)

2.10.1
Orthogonal Projection in GLS

We previously showed that the orthogonal projection matrix

\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top},\qquad(\text{project onto $\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})$})

is an orthogonal projection onto the subspace
\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.
Let
\widetilde{\bm{X}}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{X}
,
We also observe that

\displaystyle\bm{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}

\displaystyle=\widetilde{\bm{X}}(\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}})^{-1}\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top}

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\underbrace{\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}_{\triangleq\bm{H}_{2}},\qquad(\text{project onto $\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}=\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{X})$})

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{H}_{2}

is the orthogonal projection onto the subspace
\mathcal{V}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}=\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{X})
.
That is, the prediction
\widehat{\bm{y}}
becomes
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{H}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\bm{y}
in the GLS problem (and
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\bm{H}\bm{y}
in the LS case).
This also implies

\bm{H}_{2}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1},\qquad(\text{project onto $\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})$})

is also an orthogonal projection onto the subspace
\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

Before discussing the properties of orthogonal projections in the context of generalized least squares, it is important to clarify the concept of “symmetry.”
While a matrix
\bm{A}
is considered symmetric if
\bm{A}=\bm{A}^{\top}
, a more general definition of symmetry arises when considering inner products.

To see this, the definition of an inner product must satisfy three fundamental properties:

Definition 127
(Inner product).

In most cases, a vector norm can be derived from the inner product of vectors (the inner product of vectors
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
is given by
\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle
), which satisfies the following three conditions:

Commutativity.
\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle=\langle\bm{y},\bm{x}\rangle
for any
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.

Linearity.
\langle\lambda_{1}\bm{x}_{1}+\lambda_{2}\bm{x}_{2},\bm{y}\rangle=\lambda_{1}\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle+\lambda_{2}\langle\bm{x}_{2},\bm{y}\rangle
for any
\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\in\real
and
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.

Positive definiteness.
\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}\rangle\geq 0
for any
\bm{x}\in\real^{n}
, and
\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}\rangle=0
if and only if
\bm{x}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

Using this notion of an inner product, we can now define a more general form of symmetry:

Definition 128
(Symmetric in terms of inner product).

A matrix
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
is said to be symmetric (with respect to an inner product) if for all
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, such that
\langle\bm{x},\bm{A}\bm{y}\rangle=\langle\bm{A}\bm{x},\bm{y}\rangle
.
Some specific examples include:

1.

For the standard inner product
\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{y}
, symmetric
\bm{A}
means
\bm{A}=\bm{A}^{\top}
.

2.

Given a positive definite matrix
\bm{Z}
, consider the inner product
\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle_{\bm{Z}}=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{Z}\bm{y}
; see Problem
. Symmetric
\bm{A}
means
\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{Z}\bm{A}\bm{y}=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{Z}\bm{y}
.
This leads to the definition of the generalized norm, defined as
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}_{\bm{Z}}=\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}\right\rangle_{\bm{Z}}
, also known as the
\bm{Z}
-norm. When
\bm{Z}=\bm{I}
, this reduces to the standard inner product, standard symmetry, and standard
\ell_{2}
norm, respectively.

With this generalized definition of symmetry based on inner products, we can extend the idea of orthogonal projection accordingly. Specifically, we define a projection to be orthogonal in terms of the given inner product, which results in the concept of a
generalized orthogonal projection
.
Then, we can check that
\bm{H}_{2}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}
is symmetric in terms of
\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}
such that

\bm{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y}=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{H}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y},

for all
\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
.

Lemma 129
(Genralized orthogonal projection in GLS).

Consider the GLS problem

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}),

where
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is fixed and positive definite,
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full rank with
n\geq p
(i.e., rank is
p
).
Then,

\bm{H}_{2}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}

is a generalized orthogonal projection that projects onto the column space of
\bm{X}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We prove
\bm{H}_{2}
is an orthogonal projection by showing that it is idempotent and symmetric, and it projects onto the column space of
\bm{X}
.
It can be readily verified that

\bm{H}_{2}^{2}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}=\bm{H}_{2},

and

\displaystyle\langle\bm{x},\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y}\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}

\displaystyle=\bm{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y}=\bm{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\left(\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\right)\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{H}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}=\langle\bm{H}_{2}\bm{x},\bm{y}\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}.

Since
\bm{H}_{2}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\triangleq\bm{X}\bm{C}
, the columns of
\bm{H}_{2}
are combinations of the columns of
\bm{X}
, thus
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H}_{2})\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.
By Lemma
, we have

\displaystyle\mathrm{rank}(\bm{H}_{2})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{H}_{2})=\mathrm{tr}\big(\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\big)

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}\big((\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}\big)=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{I}_{p})=p,

where the third equality follows from the fact that the trace of a product is invariant under cyclical permutations of the factors.
Thus, the rank of
\bm{H}_{2}
equals the rank of
\bm{X}
. We conclude that
\mathcal{C}(\bm{H}_{2})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.
Therefore,
\bm{H}_{2}
is a generalized orthogonal projection onto the column space of
\bm{X}
.

The result on minimum distance in orthogonal projection (Theorem
) can also be extended to the generalized case under the
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}
-norm.

{theoremHigh}
[Minimum distance in generalized orthogonal projection]
Let
\mathcal{V}
be a subspace of
n
, and let
\bm{H}_{2}
be a generalized orthogonal projection with respect to
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}
-inner product onto
\mathcal{V}
.
Then, it follows that

\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}\leq\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}},\qquad\forall\,\bm{v}\in\mathcal{V}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We find that
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{H}_{2}
,
\bm{H}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}
, and
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{H}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2}
are all symmetric (with respect to the first inner product in Definition
, i.e., the standard symmetry).
Therefore, they all admit a spectral decomposition. By trial and error, the right way is to decompose

\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{H}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top},

where
\bm{Q}=[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}]
is the column partition of
\bm{Q}
, and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n})
contains the eigenvalues of
(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{H}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2})
. Let
\dim(\mathcal{V})=r
.
We notice that
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{H}_{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2}
is symmetric and idempotent such that its only possible eigenvalues are 1 and 0 by Lemma
. Without loss of generality, let
\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\ldots=\lambda_{r}=1
and
\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_{r+2}=\ldots=\lambda_{n}=0
.
Then, we have

\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{n}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
n
.

\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\mathcal{V}
, which is the subspace
\mathcal{V}
rotated by
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}
. So for any vector
\bm{v}\in\mathcal{V}
, let
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\bm{a}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{v}}
, we have
\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}=0
for
i\in\{r+1,r+2,\ldots,n\}
.

Again, let
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\bm{z}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{y}}
.
Since
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{H}_{2}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{y}-\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{y}-\bm{Q}^{\top}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{z}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{z}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}-\lambda_{i}\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}=0+\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}(\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i}-\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}+\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}(\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{q}_{i})^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{z}-\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{z}-\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{v}\right\rVert_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}}^{2},

which completes the proof.

In previous discussions, for any orthogonal projection matrix
\bm{H}
, we established Pythagoras’ theorem and the orthogonal property in ordinary least squares (i.e., with inner product denoted by

In previous discussions, we established Pythagoras’ theorem and the orthogonal property for any orthogonal projection matrix
\bm{H}
in the context of ordinary least squares, where the inner product is defined as

\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{y}
.
These properties are expressed as:

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2};

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}

\displaystyle=(\bm{H}\bm{y})^{\top}\left((\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{y}\right).

Analogously, in the generalized orthogonal projection, we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}+\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{H}_{2})\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}};

\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{H}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{H}_{2})\bm{y}+\bm{y}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}-\bm{H}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{H}_{2})\bm{y},

and

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}

\displaystyle=\langle\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y},(\bm{I}-\bm{H}_{2})\bm{y}\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}=(\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\left((\bm{I}-\bm{H}_{2})\bm{y}\right).

2.10.2
Equivalence between OLS and GLS

In Theorem
, we prove that for any orthogonal projection
\bm{H}
, the inequality
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{H}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
holds for all
\bm{v}\;\in\mathcal{V}\triangleq\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
. In the context of generalized least squares, the analogous result holds for any generalized orthogonal projection matrix
\bm{H}_{2}
:
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{H}_{2}\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}}\leq\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{v}\right\rVert^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}},\,\,\forall\,\bm{v}\in\mathcal{V}\triangleq\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, where
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is positive definite.
Although OLS and GLS generally yield different estimates, we now show that under certain conditions, these two estimators are in fact equivalent.

{theoremHigh}
[Equivalence between OLS and GLS]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full rank
p
, and let
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
be a positive definite matrix.
The ordinary least squares estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
is equivalent to the GLS estimate
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}
if and only if

\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Suppose
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Then for all
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, we must have

(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y},

which implies

(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}.

Taking the transpose of both sides gives

\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}.

Since
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
and
(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}
are nonsingular matrices, this transformation reflects a change of basis. Therefore, it follows that
\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.

Conversely, suppose
\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})=\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, there must be a nonsingular matrix
\bm{A}
such that
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}=\bm{X}\bm{A}
(columns of
\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}
are combinations of columns of
\bm{X}
, and the combinations are given by
\bm{A}
). That is
\bm{X}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{X}\bm{A}
. Then, we have

\displaystyle(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\big({\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{X}\bm{A})}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}\big)^{-1}{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{X}\bm{A})}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\big(\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X}\big)^{-1}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y},

which completes the proof.

2.11
Total Least Squares (TLS) and Other Issues

In this discussion, we assume
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full rank with
n\geq p
, ensuring that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is invertible.
However, if two or more columns of
\bm{X}
are perfectly correlated, the matrix
\bm{X}
becomes deficient, and
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
becomes singular.
To address this issue, one can choose
\boldsymbol{\beta}
that minimizes
\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
while satisfying the normal equation.
That is, we select the least squares solution with the smallest magnitude.
In Sections
and
, we briefly discuss how to use UTV decomposition and SVD to address this rank-deficient least squares problems.

\paragrapharrow

Regularizations and stability.
However, a common problem that arise in the ordinary least square solution is the near-singularity of
\bm{X}
.
Let the full SVD of
\bm{X}
be
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}\in\real^{n\times p}
, where
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times p}
are orthogonal, and the main diagonal of
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{n\times p}
contains the singular values. Consequently,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{V}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\bm{V}^{\top}\triangleq\bm{V}\bm{S}\bm{V}^{\top}
, where
\bm{S}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathrm{diag}([\sigma_{1}^{2},\sigma_{2}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2}])\in\real^{p\times p}
contains the squared singular values of
\bm{X}
. When
\bm{X}
is nearly singular,
\sigma_{p}^{2}\approx 0
, making the inverse operation
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}=\bm{V}\bm{S}^{-1}\bm{V}^{\top}
numerically unstable.
As a result, the solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{LS}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
may diverge.
To address this issue, we typically add an
\ell_{2}
regularization term to obtain the solution for the following optimization problem:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{Tik}}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(2.56)

This method is known as the
Tikhonov regularization method
(or simply the
\ell_{2}
regularized method)
(
Tikhonov 1963
)
.
The gradient of the problem is
2(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\lambda\bm{I})\boldsymbol{\beta}-2\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
. Thus, the least squares solution is given by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{Tik}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}.

The inverse operation becomes
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}=\bm{V}(\bm{S}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{V}^{\top}
, where
\widetilde{\bm{S}}\triangleq(\bm{S}+\lambda\bm{I})=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2}+\lambda,\sigma_{2}^{2}+\lambda,\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2}+\lambda)
.
The solutions for OLS and Tikhonov regularized LS are given, respectively, by

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{LS}}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{V}\left(\bm{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right)\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y};

(2.57)

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{Tik}}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{V}\left((\bm{S}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right)\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y},

(2.58)

where the main diagonals of
\left(\bm{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right)
are
\mathrm{diag}(\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}},\frac{1}{\sigma_{2}},\ldots,\frac{1}{\sigma_{p}})
; and the main diagonals of
\left((\bm{S}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right)
are
\mathrm{diag}(\frac{\sigma_{1}}{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\lambda},\frac{\sigma_{2}}{\sigma_{2}^{2}+\lambda},\ldots,\frac{\sigma_{p}}{\sigma_{p}^{2}+\lambda})
. The latter solution is more stable if
\lambda
is greater than the smallest nonzero squared singular value.
The condition number becomes smaller if the smallest singular value
\sigma_{p}
is close to zero:

\kappa(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})=\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{\sigma_{p}^{2}}\qquad\rightarrow\qquad\kappa(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\lambda\bm{I})=\frac{\lambda+\sigma_{1}^{2}}{\lambda+\sigma_{p}^{2}}.

Tikhonov regularization effectively prevents divergence in the least squares solution

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{LS}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
when the matrix
\bm{X}
is nearly singular or even rank-deficient. This improvement enhances the convergence properties of both the LS algorithm and its variants, such as alternating least squares, while addressing identifiability issues in various settings
(
Zhang 2017
)
. As a result, Tikhonov regularization has become a widely applied technique.

2.11.1
Different Least Squares Problems

In standard linear regression, the ordinary least squares method assumes that errors occur only in the response vector
\bm{y}
, while the data matrix
\bm{X}
is considered exact. However, in many real-world applications, both the data matrix
\bm{X}
and the response
\bm{y}
may be subject to measurement errors.
We then discuss different forms of least squares problems.

\paragrapharrow
Data least squares.
The least squares problem can be viewed as an optimization problem of the following form:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{LS}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{LS}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta},\widetilde{\bm{y}}}\left\lVert\widetilde{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t. }\quad\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}),

(2.59)

where
\widetilde{\bm{y}}
represents a perturbation of
\bm{y}
, i.e., a noise in the output variables.
While the OLS method accounts for errors in the response variable
\bm{y}
, the
data least sqaures (DLS)
method considers errors in the predictor variables:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{DLS}},\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{\text{DLS}}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta},\widetilde{\bm{X}}}\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert\widetilde{\bm{X}}\big\rVert_{F}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bm{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}),

(2.60)

where
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
represents a perturbation of
\bm{X}
(i.e., a noise in the predictor variables).
That is,
(\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}})\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{DLS}}=\bm{y}
, assuming the measured response
\bm{y}
is noise-free.
The Lagrangian function and its gradient w.r.t.
\boldsymbol{\beta}
are, respectively, given by

\displaystyle L(\boldsymbol{\beta},\widetilde{\bm{X}},\boldsymbol{\lambda})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(\widetilde{\bm{X}}\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top})+\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\top}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y});

\displaystyle\nabla_{\widetilde{\bm{X}}}L(\boldsymbol{\beta},\widetilde{\bm{X}},\boldsymbol{\lambda})

\displaystyle=\widetilde{\bm{X}}+\boldsymbol{\lambda}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0}\quad\implies\quad\widetilde{\bm{X}}=-\boldsymbol{\lambda}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top},

where
\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\real^{n}
is a vector of Lagrange multipliers.
Substituting the value of the vanishing gradient into
(\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}})\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
yields
\boldsymbol{\lambda}=\frac{\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
\widetilde{\bm{X}}=-\frac{(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y})\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Therefore, using the invariance of cyclic permutation of factors in trace, the objective function becomes

\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\frac{(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y})^{\top}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y})}{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(2.61)

\paragrapharrow

Total least squares. Similar to the data least squares approach, the
total least squares (TLS)
method considers errors in both the predictor variables and the response variables. The TLS problem can be formulated as:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{TLS}},\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{\text{TLS}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{TLS}}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta},\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}}\big\lVert[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]\big\rVert_{F}^{2},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad(\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}})\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}),

(2.62)

where
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
and
\widetilde{\bm{y}}
are perturbations in the predictor variables and the response variable, respectively.
Let
\bm{C}\triangleq[\bm{X},\bm{y}]\in\real^{n\times(p+1)}
,
\bm{D}\triangleq[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]\in\real^{n\times(p+1)}
, and
\boldsymbol{\gamma}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\beta}\\
-1\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
, the problem can be equivalently stated as

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{TLS}},\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{\text{TLS}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}_{\text{TLS}}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma},\bm{D}}\left\lVert\bm{D}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bm{D}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=-\bm{C}\boldsymbol{\gamma},

(2.63)

\paragrapharrow

Scaled total least squares.

Paige and Strakoš 2002
presents a unified framework that includes OLS, DLS, and TLS as special cases within the following optimization problem:

\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta},\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}}\big\lVert[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\gamma\widetilde{\bm{y}}]\big\rVert_{F}^{2},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad(\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}})\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}),

(2.64)

where
\gamma
is a given positive scaling parameter.
For small values of
\gamma
, perturbations in
\bm{y}
will be favored.
In the limit as
\gamma\rightarrow 0
, the solution equals the ordinary LS solution.
Conversely, in the limit when
\gamma\rightarrow\infty
, it reduces to the data least squares.

2.11.2
Minimum Perturbation in Total Least Squares

Writing the constraint
(\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}})\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}}
as

[\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}},\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}}]\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\beta}\\
-1\end{bmatrix}=\boldsymbol{0}

(2.65)

shows that the matrix
[\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}},\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}}]
is rank-deficient and that
[\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top},-1]^{\top}
is a right singular vector corresponding to a zero singular value:
[\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top},-1]^{\top}\in\mathcal{N}([\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}},\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}}])
(Theorem
). The TLS problem can be analyzed using the SVD of the augmented matrix:

\bm{C}\triangleq[\bm{X},\bm{y}]=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}=\sum_{i=1}^{p+1}\sigma_{i}\bm{u}_{i}\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}.

(2.66)

Suppose
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full column rank.
Note that as long as the observation vector
\bm{y}
does not lie entirely in the subspace spanned by the columns of matrix
\bm{X}
, the augmented matrix
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
has rank
p+1
. That is, the
p+1
columns of
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
are linearly independent. The
p+1
,
n
-dimensional columns of the matrix
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
span the
p
dimensional space spanned by
\bm{X}
and a component that is normal to the subspace spanned by
\bm{X}
.

For the solution
\boldsymbol{\beta}
to be
unique
, the matrix
[\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}},\;\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}}]
must have exactly
p
linearly independent columns. Since this matrix has
p+1
columns in all, it must be rank-deficient by 1. Therefore, the goal of solving the minimization problem (
) can be restated as the goal of finding the “smallest” matrix
[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]
that changes
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
with rank
p+1
to
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]+[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]
with rank
p
. The Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem (Theorem
) provides the means to do so, by defining
[[\bm{X},\bm{y}]+[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]]
as the “best” rank-
p
approximation to
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
. Dropping the smallest singular value of
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
eliminates the least amount of information from the data and ensures a unique solution (assuming
\sigma_{p+1}
is not very close to
\sigma_{p}
):

\widetilde{\bm{C}}\triangleq[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]=-\sigma_{p+1}\bm{u}_{p+1}\bm{v}_{p+1}^{\top},

(2.67)

and
\min_{\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}}\big\lVert[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]\big\rVert_{F}=\sigma_{p+1}
. Multiplying (
) from the right with
\bm{v}_{p+1}
and using (
) gives

[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]\bm{v}_{p+1}=-\sigma_{p+1}\bm{u}_{p+1}=-[\bm{X},\bm{y}]\bm{v}_{p+1}\quad\implies\quad[\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}},\bm{y}+\widetilde{\bm{y}}]\bm{v}_{p+1}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(2.68)

Then the TLS can be categorized into two forms:

Generic TLS.

v_{p+1,p+1}\neq 0
, i.e., the
(p+1)
-th component of
\bm{v}_{p+1}
is nonzero.
Then (
) and (
) show that the TLS solution is obtained by scaling
\bm{v}_{p+1}
so that its last component is
-1
:

\begin{bmatrix}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{TLS}}\\
-1\end{bmatrix}=-\frac{1}{\gamma}\bm{v}_{p+1},\quad\text{with }\gamma\triangleq\bm{e}_{p+1}^{\top}\bm{v}_{p+1}.

(2.69)

Finally, the “curve-fit” or prediction is provided by
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{\text{TLS}}=(\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}})\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{TLS}}
, which requires the parameters,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{TLS}}
, as well as the perturbation in the predictor variables,
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
.
Parameter values obtained from TLS cannot be compared directly to those from OLS because the TLS solution is in terms of a different basis (here
\bm{X}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}
instead of
\bm{X}
). This last point complicates the application of TLS to curve-fitting problems in which a parameterized functional form
\widehat{y}(\bm{x};\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is ultimately desired. Computing
\widehat{\bm{y}}
directly using
\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{TLS}}
can give bizarre results.

Nongeneric TLS.

v_{p+1,p+1}=0
. The TLS problem fails to have a solution. Nongeneric TLS problems can be treated by adding constraints on the solution
(
Van Huffel and Vandewalle 1989
;
Van Huffel and Vandewalle 1992
;
Markovsky and Van Huffel 2007
)
.

\paragrapharrow

Normal equation for TLS.
Alternatively, from the relationship between the SVD of
\bm{C}=[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
and the spectral decomposition of the symmetric matrix
\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C}
, it follows that the TLS solution
\boldsymbol{\beta}
can be characterized by the following normal equation:

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}&\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}\\
\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{X}&\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}\end{bmatrix}\bm{v}=\sigma_{p+1}^{2}\bm{v},\quad\bm{v}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\beta}\\
-1\end{bmatrix},

(2.70)

where
\sigma_{p+1}^{2}
is the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix
\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{C}
, and
\bm{v}
is a corresponding eigenvector. From (
) it follows that

(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}-\sigma_{p+1}^{2}\bm{I}_{p})\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sigma_{p+1}^{2}.

(2.71)

In the first equation of (
), a positive multiple of the unit matrix is subtracted from the matrix of normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
. This shows that TLS can be considered as a procedure for deregressionalizing the LS problem. (Compare with Tikhonov regularization, where a multiple of the unit matrix is added to improve the conditioning; see (
2.58
)). From a statistical point of view, TLS can be interpreted as removing bias by subtracting the error covariance matrix estimated by
\sigma_{p+1}^{2}\bm{I}
from the data covariance matrix
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
.

Let further
\widehat{\sigma}_{i}
,
i=1,2,\ldots,p
, be the singular values of
\bm{X}
. The
interlacing property of singular values
shows :

\sigma_{1}\geq\widehat{\sigma}_{1}\geq\ldots\geq\sigma_{p}\geq\widehat{\sigma}_{p}\geq\sigma_{p+1}.

The condition
\widehat{\sigma}_{p}>\sigma_{p+1}
ensures that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}-\sigma_{p+1}^{2}\bm{I}
is symmetric positive definite by the eigenvalue characterization theorem (Theorem
) and that the TLS problem has a
unique
solution.

2.12
Alternating Least Squares (ALS)

The explosion of data from advancements in sensor technology and computer hardware poses new challenges for data analysis.
The substantial volume of data often contains noise and other distortions, requiring pre-processing for the application of deductive science.
For instance, signals received by antenna arrays often are contaminated by noise and other degradations.
Effectively analyzing such data requires reconstruction or representation in a manner that minimizes inaccuracies while maintaining certain feasibility conditions.

Moreover, data collected from complex systems often arises from multiple interrelated variables acting together.
When these variables lack clear definitions, the information contained in the original data may be overlapping and unclear. By creating a reduced system model, we can achieve a level of accuracy that is close to the original system.
The standard approach involves removing noise, reducing the model, and reconstructing feasibility by replacing the original data with a lower-dimensional representation obtained through subspace approximation.
Consequently, low-rank approximations or low-rank matrix decompositions play a important role in
a wide range of applications.

Low-rank matrix decomposition stands out as a potent technique in machine learning and data mining for representing a given matrix as the product of two or more matrices with lower dimensions.
This method captures the essential structure of a matrix while disregarding noise and redundancies.
Common techniques for low-rank matrix decomposition include singular value decomposition (SVD), principal component analysis (PCA), multiplicative update nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), and the alternating least squares (ALS) approach introduced in this section.

For example, in the Netflix Prize competition
(
Bennett et al. 2007
)
, the objective is to predict the users’ ratings for different movies based on their existing ratings for other movies.
We use indices
n=1,2,\ldots,N
for
N
movies and
p=1,2,\ldots,P
for
P
users.
The rating of the
p
-th user for the
n
-th movie is denoted by
x_{np}
.
Let
\bm{X}
be an
N\times P
rating matrix with columns
\bm{x}_{p}\in\real^{N}
containing ratings provided by the
p
-th user. Note that numerous ratings
\{x_{np}\}
are missing, and our objective is to accurately predict these absent ratings.

We formally consider algorithms for solving the following problem: Approximating the matrix
\bm{X}
through factorization into an
N\times K
matrix
\bm{W}
and a
K\times P
matrix
\bm{Z}
.
Typically,
K
is chosen to be smaller than both
N
and
P
, ensuring reduced dimensions for
\bm{W}
and
\bm{Z}
compared to the original matrix
\bm{X}
.
This dimensional reduction yields a compressed version of the original data matrix.
Deciding the appropriate value for
K
is crucial in practice, and its selection is often problem-dependent.

The factorization holds significance; let
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{P}]
and
\bm{Z}=[\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{z}_{P}]
be the column partitions of
\bm{X}
and
\bm{Z}
, respectively.
Then,
\bm{x}_{p}=\bm{W}\bm{z}_{p}
, implying that each column
\bm{x}_{p}
is approximated by a linear combination of the columns of
\bm{W}
, weighted by the components in
\bm{z}_{p}
.
Thus, the columns of
\bm{W}
can be viewed as containing the column basis of
\bm{X}
.

To achieve the approximation
\bm{X}\approx\bm{W}\bm{Z}
, a suitable loss function must be established for measuring the distance between
\bm{X}
and
\bm{W}\bm{Z}
.
In this context, we opt for the Frobenius norm (Definition
) between two matrices, which vanishes to zero if
\bm{X}=\bm{W}\bm{Z}
, and the advantage will be evident shortly.

To simplify the problem, let’s first assume the absence of missing ratings.
We project data vectors
\bm{x}_{p}\in\real^{N}
into a lower dimension
\bm{z}_{p}\in\real^{K}
with
K<\min\{N,P\}

in a manner that minimizes the
reconstruction error
, as measured by the Frobenius norm (assuming
K
is known):

\mathop{\min}_{\bm{W},\bm{Z}}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2},

(2.72)

where
\bm{W}=[\bm{w}_{1}^{\top};\bm{w}_{2}^{\top};\ldots;\bm{w}_{N}^{\top}]\in\real^{N\times K}
and
\bm{Z}=[\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{z}_{P}]\in\real^{K\times P}
contain
\bm{w}_{n}
’s and
\bm{z}_{p}
’s as
rows and columns
, respectively. The loss formulation in (
) is referred to as the
per-example loss
.
It can be equivalently expressed as

L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

Furthermore, the loss function
L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)
is convex concerning
\bm{Z}
given
\bm{W}
, and vice versa. Therefore, we can first minimize it with respect to
\bm{Z}

while keeping
\bm{W}
fixed, and subsequently minimize it with respect to
\bm{W}
with
\bm{Z}
fixed.
This results in two optimization problems, denoted by ALS1 and ALS2:

\left\{\begin{aligned} \bm{Z}&\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{Z}}L(\bm{W},\bm{Z});\qquad\text{(ALS1)}\\
\bm{W}&\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{W}}L(\bm{W},\bm{Z}).\qquad\text{(ALS2)}\end{aligned}\right.

This is referred to as the
coordinate descent algorithm
, wherein we alternate between optimizing the least squares concerning
\bm{W}
and
\bm{Z}
.
Therefore, it is also called the
alternating least squares (ALS)
algorithm
(
Comon et al. 2009
;
Takács and Tikk 2012
;
Giampouras et al. 2018
)
.
The convergence is guaranteed if the loss function
L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})
decreases at each iteration.

Remark 130
(Convexity and global minimum).

While the loss function defined by Frobenius norm
\left\lVert\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
is convex either with respect to
\bm{W}
when
\bm{Z}
is fixed or vice versa, it lacks joint convexity in both variables simultaneously. Consequently, identifying the global minimum is infeasible.
Nevertheless, the convergence is guaranteed to reach local minima.

Given
\bm{W}
, Optimizing
\bm{Z}

Let’s now explore the problem of
\bm{Z}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{Z}}L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})
.
With
\bm{W}
fixed, we can represent
L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})
as
L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})
(or more concisely, as
L(\bm{Z})
) to emphasize the variable of
\bm{Z}
:

\displaystyle L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\big\lVert\bm{W}[\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{z}_{P}]-[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{P}]\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{W}\bm{z}_{1}-\bm{x}_{1}\\
\bm{W}\bm{z}_{2}-\bm{x}_{2}\\
\vdots\\
\bm{W}\bm{z}_{P}-\bm{x}_{P}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Now, if we define

\widetilde{\bm{W}}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{W}&\boldsymbol{0}&\ldots&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{W}&\ldots&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\ldots&\bm{W}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\in\real^{NP\times KP},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\widetilde{\bm{z}}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{z}_{1}\\
\bm{z}_{2}\\
\vdots\\
\bm{z}_{P}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\in\real^{KP},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\widetilde{\bm{a}}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{x}_{1}\\
\bm{x}_{2}\\
\vdots\\
\bm{x}_{P}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\in\real^{NP},

then the (ALS1) problem an be equivalently transformed into the ordinary least squares problem, aiming to minimize
\big\lVert\widetilde{\bm{W}}\widetilde{\bm{z}}-\widetilde{\bm{a}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
concerning
\widetilde{\bm{z}}
. The solution is then given by

\widetilde{\bm{z}}=(\widetilde{\bm{W}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{W}})^{-1}\widetilde{\bm{W}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{a}}.

However, it is not advisable to employ this approach for obtaining the result, as computing the inverse of
\widetilde{\bm{W}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{W}}
requires
2(KP)^{3}
flops
(
Lu 2021b
)
.
Instead, a more direct method to solve the (ALS1) problem is to determine the gradient of
L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})
concerning
\bm{Z}
(assuming all the partial derivatives of this function exist):

\displaystyle\nabla L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})

\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\,\,\mathrm{tr}\left((\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X})(\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X})^{\top}\right)}{\partial\bm{Z}}=2\bm{W}^{\top}(\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X})\in\real^{K\times P},

(2.73)

When the loss function is a differentiable function of
\bm{Z}
, we can determine the least squares solution using differential calculus. And a minimum of the function

L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})
must be a root of the equation (Proposition
):

\nabla L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})=\boldsymbol{0}.

By solving the equation above, we derive the “candidate” update for
\bm{Z}
, which corresponds to the minimizer of
L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})
:

{\bm{Z}=(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{X}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{Z}}L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W}).}

(2.74)

This requires
2K^{3}
flops to compute the inverse of
\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W}
, a notable improvement compared to
2(KP)^{3}
flops to get the inverse of
\widetilde{\bm{W}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{W}}

(
Lu 2021b
)
.
Before we declare a root of the equation above is actually a minimizer rather than a maximizer (that’s why we call the update a “candidate” update), we need to verify the function is convex.
In the case where the function is twice differentiable, this confirmation can be equivalently achieved by verifying (see Problem
):

\nabla^{2}L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})\succ\boldsymbol{0}.\penalty\

That is, the Hessian matrix is positive definite. To see this, we explicitly express the Hessian matrix as

\nabla^{2}L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})=2\widetilde{\bm{W}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{W}}\in\real^{KP\times KP},

(2.75)

which has full rank if
\bm{W}\in\real^{N\times K}
has full rank and
K<N
(Lemma
).

Remark 131
(Positive definite Hessian if
\bm{W}
has full rank).

We assert that if
\bm{W}\in\real^{N\times K}
has full rank
K
with
K<N
, then
\nabla^{2}L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})
is positive definite. This assertion is supported by verifying that when
\bm{W}
has full rank, the equation
\bm{W}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
only holds true when
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
, since the null space of
\bm{W}
is of dimension 0. Therefore,

\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}(2\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})\boldsymbol{\beta}>0,\qquad\text{for any nonzero vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{K}$}.

The challenge now is to confirm
whether
\bm{W}
possesses full rank, ensuring the positive definiteness of the Hessian of
L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})
; otherwise, we cannot claim the update of
\bm{Z}
in Equation (
) reduces the loss (due to convexity), thereby enhancing the matrix decomposition’s approximation of the original matrix
\bm{X}
through
\bm{W}\bm{Z}
in each iteration.
We will shortly come back to the positive definiteness of the Hessian matrix in the sequel, relying on the following lemma.

Lemma 132
(Rank of
\bm{Z}
after updating).

Suppose
\bm{X}\in\real^{N\times P}
has full rank with
N\leq P
and
\bm{W}\in\real^{N\times K}
has full rank with
K<N
(i.e.,
K<N\leq P
).
Then the update of
\bm{Z}=(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{X}\in\real^{K\times P}
in Equation (
) has full rank.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W}\in\real^{K\times K}
has full rank if
\bm{W}
has full rank (Lemma
), it follows that
(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}
has full rank.

Suppose
\bm{W}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
, it implies that
(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Thus, the following two null spaces satisfy:

\mathcal{N}(\bm{W}^{\top})\subseteq\mathcal{N}\left((\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\right).

Furthermore, suppose
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is in the null space of
(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}
such that
(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
. And since
(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}
is invertible, this implies
\bm{W}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{0}
, and

\mathcal{N}\left((\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\right)\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\bm{W}^{\top}).

Combining the two results yields that

\mathcal{N}(\bm{W}^{\top})=\mathcal{N}\left((\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\right).

(2.76)

Hence,
(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}
has full rank
K
. Let
\bm{T}\triangleq(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\in\real^{K\times N}
, and suppose
\bm{T}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
. This implies
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{T}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
, and

\mathcal{N}(\bm{T}^{\top})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{T}^{\top}).

Similarly, suppose
\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{T}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})=\boldsymbol{0}
. Since
\bm{X}
has full rank with the dimension of the null space being 0:
\dim\left(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})\right)=0
,
(\bm{T}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})
must be zero. The claim follows since
\bm{X}
has full rank
N
with the row space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
being equal to the column space of
\bm{X}
, where
\dim\left(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\right)=N
and the
\dim\left(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})\right)=N-\dim\left(\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})\right)=0
. Therefore,
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is in the null space of
\bm{T}^{\top}
if
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{T}^{\top}
:

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{T}^{\top})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\bm{T}^{\top}).

By “sandwiching” again,

\mathcal{N}(\bm{T}^{\top})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{T}^{\top}).

(2.77)

Since
\bm{T}^{\top}
has full rank
K<N\leq P
, it follows that
\dim\left(\mathcal{N}(\bm{T}^{\top})\right)=\dim\left(\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{T}^{\top})\right)=0
.
Therefore,

\bm{Z}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{T}^{\top}
has full rank
K
.
We complete the proof.

Given
\bm{Z}
, Optimizing
\bm{W}

Similarly, given
\bm{Z}
fixed, express
L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})
as
L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})
(or more concisely, as
L(\bm{W})
) to emphasize the variable of
\bm{W}
:

\begin{aligned} L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})&=\left\lVert\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.\end{aligned}

A direct approach to solve the optimization of (ALS2) involves finding the gradient of
L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})
with respect to
\bm{W}
:

\displaystyle\nabla L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})

\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\,\,\mathrm{tr}\left((\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X})(\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X})^{\top}\right)}{\partial\bm{W}}=2(\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X})\bm{Z}^{\top}\in\real^{N\times K}.

Similarly, the “candidate” update for
\bm{W}
can be obtained by locating the root of the gradient
\nabla L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})
:

{\bm{W}^{\top}=(\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{Z}\bm{X}^{\top}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{W}}L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z}).}

(2.78)

Again, it is important to highlight that the provided update is merely a “candidate” update.
Further verification is required to determine whether the Hessian is positive definite or not.
The Hessian matrix is expressed as follows:

\displaystyle\nabla^{2}L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})=2\widetilde{\bm{Z}}\widetilde{\bm{Z}}^{\top}\in\real^{KN\times KN}.

(2.79)

Therefore, by analogous analysis, if
\bm{Z}
has full rank with
K<P
, the Hessian matrix is positive definite.

Lemma 133
(Rank of
\bm{W}
after updating).

Suppose
\bm{X}\in\real^{N\times P}
has full rank with
N\geq P
and
\bm{Z}\in\real^{K\times P}
has full rank with
K<P
(i.e.,
K<P\leq N
).
Then the update of
\bm{W}^{\top}=(\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{Z}\bm{X}^{\top}
in Equation (
) has full rank.

The proof of Lemma
is similar to that of Lemma
, and we shall not repeat the details.

\paragrapharrow

Key observation.
Combining the observations in Lemma
and Lemma
, as long as we
initialize
\bm{Z}
and
\bm{W}
to have full rank
, the updates in Equations (
) and (
) are reasonable
since the Hessians in Equations (
) and (
) are positive definite
.

Note that we need an additional condition to satisfy
both Lemma

and Lemma
:
N=P
, i.e., there must be an equal number of movies and users.
We will relax this condition through regularization.

We summarize the process in Algorithm
.

Algorithm 1

Alternating Least Squares

1:

Matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{N\times P}

with
N=P
;

2:

Initialize
\bm{W}\in\real^{N\times K}
,
\bm{Z}\in\real^{K\times P}

with full rank and
K<N=P
;

3:

Choose a stop criterion on the approximation error
\delta
;

4:

Choose the maximal number of iterations
C
;

5:

iter=0
;
\triangleright
Count for the number of iterations

6:

while

\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{W}\bm{Z}\right\rVert_{F}>\delta
and
iter<C

do

7:

iter=iter+1
;

8:

\bm{Z}=(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{X}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{Z}}L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})
;

9:

\bm{W}^{\top}=(\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{Z}\bm{X}^{\top}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{W}}L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})
;

10:

end

while

11:

Output
\bm{W},\bm{Z}
;

Regularization: Extension to General Matrices

Tikhonov regularization
or simply
regularization
is a machine learning technique employed to prevent overfitting and enhance model generalization; see Section
. Overfitting occurs when a model becomes excessively complex, closely fitting the training data but performing poorly on unseen data.
To address this issue, regularization introduces a constraint or penalty term into the loss function used for model optimization. This discourages the development of overly complex models, striking a balance between model simplicity and effective training data fitting.
Common types of regularization include
\ell_{1}
regularization,
\ell_{2}
regularization, and elastic net regularization (a combination of
\ell_{1}
and
\ell_{2}
regularization).
Regularization finds extensive application in machine learning algorithms such as linear regression, logistic regression, and neural networks.

In the context of the alternating least squares problem, we can introduce a
\ell_{2}
regularization term to minimize the following loss:

L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})=\left\lVert\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lambda_{w}\left\lVert\bm{W}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lambda_{z}\left\lVert\bm{Z}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},\qquad\lambda_{w}>0,\lambda_{z}>0,

(2.80)

where the gradient with respect to
\bm{Z}
and
\bm{W}
are given respectively by

\left\{\begin{aligned} \nabla L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})&=2\bm{W}^{\top}(\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X})+2\lambda_{z}\bm{Z}\in\real^{K\times P};\\
\nabla L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})&=2(\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X})\bm{Z}^{\top}+2\lambda_{w}\bm{W}\in\real^{N\times K}.\end{aligned}\right.

(2.81)

The Hessian matrices become:

\left\{\begin{aligned} \nabla^{2}L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})&=2\widetilde{\bm{W}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{W}}+2\lambda_{z}\bm{I}\in\real^{KP\times KP};\\
\nabla^{2}L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})&=2\widetilde{\bm{Z}}\widetilde{\bm{Z}}^{\top}+2\lambda_{w}\bm{I}\in\real^{KN\times KN},\\
\end{aligned}\right.

(2.82)

which are positive definite due to the perturbation introduced by the regularization.

The regularization ensues that the Hessian matrices become positive definite, even if
\bm{W}
and
\bm{Z}
are rank-deficient
.
Consequently, matrix decomposition can be extended to any matrix, irrespective of whether
N>P
or
N<P
. In rare cases,
K
can be chosen as
K>\max\{N,P\}
to obtain a
high-rank approximation
of
\bm{X}
.
However, in most scenarios, we want to find the
low-rank approximation
of
\bm{X}
with
K<\min\{N,P\}
. For instance, ALS can be utilized to find low-rank neural networks or transformer structures, reducing the memory usage of neural networks while enhancing performance
(
Lu 2021b
;
Lu et al. 2025
)
.
Therefore, the minimizers can be determined by identifying the roots of the gradient:

\displaystyle\bm{Z}

\displaystyle=(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W}+\lambda_{z}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{X}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{W}^{\top}=(\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top}+\lambda_{w}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{Z}\bm{X}^{\top}.

(2.83)

The regularization parameters
\lambda_{z},\lambda_{w}\in\real
are used to balance the trade-off
between the accuracy of the approximation and the smoothness of the computed solution. The selection of these parameters is typically problem-dependent and can be obtained through
cross-validation
. Again, we summarize the process in Algorithm
.

Algorithm 2

Alternating Least Squares with Regularization

1:

Matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{N\times P}
;

2:

Initialize
\bm{W}\in\real^{N\times K}
,
\bm{Z}\in\real^{K\times P}

randomly without condition on the rank and the relationship between
N,P,K
;

3:

Choose a stop criterion on the approximation error
\delta
;

4:

Choose regularization parameters
\lambda_{w},\lambda_{z}
;

5:

Choose the maximal number of iterations
C
;

6:

iter=0
;
\triangleright
Count for the number of iterations

7:

while

\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{W}\bm{Z}\right\rVert_{F}>\delta
and
iter<C

do

8:

iter=iter+1
;

9:

\bm{Z}=(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W}+\lambda_{z}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{X}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{Z}}L(\bm{Z}\mid\bm{W})
;

10:

\bm{W}^{\top}=(\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top}+\lambda_{w}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{Z}\bm{X}^{\top}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{W}}L(\bm{W}\mid\bm{Z})
;

11:

end

while

12:

Output
\bm{W},\bm{Z}
;

2.12.1
Missing Entries and Rank-One Update

Since matrix decomposition via ALS is extensively used in the context of Netflix recommender data, where a substantial number of entries are missing due to users not having watched certain movies or choosing not to rate them for various reasons.
In this scenario, the low-rank matrix decomposition problem is also known as
matrix completion
that can help recover unobserved entries
(
Jain et al. 2017
)
.
To address this, we can introduce an additional mask matrix
\bm{M}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times P}
, where
m_{np}\in\{0,1\}
indicates whether user
p
has rated movie
n
or not. Therefore, the loss function can be defined as

L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{M}\circ\bm{X}-\bm{M}\circ(\bm{W}\bm{Z})\right\rVert_{F}^{2},

where
\circ
represents the
Hadamard product
between matrices.
The above formulation concisely expresses our goal of finding a completion of the ratings matrix that is both of low rank and consistent with observed user ratings.
To find the solution to this problem, we decompose the updates in Equation (
) into:

\left\{\begin{aligned} \bm{z}_{p}&=(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W}+\lambda_{z}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{x}_{p},&\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,&\text{for $p\in\{1,2,\ldots,P\}$};\\
\bm{w}_{n}&=(\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top}+\lambda_{w}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{Z}\bm{b}_{n},&\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,&\text{for $n\in\{1,2,\ldots,N\}$},\end{aligned}\right.

(2.84)

where
\bm{Z}=[\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{z}_{P}]
and
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{P}]
represent the column partitions of
\bm{Z}
and
\bm{X}
, respectively. Similarly,
\bm{W}^{\top}=[\bm{w}_{1},\bm{w}_{2},\ldots,\bm{w}_{N}]
and
\bm{X}^{\top}=[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{N}]
are the column partitions of
\bm{W}^{\top}
and
\bm{X}^{\top}
, respectively. This decomposition of the updates indicates the updates can be performed in a column-by-column fashion (the rank-one updates).

\paragrapharrow

Given
\bm{W}
.
Let
\bm{o}_{p}\in\{0,1\}^{N}
represent the movies rated by user
p
, where
o_{pn}=1
if user
p
has rated movie
n
, and
o_{pn}=0
otherwise. Then the
p
-th column of
\bm{X}
without missing entries can be denoted using the Matlab-style notation as
\bm{x}_{p}[\bm{o}_{p}]
.
And we want to approximate the existing entries of the
p
-th column by
\bm{x}_{p}[\bm{o}_{p}]\approx\bm{W}[\bm{o}_{p},:]\bm{z}_{p}
, which is indeed a rank-one least squares problem:

\displaystyle\bm{z}_{p}

\displaystyle=\left(\bm{W}[\bm{o}_{p},:]^{\top}\bm{W}[\bm{o}_{p},:]+\lambda_{z}\bm{I}\right)^{-1}\bm{W}[\bm{o}_{p},:]^{\top}\bm{x}_{p}[\bm{o}_{p}],\quad\text{for $p\in\{1,2,\ldots,P\}$}.

(2.85)

Moreover, the loss function with respect to
\bm{z}_{p}
and
\bm{Z}
can be described, respectively, by

\displaystyle L(\bm{z}_{p}|\bm{W})

\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\bm{o}_{p}}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{and}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,L(\bm{Z}|\bm{W})=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\ \sum_{n\in\bm{o}_{p}}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2}.

\paragrapharrow

Given
\bm{Z}
.
Similarly, if
\bm{p}_{n}\in\{0,1\}^{P}
denotes the users who have rated movie
n
, with
p_{np}=1
if movie
n
has been rated by user
p
, and
p_{np}=0
otherwise. Then the
n
-th row of
\bm{X}
without missing entries can be denoted by the Matlab-style notation as
\bm{b}_{n}[\bm{p}_{n}]
. We want to approximate the existing entries of the
n
-th row by
\bm{b}_{n}[\bm{p}_{n}]\approx\bm{Z}[:,\bm{p}_{n}]^{\top}\bm{w}_{n}
,

which is again a rank-one least squares problem:

\displaystyle\bm{w}_{n}

\displaystyle=(\bm{Z}[:,\bm{p}_{n}]\bm{Z}[:,\bm{p}_{n}]^{\top}+\lambda_{w}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{Z}[:,\bm{p}_{n}]\bm{b}_{n}[\bm{p}_{n}],\quad\text{for $n\in\{1,2,\ldots,N\}$}.

(2.86)

Similarly, the loss function with respect to
\bm{w}_{n}
and
\bm{W}
can be described, respectively, by

\displaystyle L(\bm{w}_{n}|\bm{Z})

\displaystyle=\sum_{p\in\bm{p}_{n}}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{and}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,L(\bm{W}|\bm{Z})=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{p\in\bm{p}_{n}}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2}.

The procedure is once again presented in Algorithm
.
Other approaches, such as
singular value projection (SVP)
, also exist to address the matrix completion problem. At a high level, SVP is a type of projected gradient descent (PGD) method that updates iteratively via gradient descent, projecting the updated matrix into a low-rank form through singular value decomposition at each step. However, the alternating least squares approach generally outperforms SVP in the context of matrix completion, so we will not delve into SVP here. For more details, refer to
Jain et al. 2017
.

Alternating Least Squares with Missing Entries and Regularization

1:

Matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{N\times P}
;

2:

,
\bm{Z}\in\real^{K\times P}

randomly without condition on the rank and the relationship between
N,P,K
;

3:

\delta
;

\lambda_{w},\lambda_{z}
;

5:

from
\bm{X}
;

6:

Choose the maximum number of iterations
C
;

7:

;
\triangleright
Count for the number of iterations

8:

while

\left\lVert\bm{M}\circ\bm{X}-\bm{M}\circ(\bm{W}\bm{Z})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}>\delta
and

do

9:

iter=iter+1
;

10:

for

p=1,2,\ldots,P

do

\bm{z}_{p}\leftarrow\left(\bm{W}[\bm{o}_{p},:]^{\top}\bm{W}[\bm{o}_{p},:]+\lambda_{z}\bm{I}\right)^{-1}\bm{W}[\bm{o}_{p},:]^{\top}\bm{x}_{p}[\bm{o}_{p}]
;
\triangleright

p
-th column of
\bm{Z}

;
\triangleright

n
-th column of
\bm{W}^{\top}

2.12.2
Vector Inner Product and Hidden Vectors

We have observed that the ALS algorithm seeks to find lower-dimensional matrices
\bm{W}
and
\bm{Z}
such that their product
\bm{W}\bm{Z}
can approximate
\bm{X}\approx\bm{W}\bm{Z}
in terms of the squared loss:

\mathop{\min}_{\bm{W},\bm{Z}}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2},

that is, each entry
x_{np}
in
\bm{X}
can be approximated as the inner product of two vectors
\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}
. The geometric definition of the vector inner product is given by

\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}=\left\lVert\bm{w}_{n}\right\rVert_{2}\cdot\left\lVert\bm{z}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}\cos\theta,

where
\theta
represents the angle between vectors
\bm{w}_{n}
and
\bm{z}_{p}
. Thus, if the vector norms of
\bm{w}_{n}
and
\bm{z}_{p}
are determined, the smaller the angle, the larger the inner product.

In the context of Netflix data, movie ratings range from 0 to 5,
with higher ratings indicating a stronger user preference for the movie.
If
\bm{w}_{n}
and
\bm{z}_{p}
fall sufficiently “close,” the value
\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}
becomes larger.
This concept elucidates the essence of ALS, where
\bm{w}_{n}
represents the features or attributes of movie
n
, while
\bm{z}_{p}
encapsulates the features or preferences of user
p
.
In other words, ALS associates each user with a
latent vector of preference
and each movie with a
latent vector of attributes
.
Furthermore, each element in
\bm{w}_{n}
and
\bm{z}_{p}
signifies a specific feature. For example, it could be that the second feature
w_{n2}
(
w_{n2}
denotes the second element of vector
\bm{w}_{n}
) represents whether the movie is an action movie or not, and
z_{p2}
might denote whether user
p
has a preference for action movies. When this holds true, then
\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}
becomes large and provides a good approximation of
x_{np}
.

In the decomposition
\bm{X}\approx\bm{W}\bm{Z}
, it is established that the rows of
\bm{W}
contain the hidden features of the movies, and the columns of
\bm{Z}
contain the hidden features of the users.
Nevertheless, the explicit meanings of the rows in
\bm{W}
or the columns in
\bm{Z}
remain undisclosed.
Although they might correspond to categories or genres of the movies, fostering underlying connections between users and movies, their precise nature remains uncertain.
It is precisely this ambiguity that gives rise to the terminology “latent” or “hidden.”
