Chapter 3
Numerical Methods for Least Squares Approximations

3.1
General Ideas and Indirect Methods

W
When considering how long it takes to solve least squares (LS) problems, one can choose between two main types of methods: direct methods and indirect (or iterative) methods. Below is a brief overview of
direct methods
for solving LS problems:

Cholesky decomposition.
If the design matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full column rank and is well-conditioned, then one can use the Cholesky decomposition to compute an upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}
such that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
.
Once this decomposition is obtained, the normal equation
\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
can be solved efficiently.

QR decomposition.

Slightly slower but more numerically stable than Cholesky—especially when
\bm{X}
is rank-deficient or ill-conditioned—this method involves computing the QR decomposition
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
, where
\bm{Q}
is orthogonal and
\bm{R}
is upper triangular. The LS solution is then obtained by solving:
\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}
.

SVD.

More computationally expensive but even more stable—particularly for very ill-conditioned matrices—the SVD computes:

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
, where this is the reduced SVD.
The LS solution is then given by:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}.

For further details, see Section
.

The computational complexity of all these direct methods is
\mathcal{O}(np^{2})
. That is, although the numerical stability and constant factors differ among the methods, all three classes of algorithms asymptotically require time proportional to
np^{2}
. In most cases, using QR decomposition offers a good balance between speed and stability.

Another broad class of algorithms for solving LS and other problems are
iterative methods
, among which gradient descent is the simplest example.

In this chapter, we will introduce approaches based on indirect (iterative) methods, as well as those using Cholesky and QR decompositions, including their computational aspects. The solution via SVD was already discussed in Section
. Computing the SVD requires more background knowledge and will not be covered here. For more information, refer to, for example,
Golub and Van Loan 2013
,
Lu 2021b
, and
Björck 2024
.

Indirect Methods and Gradient Descent

The general ideas or called indirect methods for solving least squares problems are those using descent methods to obtain the solution.
The
gradient descent
(GD) method is a specific type of descent method used to find the (local or global) minimum of a differentiable function, whether convex or non-convex. This function is commonly referred to as the
cost function
(also known as the
loss function
or
objective function
).
It stands out as one of the most popular algorithms to perform optimization and by far the
most common way to optimize machine learning, deep learning, and various optimization problems.
This is especially true for optimizing neural networks and transformer networks
(
LeCun et al. 2015
;
Goodfellow et al. 2016
;
Vaswani et al. 2017
)
.
In the context of machine learning, the cost function measures the difference between a model’s predicted output and the actual output. Neural networks, transformer networks, and machine learning models in general seek to find a set of parameters
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{n}
(also known as weights, coefficients) that optimize an objective function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
. This is expressed as the unconstrained optimization problem (P1):

\textbf{(P1)}:\qquad\text{Find}\quad\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}).

Denoting
t=1,2,\ldots
as the iteration number, iterative methods generate a sequence of vectors:

\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(2)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(T)}\in\mathrm{dom}(f)

(3.1)

such that as
T\rightarrow\infty
, the sequence converges to the optimal solution
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
, and the objective function value
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(T)})
approaches the optimal minimum
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})
, under certain mild conditions.
At each iteration
t
, an
update step (or a descent step)

\bm{h}^{(t)}
is applied to update the parameters. Denoting the parameters at the
t
-th iteration as
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
, the update rule is given by:

(\textbf{GD update}):\qquad\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\bm{h}^{(t)}.

(3.2)

\paragrapharrow

Gradient descent.
The most basic form of gradient descent is the
vanilla update
, where the parameters move in the opposite direction of the gradient. This follows the
steepest descent direction
since gradients are orthogonal to level curves (also known as level surfaces, see Lemma
):

\bm{h}^{(t)}=-\eta_{t}\bm{g}^{(t)}\triangleq-\eta_{t}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}),

(3.3)

where the positive value
\eta_{t}
denotes the
learning rate (or stepsize, step length, step size)
that depends on specific problems.
The term
\bm{g}^{(t)}\triangleq\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\in\real^{n}
represents the gradient of the parameters.
The learning rate
\eta_{t}
controls how large of a step to take in the direction of negative gradient so that we can reach a (local) minimum.
The method that follows the negative gradient direction (i.e.,
\bm{d}^{(t)}\triangleq-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
in Algorithm
) is called the
steepest descent method (or gradient method)
.
The choice of descent direction is “the best” (locally; see (
)) and we could combine it with an exact line search to determine the learning rate
(
Lu 2025
)
. A method like this converges, but the final convergence is linear and often very slow.

Examples in
Madsen and Nielsen 2010
;
Boyd 2004
show how the gradient descent method with exact line search and finite computer precision can fail to find the minimizer of a second degree polynomial. However, for many problems, it performs well in the early stages of the iterative process.
Considerations like this has lead to the so-called
hybrid methods
, which—as the name suggests—are based on two different methods. One which is good in the initial stage, like the
gradient method
, and another method which is good in the final stage, like
Newton’s method
. A key challenge with hybrid methods is designing an effective mechanism to switch between the two approaches at the appropriate time.

In (
),
\bm{h}^{(t)}
is referred to as a
descent step
. While a direction
\bm{d}^{(t)}
satisfying the condition
\left\langle\bm{g}^{(t)},\bm{d}^{(t)}\right\rangle<0
is called a
descent direction
. In most cases, the relationship between the descent step and descent direction follows a scale by the learning rate:

\displaystyle\textbf{(Descent direction)}:\qquad

\displaystyle\bm{d}^{(t)}=-\bm{g}^{(t)};

(3.4)

\displaystyle\textbf{(Descent step)}:\qquad

\displaystyle\bm{h}^{(t)}=\eta_{t}\bm{d}^{(t)}.

In many cases, when the learning rate is equal to 1, the above two terms are used
interchangeably
, then the descent direction and the descent step are the same; for example, in Newton’s method.

\paragrapharrow

Gradient descent by calculus
An intuitive analogy to understand gradient descent is to imagine the path of a river starting from a mountain peak and flowing downhill to reach the lowest point at its base.
Similarly, the goal of gradient descent is to find the lowest point in the landscape defined by the objective function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
, where
\boldsymbol{\theta}
represents a
n
-dimensional input variable. Our task is to use an algorithm that guides us to a (local) minimum of
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
.
To better understand this process, consider moving a ball a small distance
h_{1}
along the
\theta_{1}
axis, a small amount
h_{2}
along the
\theta_{2}
axis, and so on up to
h_{n}
along the
\theta_{n}
axis.
Calculus informs us of the variation in the objective function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
as follows:

\Delta f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\approx\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{1}}h_{1}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{2}}h_{2}+\ldots+\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{n}}h_{n}.

Our challenge is to choose
h_{1},h_{2},\ldots,h_{n}
such that they cause
\Delta f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
to be negative, thereby decreasing the objective function towards minimization.
Let
\bm{h}=[h_{1},h_{2},\ldots,h_{n}]^{\top}
denote the vector of changes in
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, and let
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})=[\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{1}},\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{2}},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{n}}]^{\top}
denotes the gradient vector of
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
. Then it follows that

\Delta f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\approx\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{1}}h_{1}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{2}}h_{2}+\ldots+\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{n}}h_{n}=\left\langle\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}),\bm{h}\right\rangle.

In the context of descending the function, our aim is to ensure that
\Delta f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
is negative.
This ensures that moving from
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
to
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\bm{h}^{(t)}
(from
t
-th iteration to
(t+1)
-th iteration) results in a reduction of the loss function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)})=f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})+\Delta f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
, given that
\Delta f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\leq 0
.
It can be demonstrated that if the update step is defined as
\bm{h}^{(t)}=-\eta_{t}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
, where
\eta_{t}
is the learning rate, the following relationship holds:

\Delta f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\approx-\eta_{t}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})=-\eta_{t}\big\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 0.

Specifically,
\Delta f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})<\boldsymbol{0}
unless we are already at the optimal point with zero gradients.
This analysis validates the approach of gradient descent.

\paragrapharrow

Gradient descent for convex functions.
We further explore the application of gradient descent in (unconstrained) convex problems.
If the objective function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
is (continuously differentiable) convex, then the relationship
\left\langle\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}),(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rangle\geq 0
implies
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)})\geq f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
. This can be derived from the gradient inequality of a continuously differentiable convex function, i.e.,
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)})-f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\geq\left\langle\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}),(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rangle
; see Theorem
.

In this sense, to ensure a reduction in the objective function from the point
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
to
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}
, it is imperative to ensure
\left\langle\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}),(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rangle\leq 0
.
In the context of gradient descent, the choice of
\eta_{t}\bm{d}^{(t)}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
aligns with the negative gradient
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
. However, there are many other descent methods, such as
(non-Euclidean) greedy descent
,
normalized steepest descent
,
Newton step
, and so on. The core principle of these methods is to ensure that
\left\langle\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}),(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rangle=\left\langle\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}),\eta_{t}\bm{d}^{(t)}\right\rangle\leq 0
, provided the objective function is convex.

\paragrapharrow

Gradient descent with momentum.

Gradient descent with momentum
is an improvement over basic gradient descent, frequently used in machine learning and deep learning to minimize the loss function and update model parameters. While standard gradient descent updates parameters solely based on the current gradient, momentum-based gradient descent introduces a
momentum
term to accelerate convergence and smooth the optimization path.

In this approach, the momentum term enables the algorithm to build velocity in directions with a steady but small gradient, helping it overcome local minima and saddle points. By incorporating a fraction of the previous update into the current one, this technique mimics inertia, allowing the algorithm to continue moving in the same direction despite minor fluctuations in the gradient. Consequently, this method not only speeds up convergence but also reduces oscillations, particularly in regions where the surface curvature varies significantly across different dimensions.
At each iteration
t
, the process involves two key steps:

\displaystyle\textbf{(Velocity update)}:\qquad\bm{d}^{(t)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\rho\bm{d}^{(t-1)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)});

(3.5a)

\displaystyle\textbf{(Parameter update)}:\qquad\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\bm{d}^{(t)}.

(3.5b)

By incorporating past gradients into the update rule, gradient descent with momentum enables more efficient traversal across the error surface, particularly in complex landscapes, leading to faster convergence and improved performance.
In summary, the gradient descent with momentum approach is advantageous for the following reasons
(
Lu 2025
)
:

At saddle points, the gradient of the cost function becomes nearly zero or entirely negligible. This results in minimal or no updates to the weights, causing the learning process to stagnate and effectively halt.

The trajectory taken by the gradient descent method tends to be quite erratic, even when employing mini-batch processing. This jittery path can impede efficient convergence towards the minimum.

\paragrapharrow

Steepest descent.
The linear approximation theorem (Theorem
) states that

f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\eta\bm{d})=f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})+\eta\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})+\mathcal{O}(\left\lVert\eta\bm{d}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}).

(3.6)

From (
) and by the definition of directional derivative, we observe that when taking a step
\eta\bm{d}
with a positive stepsize
\eta
, the relative reduction in function value satisfies

\lim_{\eta\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})-f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\eta\bm{d})}{\eta\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert_{2}}=-\frac{1}{\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert_{2}}\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})=\big\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\big\rVert_{2}\cos(\phi),

where
\phi
is the angle between the vectors
\bm{d}
and
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
. This equation indicates that we get the greatest gain rate if
\phi=0
, meaning the optimal descent direction is the steepest descent direction
\bm{d}_{\text{sd}}^{(t)}
, given by

\bm{d}_{\text{sd}}^{(t)}=-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}).

(3.7)

That is, the steepest descent method coincides with the gradient descent method.

\paragrapharrow

Stochastic gradient descent.
In many cases, the function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
is defined over a datasets
\mathcal{D}=\{\bm{s}_{1},\bm{s}_{2},\ldots,\bm{s}_{D}\}
such that
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
and its gradient
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
can be expressed as

f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\triangleq f(\mathcal{D};\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}f(\bm{s}_{d};\boldsymbol{\theta})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\triangleq\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\nabla f(\bm{s}_{d};\boldsymbol{\theta}),

(3.8)

respectively.
While if we follow the negative gradient of a single sample or a batch of samples iteratively, the local estimate of the direction can be obtained and is known as the
stochastic gradient descent
(SGD)
(
Robbins and Monro 1951
)
.
The SGD method can be categorized into two types:

The strict SGD:
Computes the gradient using only one randomly selected data point per iteration:
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\approx\nabla f(\bm{s}_{d};\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
.

The mini-batch SGD:
A compromise between full gradient descent and strict SGD, where a small subset (mini-batch) of the dataset is used to compute an estimate of the gradient:
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\approx\frac{1}{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\sum_{d\in{\mathbb{S}}}\nabla f(\bm{s}_{d};\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
.

The SGD method is particular useful when the number of
training entries
(i.e., the data used for updating/training the model, while the data used for final evaluation is called the
test entries or test data
) are substantial, as computing the full gradient can be computationally expensive or even resulting in that the gradients from different input samples may cancel out and the final update is small.
However, since the gradient is estimated using only a subset of the data, the updates can be noisy.
In the SGD framework, the objective function is stochastic, composed of a sum of subfunctions evaluated at different subsamples of the data. However, a drawback of the vanilla update (both GD and SGD) lies in its susceptibility to getting trapped in local minima
(
Rutishauser 1959
)
.

\paragrapharrow

Choice of stepsize.
For a small stepsize, gradient descent ensures a monotonic improvement at every iteration, guaranteeing convergence, albeit to a local minimum. However, the speed of the vanilla gradient descent method is generally slow, and it can exhibit a linear rate in case of poor curvature conditions.
While choosing a stepsize larger than an optimal threshold may cause divergence in terms of the objective function.
Determining an optimal learning rate (whether global or per-dimension) becomes more of an art than science for many problems.
Previous work has attempted to alleviate the need for manually selecting a global learning rate
(
Zeiler 2012
;
Lu 2023a
)
, though such methods remain sensitive to other hyper-parameters. Alternatively,
(exact or inexact) line search strategies
can be applied to determine the stepsize more systematically
(
Lu 2025
)
.

\paragrapharrow

Descending Property.
Most (if not all) optimization methods incorporate mechanisms to enforce the descending property:

f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)})<f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}).

(3.9)

This prevents convergence to a maximizer and also makes it less probable that we get convergence to a
saddle point
(a vanishing gradient point that is neither a local minimum point nor a maximum point of the cost function).
If the objective function has several minimizers, the final solution depends on the starting point
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}
. We do not know which of the minimizers that will be found; the specific minimizer found is not necessarily the one closest to
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}
.

As mentioned previously, in many cases the method produces vectors which converge towards the minimizer in two clearly different stages: the “global stage” where
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}
is far from the solution and we want the method to produce iterates which move steadily towards the optimizer
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
, and the “final stage” where
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
is close to
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
and seek faster convergence.

The global convergence properties of a method describe its behavior when initialization occurs at a point
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}
, which is not close to a (local) minimizer
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
.
Ideally, the iterates should move steadily toward a neighborhood of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
. For instance, there are methods for which it is possible to prove that any accumulation point (i.e., limit of a subseries) of
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}\}_{t>0}
is a stationary point, meaning the gradient vanishes:

\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}\qquad\text{ for }\qquad t\rightarrow\infty.

While this does not eliminate the possibility of convergence to a saddle point or maximizer, the descending property (
) typically prevents such cases in practice.
In this “global phase”, our primary concern is ensuring that losses do not increase (except for possibly the initial steps).
To analyze convergence in terms of iterates rather than function values, a natural potential function is

e_{t}\triangleq\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2},\quad
where
\bm{e}^{(t)}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
.

Let
\{\bm{e}^{(t)}\}_{t>0}
denote the error sequence. The requirement for progress is:

\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}<\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}\qquad\text{ for }\qquad t>t^{\prime}.

In the final stages of the iteration where the
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
are close to
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
, we expect faster convergence.
Local convergence analysis describes how quickly the iterates approach
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
to a desired accuracy. Some methods exhibit linear convergence:

\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}\leq c_{1}\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2},\quad\text{with }0<c_{1}<1\text{ and }\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}\text{ close to }\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}.

However, higher-order convergence is preferable. For instance, quadratic convergence satisfies:

\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}\leq c_{2}\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\text{with }c_{2}>0\text{ and }\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}\text{ close to }\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}.

Few practical methods achieve quadratic convergence, but superlinear convergence is a common goal:

{\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}}/{\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}}\rightarrow 0\quad\text{ for }t\rightarrow\infty.

Superlinear convergence is faster than linear convergence, though typically not as rapid as quadratic convergence.

\paragrapharrow

Framework of a descent method.

Algorithm 4

Structure of Descent Methods

1:

A function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
;

2:

Input:
Initialize
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}
;

3:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

4:

Find a descent direction
\bm{d}^{(t)}
such that
\left\langle\bm{d}^{(t)},\bm{g}^{(t)}\right\rangle<0
;

5:

Pick a stepsize
\eta_{t}
;

6:

\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\eta_{t}\bm{d}^{(t)}
;

7:

end

for

8:

(Output Option 1) Output
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{final}}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(T)}
;

9:

(Output Option 2) Output
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{avg}}\leftarrow\frac{1}{T}(\sum_{t=1}^{t}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
or
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{2t}{T(T+1)}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
;

10:

(Output Option 3) Output
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{best}}\leftarrow\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{t\in\{1,2,\ldots,T\}}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
;

The methods presented in this book are descent methods, meaning they satisfy the descending condition (
) at each iteration. Each iteration consists of:

Finding a descent direction
\bm{d}^{(t)}
at the
t
-th iteration.

Determining a stepsize
\eta_{t}
giving a good decrease in the function value.

This sequence of operations forms the foundation of descent algorithms, see Algorithm
.
The search direction
\bm{d}^{(t)}
at each iteration must be a descent direction.
This ensures that we can reduce
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
by choosing an appropriate walking distance, and thus we can satisfy the descending condition (
).

\paragrapharrow

Stopping criteria.
Ideally, a stopping criterion should indicate when the current error is sufficiently small:

\textbf{(ST1)}:\qquad\big\lVert\bm{e}^{{(t)}}\big\rVert_{2}<\delta_{1}.

Another ideal condition would be when the current function value is close enough to the minimum:

\textbf{(ST2)}:\qquad f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})-f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})<\delta_{2}.

Both conditions reflect the convergence
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
.
However, they are impractical because
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
and
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})
are (in most cases) unknown .
Instead, we rely on approximations:

\textbf{(ST3)}:\qquad\big\lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon_{1}\qquad\text{or}\qquad f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})-f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)})<\varepsilon_{2}.

(3.10)

We must emphasize that even if (
) is fulfilled with small
\varepsilon_{1}
and
\varepsilon_{2}
, it does not guarantee that
\big\lVert\bm{e}^{{(t)}}\big\rVert_{2}
or
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})-f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})
are small.

Another form of convergence, mentioned earlier in this section, is
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}
for
t\rightarrow\infty
. This leads to another commonly used stopping criterion:

\textbf{(ST4)}:\qquad\big\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\big\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon_{3},

(3.11)

which is included in many implementations of descent methods.

Another useful approach involves leveraging the property of converging function values.
The quadratic approximation (Theorem
) of
f
at
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
is

f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\approx f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})+(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})+\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}).

Since
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
is a local minimizer, we have
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\bm{H}^{*}\triangleq\nabla^{2}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})
is positive semidefinite. This simplifies to:

f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})-f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})\approx\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*})^{\top}\bm{H}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}).

Thus, another stopping criterion can be defined as:

\textbf{(ST5)}:\qquad\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\bm{H}^{(t)}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})<\varepsilon_{4}\quad\text{with}\quad\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}\approx\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}.

Here,
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
is approximated by
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
and
\bm{H}^{*}
is approximated by

\bm{H}^{(t)}\triangleq\nabla^{2}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}).

In the following sections, we delve into a detailed exploration of the gradient descent method, examining its variations and adaptations from different perspectives. This comprehensive analysis aims to provide a deeper understanding of the algorithm, its formulations, challenges, and practical applications.

3.1.1
Gradient Descent by Greedy Search and Variants

We now consider the
greedy search
method such that
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
under some mild conditions.
The linear approximation theorem (Theorem
) shows that

f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\eta\bm{d})=f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})+\eta\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})+\mathcal{O}(\left\lVert\eta\bm{d}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}).

(3.12)

For small values of
\eta
, the term
\mathcal{O}(\left\lVert\eta\bm{d}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})
becomes negligible compared to the middle term. Therefore, we can approximate
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\eta\bm{d})
as

f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}+\eta\bm{d})\approx f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})+\eta\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}),

(3.13)

when
\eta
is sufficiently small.
The second term on the right-hand side,
\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
, is the
directional derivative
of
f
at
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
in the direction
\bm{d}
.
To reiterate, it indicates the approximate change in
f
for a small step
\bm{d}
. The step
\bm{d}
is a descent direction if the directional derivative is negative.

To address how to choose
\bm{d}
to make the directional derivative as negative as possible, note that since the directional derivative
\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
is linear in
\bm{d}
, it can be made arbitrarily negative by increasing
\bm{d}
(provided
\bm{d}
is a descent direction, i.e.,
\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})<0
). To make this question meaningful, we must limit the size of
\bm{d}
, or normalize by its length.

Let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
be any norm on
n
. We define a
normalized greedy descent direction
(with respect to the norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
) as

\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}\in\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{d}}\left\{\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\text{ s.t. }\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert=1\right\}.

(3.14)

(Note that there may be multiple minimizers.) A normalized greedy descent direction
\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}
is a step of unit norm that provides the largest decrease in the linear approximation of
f
.
By the definition of the dual norm (
), it follows that
\left\langle\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)},\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rangle=-\left\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rVert_{*}
, where
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{*}
denotes the dual norm.

Since the problem in (
) can equivalently be stated using the constraint
\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert\leq 1
,
\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}
also lies within the set of primal counterparts of
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
, whose existence is shown in Definition
.

It is also convenient to consider an unnormalized greedy descent step
\bm{d}_{\text{ugd}}^{(t)}
by scaling the normalized greedy descent direction in a particular way:

\bm{d}_{\text{ugd}}^{(t)}\triangleq\left\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rVert_{*}\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}.

(3.15)

The reason for this particular unnormalization is that it aligns with the negative gradient (the steepest descent direction) when the underlying norm is the
\ell_{2}
norm.
Note that for the greedy descent step, we have

\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\bm{d}_{\text{ugd}}^{(t)}=\left\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rVert_{*}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})^{\top}\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}=-\left\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rVert_{*}^{2}.

However, when the exact line search method is used to find the learning rate, scale factors in the descent direction do not affect the outcome, so either the normalized or unnormalized direction can be used.

\paragrapharrow

Greedy search for
\ell_{2}
norm.
If we take the norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
to be the
\ell_{2}
norm, we find that the greedy descent direction in (
) is simply the negative gradient, i.e.,

\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}=-\frac{\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})}{\big\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\big\rVert_{2}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{d}_{\text{ugd}}^{(t)}=-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}).

(3.16)

The greedy descent method for the
\ell_{2}
norm coincides with the gradient descent method (or the steepest descent method).
The above equality also shows that the unnormalized greedy search direction corresponds to the negative gradient direction or the steepest descent direction.

\paragrapharrow

Greedy search for
\ell_{1}
norm.
As another example, consider the greedy descent method for the
\ell_{1}
norm. A normalized greedy descent direction can be characterized as

\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}\in\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{d}}\left\{\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\text{ s.t. }\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1\right\}.

We use ‘
\in
’ since the solution of the problem may not be unique.
Let
i
be any index for which
\left\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rVert_{\infty}=\left\lvert(\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}))_{i}\right\rvert
.
By the definition of the
\ell_{\infty}
norm and the dual norm (Definition
and (
)), a normalized greedy descent direction
\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}
for the
\ell_{1}
norm is given by

\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}=-\sign\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{i}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right)\bm{e}_{i},

where
\bm{e}_{i}
is the
i
-th unit basis vector (see Example
). An unnormalized greedy descent step is then

\bm{d}_{\text{ugd}}^{(t)}=\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}\left\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rVert_{\infty}=-\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{i}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\bm{e}_{i}.

which is a descent direction since
\left\langle\bm{d}_{\text{ugd}}^{(t)},\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rangle<0
(assuming
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\neq\boldsymbol{0}
).
Thus, the normalized greedy descent step in the
\ell_{1}
norm can always be chosen to be a (positive or negative) standard basis vector, representing the coordinate axis direction along which the approximate decrease in
f
is greatest.
Note that the index for which
\big\lVert\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\big\rVert_{\infty}=\big\lvert(\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}))_{i}\big\rvert
may not be unique (see Example
). In such cases, a convex combination of these descent directions can be used as the final descent direction.

The greedy descent algorithm in the
\ell_{1}
norm has a natural interpretation: At each iteration we select a component of
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
with maximum absolute value (though the component may not be unique), and then decrease or increase the corresponding component of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
, according to the sign of
(\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}))_{i}
. The algorithm is sometimes called a
coordinate-descent algorithm
because only one component of the variable
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is updated at each iteration, potentially simplifying or even trivializing the line search.

\paragrapharrow

Greedy search for
\bm{Q}
-norm.
We further consider the
\bm{Q}
-norm:

\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{\bm{Q}}=(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\theta})^{1/2}=\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{2}

(3.17)

for any
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{n}
,
where
\bm{Q}
is positive definite. The normalized greedy descent direction is given by

\displaystyle\bm{d}_{\text{ngd}}^{(t)}

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{d}}\left\{\bm{d}^{\top}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\text{ s.t. }\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert_{\bm{Q}}\leq 1\right\}=-\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{-1/2}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})\right\rVert_{2}^{-1/2}\bm{Q}^{-1}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}).

This can be solved using the KKT conditions or the definition of the dual norm.
The dual norm is given by
\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{*}=\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{\bm{Q}^{-1}}
for any
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{n}
, so the greedy descent step with respect to
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\bm{Q}}
is given by

\bm{d}_{\text{ugd}}^{(t)}=-\bm{Q}^{-1}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}).

(3.18)

This is a descent direction; see Problem
.

\paragrapharrow

Change of variables in
\bm{Q}
-norm.

An interesting alternative interpretation of the greedy descent direction
\bm{d}_{\text{ugd}}^{(t)}
is as the gradient search direction after applying a change of coordinates to the problem. Let
\widetilde{\bm{x}}\triangleq\bm{Q}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\theta}
; thus,
\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{\bm{Q}}=\left\lVert\widetilde{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}
. Using this change of coordinates, we can solve the original problem of minimizing
f
by solving the equivalent problem of minimizing the function
\widetilde{f}:\real^{n}\rightarrow\real
, given by

\widetilde{f}(\widetilde{\bm{x}})\triangleq f(\bm{Q}^{-1/2}\widetilde{\bm{x}})=f(\boldsymbol{\theta}).

If we apply the gradient method to
\widetilde{f}
, the search direction at a point
\widetilde{\bm{x}}^{(t)}
(which corresponds to the point
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}=\bm{Q}^{-1/2}\widetilde{\bm{x}}^{(t)}
for the original problem) is

\widetilde{\bm{d}}^{(t)}=-\nabla\widetilde{f}(\widetilde{\bm{x}}^{(t)})=-\bm{Q}^{-1/2}\nabla f(\bm{Q}^{-1/2}\widetilde{\bm{x}}^{(t)})=-\bm{Q}^{-1/2}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}).

Since
\widetilde{\bm{x}}=\bm{Q}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\theta}
by definition, the search direction in the original space is obtained by mapping
\widetilde{\bm{d}}^{(t)}
back using
\bm{Q}^{-1/2}
:

\bm{d}^{(t)}=\bm{Q}^{-1/2}\widetilde{\bm{d}}^{(t)}=-\bm{Q}^{-1}\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})

which corresponds to the unnormalized greedy search direction in (
). In other words, the greedy descent method in the
\bm{Q}
-norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\bm{Q}}
can be thought of as the gradient method applied to the problem after the change of variables
\widetilde{\bm{x}}^{(t)}=\bm{Q}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}
for each iteration
t
.

3.1.2
Geometrical Interpretation of Gradient Descent

Lemma 134
(Direction of gradients).

An important fact is that gradients are orthogonal to level curves (also known as level surfaces).

Proof
[of Lemma
: Informal]
To prove this, we need to show that the gradient is orthogonal to the tangent of the level curve. Let’s start with the two-dimensional case. Suppose the level curve has the form
f(x,y)=c
.
This equation implicitly defines a relationship between
x
and
y
, such that
y=y(x)
, where
y
can be considered as a function of
x
. Therefore, the level curve can be expressed as:

f(x,y(x))=c.

Applying the chain rule gives us:

\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\underbrace{\frac{dx}{dx}}_{=1}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dx}=0.

This implies that the gradient is perpendicular to the tangent vector:

\left\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial x},\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right\rangle\cdot\left\langle\frac{dx}{dx},\frac{dy}{dx}\right\rangle=0.

Now, let’s generalize this to higher dimensions. Consider a level set defined by a vector
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{n}
:
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})=f(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\ldots,\theta_{n})=c
. Each variable
\theta_{i}
can be regarded as a function of a parameter
t
along the level set
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})=c
:
f(\theta_{1}(t),\theta_{2}(t),\ldots,\theta_{n}(t))=c
. Differentiating both sides with respect to
t
using the chain rule yields:

\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{1}}\frac{d\theta_{1}}{dt}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{2}}\frac{d\theta_{2}}{dt}+\ldots+\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{n}}\frac{d\theta_{n}}{dt}=0.

Therefore, the gradients is perpendicular to the tangent in the
n
-dimensional case:

\left\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{1}},\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{2}},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{n}}\right\rangle\cdot\left\langle\frac{d\theta_{1}}{dt},\frac{d\theta_{2}}{dt},\ldots,\frac{d\theta_{n}}{dt}\right\rangle=0.

This completes the proof.

The lemma above provides a profound geometric interpretation of gradient descent. In the process of minimizing a (convex) function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
, gradient descent strategically moves in the direction opposite to the gradient, which reduces the loss. Figure
illustrates a two-dimensional scenario where
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
guides the decrease in loss for a (convex) function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
.

(a)

A two-dimensional convex function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
.

(b)

f(\boldsymbol{\theta})=c
is a constant.

Figure 3.1:
Figure
shows a convex function surface plot and its contour plot (
blue
=low,
yellow
=high), where the upper graph represents the surface plot, and the lower one is its projection (i.e., contour). Figure
:
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
directs the reduction in loss for the convex function
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
.

3.1.3
Geometrical Interpretation of Regularization

Figure 3.2:
Constrained gradient descent with
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq C
. The
green
vector
\bm{w}
is the projection of
\bm{v}_{1}
into
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq C
, where
\bm{v}_{1}
is the component of
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
perpendicular to
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}
. The right picture shows the next step after the update in the left picture.
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}
denotes the optimal solution of {
\min f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
}.

Regularization
is a machine learning technique employed to prevent overfitting and improve model generalization; see Sections
and
. Overfitting occurs when a model is overly complex and fits the training data too closely, resulting in poor performance on unseen data.
To mitigate this issue, regularization introduces a constraint or a penalty term into the loss function used for model optimization, discouraging the development of overly complex models.
This creates a trade-off between having a simple, generalizable model and fitting the training data well.
Common types of regularization include
\ell_{1}
regularization,
\ell_{2}
regularization (Tikhonov regularization), and elastic net regularization (a combination of
\ell_{1}
and
\ell_{2}
regularizations).
Regularization finds extensive applications in machine learning algorithms such as linear regression, logistic regression, and neural networks.

Gradient descent also reveals the geometric significance of regularization. To avoid confusion, we denote the loss function without regularization by
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
and the loss with the
\ell_{2}
regularization by
F(\boldsymbol{\theta})\triangleq f(\boldsymbol{\theta})+\lambda\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, where
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}):\real^{n}\rightarrow\real
.
When minimizing
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
, the descent method searches for a solution in
n
.
However, in machine learning, an exhaustive search across the entire space may lead to overfitting. A partial remedy involves searching within a subset of the vector space, such as searching in
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}<C
for some constant
C
. That is,

\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,\big\{f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{s.t.}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq C\big\}.

This constrained search helps prevent overfitting by introducing regularization through the addition of a penalty term in the optimization process.
In the previous discussion, a basic gradient descent approach proceeds in the direction of
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
, updating
\boldsymbol{\theta}
by
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{+}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}-\eta\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
for a small stepsize
\eta
.
When the level curve is
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})=c_{1}
and the descent approach is situated at
\boldsymbol{\theta}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}
, where
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}
is the intersection of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}=C
and
f(\boldsymbol{\theta})=c_{1}
, the descent direction
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})
will be perpendicular to the level curve of
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})=c_{1}
, as shown in the left picture of Figure
.
However, if we further restrict that the optimal value can only be in the subspace
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq C
, the trivial descent direction
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})
will lead
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}-\eta\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})
outside of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq C
.

To address this, the step
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})
is decomposed into

-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})=a\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}+\bm{v}_{1},

where
a\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}
is the component perpendicular to the curve of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}=C
, and
\bm{v}_{1}
is the component parallel to the curve of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}=C
. Keeping only the step
\bm{v}_{1}
, then the update

\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2}=\text{project}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}+\eta\bm{v}_{1})=\text{project}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}+\eta\underbrace{(-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})-a\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})}_{\bm{v}_{1}}\right)

will lead to a smaller loss from
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})
to
f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2})
while still satisfying the constraint
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq C
.
This technique is known as the
projected gradient descent

(
Beck 2017
;
Lu 2025
)
. It is not hard to see that the update
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2}=\text{project}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}+\eta\bm{v}_{1})
is equivalent to finding a vector
\bm{w}
(depicted by the
green
vector in the left panel of Figure
) such that
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}+\bm{w}
lies inside the curve of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq C
. Mathematically, the vector
\bm{w}
can be obtained as
-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})-2\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}
for some
\lambda
, as shown in the middle panel of Figure
. This aligns with the negative gradient of
F(\boldsymbol{\theta})=f(\boldsymbol{\theta})+\lambda\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
such that

-\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})=-\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})-2\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1},

and

\displaystyle\bm{w}

\displaystyle=-\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1})\qquad\implies\qquad\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}+\bm{w}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}-\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}).

In practice, a small stepsize
\eta
can be applied to prevent crossing the curve boundary of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq C
:

\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}-\eta\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{1}).

3.1.4
ALS via Gradient Descent

In Algorithm
,
, and
, we reduce the loss of the low-rank approximation or the alternating least squares (ALS) problem through the inversion of matrices (e.g., using LU decomposition
(
Lu 2021b
)
).
The reality, however, is frequently far from straightforward, particularly in the big data era of today. As data volumes explode, the size of the inversion matrix will grow at a pace proportional to the cube of the number of samples, which poses a great challenge to the storage and computational resources.
On the other hand, this leads to the creation of an ongoing development of the gradient-based optimization technique.
The
gradient descent (GD)
method and its variant, the
stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
method, are among them the simplest, fastest, and most efficient methods. Convex loss function optimization problems are frequently solved using this type of approach. We now go into more details about its principle in the ALS context.

Gradient Descent

In Equation (
), we derive the column-by-column update rules for ALS directly from the full matrix approach outlined in Equation (
) (with regularization taken into account).
To understand the underlying concept, consider the loss function with regularization, as given by Equation (
).
When minimizing the loss in (
) with respect to
\bm{z}_{p}
, we can break down the loss as follows:

\displaystyle L(\bm{z}_{p})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{W}\bm{Z}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{w}\left\lVert\bm{W}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{z}\left\lVert\bm{Z}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{W}\bm{z}_{p}-\bm{x}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{z}\left\lVert\bm{z}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+C_{z_{p}},

(3.19)

where
C_{z_{p}}
is a constant with respect to
\bm{z}_{p}
, and
\bm{Z}=[\bm{z}_{1},\bm{z}_{2},\ldots,\bm{z}_{P}]
and
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{P}]
represent the column partitions of
\bm{Z}
and
\bm{X}
, respectively.
The gradient and the root are given, respectively, by

\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{z}_{p}}L(\bm{z}_{p})=\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{z}_{p}-\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{x}_{p}+\lambda_{z}\bm{z}_{p}\quad\implies\quad\bm{z}_{p}=(\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{W}+\lambda_{z}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{x}_{p},\,\,\forall\,p.

This solution corresponds to the first update rule in the column-wise update in Equation (
).
Similarly, when minimizing the loss with respect to
\bm{w}_{n}
, we have:

\displaystyle L(\bm{w}_{n})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{W}-\bm{X}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{w}\left\lVert\bm{W}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{z}\left\lVert\bm{Z}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{w}_{n}-\bm{b}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{w}\left\lVert\bm{w}_{n}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+C_{w_{n}},

(3.20)

where
C_{w_{n}}
is a constant with respect to
\bm{w}_{n}
, and
\bm{W}^{\top}=[\bm{w}_{1},\bm{w}_{2},\ldots,\bm{w}_{N}]
and
\bm{X}^{\top}=[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,

\bm{b}_{N}]
represent the column partitions of
\bm{W}^{\top}
and
\bm{X}^{\top}
, respectively.
Analogously, taking the gradient with respect to
\bm{w}_{n}
, it follows that

\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{w}_{n}}L(\bm{w}_{n})=\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{w}_{n}-\bm{Z}\bm{b}_{p}+\lambda_{w}\bm{w}_{n}\quad\implies\quad\bm{w}_{n}=(\bm{Z}\bm{Z}^{\top}+\lambda_{w}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{Z}\bm{b}_{n},\,\,\forall\,n.

This solution corresponds to the second update rule in the column-wise update in Equation (
):

Now suppose we express the iteration number (
t=1,2,\ldots
) as the superscript, and we want to find the updates
\{\bm{z}^{(t+1)}_{p},\bm{w}^{(t+1)}_{n}\}
in the
(t+1)
-th iteration base on
\{\bm{Z}^{(t)},\bm{W}^{(t)}\}
in the
t
-th iteration:

\left.\begin{aligned} \bm{z}^{(t+1)}_{p}&\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{z}_{p}^{(t)}}L(\bm{z}_{p}^{(t)})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{w}_{n}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{w}_{n}^{(t)}}L(\bm{w}_{n}^{(t)}).\end{aligned}\right.

For simplicity, we will only derive for
\bm{z}^{(t+1)}_{p}\leftarrow\mathop{\arg\min}_{\bm{z}_{p}^{(t)}}L(\bm{z}_{p}^{(t)})
, and the derivation for the update on
\bm{w}_{n}^{(t+1)}
will follow a similar process.
With this insight, the gradient descent update for the ALS algorithms is provided in Algorithm
.

It’s noteworthy that the ALS without GD (Algorithm
) lacks explicit parameters like step size.
This characteristic can be both advantageous and disadvantageous.
On one hand, it absolves the user from the time-consuming task of fine-tuning parameters, making the method more accessible and less demanding.
On the other hand, this absence of adjustable parameters also restricts the user’s control to directly influence the progression of the algorithm, leaving the convergence of ALS entirely contingent upon the inherent structure of the optimization problem at hand.

In practical applications, it is customary to alternate between the pure ALS iterations outlined in Algorithm
and the modified, gradient-descent variants mentioned in this section. These descent adaptations offer the user a degree of control through a tunable step length parameter, allowing for a more customized approach to the optimization process.

Stochastic Gradient Descent

The gradient descent method is a valuable optimization algorithm; however, it exhibits certain limitations in practical applications.
To comprehend the issues associated with the gradient descent method, we consider the mean squared error (MSE) derived from (
):

\frac{1}{NP}\mathop{\min}_{\bm{W},\bm{Z}}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2}.

(3.21)

The MSE requires calculating the residual
e_{np}\triangleq(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p})^{2}
for each observed entry
x_{np}
, representing the squared difference between predicted and actual values. The total sum of residual squares is denoted by
e=\sum_{n,p=1}^{NP}e_{np}
.
In cases with a substantial number of training entries (i.e., large
NP
), the entire computation process becomes notably slow.
Additionally, the gradients from different input samples may cancel out, resulting in small changes in the final update.
As mentioned previously, researchers have enhanced the gradient descent method with the
stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
method to address these challenges.
In the SGD algorithm, instead of calculating the full gradient of the objective function with respect to the parameters across all samples in the data set, which can be computationally expensive, the algorithm takes a more efficient approach. It randomly chooses one sample and calculates the gradient of the objective function with respect to the parameters using only this single sample.
This gradient estimate is then used to update the parameters in the direction that minimizes the objective function.
By using a single sample at each iteration, the SGD algorithm provides a fast and often sufficient approximation of the full gradient, making it particularly useful for large data sets.

In particular, we consider again the per-example loss:

L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{w}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\lVert\bm{w}_{n}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{z}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\left\lVert\bm{z}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

As we iteratively reduce the loss term
l(\bm{w}_{n},\bm{z}_{p})=\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{np}-\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{w}\left\lVert\bm{w}_{n}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{z}\left\lVert\bm{z}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for all
n\in\{1,2,\ldots,N\},p\in\{1,2,\ldots,P\}
(referred to as the per-example loss term), the overall loss
L(\bm{W},\bm{Z})
decreases accordingly.
This process is also known as
stochastic coordinate descent
. The gradients with respect to
\bm{w}_{n}
and
\bm{z}_{p}
, and their roots are given, respectively, by

\left\{\begin{aligned} \nabla_{\bm{z}_{p}}l(\bm{z}_{p})&=\bm{w}_{n}\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}\bm{z}_{p}+\lambda_{z}\bm{z}_{p}-x_{np}\bm{w}_{n}&\implies&\,\,\bm{z}_{p}=x_{np}(\bm{w}_{n}\bm{w}_{n}^{\top}+\lambda_{z}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{w}_{n};\\
\nabla_{\bm{w}_{n}}l(\bm{w}_{n})&=\bm{z}_{p}\bm{z}_{p}^{\top}\bm{w}_{n}+\lambda_{w}\bm{w}_{n}-x_{np}\bm{z}_{p}&\implies&\,\,\bm{w}_{n}=x_{np}(\bm{z}_{p}\bm{z}_{p}^{\top}+\lambda_{w}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{z}_{p}.\end{aligned}\right.

Alternatively, the update can be performed using gradient descent. Since we update based on the per-example loss, this approach is also known as the
stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
:

\left.\begin{aligned} \bm{z}_{p}&\leftarrow\bm{z}_{p}-\eta_{z}{\nabla_{\bm{z}_{p}}l(\bm{z}_{p})}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{w}_{n}\leftarrow\bm{w}_{n}-\eta_{w}{\nabla_{\bm{w}_{n}}l(\bm{w}_{n})}\end{aligned}\right.

The stochastic gradient descent update for ALS is formulated in Algorithm
.
It is possible that the gradient descent or stochastic gradient descent algorithm may fail to converge. In such cases, it is appropriate to re-run the algorithm using a smaller learning rate.
And in practice, the values of
n
and
p
in the algorithm can be randomly generated, which is why the method is termed “stochastic.”

3.2
LS via Cholesky Decomposition

As mentioned in Chapter
, the LS problem can be solved using the Cholesky decomposition. We begin by providing ways to compute the Cholesky decomposition of a positive definite matrix.

\paragrapharrow

Computing Cholesky decomposition recursively.
To compute the Cholesky decomposition, we start by writing out the equality
\bm{A}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
, where
\bm{R}
is upper triangular:

\displaystyle\bm{A}=\begin{bmatrix}a_{11}&\bm{A}_{1,2:n}\\
\bm{A}_{2:n,1}&\bm{A}_{2:n,2:n}\end{bmatrix}

\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}r_{11}&0\\
\bm{R}_{1,2:n}^{\top}&\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}r_{11}&\bm{R}_{1,2:n}\\
0&\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r_{11}^{2}&r_{11}\bm{R}_{1,2:n}\\
r_{11}\bm{R}_{1,2:n}^{\top}&\bm{R}_{1,2:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{1,2:n}+\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}\end{bmatrix}.

Since the diagonals of
\bm{R}
are positive when
\bm{A}
is positive definite (Theorem
),
this allows us to determine the first row of
\bm{R}
by

r_{11}=\sqrt{a_{11}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{R}_{1,2:n}=\frac{1}{r_{11}}\bm{A}_{1,2:n}.

Let
\bm{A}_{2}\triangleq\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}
. The equality
\bm{A}_{2:n,2:n}=\bm{R}_{1,2:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{1,2:n}+\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}
and the symmetry of
\bm{A}
indicate

\displaystyle\bm{A}_{2}=\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}

\displaystyle=\bm{A}_{2:n,2:n}-\bm{R}_{1,2:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{1,2:n}=\bm{A}_{2:n,2:n}-\frac{1}{a_{11}}\bm{A}_{2:n,1}\bm{A}_{1,2:n},

where
\bm{A}_{2}
is known as the
Schur complement
of
a_{11}
in
\bm{A}
and has a size of
(n-1)\times(n-1)
. To obtain
\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}
, we must compute the Cholesky decomposition of the matrix
\bm{A}_{2}
of shape
(n-1)\times(n-1)
.
This implies a recursive algorithm to computing the Cholesky decomposition of a PD matrix
\bm{A}
, and the procedure is outlined in Algorithm
.

Algorithm 7

Cholesky Decomposition via Recursive Algorithm

1:

Positive definite matrix
\bm{A}
with size
n\times n
;

2:

Calculate first row of
\bm{R}
by
r_{11}\leftarrow\sqrt{a_{11}},\bm{R}_{1,2:n}\leftarrow\frac{1}{r_{11}}\bm{A}_{1,2:n}
;

3:

Compute the Cholesky decomposition of the
(n-1)\times(n-1)
matrix

\bm{A}_{2}\leftarrow\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{2:n,2:n}=\bm{A}_{2:n,2:n}-\frac{1}{a_{11}}\bm{A}_{2:n,1}\bm{A}_{1,2:n};

{theoremHigh}

[Algorithm complexity: Cholesky recursively
(
Lu 2021b
)
]
Algorithm
requires
\sim(1/3)n^{3}
flops to compute the Cholesky decomposition of an
n\times n
positive definite matrix.

The Cholesky decomposition computation mentioned above has an important application in testing the positive definiteness of a symmetric matrix. To perform the test, one can apply the algorithm mentioned above and declare the matrix as positive definite if the algorithm completes without encountering any negative or zero pivots (as described in step 1 above). Otherwise, if the algorithm encounters such pivots, the matrix is deemed not positive definite.

To end up this section, we provide the full pseudo code for Algorithm
as shown in Algorithm
(compare the two algorithms).

Algorithm 8

Cholesky Decomposition via Recursive Algorithm: Full Pseudo Code

1:

Positive definite matrix
\bm{A}
with size
n\times n
;

2:

for

k=1
to
n

do

\triangleright
compute the
k
-th row of
\bm{R}

3:

r_{kk}\leftarrow\sqrt{a_{kk}}
;
\triangleright
first element of
k
-th row

4:

\bm{R}_{k,k+1:n}\leftarrow\frac{1}{r_{kk}}\bm{A}_{k,k+1:n}
;
\triangleright
the rest elements of
k
-th row

5:

\bm{A}_{k+1:n,k+1:n}\leftarrow\bm{A}_{k+1:n,k+1:n}-\bm{R}_{k,k+1:n}^{\top}\bm{R}_{k,k+1:n}
;

6:

end

for

7:

Output
\bm{A}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
.

\paragrapharrow

An alternative perspective of the recursive algorithm.
Since
\bm{L}\triangleq\bm{R}^{\top}
is lower triangular. The lower triangular factor
\bm{L}
can be computed as a product of a series of lower triangular matrices.
To see this, we have

\bm{A}=\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix}a_{11}&\bm{A}_{1,2:n}\\
\bm{A}_{2:n,1}&\bm{A}_{2:n,2:n}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}l_{11}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{L}_{21}&\bm{L}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}l_{11}&\bm{L}_{21}^{\top}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{L}_{22}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}\triangleq\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}.

Then we still have

\begin{bmatrix}a_{11}&\bm{A}_{1,2:n}\\
\bm{A}_{2:n,1}&\bm{A}_{2:n,2:n}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}l_{11}^{2}&l_{11}\bm{L}_{21}^{\top}\\
l_{11}\bm{L}_{21}&\bm{L}_{21}\bm{L}_{21}^{\top}+\bm{L}_{22}\bm{L}_{22}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\implies\begin{cases}l_{11}&=\sqrt{a_{11}};\\
\bm{L}_{21}&=\frac{1}{l_{11}}\bm{A}_{2:n,1};\\
\bm{L}_{22}\bm{L}_{22}^{\top}&=\bm{A}_{2:n,2:n}-\bm{L}_{21}\bm{L}_{21}^{\top}.\end{cases}

The second perspective involves constructing
n+1
set of
n\times n
matrices:
\bm{A}^{(1)},\bm{A}^{(2)},\ldots,\bm{A}^{(n+1)}
, where
\bm{A}^{(1)}\triangleq\bm{A}
, and we want to obtain
\bm{A}^{(n+1)}=\bm{I}
via the relation:

\bm{A}^{(i)}=\bm{L}^{(i)}\bm{A}^{(i+1)}\bm{L}^{(i)^{\top}},\ \forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.

(3.22)

If these
\bm{L}^{(i)},\ \forall\,i
are lower triangular, then we obtain the Cholesky decomposition by

\bm{A}=(\bm{L}^{(1)}\bm{L}^{(2)}\ldots\bm{L}^{(n)})(\bm{L}^{(1)}\bm{L}^{(2)}\ldots\bm{L}^{(n)})^{\top}\triangleq\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}.

This is indeed the case. To see this, we can construct

\bm{A}^{(i)}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{i-1}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&a_{ii}&\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{b}_{i}&\bm{B}^{(i)}\end{bmatrix}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{L}^{(i)}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{i-1}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&\sqrt{a_{ii}}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\frac{1}{\sqrt{a_{ii}}}\bm{b}_{i}&\bm{I}_{n-i}\end{bmatrix},

satisfying
\bm{A}^{(i)}=\bm{L}^{(i)}\bm{A}^{(i+1)}(\bm{L}^{(i)})^{\top}
:

\displaystyle\bm{A}^{(i+1)}

\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{i-1}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}^{(i)}-\frac{1}{a_{ii}}\bm{b}_{i}\bm{b}_{i}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{i}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&a_{i+1,i+1}&\bm{b}_{i+1}^{\top}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{b}_{i+1}&\bm{B}^{(i+1)}\end{bmatrix}.

Therefore,
\bm{A}
can be decomposed as a set of lower triangular matrices in (
).
Using the result in Exercise
can show that the algorithm for this perspective is equivalent to Algorithm
.
