.

\paragrapharrow

Computing Cholesky decomposition element-wise.

It is also common to compute the Cholesky decomposition using element-wise equations derived directly from solving the matrix equation
\bm{A}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
. Observing that the
(i,j)
-th entry of
\bm{A}
is given by
a_{ij}=\bm{R}_{:,i}^{\top}\bm{R}_{:,j}=\sum_{k=1}^{i}r_{ki}r_{kj}
if
i<j
. This further implies the following recurrence relation: if
i<j
, we have

\displaystyle a_{ij}

\displaystyle=\bm{R}_{:,i}^{\top}\bm{R}_{:,j}=\sum_{k=1}^{i}r_{ki}r_{kj}=\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}r_{ki}r_{kj}+r_{ii}r_{ij}\implies r_{ij}=(a_{ij}-\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}r_{ki}r_{kj})/r_{ii},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{if }i<j.

For the diagonal entries (
i=j
), we have:

\displaystyle a_{jj}

\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{j}r_{kj}^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}r_{kj}^{2}+r_{jj}^{2}

\displaystyle\implies r_{jj}=\sqrt{a_{jj}-\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}r_{kj}^{2}}.

If we equate the elements of
\bm{R}
by taking a column at a time and start with
r_{11}=\sqrt{a_{11}}
, the element-level algorithm is formulated in Algorithm
.

Algorithm 9

Cholesky Decomposition Element-Wise:
\bm{A}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}

1:

Positive definite matrix
\bm{A}
with size
n\times n
;

2:

Calculate first element of
\bm{R}
by
r_{11}\leftarrow\sqrt{a_{11}}
;

3:

for

j=1
to
n

do

\triangleright
Compute the
j
-th column of
\bm{R}

4:

for

i=1
to
j-1

do

5:

r_{ij}\leftarrow(a_{ij}-\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}r_{ki}r_{kj})/r_{ii}
, since
i<j
;

6:

end

for

7:

r_{jj}\leftarrow\sqrt{a_{jj}-\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}r_{kj}^{2}}
;

8:

end

for

9:

Output
\bm{A}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
.

On the other hand, Algorithm
can be modified to compute the Cholesky decomposition in the form
\bm{A}=\bm{L}\bm{D}\bm{L}^{\top}
, where
\bm{L}
is unit lower triangular and
\bm{D}
is diagonal, as outlined in Algorithm
, whose Step 3 and Step 5 are derived from (since
l_{ii}=1,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
):

\displaystyle a_{jj}

\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}d_{kk}l_{jk}^{2}+d_{jj};

\displaystyle a_{ij}

\displaystyle=d_{jj}l_{ij}+\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}d_{kk}l_{ik}l_{jk},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{if }i>j.

Exercise
\thetheo

Derive the complexity of Algorithm
.

This form of Cholesky decomposition is useful for determining the condition number of a PD matrix
(
Lu 2021b
)
.
In essence, the condition number of a function measures the sensitivity of the output value to small changes in the input; a smaller condition number indicates better numerical stability.
For positive definite linear systems, the condition number is defined as the ratio of the largest eigenvalue to the smallest eigenvalue.
The condition number of a positive definite matrix is lower bounded by the diagonal matrix in the Cholesky decomposition (see Problem
):

\text{cond}(\bm{A})\geq\text{cond}(\bm{D}).

(3.23)

This can be proven by showing that
\lambda_{\max}\geq d_{\max}
and
\lambda_{\min}\leq d_{\min}
, where
\lambda_{\max}
and
\lambda_{\min}
are the largest and smallest eigenvalue of
\bm{A}
, and
d_{\max}
and
d_{\min}
are the largest and smallest diagonals of
\bm{D}
.
Therefore, this form of the Cholesky decomposition can be utilized to modify Newton’s method; see
(
Lu 2025
)
.

Algorithm 10

Cholesky Decomposition Element-Wise:
\bm{A}=\bm{L}\bm{D}\bm{L}^{\top}

1:

Positive definite matrix
\bm{A}
with size
n\times n
;

2:

for

j=1
to
n

do

\triangleright
Compute the
j
-th column of
\bm{L}

3:

l_{jj}\leftarrow 1
;

4:

c_{jj}\leftarrow a_{jj}-\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}d_{kk}l_{jk}^{2}
;

5:

d_{jj}\leftarrow c_{jj}

6:

for

i=j+1
to
n

do

7:

c_{ij}\leftarrow a_{ij}-\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}d_{kk}l_{ik}l_{jk}
, since
i>j
;

8:

l_{ij}\leftarrow\frac{c_{ij}}{d_{jj}}
;

9:

end

for

10:

end

for

11:

Output
\bm{A}=\bm{L}\bm{D}\bm{L}^{\top}
, where
\bm{D}=\mathrm{diag}(d_{11},d_{22},\ldots,d_{nn})
.

3.2.1
Full Rank Case

The classical method for solving a linear least squares problem
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}
,
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, is to form and solve the symmetric normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
. If
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, then
\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
implies that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
. Hence

\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}>0,\quad\forall\,\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p},\quad\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq\boldsymbol{0},

(3.24)

and
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is positive definite. Conversely, a symmetric positive definite matrix is nonsingular. If it were singular, there would be a vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
such that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
. But then
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=0
, which is a contradiction.

\paragrapharrow

Normal equation of the first kind.

Substituting the Cholesky factorization
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
into the normal equation gives
\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}
, where
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\triangleq\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
. Hence, the solution is obtained by solving two triangular systems:

\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{u}=\boldsymbol{\alpha},\qquad\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{u}.

(3.25)

This method is easy to implement and often faster than other direct solution methods. It works well unless
\bm{X}
is ill-conditioned.

It is often preferable to work with the Cholesky factorization of the cross-product of the augmented matrix
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
:

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}^{\top}\\
\bm{y}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}&\bm{y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}&\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}\\
\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{X}&\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}\end{bmatrix},

(3.26)

when solving a least squares problem. If
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, then the Cholesky factor of the cross-product (
),

\bm{S}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}&\bm{v}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\rho\end{bmatrix},

(3.27)

exists, where we may have
\rho=0
. Forming
\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{S}
shows that

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R},\qquad\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{v}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y},\qquad\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{v}+\rho^{2}.

Hence,
\bm{R}
is the Cholesky factor of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
, and the least squares solution is obtained from
\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{v}
. Since
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
is orthogonal to
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, we have

\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=(\bm{e}+\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{R}^{-1}\bm{R}^{-\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{v},

and hence
\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\rho^{2}=\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{v}
and
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}=\rho
.

\paragrapharrow

Cholesky QR factorization.
On the other hand, let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
have full column rank, and let
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
be its Cholesky factorization.
Define
\bm{Q}_{1}\triangleq\bm{X}\bm{R}^{-1}\in\real^{n\times p}
. Then,

\bm{X}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}=\bm{I}_{p}

(3.28)

is the
Cholesky QR factorization
of
\bm{X}
. The semi-orthogonal factor
\bm{Q}_{1}
can be obtained as the unique solution of the lower triangular matrix equation
\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}=\bm{X}^{\top}
by forward substitution. In this setting, the normal equation simplifies to
\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}
or

\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}.

In the real case, the computational cost of this Cholesky QR algorithm is
\sim 2np^{2}+p^{3}/3
flops.
More accurate methods for computing the QR factorization (
) directly from
\bm{X}
are described in Section
.

\paragrapharrow

Normal equation of the second kind.
For a consistent underdetermined linear system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
, the solution to the least-norm problem
\min\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}
subject to
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
satisfies the normal equation of the second kind in (
):

\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{y}.

If
\bm{X}
has full row rank, then
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}
is symmetric positive definite, and the Cholesky factorization
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
exists. Then
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
is obtained by solving

\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{w}=\bm{y},\qquad\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{w}.

(3.29)

3.2.2
Modifying LS: Adding or Deleting a Data/Row

Updating linear systems after low-rank modifications of the system matrix is a common practice in machine learning, statistics, and many other fields.
However, it is widely recognized that such updates can introduce significant instabilities due to round-off errors
(
Seeger 2004
)
.
When the system matrix is positive definite, employing a representation based on Cholesky decomposition is usually preferable as it provides improved numerical stability
(
Gill et al. 1974
;
Bojanczyk et al. 1987
;
Chang 1997
;
Davis and Hager 1999
;
Seeger 2004
;
Chen et al. 2008
;
Davis 2008
;
Higham 2009
)
.

On the other hand, many applications require the solution of a least squares problem after the data have been modified by adding (updating) or deleting (downdating) observations. Examples arise in regression problems, optimization, signal processing, and prediction in control
theory
(
Björck 2024
)
.
In this section, we will present a proof for the rank-one update/downdate using Cholesky decomposition.

Rank-One Update

Note that we follow the dimension notation of the underlying matrix for the Cholesky decomposition such that
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
. However, the LS notation uses
\bm{A}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\in\real^{p\times p}
.

A rank-one update
\bm{A}^{\prime}
of a matrix
\bm{A}
by a new data vector
\bm{v}
is of the form:

\displaystyle\bm{A}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\bm{A}+\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top},\quad\text{with}\quad\bm{A}\triangleq\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\ \text{ and }\ \bm{A}^{\prime}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}^{\top}&\bm{v}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize^{\top}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}\\
\bm{v}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize,

\displaystyle\downarrow

\displaystyle\downarrow

\displaystyle\bm{R}^{\prime\top}\bm{R}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}+\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}.

If the Cholesky factor
\bm{R}
of
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
has already been computed, we can efficiently obtain the Cholesky factor
\bm{R}^{\prime}
of
\bm{A}^{\prime}
.
Note that
\bm{A}^{\prime}
differs from
\bm{A}
only by the symmetric rank-one matrix.
Therefore, we can compute
\bm{R}^{\prime}
from
\bm{R}
using the rank-one Cholesky update, which takes
\mathcal{O}(n^{2})
operations, each saving from
\mathcal{O}(n^{3})
complexity if we were to recompute the Cholesky decomposition of
\bm{A}^{\prime}
from scratch,
given that we know
\bm{R}
, the Cholesky decomposition of
\bm{A}
up front.
That is, we want to compute the Cholesky decomposition of
\bm{A}^{\prime}
via that of
\bm{A}
.
To see this,
suppose there exists a set of orthogonal matrices
\bm{Q}_{n}\bm{Q}_{n-1}\ldots\bm{Q}_{1}
such that

\bm{Q}_{n}\bm{Q}_{n-1}\ldots\bm{Q}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}.

Then we find out the expression for the Cholesky factor of
\bm{A}^{\prime}
by
\bm{R}^{\prime}
.
Specifically, multiplying the left-hand side of the above equation by its transpose yields

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}&\bm{R}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\ldots\bm{Q}_{n-1}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{n}^{\top}\bm{Q}_{n}\bm{Q}_{n-1}\ldots\bm{Q}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}+\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}.

Similarly, multiplying the right-hand side by its transpose gives

\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{R}^{\prime\top}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{R}^{\prime\top}\bm{R}^{\prime},

which matches the left-hand side equation.
Givens rotations
are examples of such orthogonal matrices that can transfer
\bm{R}
and
\bm{v}
into
\bm{R}^{\prime}
.

Definition 135
(
n
-th Order Givens Rotation).

A Givens rotation is represented by a matrix of the following form

\bm{G}_{kl}=\begin{bmatrix}1&&&&&&&&&\\
&\ddots&&&&&&&&\\
&&1&&&&&&&\\
&&&c&&&&s&&\\
&&&&1&&&&&\\
&&&&&\ddots&&&&\\
&&&&&&1&&&\\
&&&-s&&&&c&&\\
&&&&&&&&1&\\
&&&&&&&&&\ddots\end{bmatrix}_{n\times n},

where the
(k,k),(k,l),(l,k),(l,l)
entries are
c,s,-s,c
, respectively, and
s=\sin\theta
and
c=\cos\theta
for some
\theta
.

Let
\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}\in\real^{n}
be the zero vector except that the entry
k
is 1 (the
k
-th unit basis vector). Then, mathematically, the Givens rotation defined above can be denoted by

\bm{G}_{kl}\triangleq\bm{G}_{kl}(\theta)=\bm{I}+(c-1)(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}^{\top})+s(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}^{\top}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{l}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}^{\top}),

where the subscripts
k
and
l
indicate that the rotation occurs
in plane
k
and
l
.

Specifically, one can also define the
n
-th order Givens rotation, where
(k,k),

(k,l),

(l,k),

(l,l)
entries are
c,{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}-s,s},c
respectively (note the difference in the sign of
s
). The underlying principles remain the same.

Exercise
\thetheo

Show that
\bm{G}_{kl}(-\theta)^{-1}=\bm{G}_{kl}(\theta)
.
Hint: Use the orthogonality of
\bm{G}_{kl}(\theta)
.

It can be easily verified that an
n
-th order Givens rotation is an orthogonal matrix, and its determinant is 1. For any vector
\bm{x}=[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}]^{\top}\in\real^{n}
, the result of applying a Givens rotation
\bm{G}_{kl}
to
\bm{x}
is
\bm{y}=\bm{G}_{kl}\bm{x}
, where

\left\{\begin{aligned} &y_{k}=c\cdot x_{k}+s\cdot x_{l},\\
&y_{l}=-s\cdot x_{k}+c\cdot x_{l},\\
&y_{j}=x_{j}.&(j\neq k,l)\end{aligned}\right.

That is, a Givens rotation applied to
\bm{x}
rotates two components of
\bm{x}
by some angle
\theta
, while keeping all other components unchanged.

Now, let’s consider a Givens rotation of order
(n+1)
, where the rotation is indexed from
0
to
n
. This rotation can be expressed as

\bm{G}_{k}\triangleq\bm{I}+(c_{k}-1)(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}^{\top})+s_{k}(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}^{\top}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}^{\top}),

where
c_{k}=\cos\theta_{k},s_{k}=\sin\theta_{k}
for some
\theta_{k}
,
\bm{G}_{k}\in\real^{(n+1)\times(n+1)}
, and
\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}\in\real^{n+1}
is a zero vector except that the
(k+1)
-th entry is 1.

Taking out the
k
-th column of the following equation

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix},

where we let the
k
-th element of
\bm{v}
be
v_{k}
, and the
k
-th diagonal of
\bm{R}
be
r_{kk}
.
We realize that
\sqrt{v_{k}^{2}+r_{kk}^{2}}\neq 0
,
and let
c_{k}\triangleq\frac{r_{kk}}{\sqrt{v_{k}^{2}+r_{kk}^{2}}}
,
s_{k}\triangleq-\frac{v_{k}}{\sqrt{v_{k}^{2}+r_{kk}^{2}}}
. Then we have

\left\{\begin{aligned} &v_{k}\rightarrow c_{k}v_{k}+s_{k}r_{kk}=0;\\
&r_{kk}\rightarrow-s_{k}v_{k}+c_{k}r_{kk}=\sqrt{v_{k}^{2}+r_{kk}^{2}}=r^{\prime}_{kk}.\\
\end{aligned}\right.

That is,
\bm{G}_{k}
will introduce a zero value to the
k
-th element of
\bm{v}
and a nonzero value to
r_{kk}
.

This finding above is crucial for the rank-one update. And we obtain

\bm{G}_{n}\bm{G}_{n-1}\ldots\bm{G}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}.

For each Givens rotation, it takes
6n
flops. And there are
n
such rotations, which requires
6n^{2}
flops if keeping only the leading term. The complexity to calculate the Cholesky factor of
\bm{A}^{\prime}
is thus reduced from
\frac{1}{3}n^{3}
to
6n^{2}
flops using the rank-one update, provided that we already know the Cholesky factor of
\bm{A}
.

The above algorithm is also essential for reducing the complexity in the posterior calculation of Bayesian inference for Gaussian mixture model
(
Lu 2021a
)
. At each stage,
k
new samples are added or removed from an existing cluster, which corresponds to applying
k
rank-one updates.

Rank-One Downdate

Let us consider the scenario where we have computed the Cholesky factor of
\bm{A}
, and
\bm{A}^{\prime}
is the rank-one downdate of
\bm{A}
given by the following expression:

\displaystyle\bm{A}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\bm{A}-\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top};

\displaystyle\downarrow

\displaystyle\downarrow

\displaystyle\bm{R}^{\prime\top}\bm{R}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}-\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}.

The algorithm is similar by proceeding as follows:

\bm{G}_{1}\bm{G}_{2}\ldots\bm{G}_{n}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}.

(3.30)

Again, the set of Givens rotations
\bm{G}_{k}=\bm{I}+(c_{k}-1)(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}^{\top})+s_{k}(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}^{\top}-\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{0}^{\top})

for
k\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}

can be constructed as follows:

Taking out the
k
-th column of the following equation

\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}.

We realize that
r_{kk}\neq 0
,
and let
c_{k}\triangleq\frac{\sqrt{r_{kk}^{2}-v_{k}^{2}}}{r_{kk}}
,
s_{k}\triangleq\frac{v_{k}}{r_{kk}}
. Then, we have

\left\{\begin{aligned} &0\rightarrow s_{k}r_{kk}=v_{k};\\
&r_{kk}\rightarrow c_{k}r_{kk}=\sqrt{r_{kk}^{2}-v_{k}^{2}}=r^{\prime}_{kk}.\\
\end{aligned}\right.

This requires
r^{2}_{kk}>v_{k}^{2}
to make
\bm{A}^{\prime}
to be positive definite. Otherwise,
c_{k}
as defined above will not exist.

Again, one can verify that, multiplying the left-hand side of Equation (
) by its transpose, we have

\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{R}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\bm{G}_{n}^{\top}\ldots\bm{G}_{2}^{\top}\bm{G}_{1}^{\top}\bm{G}_{1}\bm{G}_{2}\ldots\bm{G}_{n}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}.

And multiplying the r.h.s. by its transpose, we have

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}&\bm{R}^{\prime\top}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}+\bm{R}^{\prime\top}\bm{R}^{\prime}.

This results in
\bm{R}^{\prime\top}\bm{R}^{\prime}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}-\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}
.

3.2.3
Rank-Deficient Case

If the columns of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
are linearly dependent, then
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r<p
, and the matrix appearing in the normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is positive semidefinite.
In this case, the Cholesky factor
\bm{R}
must have
n-r
zero diagonal elements.
By employing symmetric pivoting during the factorization process, these zero entries can be arranged to appear at the end of the diagonal.

{theoremHigh}
[Semidefinite Cholesky decomposition, a.k.a., semidefinite rank-revealing decomposition]
Let
\bm{A}\in\real^{n\times n}
be a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix of rank
r<n
. Then it can be factored as

\bm{P}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{P}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R},\quad\text{with}\quad\bm{R}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},

where
\bm{P}
is a permutation matrix, and
\bm{R}_{11}\in\real^{r\times r}
is upper triangular with positive diagonal elements.
Although such decompositions for
\bm{A}
is not unique, the decomposition for
\bm{P}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{P}
is unique.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The proof is constructive and follows a similar approach to the second perspective used for computing the Cholesky decomposition, as described in Section
.
The algorithm begins with
\bm{A}^{(1)}=\bm{A}
and generates a sequence of matrices defined as

\bm{A}^{(k)}=[a_{ij}^{(k)}]=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{k-1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}^{(k)}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize,\quad k=1,2,\ldots,\quad\text{with }\bm{B}^{(k)}\in\real^{(n-k+1)\times(n-k+1)}.

At the beginning of step
k
we select the largest diagonal element of
\bm{A}^{(k)}
,

s_{q}^{(k)}=\max_{k\leq i\leq n}a_{ii}^{(k)},

and interchange rows and columns
q
and
k
to bring this into pivot position; that is,
s_{p}
appears in the (
k-1,k-1
) position of
\bm{P}^{(k)\top}\bm{A}^{(k)}\bm{P}^{(k)}
, where the permutation matrix
\bm{P}^{(k)}
has the form

\bm{P}^{(k)}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{k-1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\widetilde{\bm{P}}^{(k)}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize,

and
\widetilde{\bm{P}}^{(k)}\in\real^{(n-k+1)\times(n-k+1)}
is a smaller permutation matrix.
This pivot must be positive for
k<r
, because otherwise
\bm{B}^{(k)}=\boldsymbol{0}
, which implies that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{A})<r
. Next, the elements in the permuted
\bm{A}^{(k)}
are transformed according to the Cholesky Algorithm
:

\displaystyle r_{kk}

\displaystyle=\sqrt{a_{kk}^{(k)}},\quad r_{kj}=a_{kj}^{(k)}/r_{kk},\quad j=k+1:n,

\displaystyle a_{ij}^{(k+1)}

\displaystyle=a_{ij}^{(k)}-r_{ki}r_{kj},\quad i,j=k+1:n.

This process is equivalent to subtracting a symmetric rank-one matrix
\bm{r}_{j}\bm{r}_{j}^{\top}
from
\bm{A}^{(k)}
, where
\bm{r}_{j}=\bm{e}_{j}^{\top}\bm{R}
is the
j
-th row of
\bm{R}
. The algorithm stops when
k=r+1
. Then all the remaining diagonal elements are zero, which implies that
\bm{A}^{(r+1)}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{r}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
.

Construction algorithm.

Below contains more constructive analysis.
Following the second perspective for computing the Cholesky decomposition in Section
,
we can construct

\bm{P}^{(k)\top}\bm{A}^{(k)}\bm{P}^{(k)}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{k-1}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&a_{kk}^{(k)}&\bm{b}_{k}^{\top}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{b}_{k}&\bm{B}^{(k)}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{L}^{(k)}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{k-1}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&\sqrt{a_{kk}^{(k)}}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\frac{1}{\sqrt{a_{kk}^{(k)}}}\bm{b}_{k}&\bm{I}_{n-k}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize,

satisfying
\bm{P}^{(k)\top}\bm{A}^{(k)}\bm{P}^{(k)}=\bm{L}^{(k)}\bm{A}^{(k+1)}(\bm{L}^{(k)})^{\top}
:

\displaystyle\bm{A}^{(k+1)}

\displaystyle=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{k-1}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}^{(k)}-\frac{1}{a_{kk}^{(k)}}\bm{b}_{k}\bm{b}_{k}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{k}&0&\boldsymbol{0}\\
0&a_{k+1,k+1}^{(k+1)}&\bm{b}_{k+1}^{\top}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{b}_{k+1}&\bm{B}^{(k+1)}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

However, we notice that these permutation matrices
\bm{P}^{(1)},\bm{P}^{(2)},\ldots,\bm{P}^{(r)}
are used to permute two columns; therefore, they are symmetric satisfying
\bm{P}^{(k)}\cdot\bm{P}^{(k)}=\bm{I}
for all
k
.
Let
\bm{P}\triangleq\bm{P}^{(1)}\bm{P}^{(2)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(r)}
.
Since
(\bm{A}^{(r+1)})^{2}=\bm{A}^{(r+1)}
,
\bm{A}^{(1)}=\bm{A}
can be expressed as

\displaystyle\bm{P}^{\top}\bm{A}^{(1)}\bm{P}\triangleq\bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top};

(3.31)

\displaystyle\bm{L}\triangleq\left\{\bm{P}^{(r)}\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(2)}\bm{P}^{(1)}\right\}\left\{\bm{P}^{(1)}\bm{L}^{(1)}\right\}\left\{\bm{P}^{(2)}\bm{L}^{(2)}\right\}\ldots\left\{\bm{P}^{(r)}\bm{L}^{(r)}\right\}\bm{A}^{(r+1)}.

(3.32)

To complete the proof, it suffice to show that
\bm{L}
is lower triangular with the rank-revealing property.
On the other hand, each lower triangular
\bm{L}^{(k)}
can be written as

\bm{L}^{(k)}=\bm{I}-\bm{l}_{k}\bm{e}_{k}^{\top}\quad\text{with}\quad\bm{l}_{k}=[\boldsymbol{0}_{k-1},l_{k},l_{k+1},\ldots,l_{n}]^{\top},

where
\bm{e}_{k}
is the
k
-th standard unit basis, and
\bm{l}_{k}
is a vector containing
k-1
zeros. Note that
1-l_{k}\equiv\sqrt{a_{kk}^{(k)}}
in this notation.
For
k\in\{1,2,\ldots,r-1\}
, define

\displaystyle\bm{M}_{k}

\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{P}^{(r)}\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(k+1)}\bm{L}^{(k)}\bm{P}^{(k+1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\bm{P}^{(r)}

\displaystyle=\bm{P}^{(r)}\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(k+1)}(\bm{I}-\bm{l}_{k}\bm{e}_{k}^{\top})\bm{P}^{(k+1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\bm{P}^{(r)}

\displaystyle=\bm{I}-(\bm{P}^{(r)}\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(k+1)}\bm{l}_{k})(\bm{e}_{k}^{\top}\bm{P}^{(k+1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\bm{P}^{(r)})

\displaystyle=\bm{I}-(\bm{P}^{(r)}\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(k+1)}\bm{l}_{k})\bm{e}_{k}^{\top},

where the last equality follows since
\bm{e}_{k}^{\top}\bm{P}^{(k+1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\bm{P}^{(r)}=\bm{e}_{k}^{\top}
.
This implies
\bm{M}_{k}
is lower triangular with its
k
-th column representing a permuted version of
\bm{L}^{(k)}
.
Therefore, it holds that

\displaystyle\bm{M}_{1}\bm{M}_{2}\ldots\bm{M}_{r-1}=\left\{\bm{P}^{(r)}\bm{P}^{(r-1)}\ldots\bm{P}^{(2)}\right\}\left\{\bm{L}^{(1)}\bm{P}^{(2)}\right\}\left\{\bm{L}^{(2)}\bm{P}^{(3)}\right\}\ldots\left\{\bm{L}^{(r-1)}\bm{P}^{(r)}\right\};

\displaystyle\bm{L}\equiv\bm{M}_{1}\bm{M}_{2}\ldots\bm{M}_{r-1}\bm{L}^{(r)}\bm{A}^{(r+1)}.

From the above analysis,
\bm{M}_{1}\bm{M}_{2}\ldots\bm{M}_{r-1}
is lower triangular, and
\bm{L}^{(r)}\bm{A}^{(r+1)}
has the form

\bm{L}^{(r)}\bm{A}^{(r+1)}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{M}_{11}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{M}_{21}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize,\quad\text{with lower triangular $\bm{M}_{11}$}.

Therefore,
\bm{L}=\bm{M}_{1}\bm{M}_{2}\ldots\bm{M}_{r-1}\bm{L}^{(r)}\bm{A}^{(r+1)}
has the desired form

\bm{L}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{L}_{11}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{L}_{21}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize,\quad\text{with lower triangular $\bm{L}_{11}$}.

This completes the proof.

Since all the reduced matrices
\bm{A}^{(k)}
are symmetric positive semidefinite, their maximum elements lie on the diagonal (Corollary
).
Hence, the pivot selection the proof described above is equivalent to
complete pivoting
. The algorithm produces a matrix
\bm{R}
whose diagonal elements in
\bm{R}
form a nonincreasing sequence

r_{11}\geq r_{22}\geq\ldots\geq r_{nn}.

(3.33)

In fact, the following stronger inequalities also hold:

r_{kk}^{2}\geq\sum_{i=k}^{j}r_{ii}^{2},\qquad j=k+1,\ldots,n,\ k=1,2,\ldots,r;

(3.34)

see Section
.

The proof given above is constructive and can be directly used to compute the semidefinite Cholesky decomposition; see Algorithm
.
However, this approach may appear somewhat complicated. A more concise proof is presented below using the spectral decomposition (Theorem
) and the column-pivoted QR decomposition (which will be introduced in Theorem
).

Proof
[of Theorem
: an alternative proof]
The “nonsingular” factor of the PSD matrix
\bm{A}
is given by
\bm{A}=\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z}
, where
\bm{Z}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\bm{Q}^{\top}
, and
\bm{A}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
is the spectral decomposition of
\bm{A}
.
The rank of matrix
\bm{A}
is the number of nonzero eigenvalues (here, the number of positive eigenvalues since
\bm{A}
is PSD). Therefore, only
r
components in
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}
are nonzero, and
\bm{Z}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\bm{Q}^{\top}
contains only
r
independent columns, i.e.,
\bm{Z}
is of rank
r
. By utilizing the column-pivoted QR decomposition, we have

\bm{Z}\bm{P}=\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},

where
\bm{P}
is a permutation matrix,
\bm{R}_{11}\in\real^{r\times r}
is upper triangular with positive diagonals, and
\bm{R}_{12}\in\real^{r\times(n-r)}
. Therefore,

\bm{P}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{P}=\bm{P}^{\top}\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z}\bm{P}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}_{12}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{with}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\bm{R}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}.

Thus, we find the rank-revealing decomposition for the semidefinite matrix:
\bm{P}^{\top}\bm{A}\bm{P}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
.

Algorithm 11

Semidefinite Cholesky Decomposition

1:

Positive semidefinite matrix
\bm{A}
with size
n\times n
;

2:

Set
p_{i}=i
,
i=1,2,\ldots,n
;

3:

\bm{R}\leftarrow\bm{A}

4:

for

k=1
to
n

do

5:

Find
s
such that
r_{ss}=\max_{k\leq i\leq n}r_{ii}
;

6:

Swap rows and columns
k
and
s
of
\bm{A}
and swap
p_{k}
and
p_{s}
;

7:

r_{kk}=\sqrt{r_{kk}}
;

8:

for

j=k+1
to
n

do

9:

r_{kj}=r_{kj}/r_{kk}
;

10:

end

for

11:

for

j=k+1
to
n

do

12:

for

i=k+1
to
j

do

13:

r_{ij}=r_{ij}-r_{ki}r_{kj}
;

14:

end

for

15:

end

for

16:

end

for

17:

Set
\bm{P}
to the matrix whose
j
-th column is the
p_{j}
-th column of
\bm{I}
;

18:

Output
\bm{P},\bm{R}
.

Rounding errors can cause negative elements to appear on the diagonal in the Cholesky algorithm, even if
\bm{Z}
is positive semidefinite. Similarly, the computed reduced matrix will in general be nonzero after
r
steps even when
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Z})=r
.
This situation raises questions about the appropriate time to terminate the Cholesky factorization of a semidefinite matrix. One approach is to stop the process when

\max_{k\leq i\leq n}a_{ii}^{(k)}\leq 0,

and set
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{Z})=k-1
.
However, this approach might lead to unnecessary computations in eliminating negligible elements. Considering the computational cost, we recommend using the following stopping criterion:

\max_{k\leq i\leq n}a_{ii}^{(k)}\leq c_{n}\epsilon r_{11}^{2},

where
\epsilon
denotes the unit roundoff error,
c_{n}
is a modest constant
(
Higham 1989
;
Higham 2002
)
.

\paragrapharrow

Rank-deficient normal equation.
In the context of least squares problem with the normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
, where
\bm{P}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}=\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
is the semidefinite Cholesky decomposition.
In the rank-deficient case, the permuted normal equation become

\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\qquad\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\bm{P}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}).

With
\widetilde{\bm{u}}\triangleq\bm{R}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we obtain

\bm{R}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{u}}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}_{12}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{1}\\
\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1}\\
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\triangleq\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},

where
\bm{R}_{11}\in\real^{r\times r}
is nonsingular. The triangular system
\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{1}=\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1}
determines
\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{1}\in\real^{r}
. From

\bm{R}_{11}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}=\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{1}-\bm{R}_{12}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2},

(3.35)

where
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}^{\top},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}^{\top}]^{\top}
, we can determine
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}
for an arbitrarily chosen
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
.
This reflects the fact that a consistent singular system has infinitely many solutions.
Finally, the permutations are undone to determine
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Setting
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
we get a basic solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}=[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r1}^{\top},\boldsymbol{0}]^{\top}
with only
r=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
nonzero components in
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, corresponding to the first
r
columns in
\bm{X}\bm{P}
.
This is particularly useful when seeking a good least squares fit of
\bm{y}
using as few variables as possible (variable selection; see Section
).

\paragrapharrow

Minimum-norm solution.

The minimum-norm solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
is the one that minimizes
\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}=\big\lVert\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}
.
After obtaining the basic solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}
,
\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{1}
can be determined from (
) as
\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{1}=\bm{R}_{11}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r1}
.
This again shows that any solution
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}^{\top},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}^{\top}]^{\top}
satisfies

\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{1}=\bm{R}_{11}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r1}=\bm{R}_{11}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}+\bm{R}_{12}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\qquad\implies\qquad\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r1}-\bm{R}_{11}^{-1}\bm{R}_{12}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}.

(3.36)

Thus, the minimum-norm of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
can be obtained from the full-rank least squares problem

\min_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in\real^{p-r}}\left\lVert\begin{bmatrix}\bm{F}\\
-\bm{I}_{p-r}\end{bmatrix}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}-\begin{bmatrix}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\right\rVert_{2},\qquad\bm{F}\triangleq\bm{R}_{11}^{-1}\bm{R}_{12}\in\real^{r\times(p-r)}.

(3.37)

The basic solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r1}
can be computed in about
r^{2}(p-r)
flops. Note that
\bm{F}
can overwrite
\bm{R}_{12}
. Then
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
can be computed from the normal equation,

(\bm{F}^{\top}\bm{F}+\bm{I}_{p-r})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}=\bm{F}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r1},

using a Cholesky decomposition of
(\bm{F}^{\top}\bm{F}+\bm{I}_{p-r})
. When
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
has been determined, we have
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r1}-\bm{F}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
. This method requires about
r(p-r)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(p-r)^{3}
flops
(
Deuflhard and Sautter 1980
)
.
The final solution once again involves an undo of the permutation
\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

3.3
LS via QR Decomposition

3.3.1
Full Rank Case

We begin by presenting the least squares solution for the full-rank case using QR decomposition. Other related problems—such as the minimum-norm problem—will be discussed later.
In the least squares solution (Theorem
),
computing the inverse of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
can be numerically unstable or computationally intensive. To avoid this, we can instead use the QR decomposition to compute the least squares solution more efficiently and accurately, as shown in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[LS via QR for full column rank matrix]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
n\geq p
and full column rank, and suppose
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
is its full QR decomposition, where
\bm{Q}\triangleq[\bm{Q}_{1},\bm{Q}_{2}]\in\real^{n\times n}
(
\bm{Q}_{1}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{Q}_{2}\in\real^{n\times(n-p)}
) is an orthogonal matrix,
\bm{R}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\in\real^{n\times p}
is an upper triangular matrix appended by additional
n-p
zero rows, and
\bm{R}_{1}\in\real^{p\times p}
is the square upper triangular matrix within
\bm{R}
.
Then for any response vector
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, the LS solution to
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
is given by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}\bm{c}_{1},\quad\text{with }\begin{bmatrix}\bm{c}_{1}\\
\bm{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\triangleq\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y},

where
\bm{c}_{1}
contains the first
p
components of
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}
.
The error component is

\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
is the full QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
and
n\geq p
, the last
n-p
rows of
\bm{R}
are zero as shown in Figure
. Then,
\bm{R}_{1}\in\real^{p\times p}
is the square upper triangular in
\bm{R}
and

\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{R}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}.

Write out the loss function,

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{=}}\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{R}_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{c}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{c}_{2}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where
\bm{c}_{1}
is the first
p
components of
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}
,
\bm{c}_{2}
is the last
n-p
components of
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}
, and the equality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from the invariance under orthogonal transformations.
Then the OLS solution can be calculated by performing backward substitution on the upper triangular system
\bm{R}_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{c}_{1}
, i.e.,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}\bm{c}_{1}
.

Note that when
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, the pseudo-inverses of
\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}^{\top}
can be expressed in terms of the QR factorization as

\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(\bm{X}^{\top})^{+}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}.

Since
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
, we again obtain by Theorem
that

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{y},\quad\text{with }\bm{c}_{1}\equiv\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}.

The inverse of an upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}_{1}\in\real^{p\times p}
requires
\frac{1}{3}p^{3}
flops. However, the inverse of a basic
p\times p
nonsingular matrix (in our case, the inverse of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
) requires
2p^{3}
flops
(
Lu 2021b
;
Lu 2022c
)
.
Therefore, using QR decomposition for OLS instead of directly inverting matrices significantly reduces computational complexity.

3.3.2
Gram-Schmidt QR

Although the Householder (or Givens; see, for example,
Lu 2021b
for more details) algorithm is more commonly used to compute the QR decomposition, we also present the Gram-Schmidt process. This method serves as the foundation for the elliptic MGS approach used in solving generalized least squares problems; see Section
for further details.

3.3.3
Classical Gram-Schmidt (CGS) Process

We express the reduced QR decomposition in the form
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
, where
\bm{Q}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{R}\in\real^{p\times p}
.
The semi-orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}
can be computed efficiently using the
Gram-Schmidt process
.
Extending the concept from Equation (
) to the
k
-th term, we obtain

\displaystyle\bm{x}_{k}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}(\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k})\bm{q}_{i}+\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}(\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k})\bm{q}_{i}+\left\lVert\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2}\cdot\bm{q}_{k},

indicating that we can gradually orthonormalize
\bm{X}
to obtain an orthonormal set
\bm{Q}=[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{p}]
by

\left\{\begin{aligned} r_{ik}&=\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k},\,\,\,\,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,k-1\};\\
\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}&\triangleq\bm{x}_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i};\\
r_{kk}&=\left\lVert\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2};\\
\bm{q}_{k}&=\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}/r_{kk}.\end{aligned}\right.

(3.38)

The procedure is summarized in Algorithm
.

Algorithm 12

Reduced QR Decomposition via Gram-Schmidt Process

1:

Matrix
\bm{X}
has linearly independent columns with size
n\times p
and
n\geq p
;

2:

for

k=1
to
p

do

\triangleright
compute the
k
-th column of
\bm{Q},\bm{R}

3:

for

i=1
to
k-1

do

4:

r_{ik}\leftarrow\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k}
;

5:

end

for

6:

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i}
;

7:

r_{kk}\leftarrow\left\lVert\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2}
;

8:

\bm{q}_{k}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}/r_{kk}
;

9:

end

for

10:

Output
\bm{Q}=[\bm{q}_{1},\ldots,\bm{q}_{p}]
and
\bm{R}
with entry
(i,k)
being
r_{ik}
.

{theoremHigh}

[Algorithm complexity: reduced QR via Gram-Schmidt
(
Lu 2021b
)
]
Algorithm
requires
\sim 2np^{2}
flops to compute the reduced QR decomposition of an
n\times p
matrix with linearly independent columns and
n\geq p
.

Orthogonal Projection: Preliminary for MGS

Upon revisiting Equation (
), i.e., step 2 to step 6 in Algorithm
, we observe that the first two equalities imply that

\left.\begin{aligned} r_{ik}&=\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k},\,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,k-1\}\\
\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}&\triangleq\bm{x}_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i}\\
\end{aligned}\right\}\rightarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}=\bm{x}_{k}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k}=(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{k},

(3.39)

where
\bm{Q}_{k-1}\triangleq[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}]
. This implies that
\bm{q}_{k}
can be obtained by

\bm{q}_{k}=\frac{\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}}{\left\lVert\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2}}=\frac{(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{k}}{\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{k}\right\rVert_{2}}.

The matrix
(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})
in the above equation is known as an
orthogonal projection matrix
that projects
\bm{x}_{k}

along
the column space of
\bm{Q}_{k-1}
,
i.e., it projects a vector so that the projected vector is perpendicular to the column space of
\bm{Q}_{k-1}
; see Section
.
Consequently,
\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}
or
\bm{q}_{k}
calculated in this way will be orthogonal to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{Q}_{k-1})
, residing in the null space of
\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top}
, i.e., the space of
\mathcal{N}(\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})
by the fundamental theorem of linear algebra (Theorem
).

Let
\bm{P}_{1}\triangleq(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})
. It can be shown that
\bm{P}_{1}=(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})
is an orthogonal projection matrix such that
\bm{P}_{1}\bm{v}
will project the vector
\bm{v}
onto the null space of
\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top}
.
Additionally, let
\bm{P}_{2}\triangleq\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top}
; then,
\bm{P}_{2}
is also an orthogonal projection matrix such that
\bm{P}_{2}\bm{v}
will project the vector
\bm{v}
onto the column space of
\bm{Q}_{k-1}
(Proposition
;
\bm{P}_{2}
is called a
complementary projector
of
\bm{P}_{1}
, vice versa).
Therefore, we conclude the presence of two orthogonal projections:

\left\{\begin{aligned} \bm{P}_{1}&=\bm{I}-\bm{P}_{2}:&\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,&\text{project onto $\mathcal{N}(\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})$, {along} the column space of $\bm{Q}_{k-1}$;}\\
\bm{P}_{2}&=\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top}:&\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,&\text{project onto $\mathcal{C}(\bm{Q}_{k-1})$, {onto} the column space of $\bm{Q}_{k-1}$}.\end{aligned}\right.

An additional result to note arises when the columns of
\bm{Q}_{k-1}
are mutually orthonormal. In this case, we can observe the following decomposition:

\bm{P}_{1}=\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top}=(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{1}\bm{q}_{1}^{\top})(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top})\ldots(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{k-1}\bm{q}_{k-1}^{\top}),

(3.40)

where
\bm{Q}_{k-1}=[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}]
and each
(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{i}\bm{q}_{i}^{\top})
serves to project a vector onto the perpendicular space of
\bm{q}_{i}
.

Modified Gram-Schmidt (MGS) Process

To emphasize the modified Gram-Schmidt process and to make a connection to the equivalent projection in Equation (
), we begin by illustrating a lemma that presents an alternative approach for obtaining the entries in the upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}
of the QR decomposition.

Lemma 136
(Modified Gram-Schmidt).

Given a vector set
[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{k-1},\bm{x}_{k}
], where the first
k-1
column are spanned by
k-1
orthonormal vectors
[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}]
:

\mathcal{C}([\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{i}])=\mathcal{C}([\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{i}]),\,\,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,k-1\}.

Therefore,
r_{ik}=\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k}
represents the magnitude of the projection of
\bm{x}_{k}
on the vector
\bm{q}_{i}
(since
\bm{q}_{i}
is of unit length). Then it follows that

\displaystyle\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k}

\displaystyle=\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}(\bm{x}_{k}\underbrace{-r_{1k}\bm{q}_{1}-r_{2k}\bm{q}_{2}-\ldots-r_{i-1,k}\bm{q}_{i-1}}_{\text{orthogonal to $\bm{q}_{i}$}})

\displaystyle=\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\big(\bm{x}_{k}-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}r_{jk}\bm{q}_{j}\big),\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,k-1\}.

This can be easily verified since
\bm{q}_{i}
is orthonormal to
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{i-1}\}
. This observation implies another update for the
k
-th column of
\bm{R}
.

The lemma above reveals a second algorithm to compute the reduced QR decomposition of a matrix, as shown in Algorithm
of which the algorithm on the left is identical to Algorithm
(with slight modifications) to highlight the differences.

)

\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full column rank;

2:

for

k=1
to
p

do

;

4:

for

i=1

\boxed{r_{ik}\leftarrow\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k}}
;

;   (
\dagger
)

7:

end

for

r_{kk}\leftarrow\left\lVert\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2}
;

9:

\bm{q}_{k}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}/r_{kk}
;

10:

end

for

Algorithm 14

MGS

1:

\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full column rank;

2:

for

k=1
to
p

do

3:

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}
;

4:

for

i=1
to
k-1

do

5:

\boxed{r_{ik}\leftarrow\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}}}
;

6:

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}-r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i}
;   (
\ast
)

7:

for

r_{kk}\leftarrow\left\lVert\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2}
;

9:

\bm{q}_{k}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}/r_{kk}
;

10:

end

for

The process described above is referred to as the
modified Gram-Schmidt (MGS) process
, whereas the previous one is also known as the
classical Gram-Schmidt (CGS) process
. In theory, both CGS and MGS are equivalent in the
sense that they compute exactly the same QR decompositions when exact arithmetic is employed. However, in practice, with the presence of round-off errors, the orthonormal columns of
\bm{Q}
computed by MGS tend to be “more orthonormal” than those computed by CGS.

To see the equivalence of the above two algorithms,
we note that the equality (
\dagger
) in Algorithm
is equivalent to

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}=\bm{x}_{k}-(\bm{q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k})\bm{q}_{1}-(\bm{q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k})\bm{q}_{2}-\ldots-(\bm{q}_{k-1}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k})\bm{q}_{k-1}=(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{k}.

(3.41)

And
the equality (
\ast
) in Algorithm
can be reformulated as (via the step 4 and step 5 of the algorithm)

\displaystyle\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}

\displaystyle:=\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}-r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i}=\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}-(\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp})\bm{q}_{i}=\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}-\bm{q}_{i}\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}=(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{i}\bm{q}_{i}^{\top})\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}.

That is,
\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}
will be updated by

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}=\left\{(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{k-1}\bm{q}_{k-1}^{\top})\ldots\left[(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top})\left((\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{1}\bm{q}_{1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{k}\right)\right]\right\},

(3.42)

where the nested parentheses in MGS denote the computation order.
The comparison of (
) and (
) matches the orthogonal projection matrix equality in Equation (
) that

\displaystyle\bm{P}_{1}

\displaystyle=\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top}=(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{1}\bm{q}_{1}^{\top})(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top})\ldots(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{k-1}\bm{q}_{k-1}^{\top})=\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{i}\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}),

where
\bm{Q}_{k-1}=[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}]
.

(a)

CGS, step 1:
blue
vector; step 2:
green
vector; step 3:
purple
vector.

(b)

MGS, step 1:
blue
vector; step 2:
purple
vector.

Figure 3.3:
CGS vs MGS in three-dimensional space, where
\bm{q}_{2}^{\prime}
is parallel to
\bm{q}_{2}
so that projecting onto
\bm{q}_{2}
is equivalent to projecting onto
\bm{q}_{2}^{\prime}
.

\paragrapharrow

What’s the difference?
Taking a three-column matrix
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\bm{x}_{3}]
as an example. Suppose we have already computed
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
such that
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2}\}
, and we want to proceed to compute
\bm{q}_{3}
.

In the CGS algorithm, the orthogonalization of column
\bm{x}_{3}
against columns
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
is achieved by projecting the original column
\bm{x}_{3}
of
\bm{X}
onto
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
, respectively, followed by subtracting these projections at once:

\left\{\begin{aligned} \bm{x}_{3}^{\perp}&=\bm{x}_{3}-(\bm{q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{x}_{3})\bm{q}_{1}-(\bm{q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{x}_{3})\bm{q}_{2}\\
&=\bm{x}_{3}-(\bm{q}_{1}\bm{q}_{1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{3}-\boxed{(\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top}){\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\bm{x}_{3}}};\\
\bm{q}_{3}&={\bm{x}_{3}^{\perp}}/{\left\lVert\bm{x}_{3}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2}},\end{aligned}\right.

(3.43)

as shown in Figure
.

In the MGS algorithm, on the other hand, the components along each
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
are immediately subtracted out of the rest of the column
\bm{x}_{3}
as soon as the vectors
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
are computed.
Therefore, the orthogonalization of column
\bm{x}_{3}
against
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
is not performed by projecting the original column
\bm{x}_{3}
against
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
as it is in CGS, but rather against a vector obtained by subtracting from that column
\bm{x}_{3}
of
\bm{X}
the components in the direction of
\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}
successively. This is important because the error components of
\bm{q}_{3}
in
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
will be smaller (we will discuss this further in the following paragraphs).

More precisely, in the MGS algorithm, the orthogonalization of column
\bm{x}_{3}
against
\bm{q}_{1}
is performed by subtracting the component of
\bm{q}_{1}
from the vector
\bm{x}_{3}
:

\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}=(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{1}\bm{q}_{1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{3}=\bm{x}_{3}-(\bm{q}_{1}\bm{q}_{1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{3},

where
\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}
represents the component of
\bm{x}_{3}
that lies in a space perpendicular to
\bm{q}_{1}
. And the further step is performed by

\displaystyle\bm{x}_{3}^{(2)}=(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top})\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}

\displaystyle=\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}-(\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top})\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}

(3.44)

\displaystyle=\bm{x}_{3}-(\bm{q}_{1}\bm{q}_{1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{3}-\boxed{(\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top}){\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}}},

where
\bm{x}_{3}^{(2)}
represents the component of
\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}
that lies in a space perpendicular to
\bm{q}_{2}
. And we highlight the difference from the CGS algorithm in Equation (
) using
[formula]
text.
As a result,
\bm{x}_{3}^{(2)}
corresponds to the component of
\bm{x}_{3}
that lies in the space perpendicular to
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
, as shown in Figure
.

Main Difference and Catastrophic Cancellation

The key difference between the CGS and MGS processes lies in the fact that
\bm{x}_{3}
can generally have large components in
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2}\}
.
In such cases, one starts with large
values and ends up with small values that yields significant relative errors in them.
This phenomenon is commonly referred to as
catastrophic cancellation
.
Whereas,
\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}
lies in the direction perpendicular to
\bm{q}_{1}
and carries only a small “error” component in the direction of
\bm{q}_{1}
. Comparing the
boxed
terms in Equations (
) and (
), it is not hard to see that
(\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top})\bm{x}_{3}^{(1)}
in Equation (
) is more accurate based on the above argument. And thus, because of the much smaller error in this projection factor, the MGS introduces smaller orthogonalization error at each subtraction step compared to the CGS method. In fact, it can be shown that the final
\bm{Q}
obtained in the CGS satisfies

\left\lVert\bm{I}-\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\mathcal{O}(\epsilon\kappa^{2}(\bm{X})),

where
\kappa(\bm{X})
is a value larger than 1 determined by
\bm{X}
.
Whereas, in MGS, the error satisfies

\left\lVert\bm{I}-\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\mathcal{O}(\epsilon\kappa(\bm{X})).

That is, the
\bm{Q}
obtained via MGS is “more orthogonal.”
Therefore, we summarize the difference between the CGS and MGS processes for obtaining
\bm{q}_{k}
from the
k
-th column
\bm{x}_{k}
of
\bm{X}
, given the orthonormalized vectors
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}\}
:

\displaystyle\text{(CGS)}:

\displaystyle\text{obtain $\bm{q}_{k}$ by normalizing $\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}=(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{k-1}\bm{Q}_{k-1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{k}$;}

\displaystyle\text{(MGS)}:

\displaystyle\text{obtain $\bm{q}_{k}$ by normalizing $\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}=\big\{(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{k-1}\bm{q}_{k-1}^{\top})\ldots\big[(\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{2}\bm{q}_{2}^{\top})\big((\bm{I}-\bm{q}_{1}\bm{q}_{1}^{\top})\bm{x}_{k}\big)\big]\big\}$.}

\paragrapharrow

Comparison with the Householder algorithm.
Although both methods have their advantages, in practice, MGS usually outperforms CGS; see examples in
Lu 2021b
.
However, MGS can still fall victim to the
catastrophic cancellation
problem. Suppose, in iteration
k
of the MGS Algorithm
,
\bm{x}_{k}
is almost in the span of
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}\}
. This will result in that
\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}
has only a small component that is perpendicular to
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}\}
, whereas the “error” component in the
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}\}
will be amplified, resulting in
\bm{Q}
being less orthonormal.
As mentioned earlier, both the CGS and MGS methods suffer from the same main disadvantage: they obtain the orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}
through the upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}
. Specifically, for
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
\bm{Q}
can be obtained by using the following equation:

\bm{Q}=\bm{X}\underbrace{\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}\bm{R}_{2}^{-1}\ldots\bm{R}_{p}^{-1}}_{\bm{R}^{-1}}.

In this case, the Householder algorithm—that will be introduced in the sequel—finds a successive set of orthogonal matrices
\{\bm{Q}_{1},\bm{Q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{Q}_{l}\}
such that
\bm{Q}_{l}\ldots\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{X}
is triangularized, then
\bm{Q}=(\bm{Q}_{l}\ldots\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{Q}_{1})^{\top}
will be “more” orthogonal than that in the CGS or MGS method since the condition numbers for the orthogonal matrices are all 1.

Row-Wise MGS, Recursive Algorithm and Other Issues

The algorithms presented in Algorithm
and
are used to calculate the entries of the upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}
in an element-wise and column-by-column manner.
Suppose
\bm{X}
has column partition
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{X}_{2}]
, where
\bm{X}_{2}=[\bm{x}_{2},\bm{x}_{3},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]\in\real^{n\times(p-1)}
. Notice in the CGS Algorithm
, the first row of
\bm{R}
can be obtained by

\left.\begin{aligned} r_{11}&=\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}\\
r_{1k}&=\bm{q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k},\,\,\,\forall\,k\in\{2,3,\ldots,p\}\end{aligned}\right\}\qquad\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\left\{\begin{aligned} r_{11}&=\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}\\
\bm{r}_{12}^{\top}&=\bm{q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}_{2},\,\,\,\bm{r}_{12}=[r_{12},r_{13},\ldots,r_{1p}].\end{aligned}\right.

Therefore, the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
is given by

\bm{X}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{x}_{1}&\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{q}_{1}&\bm{Q}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}r_{11}&\bm{r}_{12}^{\top}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{R}_{22}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r_{11}\bm{q}_{1}&\bm{q}_{1}\bm{r}_{12}^{\top}+\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{R}_{22}\end{bmatrix},

where the matrix
\bm{Q}_{2}\in\real^{n\times(p-1)}
consists of mutually orthonormal columns and
\bm{R}_{22}\in\real^{(p-1)\times(p-1)}
is upper triangular.
Consequently,
\bm{Q}_{2}\bm{R}_{22}
represents the reduced QR decomposition of
\bm{X}_{2}-\bm{q}_{1}\bm{r}_{12}^{\top}
, which reveals a recursive algorithm for computing the reduced QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
.
This approach is equivalent to the MGS method that subtracts each component in the span of
\{\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}\}
when computing column
k
of
\bm{Q}
(i.e., equality (
*
) in Algorithm
). The process is described in Algorithm
.

\paragrapharrow

Full QR decomposition.
A full QR decomposition of an
n\times p
matrix with linearly independent columns extends the process by appending additional
n-p
orthonormal columns to
\bm{Q}
, thereby transforming it into an
n\times n
orthogonal matrix. Simultaneously,
\bm{R}
is augmented with rows of zeros to attain an
n\times p
upper triangular matrix.
We refer to the additional columns in
\bm{Q}
as
silent columns
and the additional rows in
\bm{R}
as
silent rows
. The comparison between the reduced and the full QR decompositions is shown in Figure
.

\paragrapharrow

Dependent columns.
In our earlier discussions, we assumed that the matrix
\bm{X}
has linearly independent columns. While this condition simplifies our analysis, it is not strictly required for all scenarios.
Consider step
k
Algorithm
, where
\bm{x}_{k}
lies in the plane spanned by
\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}
(which is equivalent to the space spanned by
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{k-1}
), indicating that the vectors
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{k}
are dependent.
Then
r_{kk}
will be zero and
\bm{q}_{k}
cannot be determined due to division by zero.
In such cases, we can arbitrarily choose
\bm{q}_{k}
to be any normalized vector that is orthogonal to
\mathcal{C}([\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}])
and proceed with the Gram-Schmidt process.
We reformulate the step
k
in the algorithm as follows:

\bm{q}_{k}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\big(\bm{x}_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i}\big)/r_{kk},\qquad r_{ik}=\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k},r_{kk}=\big\lVert\bm{x}_{k}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i}\big\rVert_{2},&\mathrm{if\,}r_{kk}\neq 0,\\
&\text{pick one in\,}\mathcal{C}^{\bot}([\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}]),\text{ and normalize},\qquad&\mathrm{if\,}r_{kk}=0.\end{aligned}\right.

This idea can be further extended such that, when
\bm{q}_{k}
does not exist, we simply skip the current step and add the silent columns at the end of the process. Consequently, the QR decomposition of a matrix with dependent columns is not unique.

Moreover, this insight also aids in determining the linear independence of a set of vectors.
Whenever
r_{kk}
in Algorithm
becomes zero, we report the vectors
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{k}
are dependent and terminate the algorithm for “
independence checking
.”

3.3.4
LS by Householder QR

Householder matrices
, also known as
Householder reflectors
, which can reflect vectors, play a crucial role in numerical linear algebra for tasks such as solving linear systems, addressing least squares problems, and deriving Hessenberg forms
(
Golub and Van Loan 2013
;
Lu 2021b
)
. In this section, we present how Householder reflectors can be used to prove the existence of and compute the QR decomposition.

Computing QR via Householder

\paragrapharrow

Householder reflectors.
Let’s begin with the formal definition of a Householder reflector, exploring its properties thereafter.

Definition 137
(Householder reflector).

Let
\bm{u}\in\real^{n}
be a unit vector (
\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert_{2}=1
).
The matrix
\bm{H}=\bm{I}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}
is referred to as a Householder reflector, a.k.a., a Householder transformation. We call this
\bm{H}
the Householder reflector associated with the unit vector
\bm{u}
, where the unit vector
\bm{u}
is also known as the Householder vector.
When a vector
\bm{x}
is multiplied by
\bm{H}
, it undergoes reflection with respect to the hyperplane
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{u}\}^{\perp}
.

Note that if
\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert_{2}\neq 1
, we can define the Householder reflector
\bm{H}
as
\bm{H}=\bm{I}-2\frac{\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}}{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{u}}
.

From the definition of the Householder reflector, we can derive the following corollary, which states that certain vectors remain unchanged under the action of the Householder reflector.

Corollary 138
(Unreflected by Householder).

Let
\bm{u}\in\real^{n}
be given with
\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, and define the Householder reflector as
\bm{H}=\bm{I}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}
.
The Householder reflector leaves any vector
\bm{v}
perpendicular to
\bm{u}
unchanged; that is,
\bm{H}\bm{v}=\bm{v}
if
\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{v}=0
.

The proof is straightforward since
(\bm{I}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top})\bm{v}=\bm{v}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{v}=\bm{v}
.

Suppose
\bm{u}
is a unit vector with
\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, and let
\bm{v}
be a vector perpendicular to
\bm{u}
. Then any vector
\bm{x}
in the plane can be decomposed into two components:

\bm{x}=\bm{x}_{\bm{u}}+\bm{x}_{\bm{v}},

where the first component
\bm{x}_{\bm{u}}
is parallel to
\bm{u}
and the second one
\bm{x}_{\bm{v}}
is perpendicular to
\bm{u}
(i.e., parallel to
\bm{v}
).
Referring to Section
on vector projections,
\bm{x}_{\bm{u}}
can be computed as
\bm{x}_{\bm{u}}=\frac{\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}}{\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{u}}\bm{x}=\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{x}
, representing the projection of
\bm{x}
onto
\bm{u}
.
Applying the Householder reflector associated with
\bm{u}
to the vector
\bm{x}
, we obtain:

\bm{H}\bm{x}=(\bm{I}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top})(\bm{x}_{\bm{v}}+\bm{x}_{\bm{u}})=\bm{x}_{\bm{v}}-\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{x}=\bm{x}_{\bm{v}}-\bm{x}_{\bm{u}},

which means the Householder reflector transforms
\bm{x}_{\bm{v}}+\bm{x}_{\bm{u}}
into
\bm{x}_{\bm{v}}-\bm{x}_{\bm{u}}
.
In other words, the space perpendicular to
\bm{u}
acts as a mirror, and any vector
\bm{x}
is reflected by the Householder reflector associated with
\bm{u}
(i.e., reflected by the hyperplane
\mathrm{span}\{\bm{u}\}^{\perp}
).
The situation is illustrated in Figure
.

Figure 3.4:
Demonstration of the Householder reflector. The Householder reflector obtained by
\bm{H}=\bm{I}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}
, where
\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, will reflect a vector
\bm{x}
along the plane perpendicular to
\bm{u}
. Specifically, it transforms
\bm{x}=\bm{x}_{\bm{v}}+\bm{x}_{\bm{u}}
into
\bm{x}_{\bm{v}}-\bm{x}_{\bm{u}}
.

The previous discussion explains how to determine the reflected vector using the Householder reflector.
However, an additional question arises: If we know in advance that two vectors are reflections of each other, how can we find the corresponding Householder reflector?
The property is crucial for computing the QR decomposition, where we aim to reflect/transform a column into a specific form.

Corollary 139
(Reflection theorem: finding the Householder reflector).

Suppose
\bm{x}
is reflected to
\bm{y}
by a Householder reflector, with
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}
. The (unique) Householder reflector can be obtained by

\bm{H}=\bm{I}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top},\text{ where }\bm{u}=\frac{\bm{x}-\bm{y}}{\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}}.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
Write out the equation, we have

\displaystyle\bm{H}\bm{x}

\displaystyle=\bm{x}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{x}=\bm{x}-2\frac{(\bm{x}-\bm{y})(\bm{x}^{\top}-\bm{y}^{\top})}{(\bm{x}-\bm{y})^{\top}(\bm{x}-\bm{y})}\bm{x}=\bm{x}-(\bm{x}-\bm{y})=\bm{y}.

Note that the condition
\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}
is required to prove the result.

Householder reflectors are useful for setting a block of components of a given vector to zero. Particularly, it is often desirable to set the vector
\bm{a}\in\real^{n}
to zero, except for the
i
-th element.
In such cases, the Householder vector can be chosen as:

\bm{u}=\frac{\bm{a}-r\bm{e}_{i}}{\left\lVert\bm{a}-r\bm{e}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}},\qquad\text{where }r=\pm\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2},

which is a reasonable Householder vector since
\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert r\bm{e}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lvert r\right\rvert
. We carefully notice that when
r=\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}
,
\bm{a}
is reflected to
\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}\bm{e}_{i}
via the Householder reflector
\bm{H}=\bm{I}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}
; conversely, when
r=-\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}
,
\bm{a}
is reflected to
-\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}\bm{e}_{i}
.

Recalling from Section
, we claimed the Householder method (or the Givens method) utilizes a set of orthogonal matrices to triangularize the matrix, thereby obtaining the QR decomposition and achieving a higher level of orthogonality in this context. The Householder reflector serves as one such orthogonal matrix for this purpose.
In the following remark, we present additional properties of the Householder reflector.

Remark 140
(Householder properties).

A Householder reflector
\bm{H}
possesses the following properties:

\bm{H}\bm{H}=\bm{I}
, i.e., reflecting a vector twice is equivalent to not reflecting it at all.

Symmetry:
\bm{H}=\bm{H}^{\top}
.

Orthogonality:
\bm{H}^{\top}\bm{H}=\bm{H}\bm{H}^{\top}=\bm{I}
such that the Householder reflector is an orthogonal matrix.

\bm{H}\bm{u}=-\bm{u}
, if
\bm{H}=\bm{I}-2\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}
.

Unit eigenvalues: the eigenvalue of
\bm{H}
is either
1
or
-1
. Given an eigenpair
(\lambda,\bm{x})
of
\bm{H}
, it follows that
\left\lVert\bm{H}\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\lambda\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2}
. Therefore,
\lambda=\pm 1
.

The determinant of a Householder reflector is
-1
.

\paragrapharrow

*Householder QR decomposition.
To reiterate, as discussed in the Gram-Schmidt section, QR decomposition involves using a triangular matrix to orthogonalize a matrix
\bm{X}
.
Building upon this concept, if we have a sequence of orthogonal matrices that can successively transform
\bm{X}
into an upper triangular form, we can also construct the QR decomposition.
In particular, suppose we have an orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}_{1}
that introduces zeros into all entries of the first column of
\bm{X}
except for the element at position (1,1);
and similarly, an orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}_{2}
that introduces zeros into the second column except for the elements at positions (2,1) and (2,2);

\ldots
. Then we can also find the QR decomposition.
To achieve this zero introduction, we could reflect the columns of the matrix to a basis vector
\bm{e}_{1}
whose entries are all zero except the first entry.

Let
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]\in\real^{n\times p}
be the column partition of
\bm{X}
, and define further

r_{1}\triangleq\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2},\qquad\bm{u}_{1}\triangleq{\bm{x}_{1}-r_{1}\bm{e}_{1}},\qquad\bm{H}_{1}\triangleq\bm{I}-\tau_{1}\bm{u}_{1}\bm{u}_{1}^{\top},\qquad\tau_{1}\triangleq\frac{1}{\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}-r_{1}\bm{e}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}},

(3.45)

where
\bm{e}_{1}
here is the first unit basis in
n
, i.e.,
\bm{e}_{1}=[1;0;0;\ldots;0]\in\real^{n}
.
Then,

\bm{H}_{1}\bm{X}=[\bm{H}_{1}\bm{x}_{1},\bm{H}_{1}\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{H}_{1}\bm{x}_{p}]\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}r_{1}&\bm{R}_{1,2:p}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{B}_{2}\end{bmatrix},

(3.46)

which reflects
\bm{x}_{1}
to
r_{1}\bm{e}_{1}
and introduces zeros below the diagonal in the first column. We observe that the entries below
r_{1}
become zero after this specific reflection. Notice that we reflect
\bm{x}_{1}
to
\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}\bm{e}_{1}
, where both vectors have the same length, rather than reflect
\bm{x}_{1}
to
\bm{e}_{1}
directly to match the requirement stated in Corollary
.

It should be noted that the choice of
r_{1}
is
not unique
. To ensure
numerical stability
, it is desirable to set
r_{1}=-\text{sign}(a_{11})\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}
, where
a_{11}
represents the first component of
\bm{x}_{1}
.
Alternatively, one can also choose
r_{1}=\text{sign}(a_{11})\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}
, as long as
\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}
is equal to
\left\lVert r_{1}\bm{e}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}
.
However, if we require the diagonal entries of the upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}
to be positive—so that the QR decomposition is unique—it becomes necessary to select a positive value for
r_{1}
.

Next, we can apply this process to
\bm{B}_{2}
in (
) to transform the entries below the entry (2,2) into zeros.
Note that we do not apply this process to the entire matrix
\bm{H}_{1}\bm{X}
but only to the submatrix
\bm{B}_{2}
in it because we have already introduced zeros in the first column, and reflecting again will reintroduce nonzero values back and destroy what have accomplished.

Suppose
\bm{B}_{2}=[\bm{b}_{2},\bm{b}_{3},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}]
is the column partition of
\bm{B}_{2}
, and define

r_{2}\triangleq\left\lVert\bm{b}_{2}\right\rVert_{2},\quad\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{2}\triangleq{\bm{b}_{2}-r_{2}\bm{e}_{1}},\quad\widetilde{\bm{H}}_{2}\triangleq\bm{I}-\tau_{2}\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{2}\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{2}^{\top},\quad\tau_{2}=\frac{1}{\footnotesize\left\lVert\bm{b}_{2}-r_{2}\bm{e}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}},\quad\bm{H}_{2}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\widetilde{\bm{H}}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

(3.47)

In this context,
\bm{e}_{1}
denotes the first unit basis in
n-1
, and
\bm{H}_{2}
is also an orthogonal matrix since
\widetilde{\bm{H}}_{2}
is orthogonal.
Note that
\bm{H}_{2}
is also an Householder reflector since it can can be equivalently denoted as
\bm{H}_{2}=\bm{I}-2\bm{u}_{2}\bm{u}_{2}^{\top}
with
\bm{u}_{2}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\widetilde{\bm{u}}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
.
Applying
\widetilde{\bm{H}_{2}}
or
\bm{H}_{2}
yields

\widetilde{\bm{H}_{2}}\bm{B}_{2}=[\bm{H}_{2}\bm{b}_{2},\bm{H}_{2}\bm{b}_{3},\ldots,\bm{H}_{2}\bm{b}_{p}]\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}r_{2}&\bm{R}_{2,3:p}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{C}_{3}\end{bmatrix},

and

\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}\bm{X}=[\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}\bm{x}_{1},\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}\bm{x}_{p}]\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}r_{1}&r_{12}&\bm{R}_{1,3:p}\\
0&r_{2}&\bm{R}_{2,3:p}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{C}_{3}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

The same process can go on. And if
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, after
p
stages, we will finally triangularize
\bm{X}=(\bm{H}_{p}\bm{H}_{p-1}\ldots\bm{H}_{1})^{-1}\bm{R}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
. Since the
\bm{H}_{i}
’s are symmetric and orthogonal (Remark
), we have orthogonal
\bm{Q}=(\bm{H}_{p}\bm{H}_{p-1}\ldots\bm{H}_{1})^{-1}=\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}\ldots\bm{H}_{p}
.

An example of a
5\times 4
matrix is shown as follows, where
\boxtimes
represents a value that is not necessarily zero, and
boldface
indicates the value has just been changed:

\displaystyle\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{X}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{H}_{1}}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{H}_{1}\bm{X}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{H}_{2}}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}\bm{X}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{H}_{3}}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{H}_{3}\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}\bm{X}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{H}_{4}}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&\bm{0}\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{H}_{4}\bm{H}_{3}\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}\bm{X}}.

The Householder algorithm is a procedure that transforms a matrix into triangular form through a sequence of orthogonal matrix operations. In the Gram-Schmidt process (both CGS and MGS), we use a triangular matrix to orthogonalize the matrix.
In contrast, the Householder algorithm employs orthogonal matrices for matrix triangularization.
The difference between these two approaches can be summarized as follows:

Gram-Schmidt algorithm: triangular orthogonalization;

Householder algorithm: orthogonal triangularization.

We further notice that, in the Householder algorithm, a set of orthogonal matrices are applied so that the QR decomposition obtained is a
full
QR decomposition. Whereas, the direct QR decomposition obtained by CGS or MGS is a
reduced
decomposition (although the silent columns or rows can be further added to find the full version).

{theoremHigh}

[Algorithm complexity: QR via Householder
(
Lu 2021b
)
]
Householder QR algorithm requires
\sim 2np^{2}-\frac{2}{3}p^{3}
flops to compute a full QR decomposition of an
n\times p
matrix with linearly independent columns and
n\geq p
. Further, if
\bm{Q}
is needed explicitly
,
an additional
\sim 4n^{2}p-2np^{2}
flops are required.
