Least Squares Problems using Householder QR

\paragrapharrow

LS via Householder QR.
When using the Householder QR algorithm to solve the least squares problem, the factor
\bm{Q}
is not explicitly formed but implicitly defined as
\bm{Q}=\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}\ldots\bm{H}_{p}
.
By Theorem
,
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}
and the residual vector
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
can be obtained as:

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{c}_{1}\\
\bm{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{H}_{p}\ldots\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}\bm{y},\qquad\bm{e}=\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}\ldots\bm{H}_{p}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.

The Householder QR factorization can be applied to the extended matrix
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
,

[\bm{X},\bm{y}]=\widetilde{\bm{Q}}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}&\bm{c}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\rho\bm{e}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\quad\widetilde{\bm{Q}}=\bm{H}_{1}\ldots\bm{H}_{p}\bm{H}_{p+1}.

Then
\bm{R}_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{c}_{1}
and the residual and its norm are given by

\bm{e}=\bm{H}_{1}\ldots\bm{H}_{p}\bm{H}_{p+1}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\rho\bm{e}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert_{2}=\rho\geq 0.

The (Q-less) Householder QR factorization requires
\sim 2np^{2}-\frac{2}{3}p^{3}
flops, and computing
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}
and solving
\bm{R}_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{c}_{1}
require a further
\sim 4np-p^{2}
flops. If one wants not only
\left\lVert\bm{e}\right\rVert_{2}
but also
\bm{e}
, another
4np-2p^{2}
flops are needed. This can be compared to the method of normal equation using the Cholesky decomposition, which requires
\sim np^{2}+\frac{1}{3}p^{3}
flops for the factorization and
\sim 2(np+p^{2})
flops for each right-hand side. For
n=p
this is about the same as for the Householder QR method, but for
n\gg p
, the Householder method is roughly twice as expensive.

\paragrapharrow

Minimum-Norm LS via Householder QR.
Similarly, we consider the underdetermined and consistent linear system
\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{z}
, where
\bm{X}^{\top}\in\real^{p\times n}
has full row rank
p
. Then the minimum-norm solution
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\real^{n}
can also be computed using the Householder QR factorization of
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
.
Recall that the minimum-norm solution must satisfy the normal equation of the second kind in (
).
From the factorization, we have
\bm{X}^{\top}=[\bm{R}_{1}^{\top},\boldsymbol{0}]\bm{Q}^{\top}
, and thus the system becomes

\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=[\bm{R}_{1}^{\top},\boldsymbol{0}]\bm{d}=\bm{z},\quad\text{with }\bm{d}\triangleq\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\bm{d}_{1}\\
\bm{d}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.

Since the
\ell_{2}
norm is orthogonally invariant, i.e.,
\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert_{2}
, the problem reduces to
\min\left\lVert\bm{d}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}
subject to the constraint
\bm{R}_{1}^{\top}\bm{d}_{1}=\bm{z}
.
Because
\bm{d}_{1}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}\bm{z}
is uniquely determined by this constraint, the minimum-norm solution is obtained by setting
\bm{d}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
, and

\bm{R}_{1}^{\top}\bm{d}_{1}=\bm{z},\qquad\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{d}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}.

\paragrapharrow

Augmented LS problem via Householder QR.
As mentioned in (
), both the least squares and minimum-norm problems are special cases of the following augmented LS problem:

(\text{AuLS}):\qquad\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}&\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\\
\boldsymbol{\beta}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{y}\\
\bm{z}\end{bmatrix},\quad\bm{y}\in\real^{n},\quad\bm{z}\in\real^{p},

(3.48)

where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
. From the QR factorization of
\bm{X}
we obtain

\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}\qquad\text{and}\qquad[\bm{R}_{1}^{\top},\boldsymbol{0}]\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{z}.

Multiplying the first equation by
\bm{Q}^{\top}
and the second by
\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}
, we obtain:

\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}\qquad\text{and}\qquad[\bm{I}_{p},\boldsymbol{0}]\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}\bm{z}.

From the second equation, we can determine the first
p
components of
\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}
.
These can then be substituted into the first equation to solve for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
The last
n-p
components of
\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}
are obtained from the last
n-p
equations in the first equation. The resulting QR algorithm for solving the augmented system (
) using QR factorization is summarized below.

{theoremHigh}

[Augmented LS solution by QR]
Compute the QR factorization of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
, and

\displaystyle\bm{d}_{1}

\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{R}_{1}^{-\top}\bm{z},\qquad\bm{c}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\bm{c}_{1}\\
\bm{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\triangleq\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}

(3.49)

\displaystyle\implies\quad\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}(\bm{c}_{1}-\bm{d}_{1}),\qquad\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{d}_{1}\\
\bm{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.

(3.50)

When
\bm{z}=\boldsymbol{0}
, then
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}\bm{c}_{1}
recovers the least squares solution presented in Theorem
; when
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}
, then
\bm{c}_{1}=\boldsymbol{0}
obtains the minimum-norm solution for the consistent system.

The algorithm involves solving triangular systems with
\bm{R}_{1}
and
\bm{R}_{1}^{\top}
, as well as multiplying vectors by
\bm{Q}
and
\bm{Q}^{\top}
.
These operations amount to a total of approximately
8np-2p^{2}
flops.

\paragrapharrow

Weighted LS problems.
We will discuss numerical methods for solving the generalized least squares problems (
2.44
) in Section
, of which the WLS problem is a special case.
The WLS problem can be formulated as

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{W}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\bm{W}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}=\mathrm{diag}(w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{n}),

(3.51)

where weights
w_{i}
can be understood such that the weighted residuals
e_{i}=w_{i}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})_{i}
have equal variance; see Remark
.
Note that the solution to (
) is scale-invariant, i.e., it does not change if
\bm{W}
is multiplied by a nonzero scalar. Therefore, without loss of generality, we can assume in the following that
w_{i}\geq 1
, and that the rows of
\bm{X}
are normalized so that
\max_{1\leq j\leq p}\left\lvert x_{ij}\right\rvert=1
,
i=1,2,\ldots,n
.
The solution to the WLS problem (
) satisfies the normal equation; see (
):

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{2}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{2}\bm{y}.

(3.52)

A more numerically stable solution method involves using the
weighted QR factorization

\bm{W}\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
. The solution to (
) is then obtained by solving

\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{y},

(3.53)

thus avoiding the need to explicitly square the weight matrix
\bm{W}
.

For a consistent underdetermined system
\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{z}
, the unique solution of the
weighted minimum-norm problem

\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\left\lVert\bm{W}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\text{s.t. }\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{z}

(3.54)

is given by the generalized normal equation of the second kind; see (
):

(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{2}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\bm{z},\qquad\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{W}^{2}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\gamma}.

(3.55)

Again, using the weighted QR factorization
\bm{W}\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
leads to a more accurate solution by avoiding squaring the weight matrix:

\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{W}\bm{Q}\bm{R}^{-\top}\bm{z}.

(3.56)

3.3.5
Modifying LS: Appending or Deleting a Covariate/Column

In Section
, we discussed how to use the Cholesky decomposition to add or delete a data in the least squares problem efficiently.
In certain applications, such as the
F
-test for least squares via QR decomposition (see Section
), there arises a need to remove or add a column/covariate to the observed matrix. The objective is to efficiently obtain the QR decomposition of the modified matrix.

\paragrapharrow

Deleting a column.
Suppose the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is given by
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
, where the column partition of
\bm{X}
is
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]
. Now, if we delete the
k
-th column of
\bm{X}
, resulting in
\bm{X}^{\prime}\triangleq[\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{k-1},\bm{x}_{k+1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]\in\real^{n\times(p-1)}
, we want to compute the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}^{\prime}
efficiently.
Additionally, let
\bm{R}
have the following structure:

\begin{aligned} \begin{array}[]{ccccc}&\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{x}&\bm{R}_{12}&k-1\\
\bm{R}\triangleq&\boldsymbol{0}&r_{kk}&\bm{b}^{\top}&1\\
&\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{R}_{22}&n-k\\
&k-1&1&p-k&\\
\end{array},\end{aligned}\qquad\text{such that}\qquad\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{b}^{\top}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{R}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\triangleq\bm{H}

is
upper Hessenberg
.
An example is provided below to illustrate the case of a
6\times 5
matrix, where
k=3
and the
k
-th column is deleted:

\displaystyle\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{R}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}}

\displaystyle\implies\quad\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{H}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\prime}}.

Again, for columns
k
to
p-1
of
\bm{H}
, there exists a set of Givens rotations (Definition
)
\bm{G}_{k,k+1}
,
\bm{G}_{k+1,k+2}
,
\ldots
,
\bm{G}_{p-1,p}
that can be applied to introduce zeros in the subdiagonal elements
h_{k+1,k}
,
h_{k+2,k+1}
,
\ldots
,
h_{p,p-1}
of
\bm{H}
. Then the triangular matrix
\bm{R}^{\prime}
is given by

\bm{R}^{\prime}\triangleq\bm{G}_{p-1,p}\ldots\bm{G}_{k+1,k+2}\bm{G}_{k,k+1}\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\prime}.

The orthogonal matrix can be obtained through the following procedure:

\bm{Q}^{\prime}=(\bm{G}_{p-1,p}\ldots\bm{G}_{k+1,k+2}\bm{G}_{k,k+1}\bm{Q}^{\top})^{\top}=\bm{Q}\bm{G}_{k,k+1}^{\top}\bm{G}_{k+1,k+2}^{\top}\ldots\bm{G}_{p-1,p}^{\top},

(3.57)

such that
\bm{X}^{\prime}=\bm{Q}^{\prime}\bm{R}^{\prime}
.
The procedure is outlined in Algorithm
. And the
6\times 5
example is shown as follows, where
\boxtimes
represents a value that is not necessarily zero, and
boldface
indicates the value has just been changed:

\displaystyle\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{R}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k=3}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{H}=\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\prime}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{34}}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{34}\bm{H}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{45}}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\

0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&\bm{0}\\

QR Deleting a Column

1:

Matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full QR decomposition

, and

by deleting column

;

2:

\bm{H}

3:

Obtain
\bm{H}
by deleting column

\bm{R}
, that is,

;

4:

for

to

\bm{G}_{i,i+1}
with the following parameters

,

i

for

from Equation (

{theoremHigh}

[Algorithm Complexity: QR Deleting Column
(
Lu 2021b
)
]
Algorithm
requires
\sim 3p^{2}-6pk+3k^{2}
flops to compute a full QR decomposition of the matrix
\bm{X}^{\prime}\in\real^{n\times(p-1)}
.
This matrix is obtained by deleting
k
-th column from
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, assuming that the full QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
is already known.
Furthermore, if the orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}^{\prime}
needs to be formed explicitly, an additional
\sim 6n(p-k)
flops are required.

Note that the value of column
k
affects the complexity: when
k=p
, the complexity is
\sim 0
(ignoring constant terms); and when
k=1
, the complexity reaches its maximum value.

\paragrapharrow

Appending a column.
Similarly, suppose
\widetilde{\bm{X}}\triangleq[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{k},\bm{w},\bm{x}_{k+1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]
, where we append a vector
\bm{w}
to the
(k+1)
-th column of
\bm{X}
. Applying the orthogonal transformation
\bm{Q}^{\top}
, we have

\bm{Q}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}}=[\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k},\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{w},\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{x}_{k+1},\ldots,\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{x}_{p}]\triangleq\widetilde{\bm{H}}.

A set of Givens rotations
\bm{J}_{n-1,n},\bm{J}_{n-2,n-1},\ldots,\bm{J}_{k+1,k+2}
can introduce zeros in the elements
\widetilde{h}_{n,k+1}
,
\widetilde{h}_{n-1,k+1}
,
\ldots
,
\widetilde{h}_{k+2,k+1}
of
\widetilde{\bm{H}}
, thereby achieving the desired result of the updated QR decomposition. That is,

\widetilde{\bm{R}}\triangleq\bm{J}_{k+1,k+2}\ldots\bm{J}_{n-2,n-1}\bm{J}_{n-1,n}\bm{Q}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}},

is upper triangular.
Suppose
\widetilde{\bm{H}}
is a

matrix and

. An example is shown below, where
\boxtimes
represents a value that is not necessarily zero, and
boldface
indicates the value has just been changed:

\displaystyle\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{J}_{56}}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\

(3.58)

such that
\widetilde{\bm{X}}=\widetilde{\bm{Q}}\widetilde{\bm{R}}
. The procedure is formulated in Algorithm

\widetilde{\bm{Q}}_{i,:}\leftarrow c\cdot\widetilde{\bm{Q}}_{i,:}+s\widetilde{\bm{Q}}_{j,:}
, where
j=i+1
;

19:

(i+1)
-th row:
\bm{Q}_{i+1,:}\leftarrow-s\cdot\widetilde{\bm{Q}}_{i,:}+c\widetilde{\bm{Q}}_{j,:}
, where
j=i+1
;

20:

end

for

21:

Output
\widetilde{\bm{Q}}\leftarrow\widetilde{\bm{Q}}^{\top}
from Equation (
);

{theoremHigh}

[Algorithm Complexity: QR Adding Column
(
Lu 2021b
)
]
Algorithm
requires
\sim 2n^{2}+6(np+k^{2}-pk-nk)
flops to compute a full QR decomposition of the matrix
\widetilde{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times(p+1)}
, where we add a column to the
(k+1)
-th column of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and the full QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
is known. Furthermore, if the orthogonal matrix
\widetilde{\bm{Q}}
needs to be formed explicitly, an additional
\sim 6n(n-k)
flops are required.

Note that the column number
k
plays a significant role in determining the complexity.
When
k=p
, the complexity is
2n^{2}
flops. On the other hand, when
k=1
, the complexity reaches its maximum value.

\paragrapharrow

Other Real-world application.
The method described above is useful for performing efficient variable selection in least squares problems using QR decomposition. In this approach, we iteratively remove a column from the data matrix
\bm{X}
and perform an
F
-test to determine the significance of the corresponding variable. If the variable is deemed insignificant, it is removed, leading to a simpler model. A brief overview is given below; for more details, refer to Section
.

Following the setup described in Section
,
let’s consider the overdetermined system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
, where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
represents the data matrix, and
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
with
n\geq p
is the observed response.
The LS solution is obtained by minimizing
\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, and it can be expressed as
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
.

Suppose we remove a column from
\bm{X}
to obtain
\widehat{\bm{X}}
. Consequently, the LS solution changes from
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS}
to
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{LS}
.
Define

\displaystyle RSS(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{LS})

\displaystyle\triangleq\left\lVert\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{LS}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad\text{where\penalty\ }\widehat{\bm{y}}_{LS}=\widehat{\bm{X}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{LS},

\displaystyle RSS(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS})

\displaystyle\triangleq\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{y}_{LS}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad\text{where\penalty\ }\bm{y}_{LS}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS},

\displaystyle\bm{H}

\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top},

\displaystyle\widehat{\bm{H}}

\displaystyle\triangleq\widehat{\bm{X}}(\widehat{\bm{X}}^{\top}\widehat{\bm{X}})^{-1}\widehat{\bm{X}}^{\top}.

Suppose the
reduced
QR decompositions of
\bm{X}
and
\widehat{\bm{X}}
are given by
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
and
\widehat{\bm{X}}=\widehat{\bm{Q}}\widehat{\bm{R}}
.
Thus
RSS(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS})=\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{y}=\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}-(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{Q})(\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y})

and
RSS(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{LS})-RSS(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS})=\left\lVert\bm{y}_{LS}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{LS}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{H}-\widehat{\bm{H}})\bm{y}=(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{Q})(\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y})-(\bm{y}^{\top}\widehat{\bm{Q}})(\widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\top}\bm{y})
, which are the differences of two inner products.
It can be shown that
RSS(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS})\sim\sigma^{2}\chi^{2}_{(n-p)}
, which follows a Chi-square distribution, and
\sigma
is the noise level. Under the hypothesis that the deleted column is not significant, we could conclude that

T={\frac{1}{p-q}\big(RSS(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{LS})-RSS(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS})\big)}/{\frac{1}{n-p}RSS(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{LS})}\sim F_{p-q,n-p},

which is the
test statistic for the
F
-test
with
q=p-1
.
Suppose we have the data set
(\bm{x}_{1},y_{1})
,
(\bm{x}_{2},y_{2})
,
\ldots
,
(\bm{x}_{n},y_{n})
, and we observe
T=t
for this particular data set. Then

\widetilde{p}=P[T((\bm{x}_{1},y_{1}),(\bm{x}_{2},y_{2}),\ldots,(\bm{x}_{n},y_{n}))\geq t]=P[F_{p-q,n-p}\geq t].

We reject the hypothesis (i.e., the variable
k
should be removed) if
\widetilde{p}<\alpha
, for some small
\alpha
, say 0.05. This is known as the
p-value
.

3.3.6
Modifying LS: Appending or Deleting a Data/Row

Similarly, we may also need to append or delete a row/data from the observed matrix in the QR case.
In such cases, our objective is to efficiently compute the QR decomposition of the modified matrix.

\paragrapharrow

Appending a row.
Suppose the full QR decomposition of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is given by
\bm{X}=\scriptsize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
, where
\bm{X}_{1}\in\real^{k\times p}
and
\bm{X}_{2}\in\real^{(n-k)\times p}
. Now, if we append a row such that
\bm{X}^{\prime}=\scriptsize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{w}^{\top}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in\real^{(n+1)\times p}
, we aim to efficiently obtain the full QR decomposition of
\bm{X}^{\prime}
.
To achieve this, we construct a permutation matrix, denoted by
\bm{P}
, such that

\bm{P}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}&1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{I}_{k}&\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{I}_{n-k}\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\bm{P}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{w}^{\top}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{w}^{\top}\\
\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\quad\implies\quad\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\bm{P}\bm{X}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{w}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{H}

is upper Hessenberg. Similarly, a set of rotations
\bm{G}_{12},\bm{G}_{23},\ldots,\bm{G}_{p,p+1}
can be applied to introduce zeros in the elements
h_{21}
,
h_{32}
,
\ldots
,
h_{p+1,p}
of
\bm{H}
. The resulting triangular matrix
\bm{R}^{\prime}
is given by

\bm{R}^{\prime}\triangleq\bm{G}_{p,p+1}\ldots\bm{G}_{23}\bm{G}_{12}\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\bm{P}\bm{X}^{\prime}.

And the orthogonal matrix is obtained by

\bm{Q}^{\prime}\triangleq\left(\bm{G}_{p,p+1}\ldots\bm{G}_{23}\bm{G}_{12}\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\bm{P}\right)^{\top}=\bm{P}^{\top}\begin{bmatrix}1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}\end{bmatrix}\bm{G}_{12}^{\top}\bm{G}_{23}^{\top}\ldots\bm{G}_{p,p+1}^{\top}.

Thus, the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}^{\prime}
is
\bm{X}^{\prime}=\bm{Q}^{\prime}\bm{R}^{\prime}
.

Update of least squares problem.

In the context of least squares, each row of
\bm{X}
and
\bm{y}
is referred to as an
observation
.
In real-world application, new observation may be received.
When performing the optimization process from scratch, obtaining the solution of the least squares problem would require approximately
\sim 2(n+1)p^{2}-\frac{2}{3}p^{3}
flops.
Let’s consider a new observation
[\bm{x}^{\top},b]
, leading to the following reduction:

\left[\begin{array}[]{c|c}\bm{X}&\bm{y}\\
\bm{x}^{\top}&b\end{array}\right]\rightarrow\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Q}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&1\end{bmatrix}\left[\begin{array}[]{c|c}\bm{X}&\bm{y}\\
\bm{x}^{\top}&b\end{array}\right]=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}&\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{y}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{y}\\
\bm{x}^{\top}&b\end{bmatrix}}_{\triangleq\bm{Z}}

Therefore, the updated least squares solution is obtained by transforming
\bm{Z}\in\real^{(n+1)\times(p+1)}
into an upper triangular matrix (actually, we transform the left
p
columns of
\bm{Z}
into an upper triangular matrix). This can be done by a set of rotations in the
(1,n+1)
plane,
(2,n+1)
plane,
\ldots
,
(p,n+1)
plane that introduce zero to
(n+1,1),(n+1,2),\ldots,(n+1,p)
-th entry of
\bm{Z}
, respectively.
The computational cost for this operation is
\mathcal{O}(np)
flops.

\paragrapharrow

Deleting a row.
Conversely, suppose
\bm{X}=\scriptsize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{w}^{\top}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in\real^{n\times p}
, where
\bm{X}_{1}\in\real^{k\times p}
and
\bm{X}_{2}\in\real^{(n-k-1)\times p}
. The full QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
is given by
\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
, where
\bm{Q}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{R}\in\real^{n\times p}
. We want to compute the full QR decomposition of

\widetilde{\bm{X}}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}
efficiently (assuming
n-1\geq p
). Analogously, we can construct a permutation matrix

\bm{P}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}&1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{I}_{k}&\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{I}_{n-k-1}\end{bmatrix}\implies\bm{P}\bm{X}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}&1&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{I}_{k}&\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{I}_{n-k-1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{w}^{\top}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{w}^{\top}\\
\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{P}\bm{Q}\bm{R}\triangleq\bm{M}\bm{R},

where
\bm{M}\triangleq\bm{P}\bm{Q}
is an orthogonal matrix.
Let
\bm{m}^{\top}
be the first row of
\bm{M}
, and construct a set of Givens rotations
\bm{G}_{n-1,n},\bm{G}_{n-2,n-1},\ldots,\bm{G}_{1,2}
, which introduce zeros in the elements
m_{n},m_{n-1},\ldots,m_{2}
of
\bm{m}
, respectively.
By applying these rotations, we can obtain
\bm{G}_{1,2}\ldots\bm{G}_{n-2,n-1}\bm{G}_{n-1,n}\bm{m}=\alpha\bm{e}_{1}
, where
\alpha=\pm 1
. Therefore, we obtain the following result:

\bm{G}_{1,2}\ldots\bm{G}_{n-2,n-1}\bm{G}_{n-1,n}\bm{R}\triangleq\begin{array}[]{cc}\bm{v}^{\top}&1\\
\bm{R}_{1}&n-1\\
\end{array},$$whichisupperHessenbergwith$\bm{R}_1\in\real^{(n-1)\times p}$beinguppertriangular.And$$\bm{M}\bm{G}_{n-1,n}^{\top}\bm{G}_{n-2,n-1}^{\top}\ldots\bm{G}_{1,2}^{\top}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\alpha&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{1}\end{bmatrix},$$where$\bm{Q}_1\in\real^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}$isanorthogonalmatrix.Thebottom-leftblockofthematrixaboveisazerovectorsince$\alpha=\pm 1$and$\bm{M}$isorthogonal.Toseethis,let$\bm{G}\triangleq\bm{G}_{n-1,n}^\top\bm{G}_{n-2,n-1}^\top$$\ldots\bm{G}_{1,2}^\top$,withitsfirstcolumndenotedas$\bm{g}$.Writing$\bm{M}$astherowpartition$\bm{M}= [\bm{m}^\top; \bm{m}_2^\top; \bm{m}_3^\top; \ldots, \bm{m}_{n}^\top]$,wehave$$\begin{aligned} \bm{m}^{\top}\bm{g}&=\pm 1\qquad\rightarrow\qquad\bm{g}=\pm\bm{m},\\
\bm{m}_{i}^{\top}\bm{m}&=0,\qquad\forall\,i\in\{2,3,\ldots,n\}.\end{aligned}$$Thisresultsin$$\begin{aligned} \bm{P}\bm{X}&=\bm{M}\bm{R}=(\bm{M}\bm{G}_{n-1,n}^{\top}\bm{G}_{n-2,n-1}^{\top}\ldots\bm{G}_{1,2}\top)(\bm{G}_{1,2}\ldots\bm{G}_{n-2,n-1}\bm{G}_{n-1,n}\bm{R})\\
&=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\bm{Q}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}_{1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha\bm{v}^{\top}\\
\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}_{1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{w}^{\top}\\
\widetilde{\bm{X}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}$$Thus,weobtainthat$\bm{Q}_1\bm{R}_1$isthefullQRdecompositionof$\widetilde{\bm{X}}=
\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{X}_{2}
\end{bmatrix}\normalsize$.\par\par\par\par\par

3.3.7
Modifying LS: Rank-One Changes

We have previously explored the rank-one update and downdate of the Cholesky decomposition in Section
.
The rank-one change of the matrix
\bm{X}
in the QR decomposition, denoted by
\bm{X}^{\prime}
, is defined in a similar manner:

\displaystyle\bm{X}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}+\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top},

\displaystyle\downarrow

\displaystyle\downarrow

\displaystyle\bm{Q}^{\prime}\bm{R}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\bm{Q}\bm{R}+\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top},

where if we set
\bm{X}^{\prime}=\bm{X}-(-\bm{u})\bm{v}^{\top}
, we recover the downdate form such that the update and downdate in the QR decomposition are equivalent.

To reiterate,
the rank-one update/downdate problem involves finding the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}^{\prime}
when the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
has already been computed.
Let
\bm{w}\triangleq\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{u}
, then we have

\bm{X}^{\prime}=\bm{Q}(\bm{R}+\bm{w}\bm{v}^{\top}).

Similarly,
there exists a set of Givens rotations
\bm{G}_{12}\bm{G}_{23}\ldots\bm{G}_{(p-1),p}
that satisfy:

\bm{G}_{12}\bm{G}_{23}\ldots\bm{G}_{(p-1),p}\bm{w}=\pm\left\lVert\bm{w}\right\rVert_{2}\bm{e}_{1},

where
\bm{G}_{(k-1),k}
represents the Givens rotation effecting in the
(k-1)
-th and
k
-th plane, which introduces zero in the
k
-th entry of
\bm{w}
.

Applying these rotations to
\bm{R}
, we obtain

\bm{G}_{12}\bm{G}_{23}\ldots\bm{G}_{(p-1),p}\bm{R}\triangleq\bm{H}_{0},

where the Givens rotations in this
reverse order
(
backward rotations
) are employed to transform the upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}
into a “simple”
upper Hessenberg matrix
.
However, if the rotations transform
\bm{w}
into
\pm\left\lVert\bm{w}\right\rVert_{2}\bm{e}_{1}
in the
forward order
(
forward rotations
), we will not obtain this upper Hessenberg
\bm{H}_{0}
.

To see this, consider a
5\times 5
matrix
\bm{R}
, an example is shown as follows, where
\boxtimes
represents a value that is not necessarily zero, and
boldface
indicates the value has just been changed. Using backward rotations results in the upper Hessenberg
\bm{H}_{0}
, which is easier to manage to update the QR decomposition:

\displaystyle\text{\parbox{70.0001pt}{Backward\\
(Right Way)}: }\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{R}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{45}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{45}\bm{R}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{34}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{34}\bm{G}_{45}\bm{R}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{23}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{23}\bm{G}_{34}\bm{G}_{45}\bm{R}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{12}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{12}\bm{G}_{23}\bm{G}_{34}\bm{G}_{45}\bm{R}}.

And the forward rotations result in a
full (non-sparse) matrix
:

\displaystyle\text{\parbox{70.0001pt}{Forward\\
(Wrong Way)}: }\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{R}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{12}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{12}\bm{R}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{23}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&0&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{23}\bm{G}_{12}\bm{R}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{34}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&0&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{34}\bm{G}_{23}\bm{G}_{12}\bm{R}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{G}_{45}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{G}_{45}\bm{G}_{34}\bm{G}_{23}\bm{G}_{12}\bm{R}}.

That is, backward rotations will preserve a lot of the zeros as they are, whereas the forward rotations will eliminate these zeros.
In general, backward rotations yield

\bm{G}_{12}\bm{G}_{23}\ldots\bm{G}_{(p-1),p}(\bm{R}+\bm{w}\bm{v}^{\top})=\bm{H}_{0}\pm\left\lVert\bm{w}\right\rVert_{2}\bm{e}_{1}\bm{v}^{\top}\triangleq\bm{H},

which is in upper Hessenberg form.
We can thus find a sequence of rotations
\bm{J}_{12},\bm{J}_{23},\ldots,\bm{J}_{(p-1),p}
such that

\bm{J}_{(p-1),p}\ldots\bm{J}_{23}\bm{J}_{12}\bm{H}\triangleq\bm{R}^{\prime}

is upper triangular.
Following the example of the
5\times 5
matrix, the triangularization process is presented below:

\displaystyle\underbrace{\bm{H}_{0}\pm\left\lVert\bm{w}\right\rVert_{2}\bm{e}_{1}\bm{v}^{\top}}_{\bm{H}}=\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{H}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{J}_{12}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{J}_{12}\bm{H}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{J}_{23}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{J}_{23}\bm{J}_{12}\bm{H}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{J}_{34}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{J}_{34}\bm{J}_{23}\bm{J}_{12}\bm{H}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bm{J}_{45}}}{{\rightarrow}}\footnotesize\mathop{{}\begin{bmatrix}\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&\boxtimes&\boxtimes&\boxtimes\\
0&0&0&\bm{\boxtimes}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
0&0&0&\bm{0}&\bm{\boxtimes}\\
\end{bmatrix}}_{\textstyle\mathstrut\bm{J}_{45}\bm{J}_{34}\bm{J}_{23}\bm{J}_{12}\bm{H}}.

And the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}^{\prime}
is then given by

\bm{X}^{\prime}=\bm{Q}^{\prime}\bm{R}^{\prime},

where

\left\{\begin{aligned} \bm{R}^{\prime}&\triangleq(\bm{J}_{(p-1),p}\ldots\bm{J}_{23}\bm{J}_{12})(\bm{G}_{12}\bm{G}_{23}\ldots\bm{G}_{(p-1),p})(\bm{R}+\bm{w}\bm{v}^{\top});\\
\bm{Q}^{\prime}&\triangleq\bm{Q}\left\{(\bm{J}_{(p-1),p}\ldots\bm{J}_{23}\bm{J}_{12})(\bm{G}_{12}\bm{G}_{23}\ldots\bm{G}_{(p-1),p})\right\}^{\top};\\
\text{(or) }\bm{Q}^{\prime\top}&\triangleq\left\{(\bm{J}_{(p-1),p}\ldots\bm{J}_{23}\bm{J}_{12})(\bm{G}_{12}\bm{G}_{23}\ldots\bm{G}_{(p-1),p})\right\}\bm{Q}^{\top}.\end{aligned}\right.

(3.59)

The procedure is outlined in Algorithm
.

We state the complexity of the rank-one update in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}
[Algorithm complexity: QR rank-one change
(
Lu 2021b
)
]
Algorithm
requires
\sim 8p^{2}
flops to compute the full QR decomposition of an
\bm{X}^{\prime}\in\real^{p\times p}
matrix with a rank-one change to
\bm{X}
, given that the full QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
is already known. Furthermore, if the orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}^{\prime}
needs to be formed explicitly, an additional
\sim 12p^{2}
flops are required.

The algorithm can be easily applied to a rectangular matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
or to the sum
\bm{X}+\bm{U}\bm{V}^{\top}
, where
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times k}
and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times k}
; see
Golub and Van Loan 2013
for more details.

3.3.8
Rank-Deficient Case

We now show that there exists a column permutation matrix
\bm{P}
such that, in the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}\bm{P}
, all diagonal elements equal to zero appear at the end.
This is referred to as the
column-pivoted QR (CPQR)
decomposition, or alternatively, the
rank-deficient QR
decomposition.

{theoremHigh}
[Column-pivoted QR decomposition]
Ler
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with rank
r
such that
r<p\leq n
.
Then there exist a permutation matrix
\bm{P}
and an orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}\in\real^{n\times n}
such that

\bm{X}\bm{P}=\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},

where
\bm{R}_{11}\in\real^{r\times r}
is upper triangular with positive diagonal elements.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r
, we can always choose a permutation matrix
\bm{P}
such that
\bm{X}\bm{P}=[\bm{X}_{1},\bm{X}_{2}]
, where
\bm{X}_{1}\in\real^{n\times r}
has linearly independent columns. The QR decomposition

\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},\quad\bm{Q}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Q}_{1}&\bm{Q}_{2}\end{bmatrix}

uniquely determines
\bm{Q}_{1}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
\bm{R}_{11}\in\real^{r\times r}
with positive diagonal elements. Then

\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}_{1}&\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}

has rank
r
. Here
\bm{R}_{22}=\boldsymbol{0}
, because
\bm{R}
cannot have more than
r
linearly independent rows.
This completes the proof.

From the CPQR decomposition and orthogonal invariance of the
\ell_{2}
norm, it follows that the least squares problem
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}
is equivalent to

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}\bm{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}\equiv\min_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\\
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\bm{d}_{1}\\
\bm{d}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\right\rVert_{2},

(3.60)

where

\bm{X}\bm{P}=\bm{Q}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}
is the CPQR of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
\bm{d}\triangleq\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{y}
and
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq\bm{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
are partitioned conformally. The general solution of (
) is given by
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{P}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\\
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\end{bmatrix}
, where

\bm{R}_{11}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}+\bm{R}_{12}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}=\bm{d}_{1},

and
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
can be chosen arbitrarily. For
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we obtain a basic least squares solution

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}^{\top},\boldsymbol{0}]^{\top}
, and

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}=\bm{P}\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}\triangleq\bm{R}_{11}^{-1}\bm{d}_{1},

(3.61)

with at most
r=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})
nonzero components. The general solution in terms of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in\real^{p-r}
(which can vary) is given by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{P}\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}-\bm{Z}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\\
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\bm{Z}\triangleq\bm{R}_{11}^{-1}\bm{R}_{12},

(3.62)

where
\bm{Z}
can be computed in
\sim r^{2}(p-r)
flops by solving the matrix equation
\bm{R}_{11}\bm{Z}=\bm{R}_{12}
using backward substitution.

\paragrapharrow

Smoothing LS and minimum-norm problems.
Another general approach to address rank deficiency is to find the solution to the least squares problem

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in{\mathbb{B}}}\left\lVert\bm{B}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2},\quad{\mathbb{B}}\triangleq\{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}=\min\},

(3.63)

where the matrix
\bm{B}
can be chosen so that
\left\lVert\bm{B}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}
is a measure of the smoothness of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
Similar to the full-rank case (
),
substituting the general solution (
) shows that the solution to (
) is given by

\min_{\bm{b}\in\real^{p-r}}\left\lVert\bm{B}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Z}\\
-\bm{I}_{p-r}\end{bmatrix}\bm{b}-\bm{B}\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\right\rVert_{2}.

(3.64)

In particular, taking
\bm{B}=\bm{I}
reduces to the minimum-norm problem, which minimizes

\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{Z}\bm{b}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{b}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

and gives the pseudo-inverse solution
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
.
It can be shown that

\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\bm{P})=\mathcal{C}\left(\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Z}\\
-\bm{I}_{p-r}\end{bmatrix}\right)

forms a (nonorthonormal) basis for
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\bm{P})
. QR factorization gives an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\bm{P})
. Note that the unique pseudo-inverse solution orthogonal to
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\bm{P})
(see Theorem
) equals the residual of the least squares problem (
) with
\bm{B}=\bm{I}
,

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{P}\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{r}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}-\bm{P}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Z}\\
-\bm{I}_{p-r}\end{bmatrix}\widehat{\bm{b}},\quad\text{with}\quad\widehat{\bm{b}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{b}}\left\lVert\bm{Z}\bm{b}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{b}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Observe that this expression takes the form of the basic solution minus a correction term lying in the null space of
\bm{X}\bm{P}
. Any particular solution can be substituted for
\bm{b}
in (
).

Computing the CPQR Decomposition

For many applications it is preferable to use a column-pivoted QR factorization (CPQR), in which the pivot column at step
k
is chosen to maximize the diagonal element
r_{kk}
.

We now explain how to implement this strategy using the Modified Gram–Schmidt (MGS) process.
Suppose that after
(k-1)
steps, the nonpivotal columns are transformed according to

\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}=\bm{x}_{j}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}r_{ij}\bm{q}_{i},\quad j=k,\ldots,p,

where
\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}
is orthogonal to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}_{k-1})=\text{span}\{\bm{q}_{1},\ldots,\bm{q}_{k-1}\}
.
In the
k
-th step we select
s
, so that

\left\lVert\bm{x}_{s}^{(k)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\max_{k\leq j\leq p}\left\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(3.65)

and interchange columns
k
and
s
. This is equivalent to choosing at the
k
-th step a pivot column with largest distance to the subspace
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}_{k-1})=\text{span}\{\bm{x}_{s_{1}},\bm{x}_{s_{2}},\ldots,\bm{x}_{s_{k-1}}\}
, where
\bm{X}_{k-1}
is the submatrix formed by the columns corresponding to the first
k-1
selected pivots.

\paragrapharrow

MGS CPQR.
Building on the recursive MGS algorithm described in Algorithm
, we can also develop a practical implementation of CPQR. This variant is presented in Algorithm
. The only difference from the standard MGS lies in the highlighted
blue
portion: before each iteration, we permute the column with the largest norm into the leading position.

As a result, we obtain a triangular matrix
\bm{R}
satisfying

r_{11}\geq r_{22}\geq\ldots\geq r_{rr}.

(3.66a)

Since
r_{kk}=\big\lVert\bm{x}_{s}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}
, and
\big\lVert\bm{x}_{s}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\max_{k\leq j\leq p}\big\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
by (
). Therefore,
r_{k,k+1}^{2}+r_{k+1,k+1}^{2}\leq\big\lVert\bm{x}_{s}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\equiv r_{kk}^{2}
.
This argument recursively shows that the diagonal elements in
\bm{R}
satisfy the stronger inequalities

r_{kk}^{2}\geq\sum_{i=k}^{j}r_{ij}^{2},\quad j=k+1,\ldots,p,\quad k=1:r.

(3.66b)

This implies that if
r_{kk}=0
, then
r_{ij}=0
,
i,j\geq k
. In particular,

\left\lvert r_{11}\right\rvert=\max_{1\leq j\leq p}\left\{\left\lvert\bm{e}_{j}^{\top}\bm{R}\bm{e}_{1}\right\rvert\mid\bm{X}\bm{P}_{1j}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}\right\},

where
\bm{P}_{1j}
is the permutation matrix that interchanges columns 1 and
j
. Then
\left\lVert\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq pr_{11}^{2}
, which yields upper and lower bounds for
\sigma_{1}(\bm{X})
,

\left\lvert r_{11}\right\rvert\leq\sigma_{1}(\bm{X})\leq\sqrt{p}\left\lvert r_{11}\right\rvert.

(3.66c)

If a diagonal element
r_{kk}
in CPQR vanishes, it follows from (
) that
r_{ij}=0
,
i,j\geq k
.

Now suppose that at an intermediate stage of CPQR, the new diagonal element satisfies
r_{k+1,k+1}\leq\delta
for some small
\delta
. Then by (
),

\left\lVert\bm{X}^{(k)}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\sqrt{p-k}\cdot\delta,

and setting
\bm{X}^{(k)}=\boldsymbol{0}
corresponds to a perturbation
\bm{E}_{k}
of
\bm{X}
, such that
\bm{X}+\bm{E}_{k}
has rank-
k
and
\left\lVert\bm{E}_{k}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\sqrt{p-k}\cdot\delta
. The matrix

\widehat{\bm{X}}=\bm{Q}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\end{bmatrix}\bm{P}^{\top},\quad\bm{Q}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Q}_{1}&\bm{Q}_{2}\end{bmatrix},

obtained by neglecting
\bm{R}_{22}
, is the best rank-
k
approximation to
\bm{X}
that differs from
\bm{X}\bm{P}
only in the last
p-k
columns. In particular, when
k=p-1
, we get
\big\lVert\widehat{\bm{X}}-\bm{X}\big\rVert_{F}=r_{pp}

(
Björck 2024
)
.

A commonly used stopping criterion for CPQR is to terminate the process when
r_{k+1,k+1}\leq\delta
.
However, this may significantly overestimate the numerical rank of
\bm{X}
. It can be shown that

\sigma_{p}\geq\frac{3\left\lvert r_{pp}\right\rvert}{\sqrt{4^{p}+6p-1}}\geq 2^{1-p}\left\lvert r_{pp}\right\rvert.

This inequality demonstrates that
\sigma_{p}
can be much smaller than
\left\lvert r_{pp}\right\rvert
for moderately large values of
p

(
Faddeev et al. 1968
)
.

Algorithm 21

Practical
CPQR via MGS (
Row-Wise and Recursively
).
The algorithm is derived from Algorithm
and a similar procedure can be derived based on Algorithm
and Algorithm
.

1:

\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with rank
r
;

2:

for

k=1
to
p

do

\triangleright
i.e., compute
k
-th column of
\bm{Q}
and
k
-th row of
\bm{R}

3:

Find the column with largest norm in
\bm{X}
, and permute to first column;

4:

\bm{x}_{1}\leftarrow\bm{X}[:,1]
;
\triangleright

1
-st column of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times(p-k+1)}

5:

r_{kk}\leftarrow\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}
;
\triangleright

\bm{x}_{1}\in\real^{n\times 1}

6:

\bm{q}_{k}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{1}/r_{kk}
;

7:

\bm{r}_{k2}^{\top}\leftarrow\bm{q}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X}_{2}
;
\triangleright

\bm{X}_{2}\triangleq\bm{X}[:,2:p]\in\real^{n\times(p-k)}
,
\bm{r}_{k2}^{\top}\in\real^{1\times(p-k)}

8:

\bm{X}\leftarrow\bm{X}_{2}-\bm{q}_{k}\bm{r}_{k2}^{\top}
;
\triangleright

\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times(p-k)}

9:

Exit when
r_{kk}=0
or
r_{kk}<\delta
;

10:

end

for

11:

Output permutations,
\bm{Q}=[\bm{q}_{1},\ldots,\bm{q}_{p}]
and
\bm{R}
with entry
(i,k)
being
r_{ik}
.

\paragrapharrow

Reduction in computational cost.
Note that, in each iteration, we need to calculate the norms of all the (remaining) columns of
\bm{X}
rather than computing the norms all at once. At iteration
k
, we need to compute the reduced QR decomposition of a matrix of size
n\times(p-k+1)
if the original matrix
\bm{X}
is of size
n\times p
. That is, extra
(p-k+1)(2n-1)
flops are required to proceed with the CPQR via MGS. Let
f(k)=(p-k+1)(2n-1)
; simple calculation can show that the additional complexity for CPQR via MGS is:

\text{extra cost = }f(1)+f(2)+\ldots+f(p)\sim np^{2}\text{ flops},

(3.67)

if only keep the leading term.

However, this additional cost in CPQR via MGS can be mitigated to some extent.
Suppose the column partition of
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]
, and let the squared norm of each column be given in the vector

\bm{l}_{a}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}l_{1}\\
l_{2}\\
\vdots\\
l_{p}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\left\lVert\bm{x}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
\left\lVert\bm{x}_{2}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
\vdots\\
\left\lVert\bm{x}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

Suppose further that
\bm{q}\in\real^{n}
is a unit-length vector such that
\bm{q}^{\top}\bm{q}=1
, and
\bm{r}\in\real^{p}
is a vector given by

\bm{r}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{q}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}r_{1}\\
r_{2}\\
\vdots\\
r_{p}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{(similar to the step 6 of Algorithm\penalty\ \ref{alg:cpqr-partial-fact-cpqr})}

Let further
\bm{B}=\bm{X}-\bm{q}\bm{r}^{\top}=[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}]
(similar to the step 7 of Algorithm
).
The vector representing the squared lengths of
\bm{B}
is given by

\bm{l}_{b}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}s_{1}\\
s_{2}\\
\vdots\\
s_{p}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\left\lVert\bm{b}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
\left\lVert\bm{b}_{2}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
\vdots\\
\left\lVert\bm{b}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
\end{bmatrix}\normalsize=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}l_{1}-r_{1}^{2}\\
l_{2}-r_{2}^{2}\\
\vdots\\
l_{p}-r_{p}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

This can be easily verified since
\bm{b}_{i}=\bm{x}_{i}-r_{i}\bm{q}=\bm{x}_{i}-(\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\bm{q})\bm{q}
such that

\left\lVert\bm{b}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{x}_{i}-r_{i}\bm{q}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=(\bm{x}_{i}-r_{i}\bm{q})^{\top}(\bm{x}_{i}-r_{i}\bm{q})=l_{i}-r_{i}^{2}.

If the column norms
\big\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}
in (
) are recomputed at each stage of MGS, this will increase the operation count of the QR factorization by 50%
(
Björck 2024
)
. Since these quantities are invariant under orthogonal transformations, this overhead can be reduced to
\mathcal{O}(np)
operations by using the recursion

\left\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-r_{kj}^{2},\quad j=k+1,\ldots,p,

to update these values. To avoid numerical problems,
\big\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}
should be recomputed from scratch whenever there has been substantial cancellation, e.g., when
\big\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k+1)}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\big\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}/\sqrt{2}
.

Coming back to step 2 of Algorithm
, suppose we have computed the squared norms of the columns from the original matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
(which requires
p(2n-1)
). The squared norms of the columns from
\bm{X}_{2}-\bm{q}_{1}\bm{r}_{12}^{\top}
(suppose
k=1
in step 7 of Algorithm
) can be obtained with an additional
2(p-1)
flops.
Over the course of the
p
iterations, the total cost is
2(p-1)+2(p-2)+\ldots+2(1)=p^{2}-p
flops. This is significantly less than the complexity of
\sim np^{2}
in Equation (
).

\paragrapharrow

CPQR for LS.

The column pivoting strategy described above is independent of the right-hand side vector
\bm{y}
, and therefore may not be the most suitable choice when solving a specific least squares problem. For example, suppose
\bm{y}
is a multiple of one of the columns in
\bm{X}
. Using standard pivoting, this situation might not be recognized until after the full QR factorization has been completed.
An alternative strategy is to select the pivot column at step
k+1
as the column for which the current residual norm
\big\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}
is maximally reduced. For MGS this is achieved by choosing as pivot the column
\bm{x}_{p}
that forms the smallest acute angle with the current residual vector
\bm{e}^{(k)}\triangleq\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(k)}
.
Therefore, the column is chosen to maximize

\frac{\big(\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}\big)^{\top}\bm{e}^{(k)}}{\big\lVert\bm{x}_{j}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}\big\lVert\bm{e}^{(k)}\big\rVert_{2}}.

This ensures that each pivot contributes the most to reducing the residual in the current iteration.

3.3.9
GLS by Elliptic MGS and Householder Methods

For a given symmetric positive definite matrix
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
,

\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}=\bm{y}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{x},\qquad\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}=(\bm{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{x})^{1/2}

(3.68)

defines a scalar inner product and the corresponding norm; see Section
.
Since the unit ball
\{\bm{x}\mid\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}\leq 1\}
forms an ellipsoid, this norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
is also referred to as an elliptic norm.
A generalized Cauchy-Schwarz inequality holds:

\left\lvert\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}.

(3.69)

Two vectors
\bm{x}
and
\bm{y}
are said to be
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-orthogonal if
\left\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}\right\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}=0
, and a matrix
\bm{Q}\in\real^{n\times p}
is
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-semi-orthogonal if
\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{Q}=\bm{I}
.

If
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]\in\real^{n\times p}
has full column rank, then an elliptic MGS algorithm can be used to compute a
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-semi-orthogonal matrix
\bm{Q}_{1}=[\bm{q}_{1},\bm{q}_{2},\ldots,\bm{q}_{p}]
and an upper triangular matrix
\bm{R}
such that

\bm{X}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R},\quad\text{with}\quad\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{Q}_{1}=\bm{I}_{p}.

(3.70)

Elliptic MGS QR Decomposition

Similar to the elementary projector in Exercise
,
an
elementary elliptic projector
has the form

\bm{P}=(\bm{I}-\bm{q}\bm{q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}),\quad\text{with }\bm{q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{q}=1

(3.71)

and satisfies
\bm{P}^{2}=\bm{I}-2\bm{q}\bm{q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}+\bm{q}(\bm{q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{q})\bm{q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}=\bm{P}
. It is easily verified that for any vector
\bm{a}
,
\bm{q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bm{P}\bm{a})=\boldsymbol{0}
, i.e.,
\bm{P}\bm{a}
is
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-orthogonal to
\bm{q}
. Note that
\bm{P}
is
not
symmetric and therefore is an oblique projector; see Definition
and Section
. Furthermore,

\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{1/2}\bm{P}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1/2}=\bm{I}-\widetilde{\bm{q}}\widetilde{\bm{q}}^{\top},\quad\text{with }\widetilde{\bm{q}}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{1/2}\bm{q}

(3.72)

is an orthogonal projector.

An updated MGS process can compute the factorization in (
); the process is shown in Algorithm
.

Algorithm 22

MGS QR (=Algorithm
)

1:

\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full column rank;

2:

for

k=1
to
p

do

3:

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}
;

4:

for

i=1
to
k-1

do

5:

{r_{ik}\leftarrow\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}}}
;

6:

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}-r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i}
;

7:

end

for

8:

\boxed{r_{kk}\leftarrow\left\lVert\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2}}
;

9:

\bm{q}_{k}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}/r_{kk}
;

10:

end

for

Algorithm 23

Elliptic MGS QR

1:

\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full column rank;

2:

for

k=1
to
p

do

3:

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}
;

4:

for

i=1
to
k-1

do

5:

{r_{ik}\leftarrow\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}}}
;

6:

\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}-r_{ik}\bm{q}_{i}
;

7:

end

for

8:

\boxed{r_{kk}\leftarrow\sqrt{\left\langle\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp},\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}\right\rangle}}
;

9:

\bm{q}_{k}\leftarrow\bm{x}_{k}^{\perp}/r_{kk}
;

10:

end

for

In addition to the
2np^{2}
flops for the standard MGS algorithms, elliptic MGS requires
2n^{2}p
flops for
p
matrix-vector products with
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
. If
n\gg p
, these operations can dominate the total computational effort.

However, if a factorization
\boldsymbol{\Phi}=\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{B}\in\real^{n\times n}
is known, then

\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}=(\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{B}\bm{x})^{1/2}=\left\lVert\bm{B}\bm{x}\right\rVert_{2},

and the operations with
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
can be replaced by operations with
\bm{B}
and
\bm{B}^{\top}
.
And the factorization in (
) can be replaced by the basic QR decomposition of
\bm{B}\bm{X}

\bm{B}\bm{X}=(\bm{B}\bm{Q}_{1})\bm{R},\quad\text{with}\quad(\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{B}^{\top})(\bm{B}\bm{Q}_{1})=\bm{I}_{p}.

(3.73)

\paragrapharrow

GLS using elliptic MGS.
The GLS problem
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
with
\boldsymbol{\Phi}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}
in (
2.44
) can be solved by an elliptic MGS QR decomposition.
If applied to the extended matrix
[\bm{X},\bm{y}]
, this gives the factorization:

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}&\bm{y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{Q}_{1}&\bm{q}_{p+1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}&\bm{z}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\rho\end{bmatrix}.

(3.74)

It follows that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}=\bm{Q}_{1}(\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{z})-\rho\bm{q}_{p+1}
, where
\bm{q}_{p+1}
is
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-orthogonal to
\bm{Q}_{1}
. Hence
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
is minimized when
\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{z}
, and the solution and residual are given by

\bm{R}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{z},\qquad\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\rho\bm{q}_{p+1}.

(3.75)

Elliptic Householder QR Decomposition

Similarly, we can obtain an
elliptic Householder QR factorization

(
Gulliksson and Wedin 1992
)
.
We begin by defining the
elliptic Householder reflection
matrix as follows.

Definition 141
(Elliptic Householder reflector).

Let
\bm{u}\in\real^{n}
be given and
\boldsymbol{\Phi}\in\real^{n\times n}
be positive definite.
The matrix

\bm{H}=(\bm{I}-\gamma\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi})\quad\text{with }\gamma\triangleq 2/(\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{u})

(3.76)

is referred to as a an elliptic Householder reflector, a.k.a., an elliptic Householder transformation.
It can be easily verified that

\bm{H}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{H}=(\bm{I}-\gamma\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top})\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bm{I}-\gamma\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi})=\boldsymbol{\Phi}.

(3.77)

Such matrices are called
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-invariant.

The product of an elliptic Householder reflection
\bm{H}
with a vector
\bm{a}
is given by

\bm{H}\bm{a}=(\bm{I}-\gamma\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi})\bm{a}=\bm{a}-\gamma(\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{a})\bm{u}.

Similar to a basic Householder reflector (Definition
), it can be verified that
\bm{H}
is also orthogonal such that that
\bm{H}^{2}=\bm{I}
and
\bm{H}^{-1}=\bm{H}
. However,
\bm{H}
is neither symmetric nor
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-orthogonal.
On the other hand, the transformation

\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{1/2}\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1/2}=\bm{I}-\gamma\widetilde{\bm{u}}\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{\top},\quad\text{with }\widetilde{\bm{u}}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{1/2}\bm{u}\ \text{ and }\ \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{1/2}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}

yields an orthogonal reflection.

It can be verified that the unit matrix
\bm{I}
is
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-invariant, and a product of
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-invariant matrices
\bm{H}=\bm{H}_{1}\bm{H}_{2}\ldots\bm{H}_{p}
is again
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-invariant. This property characterizes transformations that make the
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-norm invariant:

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2},\quad\text{if $\bm{Q}$ is orthogonal, i.e., $\bm{Q}$ is $\bm{I}$-invariant}

(3.78)

\displaystyle\implies\left\lVert\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}^{2}=(\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}^{2},\quad\text{if $\bm{H}$ is $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$-invariant}.

(3.79)

Therefore,
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
and
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{H}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y})\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
have the same solution.
Using these insights, to develop a Householder QR algorithm for solving
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
, we construct a sequence of elliptic Householder reflectors
\bm{H}_{i}
such that

\bm{H}_{p}\ldots\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y})=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\begin{bmatrix}\bm{c}_{1}\\
\bm{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},

(3.80)

where
\bm{R}_{1}
is upper triangular and nonsingular.
Therefore, an equivalent problem of the GLS problem
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
is
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{R}_{1}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{c}_{1}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
with solution
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{R}_{1}^{-1}\bm{c}_{1}
. As in the standard Householder method, this only requires that we construct an elliptic Householder reflector
\bm{H}
that maps a given vector
\bm{x}
onto a multiple of the unit vector
\bm{e}_{1}
:

\bm{H}\bm{x}=\bm{x}-\gamma(\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{x})\bm{u}=\pm\sigma\bm{e}_{1},\quad\text{with }\sigma\triangleq\frac{\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}}{\left\lVert\bm{e}_{1}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}}.

(3.81)

By the invariance of the
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
-norm (
3.79
),

\sigma\left\lVert\bm{e}_{1}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}=\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}},\ \left\lVert\bm{e}_{1}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}=(\bm{e}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{e}_{1})^{1/2},

and from (
), we have
\bm{u}=\bm{x}\pm\sigma\bm{e}_{1}
. Hence
\gamma=2/(\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{u})
, where

\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{u}=(\bm{x}\pm\sigma\bm{e}_{1})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bm{x}\pm\sigma\bm{e}_{1})=2(\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert_{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}^{2}\pm\sigma\bm{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{e}_{1}).

For stability, the sign should be chosen to maximize
\bm{u}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\bm{u}
.

3.4
LS via UTV Decomposition for Rank-Deficient Matrix

The CPQR decomposition of a rank-deficient matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r
is

\bm{X}\bm{P}=[\bm{Q}_{1},\bm{Q}_{2}]\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
, where
\bm{R}_{11}\in\real^{r\times r}

r<p
, is nonsingular.
Here,
\bm{Q}_{1}
and
\bm{Q}_{2}
provide orthogonormal bases for
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, respectively.
However, this factorization is not as useful in applications that require a basis for the nullspace
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
.
A related decomposition, known as the
complete orthogonal decomposition
, expresses a matrix using two orthogonal matrices. It is closely related to the CPQR decomposition.

{theoremHigh}
[Complete orthogonal decomposition]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
be given with rank
r
. Then it can be factored as

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{T}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{V},

where
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times p}
are two orthogonal matrices, and
\bm{T}\in\real^{r\times r}
is a rank-
r
matrix.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By utilizing the column-pivoted QR decomposition (Theorem
),
\bm{X}
can be factored as

\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize,

where
\bm{R}_{11}\in\real^{r\times r}
is upper triangular,
\bm{R}_{12}\in\real^{r\times(p-r)}
,
\bm{Q}_{1}\in\real^{n\times n}
is an orthogonal matrix, and
\bm{P}
is a permutation matrix.
Then it is not difficult to find a decomposition satisfying

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}_{12}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\triangleq\bm{Q}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{S}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},

(3.82)

where
\bm{Q}_{2}
is an orthogonal matrix, and
\bm{S}
is a rank-
r
matrix. The decomposition is reasonable because the matrix

\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}_{12}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\real^{p\times r}
has rank
r
whose columns stay in a subspace of
p
. Nevertheless, the columns of
\bm{Q}_{2}
span the entire space of
p
, where we can assume that the first
r
columns of
\bm{Q}_{2}
span the same space as that of
\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}_{12}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}
. The matrix
\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{S}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}
serves to transform
\bm{Q}_{2}
into
\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}_{12}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}
.
Then, it follows that

\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}\bm{X}\bm{P}\bm{Q}_{2}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{S}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

Let
\bm{U}\triangleq\bm{Q}_{1}
,
\bm{V}\triangleq\bm{Q}_{2}^{\top}\bm{P}^{\top}
, and
\bm{T}\triangleq\bm{S}^{\top}
, we complete the proof.

We observe that if we consider Equation (
) as the reduced QR decomposition of
\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}\\
\bm{R}_{12}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}
, then the complete orthogonal decomposition reduces to the ULV decomposition; see the next paragraph.

UTV Decomposition

The
UTV decomposition
goes further from QR and LQ decomposition by factoring the matrix into two orthogonal matrices
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\bm{T}\bm{V}
, where
\bm{U}
and
\bm{V}
are orthogonal, whilst
\bm{T}
is (upper/lower) triangular.
The resulting
\bm{T}
supports rank estimation. The matrix
\bm{T}
can be lower triangular which results in the ULV decomposition, or it can be upper triangular which results in the URV decomposition. The UTV framework shares a similar form as the singular value decomposition (SVD, see Theorem
) and can be regarded as inexpensive alternative to the SVD.

{theoremHigh}

[Full ULV decomposition
(
Hanson and Lawson 1969
)
]
Every
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
with rank
r
admits the following factorization:

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{L}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{V}^{\top},

where
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times p}
are two orthogonal matrices, and
\bm{L}\in\real^{r\times r}
is a lower triangular matrix with full rank.

The existence of the ULV decomposition is the consequence of the QR and LQ decomposition.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
For any rank-
r
matrix
\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]
, we can use a column permutation matrix
\bm{P}
(Definition
) such that the linearly independent columns of
\bm{X}
appear in the first
r
columns of
\bm{X}\bm{P}
. Without loss of generality, we assume
\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{r}
are the
r
linearly independent columns of
\bm{X}
and

\bm{X}\bm{P}=[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{r},\bm{b}_{r+1},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}].

Let
\bm{Z}=[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{r}]\in\real^{n\times r}
. Since any
\bm{b}_{i}
(
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
) is in the column space of
\bm{Z}
, we can find a transformation matrix
\bm{E}\in\real^{r\times(p-r)}
such that

[\bm{b}_{r+1},\bm{b}_{r+2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}]=\bm{Z}\bm{E}.

That is,

\bm{X}\bm{P}=[\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\ldots,\bm{b}_{r},\bm{b}_{r+1},\ldots,\bm{b}_{p}]=\bm{Z}[\bm{I}_{r},\bm{E}],

where
\bm{I}_{r}
is an
r\times r
identity matrix. Moreover,
\bm{Z}\in\real^{n\times r}
has full column rank such that its full QR decomposition is given by
\bm{Z}=\bm{U}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
, where
\bm{R}\in\real^{r\times r}
is an upper triangular matrix with full rank, and
\bm{U}
is an orthogonal matrix. This implies

\bm{X}\bm{P}=\bm{Z}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{r}&\bm{E}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{U}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{I}_{r}&\bm{E}\end{bmatrix}=\bm{U}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}&\bm{R}\bm{E}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}.

(3.83)

Since
\bm{R}
has full rank, this means

[\bm{R},\bm{R}\bm{E}]
also has full rank such that its full LQ decomposition is given by

[\bm{L},\boldsymbol{0}]\bm{V}_{0}
, where
\bm{L}\in\real^{r\times r}
is a lower triangular matrix, and
\bm{V}_{0}
is an orthogonal matrix; see Theorem
.
Substituting this into Equation (
), we have

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{L}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\bm{V}_{0}\bm{P}^{-1}.

Let
\bm{V}^{\top}\triangleq\bm{V}_{0}\bm{P}^{-1}
, which is a product of two orthogonal matrices and is also an orthogonal matrix. This completes the proof.

A second way to see the proof of the ULV decomposition is discussed in
Lu 2021b
via the rank-revealing QR (RRQR) decomposition and standard QR decomposition. However, we will not go into further detail here.

\paragrapharrow

Reduced ULV decomposition. Now suppose the ULV decomposition of matrix
\bm{X}
is

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{L}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\bm{V}^{\top}.

Let
\bm{U}_{1}\triangleq\bm{U}_{:,1:r}
and
\bm{V}_{1}\triangleq\bm{V}_{:,1:r}
, i.e.,
\bm{U}_{1}
contains only the first
r
columns of
\bm{U}
, and
\bm{V}_{1}
contains only the first
r
columns of
\bm{V}
. Then, we still have
\bm{X}=\bm{U}_{1}\bm{L}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}
. This is known as the
reduced ULV decomposition
.
The comparison between the reduced and the full ULV decomposition is shown in Figure
, where white entries are zero, and blues entries are not necessarily zero.

(a)

Reduced ULV decomposition.

(b)

Full ULV decomposition.

(c)

Reduced URV decomposition.

(d)

Full URV decomposition.

Figure 3.5:
Comparison between the reduced and full ULV, and between the reduced and full URV.

Similarly, we can also claim the URV decomposition as follows.

{theoremHigh}

[Full URV decomposition]
Every
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
with rank
r
admits the following decomposition:

\bm{X}=\bm{U}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{V}^{\top},

where
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times p}
are two orthogonal matrices, and
\bm{R}\in\real^{r\times r}
is an upper triangular matrix with full rank.

Again, there is a version of reduced URV decomposition and the difference between the full and reduced URV can be implied from the context, as shown in Figure
. The ULV and URV sometimes are collectively referred to as the UTV decomposition framework
(
Fierro and Hansen 1997
;
Golub and Van Loan 2013
)
.

We observe that the forms of ULV and URV are very close to the singular value decomposition (SVD). All of the three factor the matrix
\bm{X}
into two orthogonal matrices. Especially, there exists a set of basis for the four subspaces of
\bm{X}
in the fundamental theorem of linear algebra via the ULV and the URV. Taking ULV as an example, the first
r
columns of
\bm{U}
form an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, and the last
(n-r)
columns of
\bm{U}
form an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
. The first
r
columns of
\bm{V}
form an orthonormal basis for the row space
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, and the last
(p-r)
columns form an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{r}\},

\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{u}_{r+1},\bm{u}_{r+2},\ldots,\bm{u}_{n}\},

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(\bm{X}^{\top})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{v}_{1},\bm{v}_{2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{r}\},

\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\bm{X})=\mathrm{span}\{\bm{v}_{r+1},\bm{v}_{r+2},\ldots,\bm{v}_{p}\}.

The SVD goes further that there is a connection between the two pairs of orthonormal basis, i.e., transforming from column basis into row basis, or left null space basis into right null space basis; see Theorem
.

\paragrapharrow

Computation of URV.
The CPQR decomposition of a rank-deficient matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r
takes the form

\bm{X}\bm{P}=[\bm{Q}_{1},\bm{Q}_{2}]=\bm{Q}\bm{R}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}&\bm{R}_{12}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
, where
\bm{R}_{11}\in\real^{r\times r}
, with
r<p
, is nonsingular.
Here,
\bm{Q}_{1}
and
\bm{Q}_{2}
provide orthogonormal bases for
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
and
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}^{\top})
, respectively.
The elements in
\bm{R}_{12}
can be annihilated by postmultiplying
\bm{R}
by a sequence of Householder reflectors

[\bm{R}_{11},\bm{R}_{12}]\bm{H}_{r}\ldots\bm{H}_{2}\bm{H}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\bm{R}}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},\quad\bm{H}_{j}=\bm{I}-2\bm{u}_{j}\bm{u}_{j}^{\top},\quad j=r,r-1,\ldots,1,

where
\bm{u}_{j}
has nonzero elements only in positions
j,r+1,\ldots,p
.
The process is equivalent to a QL factorization of the transpose of the triangular factor
\bm{R}
,

\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}_{11}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\bm{R}_{12}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}=\widetilde{\bm{Q}}\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\bm{R}}^{\top}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},

and requires
2r^{2}(p-r)
flops.

This obtains the URV decomposition

\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{\bm{R}}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\bm{V}^{\top}\bm{P}^{\top},\quad\bm{V}\triangleq\bm{H}_{1}\ldots\bm{H}_{r}.

LS by UTV

In Section
, we introduced the LS solution using the full QR decomposition for matrices of full rank.
However, it often happens that the matrix may be rank-deficient. If
\bm{X}
does not have full column rank,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is not invertible.
Instead of using RRQR decomposition, we can also use the ULV/URV decomposition to compute the least squares solution, as illustrated in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[LS via ULV/URV for rank-deficient matrix]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with rank
r
and
n\geq p
. Suppose
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\bm{T}\bm{V}^{\top}
is its full ULV/URV decomposition with
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
\bm{V}^{\top}\in\real^{p\times p}
being orthogonal matrix matrices, and

\bm{T}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{T}_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize,

where
\bm{T}_{1}\in\real^{r\times r}
is a lower triangular matrix or an upper triangular matrix.
Suppose
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
is the response vector.
Then the OLS solution with minimum
\ell_{2}
norm to
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
is given by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{V}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{T}_{1}^{-1}\bm{c}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix},

where
\bm{c}_{1}
contains the first
r
components of
\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}
.

The proof follows immediately since
\bm{X}^{+}=\bm{V}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{T}_{1}^{-1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\bm{U}^{\top},
and
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}
by Theorem
.
Alternatively, a more straightforward way to show the minimum-norm solution is provided below.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\bm{T}\bm{V}^{\top}
is the full UTV decomposition of
\bm{X}
and
n\geq p
,
it follows that

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\left\lVert\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{U}\bm{T}\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{T}\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{T}_{1}\bm{e}_{1}-\bm{c}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert\bm{c}_{2}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the invariance under orthogonal transformation,
\bm{c}_{1}
is the first
r
components of
\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}
, and
\bm{c}_{2}
is the last
p-r
components of
\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}
;
\bm{e}_{1}
is the first
r
components of
\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and
\bm{e}_{2}
is the last
p-r
components of
\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
:

\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\bm{c}_{1}\\
\bm{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{V}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\bm{e}_{1}\\
\bm{e}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.

And the LS solution can be calculated by back/forward substitution of the upper/lower triangular system
\bm{T}_{1}\bm{e}_{1}=\bm{c}_{1}
, i.e.,
\bm{e}_{1}=\bm{T}_{1}^{-1}\bm{c}_{1}
. For
\boldsymbol{\beta}
to have the minimum
\ell_{2}
norm,
\bm{e}_{2}
must be zero. That is,

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{V}\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{T}_{1}^{-1}\bm{c}_{1}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

This completes the proof.

Indefinite least squares (ILS)
(
Chandrasekaran et al. 1998
)
.
For a matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
n\geq p
, and
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
, the
indefinite least squares (ILS)
problem is

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}),\quad\bm{X}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}_{1}\\
\bm{X}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\quad\bm{y}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{y}_{1}\\
\bm{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},

(3.84)

where
\bm{X}_{1}\in\real^{n_{1}\times p}
,

,
n_{1}+n_{2}=n
, and

\boldsymbol{0}&-\bm{I}_{n_{2}}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize

is the
signature matrix
. Note that
\bm{G}^{-1}=\bm{G}
.
A necessary condition for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
to be a solution of (

\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})=\boldsymbol{0}.

This implies that the residual vector
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
is
\bm{G}
-orthogonal to
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
(defined in (
3.79
)). Equivalently,
\boldsymbol{\beta}
solves the normal equation
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{y}
.

Chapter 4
Noise Disturbance and Parameter Estimation

4.1
From Random Noise to Gaussian Noise

I
In Section
, we examined the overdetermined system
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
denotes a input data matrix of full column rank,
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
represents the response vector, and the sample number
n
exceeds the number of features
p
such that the columns of
\bm{X}
are linearly independent.
The vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
contains the coefficients (or weights) of the linear model that relates the inputs to the outputs.

In Section
, we extend this framework by assuming that the observed output
\bm{y}
arises from an ideal function
g(\bm{X})
lying in the column space of
\bm{X}
:
g(\bm{X})\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.
Specifically, we model the randomness in observations through the equation:

{\mathbf{y}}=g(\bm{X})+\boldsymbol{\epsilon},

(4.1)

where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
represents a noise term.
This implies that the actual observations
\bm{y}
deviate from the true signal
g(\bm{X})=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
due to additive noise, resulting in the random variable
{\mathbf{y}}
.
This situation is illustrated in Figure
, which offers a visual interpretation of how noise affects the relationship between the “true model” and the observed data.
This visual representation provides a comprehensive overview of the problem.

Furthermore, we assume that the noise components
\epsilon_{i},\ i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
are independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and constant variance
\sigma^{2}
. For each observation
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, this leads to the following probabilistic model:

{\textnormal{y}}_{i}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x_{i1}+\beta_{2}x_{i2}+\ldots+\beta_{p-1}x_{i,p-1}+\epsilon_{i},

where
\beta_{0}
serves as the intercept or bias term.

Under the assumption of Gaussian noise, the likelihood function—representing the probability of observing the data given the model parameters—can be derived. This forms the basis for the
maximum likelihood estimator (MLE)
.
In particular, when the noise follows a normal distribution, the model corresponds to what is commonly known as the
Gauss-Markov linear model
, also referred to as
standard linear regression
or the
Gaussian linear model
.

More concretely, the likelihood function under Gaussian noise is constructed as the product of individual normal density functions. The likelihood of the observed data
\bm{y}
is therefore expressed as:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Likelihood}=\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(y_{i}\mid\bm{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta})

(4.2)
