\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(y_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{2}\right\}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\},

which follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution
\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
(Definition
), and
quantifies the plausibility of observing the dataset
\bm{y}
given the model parameters
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, input
\bm{X}
, and the assumed noise characteristics.
For computational convenience, it is standard practice to work with the
log-likelihood function
, obtained by taking the natural logarithm of the likelihood expression:

\displaystyle\text{Log-likelihood}=\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\ln\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\ln p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta}).

(4.3)

4.2
Parameter Estimation

At the beginning of this chapter, we introduced Gaussian noise into the linear model. As a result, we derived the likelihood function and the log-likelihood function, given in (
) and (
), respectively.
We have reviewed the concepts of random variables and probability distributions. In some cases, we know that a random vector
{\mathbf{x}}
follows a particular probability distribution
p(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
, but the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
of this distribution is unknown.
(e.g.,
\boldsymbol{\beta}
in the least squares model (
)).
Similarly, in a Gaussian distribution, the mean
\mu
, the variance
\sigma^{2}
, or both may be unknown.
However, if we can obtain observed data from such a random variable, we can use that data to estimate the unknown parameters of the model.
This observed data is typically referred to as “
training data
”.

Model estimation
or
parameter estimation
are methods of determining the values of parameters within a predefined model structure based on observed data .
In this section, we discuss how to estimate unknown model parameters using observed samples drawn from a given probability distribution.

4.2.1
Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

Consider a random vector
{\mathbf{x}}
, whose probability distribution is
p(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
, where
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is an unknown parameter of the distribution.
We are given a set of observations of this random variable, denoted by
\mathcal{X}=\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
, which are assumed to be i.i.d. samples from the same distribution
p(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
.

The probability of observing a single sample
\bm{x}_{i}
is
p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
. Therefore, the joint probability of observing all
n
samples is given by:

p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}).

Since the samples are i.i.d., the joint probability can be expressed as the product of individual probabilities:

p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}).

(4.4)

Now, we aim to determine the value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
that best explains the observed data. We assume
\boldsymbol{\theta}
lies in a parameter space
\Theta
. There are many possible values for
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, so we need a criterion to evaluate and compare them. A natural choice is the joint probability of the observed data under each candidate value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. Intuitively, the most plausible value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is the one that makes the observed data most probable.

This joint probability, viewed as a function of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, is called the
likelihood function
, denoted by
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})
, or simply
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
when the dataset
\mathcal{X}
is clear from context:

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})=p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}).

(4.5)

The optimal value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is the value that maximizes this likelihood function.
Therefore, the estimate of the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is given by:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}}=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}).

(4.6)

More formally, we define the maximum likelihood estimator as follows:

Definition 142
(Maximum likelihood estimator).

Let
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}
be a set of i.i.d. random samples from a distribution
F_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
with density
p(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
,
\forall\ \boldsymbol{\theta}\in\Theta
. Then the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is the value
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}}
such that

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})\leq\mathcal{L}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}}),\ \forall\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\Theta,

where
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
is the likelihood function for the i.i.d. collection. That is, the MLE of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
can be obtained by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}}=\mathop{\arg\max}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X}).

Notice that the likelihood function
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})
is a
random function
, since it depends on the random samples
\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}
. And the meaning of the likelihood function is the probability of these specific observed samples
\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
when the parameter is taken to be equal to
\boldsymbol{\theta}
rather than the probability of the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. In other words, it is the joint density of the sample, but viewed as a function of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.

Remark 143
(Estimation method vs estimator vs estimate).

Note that an estimation method is a general algorithm to produce the estimator. An estimate is the specific value that an estimator takes when observing the specific value, i.e., an estimator is a random variable and the realization of this random variable is called an estimate.

A key observation about the likelihood function is that it is defined as the product of individual probabilities
p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
.
Since each term in this product lies between 0 and 1, multiplying many such terms results in a very small number, often too small to be accurately represented by computer systems due to floating-point precision limits.
To avoid numerical underflow and simplify computation, especially during optimization, we typically work with the log-likelihood function, denoted by
\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})
or simply
\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})
when the data
\mathcal{X}
is understood:

\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})=\ln\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X}).

(4.7)

Maximizing the log-likelihood function
\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})
to obtain
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}}
is mathematically equivalent to maximizing the original likelihood function
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})
, since the logarithm is a monotone increasing function:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}}=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ln\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}).

(4.8)

\paragrapharrow

Estimation Methods For MLE.
To compute the maximum likelihood estimate, we need to maximize the (log-)likelihood function. There are three primary methods commonly used for this purpose:

1.

Analytic method
, also known as the direct solution method.
This approach involves finding critical points of the log-likelihood function by setting its gradient (i.e., vector of partial derivatives with respect to
\boldsymbol{\theta}
) equal to zero:

\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})=\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(4.9)

The solutions to this equation are called
stationary points
, which may correspond to local maxima, minima, or saddle points. Therefore, Equation (
) provides a necessary but not sufficient condition for a maximum.
The nature of these points (maximum or minimum) can be determined by the second derivative at the stationary points (see, for example,
Lu 2025
).
Not all problems can yield an analytic solution, and often it is not directly solvable.
When a unique maximum of the likelihood function exists, we refer to it as
the
maximum likelihood estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\mathop{\arg\max}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\Theta}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})
.
If the likelihood function is twice differentiable, this can be done by verifying the second derivative (Hessian matrix, see Problem
, or
Lu 2025
):

-\nabla^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})|_{\boldsymbol{\theta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\succ\boldsymbol{0}.

2.

Grid search method
.
When the parameter space
\Theta
is low-dimensional and bounded, we can discretize it into a grid of candidate values and evaluate the likelihood (or log-likelihood) at each point. The value that yields the highest likelihood is taken as the estimate. Although conceptually simple and guaranteed to find the global maximum (given a sufficiently fine grid), this method becomes computationally infeasible as the number of parameters increases, due to the exponential growth of the grid size (a problem known as the “curse of dimensionality”).

3.

Numerical method
.
These are the most widely used techniques in practice. They begin with an initial guess
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(1)}
, and iteratively update the parameter estimate using information from the gradient (and possibly the Hessian) of the log-likelihood function.
Gradient descent (ascent), Newton-Raphson, mirror descent (ascent), all fall into this category
(
Lu 2025
)
.
These iterative procedures are particularly effective in high-dimensional settings where analytic solutions are unavailable or grid search is impractical

In this chapter, we will primarily focus on deriving and applying the analytic method for computing maximum likelihood estimators.

4.2.2
Bayesian Estimation

Another related estimation method is called the
maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation
(see Section
).
Before discussing the details of MAP estimation, we first introduce the fundamental components of another widely used parameter estimation approach: the
Bayesian estimation
or the
Bayesian approach
; its application to linear models will be discussed in detail in Chapter
.
The foundational idea of Bayesian estimation is attributed to
Thomas Bayes
, who developed the concept but passed away before publishing it. Fortunately, his friend
Richard Price
continued his work and published it in 1764. The same principle was later independently rediscovered by
Laplace
at the end of the 18-th century.
In this section, we present the basic concepts of the Bayesian approach.

In MLE, the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is treated as a fixed numerical quantity, and only the variable
\mathcal{X}
is considered random.
The probability distribution of the random variable
\mathcal{X}
is described by a parametric distribution
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
, where observed samples are used to estimate the unknown parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. This leads to an estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
, which is then substituted back into the conditional probability function
p(\mathcal{X}\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
, yielding an estimated distribution for
\mathcal{X}
. This distribution can subsequently be used for predicting new samples:
p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
.

Prior Distribution and Joint Probability

A key distinction in the Bayesian framework is that unknown parameters are treated as random variables. This aligns with the Bayesian perspective on uncertainty, which treats all uncertain quantities probabilistically by modeling them as random variables and applying the laws of probability to reason about them. Unlike MLE, which focuses on finding the most likely value of a parameter, Bayesian methods aim to account for all possible values through integration over the full parameter space.

More formally, in the Bayesian framework, the model parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is treated as a random variable. A sample is generated jointly by
\boldsymbol{\theta}
and
\mathcal{X}
. Let the probability distribution of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
be
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
, known as the
prior distribution
. The random variable
\mathcal{X}
depends on
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, and thus its distribution is given by the conditional probability
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
. Together, these define a joint probability distribution from the chain rule of probability:

p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}).

Here, the conditional probability distribution
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
is the probability distribution of variable
\mathcal{X}
, which is known.
While the prior
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
reflects our initial beliefs or knowledge about the parameter before observing any data. Our ultimate goal is to determine the marginal distribution of
\mathcal{X}
, which can then be used for prediction.
There are two main approaches to achieve this:

1.

Find an estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, and then obtain the conditional probability distribution
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
. Use the conditional probability distribution
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
as the probability distribution of
\mathcal{X}
for subsequent prediction and analysis. Maximum likelihood estimation falls into this category.

2.

Use the joint distribution
p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})
to compute the marginal distribution of
\mathcal{X}
by integrating out the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
:

p(\mathcal{X})=\int p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}=\int p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}.

In this case, the marginal distribution
p(\mathcal{X})
directly accounts for all possible values of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, weighted by their prior probabilities. This is the core idea behind Bayesian estimation.

The challenge with the second approach lies in specifying the prior distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
. Without knowledge of the prior, it is not possible to compute the marginal distribution
p(\mathcal{X})
. Bayesian estimation belongs to the second method, utilizing Bayes’ theorem to update our beliefs about
\boldsymbol{\theta}
in light of observed data, thereby leading to a full
posterior distribution
over the parameter.

Bayes’ Theorem

We know that the variables
\boldsymbol{\theta}
and
\mathcal{X}
form a joint probability
p(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathcal{X})
, and these two variables are not independent of each other.
In this context, the variable
\boldsymbol{\theta}
influences the variable
\mathcal{X}
, and there exists a “cause-effect” relationship between them:
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is the “cause” or
prior
, and
\mathcal{X}
is the “effect.”
Using the chain rule of probability, the joint distribution
p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})
can be expressed as a product of conditional probabilities. Importantly, the application of the chain rule depends on the dependence (or independence) relationships between the variables, not on the order in which they appear. Therefore, the joint probability
p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})
can be decomposed in two equivalent ways:

p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\mathcal{X})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X}).

Rearranging terms yields that

p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})=\frac{p(\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})}{p(\mathcal{X})}.

(4.10)

This equation is known as
Bayes’ theorem
. To define it formally:

Bayesian modeling and statistics are fundamentally driven by Bayes’ theorem. Formally, the theorem is expressed as follows.

{theoremHigh}
[Bayes’ theorem]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}
be a sample space and let
B_{1},B_{2},\ldots,B_{K}
be a partition of
{\mathbb{S}}
such that (1).
\cup_{k}B_{k}={\mathbb{S}}
and (2).
B_{i}\cap B_{j}=\varnothing
for all
i\neq j
.
Let further
A
be any event. Then it follows that

P(B_{k}\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B_{k})P(B_{k})}{P(A)}=\frac{P(A\mid B_{k})P(B_{k})}{\sum_{i=1}^{K}P(A\mid B_{i})P(B_{i})}.

The core of Bayes’ theorem is the following transformation:

p(\text{cause}\mid\text{effect})=\frac{p(\text{cause})p(\text{effect}\mid\text{cause})}{p(\text{effect})}.

In many practical situations, we observe the “effect”—that is, we have observed values of the variable
\mathcal{X}
—but we do not know what caused this effect, i.e., the value of the variable
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is unknown. In such cases, we can use Bayes’ theorem to infer the likely cause, a process commonly referred to as
Bayesian inference
or
Bayesian estimation
.

Bayesian Inference

We consider variable
\boldsymbol{\theta}
as the “cause” variable and variable
\mathcal{X}
as the “effect” variable.
The observed value of
\mathcal{X}
represents the observed result. We express the relationship between the observed sample
\mathcal{X}
and the variable
\boldsymbol{\theta}
using Bayes’ theorem:

p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{p(\mathcal{X})},

(4.11)

where

p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})
represents the
posterior probability distribution
of the cause variable
\boldsymbol{\theta}
based on the effect
\mathcal{X}
.
The term “posterior” indicates that this distribution is updated after observing the data (i.e., after gaining experience from the effect).

p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
represents the
prior probability distribution
, which reflects our knowledge or assumptions about
\boldsymbol{\theta}
before observing the data. In practical applications, the prior can be chosen based on domain knowledge or previous experience. If no prior information is available, it is common to assume a uniform distribution for
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
.

p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
is the likelihood function, which represents the probability of observing the sample
\mathcal{X}
given the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. If the observed samples are independent and identically distributed, this term can be written as:

p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}).

p(\mathcal{X})
is referred to as the
evidence
or
marginal likelihood
. It represents the total probability of observing the data
\mathcal{X}
, regardless of the value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. It acts as a normalizing constant that ensures the posterior distribution integrates to 1 (i.e., it is a valid probability distribution). Mathematically, it is defined as:

p(\mathcal{X})=\int p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})d\boldsymbol{\theta}.

In other words, once the sample set
\mathcal{X}
is determined, the value of
p(\mathcal{X})
remains constant.

In summary, the Bayesian inference formula in (
) can be expressed in the following form:

\text{Posterior probability}=\frac{\text{Likelihood}\times\text{Prior}}{\text{Evidence}}\propto\text{Likelihood}\times\text{Prior},

(4.12)

where “
\propto
” means “proportional to” (see Problem
).
However, using (
) to infer
p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})
still has two difficulties:

1.

Choosing an appropriate prior distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
. This should ideally reflect prior knowledge about the parameters, but such information is often unavailable.

2.

Evaluating the denominator
p(\mathcal{X})
, which involves integrating over all possible values of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. The complexity of this integration depends heavily on the form of the prior
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
.

Note that, for brevity, we previously omitted the hyper-parameter from the prior distribution.
When including a hyper-parameter in the prior, Equation (
) becomes:

\displaystyle p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\alpha})

\displaystyle=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{\int_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}

(4.13)

\displaystyle=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{\int_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}\propto p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha}).

where the marginal likelihood or evidence becomes
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})
.
This form will prove useful when discussing
Occam’s Razor
and
Occam factor
in Section
.
For the remainder of this section, we will continue using the version without a hyper-parameter.

Theoretically, the prior distribution should encode any existing or priori knowledge (e.g., the parameter is sparse or dense) about the parameters. For example, a prior for a system reducing over-clustering might assign a higher probability to a larger cluster than to a small cluster
(
Lu 2021d
)
.
However, in many cases, little or no prior information is available. In such situations, we use a special type of prior called a
noninformative prior
. The purpose of a noninformative prior is to have minimal influence on the posterior distribution
(
Gelman et al. 2013
)
, allowing the data to “speak for itself.”

Another commonly used approach is the
conjugate prior
. In Bayesian inference, a conjugate prior is a prior distribution such that the resulting posterior distribution belongs to the same family of distributions as the prior. This simplifies computation and interpretation.
Conjugate priors are widely used due to their mathematical convenience. Further details can be found in Chapter
.

The elegance of Bayes’ theorem becomes apparent as it distinguishes inference from modeling. The model, encompassing the prior distribution and the likelihood, fully dictates the posterior distribution, leaving the computation of the inference as the only remaining step.
More generally, the Bayesian approach—in a nutshell—is to assume a prior distribution for any unknowns (
\boldsymbol{\theta}
in our case), and then just follow the rules of probability to answer any questions of interest. For example, when we find the parameter based on the maximum posterior probability of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, we turn to the
maximum a posteriori (MAP)
estimation; see the next section.

Prediction

The posterior distribution alllows us to compute the probability density at a new coming data point
\bm{x}_{\text{new}}
, called the
posterior predictive distribution
, by averaging over both the uncertainty in the model and in the parameters:

p(\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\mathcal{X})=\int p(\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}.

If the problem follows from a generative process
{\mathbf{y}}\sim p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})
, e.g.,
{\textnormal{y}}\sim\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}+\epsilon
in the Gauss-Markov linear model.
Then the predictive distribution is

p(\bm{y}^{\prime}\mid\bm{x}_{\text{new}},\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})=\int p(\bm{y}^{\prime}\mid\bm{x}_{\text{new}},\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}.

The posterior predictive distribution can be employed to design test statistics of interest and then compare the posterior predictive distributions to the test statistics of observed values so as to determine the best model among several candidates. This process is known as
model checking or selection
; see Chapter
.

4.2.3
Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) Estimation

One major challenge in Bayesian estimation is computing the marginal likelihood
p(\mathcal{X})
, which requires integrating over the entire parameter space. This integration can be computationally expensive or even analytically intractable.

However, if our goal is only to make predictions and not to fully characterize the posterior distribution, we may instead use a point estimate of the parameters. This approach resembles maximum likelihood estimation, but incorporates prior information.

In Bayesian estimation, one common method is to compute the expected value of the posterior distribution as the estimate of the parameters. However, calculating this expectation requires full knowledge of the posterior distribution.
Alternatively, we can use the value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
that maximizes the posterior distribution as our estimate. This is known as
maximum a posteriori (MAP)
estimation:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X}).

Formally, the MAP estimator is defined as follows.

Definition 144
(Maximum a posterior estimator).

The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the value of the parameter that maximizes the posterior distribution.
It balances information from the prior distribution and information from the likelihood.
The influence of the prior is stronger when the likelihood provides less information, and vice versa.

Recall from (
) that the denominator
p(\mathcal{X})
of the posterior probability is a constant with respect to
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.
Therefore, the posterior probability is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood:

\text{Posterior Probability}=\frac{\text{Likelihood}\times\text{Prior}}{\text{Evidence}}\propto\text{Likelihood}\times\text{Prior}.

When performing MAP estimation, it is not necessary to compute the exact form of the posterior distribution, since we are only interested in its maximum. Thus, maximizing the numerator alone suffices:

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}

\displaystyle=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})\equiv\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\text{Likelihood}\times\text{Prior}

\displaystyle=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ln\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})

\displaystyle=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\underbrace{\ln\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})}_{\text{Log-likelihood}}+\underbrace{\ln p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}_{\text{Log Prior}}.

Compared to the MLE in (
), we see that MAP estimation also maximizes the likelihood, but it includes an additional term—the log prior—which regularizes the estimate based on our prior beliefs about
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. In many ways, MAP estimation resembles maximum likelihood estimation, but it incorporates prior information, making it more robust in cases where data is limited.

In fact, incorporating a prior in MAP estimation is equivalent to adding a regularization term to the loss function. Specifically, introducing a Laplace prior for the parameters is equivalent to applying
\ell_{1}
regularization, while using a Gaussian prior corresponds to
\ell_{2}
regularization.

4.2.4
Laplace Approximation

We previously noted that the posterior distribution can be used to answer any questions of interest, including obtaining the MAP estimate:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\Theta}p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\Theta}p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}).

The
Laplace approximation
involves approximating the posterior using a Gaussian distribution centered at the mode of the posterior (i.e., the MAP estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}
), therefore approximating the posterior distribution of a model’s parameters when the exact form of that distribution is intractable or computationally expensive to calculate
(
Kass and Raftery 1995
;
MacKay 1998
;
Friston et al. 2007
)
.
Define the logarithm of the posterior distribution as

\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\ln p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\ln p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})+\ln p(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\ln p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})+\mathcal{C},

where again
\ln
is the natural logarithm (to base
e
), and
\mathcal{C}
represents a constant w.r.t.
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.
According to the quadratic approximation theorem (Theorem
), assuming that the parameter space
\Theta
is an open set (the gradient of the MAP has vanished gradient), we have

\displaystyle\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})

\displaystyle\approx\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\nabla\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})^{\top}\nabla^{2}\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})

\displaystyle=\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})^{\top}\nabla^{2}\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}),

where we let
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\triangleq\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}
for brevity.
Therefore, the log marginal likelihood can be obtained by

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \ln p(\mathcal{X})&=\ln\int p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})d\boldsymbol{\theta}=\ln\int\exp\{\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})\}d\boldsymbol{\theta}\\
&\approx\ln p(\mathcal{X}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\ln p(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\frac{p}{2}\ln(2\pi)-\frac{1}{2}\ln\left\lvert\nabla^{2}\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\right\rvert,\end{aligned}

where the last approximation comes from the definition of the multivariate Gaussian distribution, and
p
is the dimensionality of the parameter vector:
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{p}
.
Therefore, the Laplace approximation of the marginal likelihood becomes

p(\mathcal{X})_{\text{Lap}}=\underbrace{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})}_{\text{data likelihood under MAP}}\,\underbrace{p(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})}_{\text{penalty from prior}}\underbrace{\left\lvert 2\pi(\nabla^{2}\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}))^{-1}\right\rvert}_{\text{local curvature}}.

(4.14)

Thus, the Laplace approximation contains three terms: the data likelihood under the MAP estimate, a penalty term from the prior, and a volume term due to the local curvature.

While the Laplace approximation can be useful and computationally efficient, it has several drawbacks.

Gaussian assumption
: Firstly, the Laplace approximation assumes that the posterior distribution is approximately Gaussian, which might not be a good assumption, especially for multimodal posteriors or posteriors that have heavy tails or skewed distributions. This can lead to inaccurate estimates of the uncertainty around the parameters.
The Gaussian approximation is also ill-suited for parameters that are bounded, constrained, or positive, such as mixing proportions or precisions, because it assigns nonzero probability mass to values outside the valid parameter range. While this issue can often be mitigated by reparameterizing the variables (see, for example,
MacKay 1998
), there remains an undesirable aspect: in the non-asymptotic regime, the approximation lacks invariance to reparameterization.

Mode dependence
: The approximation relies heavily on the location of the mode of the posterior distribution. If the mode is not well-defined or if there are multiple modes, the Laplace approximation may perform poorly.

Curvature assumption
: The Laplace approximation assumes that the curvature of the posterior distribution around the mode is constant, which is often not the case for complex models. This can lead to poor performance when the posterior distribution has significant curvature changes over its support.

Computation of Hessian
: Computing the Hessian matrix, which is required to determine the variance of the Gaussian approximation, can be computationally expensive and unstable, particularly for models with many parameters or non-smooth likelihood functions. The computation of the volume term, which depends on the determinant of the Hessian matrix (
|\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})|
), poses another challenge. Calculating the derivatives within the Hessian requires
\mathcal{O}(np^{2})
operations, followed by
\mathcal{O}(p^{3})
operations to find the determinant, making it computationally intensive for high-dimensional problems. To simplify this process, approximations often ignore off-diagonal elements or assume a block-diagonal structure for the Hessian, effectively disregarding interdependencies among parameters.

Sensitivity to priors
: The Laplace approximation can be sensitive to the choice of prior, especially when the prior is not weakly informative. In such cases, the approximation might not accurately reflect the shape of the posterior distribution.

Dimensionality issues
: As the number of parameters increases, the Laplace approximation becomes less reliable due to the curse of dimensionality, where the volume of the parameter space grows exponentially and the Gaussian approximation becomes increasingly poor.

Despite these limitations, the Laplace approximation can still be a valuable tool, especially when used alongside other methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling or variational inference, which can provide more accurate representations of the posterior distribution
(
Hoff 2009
;
Lu 2023b
)
.

4.2.5
Mean Squared Error (MSE) of an Estimator

Let
{\mathbf{x}}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{n}
be
n
i.i.d. random vector variables, i.e., a random sample drawn from the distribution
p(\bm{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
, where
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is unknown. An
estimator
of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is any function of (only) these
n
random variables; in other words, it is a statistic
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=T({\mathbf{x}}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{n})
.
As discussed in previous sections, there are several methods available for obtaining an estimator of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, such as maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian methods.

A key challenge arises when multiple estimation methods can be applied to the same problem, leading us to choose among different estimators. In some cases, different methods may yield the same estimator (for example, in least squares estimation under certain conditions with MLE), simplifying the comparison. However, in many situations, each method results in a distinct estimator. Therefore, we need criteria to evaluate and compare their performance.
There are various measures used to assess the quality of an estimator. Some are designed for small samples, while others describe the behavior of an estimator as the sample size grows—these are known as asymptotic properties of estimators.

To evaluate how close an estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is to the true value
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, we often consider the deviation
\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{1}
or, for computational convenience, the squared error
\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
. Since
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
is itself a random variable (depending on the random sample), we must take expectation over the sampling distribution to assess its overall accuracy. This leads to the following definition:

Definition 145
(Mean squared error of an estimator).

Let
{\mathbf{x}}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{n}
be
n
i.i.d. random vector variables.
The mean squared error (MSE) or the risk function of an estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=T({\mathbf{x}}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{n})
of a parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is the function of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
defined by
\mathbb{E}[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}]
(the expectation is taken with respect to the random variables
{\mathbf{x}}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{n}
), and this is denoted as
\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})
.

Notice that the MSE quantifies the average squared difference between the estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
and the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, providing a reasonable way to assess the performance of an estimator. While other measures, such as the
mean absolute error (MAE)
, defined as
\mathbb{E}\big[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{1}\big]
, are also valid, the MSE has two main advantages: it is mathematically convenient and allows for a useful decomposition into bias and variance.

Lemma 146
(Bias-variance decomposition).

For any estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
of
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{p}
, the mean squared error of the estimator has the following decomposition:

\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}]-\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]\triangleq\left\lVert\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\theta}_{i}].

That is, a sum of a bias term and a variance term.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Write out the mean squared error

\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\big[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\big]-2\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbb{E}\big[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\big]+\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\big[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\big]-\big\lVert\mathbb{E}\big[{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\big]\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert{\mathbb{E}\big[{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\big]}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2},

which completes the proof.

The bias of an estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
of a parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is defined the difference between the expected value of the estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
and the true parameter value
\boldsymbol{\theta}
; that is,
\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}]-\boldsymbol{\theta}
. An estimator whose bias is identically equal to
\boldsymbol{0}
is called an unbiased estimator and satisfies
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}]=\boldsymbol{\theta}
for all
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.

Definition 147
(Biased and unbiased estimators).

Given the estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
of a parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, the quantity
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}]-\boldsymbol{\theta}=\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})
is called the bias of the estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
with respect to the true parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.
When the bias at some coordinate of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is positive, we have overestimation; conversely, when it is negative, we have underestimation; when the bias is zero, we refer to it as an unbiased estimator.

Suppose both
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
and
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
are unbiased estimators of an unknown parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.
Then, any linear combination of these estimators of the form
\bm{t}=w\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+(1-w)\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
, where
w
is any scalar weight, is also an unbiased estimator of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.

Thus, the MSE of an estimator has two components, one measures the
variability of the estimator (precision)
and the other measures its
bias (accuracy)
.
An estimator with good MSE performance has both low variance and low bias. To find such an estimator, one must carefully balance and control both sources of error.
While many commonly used estimators are unbiased or approximately unbiased, it’s important to note that being unbiased does not necessarily imply a small MSE. In fact, there is often a trade-off between bias and variance. A small increase in bias may lead to a significant reduction in variance, resulting in an overall improvement in MSE.
For an unbiased estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
, the bias term vanishes, and the MSE simplifies to:

\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbb{E}\big[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\big]=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\theta}_{i}]\triangleq\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}].

In this case, the MSE is simply the sum of the variances of the individual components—that is, the total variance of the estimator.

Example 148
(Estimators for Gaussian parameters).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be i.i.d. from
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
with mean
\mu
and variance
\sigma^{2}
, then the sample mean
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
is an unbiased estimator for
\mu
, and the sample variance
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}\triangleq\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\bar{{\textnormal{x}}})^{2}}{n-1}
is an unbiased estimator for
\sigma^{2}
.
To see this, we have

\mathbb{E}[\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]+\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]+\ldots+\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]}{n}=\mu.

Therefore,
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}
is an unbiased estimator.
Since

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}\left[\frac{{\textnormal{x}}_{1}+{\textnormal{x}}_{2}+\ldots+{\textnormal{x}}_{n}}{n}\right]=\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]+\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]+\ldots+\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]}{n^{2}}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n},

the MSE of
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}
is

\mathrm{MSE}(\bar{{\textnormal{x}}},\mu)=\mathbb{E}[(\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}-\mu)^{2}]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}]=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}.

It can be shown that
\frac{(n-1){\textnormal{S}}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\sim\chi^{2}_{(n-1)}
. Using the properties of the Chi-squared distribution (Definition
), we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(n-1){\textnormal{S}}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right]

\displaystyle=n-1\quad\implies\quad\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{S}}^{2}]=\sigma^{2};

\displaystyle\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}\left[\frac{(n-1){\textnormal{S}}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right]

\displaystyle=2(n-1)\quad\implies\quad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{S}}^{2}]=\frac{2\sigma^{4}}{n-1}.

Therefore,
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
is an unbiased estimator for
\sigma^{2}
, and its MSE is:

\mathrm{MSE}({\textnormal{S}}^{2},\sigma^{2})=\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{S}}^{2}-\sigma^{2})^{2}]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{S}}^{2}]=\frac{2\sigma^{4}}{n-1}.

An alternative estimator for
\sigma^{2}
of a Gaussian distribution is the maximum likelihood estimator:

\widehat{\sigma}^{2}\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\bar{{\textnormal{x}}})^{2}=\frac{n-1}{n}{\textnormal{S}}^{2}.

Therefore, we have

\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\sigma}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{n-1}{n}{\textnormal{S}}^{2}\big]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^{2}
,
such that
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}
is a biased estimator for
\sigma^{2}
. The variance of
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}
can also be calculated as

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\sigma}^{2}]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\frac{n-1}{n}{\textnormal{S}}^{2}]=\frac{(n-1)^{2}}{n^{2}}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{S}}^{2}]=\frac{2(n-1)\sigma^{4}}{n^{2}}.

The MSE of
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}
is then

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\sigma}^{2}-\sigma^{2})^{2}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\sigma}^{2}]+(\mathrm{Bias})^{2}=\frac{2(n-1)\sigma^{4}}{n^{2}}+\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^{2}-\sigma^{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{(2n-1)\sigma^{4}}{n^{2}}.

Comparing the two estimators:

\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\sigma}^{2},\sigma^{2})=\frac{(2n-1)\sigma^{4}}{n^{2}}<\frac{2n\sigma^{4}}{n^{2}}=\frac{2\sigma^{4}}{n}<\frac{2\sigma^{4}}{n-1}=\mathrm{MSE}({\textnormal{S}}^{2},\sigma^{2}).

This shows that
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}
has a smaller MSE than
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
. Therefore, by trading off some bias, we achieve a reduction in overall estimation risk when measured by MSE.

The above example does not necessarily imply that
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
should be discarded as an estimator of
\sigma^{2}
.
While
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}
may have a lower MSE, it systematically underestimates
{\sigma}^{2}
, which might make it less desirable depending on the context or interpretation.

In general, since MSE depends on the true parameter value, there is no single “best” estimator across all possible values of the parameter. Often, the MSEs of two estimators will cross—one performs better for certain parameter values, while the other performs better for others. Still, such comparisons can offer useful guidance in selecting between estimators.

One way to make the problem of finding a “best” estimator more manageable is to restrict the class of estimators considered. A common approach is to focus only on unbiased estimators and choose the one with the smallest variance. This leads to the concept of the
best unbiased estimator (BUE)
or the
minimum variance unbiased (MVU) estimator
.
If two estimators,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{1}
and
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{2}
, are both unbiased for a parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, meaning
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{1}]=\boldsymbol{\theta}
and
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{2}]=\boldsymbol{\theta}
, then their MSEs reduce to their variances. In this case, we prefer the estimator with the smaller variance.

Example 149
(Estimators for Gaussian parameters, CNT.).

Consider the same setting as in Example
. One might ask: what value of
\gamma
makes the quantity
\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{n}({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\bar{{\textnormal{x}}})^{2}
achieve the smallest MSE?
Note that when
\gamma=\frac{1}{n-1}
, we obtain the sample variance
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
from Example
; whereas when
\gamma=\frac{1}{n}
, we obtain the estimator
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}
.
Let

\displaystyle{\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma}

\displaystyle\triangleq\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{n}({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\bar{{\textnormal{x}}})^{2}=\gamma(n-1){\textnormal{S}}^{2};

\displaystyle\zeta

\displaystyle\triangleq\gamma(n-1).

Then

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma}]

\displaystyle=\gamma(n-1)\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{S}}^{2}]=\gamma(n-1)\sigma^{2}=\zeta\sigma^{2};

\displaystyle\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma}]

\displaystyle=\gamma^{2}(n-1)^{2}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{S}}^{2}]=\frac{2\zeta^{2}}{(n-1)}\sigma^{4}.

The MSE of
{\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma}
can be obtained as

\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}({\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma},\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma}]+(\mathrm{Bias})^{2}=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma}]+\left[\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma}]-\sigma^{2}\right]^{2}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma}]+(\zeta\sigma^{2}-\sigma^{2})^{2}=\frac{2\zeta^{2}}{(n-1)}\sigma^{4}+(\zeta-1)^{2}\sigma^{4}\triangleq g(\zeta)\sigma^{4},

where
g(\zeta)\triangleq\frac{2\zeta^{2}}{(n-1)}+(\zeta-1)^{2}
.
The function
g(\zeta)
reaches its minimum at
\zeta=\frac{n-1}{n+1}
.
The minimal MSE is
\mathrm{MSE}({\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma},\sigma^{2})=\frac{2}{n+1}\sigma^{4}
, with
\gamma(n-1)=\zeta=\frac{n-1}{n+1}
, i.e.,
\gamma=\frac{1}{n+1}
.
Therefore, for
\gamma=\frac{1}{n+1}
and
n>1
, we have:

\mathrm{MSE}({\textnormal{s}}^{2}_{\gamma},\sigma^{2})=\frac{2\sigma^{4}}{n+1}<\frac{(2n-1)\sigma^{4}}{n^{2}}=\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\sigma}^{2},\sigma^{2})<\frac{2\sigma^{4}}{n-1}=\mathrm{MSE}({\textnormal{S}}^{2},\sigma^{2}).

Thus, the estimator with the smallest MSE corresponds to an unbiased estimator.

Example 150
(Estimators for Laplace parameters).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be i.i.d. random variables with the probability density function
p(x\mid b)\triangleq\frac{1}{2b}\exp\left(-\frac{\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{b}\right)
(Definition
).
The maximum likelihood estimator for
b
,
\widehat{b}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}|{\textnormal{x}}_{i}|}{n}
, is unbiased.
To see this, we first calculate
\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert]
and
\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{2}]
as

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert]

\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left\lvert x\right\rvert p(x\mid b)\,dx=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left\lvert x\right\rvert\frac{1}{2b}\exp\left(-\frac{\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{b}\right)\,dx

\displaystyle=b\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x}{b}\exp\left(-\frac{x}{b}\right)d\frac{x}{b}=b\int_{0}^{\infty}te^{-t}dt=b\Gamma(2)=b

and

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{2}]

\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left\lvert x\right\rvert^{2}p(x\mid b)\,dx=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left\lvert x\right\rvert^{2}\frac{1}{2b}\exp\left(-\frac{\left\lvert x\right\rvert}{b}\right)\,dx

\displaystyle=b^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{2}}{b^{2}}\exp\left(-\frac{x}{b}\right)d\frac{x}{b}=b^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{2}e^{-t}dt=b^{2}\Gamma(3)=2b^{2}.

Therefore,

\mathbb{E}[\widehat{b}]=\mathbb{E}\left[(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\right\rvert+\ldots+\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\right\rvert)/n\right]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\right\rvert]+\ldots+\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\right\rvert]}{n}=b.

Thus,
\widehat{b}
is an unbiased estimator for
b
.
Since the estimator is unbiased, its MSE is equal to its variance:

\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{b},b)

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{b}-b)^{2}]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{b}]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}\left[\frac{\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\right\rvert+\ldots+\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\right\rvert}{n}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\right\rvert]+\ldots+\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\right\rvert]}{n^{2}}=\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\right\rvert])}{n}

\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert])^{2}}{n}=\frac{2b^{2}-b^{2}}{n}=\frac{b^{2}}{n}.

Once again, the large the sample size, the smaller the variance.

4.3
Estimation for OLS

As mentioned above, the main focus of this chapter is to derive the MLE for the OLS model (i.e., the Gauss-Markov linear model).
In this section, we will derive the analytic solutions of the MLE for OLS under both Gaussian and Laplace noise.

4.3.1
Gaussian Noise

From the likelihood arising from Gaussian disturbances, as given in (
) or its logarithmic form in (
), we can obtain the maximum likelihood estimator for the Gauss-Markov linear model.

{theoremHigh}
[MLE for LS under i.i.d. Gaussian disturbance]
Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
, which is known as the
Gauss-Markov linear model
or
Gaussian linear regression model
.
Assume that
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full rank with
n\geq p
(i.e., its rank is
p
). Then, the maximum likelihood estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is given by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}\penalty\

for all values of
\sigma^{2}
.
And the maximum likelihood estimate of
\sigma^{2}
is given by

\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

which is equal to the average sum of squares due to error.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Following Equation (
), the likelihood of this model under the given parameters
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\sigma^{2}
is

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2})=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\},

and the log-likelihood is given by

\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2})=-\frac{1}{2}\left\{n\ln 2\pi+n\ln\sigma^{2}+\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\}.

Maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood since the logarithm is a monotonically increasing function.
Thus, the MLE of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is obtained by solving

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\mathop{\arg\max}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{-(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})},

where constant terms have been omitted.
To find the solution, we solve the following optimization problem:

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}

\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\qquad\implies\qquad\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}.

Therefore, the MLE of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is given by
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
, which holds for any value of
\sigma^{2}
. This result coincides with the OLS estimator.

To find the MLE of the variance parameter
\sigma^{2}
, consider

\displaystyle\widehat{\sigma}^{2}

\displaystyle=\mathop{\arg\max}_{\sigma^{2}}\left\{\mathop{\arg\max}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2})}\right\}=\mathop{\arg\max}_{\sigma^{2}}{\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^{2})}

\displaystyle=\mathop{\arg\max}_{\sigma^{2}}{-\frac{1}{2}\left\{n\ln 2\pi+n\ln\sigma^{2}+\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\}}.

By taking the derivative with respect to
\sigma^{2}
and setting it to zero, we obtain

\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

It can also be shown that the second partial derivative of the log-likelihood functions are negative, which completes the proof.

Under Gaussian noise, the MLE of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is identical to the OLS estimator because both are derived by minimizing the same sum of squared error
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})
.
Therefore, in the following sections, we will not distinguish between the MLE and the OLS estimator of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and the two terms will be used interchangeably.

In Section
, we will show that the maximum likelihood estimator
\frac{1}{n}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
of the variance parameter is a
biased estimator
of
\sigma^{2}
(Definition
). An unbiased estimator is given by
\frac{1}{n-p}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.

\paragrapharrow

Gaussian Noise for GLS
Previously, we consider the linear model
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
and
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full column rank with
n\geq p
, i.e., rank is
p
:

{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}).

(4.15)

Now, consider a more general case in which the covariance matrix of the noise vector
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
is not diagonal:

\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega})\qquad\implies\qquad{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}).

(4.16)

where the error covariance matrix
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
is symmetric positive definite, and
\boldsymbol{\Omega}\neq\bm{I}
.
This is known as the
generalized Gauss-Markov linear model
and corresponds to the
generalized least squares (GLS)
problem defined in (
2.44
).

We can factorize
\boldsymbol{\Omega}
into its symmetric square roots
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2}
(Theorem
). Let
{\mathbf{z}}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}{\mathbf{y}}
, we have

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{z}}]=\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{z}}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}.

In other words,

{\mathbf{z}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}).

(4.17)

Comparing the form of Equation (
) with the original model in Equation (
),
we observe that
{\mathbf{z}}
now follows a standard linear model with i.i.d. Gaussian errors. This allows us to apply ordinary least squares or maximum likelihood estimation on
{\mathbf{z}}
, projecting onto the column space of
\bm{A}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1/2}\bm{X}
, to estimate
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
Using the result from Theorem
, the maximum likelihood estimators for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\sigma^{2}
can be expressed as:

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=(\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A})^{-1}\bm{A}^{\top}{\mathbf{z}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}{\mathbf{y}};

\displaystyle\widehat{\sigma}^{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}({\mathbf{z}}-\bm{A}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}({\mathbf{z}}-\bm{A}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{n}({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

Similarly, other estimators in Table
can be obtained accordingly.

{theoremHigh}

[MLE for GLS under full Gaussian disturbance]
Consider a Gauss-Markov linear model
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
with
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
of
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
and symmetric positive definite error covariance matrix
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\in\real^{n\times n}
, which is known as the
generalized Gauss-Markov linear model
.
Then, the maximum likelihood estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is given by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{y}

for all values of
\sigma^{2}
.
And the maximum likelihood estimate of
\sigma^{2}
is

\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

4.3.2
Laplace Noise

The maximum likelihood estimation framework can be applied to various types of noise models in the context of linear regression. While the Gaussian noise model is commonly used due to its mathematical convenience and desirable statistical properties, other noise models may be more appropriate depending on the nature of the data.
One such alternative is the
Laplace noise model
, which assumes zero-mean errors:

{\textnormal{y}}_{i}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x_{i1}+\beta_{2}x_{i2}+\ldots+\beta_{p-1}x_{i,p-1}+\epsilon_{i},\,\,\,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\},

where
\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{L}(0,b)
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
(Definition
).
Compared to the Gaussian distribution, the Laplace distribution has heavier tails, making it more robust to outliers or deviations from normality.
As with the Gaussian case, the likelihood function for the full dataset is the product of individual probability density functions:

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2b}\exp\left\{-\frac{\left\lvert y_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rvert}{b}\right\}.

(4.18)

Once more, we work with the log-likelihood function to simplify calculations:

\displaystyle\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)=\ln\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(-\ln(2b)-\frac{\left\lvert y_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rvert}{b}\right)=-n\ln(2b)-\frac{\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{1}}{b}.

(4.19)

Therefore, the maximum likelihood estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
can be obtained by

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{1}.

(4.20)

To find the maximum likelihood estimators for both
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
b
, we need to maximize the log-likelihood function over both parameters
(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)
.
However, unlike in the Gaussian case, there is generally no closed-form solution for these estimates. Numerical optimization techniques are therefore required to compute the MLEs.

\paragrapharrow

MLE for
\beta_{0}
.
Taking the partial derivative of
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)
with respect to
\beta_{0}
, and setting it to zero gives:

\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)}{\partial\beta_{0}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathrm{sgn}(y_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})}{b}=0,

where
\mathrm{sgn}(\cdot)
is the sign function, which takes the value
-1
if the argument is negative, 0 if the argument is zero, and 1 if the argument is positive.

\paragrapharrow

MLE for
\beta_{j}
with
j\in\{2,3,\ldots,p\}
.
Taking the partial derivative of
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)
with respect to
\beta_{j}
for
j\in\{2,3,\ldots,p\}
, and setting it to zero:

\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)}{\partial\beta_{j}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathrm{sgn}(y_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})x_{ij}}{b}=0,

\paragrapharrow

MLE for
b
.
Taking the partial derivative of
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)
with respect to
\beta_{0}
, and setting it to zero:

\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},b)}{\partial b}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(-\frac{1}{b}+\frac{\left\lvert y_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rvert}{b^{2}}\right)=0.

That is,

b=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lvert y_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rvert.

Therefore, the maximum likelihood estimator for the scale parameter
b
is simply the average absolute deviation between the observed responses and the predicted responses.

Finding analytical solutions for the MLEs under Laplace-distributed noise is generally more complex than in the Gaussian case. As a result, numerical optimization techniques such as Newton-Raphson iteration, iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS), or gradient descent are commonly used in practice. See Chapter
for more details.

4.3.3
Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE)

Under the assumption of moment conditions on the noise, as opposed to specifying its full distribution (i.e.,
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
), we demonstrate that the OLS estimator exhibits a smaller covariance matrix than any other linear unbiased estimator.
Using the bias-variance decomposition (Lemma
), we find that the bias component is zero for all unbiased estimators. Therefore, the estimator with the smallest covariance matrix becomes the optimal one in terms of mean squared error.

{theoremHigh}

[Gauss-Markov]
Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
and assume that:

1.

\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full column rank with
n\geq p
(that is, rank is
p
), so that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is invertible.

2.

\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\bm{X}]=\boldsymbol{0}
.

3.

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\bm{X}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}
, where
\bm{I}
is the
n\times n
identity matrix, and
\sigma^{2}
is a positive constant.

Note that we do not apply the stronger assumption that the noises are i.i.d. from a Gaussian distribution. Then, the OLS estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}
is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
(stated in the following). That is, for any
linear unbiased estimator

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, it holds that

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\bm{X}]-\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\bm{X}]\succeq\boldsymbol{0}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
be any linear estimator of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, which could be expressed as
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{Q}{\mathbf{y}}
.
Specifically, in the case of OLS, we have
\bm{Q}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
. Using the unbiased assumption, we get

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\beta}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\bm{X}]=\mathbb{E}[\bm{Q}{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bm{X}]=\mathbb{E}[\bm{Q}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\bm{X}]=\bm{Q}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},

which yields
(\bm{Q}\bm{X}-\bm{I})\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{0}
. We conclude that the null space of
(\bm{Q}\bm{X}-\bm{I})
is the entire space
p
, and thus,
\bm{Q}\bm{X}=\bm{I}
. The variance is then

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\bm{Q}{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bm{X}]

\displaystyle=\bm{Q}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bm{X}]\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\bm{X}]\bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q}(\sigma^{2}\bm{I})\bm{Q},

where the first equality follows from the fact of covariance under linear transformation by
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\bm{Q}{\mathbf{y}}]=\bm{Q}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}]\bm{Q}^{\top}
.
Then, it follows that

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\bm{X}]-\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\bm{X}]=\bm{Q}(\sigma^{2}\bm{I})\bm{Q}-\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\sigma^{2}\left[\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}-\bm{Q}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{Q}^{\top}\right]=\sigma^{2}\bm{Q}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{Q}^{\top}

\displaystyle=\sigma^{2}\bm{Q}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})(\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}\bm{Q}^{\top}\succeq\boldsymbol{0},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\bm{Q}\bm{X}=\bm{I}
, and the last equality follows from the fact that both
\bm{H}
and
\bm{I}-\bm{H}
are idempotent.
Note that
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\bm{X}]=\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
will be shown in Theorem
. This completes the proof.

Since there is a huge variety of candidate distributions for
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
that would be compatible with the property
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\bm{X}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}
, we cannot say very much about the exact distribution of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
or
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}
. However, under mild regularity conditions, the distribution of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is asymptotically normal for large sample sizes; see Theorem
:

\text{For large $n$, it follows that $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1})$}.

(4.21)

This asymptotic distribution is identical to the one obtained when
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
is normally distributed (as shown in Theorem
), demonstrating that OLS enjoys favorable statistical properties even without assuming normality.

The theorem shows that the OLS estimator achieves the smallest variance compared to other linear unbiased estimators.
Subsequently, in the bias-variance decomposition (Lemma
), we show that the mean squared error between the estimator of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and the true parameter
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is a sum of a bias term and a variance term.
Since OLS is unbiased, its MSE equals its variance. Among all linear unbiased estimators, OLS has the smallest variance, making it optimal in terms of MSE as well; that is, OLS estimator is the
best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE)
.

While we have established that the OLS estimator is the best linear unbiased estimator available “on hand”, one might question whether there exists an imaginary or theoretical estimator with less variance (not necessarily unbiased). This will be addressed in the next section.

4.3.4
Minimum Variance Unbiased (MVU) Estimator

In parameter estimation problems, we obtain information about an unknown parameter from a sample of data drawn from an underlying probability distribution. A natural question arises: How much information can a given sample provide about the unknown parameter? This section introduces a measure of such information. We will also see that this information measure can be used to establish bounds on the variance of estimators and to approximate the sampling distribution of an estimator based on a large sample; see Theorem
.

Fisher Information

For brevity, we consider a random variable
x
for which the p.d.f. or p.m.f. is
p(x\mid\theta)
, where
\theta
is an unknown parameter belonging to a parameter space
\Theta
.
Intuitively, if an event has a small probability, its occurrence provides significant information.
For a random variable
{\textnormal{x}}\sim p(x\mid\theta)
, if
\theta
were the true value of the parameter, the likelihood function should be large, or equivalently, the derivative log-likelihood function should be close to zero. This is the fundamental idea behind maximum likelihood estimation; see Section
.
We define
\ell(\theta;x)\triangleq\ln p(x\mid\theta)
as the log-likelihood function w.r.t.
\theta
, and it follows that

\ell^{\prime}(\theta;x)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ln p(x\mid\theta)=\frac{p^{\prime}(x\mid\theta)}{p(x\mid\theta)},

(4.22)

where
p^{\prime}(x\mid\theta)
denotes the derivative of
p(x\mid\theta)
with respect to
\theta
.
Note that
\ell^{\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})
, written with normal font
x
, denotes a random variable; whereas
\ell^{\prime}(\theta;x)
, written with an italic font
x
, denotes a particular realization of that variable.
Similarly, we denote the second order derivative of
p(x\mid\theta)
with respect to
\theta
as
p^{\prime\prime}(x\mid\theta)
.

\paragrapharrow

Fisher information for a single random variable.
From the above discussion, if
\ell^{\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})
is close to zero, the observed value is expected, and thus does not convey much information about
\theta
.
On the other hand, when the absolute values
\left\lvert\ell^{\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})\right\rvert
or
\left\lvert\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})\right\rvert
are large, the random variable provides substantial information about
\theta
.
Therefore, we can use
[\ell^{\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})]^{2}
to measure the amount of information provided by
x
. However, since
x
itself is a random variable, we should consider the average case. Thus, we introduce the following definition:

Definition 151
(Fisher information (for
\theta
)).

The Fisher information contained in the random variable
x
discussed above is defined as:

\text{(F1)}:\qquad\hbox{\pagecolor{gray!10}
$\mathbb{I}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\big(\ell^{\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})\big)^{2}\right]$
}=\int[\ell^{\prime}(\theta;x)]^{2}p(x\mid\theta)\,dx.

(4.23)

Assuming we can interchange differentiation and integration, we obtain:

\displaystyle\int p^{\prime}(x\mid\theta)\,dx

\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\int p(x\mid\theta)\,dx=0;

\displaystyle\int p^{\prime\prime}(x\mid\theta)\,dx

\displaystyle=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta^{2}}\int p(x\mid\theta)\,dx=0.

It then follows that:

\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\ell^{\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})]=\int\ell^{\prime}(\theta;x)p(x\mid\theta)\,dx=\int\frac{p^{\prime}(x\mid\theta)}{p(x\mid\theta)}p(x\mid\theta)\,dx=\int p^{\prime}(x\mid\theta)\,dx=0.

Hence, the definition of Fisher information in Definition
can be equivalently expressed as

\text{(F2)}:\qquad\hbox{\pagecolor{gray!10}
$\mathbb{I}(\theta)=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}\left[\ell^{\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})\right]$
}.

(4.24)

Moreover, observe that:

\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta;x)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left[\frac{p^{\prime}(x\mid\theta)}{p(x\mid\theta)}\right]=\frac{p^{\prime\prime}(x\mid\theta)p(x\mid\theta)-[p^{\prime}(x\mid\theta)]^{2}}{[p(x\mid\theta)]^{2}}=\frac{p^{\prime\prime}(x\mid\theta)}{p(x\mid\theta)}-[\ell^{\prime}(\theta;x)]^{2}.

(4.25)

Taking expectations:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})]

\displaystyle=\int\left[\frac{p^{\prime\prime}(x\mid\theta)}{p(x\mid\theta)}-[\ell^{\prime}(\theta;x)]^{2}\right]p(x\mid\theta)\,dx

\displaystyle=\int p^{\prime\prime}(x\mid\theta)\,dx-\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\big[\big(\ell^{\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})\big)^{2}\big]=-\mathbb{I}(\theta).

This leads to another equivalent expression for the Fisher information:

\text{(F3)}:\qquad\hbox{\pagecolor{gray!10}
$\mathbb{I}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}})]$
}=-\int\left[\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta^{2}}\ln p(x\mid\theta)\right]p(x\mid\theta)\,dx.

(4.26)

\paragrapharrow

Fisher information for multiple samples.
Now suppose that we are given a random sample
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
drawn from a distribution with the p.d.f. or p.m.f.
p(x\mid\theta)
, where the value of the parameter
\theta
is unknown.
We now aim to calculate how much information this random sample provides about the parameter
\theta
.
We denote the joint p.d.f. of
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
as

p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(x_{i}\mid\theta).

The corresponding joint log-likelihood function and its derivative (with respect to
\theta
) are given by:

\displaystyle\ell_{n}(\theta;\bm{x})

\displaystyle=\ln p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln p(x_{i}\mid\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(\theta;x_{i});

(4.27)

\displaystyle\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;\bm{x})

\displaystyle=\frac{p^{\prime}_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)}{p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell^{\prime}(\theta;x_{i}).

(4.28)

Analogous to the Fisher information defined for a single observation
x
in Definition
,
we define the Fisher information
\mathbb{I}_{n}(\theta)
contained in the random sample
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
as

(\text{F1}):\qquad\hbox{\pagecolor{gray!10}$\mathbb{I}_{n}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\big(\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})\big)^{2}\right]$}=\int\ldots\int[\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;\bm{x})]^{2}p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)dx_{1}\ldots dx_{n}.

which is an
n
-dimensional integral. Assuming that differentiation and integration can be interchanged, we obtain:

\displaystyle\int p^{\prime}_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)d\bm{x}

\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\int p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)d\bm{x}=0;

\displaystyle\int p^{\prime\prime}_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)d\bm{x}

\displaystyle=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta^{2}}\int p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)d\bm{x}=0.

It then follows that:

\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})]=\int\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;\bm{x})p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)d\bm{x}=\int\frac{p^{\prime}_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)}{p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)}p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)d\bm{x}=\int p^{\prime}_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)d\bm{x}=0.

(4.29)

Therefore, the Fisher information for the sample
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
can be expressed as:

\displaystyle(\text{F2 \& F3}):\qquad\hbox{\pagecolor{gray!10}$\mathbb{I}_{n}(\theta)=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}\left[\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})\right]=-\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\ell^{\prime\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})\right]$
}.

From the definition of
\ell_{n}(\theta;\bm{x})
, it follows that

\ell^{\prime\prime}_{n}(\theta;\bm{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta;x_{i})
,
whence we have

(\text{F4}):\qquad\mathbb{I}_{n}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\ell^{\prime\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})\right]=-\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\right]=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta;{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\right]=n\mathbb{I}(\theta).

In other words, the Fisher information contained in a random sample of size
n
is simply
n
times the Fisher information obtained from a single observation.

\paragrapharrow

Fisher information for multiple parameters.
Now suppose the distribution model involves more than one parameter. That is, consider a random variable
{\textnormal{x}}\sim p(x\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
, where
\boldsymbol{\theta}=[\theta_{1},\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{p}]^{\top}
is a vector of unknown parameters.
We denote the log-likelihood function as

\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\ln p(x\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}).

The first-order derivative (gradient) of
\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})
with respect to
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is a
p
-dimensional vector, known as the
score function
, given by

\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\left[\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\theta_{1}},\ldots,\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\theta_{p}}\right]^{\top},

The second-order derivative (Hessian) of
\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})
with respect to
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is a
p\times p
matrix defined as

\frac{\partial^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}^{2}}=\left[\frac{\partial^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\theta_{i}\partial\theta_{j}}\right],\quad\forall\,{i=1,2,\ldots,p;j=1,2,\ldots,p}.

We define the Fisher information matrix as

\hbox{\pagecolor{gray!10}
$\mathbb{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}\left(\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right)^{\top}\right]=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}\left[\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right]=-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}^{2}}\right]$
}.

(4.30)

Since the covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semi-definite, these properties hold for the Fisher information matrix as well.
The Fisher information for
n
samples is similar given by
\mathbb{I}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=n\mathbb{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
.

Example 152
(Fisher information for normal distribution).

Consider a Gaussian distribution
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
, we have

\boldsymbol{\theta}=[\mu,\sigma^{2}]^{\top}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})=-\frac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^{2})-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}.

Therefore, the gradient and Hessian are

\displaystyle\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}

\displaystyle=\left[\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\mu},\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\sigma^{2}}\right]^{\top}=\left[\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^{2}},-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}+\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2(\sigma^{2})^{2}}\right]^{\top};

\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}^{2}}

\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}&-\frac{x-\mu}{(\sigma^{2})^{2}}\\
-\frac{x-\mu}{(\sigma^{2})^{2}}&\frac{1}{2(\sigma^{2})^{2}}-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{(\sigma^{2})^{3}}\end{bmatrix}.

For
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
, since
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}-\mu]=0
and
\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{x}}-\mu)^{2}]=\sigma^{2}
, we can easily get the Fisher information matrix as
