\mathbb{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}^{2}}\right]=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}&0\\
0&\frac{1}{2\sigma^{4}}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize.

Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB)

Suppose that we have a random sample
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
drawn from a distribution with the p.d.f. or p.m.f. given by
p(x\mid\theta)
, where the value of the parameter
\theta
is unknown. We will demonstrate how to use Fisher information to determine the lower bound for the variance of an estimator of
\theta
.

Let
\widehat{\theta}=T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})=T({\mathbf{x}})
be an arbitrary estimator of
\theta
. Assume that
\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}]=m(\theta)
, and that the variance of
\widehat{\theta}
is finite.
Consider the random variable
\ell^{\prime}_{n}({\mathbf{x}}\mid\theta)
defined in (
4.28
), it was shown in (
) that
\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\ell^{\prime}_{n}({\mathbf{x}}\mid\theta)]=0
. Therefore, the covariance between
\widehat{\theta}
and
\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})
is

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta},\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\big(\widehat{\theta}-\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}]\big)\Big(\ell^{\prime}_{n}({\mathbf{x}}\mid\theta)-\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\ell^{\prime}_{n}({\mathbf{x}}\mid\theta)]\Big)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\big(\widehat{\theta}-m(\theta)\big)\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})\right]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\big(T({\mathbf{x}})-m(\theta)\big)\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[T({\mathbf{x}})\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})\right]

\displaystyle=\int\ldots\int T(\bm{x})\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;\bm{x})p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)dx_{1}\ldots dx_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\int\ldots\int T(\bm{x})p^{\prime}_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)dx_{1}\ldots dx_{n}

\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\int\ldots\int T(\bm{x})p_{n}(\bm{x}\mid\theta)dx_{1}\ldots dx_{n}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}]=m^{\prime}(\theta),

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from (
4.28
).
By the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality (Lemma
) and the definition of
\mathbb{I}_{n}(\theta)
, we obtain:

\displaystyle{}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\{\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta},\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})]\right\}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\big(\widehat{\theta}-m(\theta)\big)\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})\right]

\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}]\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}[\ell^{\prime}_{n}(\theta;{\mathbf{x}})]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}]\mathbb{I}_{n}(\theta)=n\mathbb{I}(\theta)\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}].

Thus, we arrive at the following lower bound on the variance of any estimator
\widehat{\theta}
:

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}]\geq\frac{[m^{\prime}(\theta)]^{2}}{n\mathbb{I}(\theta)}.

(4.31)

If we denote
b(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta
as the bias of the estimator
T
, the inequality can be equivalently denoted as

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}]\geq\frac{[m^{\prime}(\theta)]^{2}}{n\mathbb{I}(\theta)}\equiv\frac{[b^{\prime}(\theta)+1]^{2}}{n\mathbb{I}(\theta)}.

(4.32)

This is is called the the
Cramér-Rao lower bound
or the
information inequality
, in honor of the Swedish statistician H. Cramér and Indian statistician C. R. Rao who independently developed this inequality during the 1940s. The information inequality shows that as
\mathbb{I}(\theta)
increases, the variance of the estimator decreases, implying higher quality of estimation; that is why the quantity
\mathbb{I}(\theta)
is referred to as “information.”

If
\widehat{\theta}
is an unbiased estimator, then
b(\theta)=0
,
b^{\prime}(\theta)=0
. Hence, by the information inequality, for an unbiased estimator
\widehat{\theta}
,
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_{\theta}[\widehat{\theta}]\geq\frac{1}{n\mathbb{I}(\theta)}
.
Under certain regularity conditions, no other unbiased estimator of the parameter
\theta
based on an i.i.d. sample of size
n
can have a variance smaller than CRLB.
Formally, we formulate the result in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}
[Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB)]
Let
x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{N}
be an i.i.d. sample from a regular parametric model
p(\cdot\mid\theta)
(i.e., the model cannot switch between continuous and discrete depending on the value of
\theta
),
\Theta\in\real
. Let
T:\mathcal{X}^{N}\rightarrow\Theta
be an estimator of
\theta
, for all
N
. Assume that:

1.

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[T]<\infty
, for all
\theta\in\Theta
;

2.

\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left[\int_{\mathcal{X}^{N}}p_{{\textnormal{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{N}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N};\theta)dx\right]=\int_{\mathcal{X}^{N}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}p_{{\textnormal{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{N}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N};\theta)dx
;

3.

\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left[\int_{\mathcal{X}^{N}}T(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N})p_{{\textnormal{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{N}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N};\theta)dx\right]
=

\qquad\qquad\qquad\;\int_{\mathcal{X}^{N}}T(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N})\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}p_{{\textnormal{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{N}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N};\theta)dx
.

If we denote the bias of
T
by
b(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{N})]-\theta
, then it holds that
b(\theta)
is differentiable, and

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{N})]\geq\frac{\left(b^{\prime}(\theta)+1\right)^{2}}{N\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ln p({\textnormal{x}}_{1}\mid\theta)\right]^{2}}.

That is, the variance has a lower bound.

According to the Gauss-Markov theorem, the OLS estimator stands as the best linear unbiased estimator attainable.
Yet, the gap between this estimator and the theoretical limit of a linear estimator remains unclear.
Specifically, we seek insights into the minimum variance achievable for linear estimators and the proximity of the OLS variance to this theoretical limit.
This question is answered by CRLB.
Note that for this discussion, we assume the additional condition that the noise follows a Gaussian distribution.

By repeating the realization of
{\mathbf{y}}
from
\bm{X}
for
N
times with the same parameters, we find the variance of the OLS estimator attains the bound of CRLB for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
. We state the conclusion in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[Minimum variance unbiased (MVU) estimator]
Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
.
And assume that
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full rank with
n\geq p
(i.e., rank is
p
so that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is invertible).
Then, the OLS estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}
attains the bound of CRLB for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
For simplicity, we only prove the one-dimensional case. Interesting readers can replicate the process to find the proof for the high-dimensional CRLB.
Referring again to Equation (
), the likelihood of this model under
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\sigma^{2}
is

\displaystyle p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\},

\displaystyle\ln p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=-\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^{2})-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}-2\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}),

\displaystyle\frac{\partial\ln p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}).

For one-dimensional inputs
\bm{X}=\bm{x}
, we have

\displaystyle\frac{\partial\ln p({\mathbf{y}}\mid\bm{x},\beta)}{\partial\beta}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}(\bm{x}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}-\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}\beta),

\displaystyle\left[\frac{\partial\ln p({\mathbf{y}}\mid\bm{x},\beta)}{\partial\beta}\right]^{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\big(\bm{x}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{y}}^{\top}\bm{x}-2\beta{\mathbf{y}}^{\top}\bm{x}\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}+\beta^{2}\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}\big),

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\ln p({\mathbf{y}}\mid\bm{x},\beta)}{\partial\beta}\right]^{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}}{\sigma^{2}},

where the last equation follows from the fact that

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}},{\mathbf{y}}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{y}}^{\top}]-\beta^{2}\bm{x}\bm{x}^{\top}.

Suppose now we have
N
realizations of
\bm{y}_{i}
from the same and fixed input matrix
\bm{X}
:

{\mathbf{y}}_{i}=g(\bm{X})+\epsilon_{i},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\forall i\in\{1,2,\ldots,N\}.

Note the difference between
N
and
n
. For
n
, it means we have
n
fixed samples of
\bm{x}_{j}
on hand (i.e.,
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
). For
N
, we use the same fixed
n
samples to realize
N
different outputs
\bm{y}_{i}
(since we assume Gaussian noise disturbance that gives rises to the likelihood).
In other words, for one-dimensional case, we have
N
such
\bm{y}_{i}
’s, and each
\bm{y}_{i}\in\real^{n}
,
\forall

i\in

\{1,2,\ldots,N\}
.

So the variance has the relationship
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\geq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{N(\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x})}
, as the bias term
b^{\prime}(\beta)=0
for an unbiased estimator.
And since we have proved in Theorem
,
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\beta}_{i}]=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{(\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x})}
. Then, repeating
N
times results in
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{N(\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x})}
. This completes the proof.

It follows that, particularly for large sample sizes
N
, the OLS estimator for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
achieves performance equivalent to the theoretical optimum. This once again explains why the OLS method is fundamental to linear model estimation.

4.4
Distribution Theory for OLS

We introduce distributional theory relevant to least squares estimation under Gaussian noise. In particular, we aim to study the sampling distribution of estimators related to the least squares model. This allows us to understand their precision, construct confidence intervals, and perform hypothesis testing.

When applying the least squares estimation or maximum likelihood estimator of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}
(Theorem
), we can directly compute the expectation of the estimator as
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\mathbb{E}[(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}]
(details provided below).
Under the least squares probability model, we also assume that
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
follows some probability distribution.
Substituting into the estimator of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, therefore, we have

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}).

The distribution theory of least squares revolves around this expression.

4.4.1
Mathematical Notations

In statistical modeling, since the sample is all the information we have, any analysis we perform must be based on it—that is, as a function of the observed data, say
T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})
. Such a function is called a
statistic
or an estimator we have termed previously.

Definition 153
(Statistic).

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a sample space. For
n\geq 1
, a statistic is a function
T:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\real
.

Notice that the function
T
must not depend on the unknown parameter
\theta
, since we do not know the latter. If the function
T
depends on
\theta
, then it cannot be considered a statistic.
In general, a statistic contains less information about
\theta
than the full dataset
({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})
. However, for certain models, we can find a statistic
T
such that
T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})
retains all the relevant information about
\theta
contained in the original data. Such a statistic is called a
sufficient statistic
, because it suffices to work with
T(\cdot)
instead of the full dataset.

Definition 154
(Sufficiency).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}f_{\theta}
. A statistic
T:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\real
is called sufficient for the parameter
\theta
, if the conditional probability
\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\leq x_{1},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x_{n}\mid T=t]
does not depend on
\theta
, for all
[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]^{\top}\in\real^{n}
and all
t\in\real
.

Intuitively, once we know the value of
T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})
, the conditional distribution of the data no longer provides any additional information about
\theta
. Therefore, knowing the full dataset beyond the value of
T
does not help us determine which value of

\theta
generated the data.
This definition is often difficult to verify directly. However, the following equivalent condition is usually easier to work with in practice.

Definition 155
(Sampling distribution).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}F
, and let
T:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\real
be a statistic. The sampling distribution of
T
under the distribution
F
is defined as the probability distribution

F_{T}(t)=\Pr[T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})\leq t],\quad t\in\real.

We always apply statistics to samples, so we often suppress the dependence of the statistic on the sample values. That is, we write simply
T
instead of
T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})
.
Using this notation, the sampling distribution becomes
F_{T}(t)=\Pr[T\leq t]
.
For multi-dimensional parameters
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, the concepts of sufficiency and sampling distributions are defined analogously.

Exercise
\thetheo

Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}\text{Uniform}(0,\theta)
(see Exercise
). Show that
T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})=\max\{{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\}
is a sufficient statistic for
\theta
, and derive its sampling distribution.

Exercise
\thetheo

Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{P}(\lambda)
(Definition
). Show that the statistic
T({\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
is a sufficient statistic for
\lambda
, and derive its sampling distribution.

4.4.2
Unbiasedness under Moment Assumption

An introduction to distribution theory can begin by making assumptions only about the moments of the noise—rather than fully specifying its probability distribution—as shown below.

{theoremHigh}
[Unbiasedness under moment assumption]
Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
is a random vector of noise.
We only assume
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}
instead of
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
.
Suppose further that
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full rank with
n\geq p
(i.e., rank is
p
).
Then, the following moment properties hold:

1.

The OLS estimator (i.e., MLE) satisfies
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
.

2.

The predicted output satisfies
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}]=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{H}
, where
\bm{H}
is the orthogonal projection matrix with
\bm{H}=\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
(see Section
).

3.

The error vector
{\mathbf{e}}={\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
satisfies
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{e}}]=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{e}}]=\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since the estimator is
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}
, and we assume that
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, we have

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\boldsymbol{\beta}+(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}.

Thus, since
\bm{X}
is fixed, we obtain that

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\beta}+(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\boldsymbol{\beta},

and

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}]\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}

(4.33)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{=}}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}=\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\bm{A}{\mathbf{v}}+\bm{b}]=\bm{A}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{v}}]\bm{A}^{\top}
, and the equality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from the fact
\bm{X}
is fixed.
And since
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we obtain
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}]=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}]=\bm{X}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\bm{X}^{\top}=\sigma^{2}\bm{H}
.
Furthermore, since
{\mathbf{e}}={\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
, we have
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{e}}]=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}]=\boldsymbol{0}
and

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{e}}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}-\bm{H}{\mathbf{y}}]=(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}](\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}

\displaystyle=(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}](\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}=\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})(\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{=}}\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{H}),

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}=\bm{H}{\mathbf{y}}
, and the equality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from the fact that
(\bm{I}-\bm{H})
is an orthogonal projection.
This completes the proof.

Once again, from this lemma, we see that the maximum likelihood estimator of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is unbiased, and the expected value of the error vector is zero. This highlights why the method of maximum likelihood plays a central role in point estimation.

Computing the Covariance Matrix

In least squares problems, computing the associated covariance matrix is essential for assessing the accuracy of the estimated parameters. Specifically, as shown above, the variance of each estimated coefficient
\beta_{i}
is proportional to the
i
-th diagonal element of
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
.
Consider the full-rank linear model:
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
,
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
is a random vector with zero mean and covariance matrix
\sigma^{2}\bm{I}
.
The covariance matrix of the least squares estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is
\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
(Theorem
), where

\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}=(\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R})^{-1}=\bm{R}^{-1}\bm{R}^{-\top},

(4.34)

and
\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{R}
is the Cholesky decomposition of
\bm{X}
.
Alternatively,
\bm{X}=[\bm{Q}_{1},\bm{Q}_{2}]\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}\bm{R}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}
can be seen as the QR decomposition of
\bm{X}
.

The inverse
\bm{S}=\bm{R}^{-1}=[s_{ij}]
is also upper triangular and can be computed in
p^{3}/3
flops from the matrix equation
\bm{R}\bm{S}=\bm{I}
as follows:

\displaystyle\text{for }j=p,p-1,\ldots,1

\displaystyle\qquad s_{jj}=1/r_{jj};

\displaystyle\qquad\text{for }i=j-1,\ldots,2,1

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad s_{ij}=-\left(\sum_{k=i+1}^{j}r_{ik}s_{kj}\right)/r_{ii};

end

end

The computed elements of
\bm{S}
can overwrite the corresponding elements of
\bm{R}
in storage. Forming the upper triangular part of
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}
requires an additional
p^{3}/3
flops. This computation can be sequenced so that the elements of
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
overwrite those of
\bm{S}
directly.
The variance of the components of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is given by the diagonal elements of
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[\omega_{ij}]
:

\omega_{pp}=s_{pp}^{2}=1/r_{pp}^{2},\qquad\omega_{ii}=\sum_{j=i}^{p}s_{ij}^{2},\quad i=p-1,\ldots,1.

(4.35)

Note that the variance for
\beta_{p}
is immediately available from the last diagonal element
r_{pp}
.

Frequently,
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
appears only as an intermediate step, such as when computing the variance of a linear functional
\bm{g}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. This variance is expressed as:

\bm{g}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\bm{g}=\bm{g}^{\top}\bm{R}^{-1}\bm{R}^{-\top}\bm{g}=\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{z},

(4.36)

where
\bm{z}\triangleq\bm{R}^{-\top}\bm{g}
.
Thus, instead of evaluating
\bm{g}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\bm{g}
directly, it is more numerically stable and efficient to solve the lower triangular system
\bm{R}^{\top}\bm{z}=\bm{g}
, and then compute
\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{z}
.

Similarly, the covariance matrix of the residual vector
\bm{e}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is calculated as

\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\bm{e}}\triangleq\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top})=\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}),\quad\bm{X}=\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{R}.

(4.37)

Note that
\bm{I}-\bm{Q}_{1}\bm{Q}_{1}^{\top}
is the orthogonal projector onto the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
(Remark
).

4.4.3
Sampling Distribution of OLS under Gaussian Disturbance

In addition to understanding the moments of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, can we also gain insight into its distribution? Analogous to the way Gaussian disturbances influence the likelihood function, they also determine the exact distribution of the associated random variables.

{theoremHigh}
[Sampling distribution of LS under Gaussian disturbance] Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
. Assume
\bm{X}
is fixed and has full rank with
n\geq p
(i.e., its rank is
p
). Then,

1.

The OLS estimator satisfies
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1})
;

2.

The predicted output satisfies
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{H})
;

3.

The error vector satisfies
{\mathbf{e}}={\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{H}))
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}
and we assume that
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, we have

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\boldsymbol{\beta}+(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}.

Since both
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}
are deterministic, we can apply the affine transformation property of the multivariate normal distribution (see Lemma
), giving:

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\beta}+(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}

\displaystyle\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}(\sigma^{2}\bm{I})\left[(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\right]^{\top}\right).

Thus, it follows that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1})
.
Similarly, for
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we obtain
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{H})
.
Considering the error variable
{\mathbf{e}}={\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
, we have
{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
, then

\displaystyle\bm{e}

\displaystyle={\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}=(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\left((\bm{I}-\bm{H})\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},(\bm{I}-\bm{H})(\sigma^{2}\bm{I})(\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\right),

where the last equality comes from the fact that
(\bm{I}-\bm{H})
is an orthogonal projection onto the perpendicular space of
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, and this completes the proof.

We further show that, under the same assumptions, the error variable
{\mathbf{e}}
is independent of the predicted output and the OLS estimator.

Lemma 156
(Independence in LS under Gaussian disturbance).

Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
. Assume
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full rank with
n\geq p
(i.e., its rank is
p
). Then, the random variable
{\mathbf{e}}
is independent of
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
and
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
;

Proof
[of Lemma
]
It is straightforward that

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{e}},\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}},\bm{H}{\mathbf{y}}]=(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}},{\mathbf{y}}]\bm{H}^{\top}

\displaystyle=(\bm{I}-\bm{H})(\sigma^{2}\bm{I})\bm{H}=\sigma^{2}(\bm{H}-\bm{H})=\boldsymbol{0},

where the second equality follows from the fact that
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\bm{A}{\mathbf{v}},\bm{B}{\mathbf{w}}]=\bm{A}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{v}},{\mathbf{w}}]\bm{B}^{\top}
, given non-random matrix
\bm{A}
and
\bm{B}
.
As
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, and
\bm{X}
is the observed data matrix and is fixed,
{\mathbf{e}}
is independent of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
as well.
This completes the proof.

Using these results, we can show that
\bm{H}{\mathbf{y}}
is a sufficient statistic (Definition
) for the parameter
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
Write
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{H}{\mathbf{y}}+(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}=\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}+{\mathbf{e}}
.
Now define the
2n
-dimensional vector
{\mathbf{z}}\triangleq[\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}^{\top},{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}]^{\top}
.
Since
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
is independent of
{\mathbf{e}}
(Lemma
), conditional on
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
,
{\mathbf{e}}
always has the same distribution
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{H}))
. It follows that, conditional on
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
, the vector
{\mathbf{z}}
has a distribution whose first
n
coordinates equal
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
almost surely, and whose last
n
coordinates are
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}(\bm{I}-\bm{H}))
. Neither of those two depend on
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, proving its sufficiency.

4.4.4
t
-Distribution and
F
-Distribution

To discuss further results, we need the definitions of
t
- and
F
-distributions.
We have introduced that Chi-squared distribution is a specific case of the Gamma distribution (Definitions
and
).
In this context, we provide the formal definitions of the
t
-distribution and the
F
-distribution, with a particular emphasis on their close relationship to the Chi-squared distribution.

(a)

t
-distribution probability density
functions for different values of the parameter
n
. When increasing the degree of freedom
n
, the density gets closer to
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
.

(b)

F
-distribution probability density
functions for different values of the parameters
n
and
d
.

Figure 4.1:
t
-distribution and
F
-distribution probability density functions.

Definition 157
(
t
-distribution).

Let
y
and
z
be independent random variables such that
{\textnormal{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
and
{\textnormal{z}}\sim\chi_{(n)}^{2}
.
Then the random variable defined by
{\textnormal{x}}\triangleq\frac{{\textnormal{y}}}{\sqrt{{\textnormal{z}}/n}}
follows a
t
-distribution with
n
degrees of freedom, denoted
{\textnormal{x}}\sim t_{(n)}
. The probability density function of
\sqrt{{\textnormal{z}}/n}
is given by

h_{2}(z;n)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{2n^{n/2}}{2^{n/2}\Gamma(\frac{n}{2})}z^{n-1}\exp(-\frac{nz^{2}}{2}),&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}z\geq 0;\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}z<0.\end{aligned}\right.

And the probability density function of
y
is given by

h_{1}(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\{-\frac{y^{2}}{2}\}.

Then the probability density function of the
t
-distribution can be obtained by

\displaystyle g(x;n)

\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}t\cdot h_{1}(xt)\cdot h_{2}(t)dt=\frac{\Gamma(\frac{n+1}{2})}{\sqrt{n\pi}\Gamma(\frac{n}{2})}\left(1+\frac{x^{2}}{n}\right)^{-\frac{n+1}{2}}.

The shape of the
t
-distribution resembles that of the standard normal distribution—it is symmetric about zero.
However, it has heavier tails when
n
is small.
And when
n\rightarrow\infty
,
t
-distribution converges to
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
.
Figure
compares the
t
-distribution for various values of
n
and
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
.

Note that
t
-distribution is the univariate version of Definition
.

Definition 158
(
F
-distribution).

The
F
-distribution arises as the ratio of two independent Chi-squared distributions, each divided by its degrees of freedom.
Using
n
and
d
to denote numerator and denominator, respectively, we define

\displaystyle\frac{\frac{1}{n}\chi_{(n)}^{2}}{\frac{1}{d}\chi_{(d)}^{2}}\sim F_{n,d}.

And the probability density function is given by

f(x;n,d)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\Gamma(\frac{n+d}{2})}{\Gamma(\frac{n}{2})\Gamma(\frac{d}{2})}n^{n/2}d^{d/2}x^{\frac{n}{2}-1}\left(d+nx\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}(n+d)},&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x\geq 0;\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x<0.\end{aligned}\right.

A notable special case is that if
{\textnormal{x}}\sim t_{(n)}
, then
{\textnormal{x}}^{2}\sim F_{1,n}
.
Figure
illustrates how the shape of the
F
-distribution varies with different combinations of
n
and
d
.

4.4.5
Sampling Distribution of RSS under Gaussian Disturbance

Another crucial result we will prove is the sum of squares due to error (or called the
residual sum of squares (RSS)
)
{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}\sim\sigma^{2}\chi^{2}_{(n-p)}
, by which we can construct an unbiased estimator of
\sigma^{2}
. The distribution
\chi^{2}_{(n-p)}
is the Chi-squared distribution with
n-p
degrees of freedom (Definition
).

{theoremHigh}

[Distribution of sum of squares due to error]
Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
. Assume
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full rank with
n\geq p
(i.e., its rank is
p
). Then, we have

1.

Sum of squares due to error satisfies
{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}=\sum_{i}^{n}{\textnormal{e}}_{i}^{2}\sim\sigma^{2}\chi^{2}_{(n-p)}
, where
{\mathbf{e}}={\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
;

2.

An unbiased estimator of
\sigma^{2}
is
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}=\frac{1}{n-p}({\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}})^{\top}({\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}})=\frac{{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p}
;

3.

The random variables
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
are independent.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We realize that
\sum_{i}^{n}{\textnormal{e}}_{i}^{2}={\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}=[(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}]^{\top}[(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}]
. By expressing
{\mathbf{y}}
into
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
and using the fact that
\bm{H}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, we have:

\displaystyle(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}

\displaystyle=(\bm{I}-\bm{H})(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon},

by which we can rewrite
[(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}]^{\top}[(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}]
as

\displaystyle\sum_{i}^{n}{\textnormal{e}}_{i}^{2}

\displaystyle=[(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}]^{\top}[(\bm{I}-\bm{H}){\mathbf{y}}]=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}.

By Spectral Theorem
and Proposition
(the only possible eigenvalues of the hat matrix are 0 and 1), we can express the sum of squares due to error as
\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{e}}_{i}^{2}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}(\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\bm{I}-\bm{H}=\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bm{Q}^{\top}
is the spectral decomposition of
\bm{I}-\bm{H}
.
Given the fact that rotations on the normal distribution do not affect the distribution (Lemma
), we can define

\boldsymbol{\eta}\triangleq\bm{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}).

Thus, it follows that

\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{e}}_{i}^{2}=\boldsymbol{\eta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\eta}\sim\sigma^{2}\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{rank(\bm{I}-\bm{H})}}\sim\sigma^{2}\chi^{2}_{(n-p)},

where, according to Lemma
,

\displaystyle\mathrm{rank}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{I})-\mathrm{tr}(\bm{H})=n-\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top})

\displaystyle=n-\mathrm{tr}((\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})=n-p.

Therefore, it can be shown that
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}]=\sigma^{2}(n-p)
, leading to an unbiased estimator for
\sigma^{2}
, denoted by
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}=\frac{{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p}
.

As proved in Lemma
,
{\mathbf{e}}
is independent of
\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}
.
Then,
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}=\frac{{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p}
is independent of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
as well.
This completes the proof.

Remark 159
(Sampling distribution for GLS).

In the generalized least squares (GLS) setting described in Theorem
, the covariance matrix of the estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is given by

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{X})^{-1}\in\real^{n\times n},

(4.38)

and an unbiased estimate of
\sigma^{2}
is

S^{2}=\frac{1}{n-p}\bm{e}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{e},\quad\bm{e}\triangleq\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(4.39)

\paragrapharrow

Degree of freedom.
To see why
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
(which is the sum of squares due to error divided by
(n-p)
) is an unbiased estimator of
\sigma^{2}
, we delve into the concept of degrees of freedom.

Remark 160
(Degrees of freedom of the error vector
{\mathbf{e}}
).

The unbiased estimator
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
of
\sigma^{2}
adjusts the degree of freedom (df) of
{\mathbf{e}}
.
Specifically, if
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full column rank with
n\geq p
, then the degrees of freedom associated with
{\mathbf{e}}
is
(n-p)
.

It may not be immediately clear why
(n-p)
is referred to as the degrees of freedom of
{\mathbf{e}}
. In general, degrees of freedom represent the dimension of the space in which a vector can vary—that is, how freely it can move within that space.
Since
{\mathbf{e}}\in\real^{n}
lies orthogonal to the column space of
\bm{X}
as shown in Figure
. That is,
\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}=\boldsymbol{0}
(see Lemma
), and
{\mathbf{e}}
is in the null space of
\bm{X}^{\top}
, which has dimension
n-p
.
Thus, although
{\mathbf{e}}
resides in
n
, it is constrained by
p
linear relationships and therefore loses
p
degrees of freedom.

With this unbiased estimator of noise variance
\sigma^{2}
, we are now equipped to answer various inferential questions. Here is a typical example:

Example 161
(Application of sampling distribution).

Given any non-random vector
\bm{c}
, we wish to find the distribution for the following equation:

\frac{\bm{c}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}{{\textnormal{S}}\sqrt{\bm{c}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{c}}}.

From
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1})
, we can find
(\bm{c}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\bm{c}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{c})
. This makes

\frac{\bm{c}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}{\sigma\sqrt{\bm{c}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{c}}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

Recall that
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}\sim\frac{\sigma^{2}\chi^{2}_{(n-p)}}{n-p}
. We have
\frac{{\textnormal{S}}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\sim\frac{\chi^{2}_{(n-p)}}{n-p}
.
This implies

\frac{\bm{c}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}{{\textnormal{S}}\sqrt{\bm{c}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{c}}}\sim t_{(n-p)},

which follows a
t
-distribution (suppose
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
and
{\textnormal{y}}\sim\chi^{2}_{(n)}
; then,
\frac{{\textnormal{x}}}{\sqrt{{\textnormal{y}}/n}}\sim t_{(n)}
), and by which we could answer question of interest; for example, this result enables us to construct confidence intervals and perform hypothesis tests on individual coefficients.

For example, let
\bm{c}=\bm{e}_{k}
be the
k
-th unit basis vector. Then the confidence interval for the
k
-th coordinate is

\bm{e}_{k}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\pm t_{(n-p)}(\alpha/2){{\textnormal{S}}\sqrt{\bm{e}_{k}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{e}_{k}}}.

When
\bm{c}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}
is a new data observation, and we want to predict
y_{\text{new}}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Then the
(1-\alpha)\times 100\%
confidence interval is

\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\pm t_{(n-p)}(\alpha/2){{\textnormal{S}}\sqrt{\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}}}.

In many cases, we may model
y_{\text{new}}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon
where
\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
. Then the confidence interval becomes

\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\pm t_{(n-p)}(\alpha/2){{\textnormal{S}}\sqrt{1+\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}}}.

This is known as the prediction interval, which provides confidence bounds for a future observed response rather than for the expected value alone.

\paragrapharrow

Minimum MSE estimator of noise variance
\sigma^{2}
.
Moreover, we decompose the noise variance in terms of mean squared error, from which we could find the minimum MSE estimator of the noise variance.

Lemma 162
(Bias-variance decomposition of noise variance).

For any estimator
\bar{\sigma}^{2}
of
\sigma^{2}
, the mean squared error of the estimator have the following decomposition:

\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}(\bar{\sigma}^{2},\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(\bar{\sigma}^{2}-\sigma^{2})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[(\bar{\sigma}^{2})^{2}]-2\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}[\bar{\sigma}^{2}]+(\sigma^{2})^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\mathbb{E}[\bar{\sigma}^{2}]-\sigma^{2}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\big[\left\lVert\bar{\sigma}^{2}-\mathbb{E}(\bar{\sigma}^{2})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\big]

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\mathrm{Bias}(\bar{\sigma}^{2},\sigma^{2})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\bar{\sigma}^{2}].

In Theorem
, we showed that the MLE of
\sigma^{2}
is
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}
, which is a biased estimator of
\sigma^{2}
.
According to Theorem
, an unbiased estimator of
\sigma^{2}
is given by
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}=\frac{1}{n-p}{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}
.

Define the function
\bar{\sigma}^{2}(k)=\frac{1}{k}{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}
. Then, the MLE of
\sigma^{2}
can be denoted by
\bar{\sigma}^{2}(n)
, and the unbiased estimator
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
of
\sigma^{2}
can be expressed as
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}=\bar{\sigma}^{2}(n-p)
.
The value of
k
that minimizes the mean squared error
\mathrm{MSE}(\bar{\sigma}^{2}(k),\sigma^{2})
is
k=n-p+2
.
We thus have

\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\sigma}^{2},\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=(\frac{n-p}{n}\sigma^{2}-\sigma^{2})^{2}+\frac{2(n-p)\sigma^{4}}{{n}^{2}}=\frac{p^{2}+2(n-p)}{n^{2}}\sigma^{4};

\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}({\textnormal{S}}^{2},\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=(\frac{n-p}{n-p}\sigma^{2}-\sigma^{2})^{2}+\frac{2(n-p)\sigma^{4}}{{(n-p)}^{2}}=\frac{2\sigma^{4}}{n-p};

\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}(\bar{\sigma}^{2}(n-p+2),\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=(\frac{n-p}{n-p+2}\sigma^{2}-\sigma^{2})^{2}+\frac{2(n-p)\sigma^{4}}{{(n-p+2)}^{2}}=\frac{2n-2p}{(n-p+2)^{2}}\sigma^{4},

which implies

\mathrm{MSE}(\bar{\sigma}^{2}(n-p+2),\sigma^{2})\leq\mathrm{MSE}({\textnormal{S}}^{2},\sigma^{2}).

The result shows that
\bar{\sigma}^{2}(n-p+2)
has a smaller mean squared error than
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}
, meaning it tends to be closer to
\sigma^{2}
under this performance measure.
However,
\bar{\sigma}^{2}(n-p+2)
is biased and will underestimate
\sigma^{2}
on average . This bias raises concerns about the reliability of
\bar{\sigma}^{2}(n-p+2)
as a general-purpose estimator for
\sigma^{2}
.

In general, since MSE depends on the true parameter value, there is no single estimator that uniformly minimizes MSE across all possible values
\sigma^{2}
. Therefore, we often restrict our attention to a specific class of estimators—such as unbiased estimators—and seek the one with the lowest variance.
A commonly used approach is to focus on unbiased estimators and choose the one with minimum variance; such an estimator is called the
best unbiased estimator (BUE)
. If we further restrict our attention to linear estimators, we obtain the
best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE)
.
See Section
for a discussion about the BLUE of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.

In summary, various estimators for
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\sigma^{2}
are compared in Table
.

and
