4.4.6
Learning Curve of Least Squares under Gaussian Disturbance

To differentiate the test data error (the data we do not see), we introduce the concept of
in-sample error
(also known as the in-sample sum of squares due to error) by
\mathrm{MSE}_{\text{in}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}({\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\widehat{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i})^{2}=\frac{1}{n}{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}
for
n
available data samples.
Additionally, we define the
out-of-sample error
(also known as the out-of-sample sum of squares due to error) as the expected squared error of test data, given by
\mathrm{MSE}_{\text{out}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{y}}_{\ast}-\widehat{{\textnormal{y}}}_{\ast})^{2}]
.
We then derive the expressions for the expected in-sample error and out-of-sample error under the assumption of Gaussian noise disturbance.

{theoremHigh}
[Expectation of in-sample error under Gaussian disturbance]
Let
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
. Assume
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
is fixed and has full rank with
p<n
(i.e., its rank is
p
). Then, we have

1.

The expected in-sample error:
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MSE}_{\text{in}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\frac{n-p}{n}\sigma^{2}
;

2.

The expected out-of-sample error:
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MSE}_{\text{out}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]
converges to
\frac{n+p}{n}\sigma^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{n})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
As a recap, the sum of squares due to error is defined as

\displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\mathbf{y}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\bm{H}{\mathbf{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\bm{H}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{H}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left((\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right)^{\top}((\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon})

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
lies in
\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
, and the last two equalities arise from the fact that
\bm{I}-\bm{H}
is symmetric and idempotent.
Next, by taking the expectation of the sum of squares due to error with respect to
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, we obtain:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}\bm{e}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{H})\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\mathrm{tr}((\bm{I}-\bm{H})\cdot\sigma^{2}\bm{I})=\sigma^{2}(n-p),

where the second equality follows from the fact that: for random variable
{\mathbf{b}}
and non-random matrix
\bm{A}
, we have

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}}]=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{b}}])+\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{b}}]^{\top}\bm{A}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{b}}];

(4.40)

see Lemma
.
This expectation aligns with the outcome derived in Theorem
, where we establish that
{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}\sim\sigma^{2}\chi^{2}_{(n-p)}
with a expectation of
\sigma^{2}(n-p)
.
Consequently, we have

\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MSE}_{\text{in}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}\bm{e}]=\frac{n-p}{n}\sigma^{2}.

Note here, we can directly obtain the expectation of
{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}
from Theorem
.
The presented proof offers an alternative approach to determine the expectation of
{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}
.

For the second part of the claim,
given the test input
{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}
, test output
{\textnormal{y}}_{\ast}
, and test noise
\epsilon_{\ast}
, the test error is

\displaystyle{\textnormal{e}}_{\ast}

\displaystyle={\textnormal{y}}_{\ast}-{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\textnormal{y}}_{\ast}-{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}=({\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon_{\ast})-{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon})

\displaystyle=\epsilon_{\ast}-{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}+\left[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}-{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right]=\epsilon_{\ast}-{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}.

Then, the squared test error can be obtained by

\displaystyle{\textnormal{e}}_{\ast}^{2}

\displaystyle=(\epsilon_{\ast}-{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon})^{2}

\displaystyle=\epsilon_{\ast}^{2}-2\epsilon_{\ast}{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}+\left({\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right)\left({\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right)^{\top}

\displaystyle=\epsilon_{\ast}^{2}-2\epsilon_{\ast}{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}+{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}

Step 1.

Taking the expectation of the squared test error with respect to the test input
{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\textnormal{e}}_{\ast}^{2}]

\displaystyle=\epsilon_{\ast}^{2}-2\epsilon_{\ast}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}+\mathrm{tr}\left({\mathbf{M}}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\right)+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]^{\top}{\mathbf{M}}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}],

where
{\mathbf{M}}\triangleq(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
, and the last two components follows again from Equation (
).

Step 2.

Taking the expectation of the squared test error with respect to the test noise
\epsilon_{\ast}
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon_{\ast}}[\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\textnormal{e}}_{\ast}^{2}]]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon_{\ast}}[\epsilon_{\ast}^{2}]-2\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon_{\ast}}[\epsilon_{\ast}]\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}+\mathrm{tr}\left({\mathbf{M}}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\right)+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]^{\top}{\mathbf{M}}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]

\displaystyle=\sigma^{2}+\mathrm{tr}\left({\mathbf{M}}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\right)+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]^{\top}{\mathbf{M}}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]

Step 3.

Taking the expectation of the squared test error with respect to the input noise
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon_{\ast}}[\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\textnormal{e}}_{\ast}^{2}]]]

\displaystyle=\sigma^{2}+\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left((\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\right)\right]

(4.41)

\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\right].

Step 3.1.

For the second part of the above equation, since the trace of a product is invariant under cyclical permutations of the factors, we have:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left((\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\right)\right]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}](\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right)\right].

Following the fact that: for random variable
{\mathbf{b}}
and non-random matrix
\bm{A}
, since
{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}}
is a scalar, we have

{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}}=\mathrm{tr}({\mathbf{b}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}),

where the last equation follows from the fact that the trace of a product is invariant under cyclical permutations of the factors:

\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\bm{B}\bm{C})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{B}\bm{C}\bm{A})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{C}\bm{A}\bm{B}),

if all
\bm{A}\bm{B}\bm{C}
,
\bm{B}\bm{C}\bm{A}
, and
\bm{C}\bm{A}\bm{B}
exist.
Then, it follows that

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\top})]=\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{E}[\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}])=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}]),

where the second equality follows from the linear property of trace.

Let
{\mathbf{b}}\triangleq(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
and
\bm{A}\triangleq\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]
, then the second part of Equation (
) is

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}](\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right)\right]=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{tr}({\mathbf{b}}^{\top}\bm{A}{\mathbf{b}})]=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}])

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\right)=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\left(\frac{1}{n}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\right)^{-1}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}\frac{p}{n}\sigma^{2},

where the equality
({\dagger})
follows from the assumption that
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
, we have
{\mathbf{b}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1})
and
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\top}]=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{b}}]=\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
. And the last equation follows from the fact that
(\frac{1}{n}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
converges to
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]
as
n\rightarrow\infty
, and the trace of a
p\times p
identity matrix is
p
.

Step 3.2.

Similarly, for the third part of Equation (
), we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]^{\top}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{\top}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]^{\top}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{\ast}]]}{n},

which is an order of
\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{n})
.

Finally, we reduce Equation (
) to

\frac{n+p}{n}\sigma^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{n}).

This completes the proof.

Figure 4.2:
Learning curve of least squares under Gaussian noise disturbance.

Thus, we obtain the learning curve of least squares under Gaussian noise, as illustrated in Figure
. When the number of samples
n
significantly exceeds the dimension
p
,
both the expected in-sample error and the expected out-of-sample error converge towards the noise level.

4.5
Large-Sample Properties in LS Estimator*

4.5.1
Convergence Results

We briefly introduce fundamental convergence results and asymptotic theory in this section.
For more comprehensive discussions and proofs, see
Cameron and Trivedi 2005
;
Panaretos 2016
;
Shao 2003
;
Hansen 2007
;
Yu 2021
;
Gut 2009a
;
Wooldridge 2010
;
Hayashi 2011
;
Bickel and Doksum 2015
.

Convergence

We begin by defining convergence in distribution:

Definition 163
(Convergence in distribution).

Let
\{F_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}
be a sequence of distribution functions and
G
be a distribution function on . That is, the distribution function are

F_{n}(x)=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x],\ \forall\,n,\qquad\text{and}\qquad G(x)=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x].

We say that
F_{n}
converges in distribution to
G
, and write
F_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}G
(or
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}
) if and only if

F_{n}(x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}G(x),

for all
x
that are continuity points of
G
.

Definition 164
(Convergence in probability).

A sequence of random variables
\{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\}
is said to converge in probability to random variable
y
as
n\rightarrow\infty
, denoted
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\textnormal{y}}
, if for any
\epsilon>0
,

\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{y}}\right\rvert>\epsilon]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}0.

From the definitions above, it is clear that convergence in probability is a stronger condition than convergence in distribution. There are several other types of convergence in probability theory, such as convergence in
r
-mean and almost sure convergence. However, these will not be discussed further here.

Example 165
.

Let
\{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\}
be a sequence of random variables with

{\textnormal{x}}_{n}=(-1)^{n}{\textnormal{x}},\qquad\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}=-1]=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}=1]=\frac{1}{2}.

Then
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}
, but
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\nrightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}
.

Lemma 166
(Convergence results).

Let
\{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\}
be a sequence of random variables. Then it follows that

1.

{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}\,\,\Longrightarrow\,\,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}

2.

{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}c\,\,\Longrightarrow\,\,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}c,\qquad c\in\real.

Proof
[of Lemma
]

(i).

let
x
be any continuity point of
F_{\textnormal{x}}
, and let
\epsilon>0
. We begin by writing

\displaystyle\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x]

\displaystyle=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x,{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\leq\epsilon}]+\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x,\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon]

(4.42)

\displaystyle=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x,{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-\epsilon\leq{\textnormal{x}}\leq{\textnormal{x}}_{n}+\epsilon}]+\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x,\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon]

\displaystyle\leq\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x+\epsilon]+\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon],

where the inequality comes from the fact that
\{{\textnormal{x}}\leq x+\epsilon\}
contains
\{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-\epsilon\leq{\textnormal{x}}\leq{\textnormal{x}}_{n}+\epsilon\}
. Moreover, it follows that

\displaystyle\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon]

\displaystyle=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon,{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\leq\epsilon}]+\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon,\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon]

\displaystyle=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon,{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}{\textnormal{x}}-\epsilon\leq{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq{\textnormal{x}}+\epsilon}]+\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon,\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon]

\displaystyle\leq\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x]+\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon],

where the inequality comes from the fact that
\{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x\}
contains
\{{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon,{\textnormal{x}}-\epsilon\leq{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq{\textnormal{x}}+\epsilon\}
. This implies

\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon]-\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon]\leq\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x].

(4.43)

Combining (
) and (
) yields that

\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon]-\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon]\leq\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x]\leq\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x+\epsilon]+\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon].

Since we assume
\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\epsilon]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}0
. Then, when
n\rightarrow\infty
, we have

\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x-\epsilon]\leq\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x]\leq\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x+\epsilon],

which yields (i).

(ii).

We also have

\displaystyle\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-c\right\rvert>\epsilon]

\displaystyle=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-c>\epsilon]+\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-c<-\epsilon]

\displaystyle=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}>c+\epsilon]+\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}<c-\epsilon]

\displaystyle\leq 1-\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq c+\epsilon]+\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq c-\epsilon]

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}1-F(c+\epsilon)+F(c-\epsilon).

Since
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}c
, we have
F(c+\epsilon)=1
and
F(c-\epsilon)=0
as
c>c+\epsilon
and
c-\epsilon<c
. Therefore,

\Pr[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{n}-c\right\rvert>\epsilon]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}0,

which completes the proof.

Definition 167
(Joint convergence).

Let
\{{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\}
be a sequence of random vectors of
p
, and
{\mathbf{x}}
be a random vector of
p
. Define their distribution functions as

\displaystyle F_{{\mathbf{x}}_{n}}(\bm{x})

\displaystyle=\Pr[{\mathbf{x}}_{n1}\leq\bm{x}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{n2}\leq\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{np}\leq\bm{x}_{p}];

\displaystyle F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(\bm{x})

\displaystyle=\Pr[{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\leq\bm{x}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2}\leq\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{p}\leq\bm{x}_{p}],

for
\bm{x}=[\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{p}]^{\top}\in\real^{p}
. Then we say that
{\mathbf{x}}_{n}
converges in distribution to
{\mathbf{x}}
as
n\rightarrow\infty
if for every continuity point of
F_{{\mathbf{x}}}
we have

F_{{\mathbf{x}}_{n}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(\bm{x}).

This convergence is denoted by
{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\mathbf{x}}
.

When an estimator approaches the true value as the sample size increases indefinitely, we refer to this property as consistency. In mathematical terms, this concept is defined as follows:

Definition 168
(Consistency).

An estimator
\widehat{\theta}_{n}
of
\theta
, constructed on the basis of a sample of size
n
, is said to be consistent if
\widehat{\theta}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\theta
as
n\rightarrow\infty
.

Consistency is a desirable attribute for an estimator. When the sample size is sufficiently large, the estimator will be very close to the true value with high probability. Additionally, the concentration of an estimator around the true parameter can always be bounded using the mean squared error.

Lemma 169
.

Let
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
be an estimator of
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{p}
such that
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\theta}_{i}]<\infty,\forall i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
. Then for all
\epsilon>0
,

\Pr\left[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}\geq\epsilon\right]\leq\frac{\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\epsilon^{2}}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}\triangleq\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
. Since
\epsilon>0
, applying Markov’s inequality (see Section
) yields

\Pr\left[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}\geq\epsilon\right]=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\geq\epsilon^{2}]\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]}{\epsilon^{2}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]}{\epsilon^{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\epsilon^{2}}.

This completes the proof.

Both biased and unbiased estimators can be consistent (an example can be found in Theorem
).
Regarding mean squared error (MSE), both biased and unbiased estimators can achieve an MSE approaching zero as the sample size grows sufficiently large.

Remark 170
(Consistency).

It is important to note that while the convergence of the MSE to zero implies consistency, the reverse implication does not generally hold.

Asymptotic Theory

Five key tools, along with their extensions, play a central role in asymptotic theory.
These include the weak law of large numbers (WLLN), the central limit theorem (CLT), the continuous mapping theorem (CMT), Slutsky’s theorem, and the Delta method.
We present the main results without proof; detailed proofs can be found, for example, in the references listed at the beginning of this section.

{theoremHigh}

[
L^{2}
Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN2)]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be i.i.d. random variables with
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=\mu<\infty
and
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=\sigma^{2}<\infty
. Let
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
. Then, as
n\rightarrow\infty
,

\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mu.

Remark 171
(
L^{1}
weak law of large numbers (WLLN1)).

Actually, the same conclusion can be drawn under weaker assumptions. Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be i.i.d. random variables with
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=\mu<\infty
. It suffices to assume that
\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert]<\infty
rather than
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]<\infty
.
Then, as
n\rightarrow\infty
,

\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mu.

This result extends naturally to the multivariate case.
Let
{\mathbf{x}}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{n}
be i.i.d. random
vectors
with
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{i}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}<\infty
and
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert]<\infty
. Let
\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
.
Then, as
n\rightarrow\infty
,

\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\boldsymbol{\mu}.

The key observation in WLLN lies in the scaling by
\frac{1}{n}
, which reduces the variance of the sample mean to
\sigma^{2}/n
. causing it to vanish as
n
increases.
As a result, the sample mean converges in probability to the true mean
\mu
, or to the mean vector
\boldsymbol{\mu}
in the multivariate setting.

{theoremHigh}

[Central limit theorem (CLT)]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be i.i.d. random variables with
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=\mu<\infty
and
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=\sigma^{2}<\infty
. Let
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
. Then, as
n\rightarrow\infty
,

\sqrt{n}(\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}-\mu)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}).

Similarly, this result extends to the multivariate case. Let
{\mathbf{x}}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{n}
be i.i.d. random
vectors
with
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{i}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}<\infty
and
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\mathbf{x}}_{i}]=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
. Let
\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
. Then, as
n\rightarrow\infty
,

\sqrt{n}(\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}).

The CLT is stronger than the WLLN2 as
\sqrt{n}(\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}-\mu)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
implies
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mu
(since
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\mu,\frac{1}{n}\sigma^{2})
in CLT). However,
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mu
does not provide any information about
\sqrt{n}\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}
.

Remark 172
.

Note that if a statistic
s
asymptotically follows a Gaussian distribution
{\textnormal{s}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}],\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{s}}])
, where
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}]
and
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{s}}]
are the expectation and variance of
s
, respectively, then approximately we have:

\frac{{\textnormal{s}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}]}{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{s}}]}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

According to the definition of the Chi-squared distribution (Definition
), this implies

\frac{({\textnormal{s}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}])^{2}}{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{s}}]}\sim\chi^{2}_{(1)}.

If
s
is a vector
{\mathbf{s}}=[{\textnormal{s}}_{1},{\textnormal{s}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{s}}_{k}]^{\top}\in\real^{k}
, the above conclusion can be written in vector form as:

({\mathbf{s}}-\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{s}}])^{\top}\bm{V}^{-1}({\mathbf{s}}-\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{s}}])\sim\chi^{2}_{(k)},

where
\bm{V}
is the covariance matrix of
{\mathbf{s}}
and must be nonsingular.
Note that
({\mathbf{s}}-\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{s}}])^{\top}\bm{V}^{-1}({\mathbf{s}}-\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{s}}])
is also called the square of Mahalanobis distance between
{\mathbf{s}}
and
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{s}}]
.

In addition to the standard CLT, the following theorem presents a more general version of the central limit theorem that will often be useful.

{theoremHigh}
[Weighted sum central limit theorem (WCLT)]
Let
\{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\}
be a sequence of i.i.d. real random variables with
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=0
and
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=1
. Let
\{\eta_{n}\}
be a sequence of real constants. If

\mathop{\sup}_{1\leq i\leq n}\frac{\eta_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta_{j}^{2}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}0,

then

\frac{1}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\eta_{i}^{2}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\eta_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,1).

{theoremHigh}

[Continuous mapping theorem (CMT)]
Given a sequence of random variables
\{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\}
. If
x
is a random variable such that
\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\in\mathcal{A}]=1
and
g:\real\rightarrow\real
is continuous everywhere on
\mathcal{A}
, then,

\displaystyle{\textnormal{x}}_{n}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}\,\,\Longrightarrow\,\,g({\textnormal{x}}_{n})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}g({\textnormal{x}});

\displaystyle{\textnormal{x}}_{n}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}\,\,\Longrightarrow\,\,g({\textnormal{x}}_{n})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}g({\textnormal{x}}).

Similarly, the result can be extended to the multi-dimensional case. Given a sequence of random vectors
\{{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\}
. If
{\mathbf{x}}
is a random vector such that
\Pr[{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{A}]=1
and
g:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real^{k}
is continuous everywhere on
\mathcal{A}
, then,

\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}_{n}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbf{x}}\,\,\Longrightarrow\,\,g({\mathbf{x}}_{n})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}g({\mathbf{x}});

\displaystyle{\mathbf{x}}_{n}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbf{x}}\,\,\Longrightarrow\,\,g({\mathbf{x}}_{n})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}g({\mathbf{x}}).

The CMT was proved by
Mann and Wald 1943
and is sometimes referred to as the
Mann-Wald Theorem
. Note that the CMT allows the function
g
to be discontinuous but the probability of being at a discontinuity point is zero. For example, the function
g(u)=\frac{1}{u}
is discontinuous at
u=0
. But if
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
, then
\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}=0]=0
such that
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}^{-1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}^{-1}
.

{theoremHigh}

[Slutsky’s theorem]
Let
x
be a random variable and
c\in\real
be a constant. Suppose
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}
and
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}c
(i.e.,
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}c
). Then, it follows that

\displaystyle{\textnormal{x}}_{n}+{\textnormal{y}}_{n}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}+c;

\displaystyle{\textnormal{x}}_{n}{\textnormal{y}}_{n}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}c{\textnormal{x}};

\displaystyle{\textnormal{y}}_{n}^{-1}{\textnormal{x}}_{n}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}c^{-1}{\textnormal{x}},

when
c\neq 0
, as
n\rightarrow\infty
. (Note here,
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
,
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}
,
x
, and
c
can be understood as vectors or matrices, provided that all operations are well-defined.)

Note that one cannot replace the constant
c
with a non-degenerate random variable (or random vector, matrix) in Slutsky’s theorem. For example, take
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}=-{\textnormal{z}}+n^{-1}
and
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}={\textnormal{z}}-n^{-1}
, for
{\textnormal{z}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
. Then,
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{z}}
(since
-{\textnormal{z}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
),
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{z}}
. But for all
n
, we have
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}+{\textnormal{y}}_{n}=0
; and thus,
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}+{\textnormal{y}}_{n}
fails to converge in distribution to
2{\textnormal{z}}
.

An important application of Slutsky’s theorem is given below:

Example 173
.

Suppose
{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
and
{\mathbf{y}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
. Then
{\mathbf{y}}_{n}^{-1/2}{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{I})
.

{theoremHigh}

[General version of Slutsky’s theorem]
Let
x
be a random variable and
c\in\real
be a constant. Suppose
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{x}}
and
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}c
(i.e.,
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}c
). Let further that
g:\real\times\real
be a continuous function. Then, it follows that

\displaystyle g({\textnormal{x}}_{n},{\textnormal{y}}_{n})

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}g({\textnormal{x}},c)

as
n\rightarrow\infty
. (Note here,
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
,
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}
,
x
, and
c
can be understood as vectors or matrices as long as the operations are compatible.)

The Delta method is a direct consequence of Slutsky’s theorem and CMT.
It allows us to apply transformations to results obtained from the central limit theorem.

{theoremHigh}
[The Delta method]
Let
{\textnormal{z}}_{n}=a_{n}({\textnormal{x}}_{n}-\theta)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\textnormal{z}}
, where
a_{n},\theta\in\real
for all
n
and
a_{n}\uparrow\infty
. Let
g:\real\rightarrow\real
be differentiable at
\theta
. Then,
a_{n}(g({\textnormal{x}}_{n})-g(\theta))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}g^{\prime}(\theta){\textnormal{z}}
, provided that
g^{\prime}(\theta)\neq 0
.

In most applications,
a_{n}
in the theorem above is constructed to be
\sqrt{n}
such that
\sqrt{n}\uparrow\infty
as
n\rightarrow\infty
. The Delta method implies that, asymptotically, the randomness in a transformation of
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
is completely controlled by that in
{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
.

{theoremHigh}

[The Delta method, multi-dimensional case]
Let
{\mathbf{z}}_{n}=a_{n}({\mathbf{x}}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\theta})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\mathbf{z}}
, where
a_{n}\in\real
,
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\real^{d}
for all
n
and
a_{n}\uparrow\infty
. Let
g:\real^{d}\rightarrow\real^{p}
be continuously differentiable at
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. Then,

a_{n}(g({\mathbf{x}}_{n})-g(\boldsymbol{\theta}))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta}){\mathbf{z}},

where
J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
is the
p\times d
Jacobian matrix of
g
,

J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}g_{1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}g_{1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})&\ldots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{d}}g_{1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}g_{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta})&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}g_{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta})&\ldots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{d}}g_{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}g_{p}(\boldsymbol{\theta})&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}g_{p}(\boldsymbol{\theta})&\ldots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{d}}g_{p}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\\
\end{bmatrix}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By Taylor’s expansion (Theorem
) around
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, we have

g({\mathbf{x}}_{n})=g(\boldsymbol{\theta})+J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}^{\ast})({\mathbf{x}}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\theta}),

where
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}^{\ast}
lies between
{\mathbf{x}}_{n}
and
\boldsymbol{\theta}
such that

\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}^{\ast}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rvert<\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\right\rvert=\left\lvert a_{n}^{-1}\right\rvert\cdot\left\lvert a_{n}({\mathbf{x}}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\theta})\right\rvert=\left\lvert a_{n}^{-1}\right\rvert\cdot\left\lvert{\mathbf{z}}_{n}\right\rvert\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\boldsymbol{0},

where the convergence follows from Slutsky’s theorem. Therefore, we have
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}^{\ast}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\boldsymbol{\theta}
. By applying CMT, we have
J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}^{\ast})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
. Therefore,

\displaystyle{\mathbf{z}}_{n}=a_{n}(g({\mathbf{x}}_{n})-g(\boldsymbol{\theta}))

\displaystyle=a_{n}J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}^{\ast})({\mathbf{x}}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\theta})

\displaystyle=J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n}^{\ast})a_{n}({\mathbf{x}}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\theta})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}J_{g}(\boldsymbol{\theta}){\mathbf{z}},

where the convergence follows from Slutsky’s theorem.

Example 174
.

Suppose
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
are i.i.d. random variables with mean
\mu
and variance
\sigma^{2}<\infty
. Let
\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
. By CLT, we have

\sqrt{n}(\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n}-\mu)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}).

Given a continuously differentiable function
g(\cdot)
, the Delta method implies that

\sqrt{n}(g(\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n})-g(\mu))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}(g^{\prime}(\mu))^{2}).

Suppose further that
\{{\textnormal{y}}_{n}\}
is a sequence of random variables such that
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\sigma
. Then, by Slutsky’s theorem, we obtain

\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{g(\bar{{\textnormal{x}}}_{n})-g(\mu)}{{\textnormal{y}}_{n}}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,(g^{\prime}(\mu))^{2}).

Apart from the five basic weapons, the following Cramér-Wold device is also very useful.

{theoremHigh}
[Cramér-Wold device]
Let
\{{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\}
be a sequence of random vectors in
p
, and
{\mathbf{x}}
be a random vector in
p
. Then,

{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}{\mathbf{x}}\qquad\text{if and only if}\qquad\bm{u}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\bm{u}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}},\ \forall\,\bm{u}\in\real^{p}.

4.5.2
Assumptions Restated

For large sample asymptotic results of least squares estimators, we restate the assumptions as follows:

Assumption
\thetheo

We assume that

OLS.0 (random sampling): (
{\textnormal{y}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
),
i=1,2,\ldots,n
are i.i.d.

OLS.1 (full rank):
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
.

OLS.
1.2

\mathrm{rank}(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}]=p)
.

OLS.2 (first moment):
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid{\mathbf{x}}]={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, i.e.,
{\textnormal{y}}={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon
and
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid{\mathbf{x}}]=0
.

OLS.
2.2

{\textnormal{y}}={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon
with
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon{\mathbf{x}}]=\boldsymbol{0}
.

OLS.3 (second moment):
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i}^{2}]<\infty
, where
\epsilon_{i}
is the noise associated with the input
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
.

OLS.
3.2
(homoskedasticity):
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i}^{2}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{i}]=\sigma^{2}
.

OLS.4 (normality):
p(\epsilon\mid{\mathbf{x}})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
.

Assumption OLS.2 is equivalent to stating
{\textnormal{y}}={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon
(linear in parameters) and
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid{\mathbf{x}}]=0
(zero conditional mean).
And Assumption OLS.2 is stronger than Assumption OLS2.2.
Moreover, Assumption OLS.3.2 is stronger than Assumption OLS.3 since OLS3.2 implies the independence between
\epsilon_{i}
and
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
. The linear model under Assumption OLS.3.2 is called the
homoskedastic linear regression model
.
In most of our discussions in the previous sections, we assume OLS.0 (with fixed
\bm{x}_{i}
’s), OLS.1, OLS.2, OLS.3.2, OLS.4. That is

\displaystyle{\textnormal{y}}

\displaystyle={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid{\mathbf{x}}]

\displaystyle=0,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{2}\mid{\mathbf{x}}]

\displaystyle=\sigma^{2},

\displaystyle p(\epsilon\mid{\mathbf{x}})

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}).

However, if
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{2}\mid{\mathbf{x}}]=\sigma^{2}({\mathbf{x}})
, i.e., the noise variance depends on the input
{\mathbf{x}}
, then the errors are said to be
heteroskedastic
.

4.5.3
Asymptotics for the OLS Estimator

Asymptotic distribution of MLE

To study the asymptotic behavior of the OLS estimator, we first examine the asymptotic properties of the MLE in general.
Let
\widehat{\theta}
be the MLE of
\theta
.
To avoid confusion, let the true value of
\theta
be denoted by
\theta_{0}
.
We shall show that as the sample size
n
becomes large, the distribution of the MLE
\widehat{\theta}
is approximately normal with mean
\theta_{0}
and variance
1/n\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})
, where
\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})
is the Fisher information evaluated at
\theta_{0}
.
Since this result holds only in the limit as
n\rightarrow\infty
, we say that the MLE is
asymptotically unbiased
, and we refer to the variance of the limiting normal distribution as the
asymptotic variance
of the MLE. More precisely, we have the following theorem:

{theoremHigh}

[The asymptotic distribution of MLE]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be a sample of size
n
from a distribution for which the p.d.f. or p.m.f. is
p(x\mid\theta)
, where
\theta
is an unknown parameter.
Assume that the true value of
\theta
is
\theta_{0}
, and the MLE of
\theta
is
\widehat{\theta}
. Then the probability distribution of
\sqrt{n\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})
converges to a standard normal distribution as
n\rightarrow\infty
.
In other words, the asymptotic distribution of
\widehat{\theta}
is

\mathcal{N}\left(\theta_{0},\frac{1}{n\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}\right),

where
\mathbb{I}(\cdot)
denotes the Fisher information; see Section
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We shall prove that

\sqrt{n\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)

asymptotically. Here, we provide only a sketch of the proof; the full details are beyond the scope of this book.

Recall that the log-likelihood function is

\ell(\theta)\triangleq\ell(\theta;\bm{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln p(x_{i}\mid\theta)

and the MLE
\widehat{\theta}
satisfies
\ell^{\prime}(\widehat{\theta})=0
. We apply the linear approximation theorem of
\ell^{\prime}(\widehat{\theta})
at the point
\theta_{0}
(Theorem
), yielding

0=\ell^{\prime}(\widehat{\theta})\approx\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0})+(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{0})
.
Therefore, we have

\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0}\approx\frac{-\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0})}{\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{0})}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\approx\frac{-n^{-1/2}\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0})}{n^{-1}\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{0})}.

Now consider the numerator of this expression. Its expectation is

\mathbb{E}[-n^{-1/2}\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0})]=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ln p(x_{i}\mid\theta_{0})\right]=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0};{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\right]=0,

and its variance is

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[-n^{-1/2}\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0})]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ln p(x_{i}\mid\theta_{0})\Big)^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\big(\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0};{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\big)^{2}\right]=\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0}).

By definition, the denominator is
\frac{1}{n}\ell^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{0})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta^{2}}\ln p(x_{i}\mid\theta_{0})
.
By the law of large numbers (Theorem
), this expression converges to

\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta^{2}}\ln p({\textnormal{x}}_{i}\mid\theta_{0})\right]=-\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0}).

Thus, we can write

\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\approx\frac{-n^{-1/2}\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0})}{\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}.

Therefore, it holds that

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\right]

\displaystyle\approx\frac{\mathbb{E}[n^{-1/2}\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0})]}{\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}=0;

\displaystyle\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}\left[\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\right]

\displaystyle\approx\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[n^{-1/2}\ell^{\prime}(\theta_{0})]}{\mathbb{I}^{2}(\theta_{0})}=\frac{\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}{\mathbb{I}^{2}(\theta_{0})}=\frac{1}{\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}.

As
n\to\infty
, applying central limit theorem (Theorem
), we have

\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{1}{\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}\right)\qquad\iff\qquad\sqrt{n\mathbb{I}(\theta_{0})}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

This completes the proof.

This result shows that the MLE is asymptotically optimal, because its asymptotic variance reaches the CRLB; see Theorem
. For this reason, MLE is frequently used especially with large samples.
For a multivariate problem, similar to the scalar case, the asymptotic distribution of the MLE
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MLE}}
is approximately multivariate Gaussian distribution with the true value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0}
as the mean and
[n\mathbb{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0})]^{-1}
as the covariance matrix.
Once again,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
stands the maximum likelihood estimate of the OLS problem.
This further illustrates why the method of ordinary least squares plays such a central role in linear model estimation.

Consistency of OLS

We now show that the OLS estimator is consistent under relatively mild conditions.

{theoremHigh}
[Consistency of OLS estimator]
Let
\{{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\}
be a sequence of
n\times p
design matrices, and
\{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\}
be a sequence of
n\times 1
vectors. For each element, let
{\mathbf{y}}_{m}={\mathbf{X}}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}
, and the OLS estimator is obtained by
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}=({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}_{m}
. Suppose the model satisfies the following assumptions:

1.

OLS.0 (random sampling): (
{\textnormal{y}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
),
i=1,2,\ldots,n
are i.i.d.

2.

OLS.1.2 (full rank):
\mathrm{rank}(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}]=p)
.

3.

OLS.2.2:
{\textnormal{y}}={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon
with
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon{\mathbf{x}}]=\boldsymbol{0}
.

4.

OLS.3 (second moment):
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i}^{2}]<\infty
, where
\epsilon_{i}
is the noise associated with input
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
.

Then the least squares estimator satisfies

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, i.e.,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}
is consistent.

The assumptions OLS2.2 and OLS.3 in this context are relatively mild compared to those used earlier when deriving the OLS estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
A stronger set of assumptions, such as OLS.2 and OLS.3.2, would also lead to the same consistency result.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We begin by expressing the OLS estimator as:

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}

\displaystyle=({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}_{m}=({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m})=\boldsymbol{\beta}+({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}.

To prove consistency, it suffices to show that the second term converges in probability to zero:
({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\boldsymbol{0}
.

For
{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}
, since
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
’s are i.i.d. (OLS.0),

{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}]
as
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}]\leq\infty
implied in OLS.1.2 and by applying WLLN1. This implies
({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}]^{-1}
.

For
{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}
, similarly, since
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
’s are i.i.d. (OLS.0), we have
{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}]
by applying WLLN1 if we have
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert\epsilon{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert]<\infty
. To see why
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert\epsilon{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert]<\infty
, we have

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert\epsilon{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert^{2}\right]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}\left[|\epsilon|^{2}\right]^{1/2}<\infty,

by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (see Section
), and which is finite by Assumption OLS1.2 and OLS.3. Then,
({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}
can be expressed as

\displaystyle({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}]^{-1}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{0},

by applying Slutsky’s theorem. This completes the proof.

{theoremHigh}

[Consistency of noise estimators]
Let
\{{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\}
be a sequence of
n\times p
design matrices, and
\{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\}
be a sequence of
n\times 1
vectors. For each element, let
{\mathbf{y}}_{m}={\mathbf{X}}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}
.
The maximum likelihood estimator of the noise variance is obtained by

\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{m}=\frac{1}{n}{\mathbf{e}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}_{m}=\frac{1}{n}({\mathbf{y}}_{m}-{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m})^{\top}({\mathbf{y}}_{m}-{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}),\qquad\text{(Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theorem:mle-gaussian})}

and an unbiased estimator of the noise variance is given by

{\textnormal{S}}^{2}_{m}=\frac{1}{n-p}{\mathbf{e}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}_{m}=\frac{1}{n-p}({\mathbf{y}}_{m}-{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m})^{\top}({\mathbf{y}}_{m}-{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}).\qquad\text{(Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theorem:ss-chisquare})}

Now suppose that the linear regression model satisfies the same assumptions as in Theorem
, along with the following additional condition:

(v). OLS.
3.2
(homoskedasticity):
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i}^{2}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{i}]=\sigma^{2}
.

Then, both estimators of the noise variance are consistent:

\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\sigma^{2}
and
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\sigma^{2}
, which means
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{m}
and
{\textnormal{S}}^{2}_{m}
are consistent estimators of
\sigma^{2}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We begin by expressing the residual vector as

{\mathbf{e}}_{m}={\mathbf{y}}_{m}-{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}=(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}+{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta})-{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}+{\mathbf{X}}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}).

Thus, it follows that

\displaystyle\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{m}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}{\mathbf{e}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}_{m}=\frac{1}{n}\left\{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}+2\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m})+(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m})^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m})\right\}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}^{2}+2\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\right)(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m})+(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m})^{\top}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\right)(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m})

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\sigma^{2},

by applying the WLLN1, Theorem
, and Slutsky’s theorem.

For
{\textnormal{S}}_{m}^{2}
, it follows that

{\textnormal{S}}_{m}^{2}=\frac{n}{n-p}\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\sigma^{2}

by Slutsky’s theorem.

From the above theorem, we find two different estimators—one biased and one unbiased—can both be consistent. That is, when sample size
n
is sufficiently large, the estimates
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{m}
and
{\textnormal{S}}_{m}^{2}
become very close to each other and to the true value
\sigma^{2}
.

As previously noted, unbiasedness is not a necessary condition for consistency. This result highlights that even though
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{m}
is biased in finite samples, it still converges to the correct parameter value as
n
increases. Similarly, although
{\textnormal{S}}_{m}^{2}
is unbiased, its consistency also depends on the behavior of the estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}
and the law of large numbers.

Asymptotic Normality under Noise Moment Assumption

To study the approximate sampling distribution of the OLS estimator under the moment assumption, we introduce the following additional assumption:

Assumption OLS.5:
\mathop{\max}_{1\leq i\leq n}\left\{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}0
.

This indicates that the diagonal elements of the hat matrix
\bm{H}_{m}=\bm{X}_{m}(\bm{X}_{m}^{\top}\bm{X}_{m})^{-1}\bm{X}_{m}^{\top}
converge to zero.

Under the moment assumption, we only assume that the noise vector satisfies
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}
, rather than assuming normality:
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
.
We proved that the OLS estimator of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is unbiased such that
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{e}}]=\boldsymbol{0}
in Section
, and the sampling distribution of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1})
in Theorem
if we assume further that the noise follows from a Gaussian distribution:
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
.
However, what can we say about the sampling distribution of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
when the noise vector is not normally distributed?

We now show that, under certain regularity conditions (including Assumption OLS.5), we can approximate the sampling distribution of the OLS estimator even without assuming Gaussian errors.

{theoremHigh}
[Large sample distribution of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}
]
Let
\{{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\}
be a sequence of
n\times p
design matrices, and
\{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\}
be a sequence of
n\times 1
vectors. For each element, let
{\mathbf{y}}_{m}={\mathbf{X}}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}
. If

1.

OLS.0 (random sampling): (
{\textnormal{y}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
),
i=1,2,\ldots,n
are i.i.d.

2.

OLS.1.2:
{\mathbf{X}}_{m}
has full rank
p
for all
m\geq 1
.

3.

OLS.2 and OLS.3, the moment assumption:
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}]=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{m}
for all
m\geq 1
. That is, for each
i
-th element
\epsilon_{mi}
, we have
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{mi}]=0
and
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\epsilon_{mi}]=\sigma^{2}
.

4.

OLS.5:
\mathop{\max}_{1\leq i\leq n}\left\{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}0
.

Then the ordinary least squares estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}=({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}_{m}
satisfies

({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{1/2}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{p}),

where
\bm{I}_{p}
is a
p\times p
identity matrix.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Recall that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}=({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m})
.
Then, we have
({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{1/2}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}-\boldsymbol{\beta})=({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}
.
Let
\bm{u}\in\real^{p}
be a unit-length vector, and define the vector
\boldsymbol{\eta}_{m}\in\real^{n}
such that

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\eta}_{m}

\displaystyle=[\eta_{m1},\eta_{m2},\ldots,\eta_{mn}]^{\top}

\displaystyle=[\bm{u}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}{\mathbf{x}}_{1},\ldots\bm{u}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}{\mathbf{x}}_{n}]^{\top}

\displaystyle={\mathbf{X}}_{m}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}\bm{u},

where
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
is the
i
-th row of
{\mathbf{X}}_{m}
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
.
Then, we have

\boldsymbol{\eta}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\eta}_{m}=\bm{u}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}\bm{u}=1.

That is,
\boldsymbol{\eta}_{m}
is a unit-length random vector.
Moreover, according to Schwarz matrix inequality (see Section
), we have

\eta_{mi}^{2}\leq\left\lVert\bm{u}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}={\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}.

Therefore, by assumption:

\mathop{\max}_{1\leq i\leq n}\frac{\eta_{mi}^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{j}\eta_{mj}^{2}}=\mathop{\max}_{1\leq i\leq n}\frac{\eta_{mi}^{2}}{\boldsymbol{\eta}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\eta}_{m}}\leq\mathop{\max}_{1\leq i\leq n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\rightarrow\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}0.

Thus, by weighted sum central limit theorem in Theorem
, it follows that

\sum_{i=1}^{n}\eta_{mi}\epsilon_{mi}=\boldsymbol{\eta}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}).

That is,

\bm{u}^{\top}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})

Since we assume
\bm{u}
is a unit-length vector, then if
{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
, we have
\bm{u}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
. By Cramér-Wold device (see Theorem
), this implies that

({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1/2}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}).

We complete the proof.

The result above implies that, for large enough sample size
n
, the OLS estimator approximately follows a multivariate normal distribution:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}_{m}^{\top}\bm{X}_{m})^{-1}).

Similarly, the predicted values satisfy:

\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}_{m}=\bm{X}_{m}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{X}_{m}(\bm{X}_{m}^{\top}\bm{X}_{m})^{-1}\bm{X}_{m}^{\top})=\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{H}_{m}).

This asymptotic normality justifies the use of standard inference procedures (e.g., hypothesis testing, confidence intervals) even when the errors are not normally distributed, provided the regularity conditions hold.

Asymptotic Normality under Higher Moment Assumption

To further investigate the approximate sampling distribution of the OLS estimator under the moment assumption, we introduce the following additional condition:

Assumption OLS.6:
\quad\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{4}]<\infty
and
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert^{4}]<\infty
.

{theoremHigh}

[Large sample distribution of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}
]
Let
\{{\mathbf{X}}_{m}\}
be a sequence of
n\times p
design matrices, and
\{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\}
be a sequence of
n\times 1
vectors. For each element, let
{\mathbf{y}}_{m}={\mathbf{X}}_{m}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}
.
Suppose the model satisfies the following assumptions:

1.

OLS.0 (random sampling): (
{\textnormal{y}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
),
i=1,2,\ldots,n
are i.i.d.

2.

OLS.1.2 (full rank):
\mathrm{rank}(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}]=p)
.

3.

OLS.2.2:
{\textnormal{y}}={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon
with
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon{\mathbf{x}}]=\boldsymbol{0}
.

4.

OLS.3 (second moment):
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i}^{2}]<\infty
, where
\epsilon_{i}
is the noise associated with input
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
.

5.

OLS.6:
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{4}]<\infty
and
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert^{4}]<\infty
.

Then, the ordinary least squares estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}=({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}_{m}
satisfies

\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{V}),

where
\bm{V}=\bm{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{A}^{-1}
with
\bm{A}=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}]
and
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{2}{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}]
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
From Theorem
, we know that:

\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}-\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sqrt{n}({\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{m})^{-1}{\mathbf{X}}_{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}=\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right).

By applying Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\epsilon_{i}^{2}\right\rVert\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\right\rVert^{2}\right]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}\left[\epsilon_{i}^{4}\right]^{1/2}\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert^{4}\right]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}\left[\epsilon_{i}^{4}\right]^{1/2}<\infty,

where the second inequality follows from the Schwarz matrix inequality (see Section
), and the last inequality holds due to Assumption OLS.6.
Therefore, according to the CLT and OLS.2.2, we have

\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}=\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\boldsymbol{0}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega}).

Again, we have
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\bm{A}
. Thus,

\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\bm{A}^{-1}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{V})

by Slutsky’s theorem and the symmetry of
\bm{A}
.

Compared to Theorem
(which assumes
homoskedasticity
), we have a similar result in the Theorem
above (which assumes
heteroskedasticity
). However, in Theorem
, we do not assume the moment assumption on the noise:
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}]=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}]=\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{n}
. This results in the difference between the covariance matrices of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{m}
in the two theorems.

In the homoskedastic model,
\bm{V}
reduces to
\bm{V}_{0}=\sigma^{2}\bm{A}^{-1}
, which is the same as that in Theorem
. But the result in Theorem
is more general, as it allows for arbitrary patterns of heteroskedasticity, provided the fourth-moment conditions hold.

Gaussian MLE.
Let
x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}
be i.i.d. samples drawn from a Gaussian density
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
(Definition
).
The unique MLE of
[\mu,\sigma^{2}]
is given by

[\widehat{\mu},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}]=\left[\bar{x},\frac{1}{n}(x_{i}-\bar{x})^{2}\right],

where

Let

\mathcal{E}(\lambda)

).
Show that the unique MLE of

\widehat{\lambda}=\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{\bar{x}}.

\epsilon_{i}\sim\text{Uniform}(-a,a)
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, i.e., uniformly distributed on the interval
[-a,a]
and the density function is
p(x)=\frac{1}{2a}
for
x\in[-a,a]
. Show that a maximum likelihood estimate of the linear model is any
\boldsymbol{\beta}
satisfying
\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq a
.

Complete the proof of Theorem

Show that
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\chi_{(2)}^{2}
if and only if

(Definition
).

Prove that if
{\textnormal{x}}\sim t_{(n)}
, then
{\textnormal{x}}^{2}\sim F_{1,n}
.

7.

In Theorem
, we derived the maximum likelihood estimator of
\sigma^{2}
as:
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{n}{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}^{n}{\textnormal{e}}_{i}^{2}
. By Theorem
, we show that
the maximum likelihood estimator of
\sigma^{2}
is a biased estimator. The unbiased estimator of
\sigma^{2}
should be

{\textnormal{S}}^{2}=\frac{1}{n-p}({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{n-p}{\mathbf{e}}^{\top}{\mathbf{e}}
.
Using the definitions of overestimation and underestimation provided in Definition
, determine whether the MLE
\widehat{\sigma}^{2}
overestimates or underestimates the true variance
\sigma^{2}
.

Prove Remark

{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})
and

and
