Chapter 6
Large-Scale Least Squares Approximations

R
Randomized methods help address large-scale optimization problems by offering faster and more efficient solutions to complex linear algebra tasks, enhancing the performance of iterative solvers through better preconditioning and enable scalable solutions for handling massive datasets.
These methods can significantly aid in solving large-scale optimization problems through several key mechanisms:

Random sampling and projection.
Randomized algorithms often use randomness to perform sampling or projection operations on matrices. This involves selecting a small number of columns, rows, or elements from the matrix in a strategic manner to highlight important structural features. Alternatively, data can be projected into a lower-dimensional space while preserving key characteristics of the original dataset. The goal is to create a “sketch” of the original data—similar in essential properties but simpler and faster to process.

Improved computational efficiency.
By using these sketches, randomized methods can significantly reduce the computational burden associated with solving large-scale linear algebra problems, such as matrix multiplication, least-squares regression, and low-rank matrix approximation. As a result, they make it feasible to solve problems that would otherwise be computationally infeasible due to their size.

Scalability.
Randomized methods are designed to scale well with the size of the input data, making them ideal for applications in machine learning, statistical data analysis, and other fields where datasets continue to grow. These techniques allow for the efficient processing of large datasets on both single machines and distributed systems without compromising accuracy.

In this chapter, we will primarily introduce randomized algorithms for solving large-scale least-squares problems.

6.1
Sketched Least Squares

6.1.1
General Ideas and Subspace Embedding

This subsection will not tend to be rigorous, which is the main goal of this book.
We will collect some important theorems in this section without proof.
This subsection is standalone, which aims to introduce the fundamental notions of subspace embedding, sketching technique, and its complexity in matrix multiplication.
For further details, readers may refer to the references cited throughout the text.

Sketching Technique

Before exploring large-scale least squares approximations, we briefly review the sketching technique used in approximate matrix multiplication.
To motivate this approach, we begin with a fundamental problem: approximating the product of two matrices.
Suppose that we are given an
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
and a
p\times m
matrix
\bm{Y}
, and our goal is to compute their product
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
:

Three-loop perspective.
The most straightforward method for computing
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
is the classic three-loop algorithm.
In this approach, each entry of the resulting matrix is viewed as the inner product between a row of
\bm{X}
and a column of
\bm{Y}
:

(\bm{X}\bm{Y})_{ij}=\left\langle\bm{x}^{(i)},\bm{y}_{j}\right\rangle,\quad\forall\,i,j,

(6.1)

where
\bm{x}^{(i)}
denotes the
i
-th row of
\bm{X}
(treated as a column vector), and
\bm{y}_{j}
represents the
j
-th column of
\bm{Y}
.

Column-row perspective.
An alternative way to understand the product
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
is as the sum of
p
outer products, each of which is formed by a column of
\bm{X}
and the corresponding row of
\bm{Y}
:

\bm{X}\bm{Y}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{y}^{(i)\top}.

(6.2)

From the column-row perspective, we can attempt to construct a simplified “sketch” of the columns of
\bm{X}
and the rows of
\bm{Y}
.
These sketches are represented as matrices
\bm{C}
and
\bm{R}
, respectively, and we approximate
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
using the product
\bm{C}\bm{R}
.

Such a sketch can be constructed using a
p\times k
(with
k<p
) matrix
\bm{S}
(since we consider only linear sketches) such that
\bm{C}=\bm{X}\bm{S}\in\real^{n\times k}
and
\bm{R}=\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{Y}\in\real^{k\times m}
.
Here,
\bm{X}\bm{S}
performs a right-sketch on the columns of
\bm{X}
, while
\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{Y}
applies a left-sketch to the rows of
\bm{Y}
.
Our objective is to approximate
\bm{X}\bm{Y}
using6
\bm{X}\bm{Y}\approx\bm{C}\bm{R}=\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{Y}
, where the quality of this approximation is typically evaluated by bounding the norm of the error matrix, i.e., by providing an upper bound for
\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{Y}-\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{\xi}
, where
\xi
represents some matrix norm such as the spectral norm, Frobenius norm, or trace norm.

Of course, described this way, the sketching matrix
\bm{S}
can be anything—deterministic or randomized, efficient or intractable to compute, etc.
However, it turns out that when
\bm{S}
is randomized—based on techniques like random sampling or random projections—we often achieve better performance compared to deterministic approaches.

The randomized sketches fall into one of two categories:

Random sampling sketches.
In this case, each column of the matrix
\bm{S}
contains exactly one nonzero entry, indicating which (rescaled) column of
\bm{X}
is selected.

Random projection sketches.

That is, the matrix
\bm{S}
is dense or nearly dense, consisting of i.i.d. random variables—often drawn from a distribution such as the standard Gaussian.

Random projections are considered
data-agnostic
, meaning they can be constructed without observing the input data. In contrast, random sampling usually requires identifying and extracting important structural features from the data.

Basic versions of both methods often perform reasonably well—they typically produce acceptable approximations—but they are not always faster than solving the original problem directly. Therefore, more sophisticated variants have been developed. For example, the sketching matrix
\bm{S}
might combine a Hadamard-like transformation with uniform sampling or a sparse projection matrix. In such cases, the quality of the projection or sampling remains close to that of the basic method, but the computation is significantly faster.

However, the main goal of this chapter is to illustrate the core ideas using Gaussian sketching. For details on other techniques, readers are encouraged to consult the references provided throughout the text.

Subspace Embedding

We provide the basic concept of an
\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding for the column space of an
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
.
As we will see, this is a powerful tool for solving least squares regression problems. Throughout this section, for nonnegative real numbers
x
and
y
, we write
x\in(1\pm\varepsilon)y
to mean
x\in[(1-\varepsilon)y,(1+\varepsilon)y]
.

Definition 179
(
(1\pm\varepsilon)

\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
. Then, a
(1\pm\varepsilon)

\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding for the column space of
\bm{X}
is a matrix
\bm{S}
satisfies

\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\in(1\pm\varepsilon)\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\forall\,\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}.

In what follows, we will often use shorthand and say that
\bm{S}
is an
\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding for
\bm{X}
itself, even though the definition depends only on the column space of
\bm{X}
, not on the specific basis used to represent it.

Observe that if
\bm{S}
is a
(1\pm\varepsilon)

\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding for
\bm{X}
, then it is also a
(1\pm\varepsilon)

\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding for
\bm{Q}\in\real^{n\times r}
, where
\bm{Q}
is an orthonormal basis for the column space of
\bm{X}
and
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r
.
This is because the sets
\{\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}\}
and
\{\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\real^{r}\}
are identical.
Therefore, without loss of generality, we may assume that
\bm{X}
has orthonormal columns.
Under this assumption, the condition in Definition
becomes:

\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=(1\pm\varepsilon)\left\lVert\bm{Q}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=(1\pm\varepsilon)\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(6.3)

where the last equality follows since
\bm{Q}
has orthonormal columns.
If this requirement holds for all unit vectors
\boldsymbol{\alpha}
, then by linearity of
\bm{S}
, it holds for all
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\real^{r}
(e.g., by scaling).
Thus, the requirement can be further simplified to:

\left\lVert\bm{I}_{r}-\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{Q}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\varepsilon.

(6.4)

There are several goals in designing subspace embeddings. Two primary ones are:

To find a matrix
\bm{S}
with as few rows as possible.

To ensure that the product
\bm{S}\bm{X}
can be computed efficiently, since this is often a computational bottleneck in applications.

There are many ways to construct
\ell_{2}
-subspace embeddings, each offering different trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and other constraints. One particularly useful type is the oblivious
\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding.

Definition 180
(
(\varepsilon,\delta)
oblivious
\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding).

Let
P
be a distribution on
r\times n
matrices
\bm{S}
, where
r
is a function of
n,d,\varepsilon,
and
\delta
.
Suppose that with probability at least
1-\delta
, for any fixed
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
, a matrix
\bm{S}
drawn from distribution
P
satisfies the property that
\bm{S}
is a
(1\pm\varepsilon)

\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding for
\bm{X}
. Then we call
P
an
(\varepsilon,\delta)
oblivious
\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding.

Sarlos 2006
then proposed using Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms to construct subspace embeddings.

Definition 181
(Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform
(
Sarlos 2006
)
).

A random matrix
{\mathbf{S}}\in\real^{k\times n}
is said to form a Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) transform with parameters
\varepsilon,\delta,f
, or JLT
(\varepsilon,\delta,f)
for short, if with probability at least
1-\delta
, for any
f
-element subset
\mathcal{V}\subset\real^{n}
,
the following holds for all
\bm{v},\bm{v}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}
:

\left\lvert\left\langle\bm{S}\bm{v},\bm{S}\bm{v}^{\prime}\right\rangle-\left\langle\bm{v},\bm{v}^{\prime}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\varepsilon\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert\bm{v}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}.

If we set
\bm{v}=\bm{v}^{\prime}
, this condition reduces to the familiar statement that
\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\in(1\pm\varepsilon)\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. It turns out that if we scale all
\bm{v},\bm{v}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}
so that they are unit vectors, an equivalent condition can be formulated using only norms: specifically, we could require that

\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\in(1\pm\varepsilon)\left\lVert\bm{v}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lVert\bm{S}(\bm{v}+\bm{v}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\in(1\pm\varepsilon)\left\lVert\bm{v}+\bm{v}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

for all
\bm{v},\bm{v}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}
. In other words, the definition can be equivalently stated in terms of vector norms rather than inner products.

There are several known constructions of Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms. One of the simplest is provided by the Gaussian sketching theorem, which states that if the number of rows
k
satisfies
k=\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\ln(f/\delta))
,
then the resulting Gaussian matrix yields a valid JL transform.

{theoremHigh}
[Gaussian sketching
(
Indyk and Motwani 1998
;
Woodruff et al. 2014
)
]
Let
0<\varepsilon,\delta<1
, and let
{\mathbf{S}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}{\mathbf{G}}\in\real^{k\times n}
, where the entries
{\textnormal{g}}_{ij}
of
{\mathbf{G}}
are independent standard normal random variables. Then, if
k=\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\ln(f/\delta))
, the matrix
{\mathbf{S}}
is a JLT
(\varepsilon,\delta,f)
.

{theoremHigh}

[Gaussian sketching
(
Woodruff et al. 2014
)
]
Let
0<\varepsilon,\delta<1
, and let
{\mathbf{S}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}{\mathbf{G}}\in\real^{k\times n}
, where the entries
{\textnormal{g}}_{ij}
are independent standard normal random variables. Then, if
k=\Theta((d+\ln(1/\delta))\varepsilon^{-2})
, then for any fixed
n\times p
matrix
\bm{X}
, with probability at least
1-\delta
,
{\mathbf{S}}
is a
(1\pm\varepsilon)

\ell_{2}
-subspace embedding for
\bm{X}
; that is, simultaneously for all
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}
, it holds that
\left\lVert{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}\in(1\pm\varepsilon)\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}
.

It turns out that Theorem
provides an optimal number of rows of
{\mathbf{S}}
up to a constant factor—specifically,
\Theta(k\varepsilon^{-2})
.

After Theorem
was introduced, several improvements followed. For example,
Achlioptas 2003
showed that one can replace the Gaussian matrix
{\mathbf{G}}
in Theorem
with a matrix whose entries are i.i.d. sign random variables
Achlioptas 2003
; that is, each entry independently takes the value
1
or
-1
with equal probability. Furthermore, he showed that the distribution can be modified so that each entry of
{\mathbf{G}}
is set to
1
with probability
1/6
,
-1
with probability
1/6
, and 0 with probability
2/3
. This modification results in a sparse matrix
{\mathbf{S}}
, which allows faster computation of the product
{\mathbf{S}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\beta}
for any vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{n}
.

A significant advancement came from
Dasgupta et al. 2010
, who showed that it suffices for each column of
{\mathbf{S}}
to have only
\varepsilon^{-1}\text{poly}(\ln(f/\delta))
nonzero entries. If the
\text{poly}(f/\delta)
term is small compared to
\varepsilon^{-1}
, this represents a substantial improvement over earlier constructions, which required
\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\ln(f/\delta))
nonzero entries per column. Later,
Kane and Nelson 2014
improved this to
\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-1}\ln(f/\delta))
nonzero entries per column. This result was shown to be nearly tight by
Nelson and NguyÅn 2013
, who proved that at least
\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1}\ln(f/\delta)/\ln(1/\varepsilon))
column sparsity is necessary.

In summary, this line of work shows that applying a JLT
(\varepsilon,\delta,f)
matrix
{\mathbf{S}}
to a vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
can be done in time
\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{nnz}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\cdot\varepsilon^{-1}\ln(f/\delta))
, where
\mathrm{nnz}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
denotes the number of nonzero entries in
\boldsymbol{\beta}
. This leads to a significant speedup over Theorem
when
\varepsilon
is small. It also improves upon Theorem
, although even better results are possible in the context of
\ell_{2}
-subspace embeddings
(
Woodruff et al. 2014
)
.

Another approach aimed at speeding up the construction in Theorem
was proposed by
Ailon and Chazelle 2006
. Instead of focusing on sparsity, they sought to design matrices
{\mathbf{S}}
that can be applied to vectors
\boldsymbol{\beta}
very efficiently. The key idea is that for a vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{n}
whose
\ell_{2}
mass is approximately uniformly distributed across its coordinates, sampling a small number of coordinates uniformly at random and rescaling gives a good estimate of
\ell_{2}
-norm of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
. However, if
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is sparse or has unevenly distributed mass, uniform sampling performs poorly, as most samples may be zero.

6.1.2
Gaussian Left Sketching

We now discuss in more detail how Gaussian sketching can be applied to the least squares (LS) problem.

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
n>p
.
Now we examine a particular formulation of
\bm{S}\in\real^{m\times n}
: the
Gaussian left sketch
, or simply the
Gaussian sketch
. That is, let
{\mathbf{S}}
have i.i.d. Gaussian entries; specifically, each entry
{\textnormal{s}}_{ij}\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathcal{N}(0,1)
so that

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}]=\bm{I}

(6.5)

(since diagonals follow from a Chi-squared distribution; Definition
). Recall that the LS and sketched LS solutions are given, respectively, by

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Note that the sources of randomness in these two estimators are different. The sampling distribution of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
arises from the randomness in the sketching matrix
{\mathbf{S}}
, which induces variability through the sketched data
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}
and
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}
. In contrast, in Chapter
, the sampling distribution of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
stems from the stochasticity in the response vector
\bm{y}
, typically due to additive noise in the model.

In other words, while
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
varies across different realizations of the noise in the data,
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
varies across different realizations of the random projection matrix
{\mathbf{S}}
, assuming the original data
(\bm{X},\bm{y})
is fixed.

\paragrapharrow

Mean under Gaussian sketching.
Since
{\mathbf{S}}
is a random matrix, an important question is whether
\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]
is equal to
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, meaning that the expected value of the sketched solution equals the true least squares solution.
Assuming that
\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}
is nonsingular (which will hold with high probability when
m\gg p
), we can express the sketched solution as:

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}.

Now, decompose
\bm{y}
as
\bm{y}=\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\bm{y}^{\perp}
, where
\bm{y}^{\perp}\perp\mathcal{C}(\bm{X})
.
Substituting this decomposition into the expression for
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we obtain:

\displaystyle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}(\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\bm{y}^{\perp})

(6.6)

\displaystyle=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}^{\perp}.

Then for
\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
to hold, the term

\mathbb{E}[(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}^{\perp}]

must vanish. To see that this will happen, note that
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}
and
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}^{\perp}
are uncorrelated (
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}^{\perp}=\boldsymbol{0}
), which then implies independence. Then we can rewrite the expectation

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]

\displaystyle=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}}[(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}]\cdot\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}^{\perp}}[{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}^{\perp}]

(6.7)

\displaystyle=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}}[(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}]\cdot\boldsymbol{0}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

Thus, the expectation of the randomly projected solution matches the true least squares solution under Gaussian sketching.

\paragrapharrow

Variance under Gaussian sketching.
We also analyze the variances of:

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{E}\left[\big\lVert\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\right].

One key observation is that the variance tends to be smaller when the objective value
f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\big\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{y}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
is small. This is analogous to having low variance when the training loss is small in machine learning models.

Another thing to note is that throughout, we assume that
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{X}
and
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
are nonsingular.
In fact, if the eigenvalues of this matrix are small, i.e.,
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{X}
is nearly singular, then the variance will increase accordingly. However, we have some control over this via the construction of
\bm{S}
.

To analyze the variance, we begin by conditioning on on
\bm{S}\bm{X}
to derive a conditional distribution, and then relax this assumption to obtain a full characterization.

Fixing
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}=\bm{S}\bm{X}
.

Note that by fixing
\bm{S}\bm{X}
, the only source of randomness in
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
comes from
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}^{\perp}
.
We can express this as:

{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}^{\perp}=\begin{bmatrix}\sum_{j}{\textnormal{s}}_{1j}y_{j}^{\perp}\\
\sum_{j}{\textnormal{s}}_{2j}y_{j}^{\perp}\\
\vdots\\
\sum_{j}{\textnormal{s}}_{mj}y_{j}^{\perp}\end{bmatrix}.

Since
{\textnormal{s}}_{ij}\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathcal{N}(0,1)
, it follows that

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}\Big[\sum_{j}{\textnormal{s}}_{ij}y_{j}^{\perp}\Big]=\sum_{j}\left(y_{j}^{\perp}\right)^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{m}=\left\lVert\bm{y}^{\perp}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{m}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\triangleq\frac{1}{m}f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

Therefore, we have that
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}^{\perp}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{0},\frac{f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}{m}\bm{I}\right)
. And by (
) and Lemma
, it follows that:

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\frac{f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}{m}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{X})^{-1}\right),\qquad\text{when fixing }\bm{S}\bm{X},

(6.8)

from which it follows that

\bm{X}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{0},\frac{f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}{m}\bm{X}\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{X}\right)^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\right),\qquad\text{when fixing }\bm{S}\bm{X}.

(6.9)

Random
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}
.

Now suppose
{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}
is no longer fixed.
Although
\mathbb{E}[\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}]
is an unbiased estimator of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
,
the estimate
\mathbb{E}[(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{-1}]
introduces bias when estimating
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
, with a factor
\frac{m}{m-p-1}
.
That is, for
m>p+1
, we have

\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}\right)^{-1}\right]=\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\right)^{-1}\frac{m}{m-p-1}.

(6.10)

Therefore, if
m=p-1
for instance, the variance in (
) will blow up.

Proof
[of (
)]
Let
{\mathbf{Z}}\triangleq{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}
with rows
{\mathbf{z}}_{1},{\mathbf{z}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{z}}_{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\frac{1}{m}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
(Lemma
).
Therefore,
\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z}\sim\mathrm{Wi}(\frac{1}{m}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X},m)
and thus
(\bm{Z}^{\top}\bm{Z})^{-1}\sim\mathrm{IW}\big((\frac{1}{m}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1},m\big)
(Definitions
and
). This completes the proof.

Note that for
{\mathbf{z}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{Z})
, since
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{Z})=\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{z}}^{\top}])
, it follows that

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{z}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{tr}({\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{z}}^{\top})]=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{tr}(\bm{Z})]
,
whence we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}{m}\mathrm{tr}\left(\bm{X}\left(\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}\right)^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\right)\right]=\frac{f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}{m-p-1}\mathrm{tr}\big(\bm{X}\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\right)^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\big).

To see the specific value of
\mathrm{tr}\big(\bm{X}\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\right)^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\big)
,
notice that
\bm{X}\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\right)^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{+}
projects onto the column space of
\bm{X}
(Lemma
). Let
\bm{X}
admit the reduced SVD
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
(Figure
).
Since we assume
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is nonsingular (i.e.,
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=p
when
n>p
),
we have

\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}(\bm{X}\big(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}\big)^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{U}\bm{U}^{\top})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\mathrm{tr}(\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{U})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{I}_{p})=p=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X}),

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the cyclic invariance of traces.
So we conclude that

\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\frac{p}{m-p-1}.

(6.11)

where
f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\frac{m}{m-p-1}
provides insight into how to choose
m
when constructing
\bm{S}
in order to achieve a desired expected error.

Exercise
\thetheo

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
with full column rank
p
.
Using the results in (
), (
), and (
) to show that

\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\frac{m-1}{m-p-1}.

When
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r<p
, show that

\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\frac{m-1}{m-r-1}.

6.1.3
Special Sketching Matrices

We observed that when using random sketching, certain conditions must be satisfied to guarantee approximate optimality (e.g., recall that the Gaussian sketch requires
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{X}
to be invertible). We can also explore deterministic constructions for the sketching matrix
\bm{S}
.
Let
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
be the reduced SVD of
\bm{X}
, where
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times p},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{p\times p}
, and
\bm{V}\in\real^{p\times p}
if
\bm{X}
has full rank with
n>p
.
In this context, two notable choices for the sketching matrix
\bm{S}
arise:

\paragrapharrow
Option 1:
\bm{S}=\bm{U}^{\top}
.
Suppose we choose
\bm{S}=\bm{U}^{\top}
, i.e., the matrix containing the left singular vectors in its rows as our sketching matrix.
In this case, we have

\displaystyle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=(\bm{S}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{S}\bm{y}=(\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top})^{+}\bm{S}\bm{y}=(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top})^{+}\bm{S}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{S}\bm{y}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

Thus, by choosing
\bm{S}=\bm{U}^{\top}
, we exactly recover the least squares solution. However, this approach requires computing the left singular vectors of
\bm{X}
, which takes
\mathcal{O}(np^{2})
time. As a result, there is no computational advantage compared to solving the original (unsketched) least squares problem.

\paragrapharrow

Option 2:
\bm{S}=\bm{X}^{\top}
.
Alternatively, suppose we choose
\bm{S}=\bm{X}^{\top}
. Then we obtain:

\displaystyle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=(\bm{S}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{S}\bm{y}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-2}\bm{V}^{\top}\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

Again, this choice leads to an exact recovery of the least squares solution. However, as in the previous case, it requires computing the pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
, which also takes
\mathcal{O}(np^{2})
time. Consequently, this method again offers no computational savings compared to the standard least squares solution.

6.1.4
Variance Reduction by Averaging

In the previous sections, we showed that the average deviation of the left-sketched least squares solution from the original solution is proportional to
f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
Since this deviation corresponds to the variance of the random variable
\bm{X}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, we can reduce this variance—and thus improve our estimate of
f(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
—by averaging over multiple i.i.d. instances of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Let
{\mathbf{S}}_{1},{\mathbf{S}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{S}}_{q}
be independent sketching matrices, each of which has entries drawn independently from a scaled normal distribution
\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathcal{N}(0,1)
, such that
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{S}}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}_{i}]=\bm{I}
,
\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,q\}
. We define each sketched estimator
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}
as follows:

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert\bm{S}_{i}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{S}_{i}\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,q\}.

Now define the averaged estimator
\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
as

\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq\frac{1}{q}\sum_{i=1}^{q}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}.

This estimator
\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is unbiased because

\mathbb{E}[\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{q}\sum_{i=1}^{q}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}\right]=\frac{1}{q}\sum_{i=1}^{q}\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}]=\frac{1}{q}\sum_{i=1}^{q}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

Additionally, using the fact that the
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}
’s are independent, the variance is reduced by a factor
\frac{1}{q}
. Specifically:

\mathbb{E}[f(\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})]=\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}(\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{q}f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\frac{p}{m-p-1}.

(6.12)

The computational complexity of this averaging algorithm becomes
\mathcal{O}(q\cdot mp^{2})
.
On the other hand, when employing the non-averaging algorithm with
\bm{S}\in\real^{qm\times n}
, the computational complexity requires
\mathcal{O}(q\cdot mp^{2})
, and the expected error becomes:

\mathbb{E}[f(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})]=\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\frac{p}{qm-p-1}.

(6.13)

Since
f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\frac{p}{qm-p-1}<\frac{1}{q}f(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\frac{p}{m-p-1}
, the non-averaged method achieves better accuracy at the same computational cost. Therefore, the averaging algorithm is rarely used in practice.
However, in parallel or distributed computing environments, or on devices with limited memory, the averaging approach may still offer practical advantages due to its modular and lightweight nature.

6.1.5
Sketched Matrix Least Squares

More generally,
we consider the matrix least squares (a.k.a.,
multiple-response least squares
) problem, which is formulated as:

[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2},\ldots,\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{q}]\triangleq\widehat{\bm{B}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times q}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\bm{B}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},

(6.14)

where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{Y}\in\real^{n\times q}
.
The (left-) sketched variant of (
) is given by,

[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2},\ldots,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{q}]\triangleq\widetilde{\bm{B}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times q}}\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{X}\bm{B}-\bm{S}\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},

(6.15)

where
\bm{S}\in\real^{m\times n}
is a (Gaussian) sketching matrix.
The solution of (
) can be obtained in closed form as

\widetilde{\bm{B}}=(\bm{S}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{S}\bm{Y}
(Theorem
).

When
q=1
, this formulation reduces to the standard sketched least squares problem.
When
q>1
,
the original problem and sketched variant are

\widehat{\bm{B}}\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{B}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\widetilde{\bm{B}}\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}}\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{X}\bm{B}-\bm{S}\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

The
i
-th column of
\widetilde{\bm{B}}
satisfies

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i}}\left\lVert\bm{S}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i}-\bm{S}\bm{y}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

For a Gaussian sketching matrix
\bm{S}
, we have

\mathbb{E}\big\lVert\bm{X}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\big\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}-\bm{y}_{i}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\frac{p}{m-p-1}
,
which implies

\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}(\widetilde{\bm{B}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{q}\left\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}-\bm{y}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\frac{p}{m-p-1}=\left\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\frac{p}{m-p-1}.

Suppose that
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})=r
. By Exercise
, we then have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}(\widetilde{\bm{B}}-\widehat{\bm{B}})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\bm{B}}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\frac{r}{m-r-1};

(6.16)

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}\widetilde{\bm{B}}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\bm{B}}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\frac{m-1}{m-r-1}.

(6.17)

This result is referred to as the
left sketching optimality gap
under the Gaussian sketch
(
Pilanci
;
Halko et al. 2011
)
.

6.2
Sketched High-Dimensional Least Squares

We now consider the problem of solving the high-dimensional linear system
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
, where
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
p>n
(Section
). In general, such a system does not have a unique solution because there are more unknowns than equations. However, among all possible solutions, the minimum (
\ell_{2}
) norm solution is typically unique and well-defined; see Section
.
The minimum-norm solution is defined as follows:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}.

Similar to the least squares case, we can reduce the dimensionality of the problem by multiplying
\bm{X}
on the right by a random projection matrix
\bm{S}\in\real^{p\times m}
to form
\bm{X}\bm{S}
, where
p>m
(in most scenarios, we only consider
p>m>n
), and solve

\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{X}\bm{S}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{y}}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(6.18)

By right-multiplying
\bm{X}
by
\bm{S}
, we change the dimension of the optimization variable. Specifically, the vector being minimized—
\boldsymbol{\alpha}
—now has a smaller dimension than
\boldsymbol{\beta}
. To address this, we use the relation
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{S}\boldsymbol{\alpha}
, and hope that
\bm{S}\boldsymbol{\alpha}
provides a good approximation to the original solution
\boldsymbol{\beta}
. As we will see, this is often the case.

Let

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{X}\bm{S}\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\bm{y}}\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

and use the approximation that
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq\bm{S}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
. A solution to
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
is
(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{y}
(see Section
). Substituting into the constraint equation, when
\bm{X}\bm{S}
has full row rank, we have that

\displaystyle\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\bm{X}\bm{S}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\bm{X}\bm{S}(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{y}.

This shows that
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{S}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
is a valid solution satisfying the original constraint
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
, provided that
\bm{X}\bm{S}
has full row rank.
This also shows that the error vector

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\in\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}).

6.2.1
Gaussian Right Sketching

Let
{\mathbf{S}}\in\real^{p\times m}
with entries
{\textnormal{s}}_{ij}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathcal{N}(0,1)
be the right sketching matrix, and let
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
denote the solution to the sketched minimum-norm problem. Our estimate for
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
, defined as
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{S}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, possesses several important properties.
Similarly, we begin by assuming that
\bm{X}\bm{S}
is a fixed matrix.

Lemma 182
(Distribution of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
under fixed
\bm{X}\bm{S}
).

Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
have full row rank with
n<p
. For a fixed
\bm{X}\bm{S}\in\real^{n\times m}
of full row rank,
it follows that

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}},\frac{1}{m}\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}\bm{I}\right).

That is,
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is an unbiased estimator of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
, i.e.,
\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}
be the reduced SVD of
\bm{X}
, where
\bm{U},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{n\times n}
, and
\bm{V}_{1}\in\real^{p\times n}
.
Consider further the full right singular vector matrix
[\bm{V}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}]\in\real^{p\times p}
, where
\bm{V}_{1}\in\real^{p\times n}
and
\bm{V}_{2}\in\real^{p\times(p-n)}
. Left-multiplying
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
by
\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}
yields that

\displaystyle\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{U}^{\top}(\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{U}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}.

Similarly, left-multiplying
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
by
\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}
yields that

\displaystyle\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}.

Taking the expectation of
\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\bm{S}]\cdot\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}(\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\boldsymbol{0},

where the penultimate equality follows since
\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{2}
and
\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}
are uncorrelated, and
\mathbb{E}[\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\bm{S}]=\boldsymbol{0}
follows since
{\textnormal{s}}_{ij}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathcal{N}(0,1)
.
Now consider the expectation of the orthogonal matrix-vector product
[\bm{V}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}]^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we get that

\mathbb{E}\left[[\bm{V}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}]^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right]=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbb{E}[\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\\
\mathbb{E}[\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\equiv[\bm{V}_{1},\bm{V}_{2}]^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}.

where the last equality follows because
\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{V}_{2}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Because the expectation of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
multiplied by an orthogonal matrix is equal to
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
multiplied by the same orthogonal matrix, we can conclude that
\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
.

For the variance, let
{\mathbf{s}}_{i}
be the
i
-th row of the random matrix
{\mathbf{S}}
.
Since we fix
\bm{X}\bm{S}
and
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\mathbf{S}}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\bm{S}(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{y}={\mathbf{S}}(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}
, it follows from Lemma
that

\widetilde{\beta}_{i}={\mathbf{s}}_{i}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}\quad\implies\quad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widetilde{\beta}_{i}]=\frac{1}{m}\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}.

Therefore, the covariance matrix of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is given by
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\frac{1}{m}\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}\bm{I}
.

In Lemma
, we assume that
\bm{X}\bm{S}
is fixed rather than a random matrix. When
\bm{X}{\mathbf{S}}
is instead a random matrix, as opposed to the variance of
\bm{X}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
given in (
), we can derive the variance of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
.

{theoremHigh}
[Variance of
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}
]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
have full row rank with
n<p
. For a random
\bm{X}{\mathbf{S}}\in\real^{n\times m}
with full row rank,
it follows that

\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{p}{m-n-1}\left\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}
be the reduced SVD of
\bm{X}
, where
\bm{U},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{n\times n}
, and
\bm{V}_{1}\in\real^{p\times n}
.
Note that for
{\mathbf{z}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\bm{Z})
, since
\mathrm{tr}(\bm{Z})=\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{z}}^{\top}])
, it follows that

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{z}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{tr}({\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{z}}^{\top})]=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{tr}(\bm{Z})]
.
We then have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big\lVert\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\big[(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}})^{\top}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}})\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{tr}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}})(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}})^{\top}\big]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\frac{1}{m}\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}\cdot\bm{I}\right)\right]=\frac{1}{m}\bm{y}^{\top}\mathbb{E}[(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}]\bm{y}\cdot\mathrm{tr}(\bm{I})

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\frac{1}{m}\frac{m}{m-n-1}\cdot p(\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y})=\frac{p}{m-n-1}\bm{y}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\frac{p}{m-n-1}\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-2}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\frac{p}{m-n-1}(\bm{V}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y})^{\top}\bm{V}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=\frac{p}{m-n-1}\left\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the last equality follows from
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}=\bm{V}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}
, and the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\mathbb{E}[(\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}]=(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\frac{m}{m-n-1}
(the proof of which is similar to that of (
)).
This completes the proof.

6.2.2
Special Sketching Matrices

So far, we have assumed that
{\mathbf{S}}
is an i.i.d. Gaussian matrix in order to simplify the theoretical analysis. However, many other types of sketching matrices are possible.
Recall that
\bm{X}
can be written as
\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}
in its reduced SVD form, where
\bm{U}\in\real^{n\times n},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\real^{n\times n}
, and
\bm{V}_{1}\in\real^{p\times n}
if
\bm{X}
has full row rank with
p>n
, and that the minimum-norm solution to
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{y}
is given by
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mn}}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}
.
Similar to the left sketching technique described in Section
, the following deterministic choices for
\bm{S}
are worth considering:

\paragrapharrow

Option 1:
\bm{S}=\bm{V}_{1}\in\real^{p\times n}
.
The minimum-norm solution using this sketching matrix corresponds to the left pseudo-inverse of
\bm{X}\bm{S}
, i.e.,

\displaystyle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\bm{S}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\bm{S}(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}(\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\bm{V}_{1})^{-1}\bm{y}=\bm{V}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\bm{U}^{\top}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{+}\bm{y}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

\paragrapharrow

Option 2:
\bm{S}=\bm{X}^{\top}
.
The minimum-norm solution for this sketching matrix is:

\displaystyle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\bm{S}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\bm{S}(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{y}=\bm{X}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{y}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

These choices of
\bm{S}
yield exact solutions to the minimum-norm LS problem. However, they are equivalent to classical direct methods for solving the same problem, which contradicts the original purpose of sketching—namely, to approximately solve the optimization problem more efficiently using a JL embedding or similar dimensionality reduction technique.

6.3
Sketched Least Squares with Quantized Response

In many applications, the dimension
q
of the matrix least squares problem introduced in Section
can be extremely large, making it difficult to store the response matrix
\bm{Y}
, especially on devices with limited memory or computational resources. One possible solution is to store a quantized version of
\bm{Y}
. Fortunately, it turns out that the least squares solution obtained using Gaussian sketching with quantized responses still concentrates around the true solution; that is, the corresponding residual matrix is upper bounded
(
Saha et al. 2023
)
.

\paragrapharrow

Uniformly dithered quantizer.
We begin by considering the quantization of a scalar
\beta
satisfying
\left\lvert\beta\right\rvert\leq R
. Given a bit-budget of
B
bits, the scalar quantizer with dynamic range
R
is defined by first setting the
M\triangleq 2^{B}
quantization levels as:

q_{1}=-R,\quad q_{2}=-R+\Delta,\quad q_{3}=-R+2\Delta,\quad\ldots,\quad q_{M}=-R+(M-1)\Delta,

where the
resolution
is given by
\Delta=\frac{2R}{M-1}
.
The operation of the
uniformly dithered quantizer
is then defined as:

Q_{R,B}(\beta)=\begin{cases}q_{k+1},&\text{with probability }r\triangleq\frac{\beta-q_{k}}{\Delta},\\
q_{k},&\text{with probability }1-r,\end{cases}

(6.19)

where
k=\arg\max_{j}\{q_{j}\leq\beta\}
, meaning
\beta\in[q_{k},q_{k+1}]
.
If the input
\beta
to the quantizer lies outside this interval, i.e.,
\beta>R
or
\beta<-R
, the quantizer is said to be
saturated
.

Finally, to quantize any matrix
\bm{B}=\{\beta_{ij}\}
, we obtain
Q_{R,B}(\bm{B})
by quantizing each entry independently, i.e.,
[Q_{R,B}(\bm{B})]_{ij}\triangleq Q_{R,B}(\beta_{ij})
.
Then, we have the following result about the unbiasedness of the uniformly dithered quantizer.

Lemma 183
(Uniformly dithered quantizer).

Consider the quantization of a scalar
\beta\in[-R,+R]
, and denote the quantization error of uniformly dithered scalar quantizer with a bit-budget of
B
bits as
\epsilon\triangleq Q_{R,B}(\beta)-\beta
.
Clearly, the quantization error is bounded, satisfying
\left\lvert\epsilon\right\rvert\leq\Delta
.
Then it follows that

\mathbb{E}[\epsilon]=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\epsilon]\leq\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}=\frac{R^{2}}{(2^{B}-1)^{2}},

where the expectation
\mathbb{E}[\cdot]
is taken over the randomness introduced by the dithering in the quantizer operation.
Hence, the uniformly dithered quantizer is unbiased, and the variance of the quantization error depends only on
R
and
B
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose
\beta\in[q_{k},q_{k+1}]
, where
q_{k+1}=q_{k}+\Delta
and
\Delta=\frac{2R}{2^{B}-1}
. Then,

\mathbb{E}[Q_{R,B}(\beta)]=q_{k+1}\frac{\beta-q_{k}}{\Delta}+q_{k}\left(1-\frac{\beta-q_{k}}{\Delta}\right)=\frac{(q_{k}+\Delta)(\beta-q_{k})+q_{k}(\Delta-\beta+q_{k})}{\Delta}=\beta.

Now consider the variance:

\displaystyle\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\epsilon]=\mathbb{E}[(Q_{R,B}(\beta)-\beta)^{2}]

\displaystyle=(q_{k+1}-\beta)^{2}\left(\frac{\beta-q_{k}}{\Delta}\right)+(q_{k}-\beta)^{2}\left(\frac{q_{k+1}-\beta}{\Delta}\right)

\displaystyle=(q_{k+1}-\beta)(\beta-q_{k})\leq\max_{\beta\in[q_{k},q_{k+1}]}(q_{k+1}-\beta)(\beta-q_{k})

\displaystyle=\left(q_{k+1}-\frac{q_{k}+q_{k+1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{q_{k}+q_{k+1}}{2}-q_{k}\right)=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}=\frac{R^{2}}{(2^{B}-1)^{2}}.

This completes the proof.

\paragrapharrow

Sketched least squares with quantized response.
The sketched variant of the matrix least squares problem (
) with quantized response is given by,

\widetilde{{\mathbf{B}}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times q}}\left\lVert{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}\bm{B}-Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y})\right\rVert_{F}^{2},

(6.20)

where
{\mathbf{S}}\in\real^{m\times n}
is a Gaussian sketching matrix with entries distributed as
{\textnormal{s}}_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{m})
, and
Q\triangleq Q_{R,B}
denotes the uniformly dithered quantizer defined in (
). We assume that the dynamic range satisfies
R\geq\left\lVert{\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{+}
so that the quantizer remains unsaturated.
The solution to (
) can be written in closed form (Theorem
) as

\widetilde{{\mathbf{B}}}=({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y}).

(6.21)

Note that the norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{+}
denotes the maximum magnitude of the underlying matrix; see Problem
.

The following theorem characterizes the accuracy of the approximate solution
\widetilde{{\mathbf{B}}}
relative to the original least squares problem (
).

{theoremHigh}
[Sketched LS with quantized response]
Let
{\mathbf{S}}\in\real^{m\times n}
be a random Gaussian matrix with entries distributed as
{\textnormal{s}}_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{m})
, and
Q\triangleq Q_{R,B}
be a uniformly dithered quantizer with dynamic range
R
and bit-budget
B
. Furthermore, suppose we are given matrices
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
\bm{Y}\in\real^{n\times q}
, and define:

\widehat{\bm{B}}\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times q}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{B}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\widetilde{{\mathbf{B}}}\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}\in\real^{p\times q}}\left\lVert{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}\bm{B}-Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

Let
\mathbf{E}\triangleq Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y})-{\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y}
be the quantization error matrix.
Then, if
R\geq\left\lVert{\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{+}
and
\bm{S}\bm{X}
has full column rank, we have

\left\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\bm{B}}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}\widetilde{{\mathbf{B}}}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{m-1}{m-r-1}\left\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\bm{B}}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\frac{q\Delta^{2}}{4}\frac{\sigma_{\max}^{2}}{\sigma_{\min}^{2}}\frac{m^{2}}{(n-m-1)},

where
r=\operatorname{rank}(\bm{X})
, and
\sigma_{\max}
and
\sigma_{\min}
denote the largest and smallest singular values of
\bm{X}
, respectively.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The solution of the standard matrix least squares problem (
) can be expressed as:

\widehat{\bm{B}}=[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2},\ldots,\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{q}],\quad\text{where}\quad\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},\ \forall\,i,

and
\bm{y}_{i}\in\real^{n}
denote the
i
-th column of
\bm{Y}
. Therefore, we first analyze the vector case for the standard least squares problem:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},

(6.22)

and generalize the results by concatenating
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}
to obtain
\widehat{\bm{B}}
. The sketched variant of (
) with quantized response is given by,

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{y})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

(6.23)

The solution to (
) is available in closed form as
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{y})
(Theorem
).
Let
\bm{e}\triangleq Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{y})-{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}\in\real^{m}
denote the quantization error.
We then have,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big\lVert\bm{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\bm{y}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{y})-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}+\bm{e})-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(6.24)

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{e}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\big[\big(\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}-\bm{y}\big)^{\top}\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{e}\big]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}-\bm{y}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{e}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the last equality follows as the cross term disappears because,

\mathbb{E}\big[\big(\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}-\bm{y}\big)^{\top}\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{e}\big]=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\big[\big(\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{y}-\bm{y}\big)^{\top}\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{e}\big]=\boldsymbol{0},

(6.25)

where the last equality follows from
\mathbb{E}_{Q}[\bm{e}]=\boldsymbol{0}
when
Q
is a uniformly dithered quantizer (Lemma
).

Let
\bm{E}\triangleq\{e_{ij}\}=Q({\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y})-{\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y}\in\real^{m\times q}
denote the quantization error matrix.
Generalizing (
) to the matrix least squares problem by treating each column
\bm{y}_{i}
separately and summing over all columns yields:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big\lVert\bm{X}\widetilde{{\mathbf{B}}}-\bm{Y}\big\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}{\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{E}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

(6.26)

\displaystyle=\frac{m-1}{m-r-1}\left\lVert\bm{X}\widehat{\bm{B}}-\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{E}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},

(6.27)

where the last equality follows from (
6.17
).

Upper bounding
\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{E}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
.

We now upper bound the second term in (
6.27
). (
6.27
). Since
\left\lVert\bm{A}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A})
for any matrix
\bm{A}
, using the cyclic invariance of trace, whence we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{E}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\bm{E}^{\top}\big(({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\big)^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{E}\right)\right]

(6.28)

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\big(({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\big)^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{E}\bm{E}^{\top}\right)\right]

(6.29)

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\big(({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\big)^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\mathbb{E}_{Q}\left[\bm{E}\bm{E}^{\top}\right]\right)\right].

(6.30)

Since
R\geq\left\lVert{\mathbf{S}}\bm{Y}\right\rVert_{+}
, from (
) and Lemma
, the
(i,j)
-th entry of the quantization error matrix
\bm{E}
satisfies

\mathbb{E}\left[e_{ij}\right]=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[e_{ij}]\leq\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}=\frac{R^{2}}{(2^{B}-1)^{2}},

(6.31)

whence we have

\mathbb{E}\big[(\bm{E}\bm{E}^{\top})_{ij}\big]=\sum_{k=1}^{q}\mathbb{E}\left[e_{ik}e_{jk}\right]=\begin{cases}q\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[e_{ik}]\leq\frac{q\Delta^{2}}{4},&\text{for }i=j;\\
0,&\text{for }i\neq j.\end{cases}

(6.32)

Therefore, the expectation
\mathbb{E}_{Q}\left[\bm{E}\bm{E}^{\top}\right]
is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal elements are upper bounded by
\frac{q\Delta^{2}}{4}
.
Let
{\mathbf{Z}}\triangleq\big(({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\big)^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\in\real^{m\times m}
, which is a random matrix depends on
{\mathbf{S}}
. Then, (
6.30
) simplifies to,

\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left({\mathbf{Z}}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{Q}\big[\bm{E}\bm{E}^{\top}\big]\right)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}{\textnormal{z}}_{ii}\left(\mathbb{E}_{Q}\big[\bm{E}\bm{E}^{\top}\big]\right)_{ii}\right]\leq\frac{q\Delta^{2}}{4}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\mathrm{tr}({\mathbf{Z}})\right].

(6.33)

For the
\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\mathrm{tr}({\mathbf{Z}})\right]
term, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\mathrm{tr}({\mathbf{Z}})\right]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\right]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\leq}}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\left\lVert({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\right]\sigma_{\max}^{2}(\bm{X})

(6.34)

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{S}}}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left(({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top})^{-1}\right)\right]\sigma_{\max}^{2}(\bm{X})

(6.35)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\ddagger}}{{\leq}}\frac{\sigma_{\max}^{2}(\bm{X})}{\sigma_{\min}^{2}(\bm{X})}\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[({\mathbf{S}}{\mathbf{S}}^{\top})^{-1}\right]\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle*}}{{=}}\frac{\sigma_{\max}^{2}(\bm{X})}{\sigma_{\min}^{2}(\bm{X})}\frac{m^{2}}{(n-m-1)},

(6.36)

where the inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\left\lVert\bm{A}\bm{B}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\left\lVert\bm{A}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert\bm{B}\right\rVert_{F}
for any matrices
\bm{A}
and
\bm{B}
with appropriate dimensions, the inequality (
\ddagger
) follows from the Loewner order for matrix products , and the equality (
*
) follows from Example
. Combining (
6.30
), (
) and (
6.36
) yields,

\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}({\mathbf{S}}\bm{X})^{+}\bm{E}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{q\Delta^{2}}{4}\frac{\sigma_{\max}^{2}(\bm{X})}{\sigma_{\min}^{2}(\bm{X})}\frac{m^{2}}{(n-m-1)}.

(6.37)

This completes the proof.

Therefore, the theorem shows the residual matrix of the sketching matrix least squares problem with quantized response is bounded by the residual of the standard matrix least squares problem plus a term that depends on the condition number of the data matrix
\bm{X}
.

6.4
Least Squares Using Randomized SVD

In Section
, we introduced how to obtain the least squares solution using SVD.
However, for a large matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, calculating its SVD rquires
\mathcal{O}(np^{2})
flops, which becomes prohibitively expensive as the size of the data matrix increases.
To address this issue, a randomized algorithm samples some columns from
\bm{X}
to construct a smaller matrix
\bm{C}\in\real^{n\times m}
(
m<p
), aiming to approximate
\bm{X}
with these sampled columns, expressed as
\bm{C}=\bm{X}\bm{S}
. The goal is to minimize:

\min_{\bm{B}}\left\lVert\bm{C}\bm{B}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\min_{\bm{B}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{B}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

This is column-wise decomposable:

\displaystyle\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i}}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{S}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{x}_{i},\quad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}

\displaystyle\implies\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}}\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{S}\bm{B}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{X}.

The matrix
\bm{X}
is then approximated by
\bm{X}\approx\bm{X}\bm{S}\widehat{\bm{B}}=(\bm{X}\bm{S})(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{X}=\bm{C}\bm{C}^{+}\bm{X}
.
Given that
\bm{C}\in\real^{n\times m}
with
m<p
, the truncated SVD (TSVD) of
\bm{C}\approx\bm{U}_{k}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k}\bm{V}_{k}^{\top}
—such that
\bm{C}\bm{C}^{+}\approx\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}
—costs
\mathcal{O}(nm^{2})
, and the low-rank approximation
\underbrace{\bm{U}_{k}}_{n\times k}\underbrace{\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X}}_{k\times p}
of
\bm{X}
thus costs less than the optimal rank-
k
approximation of
\bm{X}
using the SVD of
\bm{X}
(
\mathcal{O}(np^{2})
flops).

The least squares using the rank-
k
approximation
\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X}
of
\bm{X}
then reduces the computational complexity and aligns with the goal of the norm ratio methods introduced in Section
.
The following theorem establishes an upper bound for the error introduced by this low-rank approximation:

{theoremHigh}
[Randomized Low-Rank Approximation
(
Drineas et al. 2006
)
]
Let
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and let
\bm{C}\in\real^{n\times m}
contain
m
columns of
\bm{X}
with
m<p
.
Suppose further that the rank-
k
TSVD of
\bm{C}
is
\bm{C}\approx\bm{U}_{k}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k}\bm{V}_{k}^{\top}
(
k\leq m
). Then,

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{X}_{k}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}-\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top}\right\rVert_{2};

(6.38a)

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{X}_{k}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+2\sqrt{k}\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}-\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F},

(6.38b)

where
\bm{X}_{k}
denotes the optimal rank-
k
approximation of
\bm{X}
by TSVD (Theorem
).

Equation (
) shows that the low-rank approximation by
\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X}
is bounded by two terms, where the first term is the approximation error of the exact SVD, and the second term is the spectral norm (or Frobenius norm) error in the matrix multiplication approximation.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
For brevity, we only prove (
6.38a
) here; (
6.38b
) follows similarly and is left as an exercise.
It follows that

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\max_{\left\lVert\bm{a}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lVert\bm{a}^{\top}(\bm{X}-\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X})\right\rVert_{2}=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\left\lVert\bm{b}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\bm{c}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\\
\bm{b}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k}),\bm{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})^{\perp},\\
\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=1\end{subarray}}\left\lVert(\alpha\bm{b}+\beta\bm{c})^{\top}(\bm{X}-\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X})\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{\leq}}\max_{\left\lVert\bm{c}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\bm{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})^{\perp}}\left\lVert\bm{c}^{\top}(\bm{X}-\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X})\right\rVert_{2}+\max_{\left\lVert\bm{b}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\bm{b}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})}\left\lVert\bm{b}^{\top}(\bm{X}-\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X})\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=\max_{\left\lVert\bm{c}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\bm{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})^{\perp}}\left\lVert\bm{c}^{\top}(\bm{X}-\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}\bm{X})\right\rVert_{2}=\max_{\left\lVert\bm{c}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\bm{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})^{\perp}}\left\lVert\bm{c}^{\top}\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the definition of the spectral norm (Definition
), the inequality (
{\ddagger}
) follows because
\alpha,\beta\leq 1
and
\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{U}_{k}\bm{U}_{k}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0}
can be proved by letting
\bm{b}\triangleq\bm{U}_{k}\bm{v}
with
\bm{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
.
Taking squares

\displaystyle\max_{\left\lVert\bm{c}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\bm{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})^{\perp}}\left\lVert\bm{c}^{\top}\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\max_{\left\lVert\bm{c}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\bm{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})^{\perp}}\bm{c}^{\top}\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{c}+\bm{c}^{\top}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}-\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top})\bm{c}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\leq}}\max_{\left\lVert\bm{c}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\bm{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})^{\perp}}\sigma_{k+1}^{2}(\bm{C})+\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}-\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top}\right\rVert_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{\leq}}\max_{\left\lVert\bm{c}\right\rVert_{2}=1,\bm{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\bm{U}_{k})^{\perp}}\sigma_{k+1}^{2}(\bm{X})+2\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}-\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top}\right\rVert_{2},

where the inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows from Problem
(
\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top}
and
\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}-\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top}
are symmetric such that
\sigma_{k+1}^{2}(\bm{C})\equiv\sigma_{k+1}(\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top})\equiv\lambda_{k+1}(\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top})
), and the inequality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from the matrix perturbation result

\sigma_{k+1}(\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top})-\sigma_{k+1}(\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top})\leq\left\lVert\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}-\bm{C}\bm{C}^{\top}\right\rVert_{2}
by Problem
.
This completes the proof.

\paragrapharrow

Gaussian sketching.
Another interesting problem is the low-rank reconstruction of
\bm{X}
using the sampled columns in
\bm{C}=\bm{X}\bm{S}
:

\bm{B}^{*}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}}\left\lVert\bm{C}\bm{B}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{X}.

Let
\bm{X}_{k}
denote the optimal rank-
k
approximation of
\bm{X}
(Theorem
).
It then follows that

\displaystyle\left\lVert(\bm{X}\bm{S})(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{X}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert(\bm{X}\bm{S})(\bm{X}_{k}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{X}_{k}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bm{X}_{k}^{\top}(\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}_{k}^{\top})^{+}(\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})-\bm{X}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle\triangleq\left\lVert\bm{X}_{k}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{B}}-\bm{X}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

where
\widetilde{\bm{B}}\triangleq(\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}_{k}^{\top})^{+}(\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top})=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}}\left\lVert\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}_{k}^{\top}\bm{B}-\bm{S}^{\top}\bm{X}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
by Theorem
.
This optimization problem is known as the sketched problem of
\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\bm{B}}\left\lVert\bm{X}_{k}^{\top}\bm{B}-\bm{X}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
, where the sketching is performed by
\bm{S}^{\top}
.

When treating
\bm{S}
as a Gaussian sketching matrix, (
6.17
) provides the Frobenius norm error bound:

\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}{\mathbf{S}}(\bm{X}{\mathbf{S}})^{+}\bm{X}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}_{k}^{\top}\widetilde{{\mathbf{B}}}-\bm{X}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{m-1}{m-k-1}\left\lVert\bm{X}_{k}-\bm{X}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},

(6.39)

which is valid for any
k\in\{1,2,\ldots,\mathrm{rank}(\bm{X})\}
.

\paragrapharrow

Randomized SVD.
The randomized SVD approach is closely related to the randomized low-rank approximation method introduced here.
Since
\bm{C}\bm{C}^{+}\bm{X}=(\bm{X}\bm{S})(\bm{X}\bm{S})^{+}\bm{X}\approx\bm{X}
, we can calculate the reduced QR decomposition of
\bm{X}\bm{S}=\bm{Q}\bm{R}
(
\bm{Q}\in\real^{n\times m}
and
\bm{R}\in\real^{m\times m}
, which costs
\mathcal{(}nm^{2})
; see Section
), whence we have

\bm{C}\bm{C}^{+}\bm{X}=\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\approx\bm{X},

i.e.,
\bm{Q}
approximates the column space of
\bm{X}
.
Calculating the SVD
\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}=\bm{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}\in\real^{m\times p}
(which costs
\mathcal{(}mp^{2})
), the approximate SVD of
\bm{X}
is then given by
\bm{X}\approx(\bm{Q}\bm{U})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}
.
For finding the rank-
k
low-rank approximation,

Halko et al. 2011
shows that

\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\bm{X}-\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\top}\bm{X}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left(1+\frac{4\sqrt{m}}{m-k-1}\sqrt{\min(n,p)}\right)\sigma_{k+1}.

Thus, the expected approximation error is upper bounded by this expression for any target rank
k
.
