Chapter 7
The Bayesian Approach

7.1
The Bayesian Approach

I
In contemporary statistics, Bayesian approaches have become increasingly significant and widely utilized.
Thomas Bayes came up with this idea but died before publishing it. Fortunately, his friend Richard Price carried on his work and published the work in 1764.
In this section, we outline the foundational principles of Bayesian methodology, using the
Beta-Bernoulli model
as an introductory example to highlight the benefits of Bayesian models. Additionally, we explore powerful Bayesian techniques for linear models and their relationship to ordinary least squares.

Note that we have previously introduced the Bayesian estimation method in Section
, from which the Laplace approximation method was derived (Section
). The Laplace approximation method further enables the definition of the useful BIC criterion for model selection; see Section
. Here, we briefly compare frequentist and Bayesian approaches and introduce the concept of conjugate priors.

The core idea of the Bayesian approach, in a nutshell, involves assuming a
prior
probability distribution over the unknown parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
with hyper-parameters
\boldsymbol{\alpha}
(i.e.,
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})
)—a distribution representing the plausibility of each possible value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
before observing the data.
Consequently, to infer information about
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, one considers the conditional distribution of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
given the observed data, known as the posterior distribution. The posterior reflects the plausibility of each potential value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
after taking the data into account. We then apply probability rules to address specific questions of interest
(
Fahrmeir et al. 2007
;
Hoff 2009
)
. For instance, when determining the parameter based on the maximum posterior probability of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, we refer to the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator; see Definition
.

Comparison of Frequentist and Bayesian Approaches

In the field of statistical inference, there are traditionally two distinct schools of thought: the
frequentist approach
and the
Bayesian approach
. While we will not explore their underlying philosophical differences in this discussion, we will focus on how they differ in their treatment of the parameter space.

Typically, we use a probability distribution
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
to describe a random variable. For example, we might assume that a random variable
x
follows a Bernoulli distribution. In general, any probability distribution includes one or more parameters, and only when these parameters are specified can the distribution be fully determined.

When the values of these parameters are unknown, our goal is to estimate them so that the distribution can be properly defined. Once estimated, the distribution becomes useful for making meaningful inferences or predictions. The frequentist and Bayesian approaches differ fundamentally in how they interpret and handle such unknown parameters.

\paragrapharrow

Frequentist approaches.
The frequentist approach assumes that the parameters of a probability distribution are fixed but unknown constants—essentially just numerical values.
These parameters define the distribution
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
through parameterization, and frequentists assume there exists a single true value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
within the parameter space.
The objective is to estimate this optimal (true) value. To do so, frequentists often use methods such as maximum likelihood estimation (see Section
), which seeks the value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
that makes the observed data most probable.

To estimate the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, we require a set of observed samples from the random variable
\mathcal{X}
. These samples are assumed to come from the same underlying distribution
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
, meaning they are identically distributed. Furthermore, in many cases, the samples are assumed to be independent and identically distributed.

We denote the collection of observed samples as
\mathcal{X}=\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
. The probability of observing each individual sample is given by
p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
. Assuming independence, the joint probability of observing all samples together is:

p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}),

where
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
is commonly referred to as the likelihood function.
This function is conventionally denoted by
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X})
.
The idea behind maximum likelihood estimation is to find the value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
that maximizes the likelihood of observing the given dataset.
Therefore, the maximum likelihood estimate is defined as:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}}=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathcal{X}).

Once we have estimated
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, the corresponding probability distribution becomes
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}})
, and we can use it to make predictions about new observations:

p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}})=p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}}).

\paragrapharrow

Bayesian approaches.
However, the Bayesian approach takes a fundamentally different perspective.
In Bayesian statistics, we recognize that since the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
is unknown, any value within the parameter space is, at least initially, possible. Therefore, rather than treating
\boldsymbol{\theta}
as a fixed constant, it is considered a random variable—a central tenet of the Bayesian philosophy is that all unknown quantities should be treated probabilistically.
This leads to two key ideas:

The probability distribution over the data
\mathcal{X}
is defined conditionally on the unknown parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, written as
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
. This formulation reflects a crucial difference from the frequentist perspective.

Using Bayes’ theorem (Theorem
), we reverse the relationship between the observed data
\mathcal{X}
and the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, allowing us to infer the distribution of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
given the data:

\displaystyle p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{p(\mathcal{X})}=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\int_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})}=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\int_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\propto p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}),

(7.1)

where
\mathcal{X}
represents the observed dataset or random variable, and the notation
f(x)\propto g(x)
means that
f
is proportional to
g
up to a normalizing constant.

Through Bayes’ theorem, we formally define the relationship between the random variable
\mathcal{X}
and the parameter variable
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. The term
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
in the formula represents the marginal probability distribution of the parameter variable
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, which is the probability distribution of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
before observing any data.
Therefore, we call it the
prior distribution
of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.

In practice, we typically do not know the true distribution of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, so we assume a known form for the prior.
Often, this prior depends on one or more hyper-parameters
\boldsymbol{\alpha}
, in which case we write the prior as
p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})
. Substituting this into Equation (
), we obtain:

\displaystyle p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\alpha})

\displaystyle=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{\int_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}

(7.2)

\displaystyle=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{\int_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha})}\propto p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha}).

In the remainder of this discussion, we will omit the hyper-parameter
\boldsymbol{\alpha}
for simplicity.

Given the prior distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
and the conditional probability distribution
p(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
, we observe a set of samples from the random variable
\mathcal{X}
, denoted as
\mathcal{X}=\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
.
Unlike frequentist approaches, these samples are assumed to be drawn independently from the joint distribution:
p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
; as opposed to be drawn from the conditional distribution
p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
in frequentist approaches.

Our goal is to infer the true distribution of the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
given the observed data
\mathcal{X}
.
That is, we aim to compute the posterior distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})
, which by (
) is

p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})=\frac{p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{p(\mathcal{X})}.

The conditional probability distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})
is called the
posterior distribution
of the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, because it is the probability distribution of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
under the condition of observing the samples.
This posterior distribution represents our updated belief about
\boldsymbol{\theta}
after observing the sample set. It serves as our estimate of the parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
, incorporating both the prior knowledge and the information provided by the data.

Alternatively, the posterior can be interpreted as being proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior:

\mathrm{Posterior}=\frac{\mathrm{Likelihood}\times\mathrm{Prior}}{\mathrm{Marginal\,\,likelihood}}\propto\mathrm{Likelihood}\times\mathrm{Prior},

(7.3)

where the proportionality constant is determined by the marginal likelihood (or evidence),
p(\mathcal{X})
. This formulation allows us to quantify uncertainty in the parameter estimates.

\paragrapharrow

Predictive inference.
For a new observation
\bm{x}_{\text{new}}
maximum likelihood estimation predicts using the likelihood evaluated at the MLE estimate:

p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{ML}})
.
In contrast, Bayesian inference uses the posterior distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})

to compute the predictive distribution for new samples. Assuming the generative process
p(\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})
, the predictive distribution becomes:

p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}})=\int p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})d\boldsymbol{\theta}.

If the problem follows from a generative process
{\mathbf{y}}\sim p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})
, e.g.,
{\textnormal{y}}\sim\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}+\epsilon
in the Gauss-Markov linear model.
Then the predictive distribution is

p(\bm{y}^{\prime}\mid\bm{x}_{\text{new}},\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})=\int p(\bm{y}^{\prime}\mid\bm{x}_{\text{new}},\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})d\boldsymbol{\theta}.

\paragrapharrow

Point estimates from the posterior.
Instead of using the full posterior distribution, one may summarize it using point estimates. Common choices include:

The posterior mean.
Often referred to as the
Bayesian estimate
; that is, using the expected value
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{mean}}
of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
from the posterior distribution:

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{Bayes}}\triangleq

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{mean}}=\mathbb{E}_{p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})}[\boldsymbol{\theta}]=\int\boldsymbol{\theta}p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})d\boldsymbol{\theta}\quad\implies\quad p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{mean}}).

(7.4)

The posterior median.
As one can expect, the median value
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{median}}
of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
from the posterior distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})
can also be regarded as a point estimate:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{median}}=\text{ median of }p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})\qquad\implies\qquad p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{median}}).

(7.5)

The posterior maximum.
See the following paragraphs.

Computing these point estimates requires knowing the exact form of the posterior distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})
.
However, the denominator in Bayes’ rule—the marginal likelihood or evidence in (
)—can be difficult to compute:

p(\mathcal{X})=\int p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})d\boldsymbol{\theta}.

This integral spans the entire parameter space and is often analytically intractable or computationally expensive.

To address this issue, two common strategies are used:

Using conjugate priors: If the prior and likelihood belong to conjugate families, the posterior has the same functional form as the prior, simplifying computation.

Using maximum a posterior (MAP) estimate: Instead of computing the full posterior, MAP finds the mode of the posterior distribution and avoids computing the evidence.

\paragrapharrow

Conjugate prior.
Formally, we define the conjugate prior as follows:

Definition 184
(Conjugate prior).

In Bayesian inference, if the posterior distribution and the prior distribution belong to the same probability distribution family, then this prior distribution is called a conjugate prior. Note that since the posterior distribution is obtained by multiplying the prior with the likelihood, conjugacy refers to the fact that the prior and the likelihood are conjugate. The conjugate prior, when multiplied by the likelihood, does not change the functional form of the distribution, so the posterior has the same form as the prior.

Using a conjugate prior ensures that the posterior distribution has the same form as the prior, which often allows us to derive the posterior directly without having to compute the marginal likelihood
p(\mathcal{X})
in (
). This significantly reduces the computational complexity involved in determining the posterior distribution.

For example, the conjugate prior for the likelihood function of a Gaussian distribution is itself a Gaussian distribution. Similarly, the conjugate prior for the Bernoulli likelihood is the Beta distribution, and for the categorical likelihood, it is the Dirichlet distribution. For further examples, see
Hoff 2009
;
Lu 2022a
.

Despite their advantages, conjugate priors do have limitations. First, only members of the exponential family of distributions have conjugate priors. Second, choosing a conjugate prior is often motivated more by computational convenience than by the desire to achieve more accurate parameter estimation.

\paragrapharrow

MAP estimation.
As mentioned above, in Bayesian inference, we often cannot compute the expectation of the posterior probability distribution directly. Even if we derive the exact form of the posterior distribution, calculating its expectation typically involves integration, which is analytically or computationally difficult in many cases. Therefore, an alternative point estimation method known as maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation is commonly used; see Definition
:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X}).

The idea behind MAP estimation is to use the value of
\boldsymbol{\theta}
that maximizes the posterior probability as our estimate, rather than using the expectation or median of the posterior distribution. From Equation (
), we know that the posterior is proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior:

p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})\propto p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\equiv\text{Likelihood}\times\text{Prior}.

(7.6)

To obtain the MAP estimate, we only need to maximize the numerator of the posterior (that is, the product of the likelihood and the prior), so there is no need to compute the marginal likelihood
p(\mathcal{X})
. This simplifies the computation significantly:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{X})\equiv\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}).

Once we have obtained the MAP estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}
, we can use it as a point estimate for the unknown parameter
\boldsymbol{\theta}
. This allows us to make predictions for new data points:

p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}})=p(\mathcal{X}=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}).

Furthermore, MAP estimation can be interpreted as a modified version of maximum likelihood estimation, where a prior distribution acts as a regularizer or constraint:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\{\ln p(\mathcal{X}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})+\ln p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\}.

If the prior is flat—meaning
\ln p(\boldsymbol{\theta})=0
, for instance, when
p(\boldsymbol{\theta})
is a uniform distribution over the entire parameter space—then the MAP estimate reduces exactly to the MLE.

\paragrapharrow

Frequentists V.S. Bayesian in a nutshell.
The
frequentist approach
to statistics evaluates statistical procedures based on a probability distribution over all possible data sets.
To be more specific, frequentists consider the parameter vector
\boldsymbol{\theta}
to be fixed (albeit unknown), while introducing uncertainty over possible data sets
\mathcal{X}
. Frequentist methods are often considered more objective as they avoid incorporating subjective prior information.
In contrast, Bayesian methods allow for the incorporation of prior beliefs. The Bayesian approach treats the data set
\mathcal{X}
as given, while introducing uncertainty over
\boldsymbol{\theta}
.
Moreover, though we will not use any hierarchical models in this book, Bayesian modeling is often more flexible, allowing for the specification of complex hierarchical models.
This flexibility is advantageous in cases where the underlying data-generating process is intricate.
However, statisticians nowadays tend to move comfortably between these approaches and popular statistical procedures often combine both of them, incorporating Bayesian methods for certain aspects of the analysis while using frequentist methods for others.
For instance, empirical Bayesian methods have a Bayesian spirit but are not strictly Bayesian; their analysis is frequently frequentist
(
Haugh 2021
)
.

7.2
An Appetizer: Beta-Bernoulli Model

We now formally introduce the Beta-Bernoulli model to illustrate how the Bayesian approach works.
The Bernoulli distribution models binary outcomes—that is, it assigns probabilities to two possible values, typically denoted as 0 and 1. The likelihood under this model is defined by the probability mass function of the Bernoulli distribution:

\mathrm{Bern}(x\mid\theta)=p(x\mid\theta)=\theta^{x}(1-\theta)^{1-x}\mathds{1}(x\in\{0,1\}).

This means that:

\mathrm{Bern}(x\mid\theta)=p(x\mid\theta)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &1-\theta,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x=0;\\
&\theta,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x=1,\end{aligned}\right.

where
\theta
represents the probability of observing the outcome 1, and
1-\theta
is the probability of observing 0.
The mean (or expected value) of the Bernoulli distribution is simply
\theta
.
Suppose we are given a dataset
\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}\}
, where each
x_{i}
is i.i.d. according to
\mathrm{Bern}(x\mid\theta)
. Then, the likelihood under the Bernoulli distribution is given by:

\displaystyle\text{Likelihood}=p(\mathcal{X}\mid\theta)

\displaystyle=\theta^{\sum x_{i}}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum x_{i}},

which is a distribution on
\mathcal{X}
and is called the
likelihood function
on
\mathcal{X}
.

In this model, the prior distribution follows the probability density function of the
Beta distribution
, which is defined as:

\mathrm{Prior}=\mathrm{Beta}(\theta\mid a,b)=p(\theta\mid a,b)=\frac{1}{B(a,b)}\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\mathds{1}(0\leq\theta\leq 1),

where
B(a,b)
denotes
Euler’s beta function
, serving as a normalization constant.
And
\mathds{1}(a\leq x\leq b)
is a step function that has a value of 1 when
a\leq x\leq b
and 0 otherwise (when
x<a
or
a>b
). Figure
compares different parameters for the Beta distribution.
Specifically, when
a=b=1
, the Beta distribution reduces to a
uniform distribution
over the support of
[0,1]
.

We place a Beta prior over the parameter
\theta
of the Bernoulli distribution. The posterior distribution is then obtained as follows:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Posterior}=p(\theta\mid\mathcal{X})

\displaystyle\propto p(\mathcal{X}\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid a,b)

\displaystyle=\theta^{\sum x_{i}}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum x_{i}}\times\frac{1}{B(a,b)}\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\mathds{1}(0<\theta<1)

\displaystyle\propto\theta^{a+\sum x_{i}-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-\sum x_{i}-1}\mathds{1}(0<\theta<1)

\displaystyle\propto\mathrm{Beta}\left(\theta\mid a+\sum x_{i},b+n-\sum x_{i}\right).

We observe that the posterior distribution has the same functional form as the prior. When this occurs, we refer to the prior as a
conjugate prior
(Definition
). A conjugate prior is particularly useful because it simplifies computation: it allows for straightforward derivation of the posterior probability density function, its derivatives, and even sampling from the posterior.

Using conjugate priors has a key advantage: it preserves the mathematical form of the prior during Bayesian updating. As a result, the posterior can often be expressed in closed form, eliminating the need for complex numerical methods or approximations.

Remark 185
(Prior information in Beta-Bernoulli model).

Comparing the forms of the prior and posterior distributions, we see that the hyper-parameter
a
can be interpreted as representing the number of “prior successes” (i.e., outcomes equal to 1), while
b
corresponds to the number of “prior failures” (i.e., outcomes equal to 0). The sum
a+b
reflects the strength or confidence in the prior information—effectively acting like a prior sample size.

In the Beta-Bernoulli example, similar to the maximum likelihood estimator or the method of moments (MoM)—which uses moment information to estimate model parameters—the Bayesian framework can also be used to obtain estimates. However, instead of directly estimating a single value, the Bayesian approach provides a full posterior distribution over the parameter of interest:
p(\theta\mid\mathcal{X})
.

When making predictions for new data observations, we do not use a fixed parameter value from the model
p(x_{n+1}\mid\theta)
directly. Instead, we marginalize out the uncertainty in
\theta
by integrating over the posterior distribution:

p(x_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{X})=\int p(x_{n+1}\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid\mathcal{X})d\theta.

In other words,
x_{n+1}
depends on
\mathcal{X}
. The observed data
\mathcal{X}
provide information on
\theta
, which in turn provides information on
x_{n+1}
(i.e.,
\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\theta\rightarrow x_{n+1}
).

Example 186
(Amount of data matters).

Bayesian methods can be advantageous in cases of small sample sizes or sparse data, where traditional frequentist methods may encounter difficulties.
Suppose we have three observations for the success in a Bernoulli experiment:

1.

10 out of 10 trials are observed to be success (1’s);

2.

48 out of 50 trials are observed to be success (1’s);

3.

186 out of 200 trials are observed to be success (1’s).

A common frequentist estimate of the success probability would be 100%, 96%, and 93% for cases 1, 2, and 3, respectively. However, in case 1, an observation based on only 10 trials may be unreliable, as such a small sample size makes the estimate more sensitive to noise.

Now suppose we put a
\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)
(a uniform distribution, see Figure
) prior on the Bernoulli distribution parameter.
Then the posterior probability of success for each case becomes
\frac{11}{12}=91.6\%
,
\frac{49}{52}=94.2\%
, and
\frac{187}{202}=92.6\%
, respectively.
Interestingly, under this Bayesian approach, the estimated success probability for case 1 is actually lower than for case 2, despite both having perfect success rates in the observed data. This reflects the influence of the small sample size in case 1, which results in greater shrinkage toward the prior.

This Bayesian perspective naturally incorporates both the amount of data and the observed average into the final estimate. The specific form shown here is known as Laplace’s rule of succession
(
Ollivier 2015
)
, which adjusts the observed frequency by adding one to both the count of successes and failures. This “add-one” rule avoids assigning zero probability to unseen events and corresponds to using a uniform prior in a Bayesian framework.

Remark 187
(Why Bayes?).

The previous example illustrates that Bayesian models incorporate prior information about the parameters, making them particularly effective for regularizing regression problems when data are limited. This is one reason why the Bayesian approach has attracted widespread attention over the decades.

In the Bayesian framework, the prior distribution
p(\theta)
and the likelihood function
p(x\mid\theta)
together represent a rational individual’s initial beliefs about the parameter
\theta
. Bayes’ theorem then provides an optimal method for updating these beliefs in light of new data, resulting in the posterior distribution
p(\theta\mid x)
.

The prior
p(\theta)
may not always accurately reflect true prior beliefs, and in such cases, it could be considered “incorrect” or suboptimal. However, this does not necessarily render the resulting posterior
p(\theta\mid x)
uninformative or useless. As famously stated: “All models are wrong, but some are useful”
(
Box and Draper 1987
)
. If the prior
p(\theta)
reasonably approximates our actual beliefs, then the resulting posterior
p(\theta\mid x)
will also serve as a good approximation of the updated beliefs after observing the data.

Figure 7.1:
Graphical representation of the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean prior. Orange circles represent observed and latent variables, green circles denote prior variables, and plates represent repeated variables.
In the graph,
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
,
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
,
\widetilde{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i}=\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}=\widetilde{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i}+\epsilon_{i}
.

7.3
Bayesian Linear Model: Zero-Mean Prior

We now introduce the application of Bayesian methods to linear regression models.
Consider the standard linear model:

{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon},

where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
and
\sigma^{2}
is fixed.
As discussed in Section
, the assumption of additive Gaussian noise leads naturally to a normal likelihood function. Let
\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}(\bm{x}_{1:n})=\{\bm{x}_{1},\bm{x}_{2},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\}
be the observations of
n
data points, and
\bm{y}=[y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}]
contains the corresponding responses.
Then, the joint likelihood is given by:

\mathrm{Likelihood}=\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}).

Now suppose we place a multivariate Gaussian prior with zero mean on the weight vector:

\mathrm{Prior}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}).

The graphical representation of this Bayesian linear model is shown in Figure
. Applying Bayes’ rule, which states that
“
\mathrm{Posterior}\propto\mathrm{Likelihood}\times\mathrm{Prior}
,” we obtain the posterior distribution:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Posterior}

\displaystyle=p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2})\propto p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2})p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\}\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\right\rvert^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\}

\displaystyle\propto\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1})\right\},

where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\triangleq\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}\triangleq\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y})
.
Thus, the posterior distribution is also multivariate normal (i.e., it belongs to the same family as the prior), confirming that the Gaussian prior is conjugate to the Gaussian likelihood:

\mathrm{Posterior}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}).

Note that we use
\{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\}
to denote the posterior mean and posterior covariance in the zero-mean prior model. Similarly, the posterior mean and posterior covariance in semi-conjugate prior and full conjugate prior models will be denoted by
\{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}\}
and
\{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{3}\}
, respectively (see later sections).

7.3.1
Connection to Non-Bayesian Models

We demonstrate that the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean prior generalizes certain standard Gauss-Markov linear models.

\paragrapharrow

Connection to OLS.
Importantly, in the Bayesian framework, there is no strict requirement for the design matrix
\bm{X}
to have full rank. This allows for more flexibility compared to classical linear regression.
However, if
\bm{X}
does have full column rank and we consider the limiting case where the prior becomes highly concentrated around zero, i.e.,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}
, then the posterior mean converges to the OLS estimate:

\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}\rightarrow\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}\bm{y}\qquad\text{as}\qquad\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}.

In this limit, the MAP estimate from the Bayesian model coincides with the OLS estimate.
Furthermore, the posterior distribution becomes:

\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1})\qquad\text{as}\qquad\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0},

which shares the same form as the OLS estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1})
under Gaussian disturbances (see Theorem
).

\paragrapharrow

Connection to ridge regression.
In the context of least squares approximation, the utilization of
\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
for approximating
\bm{y}
introduces two potential issues: the risk of overfitting and the possibility of
\bm{X}
lacking full rank.
Ridge regression addresses these concerns by regularizing large values of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, thereby favoring simpler models.
Instead of minimizing the squared error along:
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, ridge regression minimizes the following objective function:
\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, where
\lambda
is a hyper-parameter that controls the strength of the regularization and can be tuned as needed:

\mathop{\arg\min}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})+\lambda\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

By differentiating this expression with respect to
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and setting the gradient to zero, we obtain the closed-form estimate:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{ridge}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y},

in which case,
(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\lambda\bm{I})
is always invertible even when
\bm{X}
does not have full rank.

Now consider the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean prior. If we set
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}=\bm{I}
, the posterior mean becomes

\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
, and the posterior covariance is
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}=(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\bm{I})^{-1}
. Since
\mathrm{Posterior}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1})
, the MAP estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
becomes
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
.
This expression matches the ridge regression estimate when we identify
\sigma^{2}
with
\lambda
.
Therefore, ridge regression can be viewed as a special case of the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean Gaussian prior.
The Bayesian framework provides a probabilistic interpretation of ridge regression: it corresponds to finding the most probable value of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
given the data and the prior assumptions—namely, that the coefficients are centered at zero with unit variance.

7.3.2
Zeller’s
g
-Prior and Variable Transformation

As an illustrative example, consider modeling an individual’s weight based on various human characteristics, where one variable in the input matrix
\bm{X}
represents the person’s height in meters.
If this variable is instead expressed in centimeters, the underlying relationship remains unchanged. We can account for this change by simply dividing the corresponding coefficient in
\boldsymbol{\beta}
by 100, effectively converting centimeters back to meters.

More generally, suppose the input matrix
\bm{X}
undergoes a linear transformation such that
\widetilde{\bm{X}}=\bm{X}\bm{P}
, where
\bm{P}
is a
p\times p
invertible matrix; let the corresponding model parameter become
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Then we have:

\displaystyle\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\widetilde{\bm{X}}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

According to the
principle of invariance
, the posterior distributions of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
should be equivalent—meaning our inference should not depend on how the input features are scaled or transformed.
From earlier results, the posterior distribution of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
given
\bm{X}
is:

\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}\right),\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\right).

Similarly, for the transformed input matrix
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
, the posterior distribution of
\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
becomes:

\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\bm{y},\widetilde{\bm{X}},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\bm{P}}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}}+\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top}\bm{y}\right),{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\bm{P}}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}}+\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\bm{P}^{\top}}\right).\penalty\

Following the principle of invariance, it can be shown that this condition holds when the prior covariance matrix takes the form:
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}=k(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
, where
k>0
is a hyper-parameter. A popular specification of
k
is to relate it to the noise variance
\sigma^{2}
by
k=g\sigma^{2}
. This is called Zeller’s
g
-prior
(
Zellner 1986
)
.
Following the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean prior, the posterior of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is

\mathrm{Posterior}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}).

where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}=\frac{g\sigma^{2}}{g+1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}=\frac{g}{g+1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y})
.

7.4
Bayesian Linear Model: Semi-Conjugate Prior Distribution

We will use the Gamma distribution as the prior for the inverse variance (precision) parameter of a Gaussian distribution.
A formal definition of the Gamma distribution is provided in Definition
.
The choice of the Gamma distribution as the prior for precision is motivated by the rationale provided in
Kruschke 2014
:

“Because of its role in conjugate priors for normal likelihood function, the Gamma distribution is routinely used as a prior for precision (i.e., inverse variance). But there is no logical necessity to do so, and modern Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods permit more flexible specification of priors. Indeed, because precision is less intuitive than standard deviation, it can be more useful to give standard deviation a uniform prior that spans a wide range.”

Building on the setup introduced in Section
, we now treat
\sigma^{2}
as an unknown variable rather than a fixed constant. As before, the likelihood function is given by:

\mathrm{Likelihood}=\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}).

We define a non-zero mean Gaussian prior on the weight vector
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, along with a Gamma prior on the precision parameter
\gamma=1/\sigma^{2}
:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\mathrm{Prior:\,}}

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}({\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0});

(7.7)

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\mathrm{Hyperprior:\,}}

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}{\displaystyle\gamma=1/\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{G}(a_{0},b_{0})},

where the modifications from the previous model are highlighted in blue.
The graphical representation of this Bayesian linear model is shown in Figure
.

Figure 7.2:
Graphical representation of the Bayesian linear model with a semi-conjugate prior. Orange circles represent observed and latent variables, green circles denote prior variables, and plates represent repeated variables.
The comma “,” in the variable represents “and.” In the graph,
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
,
\gamma=1/\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{G}(a_{0},b_{0})
,
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
,
\widetilde{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i}=\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}=\widetilde{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i}+\epsilon_{i}
.

\paragrapharrow

Step 1, conditioning on
\sigma^{2}
. Then, given
\sigma^{2}
, by Bayes’ theorem “
\mathrm{Posterior}\propto\mathrm{Likelihood}\times\mathrm{Prior}
”, we obtain the conditional posterior density of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Posterior}=p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2})\propto p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2})p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\}\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\right\rvert^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})\right\}

\displaystyle\propto\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2})\right\},

where the parameters are

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}

\displaystyle\triangleq\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1};

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}

\displaystyle\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}+\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y})=\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}}+\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}\right).

Thus, the conditional posterior distribution is also Gaussian:

\mathrm{Posterior}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}).

\paragrapharrow

Connection to the zero-mean prior model.
We highlight the relationship between the zero-mean prior model and the semi-conjugate prior model as follows:

1.

\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}
here is a fixed hyper-parameter.

2.

We note that
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}
in Section
is a special case of
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
when
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

3.

And if we assume further
\bm{X}
has full rank, when
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}
,
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
approaches to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}\rightarrow\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}\bm{y}
, which converges to the OLS estimate.

4.

When
\sigma^{2}\rightarrow\infty
,
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
is approximately approaching to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
, the prior expectation of parameter. However, in the zero-mean prior model,
\sigma^{2}\rightarrow\infty
will causes
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}
to approach
\boldsymbol{0}
.

5.

Weighted average interpretation.
We can rewrite
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
as:

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}+\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}\right)

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}+\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}}{\sigma^{2}}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=(\bm{I}-\bm{A})\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}+\bm{A}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},

where
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
is the OLS estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and
\bm{A}\triangleq(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1})^{-1}\frac{\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}}{\sigma^{2}}
.
This shows that the posterior mean of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is a weighted average of the prior mean and the OLS estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
Consequently, if we set the prior parameter
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, the posterior mean of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
becomes exactly
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

\paragrapharrow

Step 2, conditioning on
\boldsymbol{\beta}
. Given
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, we again apply Bayes’ theorem to obtain the posterior distribution of the precision parameter
\gamma
:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Posterior}

\displaystyle=p(\gamma=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta})\propto p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\gamma)p(\gamma\mid a_{0},b_{0})

\displaystyle=\frac{\gamma^{n/2}}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\gamma}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\}\times\frac{{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}}{\Gamma(a_{0})}\gamma^{a_{0}-1}\exp(-b_{0}\gamma)

\displaystyle\propto\gamma(a_{0}+\frac{n}{2}-1)\exp\left\{-\gamma\left[b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right]\right\}.

Therefore, the conditional posterior of
\gamma
follows a Gamma distribution:

\mathrm{posterior\,\,of\,\,}\gamma\mathrm{\,\,given\,\,}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\gamma\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{G}\left(a_{0}+\frac{n}{2},\big[b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\big]\right).

(7.8)

\paragrapharrow

Prior information on the noise.
We can interpret the prior on
\gamma
intuitively as follows:

1.

We notice that the prior mean and posterior mean of
\gamma
are
\mathbb{E}[\gamma]=\frac{a_{0}}{b_{0}}
and
\mathbb{E}[\gamma\mid\boldsymbol{\beta}]=\frac{a_{0}+\frac{n}{2}}{b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})}
, respectively.
This suggests that the internal meaning of
2a_{0}
is the effective sample size of the prior information about the noise variance
\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{\gamma}
.

2.

As we assume
{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
, where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
, then
\frac{({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}({\mathbf{y}}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\sigma^{2}}\sim\chi_{(n)}^{2}
and
\mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\frac{n}{2}\sigma^{2}
. So the latent meaning of
\frac{b_{0}}{a_{0}}
is the prior variance of the noise.

3.

Some textbooks explicitly express
\gamma\sim\mathcal{G}(n_{0}/2,n_{0}\sigma_{0}^{2}/2)
(in which case,
n_{0}
is the prior sample size, and
\sigma_{0}^{2}
is the prior variance). While this form may seem arbitrary at first glance, it provides an intuitive way to encode prior beliefs about the magnitude and uncertainty of the noise variance.

7.4.1
Gibbs Sampling with Two Variables

Gibbs sampling was first introduced by Turchin
(
Turchin 1971
)
, and later reintroduced by the Geman brothers in the context of image restoration
(
Geman and Geman 1984
)
.
The Geman brothers named the algorithm after the physicist J. W. Gibbs, some eight decades after his death, in reference to an analogy between the sampling algorithm and statistical physics.

Gibbs sampling is particularly useful when the joint distribution is not explicitly known or is difficult to sample from directly, but the conditional distributions of each variable are known and easy to sample from. A Gibbs sampler iteratively generates a sample for each parameter or variable, conditioned on the current values of all other parameters or variables. Therefore, it operates in a componentwise manner.

For example, given some data
\mathcal{X}
and a probability distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\alpha})
, parameterized by
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\{\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{p}\}
.
In this case, we can sequentially draw samples from the full conditional distributions:

\beta_{i}^{(t)}\sim p(\beta_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta}_{-i}^{(t-1)},\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\alpha}),

(7.9)

where
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{-i}^{(t-1)}
is all current values of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
in
(t-1)
-th iteration except for
\beta_{i}
.
If the sampling continues long enough, the resulting values of
\beta_{i}
will approximate random samples from the target (posterior) distribution
p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\alpha})

In deriving a Gibbs sampler, it is often helpful to observe that

p(\beta_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta}_{-i},\mathcal{X})=\frac{p(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{p},\mathcal{X})}{p(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{-i},\mathcal{X})}\propto p(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{p},\mathcal{X}).

(7.10)

That is, the conditional distribution is proportional to the joint distribution.
This observation allows us to simplify computations by ignoring constant terms in the joint distribution that do not involve the parameter being sampled, e.g., we can discard the terms w.r.t. to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{-i}
and only pay attention to
\beta_{i}
when we want to sample from
p(\beta_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta}_{-i},\mathcal{X})
.

To illustrate briefly, suppose we have a
bivariate
joint distribution
p(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\mid\mathcal{X})
. A Gibbs sampler would iteratively draw samples from the two full conditionals: first from
p(\beta_{1}\mid\beta_{2},\mathcal{X})
, then from
p(\beta_{2}\mid\beta_{1},\mathcal{X})
.
This iterative procedure generates a sequence of realizations for
\beta_{1}
and
\beta_{2}
:

(\beta_{1}^{0},\beta_{2}^{0}),\,(\beta_{1}^{1},\beta_{2}^{1}),\,(\beta_{1}^{2},\beta_{2}^{2}),\,\ldots

which converges in distribution to the joint distribution
p(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\mid\mathcal{X})
.
For further reading on Gibbs sampling, see
Turchin 1971
;
Geman and Geman 1984
;
Müller and Quintana 2004
;
Rencher and Schaalje 2008
;
Hoff 2009
;
Gelman et al. 2013
;
Kruschke and Liddell 2018
.

Using this Gibbs sampling technique, we can construct a Gibbs sampler for the Bayesian linear model with a semi-conjugate prior discussed in Section
. The steps are as follows:

1.

Set initial values to
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\gamma=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}
.

2.

Update
\boldsymbol{\beta}
:
\mathrm{Posterior}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\gamma\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2})
.

3.

Update
\gamma
:
\mathrm{Posterior}=\gamma\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{G}\left(a_{0}+\frac{n}{2},[b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})]\right)
.

7.4.2
Zeller’s
g
-Prior

Similar to the variable transformation problem discussed in Section
, suppose the input matrix
\bm{X}
is transferred as
\widetilde{\bm{X}}=\bm{X}\bm{P}
given some
p\times p
nonsingular matrix
\bm{P}
, in which case, the model parameter is
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Then, we have

\bm{y}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\widetilde{\bm{X}}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\bm{X}\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

According to the principle of invariance, the posterior distributions of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\bm{P}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
should be identical.
Simple calculation can show that this condition is met if
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}=g\sigma^{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
.
Following the Bayesian linear model with a semi-conjugate prior, the posterior of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is

\mathrm{Posterior}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}).

where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}=\frac{g\sigma^{2}}{g+1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}=\frac{g}{g+1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y})
.

Derivation of
p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2})

Under the
g
-prior specified above, we now derive the conditional distribution
p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2})
, which will be very useful for the Bayesian variable selection procedure.
Since
{\mathbf{y}}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
, we have

\displaystyle p(\bm{y},\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2})=p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2})p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{\frac{n}{2}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\}\times\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{\frac{p}{2}}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\right\rvert^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}\right\}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{\frac{n}{2}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}}{2\sigma^{2}}+\frac{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}}{2}\right\}\frac{\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}\right\rvert^{1/2}}{\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\right\rvert^{1/2}}\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{\frac{p}{2}}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}\right\rvert^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2})}{2}\right\},

where the parameter
\boldsymbol{\beta}
only appears in the third term, which corresponds to a multivariate normal distribution with mean
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
and covariance
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}
(defined previously). Since this term integrates to 1 over all
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, we can proceed to integrate it out.
Since
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}=\frac{1}{g+1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}
such that
\frac{\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}\right\rvert^{1/2}}{\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\right\rvert^{1/2}}=\frac{1}{(g+1)^{p/2}}
. Therefore, we obtain

\displaystyle p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=\int p(\bm{y},\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2})d\boldsymbol{\beta}=\int p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2})p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2})d\boldsymbol{\beta}

(7.11)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}\right\}\cdot\frac{1}{(g+1)^{p/2}}\exp\left\{\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}\right\}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\frac{1}{(g+1)^{p/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{r}{2\sigma^{2}}\right\},

where
r\triangleq\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{y}^{\top}(\frac{g}{g+1}\bm{X}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top})\bm{y}
.

7.4.3
Bayesian Variable Selection

In Section
, we introduced variable selection using the
F
-test.
An alternative approach can be achieved through the
Bayesian variable selection
procedure.

The Model

Let
\bm{z}=[z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{p}]\in\real^{p}
be a mask vector, where each component
z_{j}\in\{0,1\}
for all
j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
. For each regression coefficient
\beta_{j}
in
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, we set
\beta_{j}=z_{j}\times b_{j}
, where
b_{j}
represents the original coefficient, and
\beta_{j}
is the final coefficient that may be included or excluded from the model based on the value of
z_{j}
.
In matrix form, this relationship can be written as:

\boldsymbol{\beta}=\bm{z}\odot\bm{b},

(7.12)

where
\odot
denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product.
Then, the model with noise disturbance can be expressed as

{\mathbf{y}}=\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=\bm{X}(\bm{z}\odot\bm{b})+\boldsymbol{\epsilon},

(7.13)

where
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
.

In Bayesian variable selection, the goal is to estimate the posterior distribution of the mask vector
\bm{z}
.
That is, we aim to determine which variables are most likely to be included in the model given the observed data.
By Bayes’ theorem, the posterior distribution of
\bm{z}
is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood:

p(\bm{z}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X})\propto p(\bm{z})p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}).

(7.14)

Alternatively, suppose we have two mask vectors
\bm{z}_{a}
and
\bm{z}_{b}
.
The ratio of their posterior probabilities is given by:

\displaystyle\text{odds}(\bm{z}_{a},\bm{z}_{b}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X})

\displaystyle=\frac{p(\bm{z}_{a}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X})}{p(\bm{z}_{b}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{p(\bm{z}_{a})}{p(\bm{z}_{b})}

\displaystyle\times

\displaystyle\frac{p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}_{a})}{p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}_{b})}

(7.15)

\displaystyle\text{Posterior odds}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\text{Prior odds}

\displaystyle\times

\displaystyle\text{Bayes factor}

where the
Bayes factor

quantifies how much the observed data favor the model associated with
\bm{z}_{a}
over the model associated with
\bm{z}_{b}
.

Derivation of the Bayes Factor

We begin by writing out the marginal likelihood related to the Bayes factor:

\displaystyle p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z})

\displaystyle=\int\int p(\bm{y},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z})d\boldsymbol{\beta}d\sigma^{2}

(7.16)

\displaystyle=\int\left(\int p(\bm{y},\boldsymbol{\beta},\mid\bm{X},\bm{z},\sigma^{2})d\boldsymbol{\beta}\right)p(\sigma^{2})d\sigma^{2}

\displaystyle=\int p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2},\bm{z})p(\sigma^{2})d\sigma^{2},

where
p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2},\bm{z})=\left(\int p(\bm{y},\boldsymbol{\beta},\mid\bm{X},\bm{z},\sigma^{2})d\boldsymbol{\beta}\right)
can be obtained from Equation (
) (under Zeller’s
g
-prior) by substituting
\bm{X}
by
\bm{X}_{z}
, where we remove the variable
i
if
z_{i}
=0.

We realize that
\gamma=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}
, and

p(\sigma^{2})=p(\gamma\mid a_{0},b_{0})=\frac{{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}}{\Gamma(a_{0})}\gamma^{a_{0}-1}\exp(-b_{0}\gamma).

Then,

\displaystyle p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\sigma^{2},\bm{z})p(\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\frac{1}{(g+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p_{z}}/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}r_{z}}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\cdot\frac{{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}}{\Gamma(a_{0})}\gamma^{a_{0}-1}\exp(-b_{0}\gamma)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\frac{1}{(g+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p_{z}}/2}}\frac{{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}}{\Gamma(a_{0})}\gamma^{a_{0}+n/2-1}\exp\left(-(b_{0}+\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}r_{z}}}{2})\gamma\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\frac{1}{(g+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p_{z}}/2}}\frac{{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}}{\Gamma(a_{0})}\frac{\Gamma(a_{n})}{{b_{n}}^{a_{n}}}\cdot\frac{{b_{n}}^{a_{n}}}{\Gamma(a_{n})}\gamma^{a_{n}-1}\exp\left(-b_{n}\gamma\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\frac{1}{(g+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p_{z}}/2}}\frac{{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}}{\Gamma(a_{0})}\frac{\Gamma(a_{n})}{{b_{n}}^{a_{n}}}\cdot\mathcal{G}(\gamma\mid a_{n},b_{n}),

where
r_{z}=\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}-\bm{y}^{\top}(\frac{g}{g+1}\bm{X}_{z}(\bm{X}_{z}^{\top}\bm{X}_{z})^{-1}\bm{X}_{z}^{\top})\bm{y}
,
p_{z}
is the number of 1’s in
\bm{z}
,
a_{n}=a_{0}+n/2
,
b_{n}=b_{0}+\frac{r_{z}}{2}
, and
\mathcal{G}(\gamma\mid a_{n},b_{n})
is the probability density function of the Gamma distribution with respect to
\gamma
with parameters
a_{n}
and
b_{n}
. Since
\gamma
only appears in the last term
\mathcal{G}(\gamma\mid a_{n},b_{n})
, which integrates to 1; from (
), we have

p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\frac{1}{(g+1)^{p_{z}/2}}\frac{{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}}{\Gamma(a_{0})}\frac{\Gamma(a_{n})}{{b_{n}}^{a_{n}}}.

Same Prior Hyper-parameter

Similarly, under models
\bm{z}_{a}
and
\bm{z}_{b}
, where we assume they share the same parameters of
a_{0}
and
b_{0}
in the two models, we have

\frac{p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}_{a})}{p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}_{b})}=\frac{(g+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p_{z_{b}}}/2}}{(g+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p_{z_{a}}}/2}}\left(\frac{2b_{0}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}r_{z_{b}}}}{2b_{0}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}r_{z_{a}}}}\right)^{a_{0}+\frac{n}{2}},

where
p_{z_{a}}
is the number of variables selected in model
\bm{z}_{a}
, and
p_{z_{b}}
is the number of variables selected in model
\bm{z}_{b}
.

Different Prior Hyper-parameter

We have previously mentioned that

1.

2a_{0}
is the prior sample size for the noise
\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{\gamma}
.

2.

\frac{b_{0}}{a_{0}}
is the prior variance of the noise.

Suppose now, given the two models
\bm{z}_{a}
and
\bm{z}_{b}
, we assume
2a_{0}=1
for both of the models (i.e., prior sample sizes for the noise are both 1), and set the
\frac{b_{0}}{a_{0}}
to be the estimated residual variance under the least squares estimate for each model, say maximum likelihood estimators:

\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{z_{a}}=\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}_{z_{a}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{z_{a}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{z_{b}}=\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}_{z_{b}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{z_{b}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

which are biased estimators for
\sigma^{2}
; see Section
.
Alternatively, we could choose the unbiased estimators, which are divided by
n-p_{z_{a}}
and
n-p_{z_{b}}
, respectively, rather than divided by
n
(see Section
). Then, we have

\frac{p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}_{a})}{p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}_{b})}=\frac{(g+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p_{z_{b}}}/2}}{(g+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}p_{z_{a}}}/2}}\left(\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{z_{a}}}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{z_{b}}}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{z_{b}}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}r_{z_{b}}}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{z_{a}}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}r_{z_{a}}}}\right)^{\frac{n+1}{2}}.

(7.17)

Notice that the ratio of the marginal probabilities is essentially
a balance between the model complexity and goodness-of-fit
:

A larger value of
p_{z_{b}}
means the model
\bm{z}_{b}
has more selected variables (more complexity), which will make the ratio larger and penalize model
\bm{z}_{b}
.

However, a more complex model will make
r_{z_{b}}
smaller, which in turn will make the ratio smaller and penalize model
\bm{z}_{a}
.

Gibbs Sampler

Given a current value
\bm{z}=[z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{p}]^{\top}
, a new value of the
j
-th variable
z_{j}
is generated by sampling from
p(z_{j}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\bm{z}_{-j})
, where
\bm{z}_{-j}
refers to the values of
\bm{z}
except the
j
-th element
z_{j}
. Specifically, we define the
intermediate parameter

o_{j}=\frac{p(z_{j}=1\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\bm{z}_{-j})}{p(z_{j}=0\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\bm{z}_{-j})}=\frac{p(z_{j}=1)}{p(z_{j}=0)}\times\frac{p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}_{-j},z_{j}=1)}{p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\bm{z}_{-j},z_{j}=0)},

where the last term can be obtained using Equation (
). For simplicity, we can assume a uniform prior on
p(z_{j})
:

p(z_{j}=1)=p(z_{j}=0)=0.5.

Then, using this intermediate parameter, the full conditional probability of
z_{j}
being equal to 1 can be obtained by

p(z_{j}=1\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\bm{z}_{-j})=\frac{o_{j}}{1+o_{j}}.

(7.18)

Therefore, given the value of
\bm{z}^{(k)}
at the
k
-th step, we can generate the next set of values
\{\bm{z}^{(k+1)},\gamma^{(k+1)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(k+1)}\}
using the following steps:

1.

Set initial values to
\boldsymbol{\beta}
,
\gamma=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}
, and
\bm{z}
if
k
=1;

2.

Update
\bm{z}
: For
j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
in random order, replace
z_{j}
with a sample from
p(z_{j}=1\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\bm{z}_{-j})
(Equation (
));

3.

Update
\boldsymbol{\beta}
:
\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\gamma,\bm{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2})
, where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}=\frac{g\sigma^{2}}{g+1}(\bm{X}_{z}^{\top}\bm{X}_{z})^{-1}
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}=\frac{g}{g+1}(\bm{X}_{z}^{\top}\bm{X}_{z})^{-1}(\bm{X}_{z}^{\top}\bm{y})
(Equation (
));

4.

Update
\gamma
:
\gamma\mid\bm{y},\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{z}\sim\mathcal{G}\left(a_{0}+\frac{n}{2},[b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{X}_{z}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{z}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]\right)
(Equation (
)).

r
(
purple
=low,
yellow
=high).

(

=high).

(

(
