7.5
Bayesian Linear Model: Full Conjugate Prior

7.5.1
Normal-Inverse-Gamma Distribution

As we have seen that the Gamma density is a conjugate prior for the precision parameter of a Gaussian distribution. The
normal-inverse-Gamma (NIG)
distribution defined as follows is a joint conjugate prior for the mean and variance parameters of a Gaussian distribution.

Definition 188
(Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) Distribution).

The joint density of normal-inverse-Gamma distribution is a density defined as

\displaystyle\mathcal{NIG}(\mu,\sigma^{2}\mid m,\kappa,r,\lambda)=\mathcal{N}(\mu\mid m,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\kappa})\cdot\mathcal{G}^{-1}(\sigma^{2}\mid r,\lambda)

(7.19)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{\mathcal{NIG}}(\kappa,r,\lambda)}(\sigma^{2})^{-\frac{2r+3}{2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\left[\kappa(m-\mu)^{2}+2\lambda\right]\right\},

where
\sigma^{2},r,\lambda>0
, and
Z_{\mathcal{NIG}}(\kappa,r,\lambda)
is a normalizing constant:

Z_{\mathcal{NIG}}(\kappa,r,\lambda)=\frac{\Gamma(r)}{\lambda^{r}}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\kappa}}.

(7.20)

Figure
illustrates several probability density functions of the normal-inverse-Gamma distribution, obtained by varying different parameter values.

The normal-inverse-Gamma defines a conjugate prior over the mean and variance parameters of a Gaussian distribution.
When the variance and mean parameters of the Gaussian distribution are not fixed with
n
data points
\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}\}
drawn i.i.d. from a normal distribution with mean
\mu
and variance
\sigma^{2}
.
The normal-inverse-Gamma
\mathcal{NIG}(m_{0},\kappa_{0},r_{0},\lambda_{0})
with
m_{0}\in\real
and
r_{0},\lambda_{0},\kappa_{0}\in\real_{+}
is a joint distribution on
\mu,\sigma^{2}
by letting

\displaystyle\mu\mid\sigma^{2}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(m_{0},\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\kappa_{0}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{G}^{-1}(r_{0},\lambda_{0})

With this prior,
\mu
and
\sigma^{2}
decouple, and the posterior conditional densities of
\mu
and
\sigma^{2}
are Gaussian and inverse-Gamma, respectively.
The joint p.d.f of NIG prior can be expressed as

p(\mu,\sigma^{2})=\mathcal{N}(m_{0},\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\kappa_{0}})\cdot\mathcal{G}^{-1}(r_{0},\lambda_{0})=\mathcal{NIG}(\mu,\sigma^{2}\mid m_{0},\kappa_{0},r_{0},\lambda_{0}).

Again, by Bayes’ theorem “
\mathrm{Posterior}\propto\mathrm{Likelihood}\times\mathrm{Prior}
,” the posterior of the
\mu
and
\sigma^{2}
parameters of a Gaussian distribution under the NIG prior is

\displaystyle p(\mu,\sigma^{2}\mid\mathcal{X},\boldsymbol{\beta})

(7.21)

\displaystyle\propto\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X}\mid\mu,\sigma^{2})\cdot\mathcal{NIG}(\mu,\sigma^{2}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta})\propto\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{N}(x_{i}\mid\mu,\sigma^{2})\cdot\mathcal{NIG}(\mu,\sigma^{2}\mid m_{0},\kappa_{0},r_{0},\lambda_{0})

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\frac{C}{(\sigma^{2})^{\frac{2r_{0}+3+n}{2}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\left[n(\overline{x}-\mu)^{2}+nS_{\overline{x}}\right]}{2\sigma^{2}}\right\}\exp\left\{-\frac{\left[2\lambda_{0}+\kappa_{0}(m_{0}-\mu)^{2}\right]}{2\sigma^{2}}\right\}

\displaystyle\propto(\sigma^{2})^{-\frac{2r_{n}+3}{2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\left[\lambda_{n}+\kappa_{n}(m_{n}-\mu)^{2}\right]\right\}\propto\mathcal{NIG}(\mu,\sigma^{2}\mid m_{n},\kappa_{n},r_{n},\lambda_{n}),

where
\boldsymbol{\beta}\triangleq\{m_{0},\kappa_{0},r_{0},\lambda_{0}\}
,
C\triangleq\frac{(2\pi)^{-n/2}}{Z_{\mathcal{NIG}}(\kappa_{0},r_{0},\lambda_{0})}
, the equality
({\dagger})
follows from (
), and

\displaystyle m_{n}

\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{\kappa_{0}m_{0}+n\overline{x}}{\kappa_{n}}=\frac{\kappa_{0}}{\kappa_{n}}m_{0}+\frac{n}{\kappa_{n}}\overline{x};\qquad

\displaystyle\kappa_{n}

\displaystyle\triangleq\kappa_{0}+n;

\displaystyle r_{n}

\displaystyle\triangleq r_{0}+\frac{n}{2};\qquad

\displaystyle\lambda_{n}

\displaystyle\triangleq\lambda_{0}+\frac{1}{2}(nS_{\overline{x}}+n\overline{x}^{2}+\kappa_{0}m_{0}^{2}-\kappa_{n}m_{n}^{2})

\displaystyle=\lambda_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\left(nS_{\overline{x}}+\frac{\kappa_{0}n}{\kappa_{0}+n}(\overline{x}-m_{0})^{2}\right),

with
S_{\overline{x}}\triangleq\sum_{n=1}^{n}(x_{n}-\overline{x})^{2}
and
\overline{x}\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}
.
Note in the above derivation, we used the expression for the likelihood of a Gaussian distribution in (
).
Furthers discussion on the posterior marginal likelihood for the NIG or NIX (normal-inverse-Chi-squared) priors can be found, for example, in
Lu 2023b
.

7.5.2
Full Conjugate Prior Model

The joint conjugate prior on the mean and variance parameters of a Gaussian distribution provides insight into constructing a full conjugate prior for the Bayesian linear model.

To develop the full conjugate Bayesian model for linear regression, we place an inverse-Gamma prior (Definition
) on the variance parameter.
Alternatively, placing a Gamma prior on the inverse variance (also known as precision),
\gamma=1/\sigma^{2}
, is mathematically equivalent to using an inverse-Gamma prior on
\sigma^{2}
itself.

Consider the same setting as the semi-conjugate prior distribution discussed in Section
, the likelihood function—given the regression coefficient
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, the design matrix
\bm{X}
, the variance scale
\sigma^{2}
—is defined as follows:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Likelihood}

\displaystyle=\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}),

which is identical to the likelihood density used in the zero-mean prior model (Section
) and the semi-conjugate model (Section
).
However, in this case, we specify:

An Gaussian prior (the covariance matrix of which is not fixed this time) over the regression coefficient
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, where the covariance matrix depends on the variance parameter
\sigma^{2}
.

An inverse-Gamma prior over the variance parameter
\sigma^{2}
, which is known as a
hyperprior
since the variance parameter
\sigma^{2}
itself is used as a parameter in the Gaussian prior; see Figure
for an illustration.

Specifically, the prior distributions are defined as:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\mathrm{Prior:\,}}

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\sigma^{2}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0});

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\mathrm{Hyperprior:\,}}

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}{\displaystyle\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{G}^{-1}(a_{0},b_{0})},

where the blue-colored terms highlight the differences from earlier models.
A graphical representation of this Bayesian linear model is provided in Figure
.

Note that, unlike in the semi-conjugate case—where we placed a Gamma prior on the precision
\gamma=1/\sigma^{2}
—here we directly use an inverse-Gamma prior on the variance
\sigma^{2}
. However, these two approaches are mathematically equivalent. This equivalence can be shown using the change-of-variables formula and computing the corresponding Jacobian “determinant”; see Problem
.

We can equivalently express the prior as what is also known as the
normal-inverse-Gamma (NIG) distribution
(compare to Definition
):

\displaystyle\mathrm{Prior:}\,\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{NIG}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0},a_{0},b_{0})

\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})\cdot\mathcal{G}^{-1}(a_{0},b_{0}),

where the normal distribution is multivariate, in contrast to the univariate version used in Definition
.

Once again, by applying Bayes’ theorem “
\mathrm{Posterior}\propto\mathrm{Likelihood}\times\mathrm{Prior}
”, we obtain the posterior distribution:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Posterior}

\displaystyle=p(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X})\propto p(\bm{y}\mid\bm{X},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2})p(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0},a_{0},b_{0})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\right\}

\displaystyle\times\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{p/2}\left\lvert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\right\rvert^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})\right\}

\displaystyle\times\frac{{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}}{\Gamma(a_{0})}\frac{1}{(\sigma^{2})^{a_{0}+1}}\exp\{-\frac{b_{0}}{\sigma^{2}}\}

\displaystyle\propto\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{p/2}}\exp\left\{\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{3}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3})\right\}

\displaystyle\times\frac{1}{(\sigma^{2})^{a_{0}+\frac{n}{2}+1}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\big[b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{3}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3})\big]\right\},

where

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{3}

\displaystyle\triangleq(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1})^{-1};

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3}

\displaystyle\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{3}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})=\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}+\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}).

Let
a_{n}\triangleq a_{0}+\frac{n}{2}+1
and
b_{n}\triangleq b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}(\bm{y}^{\top}\bm{y}+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{3}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3})
. The posterior admits conjugacy and follows a NIG distribution:

\displaystyle\mathrm{Posterior}

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^{2}\mid\bm{y},\bm{X}\sim\mathcal{NIG}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{3},a_{n},b_{n}).

Figure 7.4:
Graphical representation of the Bayesian linear model with a full conjugate prior. Orange circles represent observed and latent variables, green circles denote prior variables, and plates represent repeated variables.
The comma “,” in the variable represents “and.” In the graph,
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
,
\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{G}^{-1}(a_{0},b_{0})
,
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
,
\widetilde{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i}=\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}=\widetilde{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i}+\epsilon_{i}
.

\paragrapharrow

Connection to zero-mean prior and semi-conjugate prior models.
We highlight the connection of the full conjugate model to the zero-mean prior and semi-conjugate prior models as follows:

1.

In this model,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}
is a fixed hyper-parameter that controls the strength and direction of the prior belief about the regression coefficients
\boldsymbol{\beta}

2.

If we assume further that the design matrix
\bm{X}
has full rank, then as
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}
, the posterior mean
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3}\rightarrow\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}\bm{y}
, which converges to the OLS estimate.

3.

When
b_{0}\rightarrow\infty
, then
\sigma^{2}\rightarrow\infty
and
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3}
is approximately approaching
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
, the prior expectation of parameter. Compared to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
in Section
,
\sigma^{2}\rightarrow\infty
will make
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2}
approach
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
, where
\sigma^{2}
is a fixed hyper-parameter.

4.

Weighted average interpretation.
We can rewrite
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3}
as follows:

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\beta}_{3}

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1})^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}+\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y})

\displaystyle=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}+(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1})^{-1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}

\displaystyle=(\bm{I}-\bm{C})\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}+\bm{C}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},

where
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}
is the OLS estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, and the matrix
\bm{C}
is defined as
\bm{C}\triangleq\left(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\right)^{-1}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})
. Therefore, the posterior mean of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is a weighted average of the prior mean and the OLS estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
. Thus, if we set
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, the posterior mean of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
becomes exactly
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

5.

From
a_{n}=a_{0}+\frac{n}{2}+1
, we see that
2a_{0}
can be interpreted as the effective sample size contributed by the prior on
\sigma^{2}
. This helps quantify the influence of the prior relative to the observed data.

6.

\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{3}^{-1}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}
: The posterior inverse covariance matrix (i.e., the precision matrix) is equal to data inverse covariance
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
+ prior precision matrix. Hence, the posterior uncertainty reflects a balance between what the data tells us and what we believed a priori.

7.6
Beyond Bayesian Approach: Gaussian Process Regression

A
Gaussian process (GP)
is a powerful nonparametric Bayesian tool used primarily for regression and classification tasks. At its core, a GP defines a distribution over functions, allowing us to reason about uncertainty in function estimation. Rather than specifying a fixed functional form as in parametric models, GPs generalize this idea by assuming that any finite set of function values follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution.

Importantly, Gaussian process regression can be derived as an extension of the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean Gaussian prior on the coefficient parameter. When the feature space is implicitly defined via a kernel function—corresponding to the covariance function of the GP—the posterior distribution over functions naturally emerges without explicitly modeling parameters. This connection clarifies that Gaussian processes are not arbitrary constructs but have a firm grounding in Bayesian inference, often obscured when GPs are introduced independently of their parametric origins.

Predictive Distribution of Bayesian Linear Model with Zero-Mean Prior

Building on the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean prior introduced in Section
, the predictive distribution
g_{\ast}=g_{\ast}(\bm{x}_{\ast})
for a new data observation
\bm{x}_{\ast}
remains a Gaussian distribution:

\displaystyle p(g_{\ast}\mid\bm{x}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y},\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=\int p(g_{\ast}\mid\bm{x}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{\beta})p(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\bm{X},\bm{y},\sigma^{2})d\boldsymbol{\beta}

(7.22)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\bm{x}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y},\bm{x}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\bm{x}_{\ast}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\bm{x}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1},\bm{x}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\bm{x}_{\ast}),

where the mean of the predictive distribution corresponds to the posterior mean of the weight vector (i.e.,
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}
) multiplied by the new input
\bm{x}_{\ast}^{\top}
, and the predictive variance is a quadratic form involving
\bm{x}_{\ast}^{\top}
, indicating that the
predictive uncertainty
increases as the magnitude of the input grows.

However, this Bayesian linear model has limited expressive power and may struggle to capture complex patterns in the data. One way to address this limitation is by introducing a set of basis functions that map the original
p
-dimensional input space into a higher-dimensional space, say
q
-dimensional:

\bm{x}\in\real^{p}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})\in\real^{q}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bm{X})\in\real^{n\times q}.

Nonetheless, increasing the dimensionality introduces computational challenges. Specifically, computational complexity grows quadratically with the number of dimensions. For example, computing the predictive variance increases from
\mathcal{O}(p^{2}+p)
to
\mathcal{O}(q^{2}+q)
. Such quadratic growth becomes a significant issue when scalability and efficiency are crucial.

One way to address the computation challenges is using the kernel trick.

Remark 189
(Kernel trick).

The kernel trick can significantly reduce computational costs in high-dimensional spaces. The key requirement is that all operations depend only on inner products between input vectors.

Example 190
(Kernel trick).

For some examples, we have:

1.

The computation of
\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bm{X})^{\top}=\bm{z}\in\real^{1\times n}
involves only inner products in the input space. Therefore, we can apply the kernel trick. Each element of
\bm{z}
becomes
z_{i}=k(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{x}_{i})
, where
k(\cdot,\cdot)
denotes a kernel function.
Computing the kernel function can be more efficient than directly working in the high-dimensional space, potentially requiring less than
\mathcal{O}(q)
operations.

2.

In contrast, the computation
\bm{y}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\bm{X})
involves inner products between inputs and outputs, which cannot be expressed purely in terms of input-input dot products. Hence, the kernel trick does not apply here.

In summary, we can apply the kernel trick only when all computations involve inner products between input vectors (i.e., input-input dot products).

With this in mind, if we can reformulate Equation (
) so that all computations depend only on dot products in the input space, we can apply the kernel trick.
To achieve this, we map the original input features into a higher-dimensional space. This transformation replaces the original inputs {
\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{X}
} (the “
x
-space”
\in\real^{p}
) with their corresponding feature representations {
\boldsymbol{\phi},\boldsymbol{\Phi}
} (the “
z
-space”
\in\real^{q}
). Applying this mapping leads to the predictive distribution in the
z
-space form
:

\boxed{\begin{aligned} z\mathchar 45\relax\mathrm{Space\,Form:}\\
g_{\ast}\mid\bm{x}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y},\sigma^{2}&\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1},\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast}))\\
&=\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast})^{\top}\Big(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1}\Big)^{-1}\Big(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}\bm{y}\Big),\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast})\right),\end{aligned}}

where
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}=(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{-1})^{-1}
(see Section
) and
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\in\real^{q\times q}
. Let us define
\bm{K}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}
and
\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast})
.
Then, we can derive the identity:

\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}(\bm{K}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top},

(7.23)

where we use the matrix identity
\bm{A}\bm{B}\bm{A}+\bm{A}=\bm{A}(\bm{B}\bm{A}+\bm{I})=(\bm{A}\bm{B}+\bm{I})\bm{A}
. Note that we do not distinguish the notations of
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}
and
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}
in their notations in
x
and
z
-spaces.
However, we do distinguish the notations of
\bm{X}
in
x
-space and
\boldsymbol{\Phi}
in
z
-space, respectively.

Next, by left-multiplying Equation (
) by
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}
and right-multiplying by
(\bm{K}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}
, we transform the predictive distribution into an expression involving only inner products about the inputs:

\boxed{\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Inner\,Product\,Form:}\\
g_{\ast}\mid\bm{x}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(&\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}(\bm{K}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{y},\\
&\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}-\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}(\bm{K}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}),\end{aligned}}

where we use the
matrix inversion lemma
such that
(\bm{A}+\bm{B}\bm{C})^{-1}=\bm{A}^{-1}-\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{B}(\bm{I}+\bm{C}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{B})^{-1}\bm{C}\bm{A}^{-1}
if
\bm{A}
is nonsingular
(
Lu 2021b
)
.
Now, all terms in the input space are expressed using the forms
\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast},\,\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}
, and
\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}
, which aligns with the requirements for applying the kernel trick.

We define kernel variables as follows:

\displaystyle K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{x}_{\ast})

\displaystyle\triangleq\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast};

(7.24a)

\displaystyle K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{X})

\displaystyle\triangleq\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top};

(7.24b)

\displaystyle K(\bm{X},\bm{X})

\displaystyle\triangleq\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}.

(7.24c)

Using these definitions, we can now express the predictive distribution in kernel form:

\boxed{\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Kernel\,Form:}\\
g_{\ast}\mid\bm{x}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(&K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{X})(K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{y},\\
&K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{x}_{\ast})-K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{X})(K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}K(\bm{X},\bm{x}_{\ast})).\end{aligned}}

(7.25)

Since
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}
is positive definite (see Section
), it can be factorized using the square root decomposition
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{1/2}
(Theorem
).
Therefore, it can be absorbed into the kernel function. For example, let
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\bm{x}_{\ast})=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\ast})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}^{1/2}
,
K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{x}_{\ast})
can be denoted by
K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{x}_{\ast})=\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\bm{x}_{\ast})^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\bm{x}_{\ast})
.
Similarly,
K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{X})
can be represented as
K(\bm{x}_{\ast},\bm{X})=\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_{\ast}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}^{\top}
, and
K(\bm{X},\bm{X})
as
K(\bm{X},\bm{X})=\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}^{\top}
.

7.7
Kernels in a Nutshell

A kernel, employing basis functions, implicitly transforms the input vector
\bm{x}\in\real^{p}
into a higher-dimensional feature space
\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})\in\real^{q}
.
This transformation changes the way we compute inner products: instead of computing
\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}^{\prime}
in the original
p
-dimensional space, we compute the kernel function
k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime})
in the
q
-dimensional space.
As a result, the kernel matrix
K(\bm{X},\bm{X})
—which contains all pairwise kernel evaluations between data points—has two important properties:

1.

K
must be symmetric, i.e.,
k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=k(\bm{x}^{\prime},\bm{x})
.

2.

K
must be positive semidefinite (PSD).

Proof
[of kernel matrix
K
is PSD]
Let
k_{ij}\triangleq k(\bm{x}_{i},\bm{x}_{j})
,
\forall\,i,j\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
. And let
\bm{t}\in\real^{n}
be any real vector, we have

\displaystyle\bm{t}^{\top}K\bm{t}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}t_{i}t_{j}k_{ij}=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}t_{i}t_{j}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{i})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{j})

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_{i}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{i})\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}t_{j}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{j})\right)=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_{i}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}_{i})\right\rVert^{2}\geq 0.

This completes the proof.

At first glance, it may seem that
k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})
can be any arbitrary function of
\bm{x}
and
\bm{x}^{\prime}
. However, the requirement that the kernel matrix be positive semidefinite restricts the form of valid kernel functions. Specifically, this constraint ensures that every valid kernel corresponds to an implicit inner product in some (possibly infinite-dimensional) feature space.

Remark 191
(Kernels that are usually used: some specific kernels).

The following are examples of widely used kernel functions:

1.

Linear kernel:
k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}^{\prime}
.

2.

Polynomial kernel:
k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=(\eta+\gamma\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}^{\prime})^{Q}
with
\gamma>0,\eta\geq 0
.

3.

Gaussian kernel:
k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=\exp(-\gamma\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{x}^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2})
.
We now show that the Gaussian kernel corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature mapping. Without loss of generality, let
\gamma=1
. Then,

\displaystyle k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\exp\{-\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{x}^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}\}=\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}\}\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\prime\top}\bm{x}^{\prime}\}\exp\{2\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}^{\prime}\}

\displaystyle\underset{\mathrm{expansion}}{\overset{\mathrm{Taylor}}{=}}\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}\}\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\prime\top}\bm{x}^{\prime}\}\exp\left\{\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{(2\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}^{\prime})^{i}}{i!}\right\}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}\}\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\prime\top}\bm{x}^{\prime}\}\sqrt{\frac{2^{i}}{i!}}\sqrt{\frac{2^{i}}{i!}}(\bm{x})^{i}\cdot(\bm{x}^{\prime})^{i}\right)

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left({\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}\}\sqrt{\frac{2^{i}}{i!}}(\bm{x})^{i}}\cdot{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\prime\top}\bm{x}^{\prime}\}\sqrt{\frac{2^{i}}{i!}}(\bm{x}^{\prime})^{i}}\right)

\displaystyle={\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime})},

where
\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\exp\{-\bm{x}^{\top}\bm{x}\}\sqrt{\frac{2^{i}}{i!}}(\bm{x})^{i}
.
This shows that the Gaussian kernel maps inputs from a finite-dimensional space to an infinite-dimensional space. A similar derivation holds for general
\gamma>0
.

4.

Other valid kernels: One major advantage of using kernel methods is that we do not need to explicitly define or compute the feature mapping
\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})
. Instead, we can work directly with the kernel matrix
K
, which encodes all necessary inner products in the feature space.

7.8
Gaussian Process from Zero-Mean Prior Model

We use Gaussian processes (GPs) to model distributions over functions. GPs are a natural extension of multivariate Gaussian distributions to infinite index sets—either countably infinite or continuous. Formally, we define a Gaussian process as follows:

Definition 192
(Gaussian process).

A Gaussian process is a collection of random variables, any finite number of which have a joint Gaussian distribution. The definition does not exclude Gaussian processes with finite index sets, which would be simply Gaussian distributions.

7.8.1
Noise-Free Observations

Following the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean prior introduced in Section
, we assume a zero-mean prior on the weight coefficient
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
.
For each input observation
\bm{x}
, we define the output as
g(\bm{x})\triangleq\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
The mean and covariance of the prior over function outputs are then given by:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g(\bm{x})]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]=0,

(7.26a)

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g(\bm{x})g(\bm{x}^{\prime})]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}]\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime}).

(7.26b)

In this formulation, the prior covariance matrix is typically specified manually in the Bayesian linear model. Alternatively, it can be defined using a kernel function:

k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime}).

(7.27)

Now, suppose we have the training input design matrix
\bm{X}
, training output vector
\bm{y}
, test input design matrix
\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}
, and test output vector
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
.
Using Equation (
), we can write the joint distribution of the training outputs
\bm{y}
and the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
as:

\left[\begin{matrix}\bm{y}\\
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\end{matrix}\right]\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{0},\left[\begin{matrix}K(\bm{X},\bm{X}),&K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\\
K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X}),&K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\end{matrix}\right]\right).

Given this joint distribution, we can apply standard properties of Gaussian distributions to derive the marginal distribution of the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
.

Lemma 193
(Marginal distribution of test outputs).

Continuing from Section
, we assume a zero-mean prior on the weight coefficient
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
, and define
g(\bm{x})\triangleq\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
. Given the observed training inputs
\bm{X}
, the corresponding training outputs
\bm{y}
, and the test inputs
\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}
, the marginal distribution of the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
is:

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X},\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})K(\bm{X},\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{y},

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})-K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})K(\bm{X},\bm{X})^{-1}K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})).

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\bm{x}
and
\bm{y}
be jointly Gaussian random vectors:

\left[\begin{matrix}\bm{x}\\
\bm{y}\end{matrix}\right]\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\left[\begin{matrix}\bm{u}_{x}\\
\bm{u}_{y}\end{matrix}\right],\left[\begin{matrix}\bm{A},&\bm{C}\\
\bm{C}^{\top},&\bm{B}\end{matrix}\right]\right).

Using standard properties of multivariate Gaussian distributions, the marginal distribution of
\bm{x}
and the conditional distribution of
\bm{x}
given
\bm{y}
are

\displaystyle\bm{x}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{u}_{x},\bm{A});

(7.28a)

\displaystyle\bm{x}\mid\bm{y}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{u}_{x}+\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\bm{u}_{y}),\bm{A}-\bm{C}\bm{B}^{-1}\bm{C}^{\top});

(7.28b)

\displaystyle\bm{y}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{u}_{y},\bm{B});

(7.28c)

\displaystyle\bm{y}\mid\bm{x}

\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{u}_{y}+\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}(\bm{x}-\bm{u}_{x}),\bm{B}-\bm{C}^{\top}\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{C}).

(7.28d)

Applying these identities to our setting, where the joint distribution of
\bm{y}
and
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
follows a multivariate Gaussian, we obtain:

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X},\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})K(\bm{X},\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{y},

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})-K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})K(\bm{X},\bm{X})^{-1}K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})),

which completes the proof.

The resulting marginal distribution of the test output
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
matches the kernel form of the Bayesian linear model with a zero-mean prior given in Equation (
). The only difference is the noise term and that now we are working with vector-valued outputs instead of scalar predictions (i.e.,
g_{\ast}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
).

Remark 194
(What does a distribution over functions mean?).

When given a kernel defined as
k(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime})
, which corresponds to a zero-mean prior on the weight coefficient
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
, we obtain the following prior distribution over the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
:

\begin{matrix}\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\end{matrix}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{0},\left[\begin{matrix}K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\end{matrix}\right]\right).

Therefore, we can sample functions from
p(\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})
, where each sample represents a possible function evaluated at the test inputs
\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}
. By sampling functions, we mean generating realizations of output values corresponding to the given input points (possibly finite or infinite number of samples) and its distribution. This is precisely what is meant by a distribution over functions.

When observed data
\bm{y}
and training inputs
\bm{X}
are available, we have the prior distribution over the training outputs
\bm{y}
and test ouputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
:

\left[\begin{matrix}\bm{y}\\
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\end{matrix}\right]\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{0},\left[\begin{matrix}K(\bm{X},\bm{X}),&K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\\
K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X}),&K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\end{matrix}\right]\right).

From this, we can derive the posterior distribution of the test outputs given the observed data:

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})K(\bm{X},\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{y},

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{x}_{\ast})-K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})K(\bm{X},\bm{X})^{-1}K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})).

Using this posterior, we can sample functions from the conditional distribution
p(\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y})
, which reflect our updated beliefs about the underlying function after observing the data.

7.8.2
Noisy Observations

Following again from Section
, we assume a zero-mean prior
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
. And we define
g(\bm{x})\triangleq\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\epsilon}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})}
. Then, the mean and covariance for the prior output are:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g(\bm{x})]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]+\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\boldsymbol{0},

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g(\bm{x})g(\bm{x})]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}]\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})+2\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]\mathbb{E}[\epsilon]+\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{2}]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\sigma^{2}},

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g(\bm{x})g(\bm{x}^{\prime})]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}]\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime})+\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{\prime}]+\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]\mathbb{E}[\epsilon]+\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\epsilon^{\prime}]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime}).

That is,

\mathrm{Cov}(y_{i},y_{j})=k(\bm{x}_{i},\bm{x}_{j})\delta_{ij},

where
\delta_{ij}
is a Kronecker delta, which is equal to 1 if and only if
i=j
and 0 otherwise.
Therefore, the joint distribution of the training outputs
\bm{y}
and the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
can be expressed as:

\left[\begin{matrix}\bm{y}\\
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\end{matrix}\right]\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{0},\left[\begin{matrix}K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\sigma^{2}\bm{I}},&K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\\
K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X}),&K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\end{matrix}\right]\right).

Using Gaussian identities, we can derive the marginal distribution of the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
.

Lemma 195
(Marginal distribution of test outputs).

Following from Section
, assume a zero-mean prior
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
and define
g(\bm{x})\triangleq\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\epsilon}
, where
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})}
. Given observed training inputs
\bm{X}
, the corresponding training outputs
\bm{y}
, and the test inputs
\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}
, the marginal distribution of the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
is

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})(K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\sigma^{2}\bm{I}})^{-1}\bm{y},

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})-K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})(K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\sigma^{2}\bm{I}})^{-1}K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})).

The marginal distribution of the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
aligns with the form of Equation (
), except that now the output is a vector (i.e.,
g_{\ast}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
).

7.8.3
Further Extension, Generalized Gaussian Process

Building upon the concept of the generalized least squares introduced in Section
,
we can now assign different noise variances to individual observations. Specifically, suppose the noise covariance matrix takes the form
\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
, where
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
is a diagonal matrix. This allows each observation to have its own noise level, which is particularly useful when dealing with heteroscedastic (non-constant variance) data.
Under this assumption, the marginal distribution of the test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
becomes:

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})(K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}})^{-1}\bm{y},

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})-K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})(K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\sigma^{2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}})^{-1}K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})).

It’s important to note that the noise covariance should not depend on the input matrix
\bm{X}
. Otherwise, the kernel trick—which allows us to work implicitly in high-dimensional feature spaces—would no longer be applicable.

(a)

Use half data set.

(b)

Use entire data set.

Figure 7.5:
Comparison of using half of the data versus the full data set.

(a)

Example 196
.

We consider a dataset where the input variable represents the area of a house, and the output variable corresponds to its monthly rent. To determine the optimal parameters of the Gaussian kernel, we use cross-validation (CV).

In Figure
, the red dots represent the training inputs, the blue line signifies the MAP estimate via a GP regressor, and the shaded region indicates the 95% confidence interval.

In Figure
, the GP regressor is trained using the full dataset.
In contrast, Figure
shows results when only data points corresponding to houses smaller than 100
m^{2}
are used for training.
As expected, the model performs poorly when extrapolating beyond 100
m^{2}
, indicating that the estimator trained on limited data cannot generalize well to unseen regions of the input space.

Figure
displays four random function realizations (shown by orange lines) drawn from the posterior distribution using the full dataset. These realizations help illustrate the concept of a distribution over functions, which is central to understanding Gaussian processes.

In Figure
, we investigate how increasing the size of the dataset by repetition affects the predictions. Specifically, we repeat the dataset once, twice, three times, and four times. The yellow line in each plot represents the prediction made by ordinary least squares (OLS) regression.
Interestingly, the OLS estimate remains unchanged regardless of how many times the data is repeated. To see why, suppose the original OLS estimate is given by:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}.

Now, if we repeat the data twice, the new estimate becomes:

\displaystyle\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}

\displaystyle=\left(\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}\end{bmatrix}\right)^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{X}\\
\bm{X}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{y}\\
\bm{y}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\cdot 2\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{y}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}.

This result confirms that repeating the data does not change the OLS estimate. Similarly, repeating the data three or four times also yields the same result. Therefore, OLS treats repeated observations as redundant information.

However, this is not the case for Gaussian process regression. When the dataset is repeated, the GP estimator becomes more confident in its predictions, reflected by a reduction in predictive variance. This behavior highlights a key advantage of Bayesian models: they update their beliefs as more data becomes available.

As discussed in Section
, Bayesian models incorporate prior knowledge about the parameters, making them particularly effective for regularizing regression problems when data is scarce. The amount of observed data plays a critical role in shaping the posterior distribution, as illustrated in Example
. This example clearly demonstrates the Bayesian foundation of Gaussian process modeling.

7.9
Limitations of Gaussian Process from Non-Zero-Mean Prior*

When the prior mean
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
is not zero (see Equation (
)), and the model assumes Gaussian noise
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I})
, the predictive distribution becomes:

\displaystyle g_{\ast}\mid\bm{x}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y},\sigma^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}\Big(

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}(\bm{K}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{y}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\Big(\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Phi}+\bm{I}\Big)^{-1}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}},

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}-\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}(\bm{K}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\ast}\Big),

where we use the fact that
(\bm{A}\bm{B})^{-1}=\bm{B}^{-1}\bm{A}^{-1}
if both
\bm{A}
and
\bm{B}
are nonsingular.

Following from Section
, suppose we now assume a non-zero-mean prior
\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0})
and define
g(\bm{x})\triangleq\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\epsilon
with
\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
.
Then, the mean and covariance of the output under this prior are given by:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g(\bm{x})]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}]={\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}},

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g(\bm{x})g(\bm{x}^{\prime})]

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\beta}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}]\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\bm{x}^{\prime}).

Based on this, the joint distribution of the training outputs
\bm{y}
and test outputs
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}
can be written as:

\left[\begin{matrix}\bm{y}\\
\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\end{matrix}\right]\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\left[\begin{matrix}{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\phi(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}}\\
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\phi(\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}}\end{matrix}\right],\left[\begin{matrix}K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+\sigma^{2}\bm{I},&K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\\
K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X}),&K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})\end{matrix}\right]\right).

By Gaussian identities, the marginal distribution of test outputs is

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast}\mid\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast}\bm{X},\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}{\displaystyle\phi(\boldsymbol{g}_{\ast})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}}+K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})(K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}(\bm{y}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\phi(\bm{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}}),

\displaystyle K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{x}_{\ast})-K(\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast},\bm{X})(K(\bm{X},\bm{X})+\sigma^{2}\bm{I})^{-1}K(\bm{X},\boldsymbol{X}_{\ast})).

Note that in this formulation, we cannot express the mean of
g(\bm{x})
explicitly in terms of kernel evaluations alone. That is, there is no equivalent expression in the
z
-dimensional feature space that allows us to apply the kernel trick directly.

This limitation restricts the flexibility of models using non-zero-mean priors, especially in high-dimensional or kernel-defined spaces where working explicitly with features is infeasible. As a result, zero-mean priors are often preferred in practice for their compatibility with kernel methods and computational efficiency.

Chapter 8
Generalized Linear Model (GLM)

I
In the Gauss-Markov model (Chapter
), for each input observation
(\bm{x},y)=(\bm{x}_{i},y_{i})
,
i=1,2,\ldots,n
with
\bm{x}\in\real^{p}
, we assume the linear relationship
y=f(\bm{x})\triangleq\bm{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
This relationship is known as the
linear predictor
. The linear predictor serves as the mean of a Gaussian distribution, meaning the output variable can be described as:

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid f,\bm{x}]=f(\bm{x})\qquad\implies\qquad{\textnormal{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(f(\bm{x}),\sigma^{2}).

(8.1)

The relationship in (
) is called the
functional relationship
between predictors and the response, indicating that
p(y\mid\bm{x},f)=p(y\mid f(\bm{x}))
, with
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\bm{x},f]=f(\bm{x})
, for some function
f\in\mathcal{F}
within a suitable set of possible functions.

The Gauss-Markov setup is well-suited for regression problems where the output values are continuous.
However, when dealing with discrete, binary, or categorical output values, the assumptions of the Gauss-Markov model become less practical and may not hold true.
For instance, consider scenarios where the output represents categories (e.g., types of animals), binary outcomes (e.g., success or failure), or positive values (e.g., individual income or monthly house rent). In these cases, modeling the output as a continuous Gaussian variable does not accurately reflect the nature of the data. The primary limitation arises from the fact that the Gaussian distribution assumes a continuous range of possible outcomes, which is inappropriate for discrete or binary outputs.

To address these limitations,
generalized linear models (GLMs)
offer a more flexible framework
(
Nelder and Wedderburn 1972
;
Dobson and Barnett 2018
;
Dunn et al. 2018
;
McCullagh 2019
;
Jackson 2024
)
. GLMs extend the concept of the linear predictor to accommodate various types of response variables by linking the expected value of the response to the linear predictor through a link function. This allows the model to handle different types of distributions from the exponential family, such as binomial for binary outcomes or Poisson for count data.

The relationship between the expected value of the response variable and the linear predictor is modeled via a link function, which can be chosen based on the nature of the response variable.
The variance of the response variable can depend on its mean, allowing for
heteroskedasticity
, which is common in non-Gaussian settings.
By incorporating these features, GLMs provide a robust approach for modeling a wide array of data types, including binary, count, and categorical data. This makes them invaluable tools in fields ranging from healthcare (for predicting disease outcomes) to economics (for analyzing consumer behavior), where the responses often do not follow a normal distribution
(
Powers et al. 2005
;
Egger and Staub 2016
)
.

Thus, while the Gauss-Markov linear model provides a solid foundation for understanding relationships in continuous data, GLMs extend this capability to encompass a broader spectrum of applications and data types, enhancing the model’s flexibility and applicability across diverse domains.

8.1
A Motivating Example: Logistic Regression

In this section, we will explore a specific case that is important in its own right and serves as an introduction to the fundamental concepts of GLMs, which we will discuss in greater detail later.
For a dataset in which the response variable
y
is binary, taking values 1 or 0 to represent success or failure (presence or absence),
the expectation of
y
must fall within the interval
[0,1]
:

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid f,\bm{x}]=f(\bm{x})\in[0,1].

(8.2)

Given this requirement, the Bernoulli distribution (Equation (
)) is the appropriate probability distribution, characterized solely by the probability
\pi
that
{\textnormal{y}}=1
.
We assume a particular distributional form for
y
(in this case Bernoulli), and would like to connect
\bm{x}
with a feature of this distribution, namely its expectation, by a function
f
:

p({\textnormal{y}}=1\mid f,\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid f,\bm{x}]=f(\bm{x}).

(8.3)

Thus, with the spaces
\mathcal{Y}
for
y
and
\mathcal{X}
for
\bm{x}
established, along with a probability distribution satisfying (
), our task is to identify a suitable set of possible functions,
\mathcal{F}
.

A straightforward approach might be to apply a linear function:

f(\bm{x})=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x},

(8.4)

However, such a function may not always be suitable because, for any given value of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, there could be values of
\bm{x}
that make
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}
fall outside the interval
[0,1]
. This issue can sometimes be avoided if
\bm{x}
takes on only certain ranges of values, but this cannot be guaranteed universally. To address this, GLMs introduce a
response function
applied to the linear predictor
\eta=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}
, ensuring it falls within the correct range. Specifically, we choose a function
h:\real\to[0,1]
, setting

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid f,\bm{x}]=f(\bm{x})=h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}).

(8.5)

Such a function in the logistic regression is called the
logistic function
(a.k.a., the
sigmoid function
):

h(\eta)\triangleq\text{Sigmoid}(\eta)=\frac{e^{\eta}}{1+e^{\eta}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}.

Its inverse
h^{-1}(\pi)=\ln\left(\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\right)
, where
\pi\in(0,1)
, is known as the
logit function
.

\paragrapharrow

Logit and probit.

Alternatively, one can use the cumulative distribution function (or any other cumulative distribution function) of the standard Gaussian distribution as the response function:

\displaystyle f(\bm{x})

\displaystyle=\Phi(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Phi^{-1}(f(\bm{x}))=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x},

(8.6)

where
\Phi(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{y}\mathcal{N}(u\mid 0,1)du=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{y}\exp(-\frac{u^{2}}{2})du
is the cumulative distribution function of a standard Gaussian distribution.
Its inverse,
\Phi^{-1}
, is known as the
probit function
.
While logit and probit estimators differ when estimated probabilities are very small or close to 1, indicating large sample sizes are needed for accurate inference, both functions yield similar results, especially around probability values of 0.5. For a comparison between the logit and probit functions, see Table
.

Logit
