8.3.2
The Natural/Canonical Link

There is a particular choice of the response (or equivalently, link) function that significantly simplifies the model formulation.
This is known as the
natural link
or
canonical link
.
Recall that we have the following two expressions for the mean:

\displaystyle\mu

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\phi,\rho]=b^{\prime}(\phi);

(8.21a)

\displaystyle\mu

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\bm{x},\boldsymbol{\beta}]=h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x})=h(\eta),

(8.21b)

where (
8.21a
) holds because
p(y\mid\phi,\rho)
follows an EDF distribution (see Section
), and (
8.21b
) holds by the definition of a GLM. Following (
), we have that

\phi=(b^{\prime})^{-1}(\mu)\triangleq\psi(\mu)=\psi\big(h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x})\big).

(8.22)

The
natural link
(or
canonical link
) is defined by choosing
h\triangleq b^{\prime}
, or equivalently
g\triangleq\psi
, resulting in the equality

\phi=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}=\eta=g(\mu)=\psi(\mu).

(8.23)

As a result, the general GLM form in Equation (
) becomes

\textbf{(Natural GLM)}:\qquad p(y\mid\bm{x},\boldsymbol{\beta})=\exp\left\{\frac{(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x})y-b(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x})}{a(\rho)}+c(y,\rho)\right\}.

(8.24)

It is evident that this choice greatly simplifies the model formulation. However, other link functions can still be used when necessary, particularly since the natural link may sometimes exhibit undesirable properties.
Using the canonical link function provides several statistical advantages, the most immediate being the simplification of parameter estimation procedures.

Exercise
\thetheo

Following Example
, derive the corresponding forms for each distribution using the natural link function.

Example 207
(Standard Gauss-Markov linear model).

The standard (Gauss-Markov) linear regression model assumes that the response variable
y
follows a Gaussian distribution. The probability density function of the Gaussian distribution in the form of an EDF is expressed as:

p(y\mid\mu,\sigma^{2})=\exp\left\{\frac{y\mu-\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^{2})\right\}

(8.25)

Example
shows that the standard terms are:

\displaystyle\phi

\displaystyle=\mu;\qquad

\displaystyle b(\phi)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\phi^{2};

\displaystyle a(\rho)

\displaystyle=\rho=\sigma^{2};\qquad

\displaystyle c(y,\rho)

\displaystyle=-\frac{y^{2}}{2\rho}-\frac{1}{2}\ln(2\pi\rho).

It can be seen that the natural parameter
\phi
and its expectation
\mu
have a linear relationship, i.e.,
\phi=\mu
. In the standard linear regression model, the link function is also a linear function, so the standard linear regression model uses the natural link function. At this point,
\phi=\mu=\eta=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}
, and the model prediction value
\widehat{y}
is:

\widehat{y}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\bm{x},\boldsymbol{\beta}]=\mu=\eta=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}.

(8.26)

However, the standard linear regression model may not be appropriate when it is unreasonable to assume normality of the data or when the range of the response variable is restricted. Additionally, in many practical situations, the assumption of homoskedasticity (constant variance) does not hold, further limiting the applicability of the standard linear regression model.

Once again, GLMs extend the standard linear regression framework by relaxing these assumptions. GLMs allow us to choose an appropriate EDF distribution based on the nature of the response variable
y
, and to use a suitable link function that maps the real-valued linear predictor
\eta
to the domain of
y
.

8.3.3
Grouped Data

We have seen that in a GLM, the expected value of the response variable depends only on the natural parameter
\phi
, which in turn is a function of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
and
\bm{x}
through the linear predictor
\eta=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}
.

In principle, the dispersion
\rho
could also vary with the input features
\bm{x}
or otherwise differ from data point to data point.
In practice, however, it is typically assumed to be constant across all observations: e.g., for Poisson, exponential, Bernoulli, binomial, where
a(\rho)=1
, or Gaussian, where
a(\rho)=\sigma^{2}
; see Example
.
A common exception occurs in grouped data settings, where multiple responses may be observed for the same input
\bm{x}
.

If
p(y_{r}\mid\phi,\rho)
is an EDF for each
r\in[1,2,\ldots,m]
, with natural parameter
\phi
, log normalizer
b
, dispersion
\rho
, and function
c
.
Then, the distribution of the average response from the group data,

y\triangleq\overline{y}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{r}y_{r},

(8.27)

has a probability distribution that is also an EDF. This EDF has the same natural parameter
\phi
and log normalizer
b
as the original distribution, but
\rho
is replaced by
\frac{\rho}{m}
and the function
c
may be different and a function of
m
.

Although grouping may not always be feasible when dealing with continuous predictors, it is often beneficial to group data whenever possible, because:

it simplifies the equations.

it improves speed of convergence and hence computation time.

some theory only holds when
m\gg 1
.

Example 208
(Grouped logistic regression).

Let
\mu\equiv\pi(\bm{x})\triangleq\text{sigmoid}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x})=\frac{e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}}}{1+e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}}}
, and suppose that there are several binary values for each
\bm{x}
.
That is, our data are structured as:

\left\{(\bm{x}_{i},\{y_{ir}\}_{r\in[1,2,\ldots,m_{i}]})\right\},\quad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\},

(8.28)

where
m_{i}
denotes the number of replicates in group
i
, indexed by
r
;
n
is the total number of groups, and
M=\sum_{i}m_{i}
is the overall sample size.

If our data only consists of the total counts
\widehat{y}_{i}\triangleq\sum_{r=1}^{m_{i}}y_{ir}
,
then although the individual
y_{ir}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(\pi(\bm{x}_{i}))
, i.e., Bernoulli-distributed with parameter
\pi(\bm{x}_{i})
, the sum
\widehat{y}_{i}
’s follows a binomial distribution with parameters
m_{i}
and
\pi(\bm{x}_{i})
(Exercise
), that is:

\widehat{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i}=\sum_{r}{\textnormal{y}}_{ir}\sim\mathrm{Binom}(m_{i},\pi(\bm{x}_{i})).

(8.29)

However, it is often more convenient to model proportions or averages instead of raw counts. Specifically, we define:

{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\triangleq\frac{1}{m_{i}}\bar{{\textnormal{y}}}_{i}=\frac{1}{m_{i}}\sum_{r}{\textnormal{y}}_{ir}\sim\frac{1}{m_{i}}\mathrm{Binom}(m_{i},\pi(\bm{x}_{i})),

(8.30)

where the distribution, corresponding to a binomial variable divided by the number of trials, is known as the scaled binomial distribution; see Exercise
.

The reason for preferring the scaled values
y_{i}
over the counts
\widehat{y}_{i}
is that the expectation retains a familiar form:

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid m,\bm{x}]=\frac{1}{m}m\pi(\bm{x})=\pi(\bm{x}),

(8.31)

meaning that the expectation function can still be modelled in the same way as for binary regression, using, for example, the logistic function. There is thus no need to include
m
at the level of the expectation, only in the distribution.
It turns out this scaled binomial distribution also belongs to an EDF distribution:

\displaystyle\Pr(y\mid m,\pi)

\displaystyle=\binom{m}{my}\pi^{my}(1-\pi)^{m-my}

\displaystyle=\exp\left\{my\ln\pi+(m-my)\ln(1-\pi)+\ln\binom{m}{my}\right\}

\displaystyle=\exp\left\{\frac{y\ln\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}+\ln(1-\pi)}{\frac{1}{m}}+c(y,\frac{1}{m})\right\},

which is an EDF with

\displaystyle\phi

\displaystyle\triangleq\ln\frac{\pi}{1-\pi},\qquad a(\rho)\triangleq\frac{1}{m},\qquad b(\phi)\triangleq\ln(1+e^{\phi}),\qquad c(y,\frac{1}{m})\triangleq\ln\binom{m}{my}.

Thus, the natural parameter
\phi
is the identical to that in the Bernoulli case (Example
), but
\rho=1
is replaced by
\rho=1/m
. The dispersion thus depends on
m
. This implies that if different groups
i
have different numbers of replicates
m_{i}
, the dispersion will vary accordingly across groups:
\rho_{i}=\frac{1}{m_{i}}
.

8.4
Model Estimation for GLMs

Suppose we are given a dataset that we would like to model using a GLM. After examining the data—possibly through exploratory data analysis—we have already selected a specific type of GLM that is most appropriate for the dataset (for instance, a Poisson GLM).
Our next goal is to estimate the model parameters—in particular, to find the value of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
that best fits the data. To do this, we can apply the method of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to obtain an estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. This estimate can then be used to make predictions:

y_{\text{new}}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\bm{x}_{\text{new}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}].

One major advantage of the GLM framework is that it allows us to derive a general solution for maximum likelihood estimation that applies to all types of GLMs. This means we don’t need to develop separate parameter estimation methods for each specific GLM—such as the Poisson GLM or the exponential GLM. Instead, we can formulate a single, unified solution for the entire class of GLMs, and the estimation procedures for individual models become special cases of this general approach.

In this section, we will begin by introducing the score function and its corresponding score equation for GLMs. We will then explore how to solve the score equation using the Fisher information matrix, often within an iterative algorithm. Additionally, we will examine the theoretical properties of both the score function and the Fisher information matrix.

\paragrapharrow

Likelihood function.
Consider the grouped data setup where we have predictors and data with possible replicates
\{(\bm{x}_{i},\{y_{ir}\}_{r\in[1,2,\ldots,m_{i}]})\},\ \forall\,{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}}
(see Section
). Recall that under a GLM, given predictors
\{\bm{x}_{i}\}_{i\in[1,2,\ldots,n]}
, each response
y_{ir_{i}}
is independent of the other
y_{ir_{j}}
, and of the values of all predictors
\bm{x}_{j}
with
j\neq i
.
Therefore, the joint probability of the data—that is, the likelihood under the EDF distribution (see (
))—is given by

\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=p(\{y_{ir}\}\mid\{\bm{x}_{i}\},\boldsymbol{\beta})=p(\{y_{ir}\}\mid\{\phi_{i}\},\rho)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{r=1}^{m_{i}}p(y_{ir}\mid\phi_{i},\rho),

(8.32)

where
p(y_{ir}\mid\phi_{i},\rho)=\exp\big(\frac{y_{ir}\phi_{i}-b(\phi_{i})}{\rho}+c(y_{ir},\rho)\big)
and (see Figure
)

\displaystyle\phi_{i}

\displaystyle=\psi(\mu_{i})=\psi\big(h(\eta_{i})\big)=\psi\big(h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i})\big),\qquad\psi\triangleq(b^{\prime})^{-1}.

\paragrapharrow

Log-likelihood function.
The log-likelihood function is thus given by

\displaystyle\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle\triangleq\ln\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\ln p(\{y_{ir}\}\mid\{\phi_{i}\},\rho)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{r=1}^{m_{i}}\left(\frac{y_{ir}\phi_{i}-b(\phi_{i})}{\rho}+c(y_{ir},\rho)\right)

(8.33)

\displaystyle\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_{i}\phi_{i}-b(\phi_{i})}{\rho/m_{i}}+\sum_{r}^{m_{i}}c(y_{ir},\rho)\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{i},

where we have defined

\displaystyle y_{i}

\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{1}{m_{i}}\sum_{r}y_{ir},\qquad\ell_{i}\triangleq\frac{y_{i}\phi_{i}-b(\phi_{i})}{\rho_{i}}+\sum_{r}c(y_{ir},\rho),\qquad a(\rho)\triangleq\rho_{i}\triangleq\frac{\rho}{m_{i}}.

Note again that in the non-grouping setting, we have
a(\rho)\equiv\rho
; while in the grouping setting, we have
a(\rho)\equiv\rho_{i}\triangleq\frac{\rho}{m_{i}}
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
; see Remark
.
That is, for each group
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, the dispersion parameter is
a(\rho)=\frac{\rho}{m_{i}}
; for each single data
(\bm{x}_{i},y_{ir})
with
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
and
r\in\{1,2,\ldots,m_{i}\}
, the dispersion parameter is
\rho
.

Note that, by definition, (
), and (
), we have

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}_{i}]=\mu_{i}=b^{\prime}(\phi_{i})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}_{i}]=\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i}).

(8.34)

\paragrapharrow

Score function and score equation.
In statistics, particularly within the context of linear models and GLMs, the
score function
refers to the gradient (i.e., derivative) of the log-likelihood function with respect to the model parameters. It is commonly used to find the maximum likelihood estimates (MLEs), which are the parameter values that maximize the likelihood of observing the given data.
The score function under (
) or (
) is then given by

(\textbf{Score function}):\qquad\begin{aligned} {\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})&=\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i}\frac{\partial\ell_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i}\frac{\partial\ell_{i}}{\partial\phi_{i}}\frac{\partial\phi_{i}}{\partial\mu_{i}}\frac{\partial\mu_{i}}{\partial\eta_{i}}\frac{\partial\eta_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}};\\
&=\sum_{i}\left(\frac{y_{i}-\mu_{i}}{\rho_{i}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\right)h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})\,\bm{x}_{i}\\
&=\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{i}m_{i}(y_{i}-\mu_{i})\,\frac{1}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\,h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})\,\bm{x}_{i}.\end{aligned}

(8.35)

where, since
\mu_{i}=b^{\prime}(\phi_{i})
,
\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})=b^{\prime\prime}(\phi_{i})
,
\mu_{i}=h(\eta_{i})
, and
\eta_{i}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}
, we use the facts:

\displaystyle\frac{\partial\ell_{i}}{\partial\phi_{i}}

\displaystyle=\frac{y_{i}-b^{\prime}(\phi_{i})}{\rho_{i}}=\frac{y_{i}-\mu_{i}}{\rho_{i}};\qquad

\displaystyle\frac{\partial\phi_{i}}{\partial\mu_{i}}

\displaystyle=1/\left(\frac{\partial\mu_{i}}{\partial\phi_{i}}\right)=\frac{1}{b^{\prime\prime}(\phi_{i})}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})};

(8.36a)

\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mu_{i}}{\partial\eta_{i}}

\displaystyle=h^{\prime}(\eta_{i});\qquad

\displaystyle\frac{\partial\eta_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\bm{x}_{i}.

(8.36b)

The maximum likelihood estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
must then satisfy the
score equation
(see Proposition
):

\textbf{(Score equation)}:\qquad{\mathbb{S}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}.

(8.37)

Remark 209
(Score equation under EDFs).

Note that the dispersion parameter
\rho
cancels from the score equation, which implies that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
does not depend on
\rho
.
This is observed in the Gauss-Markov case (Theorem
), where the MLE for the least squares solution does not depend on the variance parameter
\sigma^{2}
.
This is another important property of EDFs.

During the process of finding maximum likelihood estimates, we seek the values of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
that make the score function
S(\boldsymbol{\beta})
equal to zero because these points could be where the log-likelihood function reaches its maximum. However, to ensure that we have found a maximum rather than a minimum, it’s also necessary to check the second derivatives or use other methods such as the Fisher information matrix.

In the realm of GLMs, the score equations are typically obtained by setting the score function to zero and solving for the parameters
\boldsymbol{\beta}
. Often, these equations do not have closed-form solutions, necessitating the use of numerical methods like the Newton-Raphson method or iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) to find the MLEs; see Section
.

Furthermore, the score function plays a crucial role in assessing the asymptotic properties of estimators. For example, the expected value of the score function is zero, and its variance is related to the Fisher information matrix. These properties help in deriving the asymptotic distribution of the estimator, which is essential for constructing confidence intervals and hypothesis testing.

Example 210
(Estimation of GLMs under natural link).

For the natural link (Section
),
\phi_{i}=\eta_{i}
, so Equations (
8.36a
) and (
8.36b
) combine to give

\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}=\frac{\partial\phi_{i}}{\partial\mu_{i}}\frac{\partial\mu_{i}}{\partial\eta_{i}}=\frac{\partial\phi_{i}}{\partial\eta_{i}}=1.

As a result, the score function simplifies to

{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{i}m_{i}(y_{i}-\mu_{i})\bm{x}_{i}.

\paragrapharrow

Fisher information.

To solve the score equation, we will also need the second derivative of the log-likelihood. Its negative is called the
observed Fisher information
, defined as

{\mathbb{I}}_{\mathrm{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq-\frac{\partial^{2}\ell}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}}=-\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(8.38)

Note that, at the MLE,
{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is positive semidefinite by definition. Because it is a function of the data
\{y_{i}\}
,
{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}
has a probability distribution. In practice, the observed Fisher information is often approximated by the
Fisher information
(a.k.a., the
expected Fisher information
; see Section
):

{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\mathbb{E}\left[-\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right],

(8.39)

where the expectation is taken over the joint probability distribution of the data
p(\{y_{ir_{i}}\}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\{\bm{x}_{i}\})
.

Example 211
(Poisson GLM).

Suppose
m_{i}=1
with the Poisson GLM. We have
\rho=1
by Example
.
Let the Poisson parameter be
\lambda(\bm{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta})
for each data
(\bm{x}_{i},y_{i})
such that
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\mid\bm{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta}\sim\mathcal{P}(\lambda(\bm{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta}))

Natural link.

For the natural link such that
h(\eta)=b^{\prime}(\eta)=e^{\eta}
by Example
, we have that:
\lambda(\bm{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta})=\mu(\bm{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta})=h(\eta(\bm{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta}))=e^{\eta(\bm{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta})}=e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}}
.
By Example
, we have

{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sum_{i}(y_{i}-e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}})\,\bm{x}_{i}
;
using (
), the observed Fisher information is:

{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sum_{i}e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}}\,\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}.

Since
{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
does not depend on
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}
, the expected Fisher information coincides with the observed Fisher information
{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
.

Identity link.

Now consider the identity link, where
h(\eta)=\eta
. In this case:

\lambda(\bm{x},\boldsymbol{\beta})=\mu(\bm{x},\boldsymbol{\beta})=h(\eta(\bm{x},\boldsymbol{\beta}))=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x},\qquad\mathcal{V}(\mu)=b^{\prime\prime}\big((b^{\prime})^{-1}(\mu)\big)=\mu,\qquad h^{\prime}(\eta)=1.

By (
) and (
), the score function and the observed Fisher information become:

\displaystyle{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\mu_{i})\frac{1}{\mu_{i}}\bm{x}_{i}=\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i})\frac{1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}}\bm{x}_{i}=\sum_{i}\left(\frac{y_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}}-1\right)\bm{x}_{i};

\displaystyle{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{y_{i}}{(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i})^{2}}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}.

The expected Fisher information is:

\displaystyle{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i}\frac{{\textnormal{y}}_{i}}{(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i})^{2}}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\right]=\sum_{i}\frac{\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}_{i}]}{(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i})^{2}}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}.

Note that
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\neq{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
in this case.

8.4.1
Properties of Score Function and Fisher Information

Having introduced the score function
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
and the Fisher information
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
, we now explore some of their key statistical properties.
Define
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq\frac{\partial\ell_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, where
\ell_{i}
denotes the log-likelihood for data
i
with
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
. Then, the total score function can be written as:
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sum_{i}{\mathbb{S}}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
.

\paragrapharrow

Moments of
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
.
Since
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}_{i}]=\mu_{i}
by (
), the expectation of
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
can be computed from (
) as:

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbb{S}}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\sum_{i}\frac{\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}_{i}]-\mu_{i}}{\rho_{i}}\frac{1}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})\bm{x}_{i}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(8.40)

Using (
) again, we can calculate the variance of
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
as:

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbb{S}}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\sum_{i}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}\left[\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\bm{x}_{i}({\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\mu_{i})\right]

(8.41)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\sum_{i}\left(\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\bm{x}_{i}\right)\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\mu_{i}]\left(\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\right)=\sum_{i}\left(\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})^{2}}{\rho_{i}^{2}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})^{2}}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\right)\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}]

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})^{2}}{\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\bm{A}{\mathbf{X}},\bm{B}{\mathbf{Y}}]=\bm{A}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{Y}}]\bm{B}^{\top}
for any random matrices
{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{Y}}
and fixed matrices
\bm{A},\bm{B}
with appropriate dimensions, and the last equality follows from the fact that
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}_{i}]=\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})
by (
).

\paragrapharrow

Property of
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
.
Recall from the definition of the (expected) Fisher information
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\mathbb{E}\left[-\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right]
by (
).
Taking the derivative of
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
in (
) and applying the product rule for derivatives, we have:

\displaystyle\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{i}m_{i}\bm{x}_{i}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}(y_{i}-\mu_{i})\cdot\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}+(y_{i}-\mu_{i})\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left(\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\right)\right)

(8.42)

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{\bm{x}_{i}}{\rho_{i}}\left(-\frac{\partial\mu_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\cdot\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}+(y_{i}-\mu_{i})\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left(\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\right)\right).

Therefore, the expected Fisher information is

\displaystyle{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[-\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right]=\sum_{i}\frac{\bm{x}_{i}}{\rho_{i}}\left(\frac{\partial\mu_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\mu_{i}]\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left(\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\right)\right)

(8.43)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\sum_{i}\frac{\bm{x}_{i}}{\rho_{i}}\left(h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\right)=\sum_{i}\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})^{2}}{\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\mu_{i}]=0
and

\frac{\partial\mu_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\frac{\partial\mu_{i}}{\partial\eta_{i}}\frac{\partial\eta_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}=h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}
.
Noting the expression of (
), we conclude that:

{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})],

(8.44)

which matches the definition of the Fisher information given previously in Equation (
).

Example 212
(Score function and Fisher information under natural link).

Following Example
, for the natural link, we have that
\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}=\frac{\partial\phi_{i}}{\partial\eta_{i}}=1
.
Therefore,

{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{i}m_{i}(y_{i}-\mu_{i})\bm{x}_{i}=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{\rho_{i}}\big(y_{i}-h(\eta_{i})\big)\bm{x}_{i}.

(8.45)

Let
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}\triangleq\frac{1}{\rho_{i}}\big(y_{i}-h(\eta_{i})\big)\bm{x}_{i}
such that
{\mathbb{S}}=\sum_{i}{\mathbb{S}}_{i}
. We then have

\displaystyle{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=-\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}=-\sum_{i}\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}=-\sum_{i}\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\partial\eta_{i}}\frac{\partial\eta_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i}\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\rho_{i}}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top};

(8.46)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\sum_{i}\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\rho_{i}}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}.

(8.47)

Thus, for the natural link case, we observe that
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})={\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
.
This extends the results in the Poisson GLM with natural link in Example
.

8.4.2
Iterative Solution of Score Equation

So far, we have examined how to formulate the score equation for obtaining maximum likelihood estimates. We have also established several important properties of both the score equation and Fisher information matrix.
Now, we turn our attention to the practical challenge of solving the score equation.
In general, it is not possible to find an exact closed-form solution to the score equation, except in special cases—such as in the Gauss-Markov linear model discussed in Chapter
. Therefore, we must rely on numerical methods that can be implemented using computational tools.

Generally, we have two primary options: directly optimizing the log-likelihood function
\ell
, or solving the score equation. Numerous algorithms are available for these tasks. In this context, our focus will be on one particular method:

iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS)
, which is also known as
iterative weighted least squares (IWLS)
.

Matrix Notations

To derive the iterative method for calculating the maximum likelihood estimate of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
using the score equation, it is helpful to express the problem using matrix notation. Below are the key definitions:

Let
{\mathbf{y}}\in\real^{n}
be the random vector whose components are
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}
, the observed response values.

Let
\bm{X}=[x_{ij}]\in\real^{n\times p}
be the data matrix. To abuse the notation, we let each row of
\bm{X}
be
\bm{x}_{i}
for convenience; note that the
i
-th row of a matrix is denoted as
\bm{x}^{(i)}
otherwise in this book.

Let
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\real^{n}
be the vector whose components are
\mu_{i}=h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i})
, so that
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{y}}]
.

Let
\bm{D}=[d_{ij}]\in\real^{n\times n}
be the diagonal matrix with entries
d_{ii}=h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})
.

Let
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=[\omega_{ij}]\in\real^{n\times n}
be the covariance matrix of
{\mathbf{y}}
, with entries:

\omega_{ij}=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i},{\textnormal{y}}_{j}]=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}]\delta_{ij}=\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})\delta_{ij}.

That is,

\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{1}],\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{2}],\ldots,\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{n}])=\mathrm{diag}(\rho_{1}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{1}),\rho_{2}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{2}),\ldots,\rho_{n}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{n})).

Let
\bm{G}=[g_{ij}]\in\real^{n\times n}
be the diagonal matrix with components
g_{ii}=m_{i}
, known as the
grouping matrix
.

\paragrapharrow

Score function and Fisher information.
Recall that the score function (
) and Fisher information (
) are defined as

{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sum_{i}\left(\frac{y_{i}-\mu_{i}}{\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\right)h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})\bm{x}_{i}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sum_{i}\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})^{2}}{\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}.

In terms of the matrix notation, these become

\displaystyle{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{D}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{D}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{D}\bm{X}.

(8.48)

\paragrapharrow

Natural link.
Note that for the natural link case (see Section
, Examples
,
and
),
it holds that
\frac{\partial\phi_{i}}{\partial\eta_{i}}=\frac{h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}=1
.
Thus, with the definition of
\rho_{i}=\rho/m_{i}
, we have:

h^{\prime}(\eta_{i})=\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})=\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}]}{\rho_{i}}=m_{i}\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}]}{\rho},\quad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}

Therefore, it follows that

\bm{D}=\frac{1}{\rho}\bm{G}\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\frac{1}{\rho}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{G},

whence we have

{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\frac{1}{\rho}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{G}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{G}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bm{G}\bm{X}.

(8.49)

Iterative Solution of Score Equation

\paragrapharrow

Newton-Raphson and Fisher scoring methods.
We start by recalling the Newton-Raphson method, which is commonly used to find the root (zero) of a function.
In our case, we aim to solve the score equation:

{\mathbb{S}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}.

(8.50)

Generally, for an iterative process for solving the score equation, we generate a series of parameters that converge to some point.
Denoting
t=1,2,\ldots
as the iteration number, iterative methods generate a sequence of vectors:

\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(1)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(2)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(T)},

where each new estimate is based on the previous one.
We then focus on the iteration
t
.
By the linear approximation theorem (Theorem
), we can approximate
{\mathbb{S}}
linearly at some point
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}
:

{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+\bm{d}^{(t)})={\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})+\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\bm{d}^{(t)}+\mathcal{O}\big(\big\lVert\bm{d}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\big).

Since we want
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+\bm{d}^{(t)})=\boldsymbol{0}
, ignoring the third term of the above equality, we can obtain
\bm{d}^{(t)}
approximately by:

\displaystyle\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}\bm{d}^{(t)}=-{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\iff\quad

(8.51)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\bm{d}^{(t)}={\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\iff\quad\bm{d}^{(t)}=\big({\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\big)^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}),

where we use the fact that
-\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})
by (
).
This gives us the updated estimate for the next iteration:

\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+\bm{d}^{(t)}=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+\big({\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\big)^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}).

(8.52)

Algorithm 25

Newton-Raphson or Fisher Scoring Methods for Solving Score Equation

1:

Score function
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
;

2:

Input:
Initialize
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(1)}
;

3:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

4:

Find a direction
\bm{d}^{(t)}
by (
) or (
);

5:

\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+\bm{d}^{(t)}
;

6:

end

for

7:

Return:
final
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}
;

Because computing
{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}
and its inverse can be difficult in practice, we often replace it with the expected Fisher information (
).
This modified approach is known the
Fisher scoring method
, where we compute
\bm{d}^{(t)}
by:

\bm{d}^{(t)}=\big({\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\big)^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\qquad\implies\qquad\bm{d}^{(t)}\approx\big({\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\big)^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}).

(8.53)

The complete procedure for this method is summarized in Algorithm
.

\paragrapharrow

Iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS).
We will now use (
) to derive the
iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS)
method in matrix form.
From (
) and the iterative update rule
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+\bm{d}^{(t)}
, we have that

{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\bm{d}^{(t)}={\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\qquad\iff\qquad{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)}={\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}).

(8.54)

Using the previously defined matrix notations and defining:

\bm{W}\triangleq\bm{D}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{D}

(8.55)

(
\bm{D},\boldsymbol{\Omega}
, and
\bm{W}
are all diagonal matrices), by (
8.48
), we can express the score function and Fisher information as follows:

\displaystyle{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{D}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu})=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{D}^{-1}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu});

(8.56)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

\displaystyle=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{D}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}\bm{D}\bm{X}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{X}.

(8.57)

Let
{\mathbb{S}}^{(t)}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})
,
{\mathbb{I}}^{(t)}\triangleq{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)})
,
\bm{D}^{(t)}=\mathrm{diag}(h^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)\top}\bm{x}_{1}),h^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)\top}\bm{x}_{2}),\ldots,h^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)\top}\bm{x}_{n}))
, and
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}=[h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)\top}\bm{x}_{1}),h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)\top}\bm{x}_{2}),\ldots,h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)\top}\bm{x}_{n})]^{\top}
. Then, (
) can be denoted as

\displaystyle(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}\bm{X})\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle={\mathbb{I}}^{(t)}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+{\mathbb{S}}^{(t)}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}\bm{D}^{{(t)}-1}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)})

(8.58)

\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}\widetilde{\bm{y}}^{(t)}

(8.59)

\displaystyle\implies\qquad\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)}=\big(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}\bm{X}\big)^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}\widetilde{\bm{y}}^{(t)},

(8.60)

where
\widetilde{\bm{y}}^{(t)}\triangleq\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}+\bm{D}^{{(t)}-1}(\bm{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)})
.

Thus, to find a solution for
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\boldsymbol{0}
, we can start from an arbitrary point
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(1)}
and iteratively apply (
8.60
) until a convergence criterion is met; e.g., the criterion defined by (
).
This sequence of iterated operations is called
iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS)
or
iterative weighted least squares (IWLS)
since each iteration is the solution to the following weighted least squares problem: minimize the quantity
\ell_{t}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
with respect to
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, where

\ell_{t}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq(\widetilde{\bm{y}}^{(t)}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}(\widetilde{\bm{y}}^{(t)}-\bm{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})

(8.61)

and
\bm{W}^{(t)}
is known as the
weight matrix
; see Section
.
The full procedure of IRLS is formulated in Algorithm
.

Algorithm 26

IRLS for Solving Score Equation

1:

Score function
{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
;

2:

Input:
Initialize
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(1)}
;

3:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

4:

Compute weight matrix
\bm{W}^{(t)}
and
\widetilde{\bm{y}}^{(t)}
;

5:

\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\big(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}\bm{X}\big)^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{W}^{(t)}\widetilde{\bm{y}}^{(t)}
;

6:

end

for

7:

Return:
final
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}
;

8.4.3
Estimation of Dispersion Parameter

Since the dispersion parameter
\rho
cancels out in the score equation
{\mathbb{S}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}
(Remark
), it is not necessary to estimate
\rho
in order to estimate the coefficients
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
However, the variance of the estimator
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]
does depend on
\rho
; for example, the variance of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
in the Gauss-Markov linear model depends on the variance
\sigma^{2}
, as shown in Theorem
.

Therefore, if needed or of interest, we can estimate
\rho
using the following formula:

\widehat{\rho}=\frac{1}{n-p}\sum_{i}m_{i}\frac{(y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})^{2}}{\mathcal{V}(\widehat{\mu}_{i})},

(8.62)

where
p
is the number of parameters of the model, i.e., the number of columns in
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and
\widehat{\mu}_{i}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}
.
This estimator is motivated by the fact that:

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}]=\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\mu_{i})^{2}]=\rho_{i}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})=\frac{\rho}{m_{i}}\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})\quad\implies\quad\rho=\mathbb{E}\left[m_{i}\frac{({\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\mu_{i})^{2}}{\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})}\right].

(8.63)

Hence, once we have obtained an estimate
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we can use its value and (
) to estimate
\widehat{\rho}
.
The division by
n-p
ensures unbiased estimation, similar to the reasoning in Theorem
.

Example 213
.

For the Gaussian distribution, when
{\textnormal{y}}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
with
m_{i}=1
, we have
\mathcal{V}(\mu_{i})=1
and thus,

\widehat{\rho}=\frac{1}{n-p}\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})^{2}=S^{2}.

(8.64)

This coincides with the well-known unbiased estimator of the error variance in the Gauss-Markov linear model; see Theorem
.

8.4.4
Prediction

Assume we have fitted a GLM, resulting in an estimated parameter vector
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.
The predicted value
\widehat{\bm{y}}\equiv\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
of the observed response
\bm{y}
is then given by:

\widehat{\bm{y}}=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{y}}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\bm{X}]=h(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\eta}})=h(\bm{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\equiv\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}.

(8.65)

The linear predictor
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}
is a vector where each element represents the predicted linear combination of the predictors for each observation.

When new data become available, such as a new predictor vector
\bm{x}_{\text{new}}
, the GLM can be used to make predictions for these new observations as well. The first step is to compute the corresponding linear predictor:

\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}.

Once
\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}}
is obtained, the predicted response for
\bm{x}_{\text{new}}
is found by using the response function
h(\cdot)
:

\widehat{y}_{\text{new}}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\bm{x}_{\text{new}}]=h(\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}})=h(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}).

(8.66)

Combining (
) and (
) shows that the variance of this prediction is

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}_{\text{new}}\mid\bm{x}_{\text{new}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\widehat{\rho}\mathcal{V}(h(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\text{new}})).

(8.67)

8.5
Asymptotics for GLMs*

In the previous section, we have seen how to fit a GLM to a dataset and estimate its parameters
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. In this section, we will briefly explore the asymptotic properties of GLMs, learn how to make predictions, compute confidence intervals and confidence regions, the results of which can be used in the hypothesis testing procedures (see Section
).

8.5.1
Asymptotic Properties of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

We have discussed large-sample properties of the OLS estimator in Sections
. For now, we briefly discuss the asymptotic properties of the
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
estimator in the context of GLMs
(
Fahrmeir and Kaufmann 1985
)
.
In this group setup (Section
), the term
asymptotic
refers to the scenario where
M=\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}\to\infty
. This can occur if
n\to\infty
, or if each
m_{i}\to\infty
, or through some combination of both.

Let
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
denote the true value of
\boldsymbol{\beta}
.
In what follows, we assume that
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is a consistent estimator of
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
, i.e.,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
converges in probability to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
, meaning that
\Pr\big(\big\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}\big\rVert_{2}\geq\epsilon\big)\to 0
as
n\to\infty
for any
\epsilon>0
(Definition
).
Recall that this is denoted by
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
; see Definition
. We will also abuse this notation to mean
“tends to asymptotically” for expectations
, i.e., if we write
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]\overset{a}{=}x
, that means
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}x
.

Given the assumption of consistency,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
will be close to
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
in large samples. Thus, we can expand the score function

{\mathbb{S}}
around it by Theorem
:

\displaystyle{\mathbb{S}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})+\frac{\partial{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})={\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})-{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})

(8.68)

\displaystyle\qquad\implies\qquad\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}).

\paragrapharrow

Fisher scoring method.
Previously, we stated that we often use the Fisher information in place of the observed Fisher information (known as the Fisher scoring method; see Algorithm
).
In asymptotic analyses, this substitution is generally acceptable. We can heuristically justify this by considering the behavior of the observed Fisher information matrix. Specifically, for any
\boldsymbol{\beta}
, we have:

\frac{1}{n}{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=-\frac{1}{n}\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial\ell_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\to-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\ell_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\right]={\mathbb{I}}_{1}(\boldsymbol{\beta}),

(8.69)

where
{\mathbb{I}}_{1}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
is the expected Fisher information for a single observation, and the convergence follows from the law of large numbers as
n\to\infty
(Definition
). It can be shown that
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=n{\mathbb{I}}_{1}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
, thus justifying use of
{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
in the asymptotic arguments that follow.

\paragrapharrow

Mean of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
From (
), we have:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{obs}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}).

Because convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution, this in turn implies that

\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}]\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})]=\boldsymbol{0}.

In other words, the estimator
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is asymptotically unbiased.

\paragrapharrow

Variance of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Since
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}]\overset{a}{=}\boldsymbol{0}
, we can compute its covariance as follows:

\displaystyle\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}]

\displaystyle\overset{a}{=}\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{\top}]\overset{a}{=}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}){\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{\top}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-\top}]

\displaystyle={\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}\mathbb{E}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}){\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{\top}]{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-\top}={\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})]{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-\top}

\displaystyle={\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1},

where we use the fact that
{\mathbb{I}}
is symmetric and that
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})]
; see (
).
Therefore, this concludes that

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}]\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}.

(8.70)

\paragrapharrow

Asymptotic normality.
The following is a sketch of the argument of asymptotic normality for
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
, i.e.,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
converges asymptotically to a Gaussian distribution. We begin with the expression:

{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\sum_{i}{\mathbb{S}}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})

(8.71)

where
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
is defined as
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\triangleq\frac{\partial\ell_{i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. This is a sum of independent random variables with zero mean and finite variance. As the number of terms in the sum tends to infinity, then
under a certain condition, the distribution of the sum converges in distribution to a normal distribution. Since
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})]={\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
, we have:

{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\overset{a}{\sim}\mathcal{N}\big(\boldsymbol{0},{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\big).

(8.72)

Hence,

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})\overset{a}{\sim}\mathcal{N}\big(\boldsymbol{0},{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}){\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-\top}\big).

(8.73)

Using the symmetric of
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}
is symmetric and the fact that convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution, we obtain:

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\overset{a}{\sim}\mathcal{N}\big(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}\big).

(8.74)

This result further implies that:

(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{\top}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})\overset{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{(p)},

(8.75)

where
p
denotes the number of parameters in the model (Remark
).

More formally, we state the following theorem on the asymptotic normality of the MLE in GLMs without proof. A detailed proof can be found, for example, in
Sen et al. 2010
.

{theoremHigh}
[Asymptotic normality of MLE in GLM
(
Sen et al. 2010
)
]
Assume that

1.

\boldsymbol{\beta}\in{\mathbb{B}}
for
{\mathbb{B}}
an open convex subset of
p
.

2.

The
p\times p
matrix
\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X}
is of full rank for all
n
.

3.

The information diverges, i.e.
\lambda_{\min}\left({\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\right)\to\infty
as
n\to\infty
for
\lambda_{\min}(\cdot)
the smallest eigenvalue.

4.

Given any parameter
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}
it holds that

\sup_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in{\mathbb{N}}_{\delta}(\boldsymbol{\beta})}\left\lVert{\mathbb{I}}_{n}^{-1/2}(\boldsymbol{\beta}){\mathbb{I}}_{n}^{1/2}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})-\bm{I}_{p}\right\rVert_{2}\to 0,

\forall\ \delta>0
, where
{\mathbb{N}}_{\delta}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\real^{p}\mid(\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\boldsymbol{\beta})^{\top}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta})(\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\leq\delta\}
.

Then, as
n\to\infty
, provided it exists, the MLE
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
of
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}
is unique and satisfies

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{N}\big(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0},{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})^{-1}\big).

The condition (iv) in the theorem requires that the (root) information matrix converge uniformly on compact ellipsoids centered at the true parameter value.
Just as Gauss-Markov linear models, on the other hand, this theorem can be used to perform hypothesis tests (see Section
) or confidence interval analysis (see below).

and thus we can replace
{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0})
by

in above results.

8.5.2
Prediction and Confidence Intervals

Assume a GLM has been fitted, yielding
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. If we are given a new predictor vector
\bm{x}_{\text{new}}
, we can compute

\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}

(8.76)

and use this to predict the expected response as:

\widehat{y}_{\text{new}}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\bm{x}_{\text{new}}]=h(\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}})=h(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}).

(8.77)

Next, we aim to construct confidence intervals for
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}_{\text{new}}]
. To do so, recall from Equation (
) and Exercise
that:

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\overset{a}{=}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{-1}.

(8.78)

It follows that:

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}}]=\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\bm{x}_{\text{new}}\overset{a}{=}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{-1}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}.

(8.79)

Thus, an approximate
(1-\alpha)
confidence interval for
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid\boldsymbol{\beta},\bm{x}_{\text{new}}]
is given by

\text{CI}=\left[h\left(\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}}-z_{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\sqrt{\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{-1}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}}\right),\;h\left(\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}}+z_{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\sqrt{\bm{x}_{\text{new}}^{\top}{\mathbb{I}}_{n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{-1}\bm{x}_{\text{new}}}\right)\right],

where
z_{\frac{\alpha}{2}}
represents the critical value from the standard normal distribution.
Note that in general, this is not symmetric about
h(\widehat{\eta}_{\text{new}})
due to the nonlinearity of the link function
h(\cdot)
.

8.6
Model Evaluation for GLMs

We introduced model evaluation and model selection methods for (Gauss-Markov) linear models in Chapter
. For GLMs, additional measures, methods, or variations can be applied.

8.6.1
Deviance in GLMs

Suppose we have fitted a GLM. We would like to find a measure for
goodness of fit (GOF)
, or, to put it another way, a measure for the
discrepancy
between the data
\bm{y}\in\real^{n}
and the fit
\widehat{\bm{y}}\equiv\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=[\widehat{\mu}_{1},\widehat{\mu}_{2},\ldots,\widehat{\mu}_{n}^{\top}]\in\real^{n}
, where
\widehat{\mu}_{i}=h(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i})
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
.
Note that in GLMs, the prediction
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is equal to the estimated mean
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
.
To define such a goodness-of-fit measure, we must first understand how well any GLM can potentially fit the data.

In GLMs, we define the difference in likelihoods between the saturated model and the fitted model (defined in Section
) as the
deviance statistic
, commonly denoted as
\mathrm{D}
.
More precisely, the deviance is a special case of the likelihood ratio statistic that compares the goodness of fit of the saturated model and the fitted model.

The saturated model perfectly fits the data, so its log-likelihood is theoretically the maximum possible, representing the best possible fit. Therefore, it serves as a “reference” against which the fit of our trained model can be compared. The closer the log-likelihood of the trained model is to that of the saturated model, the better the model fits the data.

Recall the general form of the EDF probability function in GLM:

p(y_{i}\mid\phi_{i},\rho)=\exp\left\{\frac{\phi_{i}y_{i}-b(\phi_{i})}{a(\rho)}+c(y_{i},\rho)\right\}

(8.80)

The natural parameter
\phi_{i}
can be expressed as a function of the expectation
\mu_{i}
. Therefore, for the fitted model, the natural parameter
\phi_{i}
can be written as
\phi_{i}(\widehat{\mu}_{i})
, and the log-likelihood function of the fitted model can be written as:

\ln\mathcal{L}_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{y_{i}\phi(\widehat{\mu}_{i})-b(\phi(\widehat{\mu}_{i}))}{a(\rho)}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(y_{i},\rho)

(8.81)

Thus, we have expressed the log-likelihood function of the fitted model as a function of
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
. Similarly, for the saturated model, since the model perfectly fits the data, its prediction is exactly equal to the observed value of the sample, i.e.,
\widehat{y}_{i}=y_{i}
. In other words, for the saturated model,
\widehat{y}_{i}=\widehat{\mu}_{i}=y_{i}
. Therefore, the log-likelihood function of the saturated model is:

\ln\mathcal{L}_{f}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{y_{i}\phi(y_{i})-b(\phi(y_{i}))}{a(\rho)}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(y_{i},\rho)

(8.82)

Note that in GLMs, the dispersion parameter
\rho
is independent of the model’s expectation
\mu
.
Because the dispersion parameter
\rho
cancels out in the score equation
{\mathbb{S}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}
(Remark
), it does not vary across observations and remains constant whether we are dealing with the saturated or the fitted model.

Now substitute these two quantities into the definition of the deviance statistic given in (
). The terms
\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(y_{i},\rho)
cancel out from both log-likelihoods:

\mathrm{D}=\frac{2}{a(\rho)}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[y_{i}\{\phi(y_{i})-\phi(\widehat{\mu}_{i})\}-b\{\phi(y_{i})\}+b\{\phi(\widehat{\mu}_{i})\}]

(8.83)

Note that the deviance statistic is defined based on the entire set of observed data. The contribution of a single observation to the overall deviance is often referred to as the
unit deviance
, denoted by
d_{i}(y_{i},\widehat{\mu}_{i})
. The total deviance for the full dataset is simply the sum of all individual unit deviances:
\mathrm{D}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}(y_{i},\widehat{\mu}_{i})
.

The deviance statistic is a special case of the log-likelihood ratio statistic, comparing the fit of the fitted model (the model we trained) and the saturated model. The saturated model achieves a perfect fit to the data, so its log-likelihood represents the theoretical maximum for the given observations.

Therefore, the deviance can serve as a measure of how well our model fits the data. However, since it is derived from the likelihood ratio framework, the deviance inherits certain statistical properties—most notably, its asymptotic distribution follows a Chi-squared distribution. Like other likelihood ratio statistics, the deviance alone cannot directly determine whether a model is “good” or “bad”; instead, hypothesis testing methods are required to make such judgments. For more information, see Section
.

Example 214
(Deviance and squared error in Gaussian GLM (Gauss-Markov model)).

In the case of the natural link function for the Gauss-Markov linear regression model, we have:
\phi=\eta=\mu
,
b(\phi)=\mu^{2}/2
,
a(\rho)=\sigma^{2}
. Therefore, the deviance is:

\displaystyle\mathrm{D}\cdot a(\rho)

\displaystyle=2\sum_{i=1}^{n}[y_{i}\{y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i}\}-y_{i}^{2}/2+\widehat{\mu}_{i}^{2}/2]=2\sum_{i=1}^{n}[y_{i}^{2}/2-y_{i}\widehat{\mu}_{i}+\widehat{\mu}_{i}^{2}/2]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})^{2}.

(8.84)

Once again, this result shows that, for the Gauss-Markov linear model, the deviance is equivalent to the sum of squared errors, as also stated in Equation (
). In fact, the concept of deviance can be seen as a generalization of the least squares criterion (or squared loss) used in classical linear regression, extended to the broader class of GLMs; see Table
for more examples.

Table 8.5:
Deviance for common types of GLMs (with non-grouped data)

Distribution

Deviance

Gaussian

\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})^{2}

Poisson

2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{y_{i}\ln(y_{i}/\widehat{\mu}_{i})-(y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})\}

Bernoulli

-2\big(\sum_{i:y_{i}=0}\ln(1-\widehat{\mu}_{i})+\sum_{i:y_{i}=1}\ln(\widehat{\mu}_{i})\big)

Gamma

2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{-\ln(y_{i}/\widehat{\mu}_{i})+(y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})/\widehat{\mu}_{i}\}

Inverse-Gaussian

\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{(y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})^{2}/(\widehat{\mu}_{i}^{2}y_{i})\}

8.6.2
Deviance-Based
R^{2}

Both
R^{2}
and
\overline{R}^{2}
(i.e., the adjusted
R^{2}
) are originally defined in the context of Gauss-Markov linear models and are not directly applicable to GLMs; see Section
.
To address this limitation, many researchers have proposed alternative versions of
R^{2}
suitable for evaluating the fit of GLM models. In this section, we introduce one such version based on the concept of deviance.

We know that the deviance statistic generalizes the idea of the residual sum of squares (RSS) in classical linear regression. Therefore, we can define an analogous version of
R^{2}
using deviance.
Let
\mathcal{L}_{0}
denote the likelihood of the null model (the model with only a constant
1
covariate, the intercept parameter), and define the deviance of the null model as the null deviance, denoted by
\mathrm{D}_{0}
:

\mathrm{D}_{0}=2\rho(\ln\mathcal{L}_{f}-\ln\mathcal{L}_{0}).

(8.85)

Similarly, let
\mathrm{D}
denote the deviance statistic of the fitted model.
The fitted model improves upon the null model by including predictor variables (corresponding to the columns of the design matrix
\bm{X}\in\real^{n\times p}
), resulting in a smaller deviance.
Recall the
R^{2}
measure (Definition
) is defined as

R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-\widehat{y}_{i})^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-\overline{y})^{2}}=1-\frac{\left\lVert\bm{y}-\widehat{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{\left\lVert\bm{y}-\overline{y}\bm{1}_{n}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}=1-\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}},

To extend this definition to GLMs, we can replace
\mathrm{RSS}
with
\mathrm{D}
and
\mathrm{TSS}
with
\mathrm{D}_{0}
to obtain a deviance-based version of
R^{2}
:

R_{D}^{2}=1-\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{D}_{0}}\in[0,1].

(8.86)

This higher the better the fitting.
This measure provides a way to assess how much better the fitted model performs compared to the null model, similar to how
R^{2}
compares the fitted model to the baseline mean model in linear regression.

8.6.3
Pearson Chi-Squared Statistic

Another commonly used goodness of fit statistic in GLMs is the
generalized Pearson Chi-squared statistic
or simply
Pearson Chi-squared statistic
.
It is defined as:

\chi^{2}_{P}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})^{2}}{a(\rho)\mathcal{V}(\widehat{\mu}_{i})},

(8.87)

where
a(\rho)\mathcal{V}(\widehat{\mu}_{i})
represents the variance of the model; see (
).
Similar to the deviance statistic, some sources omit the dispersion function
a(\rho)
and directly define it as follows:

\chi^{2}_{P_{s}}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})^{2}}{\mathcal{V}(\widehat{\mu}_{i})}.

(8.88)

However, this simplified form is not always accurate and can lead to confusion.
The term
a(\rho)
should only be omitted when
a(\rho)=1
. Some references refer to (
) as the
Pearson Chi-squared statistic
and call (
) the
scaled Pearson Chi-squared statistic
. For consistency and clarity, this book uses the full expression given in (
) as the default definition of the Pearson Chi-squared statistic unless otherwise specified.

By definition, the asymptotic distribution of the Pearson Chi-squared statistic follows a Chi-squared distribution, with degrees of freedom equal to the sample size minus the number of model parameters,
n-p
:

\chi^{2}_{P}\sim\chi^{2}_{(n-p)}.

(8.89)

The deviance statistic is based on maximum likelihood estimation, which gives it certain advantages when comparing nested models estimated using maximum likelihood methods. In the case of Gaussian models, where
\mathcal{V}(\mu)=1
and
a(\rho)=1
, the Pearson Chi-squared statistic, the deviance statistic, and the squared loss are all equivalent and exactly follow the Chi-squared distribution.

The residual sum of squares (RSS), defined as
\sum_{i}({\textnormal{y}}_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})^{2}
, is an intuitive measure that quantifies the total squared difference between observed values and model predictions. However, its magnitude can vary significantly across different datasets or modeling scenarios, making direct comparisons difficult. The Pearson Chi-squared statistic addresses this issue by normalizing the RSS with respect to the model variance. This normalization effectively expresses the residuals in terms of standard deviations, allowing for a more meaningful and interpretable comparison of model fit.

8.6.4
Residual and GLM Diagnostics

In evaluating a model, residuals measure the difference between each observed value and its corresponding fitted value. The extent to which an observation affects the estimated coefficients is known as influence.
Cox and Snell 1968
and
Pierce and Schafer 1986
have extensively discussed various definitions of residuals in GLMs. In the following, we introduce two types of residuals used in GLM analysis.

Previously, the residual is also denoted by
e_{i}=y_{i}-\widehat{y}_{i}\equiv y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i}
for each observation
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
.
These are called the
response residual
in the literature, which are simply the difference between the observed value
y_{i}
and the model’s fitted value (predicted value)
\widehat{y}_{i}
.

\paragrapharrow

Pearson residuals.
The sum of
squared Pearson residuals
equals the Pearson Chi-squared statistic:

e_{i}^{P}\triangleq\frac{y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i}}{\sqrt{a(\rho)\mathcal{V}(\widehat{\mu}_{i})}}.

(8.90)

The denominator represents the square root of the variance function, scaling the residuals to a comparable scale. A large absolute value of a residual suggests that the model does not adequately fit the specific observation. One common method for detecting outliers is to plot standardized Pearson residuals against the observed values; see Section
.

\paragrapharrow

Deviance residuals.

Deviance plays a crucial role in the derivation and inference of GLMs. Deviance residuals represent the contribution of each observation to the overall deviance. These residuals can be standardized or studentized, or both. The formula for deviance residuals is:

e_{i}^{D}\triangleq\text{sign}(y_{i}-\widehat{\mu}_{i})\sqrt{{d}_{i}^{2}},

(8.91)

where
\mathrm{D}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}
and
d_{i}=\frac{2w_{i}}{\rho}[y_{i}\{\phi(y_{i})-\phi(\widehat{\mu}_{i})\}-b\{\phi(y_{i})\}+b\{\phi(\widehat{\mu}_{i})\}]
denotes the contribution of point (or data group)
i
to the overall deviance.

In model diagnostics, deviance residuals—whether standardized or not—are often preferred over Pearson residuals because their distributional properties more closely resemble those found in linear regression models. This makes them particularly useful for identifying potential issues with model fit.

Just as in linear models (Section
), we can use deviance residuals (
e_{i}^{D}
) or Pearson residuals (
e_{i}^{P}
) in diagnostic plots—such as plotting them against observation indices or predictor variables—to detect potential violations of model assumptions. However, unlike in linear regression, these residuals are not normally distributed. This lack of normality makes it more difficult to interpret such plots and determine what patterns might indicate model problems.

To address this limitation, various transformed residuals have been proposed in the literature, including adjusted deviance residuals and Anscombe residuals
(
Pierce and Schafer 1986
;
Amin et al. 2017
)
. These transformations aim to make the residuals more closely resemble Gaussian errors, thereby improving interpretability. We will not study these, but content ourselves with checking plots for suspicious looking patterns.
